The terms **forever** and **ever** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [eternally]

In this verse, the word **enemy** is singular in form, but it refers to all enemies as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form to make this clear. Alternate translation: [The enemies are finished]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **desolation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [they are made desolate forever] or [you make them desolate forever]

Here, **cities** is spoken of as if it were a plant that could be **pulled up**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when you destroyed their cities]

Here, **remembrance** is spoken of as if it were a living being that could die. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [All remembrance of them has stopped] or [There is no longer any remembrance of them]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **remembrance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [No one remembers them at all]

The psalmist uses the words **As for them** here to indicate an emphatic contrast between what happens to the **enemy** and Yahweh. In your translation, indicate this strong contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Now speaking of the enemy]

Here, to **sit** represents the authority of the king to judge. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [reigns] or [is king]

The phrase **his throne** represents God’s rule. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He rules in order to judge people] or [He rules over people justly]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to do justly]

9.quote: וְ⁠ה֗וּא יִשְׁפֹּֽט־תֵּבֵ֥ל בְּ⁠צֶ֑דֶק יָדִ֥ין לְ֝אֻמִּ֗ים בְּ⁠מֵישָׁרִֽים
9.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. Translate them according to the decisions your team has made regarding translating parallelism in Hebrew poetry. See the Introduction to Psalms for more information. Alternate translation: [as for him, he will judge the world with righteousness, yes, he will adjudicate for the peoples with fairness] or [as for him, he will judge the people of the world with righteousness and fairness]

Here, **the world** refers to all the people in the world. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [everyone in the world]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **righteousness** and **fairness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [righteously … fairly]

9.quote: וִ֘⁠יהִ֤י יְהוָ֣ה מִשְׂגָּ֣ב לַ⁠דָּ֑ךְ מִ֝שְׂגָּ֗ב לְ⁠עִתּ֥וֹת בַּצָּרָֽה
9.text: Here the psalmist is speaking of **Yahweh** as if he were a place that people could go to for safety. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And may Yahweh protect the oppressed, may he protect them in times with distress] or [And may Yahweh provide safety for those who are oppressed, making them safe in times with distress]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **distress**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for distressing times]

Here, **your name** represents Yahweh and his reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those who know you] or [those who have heard what you do]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **knowers** and **seekers**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [people who know … people who seek you]

Here, being **the sitter** represents sitting on the throne as king. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the king] or [the ruler]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **praises**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Praise Yahweh with a song] or [Sing to praise Yahweh]
Here, **the seeker** refers to the avenger of blood, who hunts down and kills a murderer. Yahweh is the avenger in this case. See Numbers 35 for more information.

The implication is that the **seeker of vengeance** will remember to avenge for the murder of **them** (the victims calling for justice). You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [remembered to avenge those who were murdered]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **seeker**, **vengeance**, and **bloodshed**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [the one who seeks to avenge anyone who was murdered … them]

If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this double negative that consists of the negative particle **not** and the negative idea of **forget**. Alternate translation: [he surely remembers]

The psalmist is using the adjective **poor** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [poor people]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **mercy**, **affliction**, and **haters**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [Be merciful to me … how I am afflicted by those who hate me]
The implication is that Yahweh will act, not just **See**. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Take action because of]

Here, **death** is spoken of as if it were a city that had **gates** through which people enter in. If someone is near the **gates of death**, it means that he will die soon. Keeping someone from dying is spoken of as lifting him away from the gates of death. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [O you who can rescue me from death] or [O you who can keep me from dying]

The **gate** is the place of trade, business, and justice in the ancient city. If your readers would not be familiar with this, you could use the location where similar things happen in your area, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [in the central market of] or [in the place of trade and settling legal disputes of]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **praise** and **salvation**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [your praiseworthy deeds … because you saved me] or [the reasons to praise you … because you are a savior]

9.quote: נ֤וֹדַ֨ע ׀ יְהוָה֮ מִשְׁפָּ֪ט עָ֫שָׂ֥ה & נוֹקֵ֣שׁ רָשָׁ֑ע
9.text: Both the cause and the result of everything else in verses 15–16 are in the sentence **Yahweh has revealed himself, he has done justice**. The cause of the wicked nations being trapped by their own traps is Yahweh doing justice; the result is that he is revealed as being just. In your translation, use a structure that makes these connections clear. Alternate translation: [This happens because Yahweh is acting justly toward them. Yahweh reveals himself by justly causing the wicked to be ensnared]

9.quote: טָבְע֣וּ ג֭וֹיִם בְּ⁠שַׁ֣חַת עָשׂ֑וּ בְּ⁠רֶֽשֶׁת־ז֥וּ טָ֝מָ֗נוּ נִלְכְּדָ֥ה רַגְלָֽ⁠ם
9.text: People dig pits so they can catch animals that fall into them. They also hide nets to catch animals. Here digging a **pit** or hiding a **net** represents making plans to destroy people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The nations are like people who dig a pit for others and then fall into it; like people who hide a net to catch people and then get caught in it] or [The nations get caught in their own traps.]

9.quote: טָבְע֣וּ ג֭וֹיִם בְּ⁠שַׁ֣חַת עָשׂ֑וּ בְּ⁠רֶֽשֶׁת־ז֥וּ טָ֝מָ֗נוּ נִלְכְּדָ֥ה רַגְלָֽ⁠ם
9.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. Translate them according to the decisions your team has made regarding translating parallelism in Hebrew poetry. See the Introduction to Psalms for more information.

The word **himself** indicates that the object of the verb is the same as the subject of the verb. Use a way that is natural in your language to indicate that the same person fills two roles in the sentence. Alternate translation: [has revealed Yahweh]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [things justly]
See how you translated the phrase **the wicked** in [1:1](../001/001.md).

The expression **the wicked is ensnared** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the wicked person harms himself by the wicked things he does]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **work**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by what he does] or [by his own evil deeds]

Verses 17–18 form a poetic device called a chiasm where the inner two lines parallel each other and the outer two lines also parallel each other. In this case this artistic device creates a strong contrast between the verses by contrasting people forgetting God with God not forgetting the needy and contrasts the death of the wicked with the hope of the afflicted which does not die. If your language has a poetic structure that can make contrasts stand out markedly like this, consider using it here.
See how you translated the idea of “turn back” in [verse 3](../009/003.md), as this is likely connected.

Here, **are forgetful of God** is a common expression that means “they forget or ignore God.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use an expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [dismiss God] or [neglect to honor and worship God]

If the connection between **all nations** in this phrase and the **wicked** of the last phrase is not clear, you may want to show this connection. Alternate translation: [the wicked ones from all nations who are forgetful of God]

Here, **nations** represents the people in the nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [people in every nation]

The expression **the needy will not be forgotten** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [God will not always forget the needy]

The figure of speech here expresses a strongly positive meaning by using a negative word, **not**, together with an expression that is the opposite of the intended meaning. If it would be helpful in your language, you could emphasize the positive meaning. Alternate translation: [the needy will be remembered eventually]

The negation in the first clause of this verse carries over to the second half. Translate this in a way that both halves of the verse are negated (but making a positive statement as the previous note explains). Alternate translation: [indeed, the hope of the afflicted will not perish forever] or [neither will the hope of the afflicted perish forever] or (assuming the first half is translated positively) [the hope of the afflicted lives on]

Here, **hope** is spoken of as if it were something that could perish. This would mean that what they hope for does not happen. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [nor will the oppressed hope forever without results] or [someday what the afflicted hope for will happen]
Here, **Arise** represents starting to act. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Take action]

Here judging includes punishing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [let nations be judged and punished]

Here, **on your face** represents being in Yahweh’s presence, which can be considered in his courtroom (as in the UST). If it would be helpful, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [In your presence]

The expression **let nations be judged** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Judge the nations in your presence] or [Take the nations into your presence and punish them]

Here, **terror** is spoken of as something that could be **put** to the wicked, meaning to cause them to feel terror. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Make them be terrified Yahweh!] or [Terrify them Yahweh!]

Here the psalmist is speaking of **nations** as if they were living humans. There are two points: (1) nations do not last forever; they pass away or are mortal like humans, and (2) the leaders of nations are not gods, but humans who die. In both instances, they need to recognize that Yahweh is the supreme, never-ending power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May nations know they are temporary] or [May wicked human kings stop pretending to be eternal gods]

10.text:
# Psalm 10 Introduction

## Psalms 9–10 as One Psalm

Psalm 9 has a superscription but Psalm 10 does not. This fact and the acrostic nature of the two psalms (lines start with consecutive letters of the alphabet) has led many scholars to believe these two psalms may have originally been written as one psalm. The analysis of the structure of these psalms presented here will assume that. It is recommended that you follow the versification and chapter structure of other Bibles you are familiar with.

## Structure and Formatting

The outlines for psalms 9 and 10 are combined here and in the introduction to psalm 10 because they were probably originally one psalm. Your translation will probably be best if you translate them together.

1. Psalm 9:1–10 Praise of the King
2. Psalm 9:11–20 Petition the King
3. Psalm 10:1–11 Persecution of the poor
4. Psalm 10:12–18 Proclamation of the King

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

### Order and chaos

The first letter of many of the lines of these two psalms follows an acrostic (alphabetic) pattern. In some places, however, this orderly pattern is interrupted. The places where it is interrupted are places where the wicked are mentioned or acting. It is as if the presence of the wicked disrupts the orderliness over even the poetry, but it is restored and kept by Yahweh. If your language has a poetic style which can indicate order and chaos, you may wish to translate:

1. 9:1–4 in an orderly style
2. 9:5–6 in a slightly chaotic style
3. 9:7–15 in an orderly style
4. 9:16–17 in a slightly chaotic style
5. 9:18 in neither
6. 9:19–20 in an orderly style
7. 10:1 in an orderly style
8. 10:2–11 in a very chaotic style
9. 10:12–18 in an orderly style

### The fortress and the pit

There are two chiasms in psalm 9. In the first half, Yahweh is compared to a fortress (9) and, poetically, his judgment forms a barrier between the enemies and the psalmist and the oppressed.

1. People trust Yahweh (1–2)
2. Yahweh is a judge (3–4)
3. The enemy (5–6)
4. Yahweh is a king and judge (7–8)
5. People trust Yahweh (9–10)

In the second half, people’s prayers poetically encircle the wicked, causing them to fall into their own pit.

1. People pray to Yahweh for help (especially verse 13) (11–14)
2. The wicked are destroyed by their own pit (15–18)
3. People pray to Yahweh for help (19–20)

As you translate this psalm, you will probably have a structure that matches this which may or may not be meaningful in your language. You could also consider if there is a way to poetically “surround” the wicked with the prayers of Yahweh’s people and with Yahweh as judge, in the two sections.

### Adjectives used as generic nouns:

The adjectives “wicked, afflicted, innocent”, and “oppressed” are nominal adjectives used as generic nouns in these psalms. See [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-nominaladj]]; and [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-genericnoun]].
See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/writing-poetry]]

### CCBYSA

Portions of the ULT, UST, and TNs for this psalm are derivative from “Psalms, Layer by Layer” ([https://psalms.cdbr.org/w/Welcome](https://psalms.cdbr.org/w/Welcome)), “Psalm 10” ([https://psalms.cdbr.org/w/Psalm_10](https://psalms.cdbr.org/w/Psalm_10)) by Cambridge Digital Bible Research, Katie Frost, Meaghan Smith, Nikki Mustin et al, used under [CC BY](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)

See their overview video ([https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VRQZ1eytMJ8](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VRQZ1eytMJ8)) and top three exegetical issues in Psalm 10 video ([https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W4w8G32hfyI](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W4w8G32hfyI)) and their top three poetic features of Psalms 9–10 video ([https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=moXvQUAMudo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=moXvQUAMudo)) on YouTube.

10.quote: לָ⁠מָ֣ה יְ֭הוָה תַּעֲמֹ֣ד בְּ⁠רָח֑וֹק תַּ֝עְלִ֗ים לְ⁠עִתּ֥וֹת בַּצָּרָֽה
10.text: The speaker is using the question form to express his distress that Yahweh has not helped him. If you would not use the question form for this purpose in your language, you could translate this as a statement or an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, it seems as though you are far away from me and you hide from me whenever I am in trouble.]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **trouble**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when we are troubled]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **arrogance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Arrogantly]
See how you translated the phrase **the wicked** in [1:1](../001/001.md).

It is not clear who **they** are. Options include: (1) that **they** are the wicked in both cases. In that case this would either be a prediction or a wish. This would fit with what is said in [9:15–16](../009/015.md). Alternate translation: [the wicked are caught by the schemes that they themselves have planned] or [may the wicked be caught by the schemes that they themselves have planned] or (2) the first **they** is the **afflicted** and the second is the **wicked**. This would fit with the very negative outlook of 10:1–11. Alternate translation: [the afflicted are caught by the schemes that the wicked have planned]. You may wish to follow the choice that translations you are familiar with have made.

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **schemes**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [they are caught in the traps they have planned] or [they are caught in their own scheming]
Alternate translation: [For]
See how you translated the phrase **the wicked** in [1:1](../001/001.md).
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **desires**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what his soul longs to do]

It is difficult to discern who is the subject and object of both verbs in the second half of this verse. Additionally, some believe that **blesses** is an euphemism for “curses” here. The ULT seeks to offer a reasonable translation where **the wicked** is the subject throughout (occurrences of **he** in the ULT refer to **the wicked**). You may wish to follow the rendering of a translation in your region that you are familiar with. Alternate translation: [and the robber curses and disrespects Yahweh] or [and he blesses the robber whom Yahweh despises]
Alternate translation: [and … the greedy]
Alternate translation: [he spurns] or [he rejects]

Here, **the haughtiness of his nose** is a common expression of the culture that means pride or arrogance. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [In his arrogant attitude] or [In his pride]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. It is unclear **who** does not seek **what** here. It could be that (1) the wicked **seeks not** God. They do not fear him or obey him, or (2) the wicked think that God does not seek them out or notice them, to punish them. Alternate translation: [thinks God seeks not]
Alternate translation: [God is not in all his thoughts]

Here a person’s lifestyle is spoken of as if it was **ways**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [What he does endures]

Yahweh’s judgments are compared to something high above the wicked like a bird or mountain top. This could mean: (1) Yahweh’s judgments are far from his thinking; he ignores them. Alternate translation: [he pays no attention to your judgments] or (2) he does not understand Yahweh’s judgments. Alternate translation: [your judgments are beyond his comprehension]. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly.

Here, **snorts** (blowing air loudly out of the nose) is a symbolic action that expresses contempt and mocking. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [he shows that he thinks that all his enemies are weak and worthless] or [he sneers at all his enemies]

Here, **I will not be shaken** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Nothing can shake me]

**To generation and generation** is an extreme statement used for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [at any possible time]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **distress**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [be distressed]

Here, **mouth** represents speaking. To say that the **mouth is full** means he is always speaking **curses and lies and oppression**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He is constantly speaking] or [His speech is characterized by]

Here the **tongue** represents speaking. To say that these things are **under his tongue** means they are always ready to come out when he talks. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what he says is always] or [his speech is characterized by]

10.quote: אָלָ֤ה פִּ֣י⁠הוּ מָ֭לֵא וּ⁠מִרְמ֣וֹת וָ⁠תֹ֑ךְ תַּ֥חַת לְ֝שׁוֹנ֗⁠וֹ עָמָ֥ל וָ⁠אָֽוֶן
10.text: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **curses and lies and oppression** and **mischief and evil**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [Every word he speaks is harmful, false, or threatening; he always talks about mischievous plans for evil deeds]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **innocent**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [innocent people]

The **eyes** represent him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he stealthily watches for a helpless person]

This is saying that the wicked are **like a lion** because they hide, lying it wait to ambush their prey like a lion does. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state that explicitly. Alternate translation: [like a lion ambushes its prey from cover]

10.quote: יֶאֱרֹ֬ב בַּ⁠מִּסְתָּ֨ר ׀ כְּ⁠אַרְיֵ֬ה בְ⁠סֻכֹּ֗⁠ה יֶ֭אֱרֹב לַ⁠חֲט֣וֹף עָנִ֑י
10.text: In order to follow the original and highlight the parallelism with the previous verse, the ULT leaves out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. In English **ambushes** requires an object. You could supply these words or modify the sentence structure if it would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [He ambushes the afflicted in secret like a lion in cover; he ambushes them to seize them] or [He waits secretly in ambush like a lion in cover; he waits to ambush and seize the afflicted] or [He lies in wait in secret like a lion in cover; he lies in wait to seize the afflicted]

The writer speaks of the wicked person catching people as if he were a hunter using a **net** to catch animals. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He seizes the afflicted like a hunter that catches an animal in a net and drags it away]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **power**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and unfortunate people fall because he is powerful]

Here saying **in his heart** means that he thinks or believes something without necessarily speaking it out loud. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He thinks to himself] or [He believes deep down]

10.quote: שָׁ֣כַֽח אֵ֑ל הִסְתִּ֥יר פָּ֝נָ֗י⁠ו בַּל־רָאָ֥ה לָ⁠נֶֽצַח
10.text: The object of these sentences is unspoken. If it would be helpful in your language, you could supply these missing words from the context. Alternate translation: [God has forgotten my deeds; he has hidden his face from my deeds; to perpetuity he sees my deeds not.]

Here, **God has forgotten** is a common expression from the culture that means that God is not paying attention or does not care about what is happening. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [God will not make me pay] or [God does not notice]

Here, **he has hidden his face** is a common expression that means that God is deliberately ignoring or not paying attention to what is happening. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he averts his eyes] or [he does not care]

This is an exaggeration to emphasize the wicked person’s belief that God will never intervene or punish him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [what I do is completely invisible to him]

Here, **Arise** represents doing something or taking action. If it would be helpful, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Take action]

Here the **hand** represents God’s power. To **lift up** the hand means to use it. If it would be helpful, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [use your power]

Here saying **in his heart** means that he thinks or believes something without necessarily speaking it out loud. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He thinks to himself, “You will not seek] or [He believes deep down, “You will not look]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You could supply these words from the context if it would be clearer in your language. It is clearer here than in [10:3](../010/003.md) who is seeking what. The wicked think that God does not seek them out, or notice them, to punish them. Alternate translation: [You, God, will not punish me]

There is a strong contrast between what the wicked think in the previous verse and what the psalmist declares to be the truth in this verse. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [But you do seek, and you have seen] or [However you really do see]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **mischief and vexation**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [the mischievous and vexing things they do]

Here, **to take it in your hand** represents exercising power to take control of a situation. If it would be helpful, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to powerfully intervene]

Here, **arm** represents power. If it would be helpful, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Destroy the power of wicked and evil people] or [Make wicked and evil people weak]
See how you translated the phrase **the wicked** in [1:1](../001/001.md).

The psalmist is using the adjective **evil** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [and evil people]

The terms **wicked** and **evil** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [the very wicked] or [the very evil]

There is significant debate about who or what may **seek** and **find**. The interpretation suggested here is that the wicked and evil people’s arm (power for harm) is personified as looking to do the evil they have planned but is unable to because Yahweh has broken the arm (power). If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May the wicked, evil person try to use his power for harm but discover you have destroyed it]; or another common interpretation is that Yahweh will seek out (hunt down, punish) the wicked, evil person’s wickedness until he can no longer find it (because it is eradicated). Alternate translation: [Hunt down his wickedness until no more can be found]. You may wish to follow the interpretation of a translation commonly used in your region. For more information, see the Psalms layer by layer exegetical discussion at [https://psalms.cdbr.org/w/The_Division_of_Psalm_10:15](https://psalms.cdbr.org/w/The_Division_of_Psalm_10:15).

The expression **the nations have perished** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh forces foreigners to leave his land]

The implication is that the afflicted people expressed their desire for mercy to Yahweh. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [When afflicted people told you about their desire for mercy, you listened to them tell you what they needed]

Here, a strong **heart** represents courage and **you strengthen their heart** represents encouraging them. If it would be helpful, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you encourage them] or [you make them confident]

Here the psalmist speaks of the **ear** as if it were a person who could attend to, listen, or pay attention. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your ear hears] or [you listen carefully]

The implication is that Yahweh will judge in favor of the orphan and oppressed. You could include this information in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [to administer justice for] or [to judge in favor of]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You could supply these words from earlier in the sentence if it would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [terrify anyone] or [terrify the orphan and the oppressed]

11.text:
# Psalm 11 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 11 is considered to be one of the “psalms of trust.” (See the Introduction to Psalms.) He will judge the wicked and reward the righteous. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/deliverer]]; and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/good]]; and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/evil]])

1. David asserts his trust in God (1a)
2. The words of David’s advisors (1b–3)
3. David’s response to the words of his advisors (4–5)
4. David asks God to judge righteously (6–7)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Justice

David says that wicked people try to destroy righteous people, but God knows everything that evil people try to do. David says that “Yahweh is righteous” (7) and “he hates those who love to do violence” (5). David asks God to judge the wicked (6) and says that “the upright” will be rewarded by seeing his face (7). (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/justice]]; and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/save]])

11.quote: אֵ֭יךְ תֹּאמְר֣וּ לְ⁠נַפְשִׁ֑⁠י נודו הַרְ⁠כֶ֥ם צִפּֽוֹר׃ כִּ֤י הִנֵּ֪ה הָ⁠רְשָׁעִ֡ים יִדְרְכ֬וּ⁠ן קֶ֗שֶׁת כּוֹנְנ֣וּ חִצָּ֣⁠ם עַל־יֶ֑תֶר לִ⁠יר֥וֹת בְּמוֹ־אֹ֝֗פֶל לְ⁠יִשְׁרֵי־לֵֽב׃ כִּ֣י הַ֭⁠שָּׁתוֹת יֵֽהָרֵס֑וּ⁠ן צַ֝דִּ֗יק מַה־פָּעָֽל
11.text: Many Bible scholars think that David’s quote of his advisors begins with the words **Flutter like a bird to your mountain** and ends at the end of verse three. Some Bible scholars think that **Flutter like a bird to your mountain** are the only words of his advisors that David is quoting and that verses 2–3 are his own words. The ULT and UST follow option one. If a translation exists in your region that follows option two, you may wish to follow that option.

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

Here David is speaking as if Yahweh were actually a physical place of safety or shelter. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I trust in Yahweh to keep me safe] or [I depend on Yahweh to protect me]

David is using the question form to challenge what people are telling him. His question continues from this verse to the end of verse 3. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You should not say to my soul]

The psalmist is using **my soul** to represent all of himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [can you say to me]

Here the speaker’s advisors are speaking of him as if he were actually a **bird** that should fly away to safety in the mountains. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Run away and hide in the mountains] or [Escape to safety in the mountains]

The psalmist is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Listen carefully] or [Pay attention to this]
See how you translated the phrase **the wicked** in [1:1](../001/001.md). Alternate translation: [wicked men]

Here the **heart** represents where a person’s thoughts and motives exist. The phrase **upright of heart** describes people whose thoughts and motives are morally straight and righteous. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [at those who think and act righteously] or [at those who live with pure motives]

The speaker is using the question form to emphasize that the **righteous** cannot do anything if the foundations of society are destroyed. If your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement. [If the foundations are destroyed, the righteous can do nothing.] or [If the foundations are destroyed, there is nothing the righteous can do.]

This question is the end of what people are saying to David, which he uses the question form in verses 1–3 to challenge. If you chose in verse 1 to represent his challenge as a statement or exclamation, end this with a period or exclamation point.

Here the psalmist is speaking as if the principles of justice and morality were actually **foundations** of a building. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the principles of justice and morality are destroyed] or [the moral order has broken down]
See how you translated the phrase **the righteous** in [1:5](../001/005.md). Alternate translation: [righteous people]

11.quote: יְהוָ֤ה ׀ בְּֽ⁠הֵ֘יכַ֤ל קָדְשׁ֗⁠וֹ יְהוָה֮ בַּ⁠שָּׁמַ֪יִם כִּ֫סְא֥⁠וֹ
11.text: Here the psalmist is speaking of God’s presence in heaven as if he were actually in a **temple** and as if **the heavens** were a place with a **throne**. You could translate the words literally or your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is present in his holy sanctuary and rules as king from heaven]

11.quote: יְהוָ֤ה ׀ בְּֽ⁠הֵ֘יכַ֤ל קָדְשׁ֗⁠וֹ יְהוָה֮ בַּ⁠שָּׁמַ֪יִם כִּ֫סְא֥⁠וֹ
11.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and it would be good to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation, if possible. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is in his holy temple; yes, Yahweh is in the heavens, his throne] or [Yahweh is in his holy temple; indeed, Yahweh is in the heavens, his throne]

The psalmist is not distinguishing this **throne** from another throne that is not in heaven. The psalmist is showing God’s greatness compared to human rulers who rule from a throne on earth, by adding that **the heavens** are the place of God’s **throne** (where he rules from). Be sure that this is clear in your translation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is in the heavens, they are his throne] or [Yahweh’s throne is in the heavens]
Here, God’s **throne** represents his “rule.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh rules from the heavens]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [His eyes see the sons of men] or [His eyes see everything that people do]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and it would be good to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation, if possible. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [His eyes see, yes, his eyelids test] or [His eyes see, indeed, his eyelids test]

Here, **eyes** and **eyelids** represent God’s ability to see and evaluate everything people do. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [He sees, he tests]

The psalmist is using **sons of man** as a common expression of his culture to mean “all human beings.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the children of mankind] or [every human being]
See how you translated the phrase **the righteous** in [1:5](../001/005.md). Alternate translation: [righteous people]
See how you translated the phrase **the wicked** in [1:1](../001/001.md). Alternate translation: [wicked men]

The psalmist is using **soul** to represent all of Yahweh in the act of hating. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he hates]
See how you translated the phrase **the wicked** in [1:1](../001/001.md). Alternate translation: [wicked men]

11.quote: אֵ֣שׁ וְ֭⁠גָפְרִית וְ⁠ר֥וּחַ זִלְעָפ֗וֹת מְנָ֣ת כּוֹסָֽ⁠ם
11.text: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [may fire and brimstone and a scorching wind be the portion of their cup]

The phrase **fire and brimstone and a scorching wind** could refer to: (1) an actual physical judgment of fire and brimstone such as what happened to the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah in Genesis 19:24–25 (2) a judgment of some type, but not necessarily with fire and brimstone and a scorching wind. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language.

Here the psalmist is speaking as if **the portion of their cup** is what the wicked would receive as their share, like a drink that had been poured into their cup. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. If not, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what Yahweh will give them as their punishment]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [he loves those who do righteous things] or [he loves when people do what is righteous]

The psalmist is using the adjective **upright** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [upright people] or [those who do what is right]

David is using Yahweh’s **face** to represent Yahweh himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [will see him]

12.text:
# Psalm 12 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 12 has different types of themes in it. It has elements in it that belong to “lament psalms,” “psalms of trust,” and “imprecatory psalms.” See the Introduction to Psalms for more information about these types of psalms.

1. David laments that godly people seem to be no more (1)
2. The deceptive speech of wicked people (2)
3. David asks Yahweh to stop men who use their speech for evil purposes (3–4)
4. Yahweh’s response to the mistreatment of “the poor” and “the needy” (5)
5. Yahweh’s speech is perfect and trustworthy (6)
6. Yahweh’s “the poor” and “the needy” (7)
7. David observes the prideful boldness of wicked men as a result of society not condemning their evil actions (8)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Yahweh saves “the poor” and “the needy” from the oppressive acts of wicked people

Even though wicked people are temporarily succeeding in oppressing poor and needy people, Yahweh sees and will help “the poor” and “the needy” people who long for deliverance from their oppression (5). (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/save]])

### Words

A major focus of this psalm is the deceptive and prideful words that wicked people use (2–4). This psalm then shows that Yahweh’s speech, in contrast to the speech of wicked people, is morally perfect and trustworthy (6).

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]
See how you translated the term **Sheminith** in the superscription to Psalm 6.
See how you translated the phrase **the godly** in [4:3](../004/003.md). Alternate translation: [godly people]

The psalmist is using **the sons of man** as a common expression of his culture to mean “all human beings.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the human race] or [from humanity]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **Man**. He means all wicked people among mankind in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Mankind speaks with falsehood with their neighbors]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **falsehood**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [lies] or [what is untrue]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if anyone a person speaks to were actually their **neighbor**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [other people]

These two phrases, **with lip of smoothness** and **with a heart and a heart**, mean very similar things. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating a similar idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [with deceptive flattery]

The psalmist is using **lip of smoothness** as a common expression of his culture to mean “flattering speech.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with flattering words]

The psalmist is using **with a heart and a heart** as a common expression of his culture to mean “with divided loyalty” or “with deceitful intentions.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with deceitful hearts] or [speaking dishonestly]

The psalmist is using **cut off** as a common expression of the culture to mean “destroy” or “bring to an end.” See how you translated the expression “with lip of smoothness” in the previous verse. So in this context, **cut off all lips of smoothness** means “bring to an end all those who speak with flattering lips.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May Yahweh bring to an end all people who speak with flattering words] or [May Yahweh stop all people who speak with flattering speech]

Here, **tongue** represents a person who speaks. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the person speaking great things]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You could supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [May Yahweh cut off the tongue speaking great things]

The implication is that the people who are **speaking great things** are bragging and making proud claims. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [that brags] or [that makes proud claims]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [lips which say]

Here, **tongue** and **lips** represent speech and the ability to speak. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [We will prevail through what we say. We can speak as we please]

Here the wicked people are speaking of their **tongue** as if it were a weapon that could defeat others. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [By our speech we will defeat others] or [We will overpower others with our words]

The implication is that these speakers are claiming to be in complete control of what they say and do not need to answer to anyone else. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [We can say whatever we want]

The speakers are using the question **who is master over us?** as a way of making a defiant statement. They are not expecting an answer but are expressing their belief that no one has authority over them. If a speaker of your language would not use a question form for this purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [no one will be master over us!]

These two phrases **Because of oppression of the poor** and **because of the groaning of the needy** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and it would be good to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation, if possible. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Because of how the poor are being cruelly oppressed and suffering]

The psalmist is using the adjectives **poor** and **needy** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [poor people … of needy people]

Here, **groaning** represents the suffering of the needy. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [because the needy are suffering so severely that it causes them to groan] or [because of the suffering of the needy]

Yahweh is using **Now I will arise** as a common expression of the culture to indicate that he is about to take action against those who oppress the poor and needy. He is not saying that he will get out of bed or stand up from a seated position. If this expression does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Now I will take action]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **safety**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [I will keep safe]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if someone were actually **panting** for safety like a thirsty person pants for water. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he longs for it]

It might seem that the expression **he pants for** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [he pants for] or [he longs for]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if Yahweh’s **pure words** were actually refined **silver**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [are pure words, like silver]

12.quote: כֶּ֣סֶף צָ֭רוּף בַּ⁠עֲלִ֣יל לָ⁠אָ֑רֶץ מְ֝זֻקָּ֗ק שִׁבְעָתָֽיִם
12.text: Here the psalmist is speaking as if God’s promises were actually **silver refined in a furnace on the ground, purified seven** times. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. If not, you could state this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [like silver that is refined in a furnace on the ground seven times]

12.quote: כֶּ֣סֶף צָ֭רוּף בַּ⁠עֲלִ֣יל לָ⁠אָ֑רֶץ מְ֝זֻקָּ֗ק שִׁבְעָתָֽיִם
12.text: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [silver that is refined in a furnace on the ground seven times] or [pure like silver that is refined seven time in a furnace on the ground]

David is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you will keep them** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that it is Yahweh himself who will **keep** and **protect** “the poor” and “the needy” mentioned in verse 5. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [Indeed, it is you Yahweh who will keep them]

These two phrases **you will keep them** and **You will protect him** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [You yourself, Yahweh, will surely keep the poor and the needy safe]

The pronoun **them** refers to the poor and needy people, while the pronoun **him** also refers to these same people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [You yourself Yahweh will keep the poor and needy. You will protect the poor and the needy]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that the phrase **for eternity** means “forever” or “continually.” You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [forever]

12.quote: סָבִ֗יב רְשָׁעִ֥ים יִתְהַלָּכ֑וּ⁠ן כְּ⁠רֻ֥ם זֻ֝לּ֗וּת לִ⁠בְנֵ֥י אָדָֽם
12.text: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that **The wicked walk about on every side** describes. Alternate translation: [When vileness is exalted among the sons of man, the wicked ones walk about on every side]
See how you translated the phrase **the wicked** in [1:1](../001/001.md). Alternate translation: [The wicked people]

By **walk about**, the psalmist means that the wicked walk around freely doing evil things without anyone stopping them and that they walk around proudly as a result of being able to do evil things. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [walk about freely] or [walk about proudly]

The implication is that wicked people are the ones who are promoting or honoring vileness. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [when people exalt vileness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **vileness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when what is vile is exalted]

The psalmist is using **sons of man** as a common expression of his culture to mean “human beings” or “people.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [among people] or [among humanity]

13.text:
# Psalm 13 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 13 is considered to be one of the “lament psalms.” See the Introduction to Psalms for more information about the lament psalms.

1. David calls out to Yahweh regarding Yahweh’s seeming inattention to his troubles (1–2)
2. David asks Yahweh to “consider” and “answer” him and tells Yahweh what the result will be if Yahweh does not help him (3–4)
3. David expresses his trust in Yahweh’s “covenant faithfulness” and the fact that he will “rejoice” because of his hope that Yahweh will save him (5)
4. David will sing to Yahweh because of Yahweh’s kind actions towards him (6)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Yahweh’s help

In this psalm David expresses to Yahweh that he desperately needs his help or else he will die (3) resulting in his enemies rejoicing at his downfall (4). David then affirms that he trusts that Yahweh’s “covenant faithfulness” will cause Yahweh to save him from his enemies and he will “sing to Yahweh” and “rejoice” as a result of Yahweh saving him. The word “salvation” in 13:5 refers to help or deliverance from one’s enemies. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/save]]; [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/deliverer]]; and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/call-tosummon]])

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

David is probably implying the words “will you forget me,” but since the next two phrases in this verse indicates what David is asking Yahweh, you do not need to fill in the implied words in this phrase.

The implication is that **forget** means “not help.” You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Will you not help me forever] or [Will you not ever answer me]

Here, **face** represents God’s attention and favor. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [will you continue to ignore me] or [will you keep withdrawing your favor from me]
Here, **in my soul** represents David’s whole self as he experiences emotions. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language as in the UST.

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [having sorrow in my heart]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **sorrow**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [feeling sorrowful]

Here the **heart** represents where a person’s thoughts and feelings exist. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in my thoughts] or [in my inner being]

The implication is that David was distressed and in anguish throughout the entire daytime. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [daily] or [continually]

By **be high over me**, the psalmist means that his enemy will defeat him and triumph over him. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [will the one being hostile to me be exalted over me]

Here David is speaking of having energy and hope as if it were **light** coming into his eyes. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [restore my strength and hope] or [make me feel alive again]

David is using the word translated as **lest** to introduce an outcome that he does not want to happen. Because of this, he first asks God to help him so that this will not happen. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that avoiding this outcome is the purpose of the request. Alternate translation: [otherwise] or [or else]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. If it would be clearer in your language, you can supply these words from the context, as in the ULT, which supplies **sleep of**.

The psalmist is referring to death in a polite way by using the phrase **sleep the sleep of death**. Depending on what is helpful in your language, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [I die]

David is using the word translated as **Lest** to introduce an outcome that he does not want to happen. Because of this, he first asks God to help him (3) so that this will not happen. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that avoiding this outcome is the purpose of the request. Alternate translation: [Otherwise the one being hostile to me will say] or [Or else the one being hostile to me will say]

The psalmist is leaving out a word that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. Here the word is either “and” (which the ULT supplies) or “lest.” You can supply the word or words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [lest my adversaries rejoice]
The word the ULT translates as **when**, in this context, could mean: (1) “when” or (2) “because.” Alternate translation: [because]

The expression **I am shaken** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they shake me] or [they overcome me]

Here David is speaking of himself as if he were an object that could be **shaken**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am overcome] or [I am defeated]

The psalmist uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between the possibility of his enemies triumphing over him and his trust in Yahweh’s faithfulness. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Nevertheless, I] or [However, I]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in all the ways you are faithful to your covenant]
The word the ULT translates as **let my heart rejoice**, in this context, could mean: (1) “let my heart rejoice” or (2) “will rejoice.” Alternate translation: [my heart will rejoice]

Here the **heart** represents where a person’s thoughts and feelings exist. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [let everything in me rejoice]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because of the way you have saved me]

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because Yahweh has dealt bountifully with me, I will sing to him]

David could be using the past tense **he has dealt bountifully**: (1) in order to describe something that is going to happen in the future to show that the event will certainly happen. Alternate translation: [he will deal bountifully with me] or (2) to refer to things Yahweh has done for him in the past, in which case you can translate this phrase as in the ULT.

14.text:
# Psalm 14 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 14 is “wisdom psalm” that describes the difference between how righteous people and wicked people live and the difference between what happens to them. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the Introduction to Psalms.

1. A description of wicked people (1–4)
2. God punishes wicked people but helps his own people (5–7)

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **fool**. He means foolish people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [A foolish person]

Here the **heart** represents a person’s thoughts. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to himself] or [in his thoughts]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [There is no God]

These two phrases, **They are corrupt** and **they do a deed abominably**, mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [They behave in ways that are corrupt and terribly wicked]
The pronoun **They** refers to foolish people who deny God. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Such foolish people are corrupt]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **deed**. He means the deeds of foolish people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they do deeds abominably] or [what they do is abominable]

The psalmist is using **sons of man** as a common expression of his culture to mean “human beings.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [human beings]
Since the psalmist has already used the name God earlier in this sentence, it may be more natural in your language to use a pronoun here. Alternate translation: [one seeking him]

These two phrases, **The whole has turned aside** and **Together they have corrupted themselves**, mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [All have rebelled, that is, they have all become completely corrupt]

The expression **The whole** refers back to the “sons of man” in the previous verse. It may be helpful to use a term in your translation that will clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [All of mankind has turned aside]

The psalmist is speaking of people abandoning God’s ways as if they had literally **turned aside** from a path they had been walking on. He means that they stopped living in the manner in which God wants people to live. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [All people have rejected how God wants them to live] or [Everyone has stopped obeying God]

The psalmist is saying **none** and **not even one** as a generalization for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [All people are sinful]

The psalmist is using the adjective **good** as a noun to mean a certain kind of thing. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [good things] or [what is good]

14.quote: הֲ⁠לֹ֥א יָדְעוּ֮ כָּל־פֹּ֪עֲלֵ֫י אָ֥וֶן אֹכְלֵ֣י עַ֭מִּ⁠י אָ֣כְלוּ לֶ֑חֶם
14.text: The psalmist is using the question form to express amazement that wicked people oppress others without recognizing that God will judge and punish them for doing that. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [They ought to know better, the doers of iniquity, the ones eating my people as they eat bread!]

The point of this comparison is that just as someone can **eat bread** easily and quickly, so these **doers of iniquity** readily oppress and exploit vulnerable people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [the ones eating my people as readily as they eat bread]

The psalmist is speaking as if these **doers of iniquity** were actually **eating** the **people** of his nation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ones exploiting my people as readily as they eat bread]

The word the ULT translates as **There** could refer to: (1) a place. Alternate translation: [At the place God will judge the wicked] or (2) a time. Alternate translation: [At the time God will judge the wicked]

The psalmist is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [they feared greatly]

By **the generation of the righteous**, the psalmist means “the people who are righteous.” You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [is with righteous people]

The psalmist is using **{is} with** as a common expression of his culture to mean “helps.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [God helps righteous people]

The psalmist is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [righteous people]

The pronoun **You** refers to the wicked people who do the evil things that are described in the previous verses. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [You wicked people shame the counsel of the afflicted]

The psalmist is using the possessive form **the counsel of the afflicted** to mean the counsel that poor but godly people have decided to follow, that is, their decision to obey God. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [You wicked people try to humiliate the afflicted for deciding to obey God]

The psalmist is using the adjective **afflicted** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [an afflicted person] or [people in humble circumstances]

Here the psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were actually a **refuge**, that is, a place where someone can go to be safe from danger. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh protects him]

The psalmist is using **Who will give** as a common expression of his culture to introduce a fervent wish. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [O that salvation for Israel would come from Zion!] or [I fervently wish that salvation for Israel would come from Zion!]

The psalmist is using Mount **Zion**, the location of God’s sanctuary, to represent God himself in the act of providing **salvation** for **Israel**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [O that God would act from his sanctuary on Mount Zion to provide for the salvation of Israel!] or [I fervently wish that God would act from his sanctuary on Mount Zion to provide for the salvation of Israel!]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [O that God would act from his sanctuary on Mount Zion to save Israel!] or [I fervently wish that God would act from his sanctuary on Mount Zion to save Israel!]

The word that the ULT translates as **prosperity** can also mean “captivity.” If that is the meaning, then this verse could have been added to the psalm later, after the Israelites were conquered and taken into captivity. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to follow the translation that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT. Alternate translation: [When God restores the captivity of his people] or [When God brings his people back from captivity]

These two phrases, **Jacob will be glad** and **Israel will rejoice**, mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Jacob will be glad, yes, Israel will rejoice]

The psalmist is using the two names of the ancestor of the Israelites, **Jacob** and **Israel**, to represent the Israelites themselves. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The descendants of Jacob will be glad; indeed, the Israelites will rejoice]

15.text:
# Psalm 15 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 15 is considered to be one of the “wisdom psalms.” See the Introduction to Psalms for more information about the wisdom psalms. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/wise]])

1. Two parallel rhetorical questions with the same meaning (1)
2. Ten character traits of the type of person Yahweh lets enter his presence (2–5b)
3. The promised reward for the person meeting Yahweh’s requirements (5c)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### The type of person who may enter into God’s presence

Verse one begins with two questions that are both asking the same thing (parallelism). They are both rhetorical questions that are meant to make the reader think intently about the type of behaviors and attitudes that God requires. Verses 2–5b provide the answer to the questions in verse one. They indicate ten character traits that God requires. The last sentence in verse five is the conclusion to this psalm and states the promised reward for meeting Yahweh’s moral requirements. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/godly]]; and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/good]]; and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/promise]])

### Moral Conditions for Worship

Scholars have noted that this psalm contains a list of ten different conditions for those who want to participate in worship at the temple. The list consists of three positives in verse two, three negatives in verse three, two positives in verse four, followed by two negatives in verse five. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/temple]])

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

### Who do the pronouns “he,” “his,” and “him” refer to?

All occurrences of the pronouns “he,” “his,” and “him” refer to the same type of person. The person being described is not one particular person but rather anyone who exhibits the behaviors described in verses 2–5.

These two phrases, **who may sojourn in your tent** and **Who may dwell on your holy mountain**, mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [who may sojourn in your tent, yes, who may dwell on your holy mountain]

David uses these two questions to make the reader think deeply about how to live a righteous life. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for this purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or exclamations.
