Alternate translation: [this is the type of person who may sojourn in your tent. This is the type of person who may dwell on your holy mountain.]

The word **sojourn** means to be living somewhere, either temporarily or permanently, as a resident alien. By **may sojourn**, David means someone who is allowed to visit and come as a guest. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [may dwell as a guest] or [may be welcomed]

By **your tent**, David means Yahweh’s Temple that was in Jerusalem on Mount Zion. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in your temple] or [in your dwelling place]

By **your holy mountain**, David means Mount Zion, the place where Yahweh’s Temple was. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [on your holy mountain, Mount Zion]

Here, **tent** and **holy mountain** represent Yahweh’s presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [who may sojourn in your presence? Who may dwell with you]

15.quote: הוֹלֵ֣ךְ תָּ֭מִים וּ⁠פֹעֵ֥ל צֶ֑דֶק וְ⁠דֹבֵ֥ר אֱ֝מֶ֗ת בִּ⁠לְבָבֽ⁠וֹ
15.text: David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [The person who may enter your presence, Yahweh, is the one walking blamelessly, and doing righteousness, and speaking truth in his heart] or [The person who may sojourn in your house and dwell on your holy mountain is the one walking blamelessly, doing righteousness, and speaking truth in his heart]

David is speaking of how a person lives as if that were a way or path that the person was **walking** along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The one living blamelessly]

15.quote: הוֹלֵ֣ךְ תָּ֭מִים וּ⁠פֹעֵ֥ל צֶ֑דֶק וְ⁠דֹבֵ֥ר אֱ֝מֶ֗ת בִּ⁠לְבָבֽ⁠וֹ
15.text: David is not referring to a specific **one**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Those who walk blamelessly, do righteousness, and speak truth] or [Anyone who walks blamelessly, does righteousness, and speaks truth in his heart]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what is right]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **truth**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and speaking what is true]

Here the **heart** represents where a person’s thoughts and intentions exist. The phrase **speaking truth in his heart** means “speaking the truth within himself in his thoughts” and refers to a person thinking true thoughts within and then speaking out loud to others according to that truth. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly.
Here, **tongue** represents speech. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with his speech]

The psalmist is using the adjective **evil** as a noun to mean evil things. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [he does not do evil things]

By **an insult he does not raise up**, David means “an insult he does not speak.” You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [an insult he does not speak against one close to him] or [an insult he does not speak against his neighbor]

By **one close to him**, David could mean: (1) a person who has a close relationship with him. Alternate translation: [his friend] or (2) a person who lives within a close physical distance from him. Alternate translation: [his neighbor]

The psalmist is using **In whose eyes** as a common expression meaning “in the judgment of” or “in the opinion of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [In whose judgment] or [In whose opinion]

By **one being rejected**, the psalmist means one whom God has rejected or despised. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [one whom God has rejected]

The expression **one being rejected** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [He despises the person God rejects]

The implication is that he keeps his promise even when doing so will cause him difficulty or loss. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [He keeps his promises even when it costs him]

The implication is that the person does not change his oath or promise even when circumstances make it difficult or costly to keep. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and does not break his promise]

By **put out his money at interest**, the psalmist means charge interest when lending money. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [He does … charge interest when he lends his money]

David is using the adjective **innocent** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [innocent people]

David is speaking of the person God accepts as if he were an object that could be **shaken**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will ensure that the one doing these things will always live securely] or [Yahweh will protect and provide for the ones doing these things so that the circumstances of life do not overwhelm them]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **shaken**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [will remain secure for eternity]

See how you translated the phrase “I will not be shaken” in [10:6](../010/006.md) and the phrase “when I am shaken” in [13:4](../013/004.md). Alternate translation: [Nothing will ever shake the one doing these things]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that the phrase **for eternity** means “forever.” You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [will never be shaken]

16.text:
# Psalm 16 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 16 is considered to be one of the “psalms of trust.” See the Introduction to Psalms for more information about the psalms of trust.

1. David’s prayer (1)
2. David recalls what he said to Yahweh (2)
3. David’s delight in godly people (3)
4. The sorrows of those who pursue gods besides Yahweh and David’s refusal to participate in their idolatry (4)
5. David acknowledges that Yahweh is in control of his destiny and has greatly blessed him (5–6)
6. David blesses Yahweh for guiding him (7)
7. David’s resolve to continually focus on Yahweh (8a)
8. David’s trust that God will protect him from troubles (8b–c)
9. The result of David’s trust in God (9)
10. David’s trust that God will protect his life (10)
11. David’s acknowledgement that Yahweh has made him know “the path of life” and that an intimate relationship with Yahweh results in abundant and eternal joys (11)

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a “miktam.” See the discussion of that term in the introduction to Psalms.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Land and inheritance imagery in 16:5–6.

The historical and cultural background for 16:5–6 is the inheritance of land. 16:6 uses the imagery of measuring cords (lines) which were used to measure and distribute land. These verses probably also have as their background the distribution of the Promised Land to the tribes of Israel and Yahweh promising to be the inheritance of the tribe of Levi. If it would help you to better understand and translate these verses, you can read more about the inheritance of land in Joshua 18–19 and God providing for the Levites in Numbers 18:20–24.

### Messiah

In Peter’s sermon (Acts 2:14–36), he quotes Psalm 16:8–11 in 2:25–28 and then explains that David was a prophet and was speaking of the resurrection of the Messiah.
(See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/resurrection]]; and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/anoint]])

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

### What does David mean by “you will not abandon my soul to Sheol. You will not hand over your godly one to see the pit” in 16:10?

The word “Sheol” refers to the place or location of the dead (where dead people go). The word “pit” also refers to the grave. In this verse David is not saying that God will keep him from ever dying. 1 Kings 2:1–10 records that David died of old age. Here David is asserting his trust that God will save him from dying an unnatural death. In other words, he trusts that God will save him from being killed by evil men. Notice that this psalm begins with a prayer for protection. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/hades]])

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a **miktam**. Since the meaning of this word is not certain, you may wish to represent it in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language. See the discussion of that term in the Introduction to Psalms.
See how you translated the phrase “I take refuge” in [11:1](../011/001.md). Alternate translation: [I am safe because I trust in you] or [I depend on you to protect me]
The pronoun **You** refers to David himself. If this is not clear for your readers, you could use David’s name here. Alternate translation: [David said to Yahweh]

By **my good is not beyond you**, David means that he does not experience happiness apart from Yahweh and does not experience material blessings or provision apart from Yahweh. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I have no good apart from you]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **good**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [both my happiness and material provision come from you]

The term **holy ones** refers to godly people or faithful believers. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [As for the godly people] or [As for the people who are faithful to Yahweh]

David is using the adjectives **holy** and **majestic** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [As for the holy people … the majestic people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **delight**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [I fully delight in them]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **sorrows**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [They will suffer greatly, they who hasten after another god]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You could supply these words from the context, as in the ULT, if it would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [those who hasten after another god]

Here David is speaking as if those who seek out and eagerly worship other gods actually **hasten after** them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they who worship another god]

By **I will not pour out their drink offerings of blood**, the psalmist means that he will not participate in the pagan worship practices that involve offering drinks mixed with blood to false gods. You could include this information in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I will not participate in their blood offerings to other gods]

Here, **lips** represents speaking or saying something aloud. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will not speak their names] or [and I will not say their names]

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the phrase **my cup** before the phrases **the portion of my inheritance** and **holding my lot**. Alternate translation: [my cup. You are the portion of my inheritance, and you are holding my lot] or [you are my cup. You are the portion of my inheritance, and you are holding my lot]

By saying that Yahweh is **my cup** David could mean: (1) that Yahweh controls his destiny in which case he uses **cup** to refer to what one drinks and therefore, metaphorically, to what one receives in life. Alternate translation: [and the one who controls my future], or (2) [provision] in which case **cup** refers to physical provision. Alternate translation: [and the one who gives me great blessings]

Here David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were actually **the portion of my inheritance**. David is alluding to the inheritance of and distribution of land. (See the Introduction to this psalm for more information.) He means that Yahweh is his most valuable possession and the source of all his blessings and sustenance. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my most precious possession, my source of blessing]

Here David is speaking as if God were literally **holding** his lot, as if his destiny were a physical object that could be grasped in someone’s hand. He means that God controls and secures his future. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You are maintaining my lot] or [You are maintaining my destiny]

16.quote: חֲבָלִ֣ים נָֽפְלוּ־לִ֭⁠י בַּ⁠נְּעִמִ֑ים אַף־נַ֝חֲלָ֗ת שָֽׁפְרָ֥ה עָלָֽ⁠י
16.text: Here David is speaking as if his inheritance from God were actually **measuring cords** (used to divide land) that **have fallen** (were put) in **pleasant places**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. If not, you could state this as a comparison or in plain language. Alternate translation: [God has given me a delightful inheritance; indeed, what I have received is wonderful]

Here the word the ULT translates as **even** could: (1) be adding an additional thought. Alternate translation: [also,] or (2) be functioning to emphasize or assert what follows it. Alternate translation: [indeed]

Here the **kidneys** represent where a person’s thoughts and conscience exist. You may have a comparable expression in your language that you could use, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my mind instructs me]

David is speaking of **my kidneys** as if they were a living thing that could **instruct** him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh instructs my mind]

Here David assumes that readers will know that when he speaks of his mind instructing him, this happens as he thinks about Yahweh and what is pleasing to Yahweh, and probably also as he prays. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [my mind instructs me as I think about Yahweh] or [my mind instructs me as I pray and think about Yahweh]

16.quote: שִׁוִּ֬יתִי יְהוָ֣ה לְ⁠נֶגְדִּ֣⁠י תָמִ֑יד כִּ֥י מִֽ֝⁠ימִינִ֗⁠י בַּל־אֶמּֽוֹט׃ לָ⁠כֵ֤ן ׀ שָׂמַ֣ח לִ֭בִּ⁠י וַ⁠יָּ֣גֶל כְּבוֹדִ֑⁠י אַף־בְּ֝שָׂרִ֗⁠י יִשְׁכֹּ֥ן לָ⁠בֶֽטַח
16.text: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of the content of these verses, since 16:8 gives the reason for the result that 16:9 describes. Alternate translation: [My heart is glad, and my glory rejoices. Also, my flesh will dwell in security. This is because I have set Yahweh before me continually, and because he is at my right hand and I know that I will not be shaken]

The implication is that David is deliberately making Yahweh his constant focus and priority in life. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I constantly focus on Yahweh] or [In all that I do I am conscious of Yahweh]

David is using **he is at my right hand** as a common expression of his culture to mean “he is helping me” or “he is protecting me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he is helping me] or [he is protecting me]
See how you translated the similar expression in [15:5](../015/005.md).

This is a double negative. David uses the negative particle **not**, with the negative word **shaken** to express a positive meaning strongly. The phrase **I will not be shaken** means that David will remain firm and secure. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [he makes me live securely]

These two phrases **my heart is glad** and **my glory rejoices** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [my heart is glad, yes, my whole being rejoices] or [my heart is glad, yes, my glory rejoices]

Here the **heart** represents where a person’s emotions exist. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am glad] or [I feel glad]

Here, **glory** represents David’s “spirit” and by extension his feelings that come from his spirit (inner person). If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I rejoice]

Here, **flesh** represents David himself, specifically his body. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will dwell]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **security**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [securely]
David is using one part of himself, his **soul**, to mean all of him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [me]

16.quote: לֹא־תַעֲזֹ֣ב נַפְשִׁ֣⁠י לִ⁠שְׁא֑וֹל לֹֽא־תִתֵּ֥ן חֲ֝סִידְ⁠ךָ֗ לִ⁠רְא֥וֹת שָֽׁחַת
16.text: These two phrases **you will not abandon my soul to Sheol** and **You will not hand over your godly one to see the pit** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [you will save me, your faithful follower, from death] or [you will save me, a godly person, from the grave]

16.quote: לֹא־תַעֲזֹ֣ב נַפְשִׁ֣⁠י לִ⁠שְׁא֑וֹל לֹֽא־תִתֵּ֥ן חֲ֝סִידְ⁠ךָ֗ לִ⁠רְא֥וֹת שָֽׁחַת
16.text: See the Introduction to this psalm for a discussion of this phrase. Here, David is referring to Yahweh saving him from evil men who might try to kill him. David is not saying that he will not die of old age. Avoid translating this verse in a way that might make it appear that David thinks he will not die of old age.

David assumes that readers will know that **the pit** refers to the grave or death. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [You will rescue your godly one from death] or [You will rescue your godly one from the grave]

Even though David is addressing Yahweh directly, he is speaking of himself in the third person as **your godly one** to show humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a humble form in the first person. Alternate translation: [me, your godly one]

Here David is speaking of how to live as if it were actually **the path**. The phrase **of life** indicates he is speaking of living in a way that results in a joyful and blessed life in the present and in the future. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [how to live in a way that results in me being joyful and blessed, both now and in the future]

Here, **before your face** represents being in Yahweh’s presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [are in your presence … are joys] or [are with you … are pleasures]

Here, **right hand** represents God’s power and ability to give something. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [are before … with you are delights forever] or [are before … you give delights forever]

17.text:
# Psalm 17 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 17 is one of five psalms that are labeled as “prayers.” (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/deliverer]]; and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/innocent]])

1. David asks Yahweh to heed his prayer and pleads his innocence (1–5)
2. David asserts his belief that God will listen to him and answer him and will save everyone who seeks refuge in God (6–7)
3. David asks Yahweh to protect him (8–9)
4. David describes his enemies (10–12)
5. David asks Yahweh to save him by defeating his enemies who are worldly men (13–14)
6. David’s hope (15)

17.quote: שִׁמְעָ֤⁠ה יְהוָ֨ה ׀ צֶ֗דֶק הַקְשִׁ֥יבָ⁠ה רִנָּתִ֗⁠י הַאֲזִ֥ינָ⁠ה תְפִלָּתִ֑⁠י
17.text: These are imperatives, but they communicate polite requests rather than commands. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates polite requests. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please listen, Yahweh, to righteousness. Please pay attention to my cry! Please give ear to my prayer]
See how you translated this word in [11:7](../011/007.md).

David is using **Give ear** as a common expression of his culture to mean “listen” or “pay attention.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Listen to my prayer] or [Hear my prayer]

Here, **lips** represents the person who is speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Give ear to my prayer, since I speak without deceit] or [Give ear to my prayer, for I am not deceiving you]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **deceit**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [lips that do not deceive] or [lips that speak truthfully]

17.quote: מִ֭⁠לְּ⁠פָנֶי⁠ךָ מִשְׁפָּטִ֣⁠י יֵצֵ֑א עֵ֝ינֶ֗י⁠ךָ תֶּחֱזֶ֥ינָה מֵישָׁרִֽים
17.text: By using **let**, David is expressing what he desires or prays will happen. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [My vindication should come from your face; your eyes should see rightly]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **vindication**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a declaration of my innocence]

Here, **your face** represents God’s presence or his judgment. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from your presence] or [from you]

Here, **eyes** represents God’s ability to judge or evaluate. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [may you judge rightly]

Here, **my heart** represents David’s thoughts, feelings, and motives. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my thoughts] or [my inner being]

By **you have visited me in the night**, David means that God examines his heart and thoughts during the quiet hours when his true character is most evident. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [you have examined my heart at night]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context (as in the ULT) if that would be clearer in your language.

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [you have tested me and have detected nothing that displeases you]

Here, **mouth** represents “speech.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I have purposed that I will not transgress with my speech]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [mankind]

17.quote: בִּ⁠דְבַ֣ר שְׂפָתֶ֑י⁠ךָ אֲנִ֥י שָׁ֝מַ֗רְתִּי אָרְח֥וֹת פָּרִֽיץ
17.text: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [I have kept myself away from the paths of the violent by the word of your lips]

Here, **word** represents God’s oral or written communication. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [by your word] or [by what you have spoken]

Here David is speaking of how people live as if they were actually **paths** that they walk on. The phrase **paths of the violent** refers to living in a way that is characterized by unjust violence against innocent people. (David performed violent actions in the context of war but this refers to non-military violence.) If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a violent way of life] or [a destructive lifestyle characterized by violence]

David is using the adjective **violent** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [violent people]

Here David is speaking as if his obedience to God were actually **steps** that **hold firmly to** God’s **tracks**. (God’s **tracks** refer to the actions and lifestyle that God desires for people.) Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have consistently obeyed your commands; I have not disobeyed you]

The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because you will answer me God, I have called upon you]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please incline]
Here, **ear** represents hearing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Listen to me]
By **my speech**, David means his prayer. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [listen to my prayer]

The implication of **Set apart** is that David wants God to show his covenant faithfulness in a special or extraordinary way to help him in his current situation. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Show your covenant faithfulness in a special way] or [Display your covenant faithfulness remarkably]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [all the ways you are faithful to your covenant]
Here, **hand** represents the power of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [by your power]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [the ones seeking refuge in you from those rising up against them]

Here David is speaking of **the ones seeking refuge** in God as if they were literally seeking physical shelter or protection. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those who trust in you for protection]

David is using **those rising up** as a common expression of his culture to mean “those who oppose” or “enemies.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from those taking action against them] or [from those trying to harm them]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the pupil of your eye** is carefully protected, so David wants God to protect him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Protect me carefully] or [Guard me protectively]

David is speaking as if Yahweh were a bird and he were one of its chicks. Your language may have a comparable expression you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [protect me as a mother bird protects its chicks by covering them with its wings]

Here the phrase **from the faces of** was a common expression meaning “from the presence of” or “because of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the presence of]

David is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean wicked people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [wicked people] or [wicked men]

David is using the term **my soul** to mean his entire person from the perspective of his spiritual and emotional existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to me]

Here, **fat** represents their hearts or inner beings that have become hardened and unfeeling. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They have hardened their hearts] or [Their hearts have become unfeeling]

It might seem that the expression **with their mouths they speak** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [they speak with pride]

By **our steps**, David means the steps that both he and his enemies are taking as they move. The enemies are surrounding him at every point along their path. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [They have surrounded me now wherever we go] or [They have surrounded me at every point along our path]

Some ancient manuscripts read **They have surrounded me**. The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “They have surrounded us.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

By **Their eyes they have set, crouching down to the earth**, the psalmist means that his enemies are watching him carefully and getting ready to attack him like wild animals that crouch low before they pounce on their prey. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [They stare at me intently, crouched low and ready to attack]

17.quote: דִּמְיֹנ֗⁠וֹ כְּ֭⁠אַרְיֵה יִכְס֣וֹף לִ⁠טְר֑וֹף וְ֝⁠כִ⁠כְפִ֗יר יֹשֵׁ֥ב בְּ⁠מִסְתָּרִֽים
17.text: The pronoun **His** refers to the wicked person described in the previous verses. The pronoun **he** refers to this same wicked person. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The wicked person’s likeness is as a lion, the wicked person longs to tear; and as a young lion the wicked person is dwelling in hiding places]

17.quote: דִּמְיֹנ֗⁠וֹ כְּ֭⁠אַרְיֵה יִכְס֣וֹף לִ⁠טְר֑וֹף וְ֝⁠כִ⁠כְפִ֗יר יֹשֵׁ֥ב בְּ⁠מִסְתָּרִֽים
17.text: The point of this comparison is that just as **a lion** longs to tear apart its prey, so the wicked person’s **likeness** resembles a lion that longs to attack. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [He is like a lion that longs to tear apart its prey, and like a young lion hiding and waiting to attack]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [he longs to tear his prey]

17.quote: קוּמָ֤⁠ה יְהוָ֗ה קַדְּמָ֣⁠ה פָ֭נָי⁠ו הַכְרִיעֵ֑⁠הוּ פַּלְּטָ֥⁠ה נַ֝פְשִׁ֗⁠י
17.text: Here David is using imperative forms **Arise**, **confront**, **make him bow down**, and **Rescue** to communicate polite requests to God rather than commands. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please arise, Yahweh, please confront his face, please make him bow down! Please rescue my soul]

Here, **his face** represents his presence or confronting him directly. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [confront him directly] or [face him in battle]

By **make him bow down** David means “throw him to the ground” or “cause him to fall to the ground” and probably means “fall to the ground dead.” You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [make him fall down dead] or [cause him to fall to the ground defeated]

David is using one part of a person, his **soul**, to mean all of him in the act of being rescued. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [me]

David is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [from wicked people] or [from wicked men]

Here, **sword** represents power or strength used for powerful, violent action. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with your power]

17.quote: מִֽ⁠מְתִ֥ים יָדְ⁠ךָ֨ ׀ יְהוָ֡ה מִֽ⁠מְתִ֬ים מֵ⁠חֶ֗לֶד חֶלְקָ֥⁠ם בַּֽ⁠חַיִּים֮
17.text: David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Rescue me from men by your hand, Yahweh, from men of this world whose portion is in this life]

Here, **hand** represents the power of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Rescue me from evil men by your power Yahweh] or [From men, with your power Yahweh]

Here the psalmist is speaking of God providing abundantly for his people as if he would literally with his treasure **fill their belly**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you abundantly provide for them from your riches]

Here the masculine term **sons** has a generic sense that includes both sons and daughters. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both sons and daughters. Alternate translation: [with children]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **abundance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [their abundant possessions] or [great wealth]

David is using the adjective **righteousness** as a noun to mean a state or condition of being righteous. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase as in the UST.
David is using **your face** to represent all of God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [will see you]
Some Bible scholars think that the phrase **when I awake** is a reference to David’s future bodily resurrection. If it would help your readers, you could include a footnote explaining this.

The implication is that David will be satisfied when he sees God. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I will be satisfied with your presence]

18.text:
# Psalm 18 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This is a song by David about Yahweh’s deliverance. This song is also recorded in the Bible in [2 Samuel 22](../2sa/22/01.md).

1. David sings to Yahweh that he loves him and calls Yahweh his “strength” (1)
2. David describes what Yahweh is to him (2)
3. David recounts that God has answered his prayer and saved him from his enemies when he was in a dangerous situation (3–6)
4. David compares Yahweh’s act of saving him to three different natural disasters (7–14)
5. David recounts Yahweh delivering him (15–19)
6. David gives the reason Yahweh has delivered him (20–27)
7. David recounts the different things Yahweh has done for him (28–48)
8. David thanks and praises Yahweh (49)
9. Yahweh saves David his chosen king and shows covenant faithfulness to David and his descendants forever (50)

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

### Hebrew poetry

The verses of this song by David continually present two phrases that mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases with a word other than “and” in order to show that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. But you may find that in some cases it is appropriate to combine the two phrases. For example:

* both phrases

[18:23](../018/023.md) And I have been blameless with him,
and I have kept myself from my iniquity.
“And I have been blameless with him,
yes, I have kept myself from my iniquity.”

[18:21](../018/021.md) For I have kept the ways of Yahweh,
and I have not been wicked from my God.
“For I have kept the ways of Yahweh,
no, I have not been wicked from my God.”

* combined into one

[18:6](../018/006.md) In my distress I called {to} Yahweh,
and to my God I called
“In my distress I called out to Yahweh, my God”

### Extended metaphor

In [7–14](../018/007.md), David describes Yahweh coming to help him as being like the greatest natural forces that people of his culture knew, which were an earthquake ([7](../018/007.md)), a volcano ([8](../018/008.md)), and a thunderstorm ([9–14](../018/009.md)). He describes each of these forces in poetic language. In other words, after stating his topic, which is how Yahweh delivered him ([6](../018/006.md)), David then depicts it with multiple images that communicate multiple ideas. Think about how you might show in your translation that [7–14](../018/007.md), while describing three different things, all illustrate the same topic.

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]
Here **palm** and **hand** represent power or control. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the control of all his enemies]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the one who makes me strong]

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were actually a high **rock** that he could climb up to reach safety from danger. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is like a rock that keeps me safe from danger … he is like a rock to me]

Here David is speaking as if Yahweh were actually a **stronghold** or a strong structure where people go to be protected. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and my place of safety]

Here David uses **take refuge in him** as if God were a place of safety in which he could hide. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I depend on him to keep me safe] or [I trust him to protect me]

Here David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a **shield** that protected him from attack. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my protector]

David is using the possessive form to describe a **horn** that is characterized by providing **salvation**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the horn that saves me]

David is speaking of God’s power to save him as if it were a powerful **horn** of an animal. A horn was a symbol of strength in ancient Israelite culture because animals use their horns as weapons. Your language may have a comparable expression that you could use, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the one who saves me by his power] or [and the one who powerfully saves me]

The expression **being praised** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I call to Yahweh, the one whom people praise] or [I call to Yahweh, the one whom I praise]

The expression **I am saved** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [and he saves me]

Here David is speaking as if death were actually **cords** that could wrap around and bind a person. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. If not, you could state this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [Death threatened to bind me like cords] or [I was in danger of dying]

David speaks here of **torrents of wickedness** as if wickedness were a flood of rushing water that could overwhelm and destroy him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a wicked person was pursuing me relentlessly, and that terrified me]

Here, **Sheol**, the dwelling place of the dead according to Hebrew culture, represents death itself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [The cords of death surrounded me]

David is speaking as if Sheol or death actually had **cords** that it could use to bind him. This suggests he felt trapped in a situation where he thought he would die. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [I thought I was bound to die]

David speaks here of **snares of death** as if death were a hunter that could set traps for people. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [death had me in its clutches]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **distress**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [When I was distressed] or [When I felt distressed]

Here, **to his face** represents being in God’s presence or coming before him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and my call for help]

Here, **voice** represents the words David spoke in his prayer. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [He heard my prayer]

By **his temple**, David means God’s temple in heaven. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [from his heavenly temple]
David is using the term **ears** to mean hearing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he heard]

18.quote: וַ⁠תִּגְעַ֬שׁ וַ⁠תִּרְעַ֨שׁ ׀ הָ⁠אָ֗רֶץ וּ⁠מוֹסְדֵ֣י הָרִ֣ים יִרְגָּ֑זוּ וַ֝⁠יִּתְגָּֽעֲשׁ֗וּ כִּי־חָ֥רָה לֽ⁠וֹ
18.text: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Then, because it burned to him, the earth shook and trembled. The foundations of the heavens quaked and shook themselves]

The terms that the ULT translates as **shook** and **shook themselves** represent two different verbs in the original. Hebrew had more synonyms for this idea than some other languages may have. David expresses some of these with the verbs translated as **trembled** and **quaked**. It may be necessary for you to use the same words rather than different ones. However, if you do have a variety of terms for this, it would be appropriate to use different words for **shook** and **shook themselves**.

The terms **shook** and **trembled** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Then the earth shook violently]

18.quote: וַ⁠תִּגְעַ֬שׁ וַ⁠תִּרְעַ֨שׁ ׀ הָ⁠אָ֗רֶץ וּ⁠מוֹסְדֵ֣י הָרִ֣ים יִרְגָּ֑זוּ וַ֝⁠יִּתְגָּֽעֲשׁ֗וּ

This expresses how powerfully God responded to David’s prayer. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Then it was as though a violent earthquake occurred and shook the earth and the foundations of the mountains]

The terms **quaked** and **shook themselves** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [quaked mightily]
Here, **it burned to him** represents his anger. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he was angry]

18.quote: עָ֘לָ֤ה עָשָׁ֨ן ׀ בְּ⁠אַפּ֗⁠וֹ וְ⁠אֵשׁ־מִ⁠פִּ֥י⁠ו תֹּאכֵ֑ל גֶּ֝חָלִ֗ים בָּעֲר֥וּ מִמֶּֽ⁠נּוּ

David describes the opening at the top of a volcano, from which **Smoke** and **fire** and **Coals** come out, as if it were the **nose** and **mouth** of the volcano. If your readers would be familiar with what a volcano is, you could express in your translation how David is using a volcano as an image to describe Yahweh’s power. If not, you could describe in more general terms how Yahweh’s power is like fire and smoke.

David is speaking of the fire that comes from a volcano, which represents God here, as if it were a wild animal that **devoured** its prey. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and fire from his mouth completely destroyed everything] or [and fire from his mouth consumed everything]

18.quote: וַ⁠יֵּ֣ט שָׁ֭מַיִם וַ⁠יֵּרַ֑ד וַ֝⁠עֲרָפֶ֗ל תַּ֣חַת רַגְלָֽי⁠ו

The words **rode** and **flew** express a single idea. The word **flew** tells more about how he **rode**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [And he flew by riding on a cherub]

David is speaking as if God were actually riding on a **cherub** and flying through the sky. This is part of a poetic description of God’s power and swift action to help David. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he came very quickly]

David is speaking as if the wind actually had **wings** and that it could fly through the sky carrying Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and it appeared as if the wind were a great bird that was carrying him swiftly]

David is speaking as if the darkness were actually **set** like a physical object that could be arranged in place. He means that God caused darkness to surround himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [It was as if he were dwelling within the darkness of the storm]

If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

Alternate translation: [And he sent out lightning bolts like arrows and panicked them so that they scattered]

The pronoun **them** refers in each instance to David’s enemies. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and he scattered my enemies … and he panicked those enemies]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [yes, and he sent out lightnings in abundance]

Here, **height** represents “heaven” as God’s dwelling place. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from heaven]
Here, **many waters** represents the sea. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [out of the sea]

See how you translated the phrase **according to the cleanness of my hands** in [18:20](../018/020.md).

The expression **the purified** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Here, **right hand** represents the power of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and your power]

By **your humility**, David means God’s humbleness in responding to his prayers requesting help. Because God was much greater and more powerful than David, David views God’s response to his prayers as an act of humility. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and your answer to my prayers] or [and your humble answer to my prayers]

Here David’s **step** represents the place where he would step. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [You enlarge the place where I step under me]

David is speaking as if God had made the area where he needed to walk more spacious. This represents having freedom to move and act without being constrained by enemies. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [You give me room to maneuver]

David is describing one event before describing another event that preceded it. If it would be helpful your language, you may wish to relate these events in the order in which they happened, as in the UST. Alternate translation: [so that they fall under my feet and were not able to arise]
The implication is that David’s enemies fall and remain dead. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [they fall down dead]

Here David is speaking as if God were actually girding him **with valor**, as if valor were a belt or sash that could be wrapped around him. David means that God gives him courage and strength for battle. See how you translated a similar expression in [18:32](../018/032.md). Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And you make me valiant]

David means that people who try to rebel against him ultimately **bow down** as a symbolic action by which they show renewed submission to his authority. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [you make the ones rising up under me submit humbly to my authority]

David is using **the ones rising up under me** as a common expression of his culture to mean “those who rebel against my rule.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ones revolting against my rule]

David is describing a symbolic action in which victorious soldiers would make defeated enemies lie face down on the ground and then would step on their necks to demonstrate their complete triumph (as in [Joshua 10:24](../../jos/10/24.md), for example). If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [you enable me to step in complete triumph on the back of their necks]

In this verse, the words **back** and **neck** are singular in form, but they refer to all the enemies as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use plural forms of “back” and “neck.” Alternate translation: [the backs of their necks]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [you give to me the ones hating me]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [they called to Yahweh]

By **he did not answer them**, David means that Yahweh did not help his enemies as they had asked. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [but he did not do what they asked]

Here David is making a comparison between his defeated enemies and **dust upon the face of the wind**. The point of this comparison is that just as dust upon the face of the wind is completely scattered and powerless, so his enemies became completely defeated and scattered. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [And I beat them so that they scattered completely like dust blown by the wind]

Here David is speaking as if he had literally beaten his enemies into **dust** that blows away in the wind. He means that he completely defeated and destroyed them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I completely destroyed them and scattered them] or [And I crushed them completely and scattered them]

David is making a comparison between his enemies and **mud of the streets**. The point of this comparison is that just as **mud of the streets** is worthless and easily discarded, so are his defeated enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [I threw them out like worthless mud from the streets]

By **people**, David most likely means “my people” as in the parallel passage in ([2 Samuel 22:44](../../2sa/22/44.md)). You could indicate this explicitly in your translation, as in the UST, if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [You rescue me from the disputes of my people]

Here David is speaking of his leadership role as if he were the **head** of a body. Just as the head directs the rest of the body, David ruled over other nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as the ruler of nations] or [to govern the nations]

David is using one part of a person, the **ear** to represent entire people in the act of hearing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [When they listen]
David means that these people hear specifically about him. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [When they hear about me]
By **they hear me**, David means that they obey him. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [they obey me]

David is not referring to a specific **foreigner**. He means foreigners in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [sons of foreigners]

In certain contexts, biblical authors and characters use the common expression of their culture **sons of** to indicate that a person has a certain characteristic. In this case, these people have the characteristic of being foreigners or people from other nations. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly, here and in the next verse. Alternate translation: [foreigners]

By **cringe to me**, David means that foreigners will submit to him and show him respect out of fear. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [cringe before me] or [came cringing before me]

In certain contexts, biblical authors and characters use the expression **Sons of** to indicate that a person has a certain characteristic. In this case, the people whom David is describing have the characteristic of being soldiers of foreign countries that are resisting his rule. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Foreign soldiers]

Here David is speaking of foreign armies as if they were plants that **fade away** and lose their vitality. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [lose strength]

David is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling, joy. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [I rejoice that Yahweh is alive] or [How wonderful that Yahweh lives]

The expression **blessed be** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And I bless my rock]
See how you translated a similar phrase in [18:31](../018/031.md).

The expression **be exalted** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and I exalt the God of my salvation]
David is using this possessive form to describe **the God** who provides salvation to him. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the God who saves me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the God who is the rock that saves me]

Here David is speaking of conquering **peoples** as if they were being brought down physically **under** his feet. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he defeats peoples before me]

Here David is speaking of his enemies as if they were physically **arising** upward to attack him, and he speaks of God as One who will physically **lift me up** above them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you make me prevail over those who attack me] or [you protect me from those who oppose me]

David is not referring to a specific **man of violence**. He means violent people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [from violent men]

Here, **name** represents Yahweh himself, in light of his fame and reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and I will sing praise to you] or [and I will sing praise to you, Yahweh]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the one saving his king by great deeds]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and being faithful to his covenant]

The expression **his anointed** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [to the one he anointed]

Here David is speaking of his offspring as if they were actually **seed**. Just as a seed can grow into a plant that produces more seeds, David’s descendants would continue to come from his family line. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and to all who descend from him]

19.text:
# Psalm 19 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 19 is a psalm about how God has revealed himself and glorifies himself through his physical creation, and how he reveals himself through his written revelation which he gave to the Israelites through Moses.

1. The heavens declare God’s glory (1–4b)
2. The sun in the heavens (4c–6)
3. The greatness and worth of God’s word and its effect (7–9)
4. The desirableness of God’s word (10)
5. The benefit of God’s word (11–12a)
6. Closing prayer (12b–14)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Terms for God’s commands and instructions

The psalmist uses many different words to refer to God’s message to us. You could decide to use a different word for each term, but most languages will not have that many, so just use the words that your language has. In verses 7–9 there are six different terms used for things that God commanded and taught his people.

1. “The law of Yahweh” in 19:7a. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/lawofmoses]])
2. “The testimony of Yahweh” in 19:7b. Here the word “testimony” has a similar meaning to the word “law” in 19:7a, making the phrases “The law of Yahweh” and “the testimony of Yahweh” complementary. The phrase “the testimony of Yahweh” refers either to God’s entire law as a whole that he gave to the Israelites or more specifically to his law that he gave them through Moses on Mount Sinai.
3. “The precepts of Yahweh” in verse 19:8a. The word that is translated as “precepts” refers to something that is appointed or mandated so the phrase “the precepts of Yahweh” refers to the things that Yahweh mandated.
4. “The commandment of Yahweh” in 19:8b. See the note on this phrase in 19:8.
5. “The fear of Yahweh” in 19:9a. See the note on this phrase in 19:9.
6. “The judgments of Yahweh” in 19:9b. The word translated as “judgments” could also be translated as “ordinances” or “decisions” here and refers to decisions or judgments that are made. Here the phrase “the judgments of Yahweh” refers to the judicial instructions that Yahweh gave the Israelites for handling different types of situations involving people.

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

19.quote: הַ⁠שָּׁמַ֗יִם מְֽסַפְּרִ֥ים כְּבֽוֹד־אֵ֑ל וּֽ⁠מַעֲשֵׂ֥ה יָ֝דָ֗י⁠ו מַגִּ֥יד הָ⁠רָקִֽיעַ
19.text: David is speaking of **the heavens** and **the sky** as if they were living things that could declare and proclaim God’s glory and works. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [What people see in the heavens shows them the glory of God, and what they see in the sky tells them about the work of his hands]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [that God is glorious]

19.quote: הַ⁠שָּׁמַ֗יִם מְֽסַפְּרִ֥ים כְּבֽוֹד־אֵ֑ל וּֽ⁠מַעֲשֵׂ֥ה יָ֝דָ֗י⁠ו מַגִּ֥יד הָ⁠רָקִֽיעַ
19.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [The heavens are declaring the glory of God, yes, the sky is proclaiming the work of his hands]

Here, **hands** represents the power and creative ability of God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the sky is proclaiming what he has powerfully made] or [and the sky is proclaiming his mighty works]

19.quote: י֣וֹם לְ֭⁠יוֹם יַבִּ֣יעַֽ אֹ֑מֶר וְ⁠לַ֥יְלָה לְּ֝⁠לַ֗יְלָה יְחַוֶּה־דָּֽעַת
19.text: David is speaking of **Day to day** and **night to night** as if they were living things that could speak and declare knowledge. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Each day it is as if the daytime is speaking, and each night it is as if the nighttime is declaring knowledge]

Within the image of the day speaking, David is speaking of the day as if it were a spring that flows or bubbles forth water. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [It is as if each day is a spring that pours out words declaring God’s glory]

David is not referring to a specific **word**. He means words in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [words]

David assumes that readers will understand that **Day to day** means that each successive day continues to proclaim God’s glory, and **night to night** means that each successive night continues to declare knowledge about God. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Each day … and each night]
The pronoun **their** refers to the heavens. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [where the voice of the heavens is not being heard]

The expression **their voice is not being heard** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [where people do not hear their voice]

Here David speaks of the “heavens” as if they were a living thing that could speak and have their **voice** heard but remains silent. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they do not have a voice to speak]

The pronouns **Their** and **them** refer to the heavens. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The heaven’s line … the heaven’s words … in the heavens] or [The line of the heaven’s … the words of the heaven’s … in the heavens]

The Septuagint (an ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible) and the Peshitta (the Syriac translation of the Bible) read “Their voice” instead of “their line.” That may have been the original reading, particularly since it would then make this line a parallelism with the second line in the verse with “Their voice” and **their words** being parallel ideas. At one point in the process of transmission, scribes may have accidentally left out the additional Hebrew letter that would have spelled “Their voice” rather than **Their line**. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

David is speaking of the heavens as if they were living things that could speak **words**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they display God’s glory to the end of the world]

David assumes that readers will know that **their words to the end of the world** refers to the message that the heavens proclaim about God’s glory and **to the end of the world** refers to the furthest extremities of the earth. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and their message to the furthest extremities of the earth] or [and their message to the most remote parts of the earth]

David is speaking of the heavens as if they were **a tent for the sun**. He means that God has placed the sun in the skies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He has placed the sun in the heavens] or [He has put the sun in the skies]

The demonstrative pronoun **that** and the pronouns **it** and **its** all refer to the sun. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the sun … the sun rejoices … its path]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a bridegroom coming out from his chamber** is satisfied, joyful and radiant so is the sun as it rises. (Here the word **chamber** refers to a bedroom.) If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and that joyfully rises like a bridegroom coming out from his chamber] or [and it comes out joyfully and eagerly like a bridegroom leaving his bedroom]

The point of this comparison is that just as a **strong man** is eager and enthusiastic to **run**, so is the sun eager and enthusiastic to travel across the sky. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [it moves eagerly across the sky like a strong man who is eager to run a race]

David assumes that readers will know that **the end of the heavens** and **the ends of them** refer to opposite horizons where the sun appears to begin and complete its daily journey across the sky. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [From the furthest extremities of the heavens is its going forth, and its circuit to the furthest extremities of them]

The pronouns **its** in the phrase **its going forth, and its circuit** and in the phrase **its heat** all refer to the sun. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [is the sun’s going forth, and the sun’s circuit … from the sun’s heat]

The expression **nothing hidden** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and there is nothing that is able to escape from its heat]

Here the word the ULT translates as **restoring** could mean: (1) “turning back” or “converting” and refer to changing one’s mind leading them to turn from (stop) a wrong way of living and turn towards (obey) God. Alternate translation: [converting the soul] or [turning one back to God], or (2) [refreshing.] Alternate translation: [refreshing the soul] or [reviving the soul]

David is using the term **soul** to mean the entire person from the perspective of his spiritual existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [restoring the person]

David is using the adjective **simple** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [simple people] or [inexperienced people]

Here the **heart** represents a person’s inner being, where emotions and desires exist. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [causing people to rejoice]

David is not referring to a specific **commandment** of God. He means Yahweh’s entire law as a whole, which includes all Yahweh’s commandments. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the commandments of Yahweh are pure]

David is speaking of **the commandment of Yahweh** as if it were physically **pure**, like something that contains no impurities or contaminants. He means that the commandment is morally perfect and completely right. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [is totally righteous]

Here, **eyes** represents the ability to see and understand. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [giving guidance for living] or [giving insight for how to live wisely]

Here, **The fear of Yahweh** represents the obedience to his laws or commands that is the result of that reverence and that produces a clean life. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Carefully obeying the law of Yahweh keeps one clean] or [the reverence given to Yahweh that results in obedience to him produces a clean life]

David is speaking of the fear of Yahweh as if it were something that could be **clean**. He means that the fear of Yahweh causes people to obey him, which results in a life that is pure and without moral fault. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The fear of Yahweh results in a morally pure life] or [The fear of Yahweh results in obedience to him which produces a faultless life]

19.quote: הַֽ⁠נֶּחֱמָדִ֗ים מִ֭⁠זָּהָב וּ⁠מִ⁠פַּ֣ז רָ֑ב וּ⁠מְתוּקִ֥ים מִ֝⁠דְּבַ֗שׁ וְ⁠נֹ֣פֶת צוּפִֽים
19.text: The point of this comparison is that just as **gold** is valuable and therefore desirable, and as **honey** is sweet, so the commandments of Yahweh are valuable and pleasant. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [The commandments of Yahweh are extremely valuable and pleasant, like gold and honey]

The pronoun **They** refers to the “commandments” of Yahweh mentioned in the preceding verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The commandments of Yahweh are worth … the commandments of Yahweh are sweeter than honey]
