The word translated as **nectar** refers specifically to honey which drips or flows from a honeycomb. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate that explicitly by translating it as “honey.” Alternate translation: [and honey of]

19.quote: עַ֭בְדְּ⁠ךָ נִזְהָ֣ר בָּ⁠הֶ֑ם בְּ֝⁠שָׁמְרָ֗⁠ם עֵ֣קֶב רָֽב
19.text: Both occurrences of the pronoun **them** refer to the commandments and teachings of Yahweh described in verses 7–10. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [by Yahweh’s commandments your servant is warned; in obeying his commandments there is great reward]

David is speaking of himself in the third person as **your servant** to show humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a humble form in the first person. Alternate translation: [I, your servant, am warned] or [I am warned]

The expression **by them your servant is warned** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [they warn your servant] or [Yahweh warns your servant by them]

David is using the question form to emphasize that no one can fully understand all of their own sins and mistakes. If you would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate his words as a statement or an exclamation. Alternate translation: [No one can discern all his own errors!]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context, as in the ULT, if that would be clearer in your language.

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. David is asking God to forgive him. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please acquit me from hidden faults]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please keep back your servant from presumptuous ones; please do not let them rule over me]

David is speaking of himself in the third person as **your servant** to show humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a humble form in the first person. Alternate translation: [keep me back]

David is using the adjective **presumptuous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of sin. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [presumptuous sins] or [deliberate sins]

David assumes that readers will know that **them** refers to **presumptuous** sins. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [let presumptuous sins not rule over me] or [let these presumptuous sins not rule over me]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **transgression**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from doing something very wrong] or [from sinning greatly]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. David is using this form to make a humble petition to Yahweh. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [I ask that the words of my mouth … be] or [Please let the words of my mouth … be]
Here, **the words of my mouth** represent what David says by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what I say]

Here **my heart** represents where David’s thoughts and feelings exist. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and my inner thoughts] or [and what I think within myself]

Here God’s **face** represents his presence and by extension his sight. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to you] or [in your sight]
See how you translated the phrase “my strength” in [18:1](../018/001.md).

20.text:
# Psalm 20 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 20 is considered to be one of the “royal psalms.” See the Introduction to Psalms for more information about the royal psalms.

1. Prayer for the king that Yahweh would protect and help him in battle (1–2)
2. Prayer that Yahweh would accept the king’s offerings (3)
3. Prayer that Yahweh would fulfill the king’s desires and plans (4)
4. Anticipation of Yahweh giving his king victory (5)
5. Expression of confidence in Yahweh (6–8)
6. Closing prayer (9)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Trust

In verse 7 David asserts that trusting in Yahweh is better than trusting in military might. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/trust]])

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

### In verses 1–5 who do the pronouns “you” and “your” refer to?

In this psalm all occurrences of the pronouns “you” and “your” that occur in verses 1–5 are singular and refer to Yahweh’s anointed king mentioned in verse 6. Because verse 6 identifies who the pronouns “you” and “your” refer to, you do not need to make this explicit in your translation. Also, if your language has both singular and plural second person pronouns, you should use the singular forms each time you translate the pronouns “you” and “your” in verses 1–5.

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

David is using the term **day** to refer to a specific time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when you experience trouble] or [in time of trouble]

David is using the term **name** to represent the person and character of God himself, including his attributes and covenant faithfulness to deliver his people when they call on him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the God of Jacob]

David is speaking of Yahweh protecting his anointed king as if Yahweh would **set** him up on a **high** place where his enemies could not reach and harm him. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [may … keep you safe] or [may … keep you from being harmed by your enemies]

David assumes that readers will know that **help** means military assistance or deliverance from enemies. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [May he help you prevail against your adversaries with aid]

David assumes that readers will know that **the sanctuary** refers to the temple in Jerusalem, the place where God’s presence dwells. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [May he send you help from his sanctuary, the Temple]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [May he send you help from the sanctuary, yes, may he support you from Zion]

David assumes that readers will know that when God remembers someone’s offerings, he acts favorably toward that person based on those offerings. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [May he take notice of all of your offerings and act accordingly]

David is using **regard as fat** as a common expression of his culture to mean “accept” or “be pleased with.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly as in the UST.

Here the **heart** represents where a person’s desires exist. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what you desire] or [the desires of your heart]

David assumes that readers will understand that **your heart** refers to the king’s desires or wishes. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [according to your heart’s desire]

In this context, the forms of the two verbs the ULT translates as **We will shout for joy** and **we will set up our banners** could indicate: (1) a resolution of the will and therefore be translated as in the ULT, or (2) a request. Alternate translation: [May we shout for joy … may we set up our banners]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **joy** and **salvation**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [When you save us, then we will joyfully shout]

Here David is using the term **name** to represent who God is or to refer to his reputation. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and for the glory of our God]

A **banner** is a flag made from a large piece of cloth that is attached to a long pole. People, groups, and kings had their own unique banners by which they identified themselves. If your readers would not be familiar with this type of flag, you could use the name of something similar in your area, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [we will set up our flags]

Raising banners was a symbolic action by which armies showed victory. In this context it was done in order to give God the glory for helping the soldiers of the Israelite army defeat their enemies. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and in the name of our God we will raise our banners to celebrate the victory Yahweh has given us]

You may be used to indicating when David is referring to himself in the third person by saying something such as “me, his anointed.” However, we recommend that you not do that in this instance, since the term **anointed** here refers to others besides David.

David assumes that readers will know that **his anointed** refers to the king of Israel, whom God had chosen and set apart by anointing with oil. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [his anointed king]

The expression **his anointed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [the one whom he had anointed]

Here, **right hand** represents the power of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with mighty deeds by his great power to save]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with mighty deeds of his saving right hand]

David is using **These in chariots and these in horses** as a common expression of his culture to mean “Some trust in chariots and some in horses” or “Some trust in chariots and others in horses.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Some in chariots and some in horses] or [Some trust in chariots and others trust in horses]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [These trust in chariots and these trust in horses]

David assumes that readers will know that chariots and horses were military equipment that symbolized military power and strength. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [These trust in their military chariots and these in their war horses]

David uses the word **but** here to indicate a contrast between those who trust in military power and those who trust in Yahweh. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [however, we] or [in contrast, we]

David assumes that readers will know that remembering the name of Yahweh means trusting in him and calling on him for help. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [will keep in mind] or [will be confident in]

David is using the term **name** to represent who Yahweh is and his character which includes being very powerful. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh our God] or [Yahweh our powerful God]

The pronoun **They** refers to those who trust in chariots and horses (mentioned in the previous verse), while the pronoun **we** refers to David and those who trust in Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Those who trust in those things … but we who trust in Yahweh]

David assumes that readers will know that **bow down and fall** refers to being defeated in battle. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [They collapse and fall in battle]
Here, **fall** represents dying in battle. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and fall dead]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, please save]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, save the king] or [Yahweh, save us, your people]
The word the ULT translates as **the king** could belong: (1) with the second line, as in the ULT, or (2) with the first line. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, save the king! May he answer us]
David is using the term **day** to refer to a specific time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [at the time] or [when]

21.text:
# Psalm 21 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 21 is considered to be one of the “royal psalms.” See the Introduction to Psalms for more information about the royal psalms.

1. The king rejoices in Yahweh’s strength (1)
2. Yahweh’s blessing of his chosen king (2–6)
3. The king’s trust in Yahweh (7)
4. The king will defeat his enemies with Yahweh’s help (8–12)
5. Final words regarding Yahweh’s strength and power (13)

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

### Pronouns

There is a shift in how Yahweh is referred to in this psalm. In verses 1–6 David uses second person pronouns when Yahweh is addressed. In verse 7 Yahweh is referred to in the third person as “Yahweh” and as “the Most High.” In verses 8–13 David shifts back to using second person pronouns when Yahweh is being addressed. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-123person]])

In this psalm, when the pronouns “you,” “we,” “them,” “their,” and “they” are used, it may at times be unclear to whom these pronouns are referring to. For help translating these pronouns, see the notes in the individual verses where these pronouns occur. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/writing-pronouns]])

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **strength** and **salvation**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [because you are strong … and because you save me] or [because you are powerful … and because you save those who trust in you]

You may be used to indicating when David is referring to himself in the third person by saying something such as “I, the king rejoice … I exult.” However, we recommend that you not do that in this instance, since **the king** here, while including David, refers to others besides him.

David is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of joy. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [he rejoices so very much] or [he is extremely glad]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **desire**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what he desired]

Here the **heart** represents where a person’s desires exist. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what he desired] or [what he desired in his inmost being]

Here, **the request of his lips** represents what the king asked for by using his lips to speak. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and what he asked for]

Here the phrase **you meet him** could mean: (1) that Yahweh met the king. Alternate translation: [you come to him with good blessings] or [you greet him with excellent blessings], or (2) that Yahweh anticipated what the king needed and was already working ahead of time before the king prayed in order to meet his needs. Alternate translation: [you anticipated his needs and came to him with blessings of good] or [you knew what he needed and met him with blessings of good]

The implication is that God blesses the king with good things. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [with good blessings] or [with excellent blessings]
This is poetic language. If your language has a way to indicate poetry, you could use it here. Alternate translation: [with rich blessings]

David assumes that readers will know that Yahweh himself did not physically **place** a crown on David’s head but rather chose him to be king and had people crown him as king by placing a crown on his head. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [you cause to be placed]

Placing **a crown** on the king’s **head** was a symbolic action by which God showed that he was establishing the king in his royal authority and giving him honor. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [you place on his head a crown of refined gold, showing that you have established him as king]
Because the following line in this verse explains what **life** refers to, there is no need to explain this further here.

21.quote: חַיִּ֤ים ׀ שָׁאַ֣ל מִ֭מְּ⁠ךָ נָתַ֣תָּה לּ֑⁠וֹ אֹ֥רֶךְ יָ֝מִ֗ים עוֹלָ֥ם וָ⁠עֶֽד
21.text: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **life**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [He asked you that he might live, and you granted his request and gave him length of days, forever and ever]

David assumes that readers will know that **length of days** means to live for many years. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [a long life] or [a lengthy life]

21.quote: גָּד֣וֹל כְּ֭בוֹד⁠וֹ בִּ⁠ישׁוּעָתֶ֑⁠ךָ ה֥וֹד וְ֝⁠הָדָר תְּשַׁוֶּ֥ה עָלָֽי⁠ו
21.text: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **salvation**, **splendor**, and **majesty**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [You glorify him greatly by saving him; you make him splendorous and majestic]

The terms **splendor** and **majesty** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [great honor you place on him] or [magnificent glory you place on him]

David assumes that readers will know that **place on him** here means “give to him.” You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [you bestow on him] or [you give to him]

David assumes that readers will know that **him** refers to the king mentioned in the superscription and throughout the psalm. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [you bestow on the king] or [you grant the king]

21.quote: תְשִׁיתֵ֣⁠הוּ בְרָכ֣וֹת לָ⁠עַ֑ד תְּחַדֵּ֥⁠הוּ בְ֝⁠שִׂמְחָ֗ה אֶת־פָּנֶֽי⁠ךָ
21.text: The implication is that the king will rejoice in the presence of God, that is, he will rejoice because God is with him. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [you make him glad with joy because you are present with him] or [you make him rejoice because he is in your presence]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **blessings**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [you bless him eternally]
This is poetic language. If your language has a way to indicate poetry, you could use it here. Alternate translation: [you make him very glad] or [you make him exceedingly glad]

Here, **with your face** represents being in Yahweh’s presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in your presence] or [with your presence]
Translate the phrase **the king** as you did in verse one of this Psalm.

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and because he is faithful to the covenant of]
See how you translated the similar expression in [9:2](../009/002.md).
See how you translated the similar phrase “I will not be shaken” in [15:5](../015/005.md).

21.quote: תִּמְצָ֣א יָ֭דְ⁠ךָ לְ⁠כָל־אֹיְבֶ֑י⁠ךָ יְ֝מִֽינְ⁠ךָ תִּמְצָ֥א שֹׂנְאֶֽי⁠ךָ
21.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Your hand will find all of your enemies, indeed, your right hand will find those who hate you]
The pronoun **Your** refers to the king. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [You, the king’s hand] or [The king’s hand]

David is using **Your hand will find** as a common expression of his culture to mean “You will reach” or “You will overtake.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You will reach … you will overtake]
The pronoun **them** refers to the king’s enemies. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [You, the king, will make your enemies]

The point of this comparison is that just as **an oven of fire** completely consumes what is placed in it, so David is saying that God will completely destroy his enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [You will completely consume them like fire in an oven]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [You will make them as something that is burned in an oven of fire]
Here, **your face** represents your presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [at the time of your appearing]

David is using the phrase **In his nose** as a common expression of the culture to mean that Yahweh is angry. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [In his anger] or [In his wrath]

David is speaking of Yahweh destroying his enemies as if Yahweh will literally **swallow** them and burn them up with **fire**. If these images communicate well in your language, please use them. If not, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will destroy them completely, as if swallowing them or consuming them with fire]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will completely destroy them as if he was swallowing them; yes, he will consume them as if he was burning them with fire]
The pronoun **You** refers to the king. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [You, God’s king, will destroy]

David is speaking of **their fruit** and **their seed** as if his enemies’ descendants were literal **fruit** and literal **seed** that could be destroyed. If this image does not communicate well in your language, you could express this as a comparison or use plain language. Alternate translation: [their descendants … and their offspring]

David is using **from among the sons of man** as a common expression of his culture to mean “from among humanity” or “from the human race.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from among the human race] or [from among humanity]

21.quote: כִּי־נָט֣וּ עָלֶ֣י⁠ךָ רָעָ֑ה חָֽשְׁב֥וּ מְ֝זִמָּ֗ה בַּל־יוּכָֽלוּ
21.text: The pronoun **they** refers to David’s enemies. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Though his enemies stretch out evil against you; his enemies plan a plot they will not be able]

Here David is speaking of the king’s enemies’ plans to harm him as if they would physically **stretch out evil** like a net or trap. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they plan to harm you] or [they devise evil schemes against you]

David is using the adjective **evil** as a noun to mean a certain kind of thing. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [they stretch out evil things against you]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [they plan a plot they will not be able to accomplish]

David is using **you will make them shoulder** as a common expression of his culture to mean “you will make them turn and flee.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you will make them turn their backs to you] or [you will put them to flight]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language as the ULT has done by supplying the phrase **your arrows**. Alternate translation: [on your bow strings you will set your arrows]
David is using **their faces** to represent all of them in the act of fleeing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [toward them]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **strength** and **power**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [Be exalted, Yahweh, because you are strong … and we will praise you because of how powerful you are]

The implication is that this singing and praising will happen after Yahweh shows his strength by defeating the enemies. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [then we will sing and we will praise your power]

The pronoun **we** refers to David and the people of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [we, your people, will sing and we will praise you because of your power]

22.text:
# Psalm 22 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 22 contains several different but related themes of lament, prayer, trust, and hope for the future. Verses 1–21 are a lament. See the Introduction to Psalms for more information about psalms of lament. Verses 22–31 praise Yahweh for his deliverance and kingship over the nations, and the worship he will receive in the future. Many Bible scholars consider Psalm 22 to be one of the “messianic psalms” because different New Testament authors quote parts of this psalm in relation to Jesus and because Jesus quotes the first line of verse 1 while on the cross. See the Introduction to Psalms for more information about the messianic psalms. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/christ]]; and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/crucify]]; and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/lament]])

1. An anguished call to God (1–2)
2. An affirmation of God’s holiness and past deliverance of the Israelites (3–5)
3. David describes his situation (6–18)
4. A prayer for help (19–21)
5. Yahweh’s deliverance of David results in Yahweh being praised (22–26)
6. People from all parts of the world, all people groups, and rich and poor people will turn to Yahweh and worship him as king (27–29)
7. Future generations will praise Yahweh and will be told about his saving acts (30–31)

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

David is using this possessive form to mean salvation that would come to him or rescue that he would receive. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [from saving me] or [from rescuing me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from saving me] or [from helping me]

David is using this possessive form to mean words that express his groaning or words spoken while groaning. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [far from my groaning words] or [far from the words I speak while groaning]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [I call to you by day, but you do not answer, and I call to you in the night]

By **there is no silence for me**, David means that he cannot rest or find peace because he is crying out to God throughout the night. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and I cannot rest] or [and I find no peace]

Here the phrase **the praises of Israel** could (1) be using the word **praises** to represent the Tabernacle where the Israelite people offered God their praises. Alternate translation: [sitting in the praises of us Israelite people, that we give to you in your Tabernacle] or [sitting in your Tabernacle] (2) mean that Yahweh is the object of Israel’s praises. Alternate translation: [sitting as the object of the praises of Israel] or [ruling as the one whom Israel praises]
David is using the term **fathers** to mean “ancestors.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [our forefathers]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [they trusted in you]

The expression **they were rescued** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form, as in the UST, or in another way that is natural in your language.

Here David is speaking of himself as if he were a **worm**. He means that other people treat him as if he were worthless and do not care if he lives or not. If it would be helpful, you could use a comparable expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [But I am treated as if I were a worthless worm and not a human]

By **a reproach of mankind**, David means that he has become someone whom all people mock and shame. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [someone whom people mock] or [an object of shame to everyone]

The expression **despised by the people** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and the people despise me]

Here, **the lip** represents the mouth or speech. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they open their mouths wide] or [they sneer at me]

To **shake the head** was a symbolic action by which people showed contempt or mockery. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [They shake the head in mockery] or [They shake the head to show contempt]

22.quote: גֹּ֣ל אֶל־יְהוָ֣ה יְפַלְּטֵ֑⁠הוּ יַ֝צִּילֵ֗⁠הוּ כִּ֘י חָ֥פֵֽץ בּֽ⁠וֹ
22.text: This is the beginning of what David’s enemies said. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of these enemies. Alternate translation: [saying “Roll to Yahweh; let him deliver him. Let him rescue him, since he delights in him]

The enemies are using **Roll to** as a common expression of their culture to mean “commit your cause to” or “trust completely in.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Commit yourself to Yahweh] or [Trust completely in Yahweh]

In this verse, the first and third occurrence of the pronoun **him**, and the pronoun **he** refer to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [let Yahweh deliver him. Let Yahweh rescue him, since Yahweh delights in him]

The terms **deliver** and **rescue** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [let him save him]

The implication is that God was the one who brought David safely into the world at birth. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [you are the one who brought me safely into the world]

By **making me trust upon the breasts of my mother**, David means that God caused him to trust in God even when he was a nursing infant dependent on his mother. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [causing me to trust in you while I nursed at my mother’s breasts]

Here David is speaking as if he were literally **cast** upon God. He means that he has been made to rely on God from the moment of his birth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You have been caring for me from the womb] or [I have depended on you from birth]

The expression **I was cast** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [You took me as your own] or [Yahweh, you took care of me]

Here David is giving a command, **do not be far away from me**, but he intends it to communicate a polite request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [I ask you, please do not be far away from me] or [Yahweh, please do not be far away from me]

The implication is that David’s enemies or persecutors are approaching to harm him. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [for my enemies are approaching] or [for those who want to harm me are near]

22.quote: סְ֭בָבוּ⁠נִי פָּרִ֣ים רַבִּ֑ים אַבִּירֵ֖י בָשָׁ֣ן כִּתְּרֽוּ⁠נִי
22.text: Here David is speaking of his enemies as if they were **bulls** that **surround** and **encircle** him. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [Many enemies surround me like bulls; strong ones like those of Bashan encircle me]

The phrase **strong ones of Bashan** gives further information about the **Many bulls**. (David refers to **Bashan** because it was known for its rich pasturelands and so the bulls there would have been well fed and strong.) David is not distinguishing these **strong ones** from other bulls that are not strong. Be sure that this is clear in your translation. Alternate translation: [the powerful bulls of Bashan] or [the mighty bulls of Bashan]

22.quote: פָּצ֣וּ עָלַ֣⁠י פִּי⁠הֶ֑ם אַ֝רְיֵ֗ה טֹרֵ֥ף וְ⁠שֹׁאֵֽג
22.text: Here David is speaking of his enemies as if they were **a tearing and roaring lion**. He means that they are fierce and dangerous and want to destroy him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They open their mouths against me, like a fierce, roaring lion that tears apart its prey]

The point of this comparison is that just as **water** flows away and cannot be gathered back, so David feels completely drained of strength and energy. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [I am completely drained of strength like spilled water]

The expression **I am poured out** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the same idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I pour out like water] or [I flow away like water]

David says **all of my bones are dislocated** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [and my whole body is in pain] or [and I feel like my bones are coming apart]

22.quote: הָיָ֣ה לִ֭בִּ⁠י כַּ⁠דּוֹנָ֑ג נָ֝מֵ֗ס בְּ⁠ת֣וֹךְ מֵעָֽ⁠י
22.text: The point of this comparison is that just as **wax** melts and becomes soft when heated, so David’s **heart** has become weak and soft from fear and distress. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [My heart has become weak like melted wax within me]

Here David is speaking of his **heart** as if it were **wax** that has melted. This image emphasizes how completely weak and helpless he feels in his distress. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [My courage has completely failed me] or [I feel completely weak inside]

**Wax** is a soft, fatty substance that becomes liquid when heated and is used to make candles. If your readers would not be familiar with what wax is, you could use the name of a similar substance that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [like soft fat] or [like something soft that melts]

David is making a comparison between his strength and **a shard**. The point of this comparison is that just as a shard is completely dried out and brittle, so is his strength. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [My strength is completely dried up] or [I have lost my strength]

A **shard** was a piece of broken pottery. If your readers would not be familiar with what a shard is, in your translation you could use the name of a comparable object that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [like a broken piece of pottery]

The expression **my tongue is being made to cling to my gums** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [my tongue clings to my gums] or [and you, Yahweh, allow me to suffer so that my tongue clings to my gums]

Here, **dust of death** represents the grave or dying. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you lay me in the grave] or [and you bring me to death]

Here David is speaking of his enemies as if they were **dogs** that hunt in packs. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [For my enemies have surrounded me like dogs]

The Hebrew text that the ULT is translated from reads **like the lion**. Other ancient manuscripts have a verb (instead of the noun translated as **like the lion**). At one point in the process of transmission, scribes may have mistakenly changed the last letter of the verb with the meaning “they have pierced” to a different (and similar looking) letter, resulting in the word **like the lion**. All the ancient versions of the Old Testament, as well as the early Jewish sources have verb forms instead of the noun form **like the lion**. The original text probably had the verb meaning “they have pierced” instead of the noun form translated **like the lion**. For this reason, you may wish to use the verb “they have pierced.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use whatever form it uses.

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [like the lion tears my hands and my feet] or [like the lion attacks my hands and my feet]

David is speaking of his enemies as if they were a **lion** tearing at his hands and feet. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [like a lion, they have mangled my hands and my feet]

David says **I can count all my bones** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [I am so thin and emaciated that I can count many of my bones] or [I am so thin and emaciated that people can see many of my bones]

The pronoun **They** refers to David’s enemies who have surrounded him (mentioned in the previous verses as “dogs” and “a company of ones doing evil”). It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [My enemies look and they stare at me]
The implication is that David’s enemies stare at him and gloat. You could include this information, as in the UST, if that would be helpful to your readers.

David uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between his enemies who surround and torment him and Yahweh whom he calls upon for help. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [However, you] or [As for you]

22.quote: וְ⁠אַתָּ֣ה יְ֭הוָה אַל־תִּרְחָ֑ק אֱ֝יָלוּתִ֗⁠י לְ⁠עֶזְרָ֥תִ⁠י חֽוּשָׁ⁠ה
22.text: The phrases **do not be far away** and **hurry to help me** are imperatives, but they communicate polite requests rather than a commands. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [But you, Yahweh, please do not be far away. My strength, please hurry to help me]

The implication is that David wants Yahweh to come near to help him in his time of great distress. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [come near to help me] or [be close and help me]

David is emphasizing a positive meaning by using a negative word, **not**, together with a mild expression that is the opposite of the intended meaning. If it would be helpful in your language, you could emphasize the positive meaning in a strong way. Alternate translation: [be very near] or [stay close to me]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please deliver]
Here, **sword** represents “death by violence.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from death]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [deliver my only one from the hand of]

David is using **my only one** as a common expression of his culture to mean “my precious life” or “my dear life.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my precious life]

Here, **hand** represents the power of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the power of]

Here David is speaking of his enemies as if they were **the dog**. This continues the imagery from verse 16 where enemies are described as dogs that have surrounded him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my enemies]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please save me]

Here David is speaking as if his enemies were dangerous animals with **mouths** and **horns** that could attack and kill him. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [from my enemies who attack me like lions and wild oxen]

Here David is using the term **name** to represent who God is or to refer to God’s reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I will declare how wonderful you are] or [I will proclaim your character]

David is using the term **brothers** to describe people who are descended from the same ancestor. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to my fellow Israelites]

22.quote: כָּל־זֶ֣רַע יַעֲקֹ֣ב כַּבְּד֑וּ⁠הוּ וְ⁠ג֥וּרוּ מִ֝מֶּ֗⁠נּוּ כָּל־זֶ֥רַע יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
22.text: Here David is speaking of the descendants of Jacob, who Yahweh later renamed Israel, as if they were his **seed**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the term “seed” in [18:50](../018/050.md). Alternate translation: [All of the descendants of Jacob, honor him, and be terrified from him, all of you descendants of Israel]

David is using the adjective **afflicted** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the affliction of the afflicted person]

David is emphasizing a positive meaning by using a negative word, **not**, together with a mild expression that is the opposite of the intended meaning. If it would be helpful in your language, you could emphasize the positive meaning in a strong way. Alternate translation: [and he has shown his face to him] or [and he has listened to him]

David is using **hidden his face from him** as a common expression of his culture to mean “ignored him” or “refused to help him.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he has not ignored him]

David assumes that readers will know that **he heard** means God heard his prayer and responded favorably to it. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [he responded]

Here, **with you** represents “because of what you have done.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Because you have delivered me I praise you]

David is using the adjective **poor** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [The poor ones] or [Poor people]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [will praise him]

David is using **May your heart live forever** as a common expression of his culture to mean “May you live a long and prosperous life.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May you live long and prosper] or [May you have a long and blessed life]

The word **your** is plural here because David is addressing all the worshipers, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction. Alternate translation: [your hearts]

Here the phrase, **the ends of the earth**, represents the people who live in the most distant places on earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [People everywhere on earth] or [People who live in the most distant places of the earth]

The implication is that the people **will remember** Yahweh and what he has done. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [will remember Yahweh]

David is speaking as if people had been walking in one direction but then **turned** to walk toward Yahweh. He means that they will start worshiping and obeying Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and worship Yahweh] or [and start following Yahweh]

The implication is that all people groups or clans throughout the world will worship Yahweh. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [all the people groups of the world]

To **bow down** was a symbolic action by which people showed reverence and submission. Sometimes it was also done as an act of worship. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation. Alternate translation: [and all the families of the nations will bow down in worship]
Here Yahweh’s **face** represents being in front of him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in your presence]

David assumes that readers will know that here the word **to** means “belongs” and that the word **kingdom** refers to Yahweh’s “reign.” You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [For the kingship belongs to Yahweh] or [For Yahweh reigns as king]

22.quote: אָכְל֬וּ וַ⁠יִּֽשְׁתַּחֲוּ֨וּ ׀ כָּֽל־דִּשְׁנֵי־אֶ֗רֶץ לְ⁠פָנָ֣י⁠ו יִ֭כְרְעוּ כָּל־יוֹרְדֵ֣י עָפָ֑ר
22.text: David is referring to all people by naming two extremes, **the fat of the earth** (the wealthy and prosperous who were well-fed and healthy), and **the ones going down to the dust** (the dying). If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [All people will eat and will bow down; to his face will kneel every person]
See how you translated this expression in [22:27](../022/027.md).

David is using the adjective **fat** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the fat ones of the earth] or [the fat people of the earth]

Here, **the fat of the earth** represents the wealthy and prosperous people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the wealthy people of the earth] or [the prosperous people of the earth]
Here Yahweh’s **face** represents being in front of him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in his presence]

To **kneel** was a symbolic action by which people showed reverence and submission to God. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [will kneel down in worship]

These two phrases **all of the ones going down to the dust** and **even his self he kept not alive** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [all of the ones going down to the dust, that is, those who cannot keep themselves alive]

Here the phrase **the ones going down to the dust** represents people who are dying or close to death. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the ones going down to the grave] or [the ones who are dying]

The implication is that they were not able to keep themselves alive. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [even him who could not keep himself alive]

In this verse, the words **his** and **he** are singular in form, but they refer to all humans as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural forms of “his” and “he” or plural forms that include both men and women since this phrase refers to all people, as no one is able to keep themselves from eventually dying. Alternate translation: [even those who could not keep themselves alive]
See how you translated the similar expression in [22:23](../022/023.md). Alternate translation: [Descendants will serve him]

The expression **it will be told** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people will tell of the Lord to the next generation] or [people will tell the next generation about the Lord’s works]

David assumes that readers will know that **it** refers to the great works of the Lord that have been described throughout the psalm. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the next generation will be told about the great works of the lord]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [to future generations] or [to the next generation]

22.quote: וְ⁠יַגִּ֣ידוּ צִדְקָת֑⁠וֹ לְ⁠עַ֥ם נ֝וֹלָ֗ד כִּ֣י עָשָֽׂה
22.text: David is using the adjective **his righteousness** as a noun to mean something that shows God is righteous. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [and will declare to a people who will be born, that because he is righteous, he has done it]

David assumes that readers will know **that he has done it** refers to God’s acts of deliverance and salvation described throughout the psalm. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [what he has done to save his people]

23.text:
# Psalm 23 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 23 is considered to be one of the “psalms of trust.” See the Introduction to Psalms for more information about the “psalms of trust.”

1. Yahweh depicted as a good and trustworthy shepherd (1–4)
2. Yahweh depicted as a good and generous banquet host (5)
3. David affirms his trust in Yahweh’s faithful goodness and love and asserts that he will dwell with him forever (6)

## Translation Issues in this Psalm

### Metaphor

Psalm 23:1–4 is an extended metaphor in which David speaks of Yahweh as if he were a shepherd, and of himself as a sheep. Psalm 23:5 is a metaphor in which David depicts himself as a guest at a banquet at which Yahweh is the host. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-exmetaphor]]; and [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

### Referring to Yahweh in the first person and second person

In verses 1–3 and 6, David writes about Yahweh in the second person. In verses 4–5, David addresses Yahweh directly, in the first person. Yahweh’s name is used in verses 1 and 6, but in verses 2–5 pronouns are used. Second person pronouns are used in verses 2–3 when referring to Yahweh, and David addresses God directly in verses 4–5 and therefore uses first person pronouns. If your language uses pronouns, use the appropriate pronouns in verses 2–5. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-123person]])

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a **shepherd** who cares for and protects his sheep. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison as in the UST.

David is emphasizing a positive meaning by using a negative word, **nothing**, together with a mild expression, **I will lack**, that is the opposite of the intended meaning. If it would be helpful in your language, you could emphasize the positive meaning in a strong way. Alternate translation: [I will have everything I need] or [I will be completely satisfied]

23.quote: בִּ⁠נְא֣וֹת דֶּ֭שֶׁא יַרְבִּיצֵ֑⁠נִי עַל־מֵ֖י מְנֻח֣וֹת יְנַהֲלֵֽ⁠נִי
23.text: David continues to draw an extended comparison between Yahweh’s care for him and a shepherd caring for his sheep. Here David compares Yahweh’s care for him to a shepherd who brings his sheep to **green pastures** and **waters of rest**. If it would be helpful for your readers, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [He gives me what I need to be satisfied and at peace, like a shepherd who provides pasture and water for his sheep]

By **He makes me lie down**, David means “He takes me to where I can lie down” or “He lets me lie down.” You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [He takes me to green pastures where I can lie down] or [He lets me lie down in green pastures]
Here the word **to** could mean: (1) “to” as in the ULT or (2) “alongside.” Alternate translation: [alongside]

The phrase **waters of rest** could refer to: (1) still or calm bodies of water. Alternate translation: [calm waters] or [quiet waters] or (2) the location of the water and refer to bodies of water that were located at resting places. Alternate translation: [waters at resting places]

23.quote: נַפְשִׁ֥⁠י יְשׁוֹבֵ֑ב יַֽנְחֵ֥⁠נִי בְ⁠מַעְגְּלֵי־צֶ֝֗דֶק לְמַ֣עַן שְׁמֽ⁠וֹ
23.text: Here David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a shepherd who **restores** his **soul** and **leads** him **in right paths**. David means that Yahweh renews his spiritual and emotional strength and guides him to live in a way that pleases Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He renews my spiritual strength. He guides me to live righteously for the sake of his name] or [He renews my spiritual strength. He guides me regarding how to live in the right way, for the sake of name]

Here David is using the term **my soul** to mean himself from the perspective of his spiritual or emotional existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [me] or [my spiritual strength]
Here David is using the term **name** to represent who God is or to refer to God’s reputation. Alternate translation: [for the sake of his reputation] or [to bring honor to himself]

23.quote: גַּ֤ם כִּֽי־אֵלֵ֨ךְ בְּ⁠גֵ֪יא צַלְמָ֡וֶת לֹא־אִ֘ירָ֤א רָ֗ע כִּי־אַתָּ֥ה עִמָּדִ֑⁠י שִׁבְטְ⁠ךָ֥ וּ֝⁠מִשְׁעַנְתֶּ֗⁠ךָ הֵ֣מָּה יְנַֽחֲמֻֽ⁠נִי
23.text: David continues to draw an extended comparison between his relationship with God and a shepherd caring for his sheep. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the comparison. Alternate translation: [Even though I experience great danger or hardship, I will not be afraid because you protect and guide me like a shepherd protects and guides his sheep with his rod and staff]

The phrase the ULT translates as **the valley of deep darkness** could be translated: (1) as the ULT does and refer to a dark valley or ravine. Alternate translation: [through a dark valley] or (2) as [the valley of the shadow of death.] Alternate translation: [through the valley of the shadow of death]

David is using the adjective **evil** as a noun to mean things that people might do to harm him. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [I will fear no harm] or [I will fear no danger]

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [because you are with me, I will fear no evil]

Here, **rod** and **staff** represent the shepherd’s protection and guidance. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your protection and guidance comfort me]

23.quote: תַּעֲרֹ֬ךְ לְ⁠פָנַ֨⁠י ׀ שֻׁלְחָ֗ן נֶ֥גֶד צֹרְרָ֑⁠י דִּשַּׁ֖נְתָּ בַ⁠שֶּׁ֥מֶן רֹ֝אשִׁ֗⁠י כּוֹסִ֥⁠י רְוָיָֽה
23.text: David is speaking of God’s care and provision as if God were a host preparing a feast for an honored guest. The image includes arranging a table with food, anointing the guest’s head with oil as a sign of welcome and honor, and filling the guest’s cup to overflowing. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [In front of my enemies you provide for me and honor me like a host preparing a feast for a special guest]

Here, **before my face** represents being in David’s presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in my presence] or [for me]

The implication is that God provides for and protects David even when he is surrounded by those who wish to harm him. This demonstrates God’s protection and care in dangerous situations. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [while my enemies watch] or [even though my enemies are present]

In that culture, putting scented **oil** on a guest’s head was a symbolic action by which a host showed honor to and welcomed a guest. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [you have honored me by anointing my head with oil] or [you have honored and welcomed me by anointing my head with oil]

In that culture, filling a guest’s wine cup to overflowing was a symbolic action by which a host showed that they intended to abundantly and liberally provide for their guest. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [you have blessed me abundantly]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **goodness** and **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will continually show me how good he is and how faithful he is to his covenant]

The Hebrew word that the ULT translates as **and I will dwell** could be: (1) a contracted form of the Hebrew word that means “dwell,” in which case it should be translated as the ULT does, or (2) a form of the Hebrew word meaning “return.” Alternate translation: [and I will return and go]

David is using the phrase **the house of Yahweh** to refer to Yahweh’s tabernacle (tent of meeting), where Yahweh was worshiped, as if it were a **house** in which Yahweh lived. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will dwell in the tabernacle of Yahweh] or [and I will dwell in Yahweh’s sanctuary]

The implication is that David will dwell with God for his entire life. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [for my whole life] or [as long as I live]

24.text:
# Psalm 24 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 24 is a “royal psalm.” See the Introduction to Psalms for more information about the royal psalms. It is also a psalm that the Israelites used for their processional liturgy as they entered Jerusalem or as they proceeded to Yahweh’s Tabernacle on Mount Zion in Jerusalem. In this psalm there is a clear call-and-response pattern in which someone leading the procession would have called out parts of this psalm (verse 3, 8a, 10a), and those in the procession would have responded and answered with the words in verses 4–6, 8b, and 10b–c.

Among Bible scholars there are different opinions about the exact setting and context of this psalm. Because this psalm begins with “of David” the events in this psalm are most likely during David’s lifetime.

1. Yahweh created the world and it belongs to him (1–2)
2. Yahweh requires righteousness to enter his presence and rewards and vindicates those who are righteous (3–6)
3. Yahweh is the glorious and victorious king (7–10)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Righteous people

“Clean hands” and a “pure heart” (being morally pure in action and in thought and intention) are required to enter Yahweh’s presence. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/righteous]])

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

### Rhetorical Questions

David uses three rhetorical questions in this psalm. Each rhetorical question forms a unit with a response. The three rhetorical questions are found in verses 3, 8, and 10. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

By **the seas** and **the rivers** David means the waters that existed before God created the dry land. David, and people in his culture, thought of the world as being founded and placed by God upon subterranean waters. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [For he has founded it upon the waters that were there before creation] or [For he has founded it upon the deep waters under the earth]

David is using questions to cause his readers to think deeply about who is qualified to approach God. David is not asking for information, but is emphasizing that only people who meet certain requirements can approach God. If you would not use rhetorical questions for this purpose in your language, you could translate his questions as statements or exclamations. Alternate translation: [Only certain people may ascend on the mountain of Yahweh! Only certain people may stand in his holy place!]

David assumes that readers will know that **the mountain of Yahweh** and **his holy place** refer to Mount Zion in Jerusalem, where the Tabernacle of Yahweh was located. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Who may ascend Mount Zion, the mountain of Yahweh? And who may stand in his holy Tabernacle]

David is using the possessive form to describe **one** that is characterized by **clean of hands and pure of heart**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [The one who has clean hands and a pure heart]

Here, **hands** represents a person’s actions or conduct. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The one whose actions are clean and whose heart is pure] or [The one who acts righteously]

In this image, the **heart** represents a person’s thoughts, feelings, and motives, and David speaks of them as if they could be physically clean. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and whose thoughts are pure] or [and whose motives are pure]

David is using the term **soul** to mean the entire person from the perspective of his spiritual and emotional existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [who has not devoted himself to falsehood] or [who has not set his heart to worship idols] or [who has not set his heart to worship what is false]
David assumes that readers will know that **what is false** refers to idol worship. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [to idols]

The implication is that the person described in the previous verse will receive these things from God. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [He will receive]

24.quote: יִשָּׂ֣א בְ֭רָכָה מֵ⁠אֵ֣ת יְהוָ֑ה וּ֝⁠צְדָקָ֗ה מֵ⁠אֱלֹהֵ֥י יִשְׁעֽ⁠וֹ
24.text: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **blessing** and **righteousness** and **salvation**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will bless him and act righteously toward him; this is what the God who saves him will do for him]

By **and righteousness from the God of his salvation**, David means that God will vindicate this type of person by declaring that they are righteous. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and vindication from the God of his salvation] or [and God will vindicate this person by declaring him righteous]
See how you translated the similar phrase “the God of my salvation” in [18:46](../018/046.md). Alternate translation: [from the God who saves him]

Here, **generation** represents a type or class of people who have something in common. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [This is the kind of people who seek him] or [These are the people who seek him]

These two phrases **the ones seeking him** and **the ones seeking your face** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [the ones seeking him, yes, the ones seeking your face]

Here, **face** represents God’s presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the ones seeking to be in your presence] or [the ones seeking to know you intimately]

Here, **Jacob** represents the people of Israel, who are the descendants of Jacob and who sought God’s favor like Jacob did. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel] or [the descendants of Jacob]

24.quote: שְׂא֤וּ שְׁעָרִ֨ים ׀ רָֽאשֵׁי⁠כֶ֗ם וְֽ֭⁠הִנָּשְׂאוּ פִּתְחֵ֣י עוֹלָ֑ם
24.text: These two phrases **Lift up your heads, you gates** and **be lifted up, you ancient doors** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Lift up your heads, you gates, yes, be lifted up, you ancient doors]

24.quote: שְׂא֤וּ שְׁעָרִ֨ים ׀ רָֽאשֵׁי⁠כֶ֗ם וְֽ֭⁠הִנָּשְׂאוּ פִּתְחֵ֣י עוֹלָ֑ם
24.text: Here the words **gates** and **doors** could refer to: (1) the gates leading into Yahweh’s Tabernacle on Mount Zion. Alternate translation: [Lift up your heads, you Tabernacle gates, and be lifted up, you ancient doors], or (2) the gates leading into the city of Jerusalem. Alternate translation: [Lift up your heads, you city gates, and be lifted up, you ancient doors]

24.quote: שְׂא֤וּ שְׁעָרִ֨ים ׀ רָֽאשֵׁי⁠כֶ֗ם וְֽ֭⁠הִנָּשְׂאוּ פִּתְחֵ֣י עוֹלָ֑ם
24.text: David is speaking of the **gates** and **doors** that led into Yahweh’s Tabernacle as if they were living things that could lift up their heads. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Open wide the Tabernacle gates]

The expression **be lifted up** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and lift yourselves up, you ancient doors] or [and you gatekeepers, lift up the ancient doors]

David is using this possessive form to mean a king who has glory or a king who is glorious. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [so that the glorious king may come in]
In a context such as this, your language might say “go” instead of **come**. Alternate translation: [so that the King of glory may go in]

David is using the question **Who is this King of glory?** to introduce and emphasize the answer that follows. This is not a request for information, but a way to draw attention to Yahweh’s identity and attributes. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could express this as a statement or an exclamation. Alternate translation: [This is the King of glory] or [I will tell you who this King of glory is]
