See how you translated the phrase **King of glory** in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [Who is this glorious king]

The terms **strong** and **mighty** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. [Yahweh, who is very strong] or [Yahweh, the powerful one]

24.quote: שְׂא֤וּ שְׁעָרִ֨ים ׀ רָֽאשֵׁי⁠כֶ֗ם וּ֭⁠שְׂאוּ פִּתְחֵ֣י עוֹלָ֑ם וְ֝⁠יָבֹא מֶ֣לֶךְ הַ⁠כָּבֽוֹד
24.text: Here David is speaking of **gates** and **doors** as if they were people who could lift up their heads. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Open wide, you gates, and open wide, you ancient doors, so that the King of glory may come in]
See how you translated the similar expression in [24:8](../024/008.md).

David is using this possessive form to mean that Yahweh is the commander of **armies** (the army of Israel and the army of heaven made of up angels). It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, the commander of armies] or [Yahweh, who commands armies]

25.text:
# Psalm 25 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 25 has several different themes or topics within it. These include assertions of trust in Yahweh, lament (complaints about the present situation), and asking Yahweh for forgiveness of sin, deliverance from enemies and troubles, and for guidance. This psalm is an acrostic poem which follows the order of the Hebrew alphabet, with a few exceptions.

1. David’s first prayer (1–7)
2. Yahweh guides humble people in the right way to live (8–9)
3. Yahweh’s positive response to “the ones keeping his covenant and his testimonies” (10)
4. David’s second prayer (11)
5. Ways that Yahweh blesses those who fear him (12–14)
6. David looks to Yahweh for deliverance from his enemies (15)
7. David’s third prayer (16–22)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Yahweh’s guidance of David described using the metaphor of “path” and a “way”

In verses 4–5, 8–9, and 12 David describes the right way to live, the way that Yahweh desires a person to live, as a “path” and a “way.” David asks Yahweh to lead him in this proper way of living (4–5), says that Yahweh will teach humble people his “way” (8–9), and will teach those who fear him the proper “way” (12). See the individual notes in these verses for specific translation guidance. (Because David uses a parallelism in verse 4, we know that the words “ways/way” and “paths” have the same meaning in these particular verses.)

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

### Singular forms of “you” and “your.”

In verses 1–7, 11, and 16–22 David prays directly to Yahweh. Each time David uses the pronouns “you” and “your” in these verses they are the singular form (in the language he wrote in, Hebrew) because they refer to Yahweh. If your language has singular and plural forms of the pronouns “you” and “your,” make sure you use the singular forms in these verses. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-yousingular]])

David is speaking of his earnest prayer and worship as if he were to physically **lift up** his **soul** to Yahweh. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I pour out my heart] or [I come in prayer]

David is not using the phrase **My God** to mean that he is the only one who worships Yahweh nor that he possesses or controls Yahweh. Rather he uses these words to emphasize that Yahweh is the God that he worships. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [You God, whom I worship,]

David is using imperative forms, **do not let me be ashamed** and **do not let my enemies exult over me**, but he intends these as polite requests rather than commands. If the imperative forms do not communicate polite requests in your language, you could use forms that communicate polite requests. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please do not let me have shame; please do not let my enemies exult over me]

By **the ones waiting on you**, David means people who trust in Yahweh and depend on him for help. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [all those who trust in you] or [all the ones trusting in you]

David is using a double negative that consists of **not** and the negative meaning contained in the word **ashamed**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [all the ones waiting on you, you will help]

These are imperatives, but they communicate polite requests rather than commands. If the imperative forms do not communicate polite requests for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates polite requests. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please make me know your ways, Yahweh; please teach me your paths]

These two phrases **Make me know your ways, Yahweh** and **teach me your paths** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Make me know your ways, Yahweh, yes, teach me your paths]

David is speaking of how to live as if it were **paths** that he could walk along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [teach me how to live according to your will] or [teach me how I should live]

David is speaking of God’s **truth** as if it were a path that he could walk on. He means that he wants God to help him live according to God’s truth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Help me to live according to your truth]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **truth**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Lead me according to what is true] or [Lead me by your true teaching]

The expressions **Lead me in your truth** and **teach me** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Instruct me in your truth]

The verbs **Lead** and **teach** are imperatives, but they communicate polite requests rather than commands. David is humbly asking God to guide and instruct him. If the imperative form does not communicate a polite request in your language, you could use a form that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please lead me in your truth and teach me]
See how you translated the similar phrase “the God of his salvation” in [24:5](../024/005.md).
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for you are the God who saves me]

The implication is that David waits on God to help him. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I continually wait for you to help me] or [I wait on you to help me all the day]

David assumes that readers will know that when he asks God to **Remember** his compassion and covenant faithfulness, he is asking God to act according to these qualities, not simply to recall them mentally. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Act according to your compassion, Yahweh, and your covenant faithfulness]

The word translated as **Remember** is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please remember your compassion, Yahweh, and your covenant faithfulness]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **compassion** and **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [Remember how you are compassionate, Yahweh, and how you are faithful to your covenant] or [Remember to be compassionate, Yahweh, and to be faithful to your covenant]

The implication is that God has always been compassionate and faithful, not just recently. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [you have acted with compassion and covenant faithfulness since ancient times]

David is using the possessive form to describe **sins** that were committed during his **youth**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the sins I committed when I was young] or [the sinful things I did in my youth]

By **according to your covenant faithfulness remember me**, David means that he wants God to remember him with favor and blessing, not with judgment. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [because of your covenant faithfulness remember me]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **transgressions**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [or the ways I have disobeyed your instructions]
See how you translated the phrase **covenant faithfulness** in the previous verse.

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **goodness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for the sake of the fact that you are good, Yahweh]

25.quote: טוֹב־וְ⁠יָשָׁ֥ר יְהוָ֑ה עַל־כֵּ֤ן יוֹרֶ֖ה חַטָּאִ֣ים בַּ⁠דָּֽרֶךְ
25.text: David is using **therefore** to introduce a result clause that explains what follows from Yahweh being good and upright. If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because Yahweh teaches sinners the way, he is good and upright]

David is using the adjective **sinful** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [sinners]

Here David is speaking of how a person lives as if that were a **way** or path for a person to walk on. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [how to live] or [how they should conduct their lives]

25.quote: יַדְרֵ֣ךְ עֲ֭נָוִים בַּ⁠מִּשְׁפָּ֑ט וִֽ⁠ילַמֵּ֖ד עֲנָוִ֣ים דַּרְכּֽ⁠וֹ
25.text: David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a guide who **leads** people along paths and a teacher who **teaches** them the right way to take. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He guides the humble to do what is just and he shows the humble how he wants them to live]

25.quote: יַדְרֵ֣ךְ עֲ֭נָוִים בַּ⁠מִּשְׁפָּ֑ט וִֽ⁠ילַמֵּ֖ד עֲנָוִ֣ים דַּרְכּֽ⁠וֹ
25.text: David is using the adjective **humble** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [He leads humble people in justice and he teaches humble people his way]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [He leads the humble to do what is just] or [He guides the humble to act justly]

Here David is speaking of Yahweh’s actions as if they were **paths** that a person could walk along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [All the actions of Yahweh are covenant love and faithfulness]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **covenant love** and **faithfulness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [All the paths of Yahweh are loving and faithful]
David is using the term **name** to represent who Yahweh is or to refer to Yahweh’s reputation. Alternate translation: [For your sake] or [For the sake of your reputation]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [forgive me for the wrong things I have done]

25.quote: מִי־זֶ֣ה הָ֭⁠אִישׁ יְרֵ֣א יְהוָ֑ה י֝וֹרֶ֗⁠נּוּ בְּ⁠דֶ֣רֶךְ יִבְחָֽר
25.text: David is using a rhetorical question **Who is the man fearing Yahweh?** to emphasize that God is faithful to guide those who revere him. If a speaker of your language would not use a question for this purpose, you could translate this as a statement or exclamation. Alternate translation: [The man who fears Yahweh—God will teach him in the way he is to choose]

25.quote: מִי־זֶ֣ה הָ֭⁠אִישׁ יְרֵ֣א יְהוָ֑ה י֝וֹרֶ֗⁠נּוּ בְּ⁠דֶ֣רֶךְ יִבְחָֽר
25.text: The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Who are the people fearing Yahweh? He will teach them in the way they are to choose]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [anyone]

David is speaking of how a person conducts themselves as if that were **the way** or path for a person to walk on. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He will teach him how he should live]

David is using the term **soul** to mean the entire person from the perspective of his spiritual and emotional existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [He]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **good**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [His soul will remain prosperous] or [He will continue to be blessed]

By **in good**, David means in prosperity or in favorable circumstances. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in prosperity]
See how you translated the term “seed” in [18:50](../018/050.md). Alternate translation: [and his descendants]

By **will inherit the earth**, David means that their descendants will continue to live in the promised land of Israel. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [will inherit the land]

David assumes that readers will know that **the secret of Yahweh** refers to an intimate relationship with Yahweh. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s intimate friendship is for the ones fearing him] or [Yahweh shares his plans with the ones fearing him]

25.quote: עֵינַ֣⁠י תָּ֭מִיד אֶל־יְהוָ֑ה כִּ֤י הֽוּא־יוֹצִ֖יא מֵ⁠רֶ֣שֶׁת רַגְלָֽ⁠י
25.text: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because Yahweh will make my feet go out of the net, my eyes are continually toward him]

Here, **eyes** represents David’s attention and focus. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am continually focused on Yahweh]

Here David is speaking as if his troubles were a **net** that had trapped his feet and as if Yahweh could free his feet from that trap. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he will free me from my troubles like feet freed from a net] or [he will rescue me from my troubles]

David is using imperative forms, but he is communicating polite requests rather than commands. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please turn toward me and be gracious to me]

Here David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a person who could physically **Turn toward** him to give attention. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Pay attention to me]

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because I am alone and afflicted, turn toward me and be gracious to me]

The expression **afflicted** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and experiencing hardship]

Here David is speaking of **The troubles of my heart** as if they were physical objects that could become larger in size. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [My heart is filled with many troubles] or [The troubles I feel have become very great]

Here David is speaking as if his distresses were a place from which he could be brought **out**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [free me from my distresses] or [rescue me from my distresses]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **distresses**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [deliver me from the things that distress me] or [bring me out of the circumstances that distress me]

By **See**, David means “take notice of” or “pay attention to.” David is asking God to consider his difficult situation with compassion. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Consider]

The words **See** and **forgive** are imperatives, but they communicate polite requests rather than commands. If the imperative form does not communicate polite requests in your language, you could use a form that communicates polite requests. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please see my affliction and my trouble, and please forgive all of my sins]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **affliction** and **trouble**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [See how I am afflicted and troubled, and forgive all of the sinful things that I have done]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please look at] or [Please consider]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **hatred**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and they violently hate me]

David is using this possessive form **hatred of violence** to mean violent hatred. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and with violent hatred] or [and with brutal hatred]

These are imperatives, but they communicate polite requests rather than commands. If the imperatives do not communicate polite requests for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates polite requests. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please guard my life and deliver me; please do not let me have shame]

By **Guard my life**, David means protect him from his enemies who want to harm or kill him. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Protect my life]
See how you translated the phrase **for I take refuge in you** in [16:1](../016/001.md).

The terms **integrity** and **uprightness** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [May complete righteousness]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **integrity** and **uprightness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [May my honest and upright character preserve me] or [May I be preserved because I am honest and do what is right]

Here David speaks of **integrity and uprightness** as if they were people who could **preserve** or protect him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May my integrity and uprightness be the means by which you preserve me]

See how you translated the phrases “the ones waiting on you” in [25:3](../025/003.md) and “on you I wait” in [25:5](../025/005.md) where the words “waiting” and “wait” are used with the same meaning as the word **wait** in this verse.

The word **redeem** is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please redeem]

Here, **Israel** represents the Israelite people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [us Israelite people from all our troubles]

26.text:
# Psalm 26 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

1. David asks Yahweh to give him justice because of his righteous lifestyle (1–6a)
2. David vows to thank Yahweh and recount all his wondrous deeds (6b–7)
3. David proclaims that he loves to be in Yahweh’s presence in the Tabernacle (8)
4. David asks Yahweh not to punish him with the wicked (9–10)
5. David vows to live with integrity and asks Yahweh to redeem him and be gracious to him as a result (11)
6. David’s closing words (12)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Praise

The psalmist delights in praising God and doing good deeds. It is striking how this psalm uses the first person pronoun. This is an individual psalm of petition. Each of the four petitions are accompanied with various claims. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/good]])

By **Vindicate me**, David means that he wants God to prove to others that he is innocent of wrongdoing. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Prove that I am righteous] or [Show others that I am innocent]

Here David is using an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please vindicate me]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **integrity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for I have done what is right] or [for I have lived uprightly]

Here David is speaking of his manner of living and conducting himself as if it were a path he **walked**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for I have lived with integrity] or [for I have acted with integrity]

David is using imperatives to make polite requests rather than to give commands. If the imperatives do not communicate polite requests in your language, you could use a form that communicates a polite request. Alternate translation: [Please examine me, Yahweh, and test me; please try]

These two phrases, **Examine me** and **test me**, mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, examine and test me]
See how you translated the similar phrase “The righteous God examines hearts and kidneys” in [7:9](../007/009.md). Alternate translation: [try my motives and my thoughts]

David is using **before my eyes** as a common expression of his culture to mean “constantly in my thoughts” or “always in my awareness.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am always mindful of your covenant faithfulness] or [I constantly remember your covenant faithfulness]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [For the way you are faithful to your covenant]

David is speaking of living according to God’s truth as if it were a path he could **walk about** on. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I live according to your truth]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **truth**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in what is true]

Here, **sit** represents associating with or spending time with people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I do not associate with men of falsehood]

The phrase **men of falsehood** refers to people who are characterized by dishonesty, deception, or lies. David is describing those who habitually speak or act falsely. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [deceitful people] or [dishonest men]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **falsehood**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [lying men] or [men who lie]

The implication is that these people are concealing their evil intentions or dishonest behavior. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and I will not go with those who hide their evil deeds] or [and I will not go with those who hide their evil deeds and intentions]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **evil**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the ones who do evil things] or [the ones who act wickedly]
See how you translated the similar phrase “I do not sit with” in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [and I will not associate with]
See how you translated the phrase “the wicked” in [1:1](../001/001.md).

Washing hands **in innocence** was a symbolic action by which David showed that he had not done anything wrong. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [I demonstrate my innocence by washing my hands]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **innocence**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [as an innocent person] or [because I am innocent]

The expression **to cause to be heard** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [to proclaim] or [to make known]

David is speaking of the tabernacle of Yahweh as if it were a **house**, which Yahweh makes his **habitation** or dwelling place. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your tabernacle] or [the tabernacle where you are present in a special way]

David is using this possessive form, **habitation of your house**, to mean the place where Yahweh has made his special **habitation** (dwelling place). It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the house where you dwell]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please do not gather]

26.quote: אַל־תֶּאֱסֹ֣ף עִם־חַטָּאִ֣ים נַפְשִׁ֑⁠י וְ⁠עִם־אַנְשֵׁ֖י דָמִ֣ים חַיָּֽ⁠י
26.text: David assumes that readers will know that **gather** refers to God gathering wicked people to judge them. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Do not cause me to die and be judged along with the sinful, nor let me perish in judgment with men of blood] or [Do not take me away to be judged along with the sinful, nor let me perish in judgment with men of blood]
Here David is using the term **my soul** to mean himself, his very life. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [me]

David is using the adjective **sinful** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [sinful people]

David is using the possessive form to describe **men** that are characterized by violence and bloodshed. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [violent men] or [murderers]

Here, **hands** represents what these evil men do (their actions) or plan to do. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who plan an evil scheme]

The phrase **their right hand is full of bribes** could mean: (1) that these wicked men are in positions of authority and they accept bribes and make unjust decisions or rulings as a result. Alternate translation: [and their right hand is full of bribes which they have accepted] or (2) that these evil men give bribes to those in positions of authority in order to influence them to make wrong and unjust decisions. Alternate translation: [and they give bribes] or [and they pervert justice by giving bribes]
See how you translated the similar phrase “for I have walked in my integrity” in verse 1.

In this context, David is using imperative forms to make polite requests to God rather than to give commands. The words **redeem me and be gracious to me** are requests for God’s help and mercy. If the imperative forms do not communicate polite requests in your language, use a form that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please redeem me and be gracious to me]

Here David is speaking as if his **foot stands on level ground**. He means that he is in a stable and secure position because he has lived righteously. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am secure because I have lived righteously]

David assumes that readers will know that **assemblies** refers to gatherings of God’s people for worship. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in the gatherings of God’s people I will bless Yahweh]

27.text:
# Psalm 27 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 27 is considered to be one of the “psalms of trust.” See the Introduction to Psalms for more information about the psalms of trust.

1. David declares his confidence in God (1–6)
2. David prays for help (7–12)
3. David affirms his faith in God and calls on others to patiently endure (13–14)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Yahweh’s help

Because of God’s help, he has nothing to fear, no matter what happens. The psalmist shows his confidence in God; he also asks God for help.

David is speaking of **Yahweh** as if he were **light** that illuminates, guides, helps, and encourages him. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is like light to me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the one who saves me]

David is using two rhetorical questions, **whom will I fear** and **whom will I dread**, to emphasize that he does not fear anyone because Yahweh protects him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements. Alternate translation: [there is no one I fear … there is no one I dread] or [there is no one I need to fear … there is no one I need to dread]

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a physical location, a **refuge**, that could provide safety and protection. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [Yahweh protects my life like a place of refuge] or [Yahweh is like a safe place for me where I can go to be safe]

David is speaking of his enemies’ attacks as if they were wild animals trying **to devour** his **flesh**. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could state the meaning plainly or express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [to destroy me completely] or [to attack me like wild beasts]

The terms **enemies** and **the ones being hostile to me** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [my fierce enemies]

Here, **they stumbled and fell** represents being defeated. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they were defeated] or [they failed in their attack]

27.quote: אִם־תַּחֲנֶ֬ה עָלַ֨⁠י ׀ מַחֲנֶה֮ לֹֽא־יִירָ֪א לִ֫בִּ֥⁠י אִם־תָּק֣וּם עָ֭לַ⁠י מִלְחָמָ֑ה בְּ֝⁠זֹ֗את אֲנִ֣י בוֹטֵֽחַ
27.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Though an army encamps against me and war arises against me, my heart will not fear but will be confident]

In this verse, the word **army** is singular in form, but it refers to all soldiers as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning of “army” in another way. Alternate translation: [Though enemy troops encamp against me]

Here David is speaking of **my heart** as if it were the part of him that experiences fear. In your language, it may be more natural to say that David himself will not fear. Alternate translation: [I will not fear]

David is using **war arises against me** as a common expression of his culture to mean “when enemies attack me” or “when I am attacked in battle.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [though enemies attack me] or [though I am under attack]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [One thing I have asked from Yahweh, yes, this is what I will seek]

Here David is speaking of the object of his desire (dwelling in God’s tabernacle) as if it were something he could physically pursue or chase after. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that I long for] or [that I desire]
See how you translated the similar phrase “and I will dwell in the house of Yahweh for length of days” in [23:6](../023/006.md).

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were actually looking at the physical **beauty** of Yahweh with his eyes. He means that he wants to experience and appreciate Yahweh’s wonderful character and presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to experience Yahweh’s wonderful presence] or [to appreciate Yahweh’s glorious character]

David is speaking of the **temple** of Yahweh as if it were a **house** in which he lived. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in his tabernacle]

27.quote: כִּ֤י יִצְפְּנֵ֨⁠נִי ׀ בְּ⁠סֻכֹּ⁠ה֮ בְּ⁠י֪וֹם רָ֫עָ֥ה יַ֭סְתִּרֵ⁠נִי בְּ⁠סֵ֣תֶר אָהֳל֑⁠וֹ
27.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [For in the day of trouble he will hide me in his hut, yes, he will conceal me in his tent]

David assumes that readers will know that **his hut** and **his tent** refer to God’s tabernacle. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [he will hide me in his tabernacle; he will hide me in the hiding-place of his sacred tent] or [he will hide me in his tabernacle; he will hide me in the hiding-place of his tabernacle]

Here David is referring to Yahweh’s tabernacle as a **hut** and **tent** and is speaking as if Yahweh was actually hiding him from his enemies there. David means that by his being in Yahweh’s tabernacle, Yahweh will protect him from his enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he will protect me and keep me safe in his tabernacle]

David is using the term **day** to refer to a specific time of distress or difficulty. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when I have trouble] or [in times of trouble]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **trouble**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when I am troubled]

David is speaking of Yahweh protecting him and keeping him safe as if Yahweh would literally lift him up and place him on a high **rock** where he would be safe from the attacks of his enemies. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison as in the UST.

David is using **my head will be lifted up** as a common expression of his culture to mean “I will be exalted” or “I will triumph.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And now I will be exalted above]
See how you translated the phrase “his tent” in the previous verse where it is used with the same meaning. Alternate translation: [in his tabernacle]

By **sacrifices of a shout of joy**, David means sacrifices that he offers while shouting joyfully to God. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and I will joyfully shout as I sacrifice in his tent]

Here David is using the imperative forms **Hear**, **be gracious to me**, and **answer me**, but he intends to communicate polite requests rather than commands. If these imperative forms do not communicate polite requests for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates polite requests. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please hear, Yahweh, my voice when I cry out, and please be gracious to me, and answer me]

Here, **voice** represents David’s prayer or request. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my request when I cry out]

27.quote: לְ⁠ךָ֤ ׀ אָמַ֣ר לִ֭בִּ⁠י בַּקְּשׁ֣וּ פָנָ֑⁠י אֶת־פָּנֶ֖י⁠ךָ יְהוָ֣ה אֲבַקֵּֽשׁ
27.text: David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [When you said, “Seek my face,” my heart said to you, “Your face, Yahweh, I will seek.”]

The Hebrew verb the ULT translates as **Seek** is plural here because Yahweh is addressing his people or people in general who are willing to seek and trust him, and not just David. So use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Here the **heart** represents where a person’s thoughts and desires exist. David is speaking of his inner self as if it were his physical heart that could speak. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [My inner self] or [I]

Here, **face** represents being in the presence of God and also God’s favor and intervention. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [my presence and help … Your presence and help]

These are imperatives, but they communicate polite requests rather than commands. If the imperatives do not communicate polite requests for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates polite requests. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please do not hide your face from me; please do not turn your servant away in anger … Please do not abandon me or leave me]

David is using **hide your face** as a common expression of his culture to mean “reject me” or “turn away from me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Do not reject me] or [Do not turn away from me]

The terms **abandon** and **leave** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Do not forsake me]
See how you translated the phrase “God of my salvation” in [18:46](../018/046.md) where it occurs with the same meaning. Alternate translation: [the God who saves me]

Because David does not explain in what way his father and mother have left him, it is best not to add any additional explanatory information to your translation to clarify how or why his parents might have left him. It is suggested that you simply translate this phrase as it is. It may be that David’s father and mother had died by this time in his life and had not intentionally left him.

27.quote: ה֤וֹרֵ֥⁠נִי יְהוָ֗ה דַּ֫רְכֶּ֥⁠ךָ וּ֭⁠נְחֵ⁠נִי בְּ⁠אֹ֣רַח מִישׁ֑וֹר
27.text: Here David uses imperative forms, but he is making polite requests rather than giving commands. If the imperative form does not communicate a polite request in your language, then use a form that communicates polite requests. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please teach me your way, Yahweh, and please lead me on a level path]
See how you translated the similar phrase “make me know your ways” in [25:4](../025/004.md).

Here David is speaking as if Yahweh would **lead** him **on a level path**. He is picturing his life as if it were a journey and asking Yahweh to guide him along a smooth, safe route. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly as in the UST.

David is using **because of my enemies** to give the reason for the result that **lead me on a level path** describes. If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [and because of my enemies, lead me on a level path]

27.quote: אַֽל־תִּ֭תְּנֵ⁠נִי בְּ⁠נֶ֣פֶשׁ צָרָ֑⁠י כִּ֥י קָֽמוּ־בִ֥⁠י עֵֽדֵי־שֶׁ֝֗קֶר וִ⁠יפֵ֥חַ חָמָֽס
27.text: David is giving the reason why God should not give him up to his enemies. If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second and third phrases give the reasons for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because false witnesses have risen against me, and a witness of violence, do not give me up to the desire of my adversaries]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. David is asking God not to hand him over to his enemies. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please do not give me up]

David is using **give me up to the desire of** as a common expression of his culture to mean “deliver me over to” or “hand me over to.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Do not deliver me over to the desire of my adversaries]

David assumes that readers will know that **the desire of my adversaries** refers to the harmful things that his enemies want to do to him. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Do not deliver me over to my adversaries so that they can do the harmful things they desire to do to me]

David is using **have risen against me** as a common expression of his culture to mean “have taken action to oppose me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [have opposed me]

The Hebrew word that the ULT translates as **a witness of** could be either: (1) a noun that means “a testifier” or “a witness.” Alternate translation: [and a testifier of violence] or [and a violent testifier who is violent] or (2) an adjective that means “one breathing out” or “one puffing out.” Alternate translation: [and one who breathes out violence]

David is using the possessive form to describe a **witness** that is characterized by **violence**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and a violent witness] or [and a witness who speaks violently]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **violence**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and a witness who plans violent things] or [and a witness who acts violently]

27.quote: לׅׄוּלֵׅׄ֗אׅׄ הֶ֭אֱמַנְתִּי לִ⁠רְא֥וֹת בְּֽ⁠טוּב־יְהוָ֗ה בְּ⁠אֶ֣רֶץ חַיִּֽים
27.text: David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Unless I had believed that I would look on the goodness of Yahweh in the land of the living, I would have grown discouraged] or [I am certain that I will see the goodness of Yahweh in the land of the living]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **goodness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Unless I had believed that I would see Yahweh do good things for me]

David is using **in the land of the living** as a common expression of his culture to mean “while I am still alive” or “during my lifetime.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [while I am still alive] or [during my lifetime]
See how you translated the similar expressions in [25:3](../025/003.md), [25:5](../025/005.md), and [25:21](../025/021.md).

27.quote: קַוֵּ֗ה אֶל־יְה֫וָ֥ה חֲ֭זַק וְ⁠יַאֲמֵ֣ץ לִבֶּ֑⁠ךָ וְ֝⁠קַוֵּ֗ה אֶל־יְהוָֽה
27.text: The words that the ULT translates as **wait**, **your**, and **be courageous** are all singular here. David is either speaking to himself or to some other individual, or he is speaking collectively to each individual person experiencing discouragement or fear who might hear or read this psalm. So use the singular forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

The terms **Be strong** and **let your heart be courageous** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Be very courageous]

Here David is speaking of **heart** as if it were something that could be courageous. The heart represents a person’s inner being or emotions. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and be courageous within yourself] or [and be inwardly courageous]

28.text:
# Psalm 28 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 28 begins as a lament psalm and then transitions into praise, thanksgiving, and affirmation of his trust in Yahweh.

1. David prays for deliverance (1–2)
2. David asks God to judge the wicked (3–5)
3. David praises God and affirms his goodness (6–9)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Trust

David trusted God completely and God rescued him. This is similar to Psalm 7 and 17 because it is an individual psalm of lament. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/lament]])

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

### Text variant in 28:8

In 28:8 some Hebrew manuscripts contain the Hebrew word that could be literally translated as “for them” while other Hebrew manuscripts contain the word that could be literally translated as “for his people.” The Hebrew manuscript that the ULT follows contains the word that reads “for them” but the ULT translates this word as “for his people” because this word is being considered an alternate spelling of the word “for his people.” For the reasoning behind this decision, see the portion on “The Text of v. 8a” in this video produced by the “Psalms: Layer by Layer” project titled “Psalm 28: Exegetical Issues.” See the video at ([https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHlm_UCsX-A&t=1037s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHlm_UCsX-A&t=1037s))

“The Psalms: Layer by Layer” videos are part of the “Psalms: Layer by Layer” project, which is run by Scriptura (formerly Cambridge Digital Bible Research).

To visit the Psalms: Layer by Layer website go to https://psalms.scriptura.org. These videos are used under [CC BY](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
See how you translated this phrase in [18:2](../018/002.md) where it is used with the same meaning.

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please do not be deaf to me]

David is using **do not be deaf to me** as a common expression of his culture to mean “do not ignore me” or “do not refuse to answer me” (and here it specifically refers to Yahweh answering his prayers for help). If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [do not ignore my prayers]

Here, **lest, if you are deaf to me, then I will be together with the ones going down to the pit** introduces a possible condition and its consequence. David is saying that if Yahweh does not respond to his prayer, then he will die. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [If you are silent, then I will join those who go down to the grave]

David is using **the pit** as a common expression of his culture to mean “the grave” or “death.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the grave]

David is using an imperative form, but **Hear** communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please hear]

By **Hear**, David means pay attention to and respond favorably to his request. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Pay attention to]

Here, **voice** represents what David is saying by using his voice. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Hear the words of my pleas]

Here, **when I lift up my hands** was a symbolic action by which David showed that he was appealing to God for help. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [when I raise my hands in prayer]

By **your inner sanctuary of holiness**, David means the inner sanctuary of the Tabernacle where God dwelled with the Israelites in a special way. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the holy inner sanctuary in your Tabernacle]

Here David uses the possessive form **inner sanctuary of holiness** to mean the inner sanctuary of the Tabernacle that was characterized by holiness. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the most holy place where you dwell] or [your inner sanctuary that is very holy]

Here **Do not drag me away** is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please do not drag me away with the wicked]

Here David is speaking of God taking his life as if God were someone who might **drag** him away by force in order to kill him or judge and punish him. See how you translated the similar phrase “Do not gather my soul with the sinful” in [26:9](../026/009.md). If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Do not bring me away and punish me with the wicked] or [Do not let me die with the wicked]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [the wicked, that is, with the workers of iniquity] or [the wicked people who do evil deeds]

David is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase as in the UST.

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and do not drag me away with the workers of iniquity]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the ones who do wicked things, the ones speaking of peaceful things with their neighbors]

David is using the adjective **evil** as a noun to mean evil thoughts or evil intentions. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [while evil thoughts are in their hearts]

Here David is speaking of **evil** as if it were an object that could be located inside people’s **hearts**. The “heart” represents the center of a person’s thoughts and intentions. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [while they intend to do evil] or [while they have evil intentions]

David is using the imperative form **Give** to make a polite request to God rather than to give a command. If the imperative form would not communicate a polite request in your language, you could use a different form that would communicate a polite request. [Please give them … please give to them … please return to them] or [I ask that you give them … I ask that you give to them … I ask that you return to them]

28.quote: תֶּן־לָ⁠הֶ֣ם כְּ⁠פָעֳלָ⁠ם֮ וּ⁠כְ⁠רֹ֪עַ מַֽעַלְלֵ֫י⁠הֶ֥ם כְּ⁠מַעֲשֵׂ֣ה יְ֭דֵי⁠הֶם תֵּ֣ן לָ⁠הֶ֑ם
28.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Give to them according to their work, yes, according to the evil of their deeds and the work of their hands]

By **their work**, David means the evil deeds and wicked actions of his enemies that he mentioned in the previous verse. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [according to their evil actions] or [according to what their wicked deeds deserve]

Here, **work of their hands** represents the actions that they have done. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [according to their actions] or [according to what their evil deeds deserve]

By **return to them their recompense**, David means give them the punishment they deserve. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [give them the punishment they deserve]

The implication is that the wicked do not pay attention to or consider what God has done. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [they do not pay attention to the works of Yahweh] or [they do not consider the works of Yahweh]

28.quote: לֹ֤א יָבִ֡ינוּ אֶל־פְּעֻלֹּ֣ת יְ֭הוָה וְ⁠אֶל־מַעֲשֵׂ֣ה יָדָ֑י⁠ו
28.text: These two phrases **the works of Yahweh** and **the action of his hands** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [they do not give heed to what Yahweh has done]

David is speaking of God’s judgment as if it is a building **he will tear** down and **not build** up. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he will destroy them and not restore them]

The expression **Blessed be** is a passive verbal form. The psalmist is expressing his desire to praise Yahweh. If it would be unnatural to use that form for this purpose, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I bless Yahweh] or [I will praise Yahweh]

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because he has heard the voice of my pleas, blessed be Yahweh]

Here, **voice** represents the words that David spoke. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he has heard my pleas]
See how translated the similar phrase “Yahweh, my strength” in [18:1](../018/001.md).
See how you translated the phrase “my shield” in [18:2](../018/002.md) where it is used with the same meaning.

Here David is speaking of his **heart** as if it were a person who **trusts** and **exults**. The heart represents the center of his emotions and will. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I trust in him with all my being … therefore I greatly rejoice]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Yahweh makes his people strong] or [Yahweh strengthens his people]

Some ancient manuscripts read “for them” and some read **for his people**. For an explanation of the reason why the ULT reads **for his people** see the section in the Psalm 28 Introduction titled “Text variant in 28:8.”

Here David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a **refuge** that provides protection and safety. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [and he protects his anointed one like a refuge] or [and he is the one who protects his anointed one]

David is using this possessive form **refuge of help** to mean a place of protection and safety. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and a helpful refuge] or [and a refuge that provides help]

David is using the adjective **anointed** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [for his anointed king]

28.quote: הוֹשִׁ֤יעָ⁠ה ׀ אֶת־עַמֶּ֗⁠ךָ וּ⁠בָרֵ֥ךְ אֶת־נַחֲלָתֶ֑⁠ךָ וּֽ⁠רְעֵ֥⁠ם וְ֝⁠נַשְּׂאֵ֗⁠ם עַד־הָ⁠עוֹלָֽם
28.text: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, please save your people and bless your inheritance; please be their shepherd and carry them forever]

Here David is speaking of God’s people as if they were his **inheritance**. David is picturing God’s people as something valuable that belongs to God, like property or possessions that are passed down in a family. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your own people]

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a **shepherd** who would guide and protect his people as a shepherd would guide and protect his flock. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [guide and protect them like a shepherd does his flock]

David assumes that readers will know that **unto the eternity** means for all time without end. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [for all eternity]

29.text:
# Psalm 29 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 29 is a “psalm of praise.” It tells how Yahweh rules all nature.

1. A call to worship (1–2)
2. Declarations of God’s voice over creation depict natural phenomena (3–9)
3. The Lord sovereignty (10–11)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### The Cultural and Religious Background of verses 3–10

The cultural and religious background of verses 3–10 is the worship of the false gods of the nations who lived around the Israelites. Verses 3–10 are a firm declaration of Yahweh’s power and rule over the entire universe and an implicit denunciation of putting trust in false gods such as the Canaanite god Baal.

Because David does not state the historical and religious background information explicitly in verses 3–10, it is recommended that you not include this information either but if you are using footnotes or chapter introductions in your translation, you may wish to include some of the background information there if it would help your readers.

### Yahweh’s power

God is powerful. All he has to do is to speak in order to control nature.

For an overview of Psalm 29 and help understanding some of the important exegetical and poetical issues in this psalm, see the Psalms: Layer by Layer videos below. These videos are part of the Psalms: Layer by Layer project, which is run by Scriptura (formerly Cambridge Digital Bible Research).
See their overview video ([https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_aoWN_yFa0E](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_aoWN_yFa0E)) and top three exegetical issues in Psalm 29 video ([https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nnL109G57mg&t=452s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nnL109G57mg&t=452s)) and their top three poetic features of Psalm 29 video ([https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ygoKm9HWKQU&t=181s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ygoKm9HWKQU&t=181s)) on YouTube.

To visit the Psalms: Layer by Layer website go to https://psalms.scriptura.org. These videos are used under [CC BY](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)

29.quote: הָב֣וּ לַֽ֭⁠יהוָה בְּנֵ֣י אֵלִ֑ים הָב֥וּ לַ֝⁠יהוָ֗ה כָּב֥וֹד וָ⁠עֹֽז
29.text: David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Ascribe these things to Yahweh, sons of God, ascribe to Yahweh glory and strength]

David assumes that readers will know that **sons of God** refers to angels or heavenly beings. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [you angels]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **glory** and **strength**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [acknowledge that Yahweh is glorious and strong] or [praise Yahweh because he is glorious and strong]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Declare that Yahweh is glorious because of his name] or [Praise Yahweh for how glorious his name is]

David is using this possessive form **the glory of his name** to mean the glory that his name deserves. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the glory his name deserves]

David is using the term **name** to represent who Yahweh is or to refer to Yahweh’s reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the glory due to Yahweh] or [the glory Yahweh’s reputation deserves]

Here, **bow down** was a symbolic action by which people showed reverence and worship to Yahweh. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [bow down in worship to Yahweh]

The phrase **adornment of holiness** refers to the garments the Levitical priests wore while serving in Yahweh’s tabernacle. David is using the possessive form to describe **adornment** that is characterized by **holiness** because of the purpose for which it was made. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this purpose, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in holy adornment] or [in adornment that is holy]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **holiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in holy clothing]
See the Psalm 29 Introduction for more information regarding the historical and religious background of verses 3–10.

The phrase **The voice of Yahweh** could: (1) refer to the actual voice of Yahweh or (2) this phrase could mean “The thunder of Yahweh” since this phrase sometimes had that meaning in Hebrew. Alternate translation: [The thunder of Yahweh is over the waters]
By **the waters**, David means the sea and here he probably specifically means the Mediterranean Sea. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use plain language as in the UST.

29.quote: ק֥וֹל יְהוָ֗ה עַל־הַ֫⁠מָּ֥יִם & יְ֝הוָ֗ה עַל־מַ֥יִם רַבִּֽים
29.text: David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. Alternate translation: [the glorious God speaks with a voice like thunder] or [the God of glory speaks powerfully], or (2) that Yahweh sends thunder. David is using the possessive form to describe **the God** who is characterized by **glory**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the glorious God]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **power** and **majesty**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [The voice of Yahweh is powerful; the voice of Yahweh is majestic]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. David is emphasizing the awesome nature of Yahweh’s voice by using both **power** and **majesty** to describe it. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [The voice of Yahweh is very powerful]
Here, **voice** represents the sound of Yahweh’s voice. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly as in the UST.

29.quote: ק֣וֹל יְ֭הוָה שֹׁבֵ֣ר אֲרָזִ֑ים וַ⁠יְשַׁבֵּ֥ר יְ֝הוָ֗ה אֶת־אַרְזֵ֥י הַ⁠לְּבָנֽוֹן

29.quote: וַ⁠יַּרְקִידֵ֥⁠ם כְּמוֹ־עֵ֑גֶל לְבָנ֥וֹן וְ֝⁠שִׂרְיֹ֗ן כְּמ֣וֹ בֶן־רְאֵמִֽים
