By **flames of fire**, David means lightning. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [with lightning] or [with flashes of lightning]
Here, **voice** represents the sound of Yahweh’s voice. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly as in the UST.
The word **Kadesh** is the name of a place.
Here, **voice** represents the sound of Yahweh’s voice. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly as in the UST.

Here David is speaking of Yahweh’s tabernacle in Jerusalem as if it were a **temple**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and in his tabernacle]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **Glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [How glorious Yahweh is]

29.quote: יְ֭הוָה לַ⁠מַּבּ֣וּל יָשָׁ֑ב וַ⁠יֵּ֥שֶׁב יְ֝הוָ֗ה מֶ֣לֶךְ לְ⁠עוֹלָֽם
29.text: Here both times the word **sits** is used, it represents “ruling” as king since at that time kings sat on a throne from which they ruled, made decisions, and gave commands. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language as in the UST.
David assumes that readers will know that **sits** means “rules as king.” You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh sits enthroned … as]

The phrase **the flood** could refer to: (1) the water that is above the sky as in the UST, or (2) the great flood recorded in Genesis chapters 6–9 that God sent during the time of Noah. Alternate translation: [over the flood that covered the earth] or [over the Flood]

29.quote: יְֽהוָ֗ה עֹ֭ז לְ⁠עַמּ֣⁠וֹ יִתֵּ֑ן יְהוָ֓ה ׀ יְבָרֵ֖ךְ אֶת־עַמּ֣⁠וֹ בַ⁠שָּׁלֽוֹם
29.text: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **strength** and **peace**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will make his people strong; Yahweh will bless his people so that they live peacefully]

30.text:
# Psalm 30 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 30 is a psalm of praise and thanksgiving to God. The psalmist was so sick that he was near death, but God healed him.

1. Call to praise and testimony (1–5)
2. The crisis remembered (6–7)
3. The prayer for help (8–10)
4. The deliverance and vow of praise (11–12)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### The possibility of David dying from sickness

In this psalm David recounts how he was close to death and then pleaded with God. David asked God to heal him and told God that if he died, it would not benefit God, since dead people do not praise God in this life. God healed David with the result that David sings praises to God and thanks him.

30.quote: אֲרוֹמִמְ⁠ךָ֣ יְ֭הוָה כִּ֣י דִלִּיתָ֑⁠נִי וְ⁠לֹא־שִׂמַּ֖חְתָּ אֹיְבַ֣⁠י לִֽ⁠י
30.text: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because you have drawn me up and have not let the ones being hostile to me rejoice over me, I will extol you, Yahweh] or [Yahweh, because you have drawn me up and have not let the ones being hostile to me rejoice over me, I will extol you]
If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put **Yahweh** at the beginning of this verse. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, I will extol you for you have drawn me up]

Here David is speaking of God’s help as if God had physically raised him up from a lower place to a higher place. The other times the word the ULT translates as **have drawn me up** occurs in the Old Testament, it refers to drawing water out of a well with a bucket. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you have helped me] or [you have delivered me]

David is not using the phrase **my God** to mean that he is the only one who worships Yahweh nor that he possesses or controls Yahweh, but rather to emphasize that Yahweh is the God that he worships. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [You, Yahweh, God whom I worship,]

The word **Sheol** refers to the place of the dead, where dead people go, and the word **pit** also refers to the grave. These two phrases, **you have brought up my soul from Sheol** and **you have kept me alive from the ones going down to the pit**, mean basically the same thing. The second phrase emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [you have brought up my soul from Sheol, yes, you have kept me alive from the ones going down to the pit]
David is using one part of himself, his **soul**, to mean all of him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you have brought me up]

David assumes that readers will know that **the pit** refers to the grave or death. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [from the ones going down to death] or [from the ones going down to the grave]

30.quote: זַמְּר֣וּ לַ⁠יהוָ֣ה חֲסִידָ֑י⁠ו וְ֝⁠הוֹד֗וּ לְ⁠זֵ֣כֶר קָדְשֽׁ⁠וֹ׃ כִּ֤י רֶ֨גַע ׀ בְּ⁠אַפּ⁠וֹ֮ חַיִּ֪ים בִּ⁠רְצ֫וֹנ֥⁠וֹ בָּ֭⁠עֶרֶב יָלִ֥ין בֶּ֗כִי וְ⁠לַ⁠בֹּ֥קֶר רִנָּֽה
30.text: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of verse 4 and the first half of verse 5, since the first half of verse 5 gives the reason for the result that verse 4 describes. Alternate translation: [Because his anger is {for} a moment, {but} his favor is {for} a lifetime, sing praise to Yahweh, {you} his faithful ones, and give thanks at the remembrance of his holiness]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the ideas of **remembrance** and **holiness**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Here the phrase **his holiness** refers to Yahweh’s holy character and the actions that he had done in the past as a result of his holy character. Alternate translation: [when you remember how holy he is and the great things that he has done as a result]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **anger** and **favor**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [For he is angry only for a moment, but he shows kindness for a lifetime]

David is using **a moment** as a common expression of the culture to mean “a very short time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his anger is for a brief time] or [his anger is only temporary]

David is speaking of **weeping** and **rejoicing** as if they were living things that could come to a place. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [In the evening people may weep, but in the morning people will rejoice]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **ease**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when my life was easy]

The expression **I will never be shaken** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [nothing will ever shake me] or [I will always remain secure]

David is speaking of himself as if he were an object that could not be**shaken** (physically moved or disturbed). He means that he felt completely secure and believed nothing could threaten his stability or well-being. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will always be secure] or [nothing will ever threaten me]
See how you translated the word **favor** in [30:5](../030/005.md).

The phrase **you have made my mountain stand strong** could be: (1) David speaking of his security and strength as if they were **my mountain**. Alternate translation: [you have made me as secure as a mountain] or [you have given me great strength and security] (2) David using the phrase **my mountain** to refer to Mount Zion in which case David would be using Mount Zion to represent his rule as king which he would do from Mount Zion. Alternate translation: [you have made my reign secure] or [you have firmly established my rule]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [then you hid your face from me]

Here, **your face** represents Yahweh’s presence or attention (and consequently also some of the help or protection that would have come as a result). If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you withdrew your presence from me] or [you turned your attention away from me]
See how you translated the word **favor** in [30:5](../030/005.md).

30.quote: מַה־בֶּ֥צַע בְּ⁠דָמִ⁠י֮ בְּ⁠רִדְתִּ֪⁠י אֶ֫ל־שָׁ֥חַת הֲ⁠יוֹדְ⁠ךָ֥ עָפָ֑ר הֲ⁠יַגִּ֥יד אֲמִתֶּֽ⁠ךָ׃ שְׁמַע־יְהוָ֥ה וְ⁠חָנֵּ֑⁠נִי יְ֝הוָה הֱֽיֵה־עֹזֵ֥ר לִֽ⁠י
30.text: This is the beginning of what David said or prayed to Yahweh. The ULT indicates the beginning and end of David’s direct address of Yahweh with quotation marks and the UST introduces David’s words with the phrase “I said.” Consider natural ways of introducing direct quotations in your language. Alternate translation: [I prayed, “What profit is there…”]

30.quote: מַה־בֶּ֥צַע בְּ⁠דָמִ⁠י֮ בְּ⁠רִדְתִּ֪⁠י אֶ֫ל־שָׁ֥חַת הֲ⁠יוֹדְ⁠ךָ֥ עָפָ֑ר הֲ⁠יַגִּ֥יד אֲמִתֶּֽ⁠ךָ
30.text: David is using a question to emphasize that his death would not benefit God and to make the point that dead people cannot praise God. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for this purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or exclamations. Alternate translation: [There is no profit in my blood, in my descent to the pit. The dust will not praise you! It will not declare your faithfulness!]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. [What advantage is there in my death, yes, in my going down to the grave]
Here, **blood** represents “death.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in my death]

David assumes that readers will know that **the pit** refers to the dwelling place of the dead. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. (In [30:3](../030/003.md) David uses a different Hebrew word for “pit,” but there the word has the same meaning as it does here so you could see how you translated “pit” there.) Alternate translation: [to the place of the dead] or [to the abode of the dead]

Here, **dust** represents those who are dead. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Will those who are dead praise you]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way as in the UST.

Here, **Hear** represents “Listen and respond.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Listen to me and respond] or [Pay attention to me]

David is using imperative forms, but he is communicating polite requests rather than commands. If the imperative forms **Hear**, **be gracious to me**, and **be my helper** do not communicate polite requests in your language, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please hear, Yahweh, and please be gracious to me. Yahweh, please be my helper]

David assumes that readers will know **sackcloth** was a coarse material worn as a sign of mourning or distress. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [you have removed my mourning clothes and have clothed me with gladness]

Here, **gladness** represents clothing that was worn for joyous occasions that would express gladness. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [with celebratory clothes] or [with clothes worn to celebrate]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **gladness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and have covered me with clothes that show that I am glad] or [and have clothed me with celebratory clothes]

Here, **so that** marks **my glory may sing praise to you and not be silent** as the goal or purpose of “You have turned for me, my mourning into dancing; you have loosed my sackcloth and have clothed me with gladness” in the previous verse. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [for the purpose that] or [to the end that]

By **my glory**, David probably means some part of his inner being that represented where his honor was. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [my soul may sing praise to you] or [I may sing praise to you]

David is not using this possessive form **my God** to indicate that he possesses or controls Yahweh. Rather, David is using these words to indicate that Yahweh is the God whom he worships. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, the God I worship]

31.text:
# Psalm 31 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 31 is considered to be one of the “psalms of deliverance.” See the Introduction to Psalms for more information about the psalms of deliverance.

1. Declaration of trust (1–8)
2. Lament over suffering (9–13)
3. Affirmation of faith (14–18)
4. Praise and thanksgiving (19–22)
5. Final Exhortation (23–24)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Abandonment

Even though everyone deserted and despised the psalmist, God did not abandon him.

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

Here David is speaking as if Yahweh were actually a physical place of safety or shelter. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I trust in you, Yahweh, to keep me safe] or [I depend on you, Yahweh, to protect me]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please do not ever let me have shame; please deliver me in your righteousness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because you are righteous]

31.quote: הַטֵּ֤ה אֵלַ֨⁠י ׀ אָזְנְ⁠ךָ֮ מְהֵרָ֪ה הַצִּ֫ילֵ֥⁠נִי הֱיֵ֤ה לִ֨⁠י ׀ לְֽ⁠צוּר־מָ֭עוֹז
31.text: David is using imperative forms, but these communicate a polite request rather than commands. If the imperative form does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use forms in your language that communicate polite requests. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please incline your ear to me; please rescue me quickly; please be for me a rocky summit of refuge]

Here David is using the term **ear** to mean hearing or attention. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Listen and respond to me] or [Pay attention to me]

Here David is speaking as if Yahweh were actually a **rocky summit** used as a **refuge** and as if he were actually a place that had **strongholds** where he could hide and be safe from his enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [be for me like a rocky summit of refuge, and like a dwelling place of strongholds]

David is using these possessive forms, **a rocky summit of refuge** and **a dwelling place of strongholds**, to describe places that are characterized by providing refuge and strength. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive forms for this, you could express these ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [be for me a rocky summit that provides refuge, a stronghold in which to dwell]

Here David is speaking as if Yahweh were actually a large **rock** and a **stronghold** to which he could flee to be safe from his enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [you are like a rock that I can flee to for safety and like a stronghold in which I can be safe]
David is using the term **name** to refer to God’s reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language as in the UST.

The terms **lead** and **guide** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [direct me]

Here the Hebrew verbs that the ULT translates as **you lead me and guide me** could be: (1) expressing a general truth that has been part of David’s ongoing experience. If you decide this is the meaning, then you can translate the two verbs in this phrase in a similar way to the ULT. (2) expressing something that will happen in the future. Alternate translation: [you will lead me and guide me] or (3) a request that is a prayer to Yahweh. (This option is less likely since David does not use the imperative forms of these verbs as would be expected if these verbs were meant to be requests.) Alternate translation: [lead me and guide me] or [please lead me and guide me]

The implication is that David wants God to lead and guide him so that his enemies do not harm him. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [you lead me and guide me so that my enemies do not harm me]

Here David is speaking as if his enemies’ plans to harm him were a **net** that they had hidden to trap him. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Rescue me from being harmed by the plans that they have secretly made to harm me] or [Rescue me from the ambush that they have secretly set for me]

Here the Hebrew verb that the ULT translates as **You will pull me** could be: (1) expressing something that will happen in the future as in the ULT or (2) a request that is a prayer to Yahweh. (This option is less likely since David does not use the imperative form of this verb as would be expected if this was a request.) Alternate translation: [Please pull me] or [Pull me]

Here David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a **refuge**, a physical place of safety and protection from danger. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you are my protector] or [you keep me safe]

Here, **hand** represents God’s power, control and care. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Into your care] or [Into your control]

David is using the term **spirit** to mean his enlivening spirit that causes him to be physically alive. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I commit myself]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [God who is faithful to me]

Here, **the ones keeping** represents those who worship idols. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I hate those who worship]

David is using the possessive form to describe **idols** that are characterized by **worthlessness**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [worthless idols]

The terms **be glad** and **rejoice** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [I will rejoice greatly]

31.quote: בְּ⁠חַ֫סְדֶּ֥⁠ךָ אֲשֶׁ֣ר רָ֭אִיתָ אֶת־עָנְיִ֑⁠י יָ֝דַ֗עְתָּ בְּ⁠צָר֥וֹת נַפְשִֽׁ⁠י
31.text: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **covenant faithfulness** and **affliction**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [because you are faithful to your covenant, for you have seen how I have suffered; you have known how my soul is troubled]

David is using the term **soul** to mean the entire person from the perspective of his spiritual and emotional existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the troubles I have experienced] or [my inner distress]

Here, **hand** represents the power or control of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [into the power of the ones being hostile to me] or [under the control of the ones being hostile to me]

Here David is speaking of being rescued as if he had been squeezed into a narrow, dangerous space with no way to escape and God enabled him to escape into an **open space**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you have set me free from danger] or [you have rescued me from my desperate situation]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please be gracious to me]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **grief**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for I am distressed, because of my grieving my eye has wasted away]

David says **my eye has wasted away from grief** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [I cry so much that my eyes feel like they are wasting away] or [I am crying so much that my eyes hurt]

Here, **grief** represents crying. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from crying] or [because I cry so much]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [my soul and my body have wasted away from grief]

David is referring to all of himself by naming two major components, **my soul** and **my body**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all of me] or [my whole being]

31.quote: כִּ֤י כָל֪וּ בְ⁠יָג֡וֹן חַיַּ⁠י֮ וּ⁠שְׁנוֹתַ֪⁠י בַּ⁠אֲנָ֫חָ֥ה כָּשַׁ֣ל בַּ⁠עֲוֺנִ֣⁠י כֹחִ֑⁠י וַ⁠עֲצָמַ֥⁠י עָשֵֽׁשׁוּ
31.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [For my life comes to an end with sorrow, yes, my years with groaning; my strength fails from my iniquity, indeed, my bones waste away]

By **For my life has come to an end with sorrow**, David means that his life is being consumed or shortened by grief and distress. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [For my life is being consumed by sorrow] or [For sorrow is shortening my life]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **sorrow**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [sorrowfully]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because I have sinned] or [because of the wrong things I have done]

David is using one part of his body, his **bones**, to represent his entire physical being as it deteriorates. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and my entire body wastes away]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **reproach**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [I have become someone whom people reproach] or [I have become someone whom people despise]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and I have become especially a reproach to my neighbors, and I have become a dread to the ones knowing me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **dread**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the ones knowing me are afraid of me]

The expression **I have been forgotten** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [People have forgotten me]

David is making a comparison between himself and **a dead man out of mind**. The point of this comparison is that just as a dead man is completely forgotten by people, so David feels that he has been completely forgotten. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [I have been completely forgotten, just as people forget about the dead]

David is using **out of mind** as a common expression of the culture to mean “completely forgotten.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [is completely forgotten] or [whom people have completely forgotten]

Here David is comparing himself to **a broken vessel** using the word **like**. The point of this comparison is that just as a broken vessel is useless and discarded, so David feels useless and discarded by others. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [I am useless like a broken vessel] or [I am discarded like a broken vessel]

31.quote: כִּ֤י שָׁמַ֨עְתִּי ׀ דִּבַּ֥ת רַבִּים֮ מָג֪וֹר מִ⁠סָּ֫בִ֥יב
31.text: David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [For I hear the whispering of many, and there is terror on every side]

31.quote: כִּ֤י שָׁמַ֨עְתִּי ׀ דִּבַּ֥ת רַבִּים֮ מָג֪וֹר מִ⁠סָּ֫בִ֥יב
31.text: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **terror on every side** with the information about **the whispering of many**. Alternate translation: [For I hear the whispering of many and there is terror on every side]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **terror**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [terrifying things on every side]

David is using **they plan to take my life** as a common expression of the culture to mean “they plan to kill me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they plan to murder me]

David uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between his distressing circumstances and his trust in Yahweh. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [However, I] or [Yet I]

David is not using this possessive form **my God** to indicate that he possesses or controls Yahweh. Rather he is using these words to indicate that Yahweh is the God whom he worships. If it would help your readers, you could indicate this explicitly as in the UST.

Here, **hand** represents the power or control of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [My times are in your control; rescue me from the power of]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please rescue me]

David assumes that readers will know that **My times** refers to the events and circumstances of his life, including its duration. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [The events of my life] or [My life and circumstances]

The terms **the ones being hostile to me** and **the ones pursuing me** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [my relentless enemies]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please make your face shine upon your servant; save me]

David is using **Make your face shine on** as a common expression of the culture to mean “show favor to” or “be gracious to.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Show favor to] or [Be gracious to]

David is speaking of himself in the third person as **your servant** to show humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a humble form in the first person. Alternate translation: [me, your servant]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because you are faithful to your covenant]

By using **let**, the psalmist is expressing what he thinks should happen. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [the wicked should have shame; they should be silent in Sheol]

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because I have called upon you, Yahweh, do not let me have shame]

David is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are wicked]

David assumes that readers will know that **Sheol** is the place of the dead. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [let them be silent in the place of the dead]

The expression **Let lying lips be silenced** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [May God silence lying lips] or [May lying lips become silent]

Here, **lying lips** represents people who tell lies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those who lie]

David is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase as in the UST.

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **pride** and **contempt**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [proudly and contemptuously] or [in a proud and contemptuous manner]

The terms **pride** and **contempt** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [with great arrogance]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **goodness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [How incredibly good you are] or [How abundant are the good things you do]

David is speaking of God’s goodness as if it were something physical that God had **stored up** like treasure in a storehouse. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express the meaning plainly as in the UST.
See how you translated the similar phrase “I take refuge” in [31:1](../031/001.md).

The psalmist is using **sons of man** as a common expression of his culture to mean “human beings.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all people]

31.quote: תַּסְתִּירֵ֤⁠ם ׀ בְּ⁠סֵ֥תֶר פָּנֶי⁠ךָ֮ מֵֽ⁠רֻכְסֵ֫י אִ֥ישׁ תִּצְפְּנֵ֥⁠ם בְּ⁠סֻכָּ֗ה מֵ⁠רִ֥יב לְשֹׁנֽוֹת
31.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [You hide them in the safety of your presence, protecting them from those who plot against them and from cruel words]

Here David is speaking of **the hiding-place of your presence** as if it were a physical shelter where Yahweh could hide people from danger. David means that Yahweh protects people by his divine presence and power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You protect them by your presence from the plots of man]

David is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language as in the UST.

Here David is speaking of God’s protection and help as if it were a physical **shelter** in which God would hide righteous people from the accusatory words of evil people. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [you protect them from people who attack with their words as if you were hiding them in a shelter]

Here, **tongues** represents people speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from people who accuse them with their words] or [from verbal attacks]

The expression **Blessed be** is a passive verbal form. The psalmist is expressing his desire to praise Yahweh. If it would be unnatural to use that form for this purpose, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I bless Yahweh] or [Let me praise Yahweh]

31.quote: בָּר֥וּךְ יְהוָ֑ה כִּ֥י הִפְלִ֘יא חַסְדּ֥⁠וֹ לִ֝֗⁠י בְּ⁠עִ֣יר מָצֽוֹר
31.text: David is giving the reason that Yahweh should be blessed after stating that he should be blessed. If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because he has shown marvelously his covenant faithfulness to me in a besieged city, blessed be Yahweh]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [all the ways he is faithful to his covenant]

The expression **in a besieged city** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is his enemies. Alternate translation: [in a city that my enemies had surrounded]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **alarm**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when I was alarmed]

Here, **eyes** represents God’s attention or awareness. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I am cut off from your attention] or [you are no longer watching over me]

David uses the words **But indeed** here to indicate a contrast between his fearful thoughts and God’s actual response. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [However] or [Yet]
Here, **voice** represents the pleas themselves. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language as in the UST.

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [when I cried out to you, you heard the voice of my pleas]

David is using the adjective **faithful** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [faithful people] or [those who are faithful]

David is using **Be firm** as a common expression of the culture to mean “be strong.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly as in the UST.
The word **your** is plural here because David is speaking to **all the ones waiting for Yahweh**. Use the plural form in your language if your language marks that distinction.
Here the **heart** represents where a person’s thoughts and feelings exist. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly as in the UST.

David assumes that readers will know that here **waiting** refers to waiting on Yahweh to help them. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [all the ones waiting for Yahweh to help you]

32.text:
# Psalm 32 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 32 is a psalm about confession of sin. It is considered to be one of the “penitential” psalms. See the Introduction to Psalms for more information about the penitential psalms. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/confess]]; and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/sin]])

1. The type of person who God says is blessed (1–2)
2. The results of concealing one’s sin (3–4)
3. David confesses his sin to Yahweh and Yahweh forgives his sin (5)
4. David gives reasons for confessing one’s sin to Yahweh (6–7)
5. David instructs his readers (8–9)
6. Conclusion (10–11)

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a “maskil.” See the discussion of that term in the introduction to Psalms.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Confession of sin

This Psalm tells of the sorrow of unconfessed sin. It also tells of the blessing of confession and of receiving God’s forgiveness. It is a blessing when God forgives sin. Trouble comes when sin is hidden and not confessed. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/bless]]; and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/forgive]])

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

### Who is speaking in verses 8–9?

Among Bible scholars there are several different views regarding who is speaking in verses 8 and 9. Some Bible scholars think that it is David speaking, and others think that it is God speaking. Because these verses do not explicitly state who is speaking, you should not indicate who the speaker is in your translation.

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a **maskil**. Since the meaning of this word is not certain, you may wish to represent it in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language. See the discussion of that term in the Introduction to Psalms.

David is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling, what constitutes true happiness from God’s perspective. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Oh, how happy is]

The expressions **transgression is lifted up** and **covered from sin** are passive verbal forms. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [the one whose transgression God has lifted up, the one whose sin God has covered]

These two phrases **the one whose transgression is lifted up** and **the one covered from sin** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and it would be good to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation rather than combining them. It may be helpful in your language to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [the one whose transgression is lifted up, that is, whose sin is covered]

Here the phrase **the one covered from sin** means “the one whose sin is covered.” David is speaking of sin as if it were an object that could be covered. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one whose sin Yahweh takes away]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **transgression** and **sin**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [the one forgiven of the wrong things that one has done, forgiven for how that one has disobeyed you]

Here, **one whose transgression is lifted up** and **one covered from sin** represent people in general, not specific individuals. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [anyone whose transgression is lifted up, and anyone who is covered from sin]

David is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling, what constitutes true happiness from God’s perspective. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Oh, how happy is]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [any person]

32.quote: לֹ֤א יַחְשֹׁ֬ב & עָוֺ֑ן וְ⁠אֵ֖ין בְּ⁠רוּח֣⁠וֹ רְמִיָּה
32.text: The abstract nouns **guilt** and **deceit** express the ideas of being guilty and being deceitful. If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **guilt** and **deceit**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [does not reckon what he has done wrong and who is not deceitful] or [does not reckon to him what he is guilty of and who does not act deceitfully]

Here, **spirit** represents the person’s inner being or character. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and in whom there is no]

By **kept silent**, David means that he did not confess his sin to God. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [When I kept silent about my sin]

Here David is speaking as if his **bones** were actually deteriorating. He means that his body was becoming weak, and he felt as if he was ill. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my vitality was depleted]

The word translated as **through** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [which caused me to scream]

David says **through my screaming** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [through my groaning]

David is using **all of the day** as a common expression of his culture to mean “continually.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [continually]

The psalmist is referring to all of time by naming two major components, **day** and **night**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [continually] or [all of the time]

David is using **your hand was heavy upon me** as a common expression of his culture to mean that God afflicted or disciplined him severely. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly as in the UST.

The expression **My vitality was changed** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [God drained my strength] or [My strength dried up]

The point of this comparison is that just as the **heat of summer** is extremely intense and withering, so David’s **vitality was changed** due to his unconfessed sin. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [My strength was completely drained like something withered by intense heat]

These two phrases **My sin I acknowledged to you** and **my guilt I did not cover** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and it would be good to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation rather than combining them. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases with a word other than **and** in order to show that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [I confessed my sin to you—I did not hide my guilt]
See how you translated the similar expression in [32:1](../032/001.md).
See how you translated the similar expression in [32:2](../032/002.md).

Here David is speaking of **sin** and **guilt** as if they were something that could be covered. He means that he did not try to hide his sin from God. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and my guilt I did not refuse to confess]
See how you translated the similar expression in [32:1](../032/001.md).
See how you translated the similar expression in [32:1](../032/001.md). Alternate translation: [and you forgave the guilt of my sin] or [and you took away the guilt of my sin]

Here David is speaking of God’s forgiveness as if it were something that could be found. He also indicates that there is a favorable time in which to seek forgiveness. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [while there is an opportunity]

32.quote: לְ֭⁠שֵׁטֶף מַ֣יִם רַבִּ֑ים אֵ֝לָ֗י⁠ו לֹ֣א יַגִּֽיעוּ
32.text: Here David is speaking as if troubles were actually a **flood of great waters** that could overwhelm someone. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when great trouble comes, God will rescue those who trust in him]

Here, **him** represents godly people in general, not a specific person. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [to them]

Here David is speaking as if Yahweh were actually a **hiding place**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You are the one who causes me to be safe] or [You are like a hiding place for me]

These two phrases **You are a hiding place for me** and **you preserve me from distress** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and it would be good to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation rather than combining them. Alternate translation: [You protect me as my refuge; you keep me safe from trouble]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **distress**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from things that cause me trouble] or [when others afflict me]

The implication is that there will be people around the writer who will be shouting joyfully about how God has rescued him. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [You surround me with people who are celebrating your deliverance with joyful shouts]

The terms **instruct** and **teach** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [I will carefully teach you]

Here the psalmist is speaking of how a person lives as if that were a **way** or path that the person was walking along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in how you should live] or [regarding how you should live]

Yahweh is using **with my eye upon you** as a common expression of the culture to mean “watching you closely and guiding you directly.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will teach you directly] or [I will look you in the eyes when I counsel you]

The point of this comparison is that just as a **horse** and a **mule** are stubborn animals that must be controlled with bits and bridles, so are people who refuse to follow God’s guidance. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Do not be stubborn like horses and mules that must be controlled with bits and bridles]

The psalmist assumes that his readers will know that here **ornament** refers to “trappings”, functional pieces that are used on horses and mules in order to guide and restrain them. The implication of the phrase **ornament of him to curb** is that a horse or mule must be controlled by these trappings in order to guide and restrain (or **curb**) them. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [his trappings must restrain him]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [ornament of him to curb his behavior]

A **bit and bridle** is a kind of harness that fits around a horse’s head and includes a metal bar that goes in its mouth. If your readers would not be familiar with what a bit and bridle are, you could use more general terms as in the UST or explain them in a footnote.

The psalmist is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [Many are the pains of those who do wicked things]

The psalmist is speaking of **covenant faithfulness** as if it were a living thing that could protect someone by surrounding them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s faithful love will protect him] or [Yahweh’s covenant faithfulness will protect him]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [who acts faithfully toward him according to his covenant]
See how you translated the phrase **the righteous** in [1:5](../001/005.md). Alternate translation: [righteous people] or [people who do what is right]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **joy**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and shout joyfully]

Here the **heart** represents where a person’s thoughts and motives exist. The phrase **upright of heart** describes people whose thoughts and motives are morally straight and righteous. Alternate translation: [all who think and act righteously] or [all who live with pure motives]

33.text:
# Psalm 33 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 33 is a “psalm of praise” telling how great God is.

1. Call the righteous to praise Yahweh (1–3)
2. Yahweh’s word and works are true and powerful (4–9)
3. Yahweh rules over nations and cares for his people (10–19)
4. Trust and hope in Yahweh’s steadfast love (20–22)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Yahweh’s power

Yahweh is the creator and also the God of his people, Israel. Whatever he plans works out. He alone provides safety in battle.

This is an imperative, but it communicates an exhortation rather than a command. The psalmist is encouraging **righteous ones** to worship. If the imperative does not communicate an exhortation for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates an exhortation or invitation. Alternate translation: [You righteous ones should shout for joy in Yahweh]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **joy**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Rejoice]

The psalmist is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [righteous people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **praise**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for the upright should praise him]

The psalmist is using the adjective **upright** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [for those who are upright]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [give thanks with a lyre of ten strings]

A **lyre of ten** is a kind of musical instrument that has ten strings stretched across it and is plucked to produce sound. If your readers would not be familiar with what a lyre is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [a ten-stringed instrument]

This is an imperative, but it communicates an exhortation rather than a command. The psalmist is encouraging the people to worship. If the imperative does not communicate an exhortation for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates an exhortation or invitation. Alternate translation: [You should sing to him a new song]

Here the psalmist is speaking of Yahweh always speaking truth as if his **word** were standing straight or **upright**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [For Yahweh always does what he says that he will do]
Here, **the word of Yahweh** represents what Yahweh said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what Yahweh has said]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [is done in a faithful way] or [is done faithfully]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **Yahweh** who is characterized by **covenant faithfulness**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Yahweh faithfully keeps his covenant throughout the earth]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **righteousness** and **justice**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [what is righteous and fair]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [all the ways Yahweh is faithful to his covenant]

Here the psalmist is speaking of the **covenant faithfulness of Yahweh** as if it were something that could **fill** the earth like water fills a container. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [extends to everyone on the earth]

The psalmist is using **the earth** to represent everyone who lives on the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [everyone on the earth]

33.quote: בִּ⁠דְבַ֣ר יְ֭הוָה שָׁמַ֣יִם נַעֲשׂ֑וּ וּ⁠בְ⁠ר֥וּחַ פִּ֝֗י⁠ו כָּל־צְבָאָֽ⁠ם
33.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Another approach would be to combine them and express the emphasis in another way. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [By the word of Yahweh the heavens were made, indeed, by the breath of his mouth, all of their host] or [By his command, Yahweh made the heavens and everything in them]

Here, **the word of Yahweh** represents the command that Yahweh spoke using words. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [By the command of Yahweh] or [When Yahweh commanded]

The expression **were made** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language.
