Here, **the breath of his mouth** represents Yahweh speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and by what Yahweh spoke]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [all the stars in the heavens were made]

The point of this comparison is that just as a **heap** is a large mass piled together, so Yahweh gathered the sea waters together into a large mass. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [all piled together into one place]

Here the psalmist is speaking of the deep waters of the ocean as if they were goods that could be placed in **storehouses**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he contains the deep waters within their boundaries]

33.quote: יִֽירְא֣וּ מֵ֭⁠יְהוָה כָּל־הָ⁠אָ֑רֶץ מִמֶּ֥⁠נּוּ יָ֝ג֗וּרוּ כָּל־יֹשְׁבֵ֥י תֵבֵֽל
33.text: The psalmist is saying what he wants the people to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [all of the earth should fear Yahweh; all of the dwellers of the world should be in dread of him]

33.quote: יִֽירְא֣וּ מֵ֭⁠יְהוָה כָּל־הָ⁠אָ֑רֶץ מִמֶּ֥⁠נּוּ יָ֝ג֗וּרוּ כָּל־יֹשְׁבֵ֥י תֵבֵֽל
33.text: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [everyone in the world should fear Yahweh, indeed, they should all be in dread of him]
The psalmist is using the term **earth** to mean all the people who live on the earth. Alternate translation: [all the people of the earth]

33.quote: כִּ֤י ה֣וּא אָמַ֣ר וַ⁠יֶּ֑הִי הֽוּא־צִ֝וָּ֗ה וַֽ⁠יַּעֲמֹֽד
33.text: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [Because when he spoke, everything he commanded came into existence]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verbs translated as **he spoke** and **he commanded** already include this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that it was Yahweh and no other who spoke and commanded. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [he himself spoke and it came to be; he himself commanded, and it stood]
The pronoun **it** refers to the earth. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the earth came to be; he, he commanded, and the earth stood]

By **it stood**, the psalmist means that the earth came into existence or was created. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and it was created]

33.quote: יְֽהוָ֗ה הֵפִ֥יר עֲצַת־גּוֹיִ֑ם הֵ֝נִ֗יא מַחְשְׁב֥וֹת עַמִּֽים
33.text: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [Yahweh prevents the people of the nations from accomplishing what they plan]

Here, **nations** represents either the people of the nations or the leaders of the nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the counsel of the leaders of other nations]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **counsel**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what nations decide to do]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **plans**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what the people plan to do]

33.quote: עֲצַ֣ת יְ֭הוָה לְ⁠עוֹלָ֣ם תַּעֲמֹ֑ד מַחְשְׁב֥וֹת לִ֝בּ֗⁠וֹ לְ⁠דֹ֣ר וָ⁠דֹֽר
33.text: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [What Yahweh has decided will endure through all generations]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **counsel**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Everything Yahweh decides]

Here the psalmist is speaking of Yahweh’s **counsel** as if it were something that could **stand** in the sense of remaining upright and stable for all time. He means that Yahweh’s decisions are permanent and will never change or fail. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [endures forever]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [the plans of his heart stand to generation and generation]

Here the **heart** represents where Yahweh’s thoughts and intentions exist. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his intentions]

The psalmist is using **to generation and generation** as a common expression of his culture to mean “forever” or “through all time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [through all generations] or [forever]

The psalmist is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of joy or blessing. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Oh, how happy is the nation] or [How blessed will be the nation]

Here, **nation** represents the people of the nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people of the nation]

Here the psalmist is speaking of **the people** as if they were **an inheritance** that Yahweh received as a possession. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to be his own possession]

33.quote: מִ֭⁠שָּׁמַיִם הִבִּ֣יט יְהוָ֑ה רָ֝אָ֗ה אֶֽת־כָּל־בְּנֵ֥י הָ⁠אָדָֽם
33.text: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [From the heavens, Yahweh looks down, indeed he sees all the sons of man]

The psalmist is using **the sons of man** as a common expression of the culture to mean “human beings.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [humanity] or [the people]

Here the psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a person who **gazes** from a physical **place of his dwelling**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [From where he rules, he watches carefully]

Here the **hearts** represents their inner person, including thoughts and desires. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one forming all of their inner beings]

The expression **is not saved** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [A great army does not save the king]

The expression **is not delivered** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [great strength does not deliver a warrior]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by being very strong]

33.quote: שֶׁ֣קֶר הַ֭⁠סּוּס לִ⁠תְשׁוּעָ֑ה וּ⁠בְ⁠רֹ֥ב חֵ֝יל֗⁠וֹ לֹ֣א יְמַלֵּֽט
33.text: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [The horse is a falsehood for salvation, indeed, by its great strength, it does not deliver]

Here the psalmist is speaking of the horse as if it were a lie or **a falsehood** because it gives a false sense of security. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The horse gives a false sense of security]

The psalmist is using one part of an army, a **horse**, to represent the strongest part of the army. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Having an army with strong horses]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for saving anyone]

The psalmist is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look] or [Pay attention]

Here, **the eye of Yahweh** represents Yahweh’s watchful care and attention. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the watchful attention of Yahweh]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [that he will faithfully keep his covenant]

The psalmist is using **soul** to represent the people who fear Yahweh themselves from the perspective of their spiritual existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those who fear him]

The psalmist is using **Our soul** to represent the himself and the people from the perspective of their spiritual existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [We ourselves wait for Yahweh]

The terms **our help** and **our shield** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [our sure protector]

Here the psalmist is speaking of Yahweh protecting his people as if he were a battle **shield**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [is our helper and our protector]

Here the **our hearts** represents their inner person, including thoughts and desires. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [we rejoice in our inner beings]

The psalmist is using the term **name** to represent who Yahweh is and his character. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in Yahweh’s holiness]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a prayer request rather than a command. The psalmist is asking Yahweh for something. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please let your covenant faithfulness, Yahweh, be upon us]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [May you be faithful to your covenant with us, Yahweh]

34.text:
# Psalm 34 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 34 is a “psalm of thanksgiving.” It teaches that living right leads to a good life.

1. Praise Yahweh and testify of his deliverance (1–7)
2. Invite others to trust and fear Yahweh (8–14)
3. Yahweh watches over and rescues the righteous (15–22)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Yahweh’s help

Good people can have problems, but God brings them through these. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/good]])

Here, **to the face of** represents being in the presence of or in front of the king. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the presence of] or [in front of]

The pronoun in **he sent him** refers to Abimelech, while the pronouns in **him away** and **he left** refer to David. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the king sent David away and David left]

34.quote: אֲבָרֲכָ֣ה אֶת־יְהוָ֣ה בְּ⁠כָל־עֵ֑ת תָּ֝מִ֗יד תְּֽהִלָּת֥⁠וֹ בְּ⁠פִֽ⁠י
34.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [I will praise Yahweh without ceasing] or [I will bless Yahweh at all times, indeed, continually his praise is in my mouth]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **praise**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [praising him with my mouth]

Here, **my mouth** represents David’s speech. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I shall praise him with my words]
Here, **my soul** represents David himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I will boast]

David is using the adjective **humble** as a noun to mean people who are humble. If your language would not use an adjective this way, you could translate it with an equivalent expression. Alternate translation: [those who are humble]

34.quote: גַּדְּל֣וּ לַ⁠יהוָ֣ה אִתִּ֑⁠י וּ⁠נְרוֹמְמָ֖ה שְׁמ֣⁠וֹ יַחְדָּֽו
34.text: See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Let us declare together that Yahweh is great]

Here David is speaking of praising Yahweh as if Yahweh were something that they could **Magnify** or make larger. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Everyone should join me in telling others about how great Yahweh is]

This is an imperative, but it communicates an exhortation rather than a command. David is encouraging the people to worship. If the imperative does not communicate an exhortation for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates an exhortation or invitation. Alternate translation: [and we should all exalt his name]

Here, **his name** represents Yahweh himself and his reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [everything about him]

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a lost object which could be **sought** and found. He means that the people should pray to Yahweh and desire to be in his presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I asked Yahweh for help]

David is using **answered me** as a common expression of the culture to mean “acted on my behalf” in response to a request. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he acted in my behalf]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **fears**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [all the things I feared]
Here, **They** refers to those who seek Yahweh mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Those who seek Yahweh look]

David is using **look to him** as a common expression of the culture to mean to “trust in Yahweh and ask him for help.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They trust him to help them]

The psalmist is speaking of the joy and gladness those who trust Yahweh feel as if they were shining with **radiant** light. If it would be helpful for your readers, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and are glad]

The expression **let their faces not have shame** was a common expression meaning that they would not be ashamed because of some public failure or discouraged. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly or state it positively as in the UST. Alternate translation: [they should never be put to shame]

David is using the adjective **afflicted** as a noun to mean a person who is afflicted. Here David is referring to himself. If your language would not use an adjective this way, you could translate it with an equivalent expression. Alternate translation: [I was the suffering person who]

David assumes that readers will know that **Yahweh heard** means he listened to his prayer and responded favorably to it. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh did what I asked]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **troubles**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the things that were troubling him]

David is speaking of the angel protecting God’s people as if the angel were an army **encamping** around them to protect them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The angel of Yahweh stands guard around those who fear him]

David is using the possessive form to describe an **angel** that is sent by Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [The angel sent by Yahweh]

David is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of joy or blessing. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Oh, how happy is]

David is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the person who takes refuge]

David is speaking of trusting in Yahweh as if it were physically seeking shelter or **refuge** in a safe place. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he puts his trust in him]

David is speaking of experiencing Yahweh’s goodness as if it were some kind of food one could **Taste** and **see**. He means that one can discover Yahweh’s goodness by personal trial and experience. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Try for yourself and discover that Yahweh is good]

David is using the adjective **holy** as a noun to mean people who belong to Yahweh and are set apart for him. If your language would not use an adjective this way, you could translate it with an equivalent expression. Alternate translation: [his people who are set apart for him]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **lack**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [there is provision]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **lack**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [going without anything they need]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **lack**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this as modeled in the UST.

Although the term **sons** is masculine, David is using the word in a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a phrase that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [children]

David is speaking of his listeners as if they were his **sons**. He means that they are his students whom he will instruct. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [students]

34.quote: מִֽי־הָ֭⁠אִישׁ הֶ⁠חָפֵ֣ץ חַיִּ֑ים אֹהֵ֥ב יָ֝מִ֗ים לִ⁠רְא֥וֹת טֽוֹב
34.text: David is using the question form for emphasis. If you would not use the question form for that purpose in your language, you could translate this as a statement. Alternate translation: [If you want to live and enjoy a long time of seeing good, then do what follows.]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [is the person]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **life**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to live]

Here, **days** represents one’s lifespan or period of living. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to live a long time]

34.quote: נְצֹ֣ר לְשׁוֹנְ⁠ךָ֣ מֵ⁠רָ֑ע וּ֝⁠שְׂפָתֶ֗י⁠ךָ מִ⁠דַּבֵּ֥ר מִרְמָֽה
34.text: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [Do not say anything that is evil or deceptive]

David is using one part of a person, their **tongue**, to mean all of them in the act of speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [yourself from speaking evil words]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You could supply these words from context if it would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [guard your lips from speaking deceit]

David is using one part of a person, their **lips**, to mean all of them in the act of speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and yourself from deceptive speech]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **evil** and **deceit**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [from saying evil things … deceitful things]

David is speaking of doing what is evil as if it were walking on a path that a person could stop doing or **Turn away from**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Refuse to do what is evil]

This is an imperative, but it communicates an exhortation rather than a command. The psalmist is exhorting his students to stay away from evil. If the imperative does not communicate an exhortation for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates an exhortation. Alternate translation: [You should turn away from evil]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **evil**, **good**, and **peace**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [from doing what is wrong and do what is right; strive to live at peace with others and pursue living peacefully]

The terms **seek** and **pursue** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [earnestly strive to live peacefully]

Here, **eyes** represent Yahweh’s attention and watchful care. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh watchfully cares for the righteous]

David is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean people who do what is right. If your language would not use an adjective this way, you could translate it with an equivalent expression. Alternate translation: [righteous people]

Here, **ears** represents Yahweh’s attentive responsiveness to prayer. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and he listens attentively to their cry]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **cry**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [them when they cry]

Here, **face of Yahweh** represents his active presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh sets himself against the doers of evil]

Here, **their remembrance** represents the lasting legacy or memory that people leave behind. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [so that no one on earth will remember them]

The psalmist is using **cut off** as a common expression of the culture to mean “destroy” or “remove.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to remove]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **evil** and **remembrance**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [what is wicked … any trace of them]

Here, **They** refers to the righteous people mentioned in [verse 15](../034/015.md). If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the referent explicitly. Alternate translation: [Righteous people cry out]

David assumes that readers will know that **Yahweh hears** means he listens to their prayer and responds favorably to it. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh did what they asked]

Here David is speaking of Yahweh’s availability or willingness to help as if he were standing right beside or **near** to those who cry out to him for help. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will always give help]

David is using **broken of heart** as a common expression of his culture to mean “overwhelmed with grief.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to those who are overwhelmed with grief]

David is using **crushed of spirit** as a common expression of his culture to mean “in deep despair.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. # Psalm 35 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This psalm is considered to be one of the “imprecatory psalms.” See the Introduction to Psalms for more information about the imprecatory psalms.

1. Ask Yahweh to fight against adversaries (1–10)
2. Lament unjust hatred and false accusations (11–18)
3. Pray for vindication and justice from Yahweh (19–28)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Enemies

When David’s enemies were sick, he tried to comfort them, but when he was in trouble his enemies used this as a time to attack him.

## Translation Issues in this Psalm

### Imperatives

Throughout this psalm, David is requesting things from Yahweh by using an imperative form which may sound like a command in your language. If this would be impolite in your language to address a superior in this way, then use a form that would be more appropriate for addressing Yahweh with a request.

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [contend against those who fight against me]

The words **oppose** and **fight** are imperatives, but they communicate polite requests rather than commands. If the imperatives do not communicate polite requests for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. Here and throughout the psalm where this form is used, it may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, please oppose my opponents; please fight those fighting me]

David is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root in both of these phrases. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [go to battle against my enemies; fight against those who are attacking me]

David is using **rise up** as a common expression of the culture to ask Yahweh to take action. He is not telling him to get out of bed or stand up from a seated position. If this expression does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [take action]

The terms **spear** and **javelin** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Draw out your weapons]

David is using the term **my soul** to mean the entire person from the perspective of his spiritual existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [assure me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the one who rescues you]

# Psalm 36 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 36 is a “psalm of praise.” It speaks of how good God is to those who love him.

1. The depth of human sin (1–4)
2. The greatness of Yahweh’s steadfast love (5–9)
3. Prayer for continued protection and justice (10–12)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### God and man

Evil people do not think about God; but he is such a pleasure to all who honor him.

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [your judgments are like the great deep]

37.text:
# Psalm 37 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 37 is considered to be one of the “wisdom psalms.” See the Introduction to Psalms for more information about the wisdom psalms.

1. Do not envy the wicked but trust Yahweh (1–11)
2. Yahweh upholds the righteous and judges the wicked (12–20)
3. The righteous are sustained and secure in Yahweh (21–31)
4. Wait for Yahweh and observe his final justice (32–40)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Envy

Do not envy evil people. Although it appears as though they prosper, soon they will be destroyed and the good people will continue on living.

37.text: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Do not let yourself be troubled by those who do evil] or [Do not be upset about evildoers; indeed, do not be envious of the doers of unrighteousness]

The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the grass** quickly **withers** and dies, so the wicked will quickly perish. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [just as the grass quickly withers, they will quickly perish]

The point of this comparison is that just as a **green plant** will **fade** and die, so the wicked will not last. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and just as a green plant fades, they too will fade away]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **good**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the right thing]

The word translated as **feed** is used to describe what shepherds do for sheep as they care for them, and also for what sheep do as they feed themselves. So this could mean: (1) Cultivate, develop, or practice faithfulness to Yahweh (and each other). Alternate translation: [and practice faithfulness] or (2) Enjoy the faithfulness that Yahweh offers to his people. Alternate translation: [and experience Yahweh’s faithfulness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and act faithfully]

Here the **heart** represents where a person’s **desires** exist. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what you truly desire]

David is using **Roll your way upon Yahweh** as a common expression of his culture to mean to turn over or entrust your plans to Yahweh. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Commit your plans to Yahweh]

David is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **he will act** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Yahweh is the only one who can do this. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh himself will act]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the light** is clearly visible to everyone, so Yahweh will make the person’s righteousness clearly evident. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [your righteousness so that it is as clearly visible as the light]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how righteous you are]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and publicly defend your just cause]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the noonday** sun shines at its brightest, so Yahweh will make the person’s justice unmistakably clear. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and he will bring out that you are innocent so that it is as clear as the noonday sun]

David is using **Be silent to Yahweh** as a common expression of the culture to mean “wait patiently and reverently for Yahweh.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Rest quietly before Yahweh]

The word translated as **tremble** represents the written Hebrew text. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense here. Scholars have proposed that a different word with a similar spelling was intended that means “to wait” that seems to better fit the meaning of this passage. You may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [and wait]
The pronoun **him** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and tremble for Yahweh]

David is speaking of how a wicked person lives as if that were a **way** or path that the person was walking along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a wicked person’s way]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **schemes**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [carrying out wicked plans]

The terms **nose** and **wrath** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [of intense anger]

David is using the **nose** here as a common expression of the culture, **the burning of his nose** to mean “anger.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [of anger]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wrath**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [being furious]

The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [Since]

David is using **cut off** as a common expression of the culture to mean “destroy.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [evildoers will perish]

If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will cut off evildoers]

If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [they themselves will inherit the land]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [And yet a little while and then there are no more]

David is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [wicked person]
The pronoun **his** refers to the wicked person. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [where the wicked person was]

David is using the adjective **meek** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [But meek people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [living so peacefully and prosperously]

David is using the adjectives **wicked** and **righteous** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. David is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [Those who are wicked]

Here, **to** marks **bring down the poor and the needy** as the goal or purpose of the wicked preparing their weapons to kill, having **opened a sword** and **trodden their bow**. David is using the adjectives **poor** and **needy** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [those who are poor people and needy]

David is speaking of how a person lives as if that were a **way** that the person was walking along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those who live uprightly]

# Psalm 38 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 38 is a “psalm of supplication” or “lament.” It is a confession of sin and a prayer for deliverance.

1. Cry to Yahweh under discipline and distress (1–8)
2. Describe suffering and isolation (9–14)
3. Hope in Yahweh for healing and help (15–22)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### David’s sickness

The psalmist was very sick and his enemies were seeking ways to destroy him.

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional as in the UST. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, please do not continue to discipline me in your anger]
If your language does not use abstract noun for the idea of **anger** you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when you are angry]
If your language does not use abstract noun for the idea of **wrath**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [nor discipline me when you are furious]

David is speaking of Yahweh’s punishment as if it were **arrows** that had pierced him and **sunk into** his flesh. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your punishment has wounded me deeply]

David is using **your hand** as part of a common expression of his culture as seen in [Psalm 32:4](../032/004.md), “your hand was heavy upon me” to mean that Yahweh has afflicted or disciplined him severely. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you have afflicted me]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **soundness** and **indignation**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [There is no healthy part in my flesh from the face of your anger]

Alternate translation: [because of]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **peace** and **sin**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [there is nothing healthy in my body because I have sinned]

# Psalm 39 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 39 is a “psalm of supplication” or “lament.” See the Introduction to Psalms for more information about “psalms of supplication” or “laments.”

1. Struggle with silence and the weight of life (1–6)
2. Place hope in Yahweh alone (7–11)
3. Plead for mercy in light of life’s shortness (12–13)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Life

Life on earth is short. The psalmist wanted God’s healing so he can enjoy the rest of his life.

This psalm shares some characteristics of a wisdom book called Ecclesiastes but is more positive.

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

**Jeduthun** was a Levite who was one of the worship leaders in the temple during the reign of David. The expression **on Jeduthun** could mean: (1) that David gave this song to Jeduthun and his choir to perform. Alternate translation: [for Jeduthun’s choir] or (2) that singers were to perform this song in the style of Jeduthun’s choir. Alternate translation: [perform in the style of Jeduthun]

The phrase **I said** is here represented as introducing a direct quotation although it was likely an unspoken thought. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing unspoken thoughts in your language as modeled in the UST. It may not be necessary to represent this phrase explicitly.

This is an imperative, but it communicates David’s personal resolve rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a personal resolve for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a personal resolve. Alternate translation: [I resolve to guard my ways]

David is speaking of his behavior as if it were paths or **ways** where there could be a **guard** posted to control access. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [control my conduct]
David is using the term **tongue** to mean speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from sinning by what I say]

David is speaking of restraining his speech as if he were putting a **muzzle** on his **mouth** like one would muzzle an animal. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will keep silent]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **silence**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by not saying a word]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [I refrained from saying anything good]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **pain**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and my suffering increased]

The expression **was stirred up** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and my silence only made my pain worse]

David uses the word **and** here to indicate a contrast rather than adding information. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [but instead, my pain]

David is speaking of his emotional turmoil as if **fire burned** within him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my distress intensified]

The point of this comparison is that just as the time that a man **stands** or lives is frail and transient, so is **vapor** or a mere breath. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [each man’s life is frail and transient]

The point of this comparison is that just as an **image** is insubstantial and fleeting, so is a person’s life. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [a man walks about but has no real substance]

Here David is speaking of people going through life as if it were **a man** who **walks about**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [people go through life]

David is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [a person]

David is speaking of people’s pursuits as if they were **vapor**, something futile and insubstantial. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [surely they make an uproar over what is futile and worthless]
The pronoun **they** refers to people in general. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [everyone bustles around]

David assumes that readers will know that by **heaps up** he means acquiring a lot of possessions. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [He acquires possessions]
The pronoun **them** refers to the things that the person has heaped up. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [who will be getting all of those things]

The word **And** here introduces a transition from David’s reflection on the brevity of life to his direct appeal to God. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [Now then]

David is using the question form to emphasize that there is nothing worth waiting for apart from God. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [there is nothing I should wait for, Lord!]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **hope**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [What I wait hopefully for]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **transgressions**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from all the ways I have sinned against you]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **reproach**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [someone whom a fool insults]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **rebukes**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [By rebuking a man]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for the sinful things he has done]

David is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [you discipline a person]

The point of this comparison is that just as a **moth** gradually destroys clothing, so Yahweh destroys what a person treasures. David is speaking of all human existence as if it were **vapor** that quickly disappears. David is referring to dying in a polite way by using the phrase **I go and I am no more**. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [I pass away]

40.text:
# Psalm 40 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 40 is considered to be one of the “psalms of praise.” At the same time, it is a “messianic psalm” that looks forward to the triumph of Jesus Christ. The writer of Hebrews ([Hebrews 10:5–7](../../heb/10/05.md)) applies this passage ([Psalm 40:6–8](../040/006.md)) to Jesus using the ancient Greek version. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Praise Yahweh for past deliverance (1–5)
2. Commit to obey Yahweh’s will (6–10)
3. Ask Yahweh for continued help and rescue (11–17)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Sacrifices

God is not interested in sacrifices but wants people to obey him and fulfill his plans for them.

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

David is repeating forms of the verb **wait** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [I waited expectantly for]

David is speaking of Yahweh’s attentive concern for him as if Yahweh were physically bending down or **inclined** toward him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he paid close attention to me]

David assumes that readers will know that by **heard** he means Yahweh listened and responded favorably to his prayer. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and responded to]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **cry**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [me cry out]

Here David is speaking Yahweh’s rescuing him from a terrible situation as if he were lifted or **brought up** from a deep hole. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he saved me]

David is speaking as if his distress were a deep **pit** from which he could not escape. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the terrible danger I was in]

David is using the possessive form to describe a **pit** that is characterized by **tumult**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from the tumultuous pit]

David is speaking as if his desperate situation were **mud** and **mire** from which he could not free himself. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the terrible situation in which I was stuck]

David is speaking as if Yahweh’s deliverance were Yahweh physically placing his **feet on a rock**, giving him stability and safety. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he made me stable and safe]

David is speaking as if his way of living were **steps** that Yahweh made firm. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he made my way of life secure]

David is speaking of Yahweh giving him reason to sing a song of praise as if **a new song** were a physical object that he placed into his **mouth**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he made me want to sing a different song of]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **praise**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a song that says that our God is great]

David is not using the possessive form **our God** to indicate that he and his people possess or control Yahweh. Rather David is using these words to indicate that Yahweh is the God whom they worship. Alternate translation: [to the God we worship]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Many people will see what God has done for me and will reverence him]

David is using the adjective **Many** as a noun to mean a certain group of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [There will be many people who]

David is using the phrase **The happinesses of** to express a strong feeling of admiration for those who trust in Yahweh. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. If not, you could express the idea of how fortunate such a person is. Alternate translation: [Oh, how happy is the person]

David is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the one]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **trust**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the one he relies on]

David is speaking as if choosing to follow or trust the proud were physically having **turned** to face them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [has not put his trust in the proud]

David is using the adjective **proud** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [arrogant people]

By **the goers aside**, David means “those who have gone astray after falsehood.” You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and those who follow after falsehood]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **falsehood**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [lies]

David is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you have done** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Yahweh is the one who performed these wonderful deeds. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [For it is you, Yahweh my God, who has done many things]

David is not using the possessive form **my God** to indicate that he possesses or controls Yahweh. Rather David is using these words to indicate that Yahweh is the God whom he worships. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, the God I worship]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **thoughts**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and what you have planned for us]

The clause translated as **there is none to line up against you** could refer to: (1) anyone who might compare to Yahweh. Alternate translation: [there is no one to compare to you] or (2) all of the things that Yahweh has done, that cannot be listed. Alternate translation: [there is no way to enumerate them to you]

David says **they are more than to recount** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [there are too many to count]

The terms **declare** and **speak** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Should I be able to tell all about those deeds]

The pronoun **they** refers to all Yahweh’s wonderful deeds and plans. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [all those wonderful deeds are more than can be recounted]

David is using **ears you have dug for me** as a common expression of the culture to mean “you gave me the ability to hear and obey you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you have given me ears to hear] or [you have made me able to listen to you]
David is using the term **Behold** to call attention to what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look]

The expression **it is written about me** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [a prophet has written about me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **will**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what you want]

David is not using the possessive form **my God** to indicate that he possesses or controls Yahweh. Rather David is using these words to indicate that Yahweh is the God whom he worships. Alternate translation: [the God I worship]

David is speaking as if his deep commitment to Yahweh’s law were that law being physically present **in the midst of** his **inward parts**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I am deeply committed to keeping your law]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [that you are righteous]
See how you translated the similar expression in [40:7](../040/007.md).

Here, **my lips** represents David’s speech. By saying he will not **restrain** them, David means he will not stop speaking about Yahweh’s righteousness. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I will not stop telling others]

David is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you know** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Yahweh himself is fully aware of David’s faithfulness. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [Yawheh, you know this is true]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [your righteous acts]

David is using **heart** to mean the place where his thoughts and intentions exist. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [just within my own thoughts]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **faithfulness** and **salvation**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [how faithful you are and how you have saved us]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **covenant faithfulness** and **trustworthiness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [how you faithfully keep your covenant and how trustworthy you are]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **compassion**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [being compassionate]
See how you translated the same abstract nouns in [verse 10](../040/010.md).
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **evils**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [evil things]

Here David is speaking of bad things happening to him as if they were objects that **surrounded** him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [are constantly happening all around me]

David says **until there is no number** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [there are too many to count]

Here David is speaking his sins overwhelming him as if they were actually something chasing after and having caught up or **overtaken** him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my sins have caught up with me] or [my iniquities have overwhelmed me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquities**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the sins I have committed]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and I am not able to see a way out]

David says **more numerous than the hairs of my head** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [They are too many for me to count]

Here the **heart** represents where a person’s thoughts and emotions exist. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and my courage has failed me]

40.quote: רְצֵ֣ה יְ֭הוָה לְ⁠הַצִּילֵ֑⁠נִי יְ֝הוָ֗ה לְ⁠עֶזְרָ֥תִ⁠י חֽוּשָׁ⁠ה
40.text: These lines are imperatives, but they communicate a polite request or prayer rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear as modeled in the UST.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **help**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to rescue me]

By using **Let** in each of the phrases in this and the following verses, David is expressing what he desires or prays will happen. Alternate translation: [I desire that they all have shame and disgrace]

Here David is asking that his enemies be stopped as if they were walking on a path and then were blocked or **turned back**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Let them be stopped]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **shame**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how disgraced they are]

David’s enemies using **Aha! Aha!** as a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of malicious glee at his misfortune. If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how you save them]

The terms **poor** and **needy** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [in great need]

The terms **help** and **deliverer** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [my great deliverer]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **help**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the one who helps and delivers me]
See how you translated the similar expression in [40:8](../040/008.md). Alternate translation: [oh, God whom I worship]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please do not delay]

41.text:
# Psalm 41 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 41 is a “psalm of supplication” or “lament.” See the Introduction to Psalms for more information about types of psalms.

1. Blessing for those who care for the weak (1–3)
2. Cry for mercy amid betrayal and sickness (4–9)
3. Trust Yahweh for restoration and justice (10–12)
4. Conclusion of Book 1, which consists of Psalms 1–41 (13)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Enemies

The author’s best friend had become an enemy. His enemies were happy because they were sure his sickness would result in death.

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

David is using the phrase **The happinesses of** to express a strong feeling of admiration. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. If not, you could express the idea of how fortunate such a person is. Alternate translation: [Oh, how happy is the one considering]

David is using the adjective **lowly** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [people who are lowly]

David is using the possessive form to describe a **day**, time, or occasion that is characterized by **evil**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [When evil things are happening]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **evil**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [harmful things]

The expression **be called happy** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and people will call him happy]

David switches to addressing Yahweh directly in order to make his conclusion more vivid. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the third person for consistency. Alternate translation: [so may Yahweh not give him]
Here, **soul** represents “desire.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [over to the desire of his enemies]

The psalmist is speaking of the person’s time of illness as if it were **the bed of suffering** on which the person lies. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his sickbed]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **suffering**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when he suffers]

As he did in the previous verse, David switches to addressing Yahweh directly in order to make his conclusion more vivid. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the third person for consistency. Alternate translation: [Yahweh transformed]

By **transformed each bed of his in his sickness**, David means that Yahweh transforms his illness into health. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh transformed his sickness into health]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **sickness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when he is ill]

The pronoun **I** refers to David. David is stating the pronoun **I** separately for emphasis even though the verb translated as **I said** already includes this meaning. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [I, David, said]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear as modeled in the UST.

David is using the term **soul** to mean his entire person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Please make me whole again]

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Since I have sinned against you, I need you to heal me]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **evil**, you could express the same idea in another way. See how you translated the similar expression in [verse 1](../041/001.md). Alternate translation: [harmful things]

David’s enemies are using the question form to express their hostile wish that David would die. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [We wish he would die and his name would perish!]

Here, **his name** represents “his memory” or “his reputation.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and the memory of him will perish]

Here the **heart** represents where a person’s thoughts and intentions exist. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his mind plans evil]

The pronouns **he** and **his** in this verse refer to one of David’s enemies mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And if one of my enemies comes]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **worthlessness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [he speaks empty words] or [he pretends to be friendly]

Here the **heart** represents where a person’s thoughts exist so the phrase **his heart gathers iniquity to itself** means that the enemy is secretly trying to think of bad things to say about David. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he thinks of evil things he can say]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [ways to defame]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **evil**, you could express the same idea in another way. See how you translated the similar expression in [41:1](../041/001.md). Alternate translation: [things that will harm me]

David’s enemies are speaking of **A matter of wickedness** as if it were a liquid that is **poured** on a person. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Something wicked has overwhelmed him]

The expression **is poured** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Terrible things are happening to him]

This is the beginning of what David’s “haters” (enemies mentioned in the previous verse) are saying about him. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of SPEAKER. Alternate translation: [My enemies are saying, “A matter of wickedness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wickedness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [something very evil]

David’s enemies are referring to dying in a polite way by using the phrase **he who has lain down will not repeat to rise**. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [and he will die from this illness]
