David is using **the man of my peace** as a common expression of his culture to mean “my close friend” or “my trusted ally.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my closest ally]

It might seem that the expression **whom I trusted in him** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [in whom I trusted]

David is using one kind of food, **bread**, to mean food or in general so **the eater of my bread** here means “the one who shared meals with me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one who ate meals with me]

David is using **has made great the heel against me** as a common expression of the culture to mean “has greatly betrayed me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [has greatly turned against me]

Here, **so that** marks **I may repay them** as the goal or purpose of **be gracious to me and raise me up**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [in order that I may repay them]
Here, **shout** represents “triumph.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [my enemy does not triumph over me]

The pronoun **I** refers to David. David places this pronoun at the front of the sentence for emphasis, contrasting himself with his enemies. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [But as for me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **integrity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because I am honest]

Here, **to your face** represents being in front of or in the presence of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in your presence]

The expression **Blessed be** is a passive verbal form. The psalmist is expressing his desire to praise Yahweh. If it would be unnatural to use that form for this purpose, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I bless Yahweh] or [Let us all praise Yahweh]

The psalmist is not using this possessive form **the God of Israel** to indicate that the Israelites possess or control God. Rather the psalmist is using these words to indicate that God is the one whom Israel worships. Alternate translation: [who is the God whom Israel worships]

David is referring to all of time by naming two extremes, **from the everlasting** and **unto the everlasting**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from before time began and continuing forever]

42.text:
# Psalm 42–43 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalms 42 and 43 were originally one psalm. They are presented that way in many Hebrew manuscripts and ancient versions. A repeated refrain joins them together. Psalm 43 has no superscription. This psalm was divided in two in the traditional Hebrew text probably to achieve a round total of 150 psalms. See the discussion of the numbering of the psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

Psalm 42–43 is a psalm of supplication or lament. It presents all the basic elements of that type of psalm. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. First stanza (42:1–4): Description of troubles and cry for help
2. First refrain (42:5): Statement of trust
3. Second stanza (42:6–10): Description of troubles and cry for help
4. Second refrain (42:11): Statement of trust
5. Third stanza (43:1–4): Petition and vow of praise
6. Third refrain (43:5): Statement of trust

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a “maskil.” See the discussion of that term in the introduction to Psalms.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Why was a Levite worship leader far away from Jerusalem?

This psalm is one of nine psalms attributed to “the sons of Korah,” that is, to the Korahite clan, the descendants of a Levite named Korah. The members of this clan had a special responsibility for leading the Israelites in worship. They played musical instruments and sang in the temple courtyard, and they composed songs. However, some of the later kings of Judah worshiped false gods represented by idols. They tried to suppress the worship of Yahweh. Prophets, worship leaders, and faithful believers in Yahweh often had to flee for their safety. The Korahite who wrote this psalm records that he had gone to the region in the far northeast of the territory of Israel where the Jordan River begins. This territory was contested between Israel and Aram, and at the time when this psalm was written, the Arameans may have controlled the location where the psalmist was. (In 43:1, he asks God to defend him from “a nation not faithful.”) So in this psalm, he laments that he has had to flee from Jerusalem, where he joyfully led the people in worship, probably to foreign territory. But he encourages himself with the memory of those experiences, and he asks God to make it possible for him to return to the temple and worship him there once more.

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

### Repeated phrases

In 42:10, for poetic effect, the psalmist uses some the same phrases that he uses in 42:3. Similarly for poetic effect, the psalmist uses in 43:2 some of the same phrases that he uses in 42:9. And the refrain in 42:5, 42:11, and 43:5 uses the same phrases in each case. To help your readers appreciate this, we recommend that you represent the same phrases in the same way in your translation.

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. See how you translated the term “chief musician” in the superscription to Psalm 4. Alternate translation: [For the leader of worship music] or [For the music director]

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a **maskil**. Since the meaning of this word is not certain, you may wish to represent it in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language. See the discussion of that term in the Introduction to Psalms.

The psalmist of this psalm belonged to a clan of the tribe of Levi whose members led the Israelites in worship and composed many worship songs. The superscription to this psalm describes them as if they were actual **sons** or first-generation descendants of **Korah**, who was a great-grandson of Levi. They were instead later descendants of Korah. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [of the descendants of Korah] or [of the Korahites]

42.quote: כְּ⁠אַיָּ֗ל תַּעֲרֹ֥ג עַל־אֲפִֽיקֵי־מָ֑יִם כֵּ֤ן נַפְשִׁ֨⁠י תַעֲרֹ֖ג אֵלֶ֣י⁠ךָ אֱלֹהִֽים
42.text: The psalmist is using one part of himself, his **soul** or inner being, to mean all of him in the act of desiring God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [As a deer pants for streams of water, so in my inner being I pant for you, God]

42.quote: כְּ⁠אַיָּ֗ל תַּעֲרֹ֥ג עַל־אֲפִֽיקֵי־מָ֑יִם כֵּ֤ן נַפְשִׁ֨⁠י תַעֲרֹ֖ג אֵלֶ֣י⁠ךָ אֱלֹהִֽים
42.text: The point of this comparison is that just as a **deer**, when it is very thirsty in a dry place, **pants** desperately for water, so the psalmist desperately desires God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [As a deer pants desperately for streams of water, so in my inner being I pant desperately for you, God]

42.quote: כְּ⁠אַיָּ֗ל תַּעֲרֹ֥ג עַל־אֲפִֽיקֵי־מָ֑יִם כֵּ֤ן נַפְשִׁ֨⁠י תַעֲרֹ֖ג אֵלֶ֣י⁠ךָ אֱלֹהִֽים
42.text: The psalmist is speaking as if his soul were actually panting or taking short, quick breaths. He means that in his inner being, he is desperately feeling and expressing a desire for God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [As a deer pants desperately for streams of water, so in my inner being I desperately desire you, God]
See how you translated the expression “my soul” in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [In my inner being, I thirst for God]

The psalmist is speaking as if he felt physical thirst for God. He is using this image to depict his great desire for God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [In my inner being, I feel a great desire for God]

The psalmist is using the question form to express a strong desire. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I want very much to come and appear to the face of God!]
Here, **face** represents “presence.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the presence of God]

As [42:4](../042/004.md) and [43:4](../043/004.md) suggest, the psalmist is speaking of coming into the presence of God to mean coming into God’s temple. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in God’s temple again]

The psalmist is using one kind of food, **bread**, to represent food in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [My weeping is my food]

The psalmist is speaking as if he were actually eating his **weeping**. He means that he has been weeping so much that he has been unable to eat. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Instead of eating, I have been weeping]

The psalmist is using the two main components of time, **day** and **night**, to mean all of time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all the time]

The psalmist does not indicate specifically who has been **saying** what he quotes. To make clear that someone else, not the psalmist, has been saying this, the ULT supplies the indefinite pronoun **their**. It may be natural in your language to do something similar. You could also use a general expression. Alternate translation: [as they say to me] or [as people say to me]

The psalmist is saying **all the day** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [constantly]

The psalmist’s enemies are using the question form to mock him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Your God certainly does not appear to be helping you!]

The psalmist is using a verbal form that expresses a resolution. In your translation, use an appropriate verbal form to indicate this. Alternate translation: [I will remember these, and I will pour out my soul within me]

The phrases **Let me remember these** and **let me pour out my soul within me** together express a single idea. The second phrase describes the circumstances under which the psalmist is encouraging himself to do what the first phrase describes. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [Let me remember these as I pour out my soul within me] or [I will remember these as I pour out my soul within me]

The psalmist is using the demonstrative adjective **these** as a noun to mean things of a certain kind, the things he describes in the rest of the verse Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the following things]

The psalmist is speaking as if his **soul** were actually a liquid that he could **pour out**. He is encouraging himself to give full expression, in his own private reflections (**within me**), to what he is feeling deeply in his inner being. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and let me fully express to myself what I am feeling deep inside] or [as I fully express to myself what I am feeling deep inside]

42.quote: בַּ⁠סָּךְ֮ אֶדַּדֵּ֗⁠ם עַד־בֵּ֥ית אֱלֹ֫הִ֥ים בְּ⁠קוֹל־רִנָּ֥ה וְ⁠תוֹדָ֗ה הָמ֥וֹן חוֹגֵֽג
42.text: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put together the information that this **crowd** was **a multitude celebrating a festival**. Alternate translation: [with the crowd, a multitude celebrating a festival. I led them in procession to the house of God with a voice of rejoicing and praise]
See how you translated the term “house” in [5:7](../005/007.md). Alternate translation: [the temple of God]

The psalmist is using the **voice** that each person in the **crowd** used for shouting to represent the shouts of the crowd. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [with shouts of rejoicing and praise]

At the end of [42:5](../042/005.md) and the beginning of [42:5](../042/005.md), the ULT translates the traditional written Hebrew text. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense. It is different from the other two occurrences of the refrain of this psalm in [42:11](../042/011.md) and [43:5](../043/005.md). It appears that a verse division has been placed in the middle of a word, so that the prefix that means “and” in those two verses has become a suffix that means “his” in this verse. You may want to follow an alternative reading from the ancient Greek translation. Alternate translation: [the salvation of my face and my God]

The psalmist is speaking as if his **soul** had actually **bowed** itself **down** and as if it were actually **clamoring** or making noises **within** him that indicated how upset it was. He is describing his own inner feelings of despondency and agitation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Why do I feel so despondent and agitated inside]

The psalmist is using the question form to give himself a mild rebuke and to encourage himself to consider his situation from a different perspective and so come to feel differently about it. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I do not have to feel so despondent and agitated inside!]

The word that the ULT translates as **Wait** can mean simply not to do something until a certain time has passed or a certain other event has occurred. However, in many biblical contexts, it means to expect that God will do something to change an unfavorable situation that a person cannot change or that a person therefore should not try to change himself, and that is the meaning here. You may be able to use a different term to express this meaning in your language. Alternate translation: [Hope in God] or [I can hope in God]

Here the word **for** introduces not a reason but an explanation. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [after all,]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation, following the alternative reading of the ancient Greek translation: [the one who saves my face] or [the savior of my face]

The psalmist is using one part of himself, his **face**, to mean all of him in the act of receiving God’s salvation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation, following the alternative reading of the ancient Greek translation: [the one who saves me] or [my savior]

See the explanation in a note to the previous verse of how this expression was likely put at the start of this verse when a verse division was mistakenly placed in the middle of a word. You may wish to put this expression at the end of the previous verse, as many versions do, so that the refrain of this psalm will be the same in all three of its occurrences.
See how you translated the similar expression in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [I do feel despondent]

The psalmist may be using the plural term **Hermons** because: (1) Mount Hermon has three distinct peaks. Alternate translation: [and Mount Hermon] or (2) he is referring to the range of mountains that includes Mount Hermon. Alternate translation: [and the Hermon mountain range]

**Mount Mizar** seems to have been the psalmist’s specific location within the general area he describes in the earlier part of this verse. It is not known to what mountain he was referring, so it is not possible to associate it with a mountain that is known by another name today. We therefore recommend that you use the name Mount Mizar in your translation.

The psalmist is speaking as if the **sound** of the **waterfalls** he hears in the nearby forming Jordan River were actually one **Deep** (one large mass of water) **calling** to another such **deep**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. You could also express this image as a comparison, as the UST does. Alternate translation: [The powerful streams in the river make loud, echoing sounds as they flow over rock ledges as waterfalls]

The terms **breakers** and **waves** mean similar things. The term **waves** describes swellings of water that move across the surface of the ocean, and the term **breakers** describes those swellings as they crash onto the shore. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [As your waves break on the shore, the surf pounds me]

The psalmist is speaking as if he were actually in an ocean or on its shore and strong **waves** and **breakers** were crashing over him, tossing him about. He is representing how overwhelmed he feels. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. You could also express this image as a comparison, as the UST does. Alternate translation: [I am feeling overwhelmed by what you have allowed to happen]

42.quote: יוֹמָ֤ם ׀ יְצַוֶּ֬ה יְהוָ֨ה ׀ חַסְדּ֗⁠וֹ וּ֭⁠בַ⁠לַּיְלָה שיר⁠ה עִמִּ֑⁠י
42.text: As in verse 3, the psalmist is using the two main components of time, **day** and **night**, to mean all of time. See how you translated the expression “day and night” in verse 3. It would be appropriate to use similar language here, since the psalmist’s recognition of Yahweh’s covenant faithfulness and his celebration of it in worship are his intentional responses to the sorrow he described earlier. Alternate translation: [Yahweh commands his covenant faithfulness all the time, and his song is with me all the time]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Yahweh acts toward me in a way that is faithful to his covenant]

Since the psalmist is referring to a continual activity, he is likely not referring to one specific **song** that expresses one specific **prayer**. He probably means all of the songs that Yahweh enables him to compose in order to sing prayers to him. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [his songs are with me, prayers]

The psalmist is speaking of this **song** as if it were a living thing that could be **with** him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he enables me to compose songs, prayers]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to indicate that it is **God** who has given him **life** and who preserves his life. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the God who has given me life] or [the God who preserves my life]
As in [42:4](../042/004.md), the psalmist is using a verbal form that expresses a resolution. See how you translated the similar form there. Alternate translation: [I will say]
See how you translated the term “rock” in [18:2](../018/002.md). Alternate translation: [who keeps me safe]

42.quote: לָ⁠מָ֪ה שְׁכַ֫חְתָּ֥⁠נִי לָֽ⁠מָּה־קֹדֵ֥ר אֵלֵ֗ךְ בְּ⁠לַ֣חַץ אוֹיֵֽב
42.text: The psalmist is using the question form to express his feelings to God honestly and urgently. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [You appear to have forgotten me! I should not have to walk about mourning because of the oppression of the enemy!]

As in [15:2](../015/002.md) and many other places in the Psalms, the psalmist may be using the term **walk** to mean “live.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Why do I go through life] or [I should not have to go through life]

As the next verse makes clear, the psalmist is not referring to a specific **enemy**. He means all of the enemies who are oppressing him. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [because of the oppression of my enemies]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **oppression**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because of the enemies who are oppressing me]

The psalmist is speaking as if his afflicters were actually **crushing** his **bones**, that is, so badly mistreating him physically that his bones were bruised or broken. He is using this image to represent the deeply painful effect of their **reproach**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [In a way that penetrates very painfully into my inner being]

For poetic effect, the psalmist is using again the same phrases that he used in [42:3](../042/003.md). We recommend that you show this to your readers by translating the phrases here the same way that you translated them there. Alternate translation: [as they say to me constantly, “Your God certainly does not appear to be helping you!”]

42.quote: מַה־תִּשְׁתּ֬וֹחֲחִ֨י ׀ נַפְשִׁ⁠י֮ וּֽ⁠מַה־תֶּהֱמִ֪י עָ֫לָ֥⁠י הוֹחִ֣ילִי לֵֽ֭⁠אלֹהִים כִּי־ע֣וֹד אוֹדֶ֑⁠נּוּ יְשׁוּעֹ֥ת פָּ֝נַ֗⁠י וֵֽ⁠אלֹהָֽ⁠י
42.text: This is the second occurrence of the refrain in this psalm. We recommend that you show this to your readers by translating the phrases here the same way that you translated them in the first occurrence of this refrain in [42:5](../042/005.md). Alternate translation: [I do not have to feel so despondent and agitated inside! I can hope in God. After all, I will again praise him, the one who saves me and who is my God]

43.text: # Psalm 43 Introduction\n\nPsalms 42 and 43 were originally one psalm. For an introduction to what is now Psalm 43, see the introduction to Psalm 42, which discusses both psalms together.

The psalmist is speaking as if he were actually in a legal proceeding and wanted God to take his side, as if he were a judge who would **Vindicate** him or a defense attorney who would **plead** his case. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Recognize that I am innocent and defend me]

The psalmist is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. If you decide to retain the legal image in your translation, you may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternate translation: [and plead my case]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means all of the people who are acting in a **deceitful** and **unjust** way toward him. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [from these deceitful and unjust people] or [from every deceitful and unjust person]

The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **God** as being like a **refuge** for him. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [you are the God who is like a refuge to me]
See how you translated the term “refuge” in [11:1](../011/001.md). Alternate translation: [you are the God who protects me]

43.quote: לָ⁠מָ֪ה זְנַ֫חְתָּ֥⁠נִי לָֽ⁠מָּה־קֹדֵ֥ר אֶתְהַלֵּ֗ךְ בְּ⁠לַ֣חַץ אוֹיֵֽב
43.text: See how you translated the similar questions in [42:9](../042/009.md). Alternate translation: [You appear to have rejected me! I should not have to walk about mourning because of the oppression of the enemy!]

For poetic effect, the psalmist is using again the same phrases that he used in [42:9](../042/009.md). We recommend that you show this to your readers by translating the phrases here the same way that you translated them there. Alternate translation: [I should not have to go through life mourning because of the enemies who are oppressing me!]

While the psalmist uses essentially the same language here as in [42:9](../042/009.md), he uses a different form of the verb translated as **walk**. The form used here can indicate repeated action, and that seems to be the sense in this context. Your language may have a comparable verbal form that you can use in your translation. If not, you may be able to use a different verb or expression. Alternate translation: [Why do I wander about]

The psalmist is speaking of God’s **light** and **truth** as if they were living things that God could **Send out** and that could **lead** the psalmist and **bring** him home. By **your light**, the psalmist probably means “the light of your face,” as in [4:6](../004/006.md). This represents God’s favor, as if God were smiling and looking brightly at someone. By **faithfulness**, the psalmist probably means God’s covenant faithfulness, as in [42:8](../042/008.md), that is, God’s commitment to fulfill the promises he has made to help people who are loyal to him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Extend your favor and faithfulness to me, and exhibit those qualities as you lead me. Exhibit those qualities in order to bring me]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **them** separately, even though the verb translated as **let them lead me** already includes this meaning. He is doing this because he is speaking of God’s **light** and **faithfulness** as if they were people and he wants to emphasize the personal role that he would like these qualities to take. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [let them be the ones who lead me]

The psalmist is not using the possessive form to ascribe **holiness** to the mountain where God’s **dwellings** are located. Instead, he is using the possessive form to indicate that God consecrated or set apart this mountain as a place where he would dwell, that is, where he would be present in a special way in his temple. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this purpose, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to the mountain that you have set apart] or [to the mountain that you have consecrated]

The psalmist is using the plural form **dwellings** where he could have used the singular form, since the context indicates that he is referring to the temple in Jerusalem (“the house of God,” [42:4](../042/004.md), the location of “the altar of God,” [43:4](../043/004.md)). This suggests that he is using the plural form to emphasize the magnificence of the temple and especially its sacred character as a place where God is present in a special way. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the singular and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [your sacred temple]

The psalmist is speaking of God in the third person even though he is addressing him directly. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the second person. Alternate translation: [to your altar, O God, to you, the God of the joy of my gladness]

The psalmist is using the possessive expression **the joy of my gladness** to describe **joy** that is characterized by **gladness**, that is, great joy. He is using the fuller possessive expression **the God of the joy of my gladness** to describe God as the one who gives him this great joy. If a speaker of your language would not use possessive forms for these purposes, you could express these ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [the God who gives me great joy]

43.quote: מַה־תִּשְׁתּ֬וֹחֲחִ֨י ׀ נַפְשִׁ⁠י֮ וּֽ⁠מַה־תֶּהֱמִ֪י עָ֫לָ֥⁠י הוֹחִ֣ילִי לֵֽ֭⁠אלֹהִים כִּי־ע֣וֹד אוֹדֶ֑⁠נּוּ יְשׁוּעֹ֥ת פָּ֝נַ֗⁠י וֵֽ⁠אלֹהָֽ⁠י
43.text: This is the third occurrence of the refrain in this psalm. We recommend that you show this to your readers by translating the phrases here the same way that you translated them in the first two occurrences of this refrain in [42:5](../042/005.md) and [42:11](../042/011.md). Alternate translation: [I do not have to feel so despondent and agitated inside! I can hope in God. After all, I will again praise him, the one who saves me and who is my God]

44.text:
# Psalm 44 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 44 is a psalm of supplication or lament. It presents most of the basic elements of that type of psalm, but in a different order than is common. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Statement of trust (1–8) including a short petition (4b)
2. Description of troubles (9–16, 22, 25)
3. Claim of innocence (17–21)
4. Cry for help (23–24)
5. Petition (25)

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a “maskil.” See the discussion of that term in the introduction to Psalms.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### If God had “scattered” the people “among the nations” (v. 11), how did they still have “armies” (v. 9)?

It seems likely that this psalm was written not after the people of Judah had been deported to Babylon but while they were still in their land, ruled by a godly king, but suffering military defeats that led to some of their cities being conquered and the people of those cities being taken away into exile. One plausible historical setting for the composition of the psalm is the reign of Hezekiah, specifically during the invasion by the Assyrian king Sennacherib in 701 B.C. Hezekiah was an exceptionally godly king, which would correspond with the psalmist’s statement that “we have not forgotten you, and we have not dealt falsely with your covenant” (v. 17). Nevertheless, the invading Assyrians repeatedly defeated the Judean defenders. They conquered most of the fortified cities in Judah and deported their inhabitants. This would correspond with the psalmist’s complaint to God that “you do not go out with our armies” (v. 9) and “you have scattered us among the nations” (v. 11). Hezekiah’s godliness, reforms, and previous military victories are described in [2 Kings 18:1–8](../2ki/18/01.md). The Assyrian invasion is described in [2 Kings 18:9–19:34](../2ki/18/09.md). And the defeat of the Assyrians by God’s miraculous power, which would be an answer to this psalmist’s prayer if that is the historical setting, is described in [2 Kings 19:35–37](../2ki/19/35.md).

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. See how you translated the term “chief musician” in the superscription to Psalm 4. Alternate translation: [For the leader of worship music] or [For the music director]

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a **maskil**. Since the meaning of this word is not certain, you may wish to represent it in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language. See the discussion of that term in the Introduction to Psalms.
See how you translated the expression “the sons of Korah” in the superscription to Psalm 42. Alternate translation: [the descendants of Korah] or [the Korahites]

Here and throughout this psalm, the psalmist is applying the terms **we**, **our**, and **us** to himself and his fellow Judeans but not to God, to whom he is speaking. So use the exclusive forms of those terms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

It might seem that the expression **with our ears** adds extra information to this statement that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you may choose not to represent this expression in your translation. However, it does add some emphasis, and you may also choose to reflect that emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [we have heard] or [we have clearly heard]
See how you translated the term “fathers” in [22:4](../022/004.md). Alternate translation: [our forefathers]

The psalmist is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [the work you did]

The psalmist is using the term **days** to mean “time,” since time consists of days. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in their time]

The **fathers** or ancestors who **recounted** the **work** described in verses 2 and 3 did not experience it personally. The psalmist is using them generally to represent earlier generations of Israelites and specifically to represent the generation that conquered and occupied the land of Canaan. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [for the generation that conquered and occupied the land of Canaan]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **antiquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in ancient times]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **You** separately, even though the verb translated as **you drove out** already includes this meaning. He is doing that in order to emphasize a contrast between what the Israelites did not do, as described in the next verse, and what God did. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [You were the one who drove out]
Here, **hand** represents “power.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [by your power]

In each case, the pronoun **them** refers to the “fathers” or ancestors of the Israelites mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [but you planted our ancestors … but you sent our ancestors]

The psalmist is speaking as if God had actually **planted** the Israelites in the land of Canaan, as if they had been plants. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but you settled our ancestors there]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [but you sent them into the land] or [but you sent our ancestors into the land]

While it is true that God **sent** the Israelites into the land of Canaan in the sense that he commanded them to go there, the sense here seems to be that God actively propelled them into the land by helping them. That was in contrast to the way he **caused harm** to the nations he drove out. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be

Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but a complementary truth by way of concession. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [Indeed,] or [Admittedly,]

The psalmist is using one kind of weapon, a **sword**, to mean weapons in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with their weapons] or [militarily]
Here, **arm** represents “power.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and their own power]

44.quote: כִּֽי־יְמִֽינְ⁠ךָ֣ וּ֭⁠זְרוֹעֲ⁠ךָ וְ⁠א֥וֹר פָּנֶ֗י⁠ךָ כִּ֣י רְצִיתָֽ⁠ם
44.text: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [but your right hand and your arm and the light of your face saved them, for you favored them]

44.quote: כִּֽי־יְמִֽינְ⁠ךָ֣ וּ֭⁠זְרוֹעֲ⁠ךָ וְ⁠א֥וֹר פָּנֶ֗י⁠ךָ כִּ֣י רְצִיתָֽ⁠ם
44.text: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [but because you favored them, your right hand and your arm and the light of your face saved them]

In this context, the terms **right hand** and **arm** mean similar things, since they both represent power. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [but your very strong power]

The **light** of God’s **face** represents his favor, as if he were smiling and looking brightly at someone. See how you translated the similar expression in [4:6](../004/006.md). Alternate translation: [and the favor you showed them]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **he** for clarity and emphasis. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [You are the one who is my king]
Since the psalmist uses first-person plural pronouns throughout most of this psalm, you may wish to use one here, as the UST does. Alternate translation: [our king]

The psalmist is speaking of the **salvation of Jacob** as if it were a living thing that God could **Command**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Bring about the salvation of Jacob]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Act to save Jacob]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please command]

The psalmist is using the name **Jacob** to represent the Israelite people, who were descendants of a man named Jacob. God gave him the name Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [us Israelites]

The psalmist is speaking as if the Israelite army were actually a horned animal that would **gore** and **trample** an opposing army as if it were another animal. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [we push back … we defeat]

In this context, God’s **name** seems to represent his authority. The psalmist seems to mean that since God assigned the land of Canaan to the Israelites, when they fight to defend that territory, they are doing so on his authority. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [by your authority]

The psalmist is speaking of the **adversaries** of Israel as if they were physically **arising** to a higher elevation. See how you translated the similar expression in [18:48](../018/048.md). Alternate translation: [the ones attacking us]
As in verse 3, here the word **For** introduces not a reason but a complementary truth. Alternate translation: [Indeed,]

44.quote: לֹ֣א בְ⁠קַשְׁתִּ֣⁠י אֶבְטָ֑ח וְ֝⁠חַרְבִּ֗⁠י לֹ֣א תוֹשִׁיעֵֽ⁠נִי
44.text: The psalmist is using two kinds of weapons, his **bow** and his **sword**, to mean weapons in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I do not rely on my weapons, no, those weapons do not save me]

44.quote: לֹ֣א בְ⁠קַשְׁתִּ֣⁠י אֶבְטָ֑ח וְ֝⁠חַרְבִּ֗⁠י לֹ֣א תוֹשִׁיעֵֽ⁠נִי
44.text: If you decided to use first-person plural pronouns in verse 4, you may wish to do that here as well. Alternate translation: [We do not trust in our bows, and our swords do not save us] or [We do not rely on our weapons, no, those weapons do not save us]

The psalmist is speaking of his **sword** as if it were a living thing that could **save** him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I do not win victories with my sword]

The psalmist is saying **all of the day** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [continually]

In this context, God’s **name** seems to represent his reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and we will praise your reputation] or [and we will praise you for who you are]
See how your translation team decided at [3:2](../003/002.md) to represent the term “Selah.”

The psalmist is speaking as if God would previously **go out** physically with the Israelite **armies**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you no longer help our armies]

The psalmist may not mean to say that God is actively opposing the Judeans. He may be describing the consequences of God no longer helping them. Alternate translation: [You oblige us to turn back from the enemy]

In this context, the expression **for themselves** has the sense of “as they wish” or “at will,” that is, without any resistance. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [at will]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **sheep** that are characterized by being slaughtered and eaten as **food**. In context, the emphasis seems to be on the slaughtering, as the parallel phrase “sheep of slaughter” in verse 22 indicates. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [like sheep that are slaughtered]

The point of this comparison is that just as **sheep** that people slaughter for **food** are very vulnerable and easily killed, so the Judeans have become very vulnerable. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. The point of comparison is the same in verse 22. Alternate translation: [very vulnerable, like sheep that are slaughtered]

The psalmist means that God has not become greater in terms of wealth. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and you have not increased in wealth]

44.quote: תְּשִׂימֵ֣⁠נוּ חֶ֭רְפָּה לִ⁠שְׁכֵנֵ֑י⁠נוּ לַ֥עַג וָ֝⁠קֶ֗לֶס לִ⁠סְבִיבוֹתֵֽי⁠נוּ
44.text: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [You have made us a reproach to our neighbors, and you have made us a scorn and a derision to the ones around us]

44.quote: תְּשִׂימֵ֣⁠נוּ חֶ֭רְפָּה לִ⁠שְׁכֵנֵ֑י⁠נוּ לַ֥עַג וָ֝⁠קֶ֗לֶס לִ⁠סְבִיבוֹתֵֽי⁠נוּ
44.text: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **reproach**, **scorn**, and **derision**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [You have given our neighbors occasion to reproach us, and you have given the ones around us occasion to scorn and deride us]

The psalmist does not mean that God has made the Judeans something that causes **reproach** to their **neighbors**. He means that they have become an object of their neighbors’ reproach. He means the same thing when he uses the terms **scorn** and **derision**. If you retain these abstract nouns in your translation, you could indicate this explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [You have made us an object of reproach to our neighbors, an object of scorn and derision]

In this culture, shaking or wagging one’s head at a person or group was a symbolic action by which people showed contempt and expressed mockery toward that person or group. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [a group at which individuals among the peoples shake their heads contemptuously]
See how you translated the phrase “all of the day” in [44:8](../044/008.md). Alternate translation: [My disgrace is continually before me]
If you decided to use first-person plural pronouns in verses 4 and 6, you may wish to do that here as well. Alternate translation: [our disgrace is before us, and the shame of our faces covers us]

The psalmist is speaking as if his **disgrace** were actually an object that was **before** or in front of him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am aware of my disgrace]

The psalmist is using one part of himself, his **face**, to mean all of him in the act of being ashamed. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and my shame covers me]

The psalmist is speaking as if **shame** were physically covering him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the shame of my face overwhelms me]

Hebrew culture associated **shame** with the **face**. If your culture does the same thing, you may wish to retain the figurative usage in your translation and express this in terms that the people of your culture would use. Alternate translation: [I have lost face, and shame overwhelms me]
Here, **face** represents “presence.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the presence of]

Together, the expressions **an enemy** and **one avenging** express a single idea. The expression **one avenging** tells what kind of **enemy** the psalmist is describing. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [a vengeful enemy]

The psalmist is speaking of the misfortunes he has described as if they were a living thing that could have **come** to the Judeans. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation, as in the UST: [All of this has happened to us]

The psalmist is speaking as if the Judeans might actually have **forgotten** their God, that is, ceased to have remember anything about him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. The meaning is similar in verse 20. Alternate translation: [but we have not neglected to worship you]

The psalmist is speaking of God’s **covenant** as if it were a person with whom the Judeans could have **dealt falsely**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and we have not dealt falsely with you by not keeping your covenant]

The psalmist is using one part of the Judeans, their **heart**, to mean all of them in the act of remaining loyal to God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [We have not turned ourselves back]

The term **heart** is singular in form, but it refers to the hearts of all of the Judeans. If you retain the image of the heart, if it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of that word. Alternate translation: [Our hearts have not turned themselves back]

The psalmist is speaking as if the Judeans were physically following God and had not **turned** to go in the opposite direction. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [We are still loyal to you]

The psalmist is using one part of the Judeans, their **steps**, to mean all of them in the act of remaining loyal to God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and we have not turned aside from your way]

The psalmist is speaking as if how God wants people to live were a **way** or path on which people were supposed to walk. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [nor have we stopped living as you want us to live]

The psalmist is using the phrase **a place of jackals** to represent a desolate area where only wild animals live. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [so that our land is now desolate]

The term **jackals** describes wild dogs that live in desolate regions. If your readers would not be familiar with what a jackal is, in your translation you could use the name of a similar animal that your readers would recognize, or you could use a general expression. Alternate translation: [wild dogs]

The psalmist is speaking as if God had actually **covered** the Judeans with a **dark shadow**. He means that God has allowed them to be in a situation in which they are in great danger of death. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you have brought us into a situation of mortal peril]

44.quote: אִם־שָׁ֭כַחְנוּ שֵׁ֣ם אֱלֹהֵ֑י⁠נוּ וַ⁠נִּפְרֹ֥שׂ כַּ֝פֵּ֗י⁠נוּ לְ⁠אֵ֣ל זָֽר׃ הֲ⁠לֹ֣א אֱ֭לֹהִים יַֽחֲקָר־זֹ֑את כִּֽי־ה֥וּא יֹ֝דֵ֗עַ תַּעֲלֻמ֥וֹת לֵֽב
44.text: If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine [44:20](../044/020.md) and [44:21](../044/021.md) into a verse bridge and put the last phrase in verse 21 at the beginning of verse 20, since it gives the reason for the result that the material in the rest of these verses describes. Alternate translation: [Since our God knows the secrets of the heart, if we had forgotten his name and spread out our palms to a foreign god, would he not have discovered this?]

In this context, **the name of our God** represents calling on God by name. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [If we had ceased to call on our God by name] or [If we had ceased to worship our God explicitly]

The psalmist is using the action of spreading out one’s **palms** toward the sky to represent prayer, since that was the characteristic posture of prayer in this culture. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and prayed]

The psalmist is using the question form to make a strong affirmation. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [God would certainly have discovered this!]

Here the **heart** represents a person’s private thoughts and memories. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the things that people do but do not tell others about]

The expression **are killed** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [our enemies are killing us]
See how you translated the same expression in [44:8](../044/008.md). Alternate translation: [continually]

The expression **are considered** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [our enemies consider us]

The psalmist is using the question form as a rebuke. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Awake! You should not be sleeping, Lord! Wake up!]

The psalmist is speaking as if God were actually **sleeping** and therefore unaware of or unconcerned about the Judeans’ situation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Take action! You should not do nothing while we are in such danger! Help us!]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a request rather than a command. (By contrast, the imperatives **Awake** and **Wake up** are urgent summonses rather than requests.) Use a form in your language that communicates a request. Alternate translation: [Please do not reject us]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Why do you hide your face, and why do you forget our affliction and our oppression]

As in the previous verse, the psalmist is using the question form as a rebuke. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You should not hide your face, and you should not forget our affliction and our oppression!]

The psalmist is speaking as if God had actually hidden his **face** so that the Judeans could not see it. He means that it is as if God had turned his face away from the Judeans rather than looking at them with a bright expression that indicated favor. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Why do you not regard us with favor] or [Please regard us with favor, and do not forget]

The psalmist is speaking as if God had once known about the **affliction** and **oppression** of the Judeans but had now forgotten about them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [neglect to do anything about]
Here the psalmist is using the word **For** to introduce a reason why God should help the Judeans. Alternate translation: [Help us because]

44.quote: שָׁ֣חָה לֶ⁠עָפָ֣ר נַפְשֵׁ֑⁠נוּ דָּבְקָ֖ה לָ⁠אָ֣רֶץ בִּטְנֵֽ⁠נוּ
44.text: The psalmist is speaking as if the Judeans had physically fallen onto the **earth** and could not get up and as if their **soul** or inner being had similarly **sunk down into the dust**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [We have no physical strength left, as if we had fallen down and could not get up, and we have no strength in our inner beings either, as if they had collapsed into the dust]

In this verse, the words **soul** and **belly** are singular in form, but they refer to the souls and bellies of all of the Judeans. If you retain the images that the psalmist is using, if it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural forms of these words. Alternate translation: [our souls have sunk … our bellies cling]

The psalmist is using one part of a person, his **belly**, to mean all of him in the act of clinging to the **earth**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [our bodies cling to the earth]

The psalmist is speaking as if each Judean’s **belly** or body were actually clinging to the **earth**. He means that it is as if each Judean had fallen and could not get up. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [our bodies have fallen to the earth and we cannot get up]

44.quote: ק֭וּמָֽ⁠ה עֶזְרָ֣תָ⁠ה לָּ֑⁠נוּ וּ֝⁠פְדֵ֗⁠נוּ לְמַ֣עַן חַסְדֶּֽ⁠ךָ
44.text: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [because of your covenant faithfulness, arise as a helper to us and redeem us]

The psalmist assumes that God will understand that by **Arise**, he means “Take action.” You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Take action]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please take action]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in order to be faithful to your covenant]

45.text:
# Psalm 45 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 45 is a royal psalm written for a king’s wedding day. At the same time, it is a Messianic psalm that looks forward to the reign of Jesus Christ. [Hebrews 1:8–9](../001/008.md) applies Psalm 45:6–7 to Jesus. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. The psalmist’s self-introduction (1)
2. Praise for the king as God’s representative who maintains justice (2–8)
3. Transition from the king to the bride (9)
4. Exhortation to the king’s bride (10–17)

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a “maskil.” See the discussion of that term in the introduction to Psalms.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Whose wedding was this?

Psalm 45 is a royal wedding song for a historical king, composed for an actual court marriage. This king was probably a descendant of David, and he was certainly loyal to Yahweh, but the psalmist does not name him, so it is uncertain exactly which king he is describing. The exalted language about the king’s eternal throne and perfectly just rule has led both ancient and modern interpreters to see this psalm as deliberately shaped to point beyond that occasion to God’s ultimate King. Because Hebrews 1:8–9 applies Psalm 45:6–7 to Christ, both Jewish and Christian traditions have often treated the psalm as Messianic, seeing the historical king and his bride as a type or foreshadowing of the ultimate King and his people. So we recommend that you not suggest in a note or in the text of your translation for which king the psalmist may have composed this wedding song.

### Why does the psalmist call the king “God” in verse 6?

As a note to this verse suggests, the Hebrew term that is often translated as “God” in other contexts was also a respectful form of address for judges. Since this verse speaks of the king as upholding justice, that title would be appropriate for him in this context. That is one likely explanation of why the psalmist uses this term. However, other interpreters suggest that the phrase “Your throne, God” could mean “Your throne of God,” that is, “your divinely ordained throne.” Translators might represent this as “The kingdom that God has given you.” One other possibility is that the psalmist could be addressing God directly but briefly in this sentence and then returning to address the king through the end of verse 9, after which he addresses the bride. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to follow the interpretation that it does. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to follow the interpretation suggested in these notes.

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. See how you translated the term “chief musician” in the superscription to Psalm 4. Alternate translation: [For the leader of worship music] or [For the music director]

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a **maskil**. Since the meaning of this word is not certain, you may wish to represent it in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language. See the discussion of that term in the Introduction to Psalms.
See how you translated the expression “the sons of Korah” in the superscription to Psalm 42. Alternate translation: [the descendants of Korah] or [the Korahites]

The superscription to this wedding psalm uses the plural form **loves** to refer to the love of the king for his new wife and the love of the queen for her new husband. It may be more natural in your language to use the singular form. Alternate translation: [A love song]

The verb that the ULT translates as **boils over** occurs only here in the Bible, but it comes from the same root as a term for a pot or cauldron, so that seems to be its meaning. However, in this context, the focus is not on the heat that causes a liquid to boil. It is on the way a boiling liquid may overflow from a pot. Particularly if your language and culture associate heat with anger, it may be helpful to express the general meaning in order not to suggest that the psalmist is angry. Alternate translation: [My heart overflows with a good matter]

Here the **heart** represents a person’s thoughts. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [My mind overflows with a good matter] or [My thoughts about a good matter are overflowing]

The psalmist is speaking as if his **heart** (his mind) were actually overflowing with the **matter** he will describe in this psalm. He means that he finds his subject so inspiring that he cannot contain his thoughts about it; that is, he must speak out loud what he thinks about it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. (See the further discussion of this in the introduction to this psalm.) Alternate translation: [My subject is so inspiring that I must express my thoughts about it aloud]

The psalmist says **I am reciting** because he has already begun to sing his composition. However, since he is referring to the part of it that will follow, in some languages it may be more natural to use a verb in the future tense here. Alternate translation: [I will recite]

The psalmist is using the plural term **works** to refer to the many elements he has incorporated into this song. In some languages it may be more natural to use a singular term to refer to his entire composition. Alternate translation: [my work] or [my composition]

The phrase that the ULT translates as **to the king** may indicate: (1) that the psalmist is performing this song for the king and directing it to him. The ULT reflects this meaning. (2) that the psalmist has composed this song about the king. Alternate translation: [about the king]

The psalmist is speaking as if his **tongue** were actually a **stylus** that belonged to a **scribe** who was able to record quickly and accurately what he heard people say. The psalmist means that even though he has many thoughts that he would like to share on this occasion, he will be able to sing them all articulately and continuously. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will be able to express all of my thoughts articulately and continuously in this song]

In verse 1, the psalmist was addressing all of his listeners. Here he begins to address the king directly. In some cultures, a person would not begin to speak to a ruler without using a specific form of address. If your culture has such a form, you could use it in your translation. Alternate translation: [Your Majesty, you are fairer than the sons of man]

45.quote: יָפְיָפִ֡יתָ מִ⁠בְּנֵ֬י אָדָ֗ם ה֣וּצַק חֵ֭ן בְּ⁠שְׂפְתוֹתֶ֑י⁠ךָ
45.text: The words **You** and **your** are singular here and in the rest of the psalm because the psalmist is always addressing an individual. So use singular forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

The psalmist is using **sons of man** as a common expression of his culture to mean “human beings.” He is not implying that the king is not a man. He means that he is **fairer** or more handsome than all the other **sons of man**. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [You are more handsome than other people]

The psalmist is making an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. (However, since an overstatement like this one was an appropriate compliment for a ruler in this culture, you may wish to retain the overstatement in your translation. The UST models one way to do that.) Alternate translation: [You are an exceptionally handsome man]

The psalmist is using or creating a special form of a verb that means “to be beautiful” by doubling its root. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [You are handsome, far more handsome than other men]

The expression **is poured** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. If you need to say who has done this action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [God has poured grace onto your lips]

The psalmist is speaking as if **Grace** had actually been **poured** onto the **lips** of the king. In context, the emphasis seems to be not on the action of pouring but on the result of pouring. When a liquid is poured onto a surface, it spreads out and covers that surface. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Grace covers your lips] or [Your lips are entirely gracious]

Here the king’s **lips** represent his speech. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Your speech is entirely gracious]

The psalmist is not using the word **Therefore** to indicate that the king’s attractive appearance and gracious speech are the reasons why **God** has **blessed** him. He means that these characteristics of the king are evidence that God has blessed him. If a term such as “therefore” would not communicate this meaning in your language, you may want to use a different connecting word or phrase to show how the following statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [This is how we know that]

The psalmist is using one action that a **warrior** would do in preparation for fighting a battle, strapping his **sword** onto his **thigh**, to refer to being equipped for battle in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Prepare yourself to do battle]

While the expression **Gird** is an imperative, the psalmist is not telling the king to do something or suggesting that he is not already doing it. Instead, the psalmist is celebrating what the king is already doing. It may be more natural in your language to express this meaning by using a form other than an imperative. Alternate translation: [You are always prepared to do battle]

As the next verse indicates, the psalmist wants the king to use his power specifically to uphold justice. This may not necessarily involve fighting an actual battle. You could indicate this in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Be prepared to use your power to uphold justice] or [You are always prepared to use your power to uphold justice]

Together the terms **glory** and **majesty** express a single idea. The word **majesty** characterizes this man as a king, and the word **glory** tells what kind of king he is, specifically when he fights for justice. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [as a glorious king]
See how you represented the term “majesty” in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [And as a king]

The phrase **prosper, ride out** expresses a single idea. The word **prosper**, meaning “succeed” or “triumph,” tells in what way the psalmist wants the king to **ride out** in his chariot. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [ride out triumphantly] or [ride out to victory]

The psalmist is speaking as if he actually wanted the king to **ride out** in his chariot to fight a battle. As in the previous verse, he wants the king to use his power to uphold justice without necessarily involve fighting an actual battle. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [use your power triumphantly]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **truth**, **humility**, and **righteousness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [to establish a reign that is truthful, humble, and righteous]

The psalmist is speaking of the king’s **right hand** as if it were a living thing that could **teach** him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May you discover that you can do fearful things with your right hand]

The psalmist is using the king’s **right hand** to represent him using his sword and shooting arrows with that hand or, more generally, to represent him fighting against his enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [May you discover that you can do fearful things by using your sword and shooting arrows] or [May you discover that you can do fearful things as you fight against your enemies]

The expression **fearful things** is a passive verbal form, a participle that the psalmist is using as a noun. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [things that terrify your opponents]

45.quote: חִצֶּ֗י⁠ךָ שְׁנ֫וּנִ֥ים עַ֭מִּים תַּחְתֶּ֣י⁠ךָ יִפְּל֑וּ בְּ֝⁠לֵ֗ב אוֹיְבֵ֥י הַ⁠מֶּֽלֶךְ
45.text: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information that the arrows are **in the heart of the enemies of the king** with the information that the **arrows are sharp**. Alternate translation: [Your arrows are sharp in the heart of the enemies of the king; the peoples fall under you]

The psalmist says that these **arrows** are **sharp** to mean that they penetrate through armor into the bodies of enemy soldiers. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Your arrows penetrate]

The psalmist is speaking as if **the peoples** who fight against the king actually **fall** down dead or wounded and he drives his chariot over them, so that they are **under** him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you win victory over the peoples]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. If you decide not to move this phrase to an earlier part of the verse, after **Your arrows are sharp**, you can supply those words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Your arrows are in the heart of the enemies of the king] or [Your arrows penetrate into the heart of the enemies of the king]

In this verse, the word **heart** is singular in form, but it refers to the hearts of all of the king’s **enemies**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “heart.” Alternate translation: [in the hearts of]

The psalmist is speaking of the king in the third person even though he is addressing him directly. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the second person. Alternate translation: [your enemies] or [your enemies, O king]
Here the king’s **throne** represents his reign. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Your reign]

The Hebrew term that is translated as “God” in most contexts can sometimes be used to refer respectfully to judges. There are probable examples of this in [Exodus 21:6](../exo/21/06.md), [Exodus 22:9](../exo/22/09.md), [Exodus 22:28](../exo/22/28.md), and [Psalm 82:1](../082/001.md). Since the rest of this verse speaks of the king enforcing justice, this seems to be another instance of that usage. (The psalmist clarifies in the next verse that the king is subject to God himself, who is his God.) To avoid the impression that the psalmist is addressing the king as if he were God or a god, it may be helpful to use a comparable respectful form of address in your language. (See the further discussion of this in the introduction to this psalm.) Alternate translation: [O royal judge]

Here the king’s **scepter** represents his rule. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [You rule your kingdom with justice]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **righteousness** and **wickedness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [You love right actions, and you hate wicked actions]

The psalmist is speaking as if **God** had actually **anointed** the king with **oil** that consisted of or imparted **joy**. The image of pouring out a fluid so that it covers someone conveys the idea of abundance. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [has given you abundant joy, more than your companions]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **joy**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [has made you very joyful, more than your companions]

The psalmist is speaking as if the king’s **garments** were actually made of the spices **Myrrh**, **aloes**, and **cassia**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all of your garments are fragrant with myrrh and aloes and cassia] or [myrrh, aloes, and cassia scent all of your garments]

**Myrrh**, **aloes**, and **cassia** are fragrant spices. If your readers would not be familiar with these spices, we do not recommend that you use the names of similar spices that your readers might recognize, since the psalmist is describing a real historical situation. Instead, you could use a general expression. Alternate translation: [Fragrant spices]

The psalmist is using the plural **palaces** where he could have used the singular form. This suggests that he is using the plural form to emphasize the vast extent of the king’s palace complex, which may include several buildings. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the singular and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [your vast palace of]

The psalmist is using **stringed instruments** to represent the music that people are playing on those instruments. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the music of stringed instruments is making you rejoice]

The psalmist is using the adjective **precious** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. (The ULT indicates this by supplying the word **ones**.) Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [are among your honored women] or [are among the ladies of your court]

The expression **is stationed** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [is standing]

Having the **queen** stand at his **right hand** (that is, on his right side) was a symbolic action by which the king honored his bride. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [in a place of honor at your right side]

Here, **gold of Ophir** represents garments decorated with that very fine gold, as verses 13 and 14 indicate. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in garments decorated with gold of Ophir]
The word **Ophir** is the name of a land that produced gold of excellent quality.

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and do that here and throughout this psalm.
