Alternate translation: [Listen carefully, daughter, and consider] or [Listen, daughter, and consider, yes, incline your ear]

The psalmist is addressing the bride with the courteous and gentle expression that wise older people in this culture used to address young people whom they were teaching. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [young lady]

The psalmist is speaking as if he wants the bride physically to **incline** her **ear**, that is, to lean over the way someone would do to pay close attention to someone. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and pay close attention]

The psalmist is speaking as if he wanted the bride actually to **forget** her nation and family. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and do not wish that you were still with your people and in the house of your father]

Here the term **house** represents the “household” of the bride’s **father**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and your family]

The psalmist is using one part of the bride, her **beauty**, to mean all of her in the act of being attractive to the king. The psalmist means that if she gives the king her exclusive devotion, as he advised her in the previous verse, not just her physical appearance but her qualities of loyalty and faithfulness will make the king appreciate and love her. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [This will make you very attractive to the king]

Bowing low to the ground in front of the king was a symbolic action by which the bride showed her acceptance of his authority over her both as her new husband and as her new king. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [prostrate yourself respectfully and submissively to him]

45.quote: וּ⁠בַֽת־צֹ֨ר ׀ בְּ֭⁠מִנְחָה פָּנַ֥יִ⁠ךְ יְחַלּ֗וּ עֲשִׁ֣ירֵי עָֽם
45.text: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from later in the verse if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [The rich of the people will entreat your face; the daughter of Tyre will do so with a gift]

The psalmist is speaking as if the city of **Tyre** were a mother and its people were its **daughter**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The people of Tyre]

The psalmist may be using one particularly wealthy and influential kingdom, **Tyre**, to represent foreign kingdoms in general. This would be complementary to **the people** of Israel or Judah whom he mentions later in the verse. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Representatives of foreign kingdoms]

The psalmist is using the adjective **rich** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the rich citizens among our people]
Here the queen’s **face** represents her “favor.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your favor]

45.quote: כָּל־כְּבוּדָּ֣ה בַת־מֶ֣לֶךְ פְּנִ֑ימָה מִֽ⁠מִּשְׁבְּצ֖וֹת זָהָ֣ב לְבוּשָֽׁ⁠הּ
45.text: In this poem celebrating the king’s wedding, the psalmist is not following a strict chronological sequence. In verse 9, he presented a portrait of the bride, groom, and attendants in their formal places at the ceremony. In verses 13–15, he describes the procession of the bride and her attendants to the ceremony. That procession took place before he started singing this song, so in some languages, it may be appropriate to describe them in a past tense. The UST models one way to do that.

By **the daughter of the king**, the psalmist means the same person whom he calls the “queen” in verse 9. (This indicates that her father is the **king** of a foreign country.) You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the royal bride]
The psalmist is using the term **within** to mean a room or apartment within the palace where the bride has dressed for her wedding. Alternate translation: [in her chamber]

The expression **will be led** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Royal officials will lead her]

The psalmist is addressing the king once again, as the pronoun **you** at the end of the verse indicates. So it may be more natural in some languages to use a second-person form here. Alternate translation: [to you, O king,]

Here, **embroidery** represents embroidered garments, that is, garments decorated with embroidery. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in embroidered garments]

The term **embroidery** describes the art of making decorative designs in cloth by using needles to work colored threads into it to make beautiful images or patterns. If your readers would not be familiar with what embroidery is, in your translation you could use a general expression. Alternate translation: [in garments decorated with colored thread]

The expression **will be brought** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Royal officials will bring her companions to you, the virgins who follow her]

The psalmist is speaking of **joy** and **rejoicing** as if they were living things that could lead the bride and her attendants into the king’s palace. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [There will be joy and rejoicing as they will enter]

The terms **joy** and **rejoicing** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [with great joy]
See how you translated the similar expression “to the king” in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [into your palace, O king]

The psalmist is using the term **fathers** to represent “ancestors,” and he is using the term **sons** to represent “descendants.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your ancestors … your descendants]
Since the psalmist is referring to multiple people (**sons** or descendants), it may be more natural in many languages to use a plural pronoun here. Alternate translation: [you will make them]

The psalmist is saying **all** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. (However, since an overstatement like this one was an appropriate compliment for a ruler in this culture, you may wish to retain the overstatement in your translation, as the UST does. See what you decided to do in verse 2.) Alternate translation: [in many parts of the world]
Here the king’s **name** represents his reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your reputation]

It might seem that this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [in every generation] or [from generation to generation]

46.text:
# Psalm 46 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 46 is a psalm of trust. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. First stanza (1–3): God as a refuge in an earthquake and an ocean storm
2. Second stanza (4–6): God as a helper in the turmoil of the nations
3. First refrain (7): Statement of trust
4. Third stanza (8–10): Yahweh as the one who ends wars
5. Second refrain (11): Statement of trust

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### What “stream” is the psalmist describing in verse 4?

Like Psalm 44, this psalm could have been written during the Assyrian invasion of Judah and siege of Jerusalem in 701 B.C. During a siege, the attacking army tried to cut off supplies of food and water to the people inside a city to make them surrender. But Jerusalem had its own water supply. The Gihon spring higher up on Mount Zion produced a steady stream of water. Kings such as Hezekiah engineered channels to bring its water safely into the city even during a siege. The psalmist is most likely referring to the life-giving stream of water from the Gihon spring and using it as a symbol of Yahweh’s care and provision for the people. The contrast between the images of this quiet stream and the violent ocean storm portrayed in the previous verse highlights the main theme of the psalm. Even in the midst of tumultuous and threatening events, Yahweh is always helping his people.

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

### Intentionally repeated terms

The psalmist uses the same verb for “roared” in verse 6 as he does for “roar” in verse 3. He uses the same verb for “shook” in verse 6 as he does for “shaking” in verse 2. He expects readers to realize as a result that he was using the sea in verse 3 to represent the “nations” he describes in verse 6 and that he was using the mountains in verse 2 to represent the “kingdoms” he describes in verse 6. So that your readers can appreciate this, we encourage you to use the same terms in your language for “roared” and “shook” in verse 6 that you use in verses 2 and 3 for “roar” and “shaking.”

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information that this is a **song** with the information that one of the **sons of Korah** wrote it. Alternate translation: [A song of the sons of Korah. On Alamoth]

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. See how you translated the term “chief musician” in the superscription to Psalm 4. Alternate translation: [For the leader of worship music] or [For the music director]
See how you translated the expression “the sons of Korah” in the superscription to Psalm 42. Alternate translation: [Of the descendants of Korah] or [Of the Korahites]
See how you translated the similar expression “On Sheminith” in the superscription to Psalm 6. Alternate translation: [Set to the tune Alamoth]

The term that the ULT translates as **Maidens** could be the name of the tune of this psalm. It might also be a musical instruction indicating that singers should perform the song in a higher range. Alternate translation: [Perform in a higher range]

The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were actually a refuge, that is, a place where people can go to be safe from danger. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the term “refuge” in [14:6](../014/006.md). Alternate translation: [God protects us and makes us strong]

The psalmist could be using the terms **refuge** and **strength** together to express a single idea. The word **strength** would tell what kind of **refuge** God is. If you follow this interpretation in your translation, and if it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [God is our strong refuge] or [God powerfully protects us]

The term **greatly** describes the degree or extent to which God is **found** to be **a help in trouble**. Translators may choose to put the focus either on the finding or the helping. Alternate translation: [being dependably found a help in trouble] or [being found a great help in trouble]

The psalmist is using the term **found** in a way characteristic of his language to mean that when one is **in trouble**, God can be **found**; that is, he is present. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He is dependably present to help in trouble]

The expression **being found** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, but a form of the verb “find” would communicate the psalmist’s meaning in your language, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural. Alternate translation: [We dependably find him a help in trouble] or [We find him a great help in trouble]

The psalmist is speaking as if the deep part of the sea were actually its **heart**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [into the depths of]

The psalmist is using the plural **seas** where he could have used the singular form. (In the next verse, he refers back to the sea using a singular pronoun.) This suggests that he is using the plural form to emphasize the vastness of the sea. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the singular and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [the vast sea]

In each instance, the pronoun **its** refers to “the seas” in the previous verse. Since that is a plural term, you may wish to use a plural pronoun or to repeat the noun for clarity. You may have chosen to use a singular form of the noun in your translation. Alternate translation: [should their waters roar and foam, should the mountains quake at their swelling] or [should the waters of the sea roar and foam, should the mountains quake at the swelling of the sea]
To translate the term **Selah** here and in verses 7 and 11, see how your translation team decided to represent that term in [3:2](../003/002.md).

The psalmist is using **the city of God** (that is, Jerusalem) to represent the people of that city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people of the city of God]

The psalmist is using the adjective **holy** as a noun to mean a certain kind of place. (The ULT indicates this by supplying the word **place**.) Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the holy dwelling place of the Most High]

The psalmist is speaking of the temple in Jerusalem as if it were a place in which God actually lived. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the holy temple of the Most High]

The psalmist is using the plural **dwellings** where he could have used the singular form. This suggests that, as in [43:3](../043/003.md), he is using the plural form to emphasize the sacred character of the temple as a place where God is present in a special way. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the singular form and express the emphasis in another way. If it would be extra information to say both “holy” and “sacred” in your translation, you could use another term to make one of those words emphatic. Alternate translation: [the very holy dwelling of the Most High] or [the very sacred temple of the Most High]

The pronouns **her** and **she** refer to the city of Jerusalem. It was common in this culture to envision a city as a mother and its residents as her children. If your language has a neuter pronoun that it uses for impersonal entities, it may be more natural to use that here. You could also repeat the noun from the previous verse. Alternate translation: [God is in the midst of the city, it will not be shaken]

The expression **will not be shaken** contains a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [no one will shake her] or [no one will shake it]

The psalmist is speaking as if the city of Jerusalem might actually be **shaken** by the “nations” he describes in the next verse. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [it will not be destroyed]

The pronoun **her**, referring to the city of Jerusalem, represents the people of that city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. See what you did in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [God will help the people of that city]

The psalmist is using **at the turning of the morning** as a common expression of his culture to refer to the time when night ends and day begins. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [at the break of day] or [as soon as it becomes light]

The psalmist is speaking as if God were going to help the people of Jerusalem at the actual **turning of the morning**, that is, as soon as it became light on a certain day. He means that the time of trouble, pictured as a dark night, will surely end as God brings deliverance. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when he brings deliverance]

The psalmist is speaking as if these **nations** might actually **roar** and these **kingdoms** might actually **shake**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Nations may attack kingdoms and devastate them]

It was characteristic of this culture to speak of thunder as if it were actually the **voice** of God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar expression in [18:13](../018/013.md). Alternate translation: [He causes thunder]

The psalmist is speaking as if God actually causes thunder in the situations he is describing. He is doing that to represent God acting powerfully. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He acts powerfully]

The psalmist is speaking as if the **earth** actually **melts**. He is using the **earth** to represent the people of the earth, specifically hostile armies. He is using the term **melts** to mean that they will dissipate, that is, cease to be an organized force and go away. Alternate translation: [armies that threaten us dissipate]

The psalmist is using a common expression of his culture to mean that Yahweh is helping the Judeans. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation, as in the UST: [is helping us]
See how you translated the similar term “refuge” in [46:1](../046/001.md). Alternate translation: [the God of Jacob is protecting us]
Here **Jacob**, the ancestor of the Israelites (whose name God changed to Israel), represents the nation that consists of his descendants. Alternate translation: [the God of us Israelites]

The psalmist is not telling his listeners to **Come** somewhere with him. He is saying **Come** to encourage them to take action. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [Come on]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **desolations**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [who makes the earth desolate]

As in verse 6, here the **earth** seems to represent the people of the earth and specifically the armies that are threatening Jerusalem. Alternate translation: [who desolates armies that threaten us] or [who destroys armies that threaten us]

The psalmist is speaking of the effects of Yahweh’s action from the perspective of looking off as far as he can see in one direction, to one **end** of the **earth**. He is using that one direction to represent how Yahweh’s action will have effects in every direction. (While in verses 6 and 9 the term “earth” had a symbolic meaning, now that Yahweh has defeated the forces opposing his people, the “earth” has the sense of a literal place.) Alternate translation: [to the ends of the earth] or [throughout the earth]

46.quote: קֶ֣שֶׁת יְ֭שַׁבֵּר וְ⁠קִצֵּ֣ץ חֲנִ֑ית עֲ֝גָל֗וֹת יִשְׂרֹ֥ף בָּ⁠אֵֽשׁ
46.text: The psalmist is not referring to a specific **bow** or **spear** or to specific **wagons**. He means those things in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [He shatters bows and spears in pieces; he burns wagons with fire]

46.quote: קֶ֣שֶׁת יְ֭שַׁבֵּר וְ⁠קִצֵּ֣ץ חֲנִ֑ית עֲ֝גָל֗וֹת יִשְׂרֹ֥ף בָּ⁠אֵֽשׁ
46.text: The psalmist does not mean that Yahweh actually does these things personally. He is speaking of the effects of Yahweh’s action of ending wars. Alternate translation: [He keeps people from using weapons and equipment to wage war]

It might seem that this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, if you retain this image in your translation, you can shorten this expression. Alternate translation: [he burns up the wagons]

This verse is a direct quotation of Yahweh. The ULT indicates that by putting the verse inside quotation marks. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could also use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says, “Be still and know that I {am} God]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and do that here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [I will be high among the nations of the earth] or [I will be high among the nations; indeed, I will be high on the earth]

Yahweh is speaking as if he were actually going to be in a **high** location. He means that he will receive honor. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. The UST models one way to do that.

46.quote: יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֣וֹת עִמָּ֑⁠נוּ מִשְׂגָּֽב־לָ֝⁠נוּ אֱלֹהֵ֖י יַעֲקֹ֣ב
46.text: This is the second instance of the refrain of this poem. The first instance is in verse 7. To help your readers appreciate this, translate this verse the same way you translated that verse.

47.text:
# Psalm 47 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 47 is a psalm of praise. It is a specific type of praise psalm, a divine enthronement psalm. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Call to worship (1)
2. Reason to worship (2–5)
3. Call to worship (6)
4. Reason to worship (7–9)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### What “peoples” and “nations” had Yahweh enabled the Israelites to subdue (v. 3)?

The psalmist does not give specific details of the victory he is celebrating. This might be a general song of praise to Yahweh, in which case verse 3 might be translated, “He subdues peoples under us and nations under our feet.” However, interpreters have suggested one likely historical occasion for the composition of this psalm. It is generally agreed that the Korahites wrote their psalms in the later years of the kingdom of Judah. During the reign of Jehoshaphat, as [2 Chronicles 20:1–30](../2ch/20/01.md) relates, a huge army of Moabite, Ammonite, and Meunite soldiers attacked Judah. The Judeans felt unable to defeat this army, but people from all over Judah gathered at the temple and Jehoshaphat prayed for Yahweh’s help. He appealed to him on the grounds that he had promised to give the land of Israel to the descendants of Abraham. Yahweh made the invading soldiers from the different countries fight against each other, so the enemy army destroyed itself. As a result, the people of the surrounding kingdoms came to fear and respect Yahweh greatly. The psalmist may be referring to this in verse 9 when he describes people from all nations worshiping “the God of Abraham.”

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

### The order of reasons and results

As the introduction to the book of Psalms discusses, the typical pattern of a psalm of praise is to issue a call to worship and then give a reason to worship. A psalm of praise may do this more than once. (This psalm does it twice.) It would be helpful to follow this pattern to show your readers how these psalms work. However, if, as a rule, your language would not give a reason after a result, you could create verse bridges for verses 1 and 2 and verses 6 and 7 in order to put the reasons before the results.

In the ULT, which follows the Hebrew order, verses 1 and 2 read this way:
Clap a palm, all peoples!
Shout to God with a voice of rejoicing.
For Yahweh, the Most High, is to be feared,
the great king over all of the earth.

In your translation, you might present them as verse 1–2 this way:
Since Yahweh, the Most High,
the great king over all of the earth, is to be feared,
Clap a palm, all peoples!
Shout to God with a voice of rejoicing.

In the ULT, verses 6 and 7 read this way:
Sing praise {to} God, sing praise!
Sing praise {to} our King, sing praise!
 For God {is} the king of all of the earth.
Sing praise {with} a maskil.

In your translation, you might present them as verse 6–7 this way:
Since God is the king of all of the earth,
Sing praise to God, sing praise!
Sing praise to our king, sing praise!
Sing praise with a maskil.

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. See how you translated the term “chief musician” in the superscription to Psalm 4. Alternate translation: [For the leader of worship music] or [For the music director]
See how you translated the expression “the sons of Korah” in the superscription to Psalm 42. Alternate translation: [of the descendants of Korah] or [of the Korahites]
Since people strike their palms together in order to applaud, it may be more natural in your language to use a plural term here. Alternate translation, as in the UST: [Clap your hands]

It might seem that to say both **Shout** and **voice** would be to express extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can use just one of these terms in your translation. Alternate translation: [Celebrate by shouting to God] or [Lift your voice to God in rejoicing]

47.quote: כִּֽי־יְהוָ֣ה עֶלְי֣וֹן נוֹרָ֑א מֶ֥לֶךְ גָּ֝דוֹל עַל־כָּל־הָ⁠אָֽרֶץ
47.text: This verse gives the reason for the result that the previous verse describes. See the discussion in the introduction to this psalm of how you might order the reason and result here and in verses 6 and 7.

47.quote: יְהוָ֣ה עֶלְי֣וֹן נוֹרָ֑א מֶ֥לֶךְ גָּ֝דוֹל עַל־כָּל־הָ⁠אָֽרֶץ
47.text: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information that Yahweh is **the great king over all of the earth** with the information that he is **the Most High**. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, the Most High, the great king over all of the earth, is to be feared]

The expression **is to be feared** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [People should fear Yahweh, the Most High]

47.quote: יַדְבֵּ֣ר עַמִּ֣ים תַּחְתֵּ֑י⁠נוּ וּ֝⁠לְאֻמִּ֗ים תַּ֣חַת רַגְלֵֽי⁠נוּ
47.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. It may be clearer in your language to connect the phrases with a word other than **and** in order to show that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Another approach would be to combine the phrases and express the emphasis in another way. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and do that here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [He has subdued peoples under us, yes, he has subdued nations under our feet] or [He has subdued many nations under our feet]

47.quote: יַדְבֵּ֣ר עַמִּ֣ים תַּחְתֵּ֑י⁠נוּ וּ֝⁠לְאֻמִּ֗ים תַּ֣חַת רַגְלֵֽי⁠נוּ
47.text: The psalmist is speaking as if Yahweh actually put **peoples** and **nations** **under** the **feet** of the Israelites. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He has enabled us to defeat peoples, yes, he has enabled us to defeat nations] or [He has enabled us to defeat many nations]

The psalmist is speaking as if the land of Canaan were something that the Israelites had inherited as a lasting possession. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the land that would be our lasting possession]

The psalmist is using **Jacob** to represent his descendants. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the pride of the descendants of Jacob, whom he loved]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **pride**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [of which the descendants of Jacob, whom he loved, are proud]
See how your translation team decided at [3:2](../003/002.md) to represent the term **Selah**.

47.quote: עָלָ֣ה אֱ֭לֹהִים בִּ⁠תְרוּעָ֑ה יְ֝הֹוָ֗ה בְּ⁠ק֣וֹל שׁוֹפָֽר
47.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Yahweh our God has gone up with a shout and the sound of a shofar]

47.quote: עָלָ֣ה אֱ֭לֹהִים בִּ⁠תְרוּעָ֑ה יְ֝הֹוָ֗ה בְּ⁠ק֣וֹל שׁוֹפָֽר
47.text: The psalmist is using the expression **gone up** to mean that God has ascended onto his throne as king. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [God has ascended his throne with a shout, Yahweh with the sound of a shofar] or [Yahweh our God has ascended his throne with a shout and the sound of a shofar]

47.quote: עָלָ֣ה אֱ֭לֹהִים בִּ⁠תְרוּעָ֑ה יְ֝הֹוָ֗ה בְּ⁠ק֣וֹל שׁוֹפָֽר
47.text: The psalmist is using God going up onto his throne to represent him assuming the role of king. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [God has become king with a shout, Yahweh with the sound of a shofar] or [Yahweh our God has become king with a shout and the sound of a shofar]

47.quote: עָלָ֣ה אֱ֭לֹהִים בִּ⁠תְרוּעָ֑ה יְ֝הֹוָ֗ה בְּ⁠ק֣וֹל שׁוֹפָֽר
47.text: As passages such as [2 Samuel 15:10](../2sa/15/10.md) and [2 Kings 9:13](../2ki/09/13.md) illustrate, shouting that a person was the king and blowing a shofar were symbolic actions by which people acclaimed that person as their new king. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of these actions in the text of your translation or in a footnote. The UST models one way to do that.

47.quote: זַמְּר֣וּ אֱלֹהִ֣ים זַמֵּ֑רוּ זַמְּר֖וּ לְ⁠מַלְכֵּ֣⁠נוּ זַמֵּֽרוּ
47.text: In each part of this verse, the psalmist is repeating the expression “sing praise” in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat expressions for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Sing praise to God enthusiastically! Yes, sing praise to our king enthusiastically!]

The psalmist is using a musical term here, **maskil**, that also occurs in the superscriptions to several psalms. Biblical scholars have different understandings of what this term means. (See the discussion in the introduction to the book of Psalms.) Since the meaning is not certain, in your translation, you may wish to represent this word in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language, as the ULT does. You could also use a general expression, as the UST does.

Since the psalmist has already used the name **God** earlier in this sentence, it may be more natural in your language to use a pronoun here. (However, the repetition of the name has a poetic effect, so you may wish to repeat the name in your own translation.) Alternate translation: [he sits on the throne of his holiness]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe a **throne**, representing God’s reign, that is characterized by **holiness**. The idea is that God’s reign is not common, that is, it is not like the usual reign of kings on earth, who are not always just in their dealings with their people. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [God reigns with perfect justice] or [he reigns with perfect justice]

The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before as modeled in the UST.

Here, **shields** represents “rulers,” since rulers are protectors. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the rulers of the earth belong to God] or [God reigns over the rulers of the earth]

The expression **is greatly exalted** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. This could mean: (1) that God has exalted himself. Alternate translation: [He has exalted himself greatly] or (2) that people should or do exalt God. Alternate translation: [People should exalt him greatly] or [People exalt him greatly]

48.text:
# Psalm 48 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 48 is a psalm of praise. It is a specific type of praise psalm, a “song of Zion.” See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Call to worship (1–3)
2. Reason to worship (4–10)
3. Call to worship (11–13)
4. Reason to worship (14)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Who were the “kings” who “advanced” against Jerusalem?

The psalmist says in verse 4 that “kings assembled themselves” and “advanced together” to attack Jerusalem. He does not give enough information to identify these kings definitively. However, it is possible to understand Psalms 44, 46, and 48 as reflecting a sequence of compositions related to the Assyrian siege of Jerusalem in 701 B.C.

Psalm 44 is a psalm of supplication that complains to Yahweh that “you do not go out with our armies” even though “we have not forgotten you and we have not dealt falsely with your covenant.” This is an urgent cry for help in a desperate and dangerous situation.

Psalm 46 is psalm of trust. Even though there is warfare in the background (“Nations may roar; kingdoms may shake”), and this warfare seems to be ongoing, the psalmist expresses confident trust that Yahweh will help Jerusalem in time to save the city.

Psalm 48 is a psalm of praise. It celebrates Jerusalem as the city that God has chosen as the place for people to worship him. In this psalm, the psalmist says in verse 8 that just as he and his contemporaries had heard from their ancestors about Yahweh’s deliverance, now they have seen it for themselves. This could be understood as an allusion back to Psalm 44:1, where the psalmist said, “God, we have heard with our ears, our fathers have recounted to us, the work you worked in their days.”

While it is not necessarily the case that all three of these psalms relate to the same historical occasion, together they do represent the sequence of crying desperately to God for help, reaching a place of confident trust in God even before he acts, and celebrating God’s deliverance after he has brought it about. This rhythm characterizes the book of Psalms as a whole. See how you can translate these three psalms, which at least come from the same group of worship leaders and the same period in the history of the kingdom of Judah, in such a way as to highlight this rhythm.
See how you translated the expression “the sons of Korah” in the superscription to Psalm 42. Alternate translation: [of the descendants of Korah] or [of the Korahites]

The expression **is being praised** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and people are praising him]

In this context, the verbal form has the implied sense that Yahweh “is to be praised” or “ought to be praised.” Your language may have a verbal form that indicates that explicitly. If so, it would be appropriate to use it here in your translation. If not, you may be able to indicate this sense in another way. Alternate translation: [and he is worthy to be praised]

Since the psalmist has used the name **Yahweh** earlier in this sentence, and since Yahweh is the same person as **our God**, it may be more natural in your language to use a pronoun here. Alternate translation: [in his city]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe a **mountain**, Mount Zion, that is characterized by **holiness**. The idea is that Yahweh set apart this mountain as a place where he would be present in a special way and where people would worship him. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [on the mountain that he set apart for himself] or [on the mountain that he made a sacred place]

Here the **earth** represents the people of the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the joy of all of the people of the earth]

The psalmist is saying **all** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [the joy of people from throughout the earth]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **joy**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [something that makes people from throughout the earth rejoice]

This could mean: (1) that the psalmist is saying where on Mount Zion the **city** of Jerusalem, and especially the temple and the royal palace, are located. Alternate translation: [on its northern slope, where the city of the great king is] or (2) that the psalmist is using the phrase **the recesses of the north** in the same way as in [Isaiah 14:13](../isa/14/13.md) to mean the distant north, where pagan nations believe the council of the gods met. The psalmist would be saying that Yahweh is the supreme God who actually rules the council of supernatural beings (as in [89:7](../089/007.md)) from his temple in Jerusalem. Alternate translation: [, the site of Jerusalem, the place from which Yahweh, the great king, rules as the supreme God]

The expression **is known** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [People know him as a stronghold] or [He has made himself known as a stronghold]
See how you translated the term “stronghold” in [46:7](../046/007.md) and [46:11](../046/011.md). Alternate translation: [as a protector]

As is characteristic in a psalm of praise, the word **For** introduces the reason why people should praise Yahweh as the psalmist has been saying they should. Alternate translation: [We should praise Yahweh because]

The psalmist is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [listen]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **They** separately, even though the verb translated as **they saw** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that this action took place at the same time as when the kings **marveled**. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [As soon as they saw it, they marveled]

The expression **were terrified** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [This terrified them]

In this clause, the psalmist is describing the result of the previous clause. It may be helpful to add a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [so they hastened themselves away]

The psalmist is speaking of **Trembling** as if it were a living thing that could have **seized** the enemy kings. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [There they trembled uncontrollably]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [pain seized them there, like that of childbearing]

The point of this comparison is not that these kings felt physical **pain** but that they cried out in anguish and distress as a woman would who was feeling the actual **pain** of **childbearing**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [they cried out uncontrollably in anguish and distress]

The word **you** is singular here and through verse 11 because the psalmist is directly addressing Yahweh. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction. Alternate translation: [you, Yahweh, shatter]

The psalmist is using **ships of Tarshish** as a common expression of his culture to mean “ocean-going ships” or “large, sturdy ships.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. If you have already translated the book of 1 Kings, see how you translated the similar expression in [1 Kings 10:22](../1ki/10/22.md). Alternate translation: [ocean-going ships] or [large, sturdy ships]
See how your translation team decided at [3:2](../003/002.md) to represent the term **Selah**.

The psalmist means that he and his fellow Judeans have **compared** the **covenant faithfulness** that God showed on this occasion with the past covenant faithfulness that their ancestors related to them, as described in the previous verse. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [We have compared your present covenant faithfulness with your past covenant faithfulness]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [We have compared how faithful you were to your covenant on this occasion with how faithful you were to your covenant in the past]

By **We**, The psalmist means himself and his fellow Judeans but not Yahweh, to whom he is speaking. So use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

In this context, God’s **name** represents his reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [People to the ends of the earth praise you, God, as your reputation deserves]

The psalmist is speaking of **righteousness** as if it were an object with which God’s **right hand** could be **full**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Your right hand is thoroughly characterized by righteousness]

Here, God’s **hand** represents his powerful activity. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You powerfully bring about righteousness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [You powerfully do what is right]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and do that here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Let Mount Zion and the daughters of Judah rejoice greatly] or [Let Mount Zion rejoice; yes, let the daughters of Judah be glad]

Here, **Mount Zion** represents the people who live on Mount Zion, that is, the people of the city of Jerusalem. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Let the people of Jerusalem rejoice]

This could mean: (1) that the psalmist is speaking of the kingdom of **Judah** were a mother and of its people as if they were her **daughters**. Alternate translation: [let the people of Judah be glad] or (2) that the psalmist is speaking specifically of the women of the kingdom of **Judah** and encouraging them to have a victory celebration, as women in this culture did. Alternate translation: [let the women of Judah hold a victory celebration]

The instances of the implied “you” in the imperatives **Circle**, **go around**, and **Count** are plural because the psalmist is addressing many people. In the next verse, the terms “your” and “you” and the instances of the implied “you” in the imperatives are plural for the same reason. So use plural forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Go all the way around Zion]

Since a mountain does not have **towers**, here **Zion** represents the city of Jerusalem. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Circle the city on Mount Zion] or [Circle Jerusalem]

The psalmist is using **put your heart to** as a common expression of his culture to mean “carefully consider.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [keep in mind her rampart] or [carefully consider her rampart]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **rampart**. He means all the ramparts of the walls of Jerusalem. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [her ramparts]

As in verse 4, here the word **For** introduces the reason why people should praise Yahweh. It is not introducing the reason why people should walk around the walls of Jerusalem. Alternate translation: [We should praise this God because he is our God]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **He** separately, even though the verb translated as **he will guide us** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize the personal role of Yahweh in guiding the Judeans. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [He is the one who will guide us]

49.text:
# Psalm 49 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 49 is a wisdom psalm that describes the difference between how righteous people and wicked people live and the difference between what happens to them. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Introduction: call to listen (1–4)
2. Reminder that all people die, just as animals do (5–13; refrain, 12)
3. The psalmist’s confident assertion that God will bring him out of Sheol (14–15)
4. Reassertion that all people die, just as animals do (16–19; refrain, 20)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Life after death

This psalm teaches that having wealth and power cannot keep anyone from dying. All people, whether they are rich or poor, will die. But in verses 14–15, the psalmist expresses his confident expectation that God will not leave him in the place where people go when they die. Instead, God will take him out of there and bring him to himself. While the belief in life after death and the resurrection from the dead is expressed more clearly in the New Testament, that belief is also expressed in the Old Testament in places such as this. Translators should translate this psalm, especially verses 14 and 15, in such a way that it is clear that this Old Testament writer had this expectation.

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. See how you translated the term “chief musician” in the superscription to Psalm 4. Alternate translation: [For the leader of worship music] or [For the music director]
See how you translated the expression “the sons of Korah” in the superscription to Psalm 42. Alternate translation: [of the descendants of Korah] or [of the Korahites]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and do that here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Listen carefully to me, all of you people who live in the world] or [Hear this, all peoples! Yes, listen, everyone who lives in the world]
The implied “you” in these imperatives is plural because the psalmist is addressing many people. So use plural forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

The psalmist is using **sons of a human** as a common expression of his culture to mean “ordinary people,” and he is using **sons of a man** as a common expression of his culture to mean “distinguished people.” If these phrases do not have those meanings in your language, you could use comparable expressions from your language that do have those meanings, or you could state the meanings plainly. Alternate translation: [both the man on the street and the man in the corner office] or [both ordinary people and distinguished people]

The psalmist is using the adjectives **rich** and **poor** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjective with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [rich people and poor people]

49.quote: פִּ֭⁠י יְדַבֵּ֣ר חָכְמ֑וֹת וְ⁠הָג֖וּת לִבִּ֣⁠י תְבוּנֽוֹת
49.text: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [My mouth will speak wisdom, and the meditation of my heart will speak understanding]

49.quote: פִּ֭⁠י יְדַבֵּ֣ר חָכְמ֑וֹת וְ⁠הָג֖וּת לִבִּ֣⁠י תְבוּנֽוֹת
49.text: The psalmist is using individual parts of a himself, his **mouth** and the **meditation of his heart**, to mean all of him in the act of speaking **wisdom** and **understanding**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [With my mouth I will speak wisdom, and from the meditation of my heart I will speak understanding]

Here the **heart** represents a person’s thoughts. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and from the meditation of my thoughts I will speak understanding]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **meditation** and **understanding**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [and from what I have meditated on in my thoughts, I will say things that will help you understand]

The psalmist is speaking as if he is going to physically **incline** his **ear**, that is, lean over the way someone would do to listen to someone. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will listen carefully to a proverb]

The psalmist is speaking of this **proverb** as if it were a living thing that could speak to him. While he actually could listen to this proverb in the sense of hearing other people quote it, he means that he will carefully consider its meaning. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [I will see what a proverb has to say to me] or [I will carefully consider the meaning of a proverb]

While the term that the ULT translates as **proverb** generally means a short, popular saying that expresses some wisdom or truth, the specific meaning in this context is a “comparison,” which many proverbs draw. The psalmist is probably referring to the comparison in the refrain in verses 12 and 20 of this psalm, that people are like beasts. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I will carefully consider the meaning of a comparison]

The psalmist is speaking as if his **enigma** (the difficult and puzzling question he is trying to solve) were a closed container that he is going to use a **harp** to **open**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will explain my enigma as I sing and accompany myself with a harp]

49.quote: לָ֣⁠מָּה אִ֭ירָא בִּ֣⁠ימֵי רָ֑ע עֲוֺ֖ן עֲקֵבַ֣⁠י יְסוּבֵּֽ⁠נִי׃ הַ⁠בֹּטְחִ֥ים עַל־חֵילָ֑⁠ם וּ⁠בְ⁠רֹ֥ב עָ֝שְׁרָ֗⁠ם יִתְהַלָּֽלוּ
49.text: If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine [49:5](../049/005.md) and [49:6](../049/006.md) into a verse bridge in order to keep together the entire question that the psalmist is asking in these verses. The psalmist is using the question form to make a confident affirmation. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I do not have to be afraid in the days of evil, when the iniquity of my heels surrounds me, the ones trusting in their wealth, and in the abundance of their treasure they boast!]

The psalmist is using the term **days** to mean “time,” since time consists of days. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [during evil times] or [during troubled times]

As the next verse indicates, the psalmist is using his **heels** to represent people who would trip him up at his heels, that is, make him fall down. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [when the iniquity of those who would trip me up surrounds me]

The psalmist is speaking as if people wanted to trip him physically and make him fall down. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [when the iniquity of those who want to cause my downfall surrounds me] or [when the iniquity of those who want to ruin me surrounds me]

The psalmist is speaking of the **iniquity** of certain people as if it were a living thing that could surround him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when iniquitous people who want to ruin me surround me]

The psalmist is using two different verb forms in parallel statements. It may be more natural in your language to use the same verb form in both statements. Alternate translation: [the ones trusting in their wealth and boasting in the abundance of their treasure]

49.quote: אָ֗ח לֹא־פָדֹ֣ה יִפְדֶּ֣ה אִ֑ישׁ לֹא־יִתֵּ֖ן לֵ⁠אלֹהִ֣ים כָּפְרֽ⁠וֹ
49.text: The psalmist is repeating forms of the verb **redeem** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [A man certainly does not redeem a brother, he does not give his ransom to God]

49.quote: אָ֗ח לֹא־פָדֹ֣ה יִפְדֶּ֣ה אִ֑ישׁ לֹא־יִתֵּ֖ן לֵ⁠אלֹהִ֣ים כָּפְרֽ⁠וֹ
49.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [A man certainly does not pay a ransom to God to redeem a brother]

The psalmist is speaking as if a fellow human being were actually another person’s **brother**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a fellow human]

49.quote: וְ֭⁠יֵקַר פִּדְי֥וֹן נַפְשָׁ֗⁠ם וְ⁠חָדַ֥ל לְ⁠עוֹלָֽם׃ וִֽ⁠יחִי־ע֥וֹד לָ⁠נֶ֑צַח לֹ֖א יִרְאֶ֣ה הַ⁠שָּֽׁחַת
49.text: If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine verses 8 and 9 into a verse bridge in order to put the information about what **the redemption of their life** means right after that phrase. Alternate translation: [For the redemption of their life, that one should live on forever, that one should not see the pit, is costly, and it ceases forever]

In this verse, the word **life** is singular in form, but it refers to the lives of all humans as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “life.” Alternate translation: [their lives]

The psalmist means that the attempt at the **redemption** of a life **ceases** in the sense that it does not succeed and must be abandoned. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and the attempt always fails]

In this context, the term **see** has the sense of “experience.” You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [that one should not experience the pit]

The psalmist is using the expression **the pit** to refer to Sheol, the realm of the dead. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [that one should not experience the grave] or [that one should not go to the realm of the dead]

Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [After all,]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [one will see the Pit]

The psalmist is using the adjective **wise** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [Wise people]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **fool** or **brute**. He means such people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [fools and brutes] or [foolish people and brutish people]

This phrase is a translation of the written Hebrew text. You may wish to follow an alternative reading from the ancient Greek translation. Alternate translation: [Their graves {are} their houses forever]

Here, what is **Inside** people represents their thoughts. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [In their thoughts]

The psalmist is using a common expression of his culture to mean that the people he is describing give new names, their own names, to **lands** or properties. If this expression does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They give their names to lands] or [They name lands after themselves]

The expressions **is likened** and **are destroyed** are passive verbal forms. If your language would not use those forms, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [He is like the beasts, which perish]
In this context, **to them** is a possessive form. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [This, their way, is their folly]

The psalmist is speaking of how people live as if that were a **way** or path that they were walking along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [This, their manner of life, is their folly]

The psalmist is speaking as if those who admire them and want to be like these presumptuous rich people were walking **after** them on the same **way** or path. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [but their followers delight]

The psalmist is using the **mouths** of these presumptuous rich people to represent what they say by using their mouths. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in their sayings]
To translate the term **Selah** here and in verse 15, see how your translation team decided to represent that term in [3:2](../003/002.md).

The point of this comparison is that just as **sheep** are vulnerable and easily killed, so these rich people are vulnerable to dying. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [As if they were vulnerable sheep]

Here the psalmist is using the pronoun **They** in a general sense, not to refer to specific people. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. If you need to say specifically who does the action, the context in the next verse indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [They are appointed] or [God appoints them]

The psalmist is speaking of **death** as if it were a living thing that could **shepherd** these people. He means that just as a shepherd keeps all of his sheep under his control so that none wander away, none of these people will get away from the realm of the dead. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. (However, since the image of a **shepherd** here extends the image of **sheep** earlier in the verse, you may wish to express both images as comparisons. The UST models one way to do that.) Alternate translation: [they will not get away from the realm of the dead]

The psalmist is speaking as if the **upright** were going to rule **in the morning** on a certain day over rich people who had been wicked. He means that the “days of evil” (that is, the troubled times) that he began describing in verse 5, pictured here as a dark night, will surely end as God delivers innocent people from oppression. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar expression in [46:5](../046/005.md). Alternate translation: [And when God delivers the upright from their oppression, they will rule over them]

The psalmist is using the adjective **upright** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [upright people]

The psalmist is speaking of **Sheol** as if it were a living thing that could **consume** the **form** or body of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and their body will decompose in the grave]

In this verse, the word **form** is singular in form, but it refers to the forms or bodies of these wicked people as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “form.” Alternate translation: [their forms] or [their bodies]
The pronoun **it** refers to the **form** of each wicked person. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [from its dwelling] or [away from where they lived]

Here, **hand** represents the power and control that a person or thing has over someone. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the control of Sheol] or [from the custody of Sheol]

Here the word **for** introduces not a reason but an explanation. Use a connecting word or phrase in your language that will show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [and he will do that by taking me]

Here the masculine term **man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [a person]

Here, a rich person’s **house** represents all of his possessions. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [when the splendor of his estate increases]
Here, **glory** represents “wealth.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [his wealth]

The psalmist assumes that readers will understand that by **go down**, he means “go down to Sheol.” You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [go down to Sheol]

The psalmist is using one part of a person, his **soul**, to mean all of him in the act of blessing himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he blesses himself]

While the term “bless” usually refers to expressing hope that good things would happen to a person, in this context, it means saying that good things have happened to a person. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [he congratulates himself]

Here the psalmist is using the pronoun **they** in a general sense, not to refer to specific people. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and people do praise you when you do well for yourself] or [and you are praised when you do well for yourself]

The words **you** and **yourself** are singular here because the psalmist is addressing each person in the audience as a representative individual who needs to consider whether what he says applies directly to him. So use singular forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction. If it does not, you may be able to communicate the meaning here in some other way. Alternate translation: [and they will praise any one of you if you do well for yourself] or [and any one of you will be praised if he does well for himself]
In a context such as this, your language might say “go” instead of **come**. Alternate translation: [he will go to the generation of his fathers]

The psalmist is using the term **fathers** to mean “ancestors.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he will come to the generation of his ancestors]

The psalmist assumes that his listeners will understand that by this phrase he means that the rich man he has been describing since verse 16 will join in death the **generation** of people that consists of his ancestors. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [he will join his ancestors in death]

The psalmist is using **they will not see light** as a common expression of his culture to mean that the rich man and his ancestors will not live on the earth again. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they will never see the light of day] or [they will never live on the earth again]

49.quote: אָדָ֣ם בִּ֭⁠יקָר וְ⁠לֹ֣א יָבִ֑ין נִמְשַׁ֖ל כַּ⁠בְּהֵמ֣וֹת
49.text: **A human in honor, but he does not understand** introduces the first part of a possible condition. What the psalmist describes in the rest of this verse is true if this condition happens. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [Suppose a human is in honor, but he does not understand. Then he is likened to the beasts]

This is the second occurrence of the refrain in this psalm. We recommend that you show this to your readers by translating the phrases here the same way that you translated them in the first occurrence of this refrain in [49:12](../049/012.md). Alternate translation: [he is like the beasts, which perish]

50.text:
# Psalm 50 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 50 is like a wisdom psalm in that it describes the difference between how righteous people and wicked people live and the difference between what happens to them. But it is a particular type of psalm that depicts God assembling and addressing the Israelites, commending those who are faithfully obeying his covenant but warning those who are acting wickedly. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. God powerfully summons the Israelites (1–6)
2. God addresses faithful Israelites (7–15)
3. God addresses wicked Israelites (16–22)
4. God reassures faithful Israelites (23)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Who was Asaph?

Asaph was an Israelite man from the tribe of Levi who was an important singer and musician during the reigns of David and Solomon. He played instruments and led people to sing songs to worship Yahweh. In addition to leading music, he also wrote songs. A dozen of the psalms are attributed to him. Psalm 50 is the psalm by Asaph that comes earliest in the book of Psalms.

### What was a “thank offering” (verses 14, 23), and why does God encourage the Israelites to make this offering?

A thank offering was one type of fellowship offering, as [Leviticus 7:12–15](../lev/07/12.md) describes. A worshiper would sacrifice an animal from his flock, and together with other food that he would bring, this would provide a celebration meal for his family and friends. At this meal, the worshiper would describe publicly how God had helped him when he was in trouble. When God encourages the Israelites to make this offering, he is effectively encouraging them to pray to him for help when they are in trouble, as verse 15 describes, so that he can rescue them and they can honor him in this way. The Israelites were already offering all of the sacrifices that the law of Moses required, but God wanted them to go beyond what was required and live in a relationship of active devotion to him. He wanted them to experience his help and offer sacrifices freely in gratitude.

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

### Repeated phrases

For poetic effect, Asaph repeats some key terms in this psalm. He says in verse 3 that God “is not silent,” showing that the situation in verse 21, where God says “I was silent,” no longer holds. In verse 8, God tells the Israelite people, “I do not accuse you regarding your sacrifices,” but in verse 21, God tells a representative wicked person, “I will accuse you” of moral wrongdoing. To help your readers appreciate these connections, we recommend that in your translation, you translate the verbs that the ULT represents as “be silent” and “accuse” the same way in both of their occurrences.

Asaph is using a possessive form to express a superlative meaning. If a speaker of your language would not use a possessive form as a superlative, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [The Supreme God] or [The God who is greater than all other gods]

Here, **the earth** represents the people who live on the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people of the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting]

Asaph is referring to the entire earth by naming two extremes, the east, where **the sun** rises, and the west, where the sun sets. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people who live everywhere on earth]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **perfection** and **beauty**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [the perfectly beautiful place]

Asaph is speaking as if God had actually **shined forth** from Zion. He is using the image of light to represent God’s presence radiating out from Zion. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [God’s presence radiates out]
By **Our**, the psalmist means to include both himself and those he is addressing, so use the inclusive form of that word if your language marks that distinction.

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **silent**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [and he is going to speak]

Asaph is using images from God’s appearance on Mount Sinai, where he made a covenant with the Israelites, to describe God’s approach to judge his people in light of that covenant on this occasion. [Exodus 19:16–18](../exo/19/16.md) describes how a great thunderstorm and a burning fire preceded Yahweh’s descent onto Mount Sinai. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. The UST models one way to do that.

Here, **to his face** represents “in front of him.” If you decide to retain this image in your translation, if it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [A fire devours in front of him]

Asaph is speaking as if this **fire** were actually devouring or eating what was in front of God. If you decide to retain this image in your translation, if it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [A fire burns up everything in front of him]

The expression **it is stormed** is a passive verbal form. If you decide to retain this image in your translation, if your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [a great storm rages]

Asaph assumes that listeners will understand that he means that God **calls** the **heavens** and the **earth** to serve as witnesses of what the Israelites promised to do when they made a covenant with Yahweh. [Deuteronomy 4:26](../deu/04/26.md) and [Deuteronomy 30:19](../deu/30/19.md) describe how Moses called upon the heavens and the earth to serve as witnesses in this way. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [He calls to the heavens above and to the earth as witnesses]

This verse is a direct quotation of God. The ULT indicates that by putting the verse inside quotation marks. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could also use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. Alternate translation: [He says, “Gather my faithful ones to me]

Asaph does not identify to whom God is giving this command. (God is not addressing the heavens and the earth. Their role is to serve as witnesses.) The focus is more on the results than on the agents. It may be more natural in your language to express this with a form other than a command form. Alternate translation: [Let my faithful ones be gathered to me]
The implied “you” in the imperative **Gather** is plural, so if you retain the command form, use its plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Asaph is using the adjective **faithful** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. (The ULT indicates this by supplying the word **ones**.) Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can use an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the ones who are faithful to me]

God is using **the cutters of my covenant** as a common expression of this culture to mean “those who made a covenant with me.” He is using the term “cut” because in some covenant ceremonies, the participants would cut up animals and then walk between the pieces.
