This was to indicate, “If I break this covenant, may I be destroyed in this same way.” It is not necessary to understand this background to covenant ceremonies in order to understand what God says in the rest of this psalm, so you do not have to use the term “cut” in your translation. You could simply say “make,” or you could use an expression from your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [those who made a covenant with me]

God is not using the phrase **by sacrifice** to refer to animals that were slaughtered and cut up when he made his covenant with the Israelites. (There is no description in the Bible of such a ceremony connected with that covenant.) He means that this covenant was sealed and was to be continually acknowledged by sacrificial worship, which is the main theme of this psalm. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [that was sealed and was to be continually acknowledged by sacrificial worship]

Asaph is speaking of the **heavens** as if they were a living thing that could **declare** God’s righteousness. This conveys two ideas. In the immediate context, the heavens witness that God has kept his part of the covenant. In the broader biblical context, as in [19:1](../019/001.md) and [97:6](../097/006.md), the characteristics of the heavens display the righteous character of God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the broader meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The heavens display his righteousness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [that he is righteous]

Asaph is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though it could be omitted, in order to emphasize that the heavens declare that God is the supreme **judge** of everyone on earth. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the emphasis here. Alternate translation: [that it is God who is judge]
See how your translation team decided at [3:2](../003/002.md) to represent the term **Selah**.

This verse begins a direct quotation of God that continues through verse 15. The ULT indicates that by putting these verses inside quotation marks. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could also use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. Alternate translation: [He says, “Hear, my people, and I will speak]

The pronouns **you** and **your** and the implied “you” in imperatives are singular here and through verse 15 because God is addressing his **people** as if they were a single individual. So use singular forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Asaph is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [listen, Israel]

Here, **Israel** represents the nation that consisted of the descendants of Jacob, whom God renamed Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [you Israelites]

50.quote: לֹ֣א עַל־זְ֭בָחֶי⁠ךָ אוֹכִיחֶ֑⁠ךָ וְ⁠עוֹלֹתֶ֖י⁠ךָ לְ⁠נֶגְדִּ֣⁠י תָמִֽיד
50.text: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Your burnt offerings are always before me, so I do not accuse you regarding your sacrifices]

Asaph is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [I will not take a bull from your house, and I will not take goats from your folds] or [I will not take a bull from your house or goats from your folds]

God is not saying that he will not accept bulls or goats from the Israelites as sacrifices. This psalm as a whole is supportive of the sacrificial system. However, its emphasis is on offering sacrifices for the right reasons. They are not something that God needs; they are a way of living in relationship with God (as verses 14 and 15 especially emphasize). You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I do not need to take a bull from your house or goats from your folds]

Here, a person’s **house** represents his “household” or “possessions.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from among your possessions]

Here and in v. 13, the psalmist is using a specific term that means male goats. If your language does not have a general term for goats but must specify whether a goat is male or female, use your term for male goats in these places.

The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

Asaph is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [every beast of the forest is mine, and the cattle on a thousand hills are mine] or [every beast of the forest and the cattle on a thousand hills belong to me]

God is using the number **a thousand** in a way that was common in this culture to mean a very large, uncountable number, not a precise figure. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the cattle on every hill] or [all cattle everywhere]

God is using the term **know** in a particular sense to mean that he owns **all the birds**. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I own]
In this context, the phrase **with me** expresses a relationship of possession. Alternate translation: [and the creature of the field is mine]

God is not referring to a specific **creature**. He means field creatures in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and every field creature is mine]

The term that the ULT translates as **creature** refers to a “moving thing,” and in this context, it probably means a “swarming thing” or insect. (In the previous verse, God described how large animals belonged to him, and in this verse, he makes the focus much smaller and thus even more comprehensive.) You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and even the insects in the fields are mine]

50.quote: אִם־אֶ֭רְעַב לֹא־אֹ֣מַר לָ֑⁠ךְ כִּי־לִ֥⁠י תֵ֝בֵ֗ל וּ⁠מְלֹאָֽ⁠הּ
50.text: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Since the world and its fulness are mine, I would not tell you if I were hungry]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **fulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and what fills it] or [and everything in it]

50.quote: הַֽ֭⁠אוֹכַל בְּשַׂ֣ר אַבִּירִ֑ים וְ⁠דַ֖ם עַתּוּדִ֣ים אֶשְׁתֶּֽה
50.text: God is using the question form to emphasize that what he is describing is certainly not true. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I certainly do not eat the flesh of bulls, and I do not drink the blood of goats!]

50.quote: זְבַ֣ח לֵ⁠אלֹהִ֣ים תּוֹדָ֑ה וְ⁠שַׁלֵּ֖ם לְ⁠עֶלְי֣וֹן נְדָרֶֽי⁠ךָ
50.text: God is speaking of himself in the third person because he is giving an authoritative command. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [Sacrifice a thank offering to me, God, and pay your vows to me, the Most High]

Asaph is using the term **day** to mean “time,” since time consists of days. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in any time of trouble]

50.quote: וְ⁠לָ֤⁠רָשָׁ֨ע ׀ אָ֘מַ֤ר אֱלֹהִ֗ים מַה־לְּ֭⁠ךָ לְ⁠סַפֵּ֣ר חֻקָּ֑⁠י וַ⁠תִּשָּׂ֖א בְרִיתִ֣⁠י עֲלֵי־פִֽי⁠ךָ׃ וְ֭⁠אַתָּה שָׂנֵ֣אתָ מוּסָ֑ר וַ⁠תַּשְׁלֵ֖ךְ דְּבָרַ֣⁠י אַחֲרֶֽי⁠ךָ
50.text: If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine [50:16](../050/016.md), which describes a result, and [50:17](../050/017.md), which gives a reason, into a verse bridge in order to put the reason before the result. Alternate translation: [But to the wicked one God says, “Since you, you hate instruction, and you cast my words behind you, what to you to recount my statutes, or that you should lift up my covenant onto your mouth?]

Asaph is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. (The ULT indicates this by supplying the word **one**.) Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can use an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [But to every wicked person]

The pronouns **you** and **your** are singular here and through verse 21 because God is addressing a representative **wicked** individual. So use singular forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

50.quote: מַה־לְּ֭⁠ךָ לְ⁠סַפֵּ֣ר חֻקָּ֑⁠י וַ⁠תִּשָּׂ֖א בְרִיתִ֣⁠י עֲלֵי־פִֽי⁠ךָ
50.text: God is using the question form to rebuke wicked people who speak as if they were loyal to his covenant but who disobey its commandments. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [It is not to you to recount my statutes, and you should not lift up my covenant onto your mouth!]

50.quote: מַה־לְּ֭⁠ךָ לְ⁠סַפֵּ֣ר חֻקָּ֑⁠י וַ⁠תִּשָּׂ֖א בְרִיתִ֣⁠י עֲלֵי־פִֽי⁠ךָ
50.text: God is using **What to you** as a common expression of this culture to mean that the person he is addressing has no valid connection with what he describes next. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You have no business recounting my statutes or lifting up my covenant onto your mouth!] or [It is not appropriate for you to recount my statutes or to lift up my covenant onto your mouth.]

God is speaking as if his **covenant** were an object that this wicked person could actually **lift up** and put on his **mouth**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [or that you should say that you are loyal to my covenant]

God is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you have** already includes this meaning. He is doing that in order to emphasize a contrast between what faithful people are doing, as described in the previous part of this psalm, and what this wicked individual is doing. Alternate translation: [for your part, you hate]

God is speaking as if his **words** were objects that this wicked person could actually **cast behind** him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you disregard my words]
God is using the term **words** to represent what he says by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what I say to you]

God is using the term **send** in a specific sense to mean “release” or “set free,” as in [Deuteronomy 15:12](../deu/15/12.md). You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [You release your mouth in evil]

God is speaking of this wicked person’s **mouth** as if it were itself a person that the wicked one could **send** away or release. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You say evil things without restraint]

God is speaking of this wicked person’s **tongue** as if it were itself a person who could **frame** (form or put together) **deceit**, which God is speaking of as if it were an object that could be assembled. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you make up deceitful things to say]

God is using **You sit** as a common expression of this culture to indicate that the action he describes next, **you speak**, is something that this wicked person does deliberately and continuously. If this expression does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You sit around speaking] or [You habitually speak]

The word that the ULT translates as **brother** is a general term that in various contexts can mean a full brother or a half-brother, a kinsman, or a fellow Israelite. The phrase **the son of your mother** explicitly describes a full brother. (It is characteristic of Hebrew poetry for the second part of a line to intensify and sharpen the first part of a line.) If your language has a general term for a relative that can include a brother, it would be appropriate to use it to translate **brother**. If not, if your language has a term for a half-brother (a son of the same father but not of the same mother), you might use that to translate **brother**, and you might use your term for a full brother (a son of the same mother and father) in the second part of the verse.

This could mean: (1) that God is referring to himself in the third person by the name he revealed to Moses in [Exodus 3:14](../exo/03/14.md). If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [You thought that I, the I AM, was like you in my being] or (2) that God is repeating forms of the verb “to be” in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. Another way to translate the original text is, “You thought that being, I was like you.” Alternate translation: [You thought that surely I was like you]

This sentence indicates the result of the reason that the previous sentence describes. It may be helpful to use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [Therefore, you thought the being of I AM was like you]

God is using the term **array**, which often describes armies forming battle lines, in a legal sense to mean that he will present evidence in a compelling order. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and I will marshal the evidence against you]
Here, **eyes** represent sight. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [for you to see]

The implied “you” in the imperative **Consider** is plural because God is addressing everyone who does not pay attention to his commandments, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

God is speaking of himself in the third person because he is giving an authoritative command. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [you who forget me, God] or [you who disregard me, God]

God is using the word translated as **lest** to introduce an outcome that he does not want to happen. Because of this, he first gives the people he is addressing an instruction to follow so that this will not happen. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that avoiding this outcome is the purpose of the instruction. Alternate translation: [Otherwise, I will tear you, and no one will be able to deliver you]

God is speaking as if he would actually **tear** wicked people into pieces the way a lion tears its victim apart. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I punish you severely]

God is speaking as if the person he is describing were actually **placing** or preparing a **way** or path on which he would walk. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the one ordering his conduct rightly]

In this context, to **look upon** salvation means to “experience” it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will make him experience the salvation of God]

God is speaking of himself in the third person because he is making an authoritative promise. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [I will make him experience my salvation]

51.text:
# Psalm 51 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 51 is a specific kind of psalm of supplication, a “penitential psalm” in which the psalmist is deeply troubled by guilt and asks God to forgive him and restore him. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. David’s plea for forgiveness (1–9)
2. David’s plea for restoration (10–15)
3. Rightly offered sacrifices (16–19)

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. See how you translated the term “chief musician” in the superscription to Psalm 4. Alternate translation: [For the leader of worship music] or [For the music director]

This superscription, referring to events described in [2 Samuel 11:1–12:25](../2sa/11/01.md), describes sexual relations in a polite way by using the phrase **had gone in to**. Depending on what is helpful in your language, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly, as the UST does. Alternate translation: [he had slept with Bathsheba]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [according to all the ways you are faithful to your covenant]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **compassions** and **transgressions**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [of ways you care for me, forgive all the ways I have sinned against you]

David is speaking of his **transgressions** as if they were words written in ink on a scroll that God could **wipe away** to erase them and make them disappear. The basic idea is that David wants God to regard his transgressions as if they had never occurred; that is, he wants God to forgive him for committing them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [completely forgive my transgressions]

The expressions **Make great** and **wash me** together express a single idea. The expression **Make great** tells in what way David wants God to **wash**him. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and do that here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Wash me thoroughly to cleanse me of my sin] or [Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity, yes, cleanse me from my sin]

This could mean (both meanings may be present): (1) that David is speaking of his **iniquity** or **sin** as if it were actually dirt or a stain that God could **wash** off of him in order to **cleanse** him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Completely take away my iniquity, yes, remove all of my sin] or (2) that David is speaking as if his **iniquity** or **sin** had made him ritually unclean and so unable to participate in the worship of God until he became ritually clean again through ceremonial washing. Alternate translation: [Take away all of my iniquity to make me acceptable to you again so that I can worship you freely]
Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an admission. Alternate translation: [Indeed,] or [Admittedly,]

David is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I know** already includes this meaning. He is doing that because he is confronting himself with the fact of his **transgressions**. Alternate translation: [I know very well that I have committed transgressions]

David is speaking of his **sin** as if it were actually an object that was **always before** him or in front of him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I am always conscious of my sin]

David is repeating the pronoun **you** for emphasis. If your language can repeat pronouns for emphasis, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [You are the only one I have sinned against]

David is saying **only** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [You are the one I have essentially sinned against]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **evil**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what is evil]
Here, **eyes** represents “perspective.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in your perspective]
David is using the term **Behold** to focus attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, here and in the next verse.

David does not mean that his **mother conceived** him as the result of a sinful act. Instead, he means that as a human being, he has been characterized by **iniquity** and **sin** for his entire life. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I have been iniquitous since I was born; indeed, I have been sinful from the time my mother conceived me]

The expression **was born** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I was in iniquity when my mother gave birth to me; indeed, I was in sin when my mother conceived me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **truth**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [trustworthiness] or [integrity]
Here the **kidneys** represents a person’s motives and intentions. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in a person’s motives]

The expression **closed** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [in the place that people close up]

David is using the verbal form **closed**, which functions here as an adjective, as a noun to mean a certain place. (The ULT indicates this by supplying the word **place**.) Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [in my inner being]

David is speaking as if he wanted God to perform the ceremony that the law of Moses describes in [Numbers 19:18](../num/19/18.md), in which a ceremonially clean person would dip a **hyssop** branch in water and sprinkle water with it to **purify** a person or place that had become ritually unclean. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. The UST models one way to do that.

The term **hyssop** describes a leafy plant, an herb that was common in Israel. Its large and numerous leaves made it ideal for use in sprinkling, especially in ceremonial contexts. If your language does not have a word for this plant, consider using a general expression. Alternate translation: [with leafy branches]

As in verse 2, David is speaking of his sin as if it were dirt that God could **wash** off of him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar image in verse 2. Alternate translation: [May you take away my sin]

David is speaking as if he would become bright white in color if God were to wash him. He is using the uniform whiteness of newly fallen snow to represent complete purity. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that I may be purer than snow]

David is using the expression **joy and gladness** to represent things that God would say to him that would make him feel those emotions. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Make me hear things that will cause me to feel joy and gladness] or [Say things to me that will make me feel joy and gladness]

David means specifically that he wants God to tell him that he has forgiven him. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Assure me that you have forgiven me, that I may feel joy and gladness]

The terms **joy** and **gladness** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [great joy]

David is using one part of himself, his **bones**, to mean all of him in the act of being **crushed**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [may I, whom you have crushed, rejoice]

David is speaking as if God had actually **crushed** him by convicting him of his sin. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [may I, whom you have deeply convicted of sin, rejoice]

David is speaking as if he wanted God to position his **face** so that it would not be visible from the place where his **sins** were. Effectively this means that he wants God not to look at his sins. However, he does not mean that he wants God to leave his sins in place but not regard them. He wants God to make his sins nowhere to be seen; that is, he wants God to forgive the sins so that it is as if he had not committed them. Alternate translation: [Make my sins nowhere to be seen]
See how you translated the same image in verse 1. Alternate translation: [and forgive all of my iniquities]

Here the **heart** represents a person’s thoughts or motives. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Give me a new capacity for pure thoughts] or [Give me a new capacity for right motives]

The expression **established** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and renew a steadfast spirit within me]

Here a person’s **spirit** represents his attitude, in this case, one of determination. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and enable me once again to be steadfastly determined to obey you]

Here God’s **face** represents his “presence.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [May you not cast me away from your presence]

David is speaking as if God might actually **cast** or throw him away from his presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May you not banish me from your presence]

David is using the possessive form to describe how God’s **Spirit** is characterized by **holiness**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and may you not take your Holy Spirit from me]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **joy** and **salvation**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [Make me joyful again that you have saved me]

David is speaking as if he wanted God to use a **willing spirit** like a cane or walking stick to **support** him, that is, to keep him from falling down. Within this image, falling down represents disobeying and sinning. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and to keep me from sinning, make me willing to obey you]

David is speaking of the manners in which God wants people to live as if they were **ways** or paths that people would be walking along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [how you want people to live]

David is speaking as if **sinners** had actually gone to some place away from God from which they would **return** to him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that sinners may repent]

Here, **blood** represents “bloodguiltiness,” that is, legal liability to punishment by death for murdering another person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from the death penalty I deserve for killing someone]

David is repeating the word **God** to emphasize that the basis of his plea is the merciful, saving character of God. If your language can repeat words for emphasis, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the emphasis. Alternate translation: [you who are God my Savior]

David is using one part of himself, his **tongue**, to mean all of him in the act of singing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [may I sing]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [about how righteous you are]

David is not asking God physically to **open** his **lips**. He means that he wants God to do something (forgive and restore him, as he has asked) that will cause him to open his lips and declare God’s praise with his mouth. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Do this, Lord, so that I may open my lips]

Here David’s **lips** represent him speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [give me something to speak about]

David is using one part of himself, his **mouth**, to mean all of him in the act of praising God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that I may declare your praise]

Here the word **For** does not introduce a reason for what immediately precedes. Instead, it introduces a general explanation for what David has been asking throughout this psalm. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [After all,]

David means specifically that God does not want a **sacrifice** and that God does not **accept a burnt offering** as the grounds on which to pardon someone who has committed murder. (The law of Moses provides for no such sacrifice.) You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [you do not delight in sacrifice in cases of murder … you do not accept a burnt offering to pardon a murderer]

David is using this possessive form not to describe **sacrifices** that **God** makes but sacrifices that God wants and accepts. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [The sacrifices that God wants] or [The sacrifices that God accepts]

The expression **broken** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [are a spirit that has broken]

David is speaking as if a person’s **spirit** were actually an object that could be **broken**. The image is of something that is broken so that it has fallen down in pieces, with lowliness representing humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [are a humble spirit]
As in verse 10, here a person’s **spirit** represents his attitude. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [are a humble attitude]

The expressions **broken** and **crushed** are passive verbal forms. If your language would not use those forms, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [A heart that an awareness of the seriousness of sin has broken and crushed]

The terms **broken** and **crushed** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [A completely broken heart] or [A heart that an awareness of the seriousness of sin has completely broken]

Here the **heart** represents a person’s inner being. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [A person who is deeply humbled by an awareness of the seriousness of his sin]

David is using Mount **Zion**, the location of the Israelite capital city of Jerusalem, to represent the people of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel]

The noun that the ULT translates as **acceptance** here comes from the same root as the verb that it translates as “accept” in verse 16. However, the perspective is broader here. David is not asking God to **Do good to Zion** based on God’s **acceptance** of him personally as a penitent and forgiven sinner. Instead, he is asking that all of the people of Israel would experience God’s renewed favor now that he, as their king, has repented. Your language may have a term that you can use in your translation to indicate this. Alternate translation: [in your favor]

David is speaking as if **Jerusalem** did not have **walls**, and he wanted God to **build** some for the city. He is using Jerusalem to represent the people of Israel and walls to represent their protection. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [strengthen the defenses of Israel] or [strongly protect us Israelites]

David is using the possessive form to describe **sacrifices** that are characterized by the **righteousness** of those offering them. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [rightly offered sacrifices]

David is using the adjective **whole** as a noun to mean a certain kind of sacrifice. (The ULT indicates this by supplying the word **one**.) Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [a burnt offering and a wholly consumed sacrifice]

Together, the expressions **a burnt offering** and **a whole one** express a single idea. The word **whole** tells to what extent this **offering** would be **burnt**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [a wholly burnt offering]

David is not referring to a specific wholly burnt offering. He means such offerings in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [wholly burnt offerings]

Here David is using the pronoun **they** in a general sense, not to refer to specific people. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Then people will offer bulls] or [Then bulls will be offered]

52.text:
# Psalm 52 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 52 is a specific kind of psalm of supplication, an “imprecatory psalm” in which the psalmist describes the actions of wicked people and asks God to judge and punish them. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Description of Doeg’s wickedness (1–4)
2. Declaration that God will punish Doeg (5–7)
3. David’s statement of his confidence in God (8–9)

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a “maskil.” See the discussion of that term in the introduction to Psalms.

As its superscription indicates, the background to this psalm is an episode related in [1 Samuel 22:6–23](../1sa/22/06.md), in which Doeg the Edomite, one of King Saul’s officers, killed Yahweh’s priests and their families. It may be helpful to read that episode before translating this psalm.

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. See how you translated the term “chief musician” in the superscription to Psalm 4. Alternate translation: [For the leader of worship music] or [For the music director]

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a **maskil**. Since the meaning of this word is not certain, you may wish to represent it in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language. See the discussion of that term in the Introduction to Psalms.

52.quote: בְּ⁠ב֤וֹא ׀ דּוֹאֵ֣ג הָ⁠אֲדֹמִי֮ וַ⁠יַּגֵּ֪ד לְ⁠שָׁ֫א֥וּל וַ⁠יֹּ֥אמֶר ל֑⁠וֹ בָּ֥א דָ֝וִ֗ד אֶל־בֵּ֥ית אֲחִימֶֽלֶךְ
52.text: This superscription is referring to events related in [1 Samuel 22:6–23](../1sa/22/06.md). If it would be helpful to your readers, you could describe these events more fully. Alternate translation: [David wrote this song when Doeg the Edomite, an officer of King Saul, came and told Saul that David, whom Saul was trying to kill, had gone to the high priest Ahimelech and that he had received help from him]
This phrase introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this phrase explicitly.

52.quote: מַשְׂכִּ֥יל לְ⁠דָוִֽד׃ בְּ⁠ב֤וֹא ׀ דּוֹאֵ֣ג הָ⁠אֲדֹמִי֮ וַ⁠יַּגֵּ֪ד לְ⁠שָׁ֫א֥וּל וַ⁠יֹּ֥אמֶר ל֑⁠וֹ בָּ֥א דָ֝וִ֗ד אֶל־בֵּ֥ית אֲחִימֶֽלֶךְ
52.text: This superscription is referring to events related in [1 Samuel 23:19–23](../1sa/23/19.md). If it would be helpful to your readers, you could describe these events more fully. Alternate translation: [This is a maskil that David wrote when he was hiding in the wilderness of Ziph from King Saul, who wanted to kill him, and the people who lived there went and told Saul that he was hiding among them]

David actually means to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of what he is saying here. While Doeg had caused great **harm** by killing all of Yahweh’s priests and their families ([1 Samuel 22:18–19](../1sa/22/18.md)), those were harmless, defenseless people, so this was not the kind of feat that a true **warrior** would **boast** about. If a speaker of your language would not say the opposite of what he meant as a way of showing how he felt about what he was saying, you could translate the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Why do you boast about killing defenseless people as if that made you a great warrior?]

David is using the question form to mock and ridicule Doeg. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You should not boast about killing defenseless people as if that made you great warrior!]

Here and through verse 5, David addresses Doeg directly, even though he knows Doeg cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to himself and to anyone who hears this song that he feels very strongly about how Doeg killed the priests of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, here and through verse 5 you could translate what David says to Doeg as if he were speaking to other people about him. Alternate translation: [Doeg should not boast about killing defenseless people as if that made him great warrior!]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [The covenant faithfulness of God lasts all of the day]

David is using the term **day** to mean “time,” since time consists of days. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The covenant faithfulness of God lasts all the time]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [God is always faithful to his covenant]

The expression **sharpened** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Like a sharp razor] or [Like a razor that someone has sharpened]

The point of this comparison is that just as a **sharpened razor** is dangerous and potentially destructive, so is Doeg’s **tongue**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Like a dangerous sharpened razor] or [Like a dangerously sharp razor]

David is speaking of Doeg’s **tongue** as if it were a living thing that could devise calamities. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what you say causes calamities]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **betrayal**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [you who have betrayed innocent people to their deaths]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and you love lying more than speaking righteousness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what is right] or [truthfully]
To translate the term **Selah** here and in verse 5, see how your translation team decided to represent that term in [3:2](../003/002.md).
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **destruction**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [all words that destroy others]

David is using the term **words** to represent what Doeg says by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to say anything that will destroy other people]

David is using one part of Doeg, his **tongue**, to represent all of him in the act of saying things that betrayed innocent people to their deaths. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you treacherous person]

The verbs in this verse are in a form that Hebrew writers could use to express either a statement or a wish. It would be consistent with the usual pattern of an imprecatory psalm (see the introduction to this psalm) for David to express a wish at this point that God would judge and punish this wicked person. However, he may also be making a confident statement about what God will do. The original audience would have heard both nuances. Use the verbal form in your language that seems most suitable. Alternate translation: [May God also tear you down forever! May he take you away and tear you from the tent and uproot you from the land of the living!]

David is speaking of Doeg as if he were actually a building or wall that God would **tear down**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [God will also destroy you]

David is describing one event before describing another event that would precede it. If it would be helpful your language, you may wish to relate these events in the order in which they would happen. Alternate translation: [He will tear you from the tent and take you away]

David is speaking as if Doeg were actually attached to or part of the **tent** in which he lived and as if God would physically **tear** him from the tent. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He will remove you from the tent you live in and take you away]

David is speaking as if Doeg were a plant that God would **uproot** from the soil. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and remove you]

David is using the adjective **living** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [from the land of people who are alive]

Here the **land of the living** represents the people who figuratively inhabit that land. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from among people who are alive]

David is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [And righteous people]

Since David has been addressing Doeg directly (even though he cannot hear him) to show that he feels strongly about what he did, you may wish to use the pronoun “you” here instead of the pronoun **him**. However, there is poetic effect in the change of pronoun. David describes in the previous verse how God will destroy Doeg, and in this verse it is as if that has already happened, so that Doeg is no longer around to address directly. Use the pronoun that will be most natural and effective in your language.

This verse is a direct quotation of the righteous people described in the previous verse. The ULT indicates that by putting this verse inside quotation marks. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could also use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. Alternate translation: [They will say, “Behold, the man]

These righteous people are using the term **Behold** to focus their listeners’ attention on what they are about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Listen]

These people are speaking of Doeg as if he should actually have made God his **refuge**, that is, the place where he could go to be safe from danger. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the term “refuge” in [14:6](../014/006.md). Alternate translation: [the man did not depend on God for protection]

The term that the ULT translates as **man** refers to a full-grown male. It is related to the word that the ULT translates as “warrior” in verse 1, and it can refer to a soldier. The people may be using it in a mocking sense, like David did in verse 1. Your language may have a word or phrase that you can use to bring out this sense in your translation. Alternate translation: [the big man]

The point of this comparison is that just as such a **tree** was secure and carefully tended, so God keeps David safe and cares for him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [But I am secure and well cared for, like a green olive tree in the house of God]

David is using the term **green** not to describe the color of this **tree** but to indicate that it is alive. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [like a living olive tree] or [like a thriving olive tree]

David is speaking of God’s sanctuary as if it were actually a **house** in which he lived. He does not mean that the tree to which he is comparing himself is actually within the sanctuary itself. There was probably a courtyard around the tent that David set up for the Box of Yahweh ([2 Samuel 6:17](../2sa/06/17.md)), just as there was a courtyard around the temple that his son Solomon later built on the same site. In such courtyards there were trees that priests planted and tended. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in the courtyard of the sanctuary of God]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in all the ways he is faithful to the covenant of]

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because you have done this, I will praise you forever]

David is using a verbal form that typically describes action completed in the past. While verbal forms are more flexible in poetry, he may be using this form to describe something that is going to happen in the future in order to show that the event will certainly happen. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use the future tense. Alternate translation: [you will do this]

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because your name is good before your faithful ones, I will await it]

Here God’s **name** represents his reputation. David means that he will wait for God to confirm his reputation for being just by judging and punishing Doeg. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I will wait for you to confirm your reputation]

Here God’s name being **before** his **faithful ones** represents it being where they can see it. In other words, God has shown them that his name is good, that is, that he deserves his good reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [you have shown your faithful ones that it is good]

David is using the adjective **faithful** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. The ULT indicates this by supplying the word **ones**. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [your faithful people]

53.text:
# Psalm 53 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 53 is a slightly modified version of Psalm 14, which is a wisdom psalm that describes the difference between how righteous people and wicked people live and the difference between what happens to them. The editor of this psalm reworked [Psalm 14:5–6](../014/005.md) into [Psalm 53:5](../053/005.md) in such a way that a foreign army that attacked the Israelites serves as a specific example of wicked people seeking to oppress innocent people, and God’s destruction of that army provides a specific example of how God judges and punishes wicked people. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. A description of wicked people (1–4)
2. God punishes wicked people but helps his own people (5–6)

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a “maskil.” See the discussion of that term in the introduction to Psalms.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Why does Psalm 53 say “God” in the places where Psalm 14 says “Yahweh”?

Except for the reworking of Psalm 14:5–6 into Psalm 53:5, Psalm 53 is essentially the same as Psalm 14, with only minor differences (such as saying “and they do” rather than just “they do” in verse 1). However, one significant difference is that in the four places where Psalm 14 uses the divine name “Yahweh,” Psalm 53 says “God.” Many interpreters believe that this is to show that God’s judgment against wicked people and help for innocent people extend beyond the community of those who are in a specific covenant relationship with him. They apply to the entire world, as the destruction of this foreign army demonstrates.
See how you translated the term “chief musician” in the superscription to Psalm 4. Alternate translation: [For the leader of worship music] or [For the music director]

The term that the ULT translates as **Weakness** could be the name of the tune of this psalm. It might also be a musical instruction indicating that singers should perform the song in a minor key or in a somber tone. Alternate translation: [perform in a minor key] or [perform in a somber tone]

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a **maskil**. Since the meaning of this word is not certain, you may wish to represent it in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language. See the discussion of that term in the Introduction to Psalms.

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **fool**. He means foolish people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [A foolish person]
Here the **heart** represents a person’s thoughts. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [thinks]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [There is no God]
The pronoun **They** refers to foolish people who deny God. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Such foolish people are corrupt]

The psalmist is using the adjective **good** as a noun to mean a certain kind of action. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase, here and in verse 3. Alternate translation: [good things]

The psalmist is using **sons of man** as a common expression of his culture to mean “human beings.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [human beings]
Since the psalmist has already used the name “God” earlier in this sentence, it may be more natural in your language to use a pronoun here. Alternate translation: [one seeking him]

The pronoun **him** refers back to “man” in the previous verse. It may be helpful to use a term in your translation that will clarify this for your readers. Another possibility would be to use a plural pronoun, as the psalmist does in the next sentence. Alternate translation: [All of mankind has turned away] or [All of them have turned away]

The psalmist is speaking as if people had physically **turned away** from God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [All of them have abandoned God]

The psalmist is saying **none** and **not even one** as a generalization for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [All people are sinful]

53.quote: הֲ⁠לֹ֥א יָדְעוּ֮ פֹּ֤עֲלֵ֫י אָ֥וֶן אֹכְלֵ֣י עַ֭מִּ⁠י אָ֣כְלוּ לֶ֑חֶם
53.text: The psalmist is using the question form to express amazement that wicked people oppress others without recognizing that God will judge and punish them for doing that. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [They ought to know better, the doers of iniquity, the ones eating my people as they eat bread!]

The point of this comparison is that just as someone can **eat bread** easily and quickly, so these **doers of iniquity** readily oppress and exploit vulnerable people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [the ones eating my people as readily as they eat bread]

The psalmist is speaking as if these **doers of iniquity** were actually **eating** the **people** of his nation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ones exploiting my people as readily as they eat bread]

The psalmist is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [they feared greatly]

53.quote: אֱלֹהִ֗ים פִּ֭זַּר עַצְמ֣וֹת חֹנָ֑⁠ךְ הֱ֝בִשֹׁ֗תָה כִּֽי־אֱלֹהִ֥ים מְאָסָֽ⁠ם
53.text: The psalmist is addressing the nation of Israel as if it were an individual, even though he knows that it cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to anyone who hears this song that he feels very strongly about how God defeated and destroyed this attacking army. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if the psalmist were speaking objectively about this army. Alternate translation: [God scattered the bones of the ones encamping against Israel. The Israelites have shamed them, for God despises them]

The psalmist is using the fact that the surviving soldiers of this army were not able to bury their fellow soldiers who were killed, so that their **bones** were left **scattered** on the field of battle, to represent how completely God defeated this army. Alternate translation: [God completely defeated and destroyed]

The psalmist is using one person who was involved in **encamping** against the Israelites, probably the king who commanded this army, to mean everyone who was involved. (This is clear from the way the psalmist says **them** later in this verse.) If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ones encamping against you] or [the soldiers who attacked you]
The word “you” is singular in both instances in this verse, so use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.
The pronoun **you** seems to refer in context to “Israel” in the next verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [against you, Israel. You have shamed them]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Who will give that the salvation of Israel will come from Zion?]

The psalmist is using **Who will give** as a common expression of his culture to introduce a fervent wish. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [O that salvation for Israel would come from Zion!] or [I fervently wish that salvation for Israel would come from Zion!]

The psalmist is using Mount **Zion**, the location of God’s sanctuary, to represent God himself in the act of providing **salvation** for **Israel**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [O that God would act from his sanctuary on Mount Zion to provide for the salvation of Israel!] or [I fervently wish that God would act from his sanctuary on Mount Zion to provide for the salvation of Israel!]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [O that God would act from his sanctuary on Mount Zion to save Israel!] or [I fervently wish that God would act from his sanctuary on Mount Zion to save Israel!]

The word that the ULT translates as **prosperity** can also mean “captivity.” If that is the meaning, then this verse could have been added to the psalm later, after the Israelites were conquered and taken into captivity. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to follow the translation that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT. Alternate translation: [When God restores the captivity of his people] or [When God brings his people back from captivity]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms. Alternate translation: [Israel will rejoice greatly] or [Jacob will be glad; indeed, Israel will rejoice]

The psalmist is using the two names of the ancestor of the Israelites, **Jacob** and **Israel**, to represent the Israelites themselves. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The descendants of Jacob will be glad; indeed, the Israelites will rejoice]

54.text:
# Psalm 54 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 54 is a psalm of supplication or lament. It includes all the basic elements of that type of psalm. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Cry for help (1–2)
2. Description of troubles (3)
3. Statement of trust (4–5a)
4. Petition (5b)
5. Vow of praise (6)
6. Renewed statement of trust (7)

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a “maskil.” See the discussion of that term in the introduction to Psalms.

As its superscription indicates, the background to this psalm is an episode related in [1 Samuel 23:19–23](../1sa/23/19.md) in which the people who lived in the wilderness of Ziph went and told Saul, who wanted to kill David, that he was hiding among them. It may be helpful to read that episode before translating this psalm.

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

### Variation between “you” and “he”

In verses 1, 2, 6, and the second part of verse 5, David addresses Yahweh directly as “you.” In verses 3, 4, 7, and the first part of verse 5, he speaks about Yahweh as “he.” This variation of pronouns reflects the flow of a psalm of supplication from a cry for help (“you”) to a description of troubles and statement of trust (“he”) to a petition and vow of praise (“you”) to a renewed statement of trust (“he”). However, if it would not be natural in your language to switch back and forth between second-person and third-person pronouns, you could use second-person pronouns throughout the psalm, as some versions do. For example, in verse 3, you might say, “They do not set you, God, before them”; in verse 4, you might say, “you, God, are a helper to me”; and in verse 7, you might say, “you deliver me from every trouble.”
See how you translated the term “chief musician” in the superscription to Psalm 4. Alternate translation: [For the leader of worship music] or [For the music director]

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a **maskil**. Since the meaning of this word is not certain, you may wish to represent it in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language. See the discussion of that term in the Introduction to Psalms.

The Ziphites were using the question form to show that they were certain about what they were saying. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [David is definitely hiding among us]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Deliver me, God, by your mighty name] or [Save me, God, by your name; yes, vindicate me by your might]

The terms **Save** and **vindicate** are imperatives, but they communicate polite requests rather than a commands. Use a form in your language that communicates a polite request in these cases and in the next verse. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make the meaning clear. Alternate translation: [Please save me … yes, please vindicate me]

David is using God’s **name** to represent the qualities that people associate with God when they hear his name; specifically in this context, his power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [by your power] or [by the power for which you have a well-deserved reputation]

David is using his **mouth** to represent what he is saying by using his mouth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to the words that I am speaking]

Here the word **For** does not introduce the reason why God should listen to David. It introduces David’s explanation of why he is praying to God for help. Use a connecting word or phrase in your language that will make this clear. Alternate translation: [You see,]

David is speaking as if the Ziphites were actually **foreigners**, even though he and they belong to the same Israelite tribe of Judah, because they are not acting toward him with the loyalty that one would expect of kinsmen. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [treacherous people]

When David says that these people **have arisen**, he does not mean that they have stood up from a sitting or lying position. He means that they have taken action, in this context hostile action. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [have taken hostile action against me]

David is using the adjective **violent** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. The ULT indicates this by supplying the word **ones**. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [and violent men]

David is speaking as if **God** were an object that these people could **set** in front of them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They have no regard for God] or [They are not mindful of God]
See how your translation team decided at [3:2](../003/002.md) to represent the term **Selah**.
David is using the term **Behold** to focus attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Listen]

David is using a common expression of his culture to mean that **the Lord** helps the **sustainers** of his **life**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the Lord helps the sustainers of my life]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Because you are faithful]

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because your name is good, Yahweh, I will praise it]
See how you translated the term “name” in verse 1. Alternate translation: [I will praise you for your character]

Here the word **For** does not introduce the reason why David is going to praise Yahweh and sacrifice to him. It introduces an explanation of why David is going to be able to do that. Use a connecting word or phrase in your language that will make this clear. Alternate translation: [After all,]

David is using one part himself, his **eye**, to mean all of him in the act of looking upon his enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I look at my enemies] or [and I personally see my enemies]

David means specifically that he sees that Yahweh has defeated his enemies. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and I personally see that Yahweh has defeated my enemies]

55.text:
# Psalm 55 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 55 is a psalm of supplication or lament. It includes all the basic elements of that type of psalm except a vow of praise. (Some elements are repeated.) See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Cry for help (1–2)
2. Description of troubles (3–8)
3. Petition (9)
4. Description of troubles (10–14)
5. Petition (15)
6. Statement of trust (16–19a)
7. Description of troubles (19b–21)
8. Statement of trust (22–23)

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a “maskil.” See the discussion of that term in the introduction to Psalms.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### What former “companion” or friend is David describing in verses 12–14 and 20–21?

Many interpreters believe that David wrote this psalm after his counselor and friend Ahithophel turned against him and supported David’s son Absalom in his rebellion against him. (These events are described in [2 Samuel 15:12–36](../2sa/15/12.md).) If so, then Ahithophel would be the former friend whom David describes in these verses. However, throughout the centuries, Christian interpreters have also seen this psalm as prophetic of Judas’s betrayal of Jesus (even though no New Testament writer directly quotes it as a Messianic prophecy that was fulfilled in the life of Jesus). For that reason, we recommend that translators take care not to translate it in a way that limits its potential meaning to the original circumstances, such as by saying in verse 13, for example, “But it was you, Ahithophel” rather than simply “But it was you.” Instead, a translation can use footnotes to describe the likely historical background of this psalm.

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

### Intentionally repeated terms

In two cases, David uses the same terms near the beginning and end of this psalm. In the first case, he does this to draw a contrast. In verse 3 he says that the wicked try to “shake” trouble onto the righteous, but in verse 22 he says that God will never allow their “shaking.” In the second case, he repeats terms to reassert something he said earlier that he would do. In verse 2, he says, “I am restless in my complaint, and let me moan.” In verse 17, after describing the trouble he is in, he says “let me complain and moan,” showing that his response to the trouble is to plead with God for help. So that your readers can appreciate these things, we encourage you, if possible, to use the same terms in your language in the later verses that you use in the earlier verses.
See how you translated the term “chief musician” in the superscription to Psalm 4. Alternate translation: [For the leader of worship music] or [For the music director]

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a **maskil**. Since the meaning of this word is not certain, you may wish to represent it in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language. See the discussion of that term in the Introduction to Psalms.

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Listen carefully, God, as I plead with you in prayer] or [Listen {to} my prayer, God! Indeed, do not hide yourself from my plea!]

The expressions **Listen** and **do not hide** are imperatives, but they communicate polite requests rather than a commands. Use a form in your language that communicates a polite request in these cases and in the next verse. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make the meaning clear. Alternate translation: [Please listen … and please do not hide]

David is speaking as if God might actually **hide** himself so that David could not find him and make a **plea** to him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and do not disregard my plea]

In this context, the expression **answer me** means more than “say something in response to me.” It means “do what I ask.” In this case, David is asking God specifically to protect him. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and protect me]

David is using a verbal form in which he is addressing himself and suggesting a course of action. (It is common in psalms of supplication for the psalmist to move back and forth between calling to God for help and making observations to himself about his own situation.) If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this with the same kind of statement form that David uses in the first part of this sentence when he says **I am restless**. Alternate translation: [and I moan]

David is not referring to a specific **enemy**. He means all of the enemies who are threatening him on this occasion, as his use of the plural pronoun **they** later in this verse indicates. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [from the voice of my enemies]

Here a person’s **voice** represents what he is saying by using his voice. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [because of what my enemies are saying]

David is using **from the face of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “because of” or “on account of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because of the oppression of the wicked]

David is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [because of the oppression of wicked people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **oppression**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because wicked people are oppressing me]

Here the expression **For** introduces more detailed information about what David’s wicked enemies are doing. Use a connecting word or phrase in your language that will make this clear. It may not be necessary to represent this expression explicitly in your translation. Alternate translation: [You see,]

David is speaking as if **trouble** were an object such as a large rock that his enemies could **shake** loose so that it would fall **onto** him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [they stir up trouble for me] or [they trouble me greatly]
Here the **nose** represents anger. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and in anger]

The verb that the ULT translates here as **persecute** means generally to “hold a grudge.” The focus in this context is not on an inner feeling of resentment but on a relentless attempt by someone holding a grudge to harm another person. If your language has a verb or phrase that describes this action, it would be appropriate to use it in your translation. Alternate translation: [they try relentlessly to harm me] or [they pursue a vendetta against me]

This statement could have a figurative meaning or a literal meaning or both. If your language has a term such as “heart” that describes an internal organ and can also represent emotions, it would be appropriate to use it here in your translation. This could mean: (1) that David is using his **heart** to represent his emotions.
