Alternate translation: [I feel very distressed inside] or (2) that David is describing physical symptoms that he is experiencing. Alternate translation: [My heart is pounding inside me] or [My heart is racing fast]

David is speaking as if the **terrors of death** were actually objects that could have **fallen onto** him. He means that he is feeling them immediately and forcefully, as if they had struck him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I feel the terrors of death strikingly]

David may be using the plural form **terrors**: (1) to indicate that the prospect of dying is making him feel a combination of fears. Alternate translation: [I feel strikingly all the fears that the prospect of dying makes a person feel] or (2) to emphasize that the fear of death is a very great fear. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a singular form and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [I feel strikingly the great fear of death]

David is speaking of **Fear and trembling** as if they were living things that could have **come** upon him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I cannot help feeling afraid and trembling]
David is speaking as if **horror** had physically **covered** him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and horror has overwhelmed me]

David has not **said** this to anyone else. He has said it to himself. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I have said to myself] or [I have thought]

Here the word **wing** is singular in form, but it refers to both of the two wings that a dove has. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural or dual form of “wing.” Alternate translation: [Who will give, the wings of a dove are to me?]

David is using **Who will give** as a common expression of his culture to introduce a fervent wish. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [O that I had the wings of a dove!] or [I fervently wish that I had the wings of a dove!]

David means implicitly that he wishes he could **dwell** somewhere safe. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and let me dwell somewhere safe]
David is using the term **Behold** to focus attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Listen]

The verbs **make distance** and **wandering** together express a single idea. The verb **wandering** tells in what way David would **make distance** between himself and his enemies. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [I would wander far away]
To translate the term **Selah** here and in verse 19, see how your translation team decided to represent that term in [3:2](../003/002.md).

Here, **an escape** represents “a place of escape.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to a place of escape] or [to a place where I am safe]

The terms **storming wind** and **tempest** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [from the raging tempest]

David is speaking as if the hostile opposition of his wicked enemies were actually a **storming wind** or **tempest**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from these looming calamities]

The verb that the ULT translates as **Swallow** means “to swallow” in every other instance in the Hebrew Bible. (For example, [Jonah 1:17](../jon/01/17.md), “Yahweh appointed a great fish to swallow Jonah.”) However, many biblical scholars believe, based on languages similar to Hebrew, that there was another verb with the same consonants that meant “confuse” and that David was using that verb here. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT. Alternate translation: [Confuse, Lord, divide their tongue] or [Lord, confuse and divide their tongue]

If this verb means **Swallow**, then David is speaking as if he wants the **Lord** actually to eat his enemies and swallow them. See how you translated the similar term “devour” in [35:25](../035/025.md). Alternate translation: [Destroy them]

Here the word **tongue** is singular in form, but it refers to the tongues of all of David’s enemies as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “tongue.” Alternate translation: [divide their tongues]

David is using the term **tongue** to represent what his enemies would by using their tongues. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [make them disagree in what they say]
Here the word **For** introduces an explanation for what David asks in the previous sentence. Use a connecting word or phrase in your language that will make this clear.

The terms **violence** and **strife** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [much violence]
To decide whether to be more specific in your translation about what **city** David is referring to, see the discussion in the introduction to this psalm of when and why he probably wrote it.

David is referring to all of time by naming its two major components, **Day** and **night**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [All the time] or [Constantly]

David is speaking of the “violence” and “strife” he mentioned in the previous verse (referring back to them here as **they**) as if they were living things that could **go around** on the walls of a city. He is speaking of them as if they were watchmen who were supposed to make sure that there was good order in the city but who instead are making sure that there is continual fighting in the city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [there is violence all around the city]

David is speaking of **iniquity** and **trouble** as if they were living things that could dwell **in the midst of** a city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and wicked people cause trouble in the midst of it]

David is speaking of **oppression** and **deceit** as if they were living things that could **depart** from the open square of a city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and oppression and deceit are continually present in it]

Here the expression **For** introduces more detailed information about the identify of one of David’s enemies. Use a connecting word or phrase in your language that will make this clear. It may not be necessary to represent this expression explicitly in your translation. Alternate translation: [You see,]

Here and in the next verse, David addresses this former **companion** directly, even though he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to himself and to anyone who hears this song that he feels very strongly about how this former friend has betrayed him. If it would be helpful in your language, here and in the next verse you could translate what David says to this former friend as if he were speaking to other people about him. Alternate translation: [But it was a man according to my valuation, my companion and my acquaintance]

David is speaking as if someone had vowed both him and his former friend to God (as [Leviticus 27:1–8](../lev/27/01.md) describes) and a priest had determined that they had the same **valuation**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a man equal to me]

Since David was the king of Israel, this **man** could not have been his actual equal in rank. David is probably describing the regard in which he held this man. Alternate translation: [a man whom I esteemed as my equal]

To decide whether to be more specific in your translation about what **companion** and **acquaintance** David is referring to, see the discussion in the introduction to this psalm of when and why he probably wrote it.

By **we** in both instances, David means himself and his former friend, whom he is addressing, so use the inclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction. However, if you translated verse 13 as if David were speaking about his friend rather than to him, then **we** would not include the people to whom he is speaking (anyone else hearing this song), so use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

David is speaking as if he and his former friend had actually **made** the **counsel** they formerly shared together **sweet**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [we who spoke together very pleasantly]

David is speaking as if God’s temple were actually a **house** in which he lived. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Since only priests could enter the temple building, David is referring to the courtyard of the temple. Alternate translation: [in the courtyard of the temple of God]

55.quote: ישימות עָלֵ֗י⁠מוֹ יֵרְד֣וּ שְׁא֣וֹל חַיִּ֑ים כִּֽי־רָע֖וֹת בִּ⁠מְגוּרָ֣⁠ם בְּ⁠קִרְבָּֽ⁠ם
55.text: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because evils {are} in their dwelling, in the midst of them, may desolations be upon them; may they go down to Sheol alive]

The pronouns **them** and **they** refer to the enemies whom David first described in verse 3. He is talking about them as a group again after focusing on a specific one of them in verses 12–14. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [May desolations be upon my enemies; may they go down]

This phrase is a translation of the written Hebrew text. Later Hebrew scribes, however, have recommended a correction in the margin of the text. You may want to follow this correction in your translation. Alternate translation: [May death seize upon them]

If this is the correct reading, David would be speaking of **desolations** as if they were objects that could be **upon** his enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May things happen to them that desolate them]

If the correct reading is “May death seize upon them,” David would be speaking of death as if it were a living thing that could seize his enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May they die without being able to resist dying]

David is alluding to the episode described in [Numbers 16:1–33](../num/16/01.md) in which men named Korah, Dathan, and Abiram rebelled against Moses, and Yahweh judged and punished them by having the ground open up so that they “went down to Sheol alive.” You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [may they go down to Sheol alive, just like the people who rebelled against Moses]

David is speaking as if **evils** actually lived with his enemies in their **dwelling**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [evil is at home with them] or [they live in an environment that is constantly evil]

Here the word **dwelling** is singular in form, but it refers to the dwellings of all of David’s enemies as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “dwelling.” Alternate translation: [are in their dwellings]

David is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I will call** already includes this meaning. He is doing that in order to emphasize a contrast between what his enemies are doing (living wickedly, without regard for God), and what he will do. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [But as for me, I will call to God]

David is referring to an entire day by naming three significant times in it, **Evening** (probably meaning sundown), **morning** (probably meaning dawn), and **noon**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Throughout the day]

David is using the term **voice** to represent what he would say by using his voice. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he will hear what I say]

David is using the term **hear** to mean that God will do what he is asking him to do, as he states confidently in the next verse. The meaning of “hear” is the same in verse 19. Alternate translation: [and he will do what I ask]

David is speaking as if God actually **redeems** him or pays a price to free him from slavery or captivity. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He rescues my life in peace from the battle against me]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. In this context, that term has the sense of “well-being.” Alternate translation: [He rescues me, alive and well, from the battle against me]
The pronoun **they** refers to David’s enemies. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [my enemies are]

This phrase is a translation of the written Hebrew text. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense, since in contexts like this, the term “answer” usually means “do what they ask” (as in verse 2). You may want to follow an alternative reading from the ancient Greek translation. Alternate translation: [and afflict them]

David is referring specifically to God **sitting** on his throne, and he is using that action to represent God ruling. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the one enthroned] or [the one ruling]

The relative pronoun **whom** refers to David’s enemies. It may be more natural in your language to use a personal pronoun and begin a new sentence here. Alternate translation: [There are no changes to them]

By **changes**, David means misfortunes, losses, and disappointments in life. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [They have no reversals of fortune] or [They enjoy continuous prosperity]
The pronoun **He** refers to David’s former friend. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [My former friend stretches out]

David is using **stretches out his hands** as a common expression of his culture to mean “commits violent acts.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [My former friend lays violent hands on his friends] or [My former friend commits violent acts against his friends]

The word “defile” means to treat something sacred as if it were common. The implication is that this former friend did not consider his **covenant** with David a sacred obligation that God would enforce. (David could be referring to a formal covenant or the implicit obligations of friendship.) As a result, he was not concerned that God would punish him if he broke the covenant. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [he breaks his covenant] or [he disregards the obligations of friendship]

David is speaking as if the things that this former friend said with his **mouth** had actually been **curds**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this image as a comparison. Alternate translation: [The things that he said were so smooth, it was as if they were curds] or [What he said caused no concern, just as a person can swallow curds without difficulty because they are smooth]

David is speaking as if this former friend’s **heart**, which represents his feelings, had actually been **war**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but secretly he felt hostile toward me]

The point of this comparison is that while soft olive **oil** is soothing to the skin, the **words** of this former friend were even more soothing and reassuring to David. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [His words were even more soothing to me than soft olive oil is to the skin]

David is speaking as if this former friend’s words had actually been **swords** that soldiers had **unsheathed** so that they were ready to use. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but they were actually dangerous and deadly]

The expression **unsheathed** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [were bare swords]

The words **you** and **your** and the implied “you” in the imperative **Cast** are singular because David is addressing himself and any individual in a similar situation who hears this song. So, use singular forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

David is speaking of the difficulties that a person might have as if they were actually a **burden** that a person was carrying and that he could **Cast** onto **Yahweh** so that he would carry it instead. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Trust Yahweh to help you with your difficulties]

David is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **he will sustain** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize the personal role that Yahweh will take in sustaining a person who trusts him. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [and he will personally sustain you]

David is using the image of **shaking** something loose so that it falls from its position (he uses the same image in verse 3) to represent other people ruining righteous people. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [he will not let the righteous down] or [he will not allow anyone to ruin the righteous]

David is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [he will not allow shaking to righteous people] or [he will not allow anyone to ruin righteous people]

David is using the term **grave** to represent the decay and destruction of physical bodies that occurs in a grave. By characterizing this **pit** in that way, he is indicating that it is the chasm beneath the earth where his culture understood dead people to be. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to the pit of destruction] or [to the pit where dead people go]

Here, **blood** represents violently shedding blood. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Men of bloodshed and treachery] or [Murderous, treacherous men]

David is using **will not halve their days** as a common expression of his culture to mean “will not even live half as long as they otherwise would have.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [will not reach middle age] or [will not even live half as long as they otherwise would have]

David is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I will trust** already includes this meaning. He is doing that in order to emphasize a contrast between what will happen to the wicked people he has just described and what he will do himself. Alternate translation: [But for my part, I will trust]

56.text:
# Psalm 56 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 56 is a psalm of supplication or lament. It includes all the basic elements of that type of psalm. (Some elements are repeated.) See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Cry for help (1a)
2. Description of troubles (1b–2)
3. Statement of trust (3–4)
4. Description of troubles (5–6)
5. Petition (7–8)
6. Statement of trust (9–11)
7. Vow of praise (12–13)

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a “miktam.” See the discussion of that term in the introduction to Psalms.

As its superscription indicates, the background to this psalm is an episode related in [1 Samuel 21:10–15](../1sa/21/10.md) in which David fled from King Saul to the Philistine city of Gath, and the Philistines, recognizing that he was a great Israelite military commander, imprisoned him. It may be helpful to read that episode before translating this psalm.

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

### Variation between “you” and “he”

In verses 1–3, 8, and 12, David addresses God directly as “you.” In verses 4 and 9–11, he speaks about him as “God.” This variation of pronouns reflects the flow of a psalm of supplication from a cry for help to a description of troubles and statement of trust to a petition to a vow of praise. However, if it would not be natural in your language to switch back and forth between second-person and third-person pronouns, you could use second-person pronouns throughout the psalm, as some versions do. For example, in verses 4, 10, and 11, you might say “I praise your word” and “in you, God, I trust.” In verse 9, you might say “you, God, are for me.”
See how you translated the term “chief musician” in the superscription to Psalm 4. Alternate translation: [For the leader of worship music] or [For the music director]

See how you translated the similar expression “On Sheminith” in the superscription to Psalm 6. Alternate translation: [Set to the tune Yonath Elem Rehoqim] or [Perform in the Yonath Elem Rehoqim style]

The words that the ULT translates as **A Faraway Silent Dove** could also mean “A Dove on Distant Oaks.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT. Alternate translation: [A Dove on Distant Oaks]

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a **miktam**. Since the meaning of this word is not certain, you may wish to represent it in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language. See the discussion of that term in the Introduction to Psalms.

This superscription is referring to events related in [1 Samuel 21:10–15](../1sa/21/10.md). If it would be helpful to your readers, you could describe these events more fully. Alternate translation: [David wrote this song when he fled from Saul to the Philistine city of Gath, hoping he would be safe there, but the Philistines seized him]

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Man tramples me, so be gracious to me, God!]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a polite request, here and in verses 7 and 8. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please be gracious to me]

David is not referring to a specific **man**. He means all of the Philistines who have captured him. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [men are trampling me] or [people are trampling me]

David is speaking as if the Philistines were actually trampling on him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly, here and in the next verse. Alternate translation: [men are harassing me] or [people are harassing me]

David is using the term **day** to mean “time,” since time consists of days. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly, here and in verses 2 and 5. Alternate translation: [All the time] or [Continually]

The words **fighting** and **oppresses** together express a single idea. David is using the word **fighting** to tell in what way **man** (representing his human opponents) **oppresses** him. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [he oppresses me hostilely] or [they oppress me hostilely]

56.quote: שָׁאֲפ֣וּ שׁ֭וֹרְרַ⁠י כָּל־הַ⁠יּ֑וֹם כִּֽי־רַבִּ֨ים לֹחֲמִ֖ים לִ֣⁠י מָרֽוֹם
56.text: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because many are fighting against me arrogantly, my enemies trample me all of the day]

David is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I will trust** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to express a commitment or resolve. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [I am resolved that the day I fear, I will trust in you]

David is using **The day** as a common expression of his culture to describe the occasion on which something might happen. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [If ever] or [When]

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put David’s statement **I praise his word** at the beginning of this verse so that it does not interrupt his statement **In God … I trust**. However, it is for emphasis and emotional impact that David introduces the information that he praises God’s word in the middle of the information that he trusts God, so if you move the former information to the beginning of the verse, you should try to convey the emphasis and emotional impact in another way. Alternate translation: [I praise God’s word, so I trust completely in him] or [I celebrate God’s promises, so I trust completely in him]

David is using the term **word** to represent **God** speaking to him by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I praise him for what he has said to me] or [I praise him for his promise to me]

Here, **flesh** represents human beings, who are made of flesh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [What will human beings do to me?]

David is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Human beings can certainly do nothing to me!]

The term that the ULT translates as **matters** can also mean “words.” So this could mean: (1) that the people David is describing are causing trouble in his affairs. Alternate translation: [they cause trouble in my affairs] or (2) that these people are figuratively reshaping, that is, distorting, what David says. Alternate translation: [they twist my words]

David is saying **all** as an overstatement for emphasis. He is referring not to every thought that his Philistine captors have but to **all of their thoughts** about him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [all of their thoughts about me]

David is stating the pronoun **they** separately, even though the verb translated as **they watch** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize the personal role that his enemies are taking in watching him. (They are not appointing others as spies but doing the spying themselves.) If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [they personally watch] or [it is they who watch]

David is using his **heels** to represent how he walks on his feet to go places. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [they watch my steps] or [they observe where I go]

Here, David’s **life** represents an opportunity to take his life or kill him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. The UST models one way to do that.

The word that the ULT translates as **Upon** could indicate: (1) that **iniquity** characterizes David’s enemies. Alternate translation: [Because of their iniquity, shall there be an escape for them] or (2) that **iniquity** is the means that David’s enemies would use to **escape** from the just consequences of their actions. Alternate translation: [Shall there be an escape for them by iniquity]

David is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Because of their iniquity, there should not be an escape for them!] or [There should not be an escape for them by iniquity!]
Here the **nose** represents anger. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [In anger]

David is speaking as if the **peoples** were actually in an elevated position and God would **make** them **go down** from there. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [destroy the peoples]

David is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you record** already includes this meaning. He is doing that in order to emphasize a contrast between what his enemies are doing to try to harm him and what God is doing to watch over him and care for him. Alternate translation: [But for your part, you record]

David is speaking as if God had actually recorded his **wandering**, that is, as if God had written down that at this point David had left Israel to live among the Philistines. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you are aware of my wandering]

David is speaking as if God actually had a leather **bag** that held fluids, such as people in this culture used to hold water or wine when traveling through arid regions, and that he wanted God to put his **tears** in it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Keep my tears close to you]

David is using his **tears** to represent the sorrows he has experienced. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Always be mindful of my sorrows]

David is using the question form to make a confident affirmation. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [After all, they are in your record.]

Earlier in this verse, David portrays God as recording the details of his **wandering**. Here he speaks as if God had actually written in that **record** about the tears he has shed. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [After all, you are aware of them]

56.quote: אָ֥֨ז יָ֘שׁ֤וּבוּ אוֹיְבַ֣⁠י אָ֭חוֹר בְּ⁠י֣וֹם אֶקְרָ֑א
56.text: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [On the day I call, then my enemies will turn back]

56.quote: אָ֥֨ז יָ֘שׁ֤וּבוּ אוֹיְבַ֣⁠י אָ֭חוֹר בְּ⁠י֣וֹם אֶקְרָ֑א
56.text: See how you translated the similar expression “The day” in verse 3. Alternate translation: [When I call, then my enemies will turn back]

56.quote: אָ֥֨ז יָ֘שׁ֤וּבוּ אוֹיְבַ֣⁠י אָ֭חוֹר בְּ⁠י֣וֹם אֶקְרָ֑א
56.text: David saying both **Then** and **on the day** (meaning “when”) for emphasis. However, in some languages this might seem to express extra information in a way that would not be natural. If so, you can use only one of these expressions. Alternate translation: [When I call, my enemies will turn back]

David means implicitly that he will **call** to God for help. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I call to you for help]

The word that the ULT translates as **for** could introduce: (1) the reason why David knows that what he has just said is true. Alternate translation: [I know this because God is for me] or (2) the content of what David knows. Alternate translation: [This I know, that God is for me]

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because God is for me, I know this]

56.quote: בֵּֽ֭⁠אלֹהִים אֲהַלֵּ֣ל דָּבָ֑ר בַּ֝⁠יהוָ֗ה אֲהַלֵּ֥ל דָּבָֽר׃ בֵּֽ⁠אלֹהִ֣ים בָּ֭טַחְתִּי לֹ֣א אִירָ֑א מַה־יַּעֲשֶׂ֖ה אָדָ֣ם לִֽ⁠י
56.text: This is the second instance of the refrain in this psalm. (It occurs here in an expanded form.) We recommend that you show this to your readers by translating the phrases here the same way that you translated them in the first occurrence of this refrain in [56:4](../056/004.md).

See how you translated the term “man” in [56:1](../056/001.md). (Although David says **man** here where he said “flesh” in verse 4, the meaning is the same in both instances of this refrain.) Alternate translation: [What will people do to me?] or [Human beings can certainly do nothing to me!]

David is using **Your vows {are} on me** as a common expression of his culture to mean that he has made vows to God that he will publicly thank him for helping him and that he is bound by those vows to keep that promise. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am under vows to you] or [I have made vows to you]

David is using the possessive form to describe not vows that God has made but **vows** that he has made to **God**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [The vows I have made to you]

David is probably not referring to several different vows he has made to God. He probably means that he has made the same vow several times, that he will sacrifice a thank-offering to God when God delivers him. If your language uses a different plural form for a repeated action than it does for separate actions, it would be appropriate to use that form here. In some languages it may be natural to use a singular form. Alternate translation: [The vow I have made to you]

Here the word **For** does not introduce the reason why David is going to make a thank-offering to God. It introduces an explanation of why David is going to be able to do that. Use a connecting word or phrase in your language that will make this clear. Alternate translation: [I will be able to do this because]

It might seem that this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [you deliver me from death] or [you rescue my life]

56.quote: הֲ⁠לֹ֥א רַגְלַ֗⁠י מִ֫⁠דֶּ֥חִי לְ֭⁠הִֽתְהַלֵּךְ לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י אֱלֹהִ֑ים בְּ֝⁠א֗וֹר הַֽ⁠חַיִּֽים
56.text: David is using the question form to make a confident assertion. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [My feet are from stumbling, so I may walk about to the face of God in the light of the living!]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Are not my feet kept from stumbling] or, as an assertion, [You keep my feet from stumbling]

David is speaking as if God actually kept his **feet** from **stumbling**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Do you not keep me safe] or, as an assertion, [You keep me safe]
David is using the image of walking to represent living. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that I may live]

Here, **to the face of** represents being in the presence of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the presence of]

Here, **light** represents the earth, which people of this culture considered to be a light place, by contrast with Sheol, the realm of the dead, which was a dark place. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the world of the living] or [on this earth, where people are alive]

David is using the adjective **living** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [living people]

57.text:
# Psalm 57 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 57 begins as a psalm of supplication or lament. It presents several of the basic elements of that type of psalm. But after the statement of trust, instead of a petition and a vow of praise, it turns into a psalm of worship. David experiences such confidence in God that instead of asking him to do something specific for him and promising to thank him publicly, David calls himself to praise God and says why he should do that. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Cry for help (1–3)
2. Description of troubles (4)
3. Refrain (5)
4. Description of troubles (6)
5. Statement of trust (7)
6. Call to worship (8–9)
7. Reason to worship (10)
8. Refrain (11)

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a “miktam.” See the discussion of that term in the introduction to Psalms.

As its superscription indicates, the background to this psalm is one of two episodes in which David fled from King Saul and hid in a cave. This could have been the cave of Adullam, as described in [1 Samuel 22:1–2](../1sa/22/01.md), or the cave of En Gedi, as described in [1 Samuel 24:1–22](../1sa/24/01.md). It may be helpful to read those episodes before translating this psalm.

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

### Variation between “you” and “he”

In verses 1, 5, 7, and 9–11, David addresses God directly as “you.” In verses 2–3, he speaks about him as “God.” This variation of pronouns reflects the flow of psalm of supplication from a cry for help to a description of troubles to a statement of trust. This psalm then becomes a psalm of worship in which David continues to address God directly. However, if it would not be natural in your language to switch back and forth between second-person and third-person pronouns, you could use second-person pronouns throughout the psalm, as some versions do. For example, in verse 2 you might say “I call to you, God Most High,” and in verse 9, you might say “May you send” and “May you reproach.”
See how you translated the term “chief musician” in the superscription to Psalm 4. Alternate translation: [For the leader of worship music] or [For the music director]

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a **miktam**. Since the meaning of this word is not certain, you may wish to represent it in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language. See the discussion of that term in the Introduction to Psalms.

This superscription is referring to one of two episodes in which David **fled** from King **Saul**, who wanted to kill him, and hid in a **cave**. This could have been the cave of Adullam, as described in [1 Samuel 22:1–2](../1sa/22/01.md), or the cave of En Gedi, as described in [1 Samuel 24:1–22](../1sa/24/01.md). If it would be helpful to your readers, you could describe these events more fully, even though the identity of this cave is not certain. Alternate translation: [David wrote this song while he was hiding in a cave to which he had fled in order to be safe from King Saul]
The superscription is using one part of Saul, his **face**, to mean all of him in his determination to kill David. Alternate translation: [from Saul, who wanted to kill him]

These are imperatives, but they communicate a polite request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please be gracious to me; God, please be gracious to me]

David is repeating a phrase in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If speakers of your language can repeat phrases for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [I ask you earnestly to be gracious to me, God]

Here the word **for** does not introduce the reason why God should be gracious to David. It introduces David’s explanation of why he wants God to be gracious to him. Use a connecting word or phrase in your language that will make this clear. It may not be necessary to represent this expression explicitly in your translation.

57.quote: בְ⁠ךָ֮ חָסָ֪יָה נַ֫פְשִׁ֥⁠י וּ⁠בְ⁠צֵֽל־כְּנָפֶ֥י⁠ךָ אֶחְסֶ֑ה עַ֝֗ד יַעֲבֹ֥ר הַוּֽוֹת
57.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [my soul takes refuge in the shadow of your wings until the calamities have passed by] or [in you my soul takes refuge, indeed, in the shadow of your wings I take refuge until the calamities have passed by]

David is using one part of himself, his **soul**, to mean all of him in the act of taking refuge in God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in you I take refuge]

David is speaking as if God were actually a **refuge** or place where he could go to be safe. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you are the one who keeps me safe]

Here the **shadow** that wings cast represents the area under the wings that they shelter. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and in the shelter of your wings I take refuge] or [and under your wings I take refuge]

David is speaking as if God were actually a bird that had **wings** and as if he were one of that bird’s chicks that would **take refuge** under those wings. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this image as a comparison. The UST models one way to do that.

David is speaking of the **calamities** he is experiencing as if it were living things that could pass by him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [until these calamities end]

David assumes that his listeners will understand that by **accomplishing**, he means that God accomplishes the purposes that he has for him. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the one accomplishing his purposes for me]

57.quote: יִשְׁלַ֤ח מִ⁠שָּׁמַ֨יִם ׀ וְֽ⁠יוֹשִׁיעֵ֗⁠נִי חֵרֵ֣ף שֹׁאֲפִ֣⁠י & יִשְׁלַ֥ח אֱ֝לֹהִ֗ים חַסְדּ֥⁠וֹ וַ⁠אֲמִתּֽ⁠וֹ
57.text: The two instances of the verb **send** in this verse are in a form that Hebrew writers could use to express either a statement or a wish. The verb **reproach** would conform to whichever sense the writer intended. At this point in this psalm of supplication, David still seems to be expressing his cry for help, so the ULT translates these verbs as expressing a wish. (See the introduction to this psalm.) However, David may also be making an anticipatory confident statement about what God will do. The original audience may have heard both nuances. Use the verbal form in your language that seems most suitable. Alternate translation: [He will send from the heavens and save me. He will reproach the one trampling me. … God will send his covenant faithfulness and his truth]

David is speaking as if he wanted God actually to **send** someone or something **from the heavens** to **save** him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May he act from the heavens to save me]
If you decide to retain the image of sending in your translation, it may be helpful to specify what God would **send**. Alternate translation: [May he send help from the heavens and save me]

David is speaking as if someone were actually **trampling** on him and as if he wanted God to say something to make the person ashamed of doing that so that he would stop. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May he stop the person who is harassing me]
To translate the term **Selah** here and in verse 7, see how your translation team decided at [3:2](../003/002.md) to represent that term.

David is speaking as if **covenant faithfulness** and **truth** were living things that God could **send** to help him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May God act in covenant faithfulness and truth to help me]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **truth** and **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways, here and in verse 10. Alternate translation: [the ways he is faithful to his covenant and his trustworthiness]

David is using one part of himself, his **soul** or inner being, to mean all of him in the situation of being **in the midst of lions**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am in the midst of lions]

The word that the ULT translates as **soul** can also mean “life.” The original audience would have heard both nuances. The implication is that David’s life is in danger, that is, he is in danger of being killed. Alternate translation: [My life is in danger because I am in the midst of lions]

David is speaking as if he were actually surrounded by **lions**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this image as a comparison. Alternate translation: [I am in the midst of men who are as dangerous as lions]

By putting the phrase **sons of man** right after **blazing ones**, David is indicating that he is making a comparison between these people and things that are **blazing** and set other things on fire. The point of this comparison is that just as fire is destructive, so these people are trying to destroy him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [I must lie down among people who are trying to destroy me]

David is using **sons of man** as a common expression of his culture to mean “human beings.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [human beings]

57.quote: שִׁ֭נֵּי⁠הֶם חֲנִ֣ית וְ⁠חִצִּ֑ים וּ֝⁠לְשׁוֹנָ֗⁠ם חֶ֣רֶב חַדָּֽה
57.text: David is using the **teeth** and **tongue** of these men to represent them speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Their speech is a spear and arrows; yes, what they say is a sharp sword]

57.quote: שִׁ֭נֵּי⁠הֶם חֲנִ֣ית וְ⁠חִצִּ֑ים וּ֝⁠לְשׁוֹנָ֗⁠ם חֶ֣רֶב חַדָּֽה
57.text: David is speaking as if what these men say with their **teeth** and **tongue** were actually **a spear and arrows** and **a sharp sword**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this image as a comparison. Alternate translation: [What they say about me is as dangerous as a spear or arrows or a sharp sword]

Here the word **tongue** is singular in form, but it refers to the tongues of all of David’s enemies as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “tongue.” Alternate translation: [and their tongues are sharp swords]

57.quote: ר֣וּמָ⁠ה עַל־הַ⁠שָּׁמַ֣יִם אֱלֹהִ֑ים עַ֖ל כָּל־הָ⁠אָ֣רֶץ כְּבוֹדֶֽ⁠ךָ
57.text: The expression **Be high** is an imperative, but it communicates a fervent wish rather than a command. Use a form in your language that will indicate this. Alternate translation: [Oh may you be high above the heavens, God, may your glory be above all of the earth]

57.quote: ר֣וּמָ⁠ה עַל־הַ⁠שָּׁמַ֣יִם אֱלֹהִ֑ים עַ֖ל כָּל־הָ⁠אָ֣רֶץ כְּבוֹדֶֽ⁠ךָ
57.text: David is speaking as if he actually wanted **God** and his **glory** to be in a physically high position relative to the **heavens** and the **earth**. In this context, God’s **glory** refers to the honor that he receives. The second part of this verse specifies in what way David wants the first part to be true. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May people honor you, God, more than anyone else in heaven or on earth]

57.quote: ר֣וּמָ⁠ה עַל־הַ⁠שָּׁמַ֣יִם אֱלֹהִ֑ים עַ֖ל כָּל־הָ⁠אָ֣רֶץ כְּבוֹדֶֽ⁠ךָ
57.text: David is referring to the entire created realm by naming its two main components, **the heavens** and **the earth**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [May people honor you, God, more than anyone else anywhere]
The pronoun **They** refers to the enemies whom David describes in verse 4. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [My enemies prepare a net for my steps]

Here, David’s **steps** represent his feet walking along a path. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [They prepare a net for my feet] or [They prepare a net, hoping I will walk into it and it will trap my feet]

David is speaking as if his enemies physically **prepare a net** to trap him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They take measures to capture me]

David is using one part of himself, his **soul** or inner being, to mean all of him in the act of bowing down. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I bow down]

David is speaking as if he physically **bows down** when he realizes that his enemies are trying to capture him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I feel despair]

Here, **to my face** represents “in front of me.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [They dig a pit in front of me; they fall into the midst of it] or [They dig a pit where they expect me to walk, hoping I will fall into it, but they fall into it instead]

David is speaking as if his enemies physically **dig a pit** (covering it to conceal it) in order to trap him, but that they fall into it themselves. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly (indicating that David is elaborating on the idea he expressed in the first part of this verse). Alternate translation: [Indeed, they do things to try to capture me, but what they do only hurts them instead]

The expression **established** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [My heart is steadfast, God, my heart is steadfast]

David is repeating a phrase in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If speakers of your language can repeat phrases for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [My heart is firmly established, God] or [My heart is firmly steadfast, God]

Here the **heart** represents a person’s feelings and intentions. David means that his confidence in God is unwavering. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have confidence in you, God, I have confidence in you] or [I have resolute confidence in you, God]

David is using a verbal form in which he is addressing himself and suggesting a course of action that is appropriate in light of what he has just said. In your translation, use an appropriate verbal form to indicate this, here and in the next verse. Alternate translation: [So I will sing and make music]

The terms **sing** and **make music** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Let me surely sing] or [So I will surely sing]

David is using the term **glory** to represent his soul. People of this culture spoke of the soul or inner being as the most noble or glorious part of a person. (The use of this term here is similar to its use in [16:9](../016/009.md), “my heart rejoices and my glory is glad,” and [30:12](../030/012.md), “my glory will make music to you.”) If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Awake, my soul]

David is addressing one part of himself, his **glory** or soul, to tell all of himself to wake up. If your language has a verbal form that is marked for self-address, you could use it here. Other languages may have other ways of showing the meaning. Alternate translation: [I must wake up] or (self-address form) [Wake up!]

David is speaking as if he were actually asleep and needed to wake up. He is actually urging himself to apply vitality and creativity to the work of praising God in song. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [I must sing in a lively way] or (self-address form) [Come on, sing in a lively way]

David is speaking of his **lyre** and **harp** as if they were living things that could wake up from sleep. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will start making music with my lyre and harp]

David is speaking of the **dawn** as if it were a living thing that he could **awaken**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will play them before the sun comes up]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [I will sing praises to you, Lord, among the peoples of other nations]

Here the word **For** introduces more detailed information about the reasons David has for singing the Lord’s praises. Use a connecting word or phrase in your language that will make this clear. It may not be necessary to represent this word explicitly in your translation. Alternate translation: [I will do this because]

David is speaking of God’s **covenant faithfulness** and **truth** as if they were physical things that could extend from the earth to the **clouds** and the **heavens**. He means that these qualities of God are immeasurably great. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. The UST models one way to do that.

David is using **is great to** as a common expression of his culture to mean “is as high as.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your covenant faithfulness reaches to the heavens] or [your covenant faithfulness is as high as the sky]
See how you translated the abstract nouns for the ideas of **covenant faithfulness** and **truth** in [verse 3](../057/003.md).

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and your truth is great to the clouds] or [and your truth is as high as the clouds]

57.quote: ר֣וּמָ⁠ה עַל־שָׁמַ֣יִם אֱלֹהִ֑ים עַ֖ל כָּל־הָ⁠אָ֣רֶץ כְּבוֹדֶֽ⁠ךָ
57.text: This is the second instance of the refrain in this psalm. We recommend that you show this to your readers by translating the phrases here the same way that you translated them in the first occurrence of this refrain in [57:5](../057/005.md).

58.text:
# Psalm 58 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 58 is a wisdom psalm that describes the difference between how righteous people and wicked people live and the difference between what happens to them. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Introduction: rebuke of wicked judges (1–2)
2. Description of wicked people (3–5)
3. Prayer that God will punish the wicked (6–8)
4. Assertion that God will punish the wicked and reward the righteous (9–11)

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a “miktam.” See the discussion of that term in the Introduction to Psalms.
See how you translated the term “chief musician” in the superscription to Psalm 4. Alternate translation: [For the leader of worship music] or [For the music director]

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a **miktam**. Since the meaning of this word is not certain, you may wish to represent it in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language. See the discussion of that term in the Introduction to Psalms.

58.quote: הַֽ⁠אֻמְנָ֗ם אֵ֣לֶם צֶ֭דֶק תְּדַבֵּר֑וּ⁠ן מֵישָׁרִ֥ים תִּ֝שְׁפְּט֗וּ בְּנֵ֣י אָדָֽם
58.text: David is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Truly in silence you do not speak righteousness! You do not judge uprightly, sons of man!]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what is right]

David is using **sons of man** as a common expression of his culture to mean “human beings.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [human beings]

Here the **heart** represents where a person’s thoughts and intentions exist. The psalmist means that they are planning and deciding to do wickedness. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in your thoughts] or [inwardly]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wickedness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [wicked things] or [evil]

Here, **hands** represents the actions of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You intentionally commit violent acts]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **violence**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [violent acts] or [violent deeds]

The psalmist is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [Those who act wickedly]

The psalmist is using **turn aside from the womb** as a common expression to mean “go astray from birth.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [go astray from birth] or [are wicked from the day they are born]

The psalmist is using **stray from the belly** as a common expression of the culture to mean “go astray from birth.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they err from birth] or [they go astray from the day they are born]

58.quote: זֹ֣רוּ רְשָׁעִ֣ים מֵ⁠רָ֑חֶם תָּע֥וּ מִ֝⁠בֶּ֗טֶן דֹּבְרֵ֥י כָזָֽב
58.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [The wicked turn aside from the womb, indeed, they stray from the belly, speaking falsehood.]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **falsehood**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [speaking lies] or [saying things that are false]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the poison of a serpent** is harmful and deadly, so is the speech or nature of the wicked. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Their words are as harmful as serpent venom] or [They are as poisonous as a serpent]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a deaf adder** does not listen, so the wicked do not listen to correction. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [They are as unheeding as a deaf adder]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [The wicked people are like]

The psalmist is speaking of the wicked as if they were snakes that could **shut** their **ears**. He means that they willfully refuse to listen. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that refuses to listen] or [that will not listen]

The psalmist is using **the voice of charmers** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the music or incantations of snake charmers.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to the music of snake charmers] or [to the incantations of those who charm snakes]

The psalmist is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [one who is charming them expertly] or [one who skillfully charms]

The expression **being made wise** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [a skilled charmer] or [an expert charmer]

58.quote: אֱֽלֹהִ֗ים הֲרָס־שִׁנֵּ֥י⁠מוֹ בְּ⁠פִ֑י⁠מוֹ מַלְתְּע֥וֹת כְּ֝פִירִ֗ים נְתֹ֣ץ ׀ יְהוָֽה
58.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [God, break their teeth in their mouth; indeed, break out the fangs of the young lions, Yahweh]

58.quote: אֱֽלֹהִ֗ים הֲרָס־שִׁנֵּ֥י⁠מוֹ בְּ⁠פִ֑י⁠מוֹ מַלְתְּע֥וֹת כְּ֝פִירִ֗ים נְתֹ֣ץ ׀ יְהוָֽה
58.text: The psalmist is speaking of the wicked people as if they were dangerous animals with **teeth** and **fangs** that could harm others. He is asking God to destroy their power to harm people, as if God were breaking the teeth of dangerous animals. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture. Alternatively, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [God, destroy the power of the wicked! Take away their ability to harm people, Yahweh]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a request. Alternate translation: [I ask you to break their teeth] or [please break their teeth]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “Please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please break out the fangs of]

The expression **May they be melted** contains a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [May God melt them] or [May Yahweh cause them to melt]

The point of this comparison is that just as **waters that run off** quickly disappear, so the psalmist wants his enemies to disappear. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like waters that vanish from sight]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [When the wicked person treads his arrows] or [When each wicked person treads his arrows]

Here, **treads** represents “shoots.” Ancient archers would step on their bows in order to bend them so that they could string them. David means “when he steps on his bow to string it and then shoots arrows from it.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [When he launches his arrows] or [When he shoots his arrows]

The point of this comparison is that just as something that is **cut off** or blunted is ineffective, so the wicked person’s **arrows** would be ineffective. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [may they be as if they were blunted] or [may they be as if they had no points]

The expression **they are cut off** contains a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh cuts them off] or [they break off]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a snail that melts** dissolves and disappears as it moves along, so the psalmist desires that his enemies would perish and vanish. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [May they be like a snail that liquifies and disappears]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [May they be destroyed like] or [May they perish like]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the miscarriage of a woman** never sees the light of day, so David’s enemies will never see **the sun**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [May they be like a stillborn baby which never experiences life]

The psalmist is referring to a stillborn child in a polite way by using the term **miscarriage**. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [May they be like a stillborn baby] or [May they be like a child who dies at birth]

The psalmist is using **Before your pots perceive the thorn** as a common expression of the culture to mean “very swiftly” or “before something can even begin.” The image refers to using thorns as quick-burning fuel to heat cooking pots, and the expression means that something will happen before the cooking process can even start. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [In an instant] or [More swiftly than you can imagine]

The psalmist is speaking of the thorns as if they could be **the living** or **the burning** (that is, either green or dry). If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [whether green or dry]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **burning**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what burns easily]

The psalmist is speaking of God’s judgment as if it were a powerful **whirlwind** that sweeps things away. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he will sweep it away with great force] or [he will lift it from sight with a strong wind]

The psalmist is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [Righteous people] or [Those who are righteous]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **vengeance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [God punish the wicked] or [the wicked being punished]

David is speaking of the righteous person as if he were a warrior who could **wash his feet in the blood** that covered a battlefield after defeating enemies. This image expresses the idea of complete victory. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He will triumph completely over the wicked] or [He will celebrate total victory over the wicked]

By **when he sees vengeance**, the psalmist means when he sees God punish the wicked. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [when he sees God take vengeance on the wicked] or [when he sees God punish those who are wicked]

The psalmist is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [wicked people] or [those who act wickedly]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Then someone will say]

The psalmist is using **fruit is to the righteous** as a common expression of the culture to mean “there is a reward for the righteous.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the righteous have a reward] or [the righteous are rewarded]

The psalmist is speaking of the reward or outcome that righteous people receive as if it were **fruit** such as that which a tree produces. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture. Alternatively, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [benefit]

The psalmist is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [is to those who act righteously] or [comes to people who are righteous]

The implication is that God actively judges the earth in contrast to the unjust judges mentioned earlier in the psalm. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [a God who actively judges the earth] or [a God who really does judge the earth]

59.text:
# Psalm 59 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 59 is a psalm of supplication or lament. It includes all the basic elements of that type of psalm. (Some elements are repeated.) See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Cry for help (1–2)
2. Description of troubles (3–4)
3. Petition (5)
4. Refrain (6)
5. Description of troubles (7)
6. Statement of trust (8–10)
7. Petition (11–13)
8. Refrain (14–15)
9. Vow of praise (16–17)

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a “miktam.” See the discussion of that term in the introduction to Psalms.

As its superscription indicates, the background to this psalm is an episode related in [1 Samuel 19:8–12](../1sa/19/08.md) in which King Saul sent men to watch David’s house so that they could kill him when he left it. It may be helpful to read that episode before translating this psalm.
See how you translated the term “chief musician” in the superscription to Psalm 4. Alternate translation: [For the leader of worship music] or [For the music director]

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a **miktam**. Since the meaning of this word is not certain, you may wish to represent it in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language. See the discussion of that term in the Introduction to Psalms.

The implication is that Saul sent men to watch David’s house in order to kill him, as recorded in 1 Samuel 19:11. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [When Saul sent men to watch David’s house to kill him]

This is an imperative, but it communicates an urgent request to God rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates an urgent request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please set me on high] or [I beg you to set me on high]

David is speaking of protection as if Yahweh could **Set** him **on high** in an unreachable place above his enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Keep me safe from them] or [Put me beyond their reach]
The pronoun **ones** refers to David’s enemies. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [away from the enemies rising up against me]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request.
