It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please deliver me]

David is using the possessive form to describe **workers** who are characterized by **iniquity**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from people who do wicked things] or [from those who practice evil]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from people who do evil things]

This is an imperative, but it communicates an urgent request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates an urgent request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please save me]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **men** who are characterized by **blood**. This refers to people who are violent or who commit murder. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and save me from violent men] or [and save me from murderers]

Here, **blood** represents violence and murder. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and save me from violent men] or [and save me from murderous men]

The psalmist is using **behold** as a common expression to draw the reader’s attention to what he is about to say. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [notice] or [see]

Here, **life** represents the whole person as the target of an attack. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to attack me] or [to murder me]

David is using the adjective **mighty** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [mighty men] or [very strong men]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [They gather against me not for my transgression and not for my sin] or [This is happening not for my transgression and not for my sin]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **transgression**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because I transgressed against you]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **sin**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because I have sinned]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [though I have done nothing wrong]

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were asleep and needed to **Awake**. David means that he wants Yahweh to take action and help him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture or you could express this meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Come to meet me]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that would be used to make a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please awaken]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [and please look at my situation]

The expression **God of armies** refers to Yahweh as the commander of the heavenly armies, meaning the angelic hosts. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [God who rules over the angelic hosts]

The psalmist is not using this possessive form **the God of Israel** to indicate that the Israelites possess or control God. Rather the psalmist is using these words to indicate that God is the one whom Israel worships. Alternate translation: [who is the God whom Israel worships]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please arise to punish] or [I beg you to arise and punish]

The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were asleep and needed to **wake up**. He means that he wants Yahweh to begin to intervene and punish the nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [come and act]

David says **all of the nations** as a generalization for emphasis. If it would be clearer in your language, you could express the emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [the hostile nations] or [these enemy nations]

The word translated as **Do not be gracious** is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please do not show favor] or [I beg you not to be gracious]

David is using the possessive form to describe **workers** who are characterized by **iniquity**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [people who are treacherous and who do wicked things] or [treacherous people who do evil]

The word **Selah** is a Hebrew word. You will need to decide if you will use this word in its Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew word, you could spell it the way it sounds in your language and then put the translation in a footnote.
The pronoun **They** refers to the enemies introduced in verses 1–3. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The psalmist’s enemies return]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a dog** is threatening and aggressive, so are the psalmist’s enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [they make threatening sounds] or [they snarl aggressively]

By **go around the city**, the psalmist means that David’s enemies are roaming around Jerusalem looking for victims. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [roam around the city looking for prey] or [prowl around the city seeking victims]

The psalmist is using **Behold** as a common expression to draw attention to what follows. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Look] or [Pay attention]

The psalmist is using **they belch out with their mouth** as a common expression of the culture to mean that his enemies speak violently or arrogantly. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they speak violent threats] or [they pour out arrogant words]

The psalmist is speaking of his enemies’ words as if they were **swords** that could physically harm people. This image emphasizes how dangerous and hurtful their speech is. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [their lips speak harmful words] or [their words are as dangerous as swords]

Here, **lips** represents speech. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in their speech] or [in what they say]

The psalmist’s enemies are using the question form for emphasis. They assume that no one hears or cares what they say. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [No one is hearing] or [No one hears us!]

The psalmist uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between the threats of his enemies and God’s response to them. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [You, however, Yahweh] or [You, Yahweh, on the other hand]

The psalmist is using **laugh at them** as a common expression of the culture to mean “scorn them” or “treat them with contempt.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [ridicule them] or [look upon them with contempt]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [But you, Yahweh, laugh at them, indeed, you mock all of the nations]

The pronoun **his** may refer to God, but some Hebrew manuscripts and many translations understand it as **my**. This would make the psalmist say that God is **my strength**, which fits better with the context where he calls God **my stronghold**. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could clarify this. Alternate translation: [my strength] or [you, my strength]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [you who are strong] or [you who strengthen me]

The psalmist is speaking of God as if he were a **stronghold**, that is, a fortified place of safety. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture. Alternatively, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [God protects me] or [God is my place of safety]

David is using the possessive form to describe **the God** who is characterized by **covenant faithfulness** toward him. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [God, who is faithful to his covenant with me] or [God, who keeps his covenant promises to me]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [who is faithfully loyal to me in his covenant] or [who faithfully keeps his covenant with me]

The psalmist is using **will make me look upon my enemies** as a common expression of the culture to mean “will cause me to see my enemies defeated” or “will enable me to see my enemies humiliated.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [will let me see my enemies defeated] or [will enable me to see myself humiliating my enemies]

The expression translated as **Do not slay them** is an imperative, but it communicates a request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a request. Alternate translation: [Please do not kill them] or [I ask that you not kill them]

David is using the word translated as **lest** to introduce an outcome that he does not want to happen. Because of this, he first gives God an instruction to follow so that this will not happen. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that avoiding this outcome is the purpose of the instruction. Alternate translation: [so that my people will not forget] or [because if you do, my people will forget]

Here David is using the pronoun **my** with **people** to refer to the nation of Israel, over whom he reigns as king. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the Israelites] or [the people of Israel]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a request to God rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a request to God. It may be helpful to use a word such as “please.” Alternate translation: [Please scatter them] or [We ask that you scatter them]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **power**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because you are powerful]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please bring them down] or [I ask you to humble them]

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a **shield** that protects the Israelites. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture. Alternatively, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [our protector]

David is using the possessive form to describe a **sin** that is characterized by **their mouth**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the sin characterized by their mouth] or [the sin that comes from their mouth]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **sin**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [For what they say that is sinful] or [For the sinful words]

Here the phrases **their mouth** and **their lips** represent what the psalmist’s enemies say. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what they say] or [their spoken words]

The expression **may they be taken in their pride** contains a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [may their pride trap them]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **pride**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because they are proud]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **the curse**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how they curse people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **lying**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and for the untruthful stories]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a request rather than a command for God to destroy his enemies. If the imperative does not communicate a request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a request. Alternate translation: [I ask that you consume them in wrath] or [Please consume them in wrath]

The psalmist is repeating forms of the verb **Consume** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Completely consume them in wrath]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wrath**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because you are angered] or [wrathfully]

David is using the phrase **that they may not be** to introduce the goal or purpose of consuming his enemies in wrath. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [so that they will no longer exist] or [in order that they will be destroyed]

Here, **that they may know** marks **that God is ruling in Jacob to the ends of the earth** as a further goal or purpose of **Consume them in wrath; consume them that they may not be**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [so that people may know] or [in order that all may know]

Here, **Jacob** represents the people of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [over Israel] or [the people of Israel]

The phrase **to the ends of the earth** was a common expression meaning “everywhere” or “throughout the entire world.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [everywhere] or [throughout the whole world]

The word **Selah** is a Hebrew word. You will need to decide if you will use this word in its Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew word, you could spell it the way it sounds in your language and then put the translation in a footnote.
This is poetic language. If your language has a way to indicate poetry, you could use it here. Alternate translation: [In the evening they return]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a dog** growls when it is threatening or angry, so the psalmist’s enemies make threatening sounds. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [they make threatening sounds like an angry dog]

Here the psalmist is stating the pronoun **They** separately, even though the verb translated as **they wander** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize the contrast between him and his enemies. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here.

David is speaking as if this were a hypothetical possibility, but he means that it is actually true. If your language does not state something as a condition if it is certain or true, or if your readers might think that what David is saying is uncertain, then you could translate this as a confident statement. Alternate translation: [When they are not full, they lodge]

Here David is using the pronoun **I** twice for emphasis. He is doing this to contrast his response to God with the actions of his enemies, which he described earlier in the psalm. If a speaker of your language would repeat a pronoun in this way for emphasis, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing this emphasis. Alternate translation: [But as for me, I]

David uses the words **But I** here to indicate a strong contrast between the enemies described in the previous verses and himself. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [As for me, however, I] or [In contrast to them, I]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [about how strong you are]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [about how you are faithful to your covenant] or [about how faithful you are to me]

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a **stronghold** that protected him from enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable figure of speech or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you are like a fortified place to me]

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were **a refuge** in which he could find safety from danger. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [and a place of safety]

David is using **in the day of trouble** as a common expression to mean “when I am in trouble.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when I am in trouble] or [in times of distress]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **trouble**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when I am troubled] or [when I experience troubles]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [you who make me strong] or [you who strengthen me]

David is speaking of God as if he were a **stronghold**, a fortified place where David could be protected from his enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture. Alternatively, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [God protects me] or [God keeps me safe from my enemies]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the God who is faithful to his covenant]

60.text:
# Psalm 60 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 60 is a psalm of supplication or lament. It includes all the basic elements of that type of psalm except a vow of praise. (Some elements are repeated.) See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Cry for help (1)
2. Description of troubles (2–3)
3. Statement of trust (4–5a)
4. Petition (5b)
5. Statement of trust (6–8)
6. Petition (9–11)
7. Statement of trust (12)

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a “miktam.” See the discussion of that term in the introduction to Psalms.

As its superscription indicates, the background to this psalm consists of two episodes related in [2 Samuel 8:3–8](../2sa/08/03.md) and [2 Samuel 8:13–14](../2sa/08/13.md) in which David was leading the Israelite army to fight against Aramean armies northeast of Israel and his general Joab had to leave and fight against the Edomite army to the south of Israel. It may be helpful to read those episodes before translating this psalm.
See how you translated the term “chief musician” in the superscription to Psalm 4. Alternate translation: [For the leader of worship music] or [For the music director]

The superscription to this psalm describes it as a **testimony**. This most likely means that the psalm is presenting the sufferings and defeats of the Israelites to Yahweh as a plea for him to help them on the basis that they are his covenant people. Alternate translation: [An appeal for help]

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a **miktam**. Since the meaning of this word is not certain, you may wish to represent it in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language. See the discussion of that term in the Introduction to Psalms.
The words **Aram Naharaim** are the name of a place.
The words **Aram Zobah** are the name of a place.
The phrase **Valley of Salt** is the name of a place.
The number **12,000** should be translated according to the conventions of your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [twelve thousand]

Here the psalmist is providing background information about the historical circumstances in which David wrote this psalm. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

David is speaking of God as if he had **broken through** the defenses of Israel like an enemy army that is breaching a wall or battle line. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you have allowed our enemies to overcome our defenses] or [you have let our defenses collapse]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please restore us]

David is speaking of the nation of Israel as if it were **the earth** that Yahweh had caused to **tremble** and **broken** as in an earthquake. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You have brought disaster on our nation; you have shattered it]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please heal its breaches]

David is speaking of the nation of Israel as if it were land that had been damaged by an earthquake and needed to be **healed**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture. Alternatively, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Restore it] or [Repair the damage]

The psalmist is using the adjective **difficult** as a noun to mean difficult things or hardship. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [difficult things] or [hardship]

The psalmist is speaking of God causing his people to be confused and helpless as if he had **made** them **drink wine** that caused **staggering**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [made us confused and helpless]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that **a banner** is a military flag used to mark a rallying point where troops assemble for safety and coordination during battle. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [a rallying flag] or [a flag to gather around for safety]

The psalmist is using **the ones fearing you** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the ones who worship and honor you with reverence.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those who worship you] or [those who approach you with reverence]

The psalmist is using **from the face of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “because of” or “on account of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because of the bow] or [on account of the bow]

The word **Selah** is a Hebrew word. You will need to decide if you will use this word in its Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew word, you could spell it the way it sounds in your language and then put the translation in a footnote.

The expression **may be delivered** contains a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [you, God, may deliver your beloved]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please save us]

Here, **right hand** represents power or strength. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with your might] or [with your strength]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please answer me]

The pronouns shift from **us** to **me** in this verse. The psalmist is speaking as an individual representative of the people, first using “us” to refer to the collective group, then using “me” to refer to himself as their leader. If it would be helpful in your language, you could clarify this shift. Alternate translation: [answer me, your servant who speaks for your people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **holiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by his holy character]

This is the beginning of what God said. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of God. Alternate translation: [God has spoken in his holiness, saying, “I will rejoice] or [God has spoken in his holiness, from which he says, “I will rejoice]

The implication is that David will divide Shechem as an inheritance among God’s people, demonstrating God’s sovereignty over the land. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I divide Shechem as an inheritance] or [I apportion Shechem to God’s people]

David is speaking of **Ephraim** as if it were **the protection of** his **head**, that is, as if the tribe were a helmet that protected him in battle. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [Ephraim protects me like a helmet] or [Ephraim is my military defense]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that while **Ephraim** was the name of one of the sons of Joseph, he and his brother, Manasseh, became patriarchs of two of the twelve tribes of Israel. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And the tribe of Ephraim]
Here, **head** represents the person himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [me]

David is speaking of **Judah** as if it were **my scepter**, the symbol of royal authority. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Judah, the source of my royal authority] or [Judah, the tribe from which my kingship comes]

David is speaking of **Moab** as if it were **the tub of his washing**, a basin used by a servant to wash his master’s feet. This image expresses that Moab has been reduced to servant status under God’s authority. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Moab is my servant] or [I will make Moab serve me like a slave]

Throwing a sandal **over Edom** was a symbolic action by which the psalmist showed that God was claiming ownership and dominion over that nation. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [I claim Edom as my own by throwing my sandal over it]

The psalmist is speaking to **Philistia**, which he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about God’s power over the Philistines. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about Philistia. Alternate translation: [Philistia will shout triumphantly over me] or [Let Philistia shout triumphantly over me]

The psalmist actually means to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of what he is saying here. If a speaker of your language would not do that, you could translate the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you have nothing to shout about]

David is using the question form to express his need for God’s help to conquer the fortified city. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I need someone to bring me into the city of fortification!] or [Only you can bring me into the city of fortification.]

The implication is that **the city of fortification** refers to a well-fortified Edomite city, likely Petra or Bozrah. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Edom’s fortified capital city]

David is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Only you will lead me to Edom!] or [You alone will lead me to Edom.]

The psalmist is using the question form to express his complaint to God. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [you have rejected us!] or [it seems you have rejected us.]

The psalmist is using **go out with our armies** as a common expression of the culture to mean “accompany our armies into battle” or “help us fight our enemies.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And you do not accompany our armies into battle] or [And you do not help us fight our enemies]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a polite request to God. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please give us help against the enemy] or [We beg you to give us help against the enemy]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [man cannot save us] or [people cannot rescue us]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [humankind] or [people]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **futility**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for the salvation of man is useless] or [for the salvation of man cannot help]

The psalmist is using **do valor** as a common expression of the culture to mean “act valiantly” or “accomplish mighty deeds.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [we will act valiantly] or [we will accomplish mighty deeds]

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he would literally **trample** Israel’s enemies with his feet. He means that Yahweh will decisively defeat them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture. Alternatively, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he will crush our adversaries] or [he will give us complete victory over our adversaries]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **he** twice for emphasis. He is doing this to stress that God alone will defeat the enemies. If a speaker of your language would use a repeated pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing this emphasis. Alternate translation: [he himself will trample our adversaries] or [it is he who will trample our adversaries]

61.text:
# Psalm 61 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 61 is a psalm of trust and petition in which the psalmist calls out to God from a distant place and expresses confidence in God as his protector.

1. Petition: The psalmist cries out for God to hear from far away (1–2)
2. Confidence: God has been a refuge and strong tower (3)
3. Desire: To dwell forever in God’s tent and under his wings (4)
4. Assurance: God has heard the psalmist’s vows and given an inheritance (5)
5. Prayer for the king: Long life in God’s presence, guarded by covenant faithfulness and truth (6–7)
6. Response: Perpetual praise and vow fulfillment (8)

The word “Selah” at the end of verse 4 marks a structural break between the personal petition (1–4) and the assurance and royal prayer (5–8).

## About the Psalm

The superscription attributes this psalm to David and directs it to the music director with stringed instruments. The psalmist speaks as someone far from God’s dwelling place (“the end of the earth,” verse 2), calling out in a time of emotional weakness. The psalm moves from personal petition to a prayer for “the king” in the third person (verses 6–7), which likely refers to David speaking of himself as king, though some interpreters see a broader reference to the Davidic line.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### God as refuge and shelter

The psalm uses a series of protection images to describe God: a high rock (verse 2), a refuge (verse 3), a tower of strength (verse 3), a tent (verse 4), and sheltering wings (verse 4). Translators should be aware that these are distinct metaphors drawn from different areas of Israelite life—geography, military defense, hospitality, and nature—all conveying the idea of safety in God’s presence. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/refuge]])

### Covenant faithfulness and truth

In verse 7, the Hebrew words “hesed” (covenant faithfulness) and “emeth” (truth, faithfulness) appear together as a pair and are personified as guardians who preserve the king. When these two terms appear together, each enriches the other, expressing God’s loyal, reliable love. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/covenantfaith]])

### Vows

Vows (solemn promises made to God) frame the second half of the psalm, appearing in both verse 5 and verse 8. In Israelite worship, a person in distress would make a vow to God, promising praise or offerings in return for deliverance. The psalmist’s commitment to fulfill these vows “day by day” reflects ongoing, not one-time, worship. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/oath]])

## Translation Issues

### Person shift: first person to third person

The psalmist speaks in the first person through verses 1–5 (“I call,” “my vows”) but shifts to the third person in verses 6–7 (“the king,” “he,” “his years”), then returns to first person in verse 8. This is likely David referring to himself as king, but some languages may need to make the referent explicit to avoid confusion.

**For the chief musician** is an instruction about who should lead people in singing or playing music with this psalm. This could refer to the person in charge of music for temple worship. If your readers would not be familiar with this role, you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the worship leader]

**On a stringed instrument** refers to a type of stringed musical instrument used in worship. This may indicate how the psalm was to be accompanied. If your readers would not be familiar with this type of instrument, you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [To be accompanied by stringed instruments] or [With music from stringed instruments]

These two phrases, **Hear my cry, God** and **listen to my prayer**, mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [God, hear my cry; yes, listen to my prayer]

These are imperatives, but they communicate polite requests rather than commands. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. Alternate translation: [Please hear my cry, God; please listen to my prayer]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **prayer**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what I pray]

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about where David calls from after the information about calling to God. Alternate translation: [I call to you from the end of the earth]

David is using **From the end of the earth** as a common expression to mean from a very distant or remote place. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [From a faraway place] or [From distant lands]

Here the **heart** represents where a person’s thoughts and feelings exist. David is speaking of his emotions as if they were physically weak. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when I am discouraged] or [when I feel weak]

The word that the ULT translates as **when** indicates that David calls to God at the same time as **my heart is faint**. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could describe the time relationship more explicitly. Alternate translation: [at times when my heart is faint] or [during the times that my heart is faint]

David is speaking of God as if God were a high **rock** that David could climb up to reach safety from danger. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [to a place of safety that is like a high rock]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. Alternate translation: [Please lead me to the rock]

61.quote: הָיִ֣יתָ מַחְסֶ֣ה לִ֑⁠י מִגְדַּל־עֹ֝֗ז מִ⁠פְּנֵ֥י אוֹיֵֽב
61.text: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [you are a refuge to me, you are a strong tower from the face of the enemy]

61.quote: הָיִ֣יתָ מַחְסֶ֣ה לִ֑⁠י מִגְדַּל־עֹ֝֗ז מִ⁠פְּנֵ֥י אוֹיֵֽב
61.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [you are a refuge to me, indeed, you are a strong tower from the face of the enemy]

The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [Because you are a refuge to me]

Here David is speaking as if God were a physical shelter. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you are a place of protection for me] or [you are a place of safety for me]

Here David is speaking as if God were a fortified **tower**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a fortress that protects me from the enemy]

David is using **from the face of** as a common expression to mean “away from the presence of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the enemy] or [when the enemy comes]

61.quote: אָג֣וּרָה בְ֭⁠אָהָלְ⁠ךָ עוֹלָמִ֑ים אֶֽחֱסֶ֨ה בְ⁠סֵ֖תֶר כְּנָפֶ֣י⁠ךָ
61.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Let me always live in your presence, taking refuge in the shelter of your wings]

Here David is speaking as if God’s presence and protection were a **tent** where he could stay as a guest. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in your presence] or [with you]

Here David is speaking as if God were a bird sheltering its young under its **wings**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [under your care] or [in your protection]
David is using this possessive form to mean the shelter that God’s wings provide. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [in the shelter that your wings provide]

The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [Because you, God, have listened to my vows]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **inheritance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what is passed to]

David is using this possessive form to mean the inheritance that belongs to those who fear God. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [what you give to those who fear your name]

Here, **your name** represents God’s reputation and character. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [who you are] or [your reputation]

The psalmist is using **Days upon days** as a common expression of the culture to mean “many days.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May you add many days to the king’s lifetime]
The phrase **the king** refers to David himself, who is speaking of himself in the third person. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [me, the king]
The pronoun **you** refers to God, while the pronoun **his** refers to the king. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [may you, God, add to the king’s years]
Here, **his years** represents “his lifetime.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to his lifetime]

The point of this comparison is that just as **generation and generation** spans a very long time, so should the king’s years be extended. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as if he would live for many generations]

David is using **to generation and generation** as a common expression of his culture to mean “throughout all generations” or “forever.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [throughout all generations]
The pronoun **he** refers to the king mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [May the king dwell forever]

Here, **to the face of God** represents being in the presence of God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the presence of God] or [before God]

The phrase **covenant faithfulness and truth** expresses a single idea. The word **truth** tells more about **covenant faithfulness**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [true covenant faithfulness] or [faithful covenant love]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please appoint covenant faithfulness and truth]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **covenant faithfulness** and **truth**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [evidences that you are truly faithful to your covenant]

David speaks of **covenant faithfulness and truth** as if they were living things that could **preserve** the king. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [ways to show the king covenant faithfulness and truth so that he is preserved]
Here, **name** represents God himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to you]

The phrase **that I may pay my vows** indicates the purpose or goal for which David will make music to God’s name. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [in order to pay my vows day after day] or [so that I may pay my vows day after day]

David is using **pay my vows** as a common expression to mean “fulfill my vows” or “do what I have vowed to do.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [fulfill my vows] or [do what I have promised]

David repeats the word **day** to emphasize the idea of continually or constantly. If your language can repeat words for emphasis, it would be appropriate to do that here. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the emphasis. Alternate translation: [day after day] or [continually]

62.text:
# Psalm 62 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 62 is a specific kind of psalm of supplication, a psalm of trust. It is a calm affirmation of reliance on God, with the troubles of the psalmist mostly in the background. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Statement of trust (1–2)
2. Description of opponents (3–4)
3. Statement of trust (5–6)
4. Exhortation to listeners (8–10)
5. Affirmation of God’s power and goodness (11–12)

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]
See how you translated the expression “on Jeduthun” in the superscription to Psalm 39.

David is using **my soul** to represent all of himself in the act of waiting silently for God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all of myself]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [He is the one who saves me]

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a **rock** that provided stability and protection. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture. Alternatively, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my foundation] or [my protector]

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a **stronghold**, a fortified place that protects people from danger. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my place of safety] or [my protector]

The expression **I will not be greatly shaken** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Nothing will shake me greatly] or [I will remain stable]

David is using the question form to express his frustration at his enemies for attacking him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You have attacked me far too long!] or [Stop attacking me!]
Here the masculine term **a man** refers to the psalmist himself. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that makes this clear as modeled in the UST.

The expression **You will be smashed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [God will smash you] or [God will crush you]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a leaning wall** and **an overthrown fence** will collapse, so the psalmist’s enemies will be destroyed. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and will collapse like a leaning wall or an overthrown fence]
The pronoun **him** refers to the psalmist. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [to cast me down from my elevation]

The psalmist is speaking of the author’s honor and status as if it were **his elevation**, a high position from which he could be cast down. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from his honored position] or [from his high status]

David is using one part of a person, his **mouth**, to mean all of him in the act of speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with their words] or [in their speech]

These two clauses, **with his mouth, they bless** and **in their inside, they curse**, mean basically opposite things. The psalmist is contrasting what his enemies say outwardly with what they feel inwardly. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition and contrast, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both clauses in your translation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make the contrast more explicit. Alternate translation: [they say kind things, but they really wish harm]

Here, **inside** represents their hearts or inner thoughts. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in their hearts] or [in their thoughts]

The word **Selah** is a Hebrew word. You will need to decide if you will use this word in its Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew word, you could spell it the way it sounds in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Pause and praise]

The psalmist is speaking to **his own soul** as if he were speaking to another person who could hear him. He is doing this to emphasize how strongly he feels about waiting for God alone. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to himself or expressing his own determination. Alternate translation: [I shall be silent before God alone] or [I tell myself to wait quietly for God alone]

The psalmist is using **my soul** to represent all of himself in the act of waiting for God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I tell myself] or [self]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **hope**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what I await] or [what I confidently wait for]

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a **rock** and a **stronghold**, solid structures that could protect him from danger. If these images communicate well in your language, please use them. If not, you could express these as comparisons. Alternate translation: [the one who protects me as would a rock and a stronghold]
If your language does not use this passive form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Nothing will shake me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way, as modeled by the UST.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and what makes me honored]

David is speaking of God as if he were **the rock of** his **strength**, that is, a high rock that he could climb up to reach safety from danger. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [God, who is like a rock that protects me and makes me strong] or [my strong protector]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the rock that strengthens me]

David is speaking of God as if he were a **refuge**, a place where he could go to be safe from danger. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my place of safety] or [my place of protection]

The word translated as **Trust** is an imperative, but it communicates an exhortation rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates an exhortation. Alternate translation: [I urge you to trust in him at all times, people]

The psalmist is using **Pour out your heart** as a common expression of the culture to mean “express your emotions openly.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Tell him honestly how you feel] or [Share your deepest emotions with him]
Here, **to his face** represents being in the presence of God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before him]

The psalmist is speaking of God as if he were **a refuge**, a safe place to which people can go to escape danger. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [is a safe place for us] or [is the one who protects us]

The word **Selah** is a Hebrew word. You will need to decide if you will use this word in its Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew word, you could spell it the way it sounds in your language and then put the translation in a footnote.

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [all people are vapor; indeed, they are a lie]

The psalmist is using **sons of a human** and **sons of a man** as common expressions of the culture to mean “people” or “human beings.” If these phrases do not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [people … people] or [human beings … human beings]

The psalmist is speaking of people as if they were **vapor**. He means that people are transient and insubstantial. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture. Alternatively, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [are fleeting] or [have no substance]

When the psalmist says that people **are a lie**, he means that humans are deceptive in appearance and cannot be relied upon. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [are unreliable] or [are deceptive]

The psalmist says **they together would be lighter than vapor** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [together they would weigh almost nothing] or [all of them together have no weight at all]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **oppression**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in oppressing others]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **robbery**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by robbing people] or [in what you rob from others]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **Wealth**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Should you become wealthy]

Here, **heart** represents a person’s desires and focus of attention. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [do not fix your desires on it] or [do not focus your attention on it]

The psalmist is using **Once** and **twice** as a common expression to mean “repeatedly” or “with certainty.” The phrase emphasizes that God’s declaration is reliable and sure. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Repeatedly] or [Most certainly]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **power**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [God is powerful]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [you are faithful to your covenant] or [you are loyal and faithful]

The psalmist is repeating the pronoun **you** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that God is the one who repays. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [you yourself repay] or [you alone repay]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [to each person]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **doing**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [according to what he does]

63.text:
# Psalm 63 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 63 is a psalm of praise. David is specifically encouraging himself to praise God for what he will do to help him. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. David’s longing for God (1–2)
2. Reason to worship (3a)
3. Call to worship (3b–6)
4. Reason to worship (7a)
5. Call to worship (7b–8)
6. God will punish David’s enemies (9–10)
7. Call to worship (11a)
8. Reason to worship (11b)

This is a superscription to a psalm. It is written in poetic language and provides historical context for the psalm. If your language has a way to indicate poetry, you could use it here. Alternate translation: [A song of David written while he was in the wilderness of Judah]

David is speaking of his intense desire for God as if his **soul** were physically **thirsting** for water. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture. Alternatively, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [My soul longs for you] or [I deeply desire to be near you]
David is using **My soul** to represent all of himself in the act of thirsting for God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I thirst]

The psalmist is speaking of his intense longing for God as if his body were physically **fainting** from weakness or exhaustion. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my whole being aches for you] or [my body grows weak with longing for you]

David is using one part of a person, his **flesh**, to mean all of him in the act of longing for God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my whole being faints for you] or [I faint for you]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [My whole being longs for you]

The terms **dryness** and **weary** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [very dry] or [extremely parched]

The word translated as **Thus** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [So] or [Because of this,]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **power**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how powerful you are]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how glorious you are]

The terms **power** and **glory** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [your awesome power] or [your magnificent strength]

The word translated as **Because** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came after. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came after. Alternate translation: [Since]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how faithful you are to your covenant] or [how faithfully you keep your covenant promises]

The psalmist says **better than life** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [more valuable than anything] or [extremely valuable]

The psalmist is using one part of a person, his **lips**, to mean all of him in the act of praising God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will praise you]

The word **Thus** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. David will bless God because of what he has just expressed in the previous verses. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [Because of this,] or [Therefore,]

Lifting up one’s palms was a symbolic action by which David showed his worship and prayer to God. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [I will lift up my palms to worship you] or [I will lift up my palms in prayer to you]

The psalmist is using the term **name** to represent who God is, particularly God’s character and authority. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because of who you are] or [because of your character]

The point of this comparison is that just as **fat and fatness** are deeply satisfying, so God’s presence satisfies the psalmist’s soul. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [My soul will be completely satisfied, just as if I had eaten the richest foods]

The terms **fat** and **fatness** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [the richest food]

By using the phrase **my soul will be full**, David is speaking as if Yahweh could satisfy him in the same way that rich food satisfies hunger. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [I will be as satisfied as if I had eaten the richest foods]
David is using **my soul** to represent all of himself in the act of being satisfied. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I]

The psalmist is using one part of a person, his **lips**, to mean all of him in the act of praising God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and with my joyful shouts]

These two phrases, **lips of joyful shouts** and **my mouth will praise**, mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [and my mouth will praise you with lips of joyful shouts]

David is using one part of a person, his **mouth**, to mean all of him in the act of praising God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I]

The word **When** indicates that David **remembering** God occurred at the same time as when he **meditates** on God. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could describe the time relationship more explicitly. Alternate translation: [As I remember you on my bed]

The term **night watches** refers to the divisions of the night during which guards were on duty. In ancient Israel, the night was typically divided into three or four such periods. If your readers would not be familiar with this, you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [during the night] or [in the hours of the night]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [When I remember you on my bed, yes, when I meditate on you in the night watches]

The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [Because] or [Since]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **help**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [one who gives help] or [helpful]

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a bird protecting him **in the shadow of** his **wings**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [while you protect me] or [as you shelter me]

David is speaking of God as if he had **wings** that cast a shadow providing protection. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture. Alternatively, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your protective shelter] or [your protection]
David is using **My soul** to represent all of himself in the act of clinging to God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I]

David is speaking of his devotion to God as if his soul physically **clings** to him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture. Alternatively, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [remains devoted to you] or [holds tightly to you]

Here, **right hand** represents the power of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your strength]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **they** separately, even though the verb translated as **they seek** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that his enemies seek his life. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [But my enemies truly seek]

The pronoun **they** refers to David’s enemies, who have not been mentioned previously in this psalm. If it would be helpful in your language, you could clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [But those who are my enemies]
David is using **my life** to represent his entire person in the act being killed. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to kill me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **devastation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to destroy me]

David is referring to death in a polite way by using the phrase **the lowest parts of the earth**. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [to the grave] or [to Sheol]

The psalmist is using **pour him into the hands of the sword** as a common expression of the culture to mean “cause him to be killed by the sword.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They will hand him over to be slain by the sword] or [They will cause him to die by the sword]

The psalmist is speaking of **the sword** as if it were a living thing that could have **hands**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the destructive power of the sword] or [death by the sword]

The psalmist is speaking of his enemies’ dead bodies as if they were **a portion of jackals**, that is, food that would be given to scavenging animals. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they will become food for wild animals]

A **jackal** is a kind of wild scavenging animal. If your readers would not be familiar with what a jackal is, you could use the name of a similar animal that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [scavengers]

The pronoun **him** is singular, but it refers to the psalmist’s enemies, who are plural. David may be referring to them collectively. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a plural form. Alternate translation: [them]
By **the king**, David means himself. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I, the king,]
The pronoun **him** refers to God. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [by God]
