The psalmist is using one part of a person, **the mouth**, to mean all of him in the act of speaking lies. The phrase **will be shut** means that they will be stopped or silenced. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [speakers of falsehood will be silenced] or [those who speak falsehood will be stopped]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **falsehood**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [false things]

The expression **will be shut** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [God will shut the mouth of speakers of falsehood] or [will stop speaking]

64.text:
# Psalm 64 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 64 is a wisdom psalm that describes the difference between how righteous people and wicked people live and the difference between what happens to them. However, it begins like a psalm of supplication, with a cry for help. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Introduction: cry for help (1–3a)
2. What wicked people do (3b–6)
3. How God will judge and punish wicked people (6–8a)
4. How other people will respond when they see this (8b–10)

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please hear my voice, God] or [I ask you to hear my voice, God]

Here, **voice** represents what David is saying in prayer. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my prayer] or [my words]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **complaint**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [as I complain to you] or [as I tell you what troubles me]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please preserve my life]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **fear**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [so that I will not be afraid of]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please hide me]

The phrases **the council of evildoers** and **the throng of the workers of iniquity** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two phrases together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [from the large group of wicked people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [iniquitous things] or [perverted acts]

64.quote: שָׁנְנ֣וּ כַ⁠חֶ֣רֶב לְשׁוֹנָ֑⁠ם דָּרְכ֥וּ חִ֝צָּ֗⁠ם דָּבָ֥ר מָֽר
64.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [have sharpened their tongue like a sword, yes, they tread their arrow, a bitter word]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a sword** is sharp and able to cut and wound, so the **tongue** of the enemies is able to harm others with their words. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [sharpened their tongue to wound like a sharp sword]

Here, **their tongue** represents what they say. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [their words] or [what they say]

The psalmist is speaking of **a bitter word** as if it were **their arrow**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They tread their cruel words as arrows]

Here, **tread** represents “shoot.” Ancient archers would step on their bows in order to bend them so that they could string them. David means “they step on their bows to string them and then shoot arrows from them.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [They shoot]

The psalmist is using the adjective **innocent** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [innocent people] or [people who are innocent]

The psalmist is speaking of **the innocent** as if they were targets that the wicked could **shoot** with arrows. He means that the wicked attack innocent people with harmful words. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture. Alternatively, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to attack the innocent with their words]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and they do not fear judgment] or [and they do not fear consequences]

The psalmist is using **strengthen for themselves an evil matter** as a common expression of the culture to mean “encourage each other in their evil plans.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [embolden one another to do evil] or [make each other more determined to carry out wicked schemes]

The evildoers are using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [No one will see them.] or [No one will see our schemes!]
The pronoun **them** refers to the snares, not to the evildoers. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Who will see the snares]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquities**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [iniquitous things] or [things that are evil]

The terms **inside of man** and **the heart** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. [The human heart is very deep] or [Man’s private thoughts are beyond knowing]

Here, **the inside of man** represents a person’s inner thoughts and motives. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The thoughts of man] or [Man’s inner motives]

Here, **the heart** represents a person’s thoughts and motives. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a person’s thoughts] or [people’s motives]

The psalmist is speaking of **the heart** as if it were something **deep** that cannot be easily explored or understood. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the heart are hidden] or [and the heart are unfathomable]

David is speaking of God judging his enemies as if he were **shooting an arrow** at them. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [God will strike his enemies suddenly, like a warrior who shoots an arrow at them]

The psalmist uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between the evildoers’ plans and God’s response. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [However, God will shoot] or [In contrast, God will shoot]

The psalmist actually means to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of what he is saying here. He describes the wounding of the wicked as happening **suddenly**, just as the wicked planned to wound the innocent suddenly (verse 4). If a speaker of your language would not do that, you could translate the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they will receive the sudden wounds they planned for others]

The pronoun **it** could refer to: (1) their tongue or (2) the arrow (see 64:7). If it would be helpful in your language, you could clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And their tongue will make them stumble] or [And the arrow will make them stumble]

Here, **their tongue** represents their harmful words. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [their own words] or [what they themselves have said]

The psalmist is saying **Everyone seeing them will flee** as a generalization for emphasis. If it would be clearer in your language, you could express the emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [All who see them will flee] or [People who see them will flee]

The psalmist is saying **all of mankind** as a generalization for emphasis. If it would be clearer in your language, you could express the emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [all people who see this] or [everyone who observes these things]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The first phrase states the general idea, and then the second phrase gives a specific example. Translate these phrases according to the decisions your team has made regarding translating parallelism in Hebrew poetry. Alternate translation: [and they will declare the work of God, certainly, they will consider his deed]

The psalmist is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [Righteous people] or [Those who do the right thing]

64.quote: יִשְׂמַ֬ח צַדִּ֣יק בַּ֭⁠יהוָה וְ⁠חָ֣סָה ב֑⁠וֹ וְ֝⁠יִתְהַֽלְל֗וּ כָּל־יִשְׁרֵי־לֵֽב
64.text: These two phrases, **The righteous will rejoice** and **the upright of heart will celebrate** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [The righteous will rejoice in Yahweh and take refuge in him; indeed, all of the upright of heart will celebrate.]

The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a safe **refuge** or shelter where the righteous could be protected from danger. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and go to him for protection] or [and trust him to keep them safe]

The psalmist is using the adjective phrase **upright of heart** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjective phrases in the same way. If not, you can translate this with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the people who are upright in heart] or [those whose hearts are upright]

Here, **heart** represents a person’s inner character and motives. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [character] or [motives]

65.text:
# Psalm 65 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 65 begins as a psalm of thanksgiving. David announces that he is paying a vow to God. He says what God has done for him: God has forgiven his sin. He invites people to share in a celebration meal. But after those standard elements, this turns into a psalm of worship. David describes the powerful things that God does, and he describes how people all over the world praise God for them. He then describes how God provides rain so that fields and pastures in meadows, hills, and valleys can produce good crops, and he depicts those places as praising God for that. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. David’s declaration that he is paying a vow (1)
2. Statement of what God has done in answer to prayer (2–3)
3. Invitation to share in a celebration meal (4)
4. Reason to worship: God powerfully controls nature and people (5–7)
5. Description of people worshiping God for this (8)
6. Reason to worship: God sends rain to make crops grow (9–11)
7. Description of fields and pastures worshiping God for this (12–13)

**For the chief musician** is an instruction about who should lead people in singing or playing music with this psalm. This could refer to the person in charge of music for temple worship. If your readers would not be familiar with this role, you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the worship leader]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **Praise**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [We are praising you in silence]

The implication is that the people are waiting silently in reverent worship before they praise God. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Waiting in silence to praise] or [Silent before worship directed]
The word **Zion** is the name of a place. It refers to Mount Zion in Jerusalem.

The expression **a vow will be paid** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is the worshipers. Alternate translation: [the worshipers will pay their vows] or [people will fulfill their vows]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **prayer**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [You who hear people when they pray;]

Here, **all flesh** represents all people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all people] or [everyone]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquities**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [The wrong things we have done]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **transgressions**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the ways we have disobeyed you]

The terms **iniquities** and **transgressions** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Our many sins overwhelm me but]

The pronoun **me** refers to the psalmist, while the pronoun “our” refers to the psalmist along with the rest of God’s people. The psalmist is speaking both personally and on behalf of the community. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [prevail against me and my people]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you cover them** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that God, to whom he is speaking, is the one forgiving them. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [you, God, you cover them]

The psalmist is using **you cover them** as a common expression of the culture to mean “you forgive them” or “you atone for them.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you forgive them] or [you atone for them]

The psalmist is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of joy or blessing. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Oh, how happy is] or [Truly blessed is]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **goodness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the good things in your house] or [how good your house is]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **holiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how holy your temple is]

Here, **your house** and **your temple** represent God’s presence at the temple in Jerusalem. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your presence in the temple … your presence in the temple]

The terms **your house** and **your temple** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [May we be full of the goodness and holiness of your holy dwelling place]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by doing what is right] or [in a righteous way]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [God who is saving us]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **confidence**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the trusted one of]

The psalmist is using **the ends of the earth** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the most distant places on earth” or “people everywhere.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the most remote places] or [people everywhere on earth]

The psalmist is referring to all of the earth by naming two extremes, **the ends of the earth** and **the distant seas**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [everywhere on earth]

The psalmist is speaking of God as if he were a builder who physically **establishes mountains** in place. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one who created the mountains by his great power]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by how strong he is]

The expression **being girded with might** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [who girds himself with might] or [who clothes himself with might]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **might**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with powerful strength] or [by being mighty]

The terms **strength** and **might** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [great power]

The psalmist is speaking of might as if it were clothing that God could wear. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture. Alternatively, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [possessing great power] or [having great might]

These two phrases **the roar of the seas** and **the roar of their waves** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [the roar of the seas, yes, the roar of their waves] or [the roaring seas and their waves]

The terms **the roar of the seas** and **the roar of their waves** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [the loud roaring of the seas]

The psalmist is speaking of **the tumult of the peoples** as if it were roaring like chaotic seas. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the unrest of the nations] or [the agitation of the peoples]

The phrases **the roar of the seas** and **the tumult of the peoples** mean basically the same thing. The psalmist is speaking of the **peoples** as if they were **seas**, comparing the noise and chaos of nations to crashing waves. The second phrase emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [the roar of the seas, that is, the tumult of the peoples]

The psalmist is using **the dwellers of the ends** as a common expression of the culture to mean “those who live in the farthest places” or “those who live at the remotest boundaries of the earth.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those who live in the most distant places] or [people in the remotest parts of the earth]

Here, **signs** represents God’s miraculous deeds. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your miraculous works] or [your mighty acts]

The psalmist is speaking of **the goings forth of the morning and the evening** as if they were living things that could **shout joyfully**. The phrase **the goings forth of the morning and the evening** represents sunrise and sunset. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the places where the sun rises and sets rejoice] or [people everywhere from sunrise to sunset shout joyfully]

The psalmist is using **the goings forth of the morning and the evening** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the east and the west” or “all the earth from sunrise to sunset.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all the earth from the east to the west] or [everywhere the sun rises and sets]

The psalmist is referring to all times of day by naming two extremes, **the morning** and **the evening**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all day long] or [at all times]

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a person who could come to **visit the earth**. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [You come to the earth and care for it] or [You attend to the earth]

The psalmist is speaking of the rain that comes from the sky as if it flowed from **the channel of God**, a heavenly waterway. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The sky is full of rain from God] or [God’s heavenly reservoir is full of water]

The pronoun **their** refers to people on earth who benefit from God’s provision. If it would be helpful in your language, you could clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [grain for people] or [grain for humanity]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [You water its furrows, you settle its ridges]

The psalmist is speaking of the growth of plants as if it were something that receives God’s **blessing**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you cause its crops to grow] or [you make it produce a good harvest]

The psalmist is speaking of God as if he were a king placing a **crown** on the year to adorn it with abundant blessings. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You adorn the year with your goodness] or [You make the year wonderful with your goodness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **goodness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how good you are] or [how generously you provide]

The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were driving a cart whose **tracks drip fatness** (that is, whose wheel ruts overflow with abundant crops). If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [you leave abundance behind you wherever you go]

Here, **tracks** represents God’s presence as he passes by, bringing blessing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [everywhere you pass by] or [the places where you have gone]

Here, **fatness** represents abundance and prosperity. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [abundance] or [rich blessings]

The psalmist is speaking of **the pastures of the wilderness** as if they were living things that could **drip** with moisture or abundance. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The pastures of the wilderness are covered with dew] or [The pastures of the wilderness are full of water]

The psalmist is speaking of **the hills** as if they were living things that could put on clothing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the hills are like people who dress themselves in joyful celebration] or [it is as if the hills wear rejoicing]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **rejoicing**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [joy] or [what makes people rejoice]

The psalmist is speaking of the hills as if they were people who could **gird on rejoicing** like a person putting on clothing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the hills are clothed with joy] or [the hills seem joyful]

The psalmist is speaking of **meadows** as if they were living things that could put on clothing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Flocks cover the meadows]

The psalmist is speaking of the meadows as if they were people who could **put on** flocks as clothing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The flocks cover the meadows] or [Flocks are spread across the meadows]

The psalmist is speaking of **the valleys** as if they were living things that could **cover themselves with grain**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [grain grows abundantly in the valleys] or [the valleys are filled with grain]

The psalmist is speaking of **the meadows** and **the valleys** as if they were living things that could **shout joyfully** and **sing**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [It is as though they shout joyfully; indeed, it is as though they sing] or [They are like people shouting joyfully and singing]

The terms **shout joyfully** and **sing** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [rejoice with loud songs]

66.text:
# Psalm 66 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 66 is a psalm of thanksgiving. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Call to worship (1–3)
2. Reason to worship (5–7)
3. Call to worship (8)
4. Reason to worship (9–12)
5. The psalmist’s declaration that he is paying a vow (13–15)
6. The psalmist’s declaration that God has answered his prayer (16–20)

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Let everyone on earth shout to God]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please make music to the glory of his name]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [glorious character]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please make his praise glorious]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **praise**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [praises]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please say to God]

The psalmist is using the question form to express amazement at God’s deeds. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Your deeds are very fearsome!]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **greatness** and **power**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [of your very great power]

Here, **cringe** represents showing false submission out of fear. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your enemies submit to you in fear]

The psalmist is saying **All of the earth bows down to you** as a generalization for emphasis. If it would be clearer in your language, you could express the emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [Everyone on earth bows down to you]

The psalmist is speaking of **the earth** as if it were a living thing that could bow down and worship. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Everyone on earth bows down]
The psalmist is using the term **name** to represent who God is or to refer to God’s reputation. Alternate translation: [to your reputation]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please come and see the works of God]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **doing**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [fearsome in what he does]

The psalmist is using **sons of man** as a common expression of the culture to mean “human beings.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [human beings]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if God had literally transformed the sea into solid ground. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He made a way through the sea on dry ground]
The pronoun **they** refers to the Israelites. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the Israelites passed through]

The psalmist is using the imperative form to communicate an exhortation. If the imperative does not communicate an exhortation for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates an exhortation. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [we should rejoice in him]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that **the sea** refers to the Red Sea and **the river** refers to the Jordan River, both of which God miraculously parted for the Israelites to cross. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the Red Sea … the Jordan River]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **might**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by being mighty]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if God had physical **eyes** that could **watch over** the nations. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he observes the nations]

See the discussion in the introduction to Psalms about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [The ones rebelling should not exalt themselves]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please bless our God, peoples]

The expression **make the sound of his praise heard** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and proclaim his praise aloud]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **praise**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [praising him]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if keeping them alive were **putting** their **soul among the living**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one keeping us alive]

Here, **our foot to slip** represents falling into danger or ruin. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and he does not allow us to stumble into disaster]

Here the psalmist is speaking of the difficulties God allowed as if God had **tested** them as a refiner tests metal. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [For you put us through difficulties to prove us]

The point of this comparison is that just as silver is purified by being heated in fire to remove impurities, so God allowed the people to go through difficulties to purify them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [you purified us through suffering just as a refiner purifies silver with fire]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **refining**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [just as silver is refined]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if the difficult circumstances were a **net** that trapped them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You allowed us to be captured]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if oppression and hardship were physical **pressure on our loins**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you placed a heavy burden on us]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if being conquered by enemies were having **man ride over our head**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You let our conquerors trample over us]

The psalmist is referring to all kinds of trials by naming two extremes, **fire** and **waters**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [we went through every kind of danger]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if prosperity and blessing were a place of **abundance** to which God brought them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but you brought us to where we prosper]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **abundance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to a place where we have all that we need]

The **burnt offerings** are a kind of sacrifice in which whole animals are burned on an altar as an offering to God. If your readers would not be familiar with what burnt offerings are, you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [with sacrifices that are totally burned on the altar]

Here, **my lips opened** represents the psalmist making vows by speaking them aloud. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [which I voiced]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [I solemnly vowed]

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about when the psalmist was in trouble before the information about what his lips and mouth did. Alternate translation: [{for} which, when trouble {was} to me, my lips opened and my mouth spoke]

66.quote: עֹ֘ל֤וֹת מֵחִ֣ים אַעֲלֶה & אֶ֥עֱשֶֽׂה בָקָ֖ר עִם־עַתּוּדִ֣ים
66.text: These two phrases **I will offer up burnt offerings of fatlings** and **I will offer cattle with male goats** mean basically the same thing. The first phrase states the general idea, and then the second phrase gives a specific example. Translate these phrases according to the decisions your team has made regarding translating parallelism in Hebrew poetry. Alternate translation: [I will offer up young animals fattened for burnt offerings … including cattle with male goats]

**Fatlings** are young animals that have been fattened for sacrifice. If your readers would not be familiar with what fatlings are, you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [burnt offerings of young, fattened animals]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know what he means. The **smoke of rams** is the fragrant smoke that rises when rams are burned as sacrifices on the altar. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [with the fragrant smoke from the burning of rams]

These are imperatives, but they communicate a polite request rather than a command. If the imperatives do not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please come, listen, and let me recount]

The psalmist is using the term **soul** to mean the entire person from the perspective of his spiritual and emotional existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [what he has done for me personally]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if his praise were something physically lifted up from his **tongue**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I praised his greatness with my words]

The psalmist is making a conditional statement that sounds hypothetical, but he knows that the condition is not true. He is stating it as a condition to show that the Lord not hearing is also not true. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that the speaker believes is not true. Alternate translation: [Suppose I had cherished iniquity in my heart]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what is wicked]
Here, **my heart** represents the psalmist’s inner thoughts. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in my mind]

The psalmist uses the word **Surely** here to indicate a contrast between the hypothetical situation in which God would not have heard (verse 18) and the reality that God did hear. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [But indeed God has heard]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **prayer**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to me as I prayed to him]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if his prayer had a **voice** that could speak. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to my words as I prayed]

The expression **Blessed be** is a passive verbal form. The psalmist is expressing his desire to praise God. If it would be unnatural to use that form for this purpose, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Let me praise Yahweh]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word for **turned away**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [who has certainly accepted my prayer]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **prayer**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [my crying to him]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [nor has he turned away his covenant faithfulness from me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [or his loyal love]

67.text:
# Psalm 67 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 67 is a psalm of thanksgiving on the occasion of an abundant harvest. It includes requests at the beginning and end for God to bless the people, but given the occasion, these have the sense of “may God continue to bless us.” So while these requests have an element of supplication, the psalm as a whole is a psalm of praise. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Request for God to bless (1–2)
2. Refrain (3)
3. Call to worship (4a)
4. Reason to worship (4b)
5. Refrain (5)
6. Reason to worship (6a)
7. Request for God to bless (6a–7)

### Allusion to Numbers

In verse 1, the psalmist says, “May God be gracious to us and bless us; may he make his face shine on us.” In [Numbers 6:25](../num/06/25.md), Yahweh told the priests to say this same thing in order to bless the Israelites. So that your readers will be able to recognize this allusion, we recommend that you translate this phrase in the same way here and in Numbers 6:25.

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

The psalmist is speaking of God showing his favor as if God’s **face** were a light that could **shine** on people. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [may he show us his favor]

Here the word **for** marks **the knowing of your way** as the goal or purpose of the psalmist’s prayer for God’s blessing in the previous verse. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [so that people may know your way]

The psalmist is speaking of how God acts as if that were a **way** or path that God walks along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [how you act]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and for the knowing of your salvation among all of the nations]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how you save people]
The pronoun **your** refers to God in both instances. Alternate translation: [God’s way … God’s salvation among all the nations]

67.quote: יוֹד֖וּ⁠ךָ עַמִּ֥ים ׀ אֱלֹהִ֑ים י֝וֹד֗וּ⁠ךָ עַמִּ֥ים כֻּלָּֽ⁠ם
67.text: These two phrases **May the peoples thank you, God** and **may the peoples thank you, all of them** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with some different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [May all the peoples thank you, God] or [May all the peoples thank you, God; indeed, may everyone in the world thank you]

67.quote: יִֽשְׂמְח֥וּ וִֽ⁠ירַנְּנ֗וּ לְאֻ֫מִּ֥ים כִּֽי־תִשְׁפֹּ֣ט עַמִּ֣ים מִישׁ֑וֹר וּ⁠לְאֻמִּ֓ים ׀ בָּ⁠אָ֖רֶץ תַּנְחֵ֣⁠ם סֶֽלָה

Alternate translation: [Because you judge the peoples {with} uprightness, and the nations on the earth, you guide them, may the nations rejoice and shout joyfully. Selah]

67.quote: תִשְׁפֹּ֣ט עַמִּ֣ים מִישׁ֑וֹר וּ⁠לְאֻמִּ֓ים ׀ בָּ⁠אָ֖רֶץ תַּנְחֵ֣⁠ם
67.text: These two phrases **you judge the peoples with uprightness** and **the nations on the earth, you guide them** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [you judge and guide all the peoples on the earth with uprightness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **uprightness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [justly]

67.quote: יוֹד֖וּ⁠ךָ עַמִּ֥ים ׀ אֱלֹהִ֑ים י֝וֹד֗וּ⁠ךָ עַמִּ֥ים כֻּלָּֽ⁠ם
67.text: This verse is a refrain that repeats the exact words of [67:3](../067/003.md). If your language has a poetic way to indicate a refrain, you could use it here. Alternate translation: [May all the peoples thank you, God]

The psalmist is speaking of **the earth** as if it were a living thing that could **give** produce. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [There has been a good harvest from the earth]

The psalmist is not using the possessive form **our God** to indicate that the people of Israel possess or control God. Rather the psalmist is using these words to indicate that God is the one whom they worship. Alternate translation: [the God whom we worship]

Here, **all of the ends of the earth** represents people everywhere on the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [people everywhere on the earth]
The pronoun **him** refers to God. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [God]

68.text:
# Psalm 68 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 68 is a divine enthronement psalm. (See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.) Many interpreters believe that David wrote this psalm for the occasion when a great crowd of Israelites brought the Box of the Covenant to a sanctuary that David had prepared for it on Mount Zion. (His son King Solomon later built a temple for Yahweh on that location.) The psalm depicts God leading the people of Israel in a procession starting at Mount Sinai, through the wilderness, into the land of Canaan to conquer it, and finally up Mount Zion to the sanctuary. The psalm then describes the actual procession of Israelites. Finally, it describes how the Israelites will be safe from their enemies now that God will be ruling as their divine king from his sanctuary.

1. The Box of the Covenant sets out (1–2)
2. A call to worship God for his power and goodness (3–6)
3. God leads the Israelites through the desert and provides water (7–10)
4. The conquest of Canaan, viewed through a victory celebration afterwards (11–14)
5. God chooses Mount Zion for his sanctuary (15–18)
6. God will defeat the enemies of the Israelites (19–23)
7. Description of the procession up Mount Zion (24–27)
8. Foreign kingdoms will worship the God of Israel and pay tribute to him (28–35)

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

### Allusion to Numbers

David begins this psalm by saying, “Let God arise, let his enemies scatter, and let the ones hating him flee from his face.” According to [Numbers 10:35](../num/10/35.md), whenever the Israelites picked up the Box of the Covenant in order to move to another place in the wilderness, Moses would say, “Arise, Yahweh, and let your enemies scatter, and let the ones hating you flee from your face.” So that your readers will be able to recognize this allusion, we recommend that you translate this phrase with the same terms here and in Numbers 10:35.

### Mountains

David speaks of mountains in significant ways in this psalm. His overall message is that the same God who first appeared to the Israelites at Mount Sinai is now ruling over them from his sanctuary in Mount Zion. As he says in a compact way in verse 17, “Sinai is in the holy place.” David also speaks of Mount Bashan, a high mountain to the northeast of Israel. In verses 15–16, he says poetically that this great mountain should not be jealous of Mount Zion. In verse 22, he uses it to represent a very high place to which enemies might try to flee, pairing it with the “depths of the sea,” a very low place. Because of the significance of these mountains in the psalm, we recommend that you use the names Sinai and Bashan at each place where they occur, spelling them the way they sound in your language. You may also want to identify Mount Zion as the mountain that David describes in verse 17, as the UST does.

### Walking

The image of walking or marching in a great procession unites all the sections of this psalm. David also uses the image of walking to mean other things. For example, in verse 21, he speaks of “the one walking ahead in his trespasses.” This represents continuing to commit sins, as the UST indicates. It may be most natural to express the idea in that way in your translation. However, if your language can use the image of walking to represent living, we recommend that you do that so that your readers can appreciate how David is using this image.

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

68.quote: יָק֣וּם אֱ֭לֹהִים יָפ֣וּצוּ אוֹיְבָ֑י⁠ו וְ⁠יָנ֥וּסוּ מְ֝שַׂנְאָ֗י⁠ו
68.text: By using **Let**, the psalmist is expressing his wish or prayer. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [I desire that God should arise and make his enemies scatter and the ones hating him flee]

These two phrases **let his enemies scatter** and **let the ones hating him flee from his face** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [may all who oppose him scatter and flee]

Here, **from his face** represents being away from God’s presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from before him]

The point of this comparison is that just as **smoke is driven away** easily and completely by wind, so should God’s enemies be easily and completely driven away. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Scatter them completely, just as smoke is scattered by the wind]

The expression **smoke is driven away** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the wind drives smoke away]

68.quote: כְּ⁠הִמֵּ֣ס דּ֭וֹנַג מִ⁠פְּנֵי־אֵ֑שׁ יֹאבְד֥וּ רְ֝שָׁעִ֗ים מִ⁠פְּנֵ֥י אֱלֹהִֽים
68.text: The point of this comparison is that just as **wax melts from the face of fire**, dissolving and disappearing before heat, so will the wicked perish before God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [just as wax dissolves when heat strikes it, let the wicked perish before God]

Here, **from the face of fire** represents being near the front surface of fire. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from the heat of fire]

By using **let**, the psalmist is expressing what he desires or prays will happen. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [the wicked should be destroyed]

The psalmist is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [wicked people]

Here, **from the face of God** represents being away from God’s presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from before God]

68.quote: וְֽ⁠צַדִּיקִ֗ים יִשְׂמְח֣וּ יַֽ֭עַלְצוּ לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י אֱלֹהִ֗ים וְ⁠יָשִׂ֥ישׂוּ בְ⁠שִׂמְחָֽה
68.text: See how your translation team has decided to represent sets of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [But let the righteous celebrate joyfully in God’s presence]

The psalmist is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [But let righteous people rejoice]
Here, **to the face of God** represents being in God’s presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before God]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **rejoicing**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [as they rejoice greatly]
See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [Sing praise to God, making music to him]

The psalmist is using the term **his name** to represent who God is and to refer to God’s reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [who he is]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [lift up a song to the one riding over the plains]

Here the psalmist is speaking of God as if he were **the one riding over the plains**, evoking the image of a powerful warrior or king who commands the open wilderness. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one who moves powerfully through the desert wastelands]

Here, **exult to his face** represents rejoicing in God’s presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [yes, exult before him]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe a father who is characterized by caring for orphans. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [A father to orphans]

Here the psalmist is speaking of God as if he were **A father of orphans**, meaning God cares for and protects those who have no earthly father. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [One who cares for orphans as a father would]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe a judge who is characterized by defending widows. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a defender of widows]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **his holiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [his holy being]

The psalmist is using the adjective **lonely** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are lonely]

The psalmist uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between those whom God blesses and those who rebel against him. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [However, the ones rebelling dwell in dryness]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if **dryness** were a place where rebels must live, representing the barrenness and hardship of life without God’s blessing. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [dwell in a barren land]

The psalmist is using the clause **when you went out to the face of your people, when you marched in the wilderness** to describe something that was ongoing. This provides the background for the events he describes in verse 8. Connect this clause to the following verse in a way that makes it clear in your language that this clause is describing something that was ongoing in the background. Alternate translation: [as you went out before your people, as you marched through the wilderness]

See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [when you marched before your people through the wilderness]

Here, **to the face of your people** represents going out in front of and leading the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before your people]

The psalmist is speaking of **the earth quaked** as if the earth were a living thing that could react with fear. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the earth trembled]

The psalmist is speaking of **the heavens dripped** as if the heavens were a living thing that could pour out rain. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [rain fell from the sky]

Here, **from the face of God** represents being in front of God, that is, in his presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from the presence of God]

68.quote: זֶ֥ה סִינַ֑י מִ⁠פְּנֵ֥י אֱ֝לֹהִ֗ים אֱלֹהֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
68.text: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. The verb “quaked” from the previous clause is implied here. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [this Sinai also quaked, from the face of God, the God of Israel]

Here, **from the face of God** represents being in front of God, that is, in his presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from the presence of God]

The psalmist is not using this possessive form **the God of Israel** to indicate that the Israelites possess or control God. Rather the psalmist is using these words to indicate that God is the one whom Israel worships. Alternate translation: [who is the God whom Israel worships]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe a **rain** that is characterized by **generosities**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [You poured out abundant rainfall]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **generosities**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [A generous rainful]

David is speaking as if the land of Israel were actually Yahweh’s **inheritance**, that is, as if it were something that belonged to him permanently because he inherited it from an ancestor. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the land that belongs to you]

The expression **when it was wearied** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [when it grew weary]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you established** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that God himself is the one who acted. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [indeed, you established it]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if God’s people were **your flock**, an animal herd cared for by a shepherd. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Your nation]
The pronoun **it** refers to the land, that is, the inheritance mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [in the land]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **goodness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because you are good]

The psalmist is using the adjective **poor** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [for those who are needy]

The psalmist is using the term **word** to represent the message or command that the Lord spoke. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The Lord speaks his command]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if the women proclaiming good news were **a great army**, a large and powerful fighting force. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the women proclaiming good news are a vast company]

The Hebrew word translated as **the women proclaiming good news** is feminine in form, indicating that those who announced the victory were specifically women. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this explicit. Alternate translation: [the female heralds]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to mean kings who command armies. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Kings who command armies]

The words **flee** and **they flee** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two words together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [they flee in great haste]

The pronoun **they** refers to the kings, while the pronoun **she** refers to the woman who stays at home. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the kings flee, and the woman who stays at home divides]

The pronoun you does not refer to God, as in verses 7–10. It is plural, and it refers to Israelite men who stayed back to care for flocks instead of going into battle. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Even if you were among the Israelite men who lay down between the sheepfolds] or [Even if you were among the Israelite men who cared for flocks instead of going into battle]

The psalmist is using **the wings of a dove covered with silver** to represent a dove statue on which the wings are covered with silver. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a dove statue whose wings are covered with silver]

David assumes that his listeners will understand that he is describing the type of plunder that even men who stayed out of battle to care for flocks will receive. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [you will still receive plunder such as a dove statue whose wings are covered with silver]

The expression **covered with silver** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [with a silver covering]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. The word “covered” from the previous clause is implied here. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and its feathers covered with greenness of gold]

68.quote: בְּ⁠פָ֘רֵ֤שׂ שַׁדַּ֓י מְלָ֘כִ֤ים בָּ֗⁠הּ תַּשְׁלֵ֥ג בְּ⁠צַלְמֽוֹן
68.text: The word **When** indicates that the scattering of kings and the snowfall on Zalmon happened at the same time. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could describe the time relationship more explicitly. Alternate translation: [As Shaddai scattered kings in it, it snowed on Zalmon]

The pronoun **it** refers to the land, the region where the battle took place. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [in the place where the enemy army had assembled]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if the whitened, fleeing armies were **it snowed on Zalmon**, comparing their scattered flight to snowfall blanketing a dark mountain. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the battlefield was white, like snow on Zalmon]

The psalmist is using **a mountain of God** as a common expression of the culture to mean “a very great mountain.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a magnificent mountain]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe a mountain that is characterized by having many peaks. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a many-peaked mountain]

68.quote: לָ֤⁠מָּה ׀ תְּֽרַצְּדוּ⁠ן֮ הָרִ֪ים גַּבְנֻ֫נִּ֥ים הָ⁠הָ֗ר חָמַ֣ד אֱלֹהִ֣ים לְ⁠שִׁבְתּ֑⁠וֹ
68.text: The psalmist is using the question form to assert that God has chosen Mount Zion as his dwelling place, not the impressive Mount Bashan. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You other mountains and peaks should not look enviously at the mountain God desired for his dwelling!]

The psalmist is speaking of **mountains, peaks** as if they were living things that could feel envy. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Why do you look enviously, O rugged mountains]

The psalmist is speaking to **mountains, peaks** that he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about God’s choice of Zion. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about the mountains. Alternate translation: [many-peaked mountains] or [dwellers among the many-peaked mountains]
The pronoun **his** refers to God. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [for God’s dwelling]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if God’s overwhelming power were **the chariotry of God**, a vast military force of chariots. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The armies of God]

The psalmist says **two myriads, thousands of repetition** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [tens of thousands upon thousands]
The pronoun **them** refers to the chariots/myriads. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [is among the chariots]

Here the psalmist is speaking of God’s victory as if it were **ascended to the height**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You have risen to supremacy]

The psalmist is using **you have taken captivity captive** as a common expression of the culture to mean that he has taken a great multitude of prisoners. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you have led a host of captives]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **captivity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [captives]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [among people]

Here, **that Yah God might dwell there** marks the entire preceding action of ascending, taking captives, and receiving gifts as the goal or purpose of those acts—namely, that God would establish his dwelling. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [so that Yah God might dwell there]

The expression **Blessed be** is a passive verbal form. The psalmist is expressing his desire to praise the Lord. If it would be unnatural to use that form for this purpose, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [We bless the Lord] or [Let me praise the Lord]

The psalmist is repeating the word **Day** in order to intensify the meaning or the emotion that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification.
