# Psalm 69 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 69 is a psalm of supplication or lament. It presents the basic elements of that type of psalm. (Some elements are repeated.) Near its end, it becomes a specific kind of psalm of supplication, an “imprecatory psalm” in which the psalmist describes the actions of wicked people and asks God to judge and punish them. Furthermore, the New Testament writers considered Psalm 69 to be a Messianic psalm that looked forward to the reign of Jesus Christ. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Cry for help (1–3)
2. Description of troubles (4)
3. Confession of sin (5–6)
4. Claim of devotion to God (7–12)
5. Statement of trust (13)
6. Petition (14–18)
7. Description of troubles (19–21)
8. Imprecation (22–28)
9. Vow of praise (29–36)

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

While New Testament writers quote this psalm in several places, we encourage translators to translate the words of the Hebrew text as they appear in the Old Testament and the words of the Greek text as they appear in the New Testament, even if, inevitably, there is some difference between the words as the ideas are expressed in different languages. We encourage translators not to try to use similar words in both places so that readers will recognize the quotations. Instead, translators can use footnotes in the New Testament to identify the source of these quotations.

Here is a list of the places where New Testament writers quote this psalm:
69:4, “The ones hating me gratuitously,” John 15:25
69:9, “zeal for your house has consumed me,” John 2:17
69:9, “the reproaches of the ones reproaching you have fallen on me,” Romans 15:3
69:21, “they made me drink vinegar for my thirst,” Matthew 27:34 and John 19:28
69:22–23, “Let their table become a snare to their faces and a trap for their welfare. Let their eyes darken from seeing, make their loins tremble continually,” Romans 11:9–10
69:25, “Let their encampment be deserted; let there not be a dweller in their tents,” Acts 1:20

# Psalm 70 Introduction

Psalm 70 is a psalm of supplication or lament. Formally, it includes only two the basic elements of that type of psalm, a cry for help and a petition. But a description of troubles and a statement of trust are implicit in the background. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Cry for help (1)
2. Petition (2–4)
3. Repeated cry for help (5)

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

### Similarity to Psalm 40

This words of this psalm are very similar to Psalm 40:13–17. If you have already translated Psalm 40, see what you did there. It may help you translate Psalm 70.

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

These two phrases **Hurry, God, to deliver me** and **Yahweh, to my help** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Hurry, Yahweh God, to deliver me and help me]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please hurry, God, to deliver me]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, hurry to my help]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **help**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to help me]

# Psalm 71 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 71 is a psalm of supplication or lament. It presents all of the basic elements of that type of psalm. (Some elements are repeated.) See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Cry for help (1–4)
2. Statement of trust (5–7)
3. Petition (8–9)
4. Description of troubles (10–11)
5. Petition (12–13)
6. Statement of trust (14–17)
7. Petition (18–21)
8. Vow of praise (22–24)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Lifelong Dependence on God

The psalmist traces reliance on God from the womb (verse 6) through youth (verse 17) to old age (verses 9, 18), asking not to be abandoned as his strength fails.

### God as Refuge and Rock

The psalmist calls God his rock, fortress, and refuge (verses 1–3, 7), using images of physical shelter to express trust in divine protection.

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a safe place where David could **take refuge**. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [I find safety]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please never let me have shame]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Because you act righteously]

These are imperatives, but they communicate a polite request rather than a command. If the imperatives do not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please deliver me and rescue me]

The terms **deliver** and **rescue** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [completely deliver me]

These are imperatives, but they communicate a polite request rather than a command. If the imperatives do not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. 72.text:
# Psalm 72 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 72 is a royal psalm that celebrates the occasion of a new king beginning his rule. It is a prayer for God to help the new Israelite king uphold justice and help needy people as his representative on earth. It also asks God to defeat the king’s foreign enemies so that he can continue to rule. This type of royal psalm is a specific kind of psalm of supplication. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Prayer that the new king will uphold justice (1–7)
2. Prayer that the new king will rule a great area (8–11)
3. Prayer that the new king will help needy people (12–14)
4. Prayer that the new king will bring blessings and be blessed (14–17)

Verses 18–20 are not part of the original psalm. They are a doxology (an expression of praise to God) that the editors of the book of Psalms added to mark the end of Book Two of the psalms. See how you translated the similar doxology in [41:13](../041/013.md).

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

### “Of Solomon”

The superscription of this psalm is “Of Solomon.” This may mean that Solomon wrote this psalm. But it may also mean that someone else wrote this psalm in honor of Solomon. If so, one likely possibility is that David wrote it for the coronation of his son as the next king. We recommend that you translate the superscription in a way that allows for this possibility as well as for the possibility that Solomon was the author.

The psalmist is using an imperative, but he is communicating a polite request to God rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [God, please give your judgments to the king]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [give your just decisions to the king, yes, give your righteousness to the king’s son]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **judgments**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [your ability to judge rightly]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [your righteous character]

See the discussion in the introduction to Psalms about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [I want him to rule from sea to sea and from the River to the ends of the earth]

The psalmist is using this possessive form to describe the farthest places on **the earth**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the farthest places on earth]
Here, **his face** represents his presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [kneel before him]

The expression **lick the dust** is an idiom that means to be completely defeated and humiliated. If your readers would not understand this, you could use an equivalent idiom or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [be completely defeated]

72.quote: לְ֭⁠פָנָי⁠ו יִכְרְע֣וּ צִיִּ֑ים וְ֝⁠אֹיְבָ֗י⁠ו עָפָ֥ר יְלַחֵֽכוּ
72.text: In both instances, the pronoun **his** refers to the king. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could state that explicitly. Alternate translation: [May desert-dwellers kneel to the king’s face, and may the king’s enemies lick the dust]

72.quote: מַלְכֵ֬י תַרְשִׁ֣ישׁ וְ֭⁠אִיִּים מִנְחָ֣ה יָשִׁ֑יבוּ מַלְכֵ֥י שְׁבָ֥א וּ֝⁠סְבָ֗א אֶשְׁכָּ֥ר יַקְרִֽיבוּ
72.text: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [May kings from distant lands, from Tarshish to Sheba and Seba, bring tribute and gifts to him]

The psalmist is using this possessive form to describe the kings who rule in **Tarshish**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the kings who rule in Tarshish]

The psalmist is using this possessive form to describe the kings who rule in **Sheba** and **Seba**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the kings who rule in Sheba and Seba]
The word **Seba** is the name of a region.

See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [And may all kings and nations submit to him and serve him]

The word **And** escalates the stated desire from the specific kings mentioned in the previous verse to **all kings** and **all nations**. Use a connector in your language that communicates this escalation. Alternate translation: [Indeed, may all kings bow down to him]

The psalmist says **all kings** and **all nations** as a generalization to emphasize how widespread the king’s dominion will be. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [kings everywhere … nations everywhere]

The word **For** introduces the reason why the kings and nations of the preceding verses should honor the king. Use a connector in your language that communicates that what follows is a reason. Alternate translation: [May they do this because he delivers]

The psalmist is using the adjective **needy** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the needy person]

The psalmist is using the adjective **poor** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the poor person]
The pronoun **him** refers to the poor person. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could state that explicitly. Alternate translation: [when no helper is available to that poor person]

72.quote: יָ֭חֹס עַל־דַּ֣ל וְ⁠אֶבְי֑וֹן וְ⁠נַפְשׁ֖וֹת אֶבְיוֹנִ֣ים יוֹשִֽׁיעַ
72.text: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [May he show compassion to weak and needy people by saving their lives]

The psalmist is using the adjectives **weak** and **needy** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [weak people and needy people]

72.quote: מִ⁠תּ֣וֹךְ וּ֭⁠מֵ⁠חָמָס יִגְאַ֣ל נַפְשָׁ֑⁠ם וְ⁠יֵיקַ֖ר דָּמָ֣⁠ם בְּ⁠עֵינָֽי⁠ו
72.text: In this verse, the pronoun **he** refers to the kings, **their** refers twice to the needy, and the pronoun **his** refers to the king. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could state that explicitly. Alternate translation: [May the king redeem the lives of the needy from oppression and from violence, and may the blood of the needy be precious in the king’s eyes]

The psalmist is using the singular **life** to refer collectively to the lives of multiple people. If your language would not use a singular noun in this way, you could use the plural form. Alternate translation: [their lives]

The words **oppression** and **violence** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two words together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [from every kind of mistreatment]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **oppression** and **violence**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [from those who oppress them and from those who harm them]

Here, **their blood** represents their lives, especially the shedding of blood through violence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [their lives]

The expression **precious in his eyes** is an idiom that means he considers it to be very valuable. If your readers would not understand this, you could use an equivalent idiom or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and may their lives be valuable to him]

The psalmist is using this possessive form to describe gold that comes from **Sheba**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from the gold that comes from Sheba]
The word **one** refers to people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could state that explicitly. Alternate translation: [may people give to him … may people pray for him]
The pronoun **they** refers to people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could state that explicitly. Alternate translation: [may people bless him]

The psalmist says **continually** and **all of the day** as generalizations to emphasize how frequently people should pray for and bless the king. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [and may one pray for him continuously; may they bless him constantly]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **abundance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [abundant grain]

Here, **the head** of the mountains represents the tops or summits of the mountains. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [on the tops of the mountains]

The point of this comparison is that the fruit of the grain will sway abundantly, just as the trees of **Lebanon** sway in the wind. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point of comparison explicit. Alternate translation: [may its fruit sway like the trees of Lebanon sway]
The pronoun **its** refers to the grain in the land. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could state that explicitly. Alternate translation: [the grain’s fruit]

The point of this comparison is that just as **grass** grows abundantly on **the earth**, so the people will flourish and multiply in the cities. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point of comparison explicit. Alternate translation: [may the people of the city flourish as abundantly as does the grass of the earth]
The pronoun **they** refers to the people. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could state that explicitly. Alternate translation: [may the people flourish from the city]

Here, **the face of the sun** represents the presence and duration of the sun. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as long as the sun shines]

The pronoun **they** refers to the nations, and the pronoun **him** refers to the king. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could state that explicitly. Alternate translation: [may the nations be blessed by the king]
If your language does not use this passive form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [may he bless them]

Here, **blessed** means to have good things done for someone. The psalmist is expressing a desire for the king to bring good things to all people. Alternate translation: [may he do good things for them]

The psalmist says **all of the nations** as a generalization to emphasize how widespread the king’s fame will be. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [nations everywhere]

72.quote: יְהִ֤י שְׁמ֨⁠וֹ לְֽ⁠עוֹלָ֗ם לִ⁠פְנֵי־שֶׁמֶשׁ֮ ינין שְׁ֫מ֥⁠וֹ
72.text: Here, **his name** represents the king’s reputation and fame. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May his reputation last forever; may his fame continue to the face of the sun]

The expression **Blessed be** is a passive verbal form. The psalmist is expressing his desire to praise Yahweh. If it would be unnatural to use that form for this purpose, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I bless Yahweh] or [Let us all praise Yahweh]

The psalmist is not using this possessive form to indicate that the Israelites possess or control God. Rather, he is using it to indicate that Yahweh is the God whom Israel worships. Alternate translation: [who is the God whom Israel worships]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [he alone can do]

Here, **blessed be** expresses praise to God. This is a doxology in which the psalmist declares that God’s glorious name is worthy of praise forever. If your readers would not understand this blessing formula, you could express this in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [may people praise his glorious name forever]

Here, **the name** represents God’s reputation and character. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his glorious reputation]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [his glorious name]

The expression **be filled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and let his glory fill all of the earth]

The psalmist is repeating the word **Amen** for emphasis as a way of concluding Book 2 of Psalms (42–72). If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [May it certainly be so]

This possessive form describes a social relationship, for **son of Jesse** identifies David as the offspring of Jesse. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [, Jesse’s son,]
If your language does not use this passive form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [end here]

73.text:
# Psalm 73 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 73 is a wisdom psalm. It explains the problem of wicked people who seem to prosper. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/wise]]; and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/evil]])

## Structure and Formatting

1. Affirmation that God is good to the righteous (1)
2. The psalmist recounts his experience of envy and confusion as he observes the prosperity of the wicked (2–16)
3. The psalmist goes to the sanctuary of God and understands what will happen to wicked people in the future (17–24)
4. The psalmist renews his commitment to God and to righteous living (25–26)
5. The psalmist’s final thoughts (27–28)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Evil people

Sometimes it seems that wicked people have no problems and that they live an easy and problem free life. Despite this, wicked people will eventually perish (18–19 and 27). In contrast, righteous people have the benefit of always having God’s presence with them during their life on earth (23), God guiding them during their life on earth (24a), and being with God in “glory” after they die. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/righteous]])

### Psalms by Asaph

There are twelve psalms attributed to Asaph; the first one is Psalm 50, which is in Book Two, and the other eleven (Psalms 73–83) are at the beginning of Book Three.

The psalmist uses the word **Surely** to emphasize the truth of what follows. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation or use a natural form in your language for expressing this emphasis. Alternate translation: [Certainly]
Here, **Israel** represents the Israelite people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to the people of Israel]

Here the psalmist speaks of the **heart** of righteous people as **pure** and not blemished by wrong and sinful thoughts in contrast to having a **heart** that is impure because of sinful thoughts and motives and therefore morally dirty. What the psalmist means by **pure** here is that the person’s **heart** is “morally pure.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly or use an equivalent expression. Alternate translation: [to the ones who think about and want what is pleasing to God] or [to those with a morally pure heart]

In Jewish culture people considered the **heart** to be the center of a persons thoughts and feelings and here, the **heart** represents the intentions, thoughts and desires of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to those who think about and want what is pure] or [to those with a pure mind] or [to those with pure thoughts]

73.quote: כִּ֭⁠מְעַט נטוי רַגְלָ֑⁠י כְּ֝⁠אַ֗יִן שפכה אֲשֻׁרָֽ⁠י
73.text: Here, **my feet** and **my steps** represent the Psalmist himself and the phrases **slipped** and **slide out** refer to abandoning doing what pleases God and instead choosing to sin. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning with an equivalent expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I was tempted to stop obeying God. It was as if my feet almost slipped and as if my steps were almost caused to slide out from under me] or [I almost stopped trusting in God; I was almost guilty of sinning against him]

73.quote: כִּ֭⁠מְעַט נטוי רַגְלָ֑⁠י כְּ֝⁠אַ֗יִן שפכה אֲשֻׁרָֽ⁠י
73.text: The phrases **my feet almost slipped** and **my steps almost were caused to slide out from under me** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine the phrases and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [my feet almost slipped] or [my feet almost slid out from under me]

The expression **my steps almost were caused to slide out** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you must state who did the action, the following verse implies that the Psalmist caused his own steps to almost slide out from under him when he looked at the “prosperity of the wicked” and did not also immediately go into “God’s sanctuary” so that he could “understand” the final “fate” of the wicked (see [Psalm 73:17](../073/017.md)). Alternate translation: [I almost caused my steps to slide out from under me]

Here the word **because** indicates that what follows it in this verse is the reason for what precedes it in [73:2](../073/002.md). Use a natural form for indicating this relationship. Alternate translation: [for]

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [when I saw the prosperity of the wicked, I was envious of the arrogant]

The Psalmist is using the adjectives **arrogant** and **wicked** as nouns in order to describe certain people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you could translate these words with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [of arrogant people when I saw the prosperity of wicked people] or [of the people who are arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the people who are wicked]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **prosperity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when I saw how prosperous the wicked were]

The word the ULT translates as **ropes** refers to ropes or bonds that constrain a person. Here the psalmist is speaking of struggles or pains as if they were **ropes** or “bonds.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning with an equivalent expression, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [struggles] or [emotional pains] or [pains]

The word the ULT translates as **until their death** could refer to: (1) the time before the death of wicked people in which case you can use the ULT as a model, or (2) the time at which wicked people die. Alternate translation: [in their death] or [at their death]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **trouble**, you could express the same idea with a verb or in some other way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [They do not have to experience difficult things like the rest of man] or [They do not suffer the way other men do]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people, and with people they are not afflicted] or [other people, and they are not afflicted like everyone else]

The expression **they are not afflicted** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you must state who did the action, the context implies that God did it. Alternate translation: [and God does not afflict them like he does the rest of man] or [and God does not afflict them like he does everyone else]
Here, the word **Therefore** introduces the result of [73:4–5](../073/004.md). You can use a natural word or phrase in your language to express this relationship. Alternate translation: [As a result]

The psalmist is speaking of **pride** as if it were a **necklace** that wicked people wear around their neck. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparison, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they wear pride like a necklace] or [pride is like a necklace which they flaunt]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **pride**, you could express the same idea in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they act pridefully for all to see, like someone who wears a necklace that they want everyone to see] or [they unashamedly act proud in front of everyone, like a person wearing a necklace that they want everyone to see]

A **necklace** is a type of jewelry worn around the neck in order to adorn the body and make a person look more attractive. If your readers would not be familiar with necklaces, you could use the name of something similar that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternately, if you are using footnotes, you could make a footnote explaining what a **necklace** is. Alternate translation: [a neck ornament for them]

The psalmist is speaking of **violence** as it were a **garment** that people wear. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning with a comparable expression, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [violence covers them like a garment] or [violence covers them like clothing]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **violence**, you could express the same idea in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they are proud of their violent actions and display them openly, as a person who wears a garment for all to see]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **imaginations**, you could express the same idea in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they are constantly imagining evil things in their hearts] or [they are constantly thinking about evil things in their hearts]

Here the psalmist speaks of the **heart** of a wicked person as if it were a container that could overflow with evil **imaginations** (thoughts). If it would be helpful to your readers, you could express the meaning using an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [their heart is constantly thinking of evil things to do] or [their heart is constantly imagining evil thoughts]

The psalmist is describing the mind of wicked people by association with their **heart**, which is where a person’s thoughts and intentions were viewed as coming from in Jewish culture. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [they constantly think of evil things to do] or [the imaginations of their inner being overflow]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the ideas of **evil** and **oppression**, you could express the same ideas in some other way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and wickedly speak about oppressing people]

The phrase **they speak from an elevated place** means “they speak arrogantly.” If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate that explicitly. Alternate translation: [they speak arrogantly]

Here, **mouth** and **tongue** represents “speech.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [They talk as if they are God who is in the heavens, and their speech goes through the earth]

The word translated as **in the heavens** could be translated as: (1) **in the heavens** as modeled by the ULT in which case the psalmist is describing the role or authority of God by association with the **heavens**, Alternate translation: [They talk with their mouth as if they are God who is in heaven] or [They talk as if they are in the position of God] or (2) “against the heavens” in which case the psalmist is describing God by association with the **heavens**. Alternate translation: [They set their mouth against the heavens] or [They set their mouth against God]

The psalmist is speaking of the **tongue** (words or speech) of wicked people as if it could go **through the earth**. What he means is that these wicked people go about talking wickedly (and bragging) as they live their daily lives on earth and proudly act as if they are not accountable to God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they constantly talk wickedly as if they rule the earth] or [and they walk about talking wickedly]
The term translated as **Therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [This is why]
This could mean: (1) “God’s people love the wicked people” or (2) “the wicked people return to this place”

The expression **are drained** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you must state who did the action, the context implies that people did it. Alternate translation: [and they drain the waters of a full cup]

The psalmist is speaking of listening to words as if they were drinking **water** out of a cup. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning with a simile or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and believe all that they say]
This could mean: (1) “God’s people listen gladly to the words of the wicked people” or (2) “the wicked people have plenty of food to eat and wine to drink”

The phrases **How does God know** and **is there knowledge in the Most High** mean basically the same thing. The second phrase emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and it would be good to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation rather than combining them. However, if it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine the phrases into one. Alternate translation: [How could God know?] or [Does God have knowledge?]

Here the word **they** could refer to: (1) wicked people. Alternate translation: [And those who are wicked say] or [And the wicked say] or (2) people who are righteous and obey God. Alternate translation: [And righteous people say] or [And godly people say]

Here wicked people are not asking for information but are using the question form to express that they do not think God knows or cares about the evil things they do. If you would not use the question form for this purpose in your language, you could translate these questions as statements or exclamations and communicate the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Surely God does not know what we are doing! Surely the Most High has no knowledge of it!] or [Surely God does not care about we are doing! Surely what we are doing does not matter to the Most High!]
This portion of this verse is a quotation of what the wicked people said or thought to themselves. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language.

The psalmist is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [See]

The Psalmist is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun in order to describe a group of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you could translate this word with an equivalent phrase. See how you translated the phrase **the wicked** in [73:3](../073/003.md). Alternate translation: [wicked ones]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **ease**, you could express the same idea in some other way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they are always comfortable] or [they are always carefree]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wealth**, you could express the same idea in some other way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they become increasingly wealthy]

Here the psalmist uses the word **Surely** to emphasize his strong thoughts and feelings about the certainty of what he states in this verse. Use a natural form in your language for expressing this emphasis. Alternate translation: [Certainly]

The psalmist is describing his thoughts and intentions by association with his **heart**, which Jews viewed as the center of a person’s thoughts and intentions. The expression **I have kept my heart clean** means he has intentionally kept his thoughts and intentions morally pure (free from sin). You may have an equivalent expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have kept my thoughts pure]

The psalmist is describing his actions by association with his **hands**, which he would use to do the actions. The psalmist is using the symbolic action of hand washing to declare his **innocence**. In that culture hand washing was a common practice that people did to publicly assert that they were innocent. (See Deuteronomy [21:6](../../deu/21/06.md) and Matthew [27:24](../../mat/27/24.md).) Here the psalmist is saying that he has **washed** his **hands in innocence** as a way to declare that he is guiltless. See how you translated the similar phrase in [Psalm 26:6](../026/006.md). If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and kept my actions pure to show that I am innocent] or [and kept my actions free from sin]

The expression **I have been stricken … and punished** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [For you have stricken me all of the day and punished me every morning] or [For you have afflicted me all of the day and punished me every morning]

The phrase **all of the day** is a common expression meaning “every day” or “constantly.” If this phrase does not have this meaning in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [constantly]

73.quote: אִם־אָ֭מַרְתִּי אֲסַפְּרָ֥ה כְמ֑וֹ הִנֵּ֤ה ד֭וֹר בָּנֶ֣י⁠ךָ בָגָֽדְתִּי
73.text: The psalmist is describing a hypothetical situation in order to tell his readers what would have happened if he had said the things he was thinking out loud. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a situation that could happen. Alternate translation: [If I had said, ‘I will recount such things,’ then I would have betrayed the generation of your children.]
The psalmist is using the term **behold** to emphasize what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [certainly]

The psalmist is speaking of God’s people, his spiritual children, as if they were his biological **children**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your followers] or [the people who obey you]

Here the author’s **eyes** represent his evaluation or estimation as he tried to understand why wicked people seemed to prosper and he suffered. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to me] or [to think about]

Here the plural word **sanctuaries** could: (1) refer to the Jerusalem temple, in which case the plural is intensifying the meaning. Alternate translation: [the great sanctuary of God] or [the great temple of God] (2) refer to the precincts of the Jerusalem temple. Alternate translation: [the precincts of the temple of God] or [the precincts of God’s temple]
Alternate translation: [then I understood their fate] or [then I understood what will happen to those who are wicked]
See how you translated the word **Surely** in [73:1](../073/001.md) where it is used with the same meaning.

The psalmist is speaking of the fact that God does not allow wicked people to have a secure future as if God had **set them in slippery places**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you do not give them a good future]

Here the word **you** refers to God and the word **them** refers to wicked people. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate that explicitly. Alternate translation: [Surely you, God, set wicked people in slippery places]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **destruction**, you could express the same idea in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [you cause them to be destroyed]
The psalmist is using the term **How** to focus attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you could use in your translation.

The expression **they are brought** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you must state who did the action, the context implies that “God” does it. Alternate translation: [God brings them]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **desolation**, you could express the same idea in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [God will destroy them as in a moment] or [they will be suddenly destroyed]
The phrase **as in a moment** means “suddenly” or “all at once.” If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate that explicitly. Alternate translation: [all at once]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The psalmist is using the phrases **They come to an end** and **they perish** together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [They come to an end] or [They perish]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **terrors**, you could express the same idea in another way that is natural in your language.

73.quote: כַּ⁠חֲל֥וֹם מֵ⁠הָקִ֑יץ אֲ֝דֹנָ⁠י בָּ⁠עִ֤יר ׀ צַלְמָ֬⁠ם תִּבְזֶֽה
73.text: The psalmist is comparing the short and temporary duration of a **dream**, which is over after a person **awakes**, to the fact that God will **despise** wicked people when he rouses himself to action and judges them. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the basis of this comparison or express this meaning in plain language. Alternate translation: [They will disappear as quickly as a dream disappears when a person awakes in the morning; Lord, when you act, you will cause them to disappear]
Alternate translation: [their form]

The phrases **When my heart was embittered** and **I was pierced in my kidneys** mean basically the same thing. The second phrase emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and it would be good to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation rather than combining them. However, if it would be helpful to your readers, you could connect the phrases with a word other than **and** in order to show that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [When my heart was embittered, yes, when I was pierced in my kidneys]

The psalmist is describing his inner being and thoughts by association with his **heart**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I was embittered] or [I was embittered within]
The psalmist is describing his feelings by association with his **kidneys**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language as modeled by the UST.

The phrase **I was not knowing** means “I was without knowledge” or “I was ignorant.” If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate that explicitly. Alternate translation: [and I was without knowledge] or [and I was ignorant]

The psalmist is speaking of his prior **stupid** and ignorant thinking and action toward God as if he had been behaving like an **animal**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning with a comparison, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I acted like an animal toward you] or [I acted and thought like an animal before you] or [I acted like a fool toward you]
Here the word **you** refers to God. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate that explicitly. Alternate translation: [with you, God]

The psalmist is speaking of God’s continual presence with him as if God were continually holding his **right hand**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning with a comparison, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you are constantly with me] or [you are constantly with me. It is as if you are holding me by my right hand]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **counsel**, you could express the same idea in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [You guide me by teaching me instructive things] or [You guide me by teaching me]

Here the term **glory** could refer to: (1) God’s presence in this life or after death. Alternate translation: [and afterward you will take me into your glorious presence] or [and after I die you will take me into your presence] (2) the glory or honor that God would give the psalmist in this life or after death because he had remained faithful and lived a righteous life. Alternate translation: [and afterward you will receive me with honor] or [and when I die you will receive me with honor] or [and at the end of my life you will receive me and honor me]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and afterward you will take me into your glorious presence] or [and afterward you will honor me when you receive me]

Here psalmist is implying the words “but you?” If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate that explicitly as modeled by the ULT. Alternate translation: [Whom have I in heaven but you?]

The psalmist is not asking for information but is using the question form for emphasis. If you would not use a rhetorical question for this purpose in your language, you could translate these words as a statement or an exclamation and communicate the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [There is no one I have in heaven but you!]
Alternate translation: [And with you I desire nothing on the earth]

The psalmist is referring to his entire body as if it were his **flesh**, and he is referring to his mind and/or spirit as if they were his **heart**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly or use an equivalent expression. Alternate translation: [I may become physically and emotionally weak] or [My body and my mind may fail] or [My body and my spirit may fail]

73.quote: כָּלָ֥ה שְׁאֵרִ֗⁠י וּ⁠לְבָ֫בִ֥⁠י צוּר־לְבָבִ֥⁠י וְ⁠חֶלְקִ֗⁠י אֱלֹהִ֥ים לְ⁠עוֹלָֽם
73.text: Alternate translation: [My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart forever]

The psalmist is speaking of **God** as if he were a **rock**. The term **rock** is associated with strength so by calling God **the rock of my heart**, he means that God is the strength of his heart. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning with a comparison, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but God, you are like a rock for my heart, and you are my portion forever] or [but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever]

The psalmist is using the term **behold** to bring attention to and emphasize the certainty of what he is about to say. Use a word or phrase that would communicate that meaning in your language. Alternate translation: [indeed]
Alternate translation: [you will destroy everyone who is unfaithful to you]
Alternate translation: [But for me, God’s companionship is my greatest good] or [But for me, God’s presence is my good]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **closeness**, you could express the same idea in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [being close to God is good for me] or [being near to God is good for me]

The psalmist speaks of **Yahweh** as if he were a physical place that a person could go to for **refuge**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning with a comparison, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Like a person runs to a shelter to keep them safe when they are in danger, so I have chosen to trust you to keep me safe]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **refuge**, you could express the same idea in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I trust the Lord, Yahweh, to protect me]

The phrase **in order to** marks **recount all your works** as the goal or purpose for which the psalmist **made the Lord, Yahweh** his **refuge**. Use a natural way in your language for indicating that this is the goal or purpose.
Alternate translation: [that I might make known to people all your works] or [that I may declare all your deeds]

74.text:
# Psalm 74 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 74 is a psalm of supplication or lament. It includes all the basic elements of that type of psalm except a vow of praise. (There is only the hint of a vow of praise in verse 21b.) See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Cry for help (1–3)
2. Description of troubles (4–9)
3. Cry for help (10–11)
4. Statement of trust (12–17)
5. Petition (18–23)

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a “maskil.” See the discussion of that term in the introduction to Psalms.

## Translation Issues in this Psalm

### Imperatives

Throughout this psalm, the psalmist is requesting things from Yahweh by using an imperative form which may sound like a command in your language. If this would be impolite in your language, then use a form that would be more appropriate for addressing Yahweh with a request.

### Parallelisms

Parallelisms arise when two phrases occur together which mean the same thing. The second phrase emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea using different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine the phrases and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one and not saying something additional. See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing.

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a **maskil**. Since the meaning of this word is not certain, you may wish to represent it in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language.

74.quote: לָ⁠מָ֣ה אֱ֭לֹהִים זָנַ֣חְתָּ לָ⁠נֶ֑צַח יֶעְשַׁ֥ן אַ֝פְּ⁠ךָ֗ בְּ⁠צֹ֣אן מַרְעִיתֶֽ⁠ךָ
74.text: Asaph is using the question form to express his anguish at God’s anger toward his people. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [God, you have rejected us forever! Your nose should not smoke against the flock of your pasture.]

Asaph is using **does your nose smoke** as a common expression of the culture to mean that God is angry. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Why are you angry]

Here Asaph is speaking of God’s people as if they were **the flock** of a shepherd, and of God as if he were a shepherd who cares for them in **your pasture**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [against the people you care for]

Asaph is using the possessive form to describe a **flock** that is associated with a **pasture**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express the idea in another way. Alternate translation: [against the flock that you pasture]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. See the Introduction to this Psalm for more information on how to translate the imperative here and throughout this Psalm. Alternate translation: [Please remember your congregation]

Asaph is using this possessive form to mean that the tribe itself is what God inherited. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the tribe that is your inheritance]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **inheritance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the tribe that you inherited] or [the people whom you have made your own]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that a sentence in many languages would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if this would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [remember this Mount Zion on which you have dwelt]

The psalmist speaks of God as if he were a person with **feet** which he could **Lift up** and come and see the ruined temple in Jerusalem. The phrase **Lift up your feet** is probably also indicating that the psalmist wants God to not only take notice but also to take notice quickly. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Come and see the perpetual ruins] or [Please do not delay any longer. Please pay attention to these perpetual ruins]

Here and other places in this psalm, **the holy place** refers to the Temple in Jerusalem that had been destroyed. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate that explicitly as modeled by the UST.

Here Asaph is speaking of the **adversaries** as if they were wild animals that **roared**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Your adversaries shouted loudly]

Setting up **signs** was a symbolic action by which the conquerors signified their victory over those conquered. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. The phrase **they have set up their signs as signs** could mean: (1) that God’s adversaries had set up their military banners as signs in the Temple. Alternate translation: [they have set up their banners as signs] or [they have set up their banners as a sign of their conquest] or (2) that God’s adversaries had set up items of worship and symbols related to their false religion. Alternate translation: [they have set up symbols and items for their pagan worship] or [they have set up idolatrous symbols and items of false worship]

The expression **It was known** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [They appeared]

The point of this comparison is that just as a woodsman swings **axes** to cut down trees **in a thicket**, so the enemies swung their weapons to destroy the carvings of the temple. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like a woodsman chopping down trees in a forest]

Here the words **And now** mark a shift from describing what the enemies did in the past to what they are doing in the present. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [Now]
The pronoun **its** refers to the holy place. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the carvings of the holy place]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. For more information on translating parallelisms, see the Introduction to this Psalm. Alternate translation: [They completely burned down and desecrated the place where you dwell]
The pronoun **They** refers to the enemies. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The enemies sent]

Asaph is using the term **name** to represent God’s presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the place called by your name by bringing it] or [the dwelling where you are present by bringing it]

Asaph is using the possessive form to describe a **dwelling** that is characterized by God’s **name**, that is, by his presence. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express the idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the dwelling place dedicated to you by burning it]

The phrase **They said in their heart** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. Alternate translation: [They thought to themselves]
Both occurrences of the pronoun **They** refer to the enemies. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The enemies said in their heart]

Asaph is using **in their heart** as a common expression of the culture to mean that the enemies thought this to themselves. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [within themselves]

Asaph is using this possessive form to mean the places that are dedicated to **God** for worship. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the places where people gather to worship God]

Here the phrase **our signs** could refer to: (1) signs that God’s prophets gave. Alternate translation: [We do not see any prophetic signs for us] or [We do not see any signs given to us from a prophet] or (2) the military banners and symbols used by the Israelite army which represented their army. Alternate translation: [We no longer see any of our military banners] or (3) the Jewish festivals and religious observances which were the outward signs of their religion. Alternate translation: [We no longer see any signs of our religion] or [All our sacred observances are gone] or [All our sacred symbols are gone]

74.quote: עַד־מָתַ֣י אֱ֭לֹהִים יְחָ֣רֶף צָ֑ר יְנָ֘אֵ֤ץ אוֹיֵ֖ב שִׁמְ⁠ךָ֣ לָ⁠נֶֽצַח
74.text: Asaph is using the question form to express his impatient plea for God to intervene. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or exclamations. Alternate translation: [God, the adversary has reproached you long enough! The enemy should not despise your name forever.]

Asaph is using the term **name** to represent God’s reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your reputation]

Asaph is using the question form to protest God’s inaction. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You should not hold back your hand, even your right hand!]

Asaph is using **hold back your hand** as a common expression of the culture to mean that God is withholding his action and not intervening. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [do you refrain from acting with your great power]

Here, **your hand, even your right hand** represents God’s power to act. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your power, even your great strength]

Here, **your bosom** represents concealment and inaction, as though God were keeping his hand tucked inside his robe instead of stretching it out to act. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your hiding place]

Asaph uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between the despair he has expressed about the destruction of the temple and his confidence in God as king. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Yet God is my king]
Asaph uses the pronoun **my** instead of “our” to express a personal declaration of trust. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [is my king whom I trust]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvations**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [mighty things to save his people]

Asaph is stating the pronoun **You** separately, even though the verb translated as **you divided** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that it was God himself who performed this mighty act. If it would be natural in your language to use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation, or you could express this emphasis in a different way. See how you as a team decide to translate this phrase and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [It was you who divided]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because you are strong]

Here Asaph is speaking of the forces of chaos as if they were **sea monsters** whose **heads** God crushed. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the powers of the chaotic waters]

Here Asaph is speaking of the forces of chaos as if they were a great sea creature called **Leviathan**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the great chaos creature]

Here Asaph is speaking of God’s defeat of Leviathan as if God had given **him as food** to people, meaning that God completely destroyed this power. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you left his remains for the people]

Here, **split open spring and wadi** refers to Yahweh breaking open the ground and causing springs and streams to flow. Alternate translation: [you caused springs and streams to flow out of the ground]

Asaph is referring to all of time by naming two extremes, **the day** and **the night**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [All hours of the day and night are also]

Here the word **also** connects two parallel statements, emphasizing that both the day and the night belong to God. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [even]

Asaph is referring to all celestial light by naming two components, **the light and the sun**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [every source of light in the sky]

Asaph is using this possessive form to mean the boundaries that mark the extent of **the earth**. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the boundaries that define the earth]

Asaph is referring to all the seasons of the year by naming two extremes, **summer and winter**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all the seasons of the year]

Here the words **Remember this** mark a shift from praising God’s mighty acts back to petitioning him for help. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [Consider this]

Even though Asaph is addressing God directly, he is speaking of him in the third person as **Yahweh** to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [the enemy has reproached you, Yahweh]

Asaph is using the term **name** to represent God’s reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [has despised your reputation]

Asaph is using the possessive form to describe the **life** that belongs to the people he calls a **dove**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express the idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the lives of your people whom you cherish]

Here Asaph is speaking of God’s people as if they were a vulnerable **dove**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your defenseless people]

Here Asaph is speaking of the enemy nation as if it were a wild **beast** that would devour its prey. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to the cruel enemy]

Asaph is using the adjective **poor** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [your poor people]

The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [because violent places fill the dark places of the land]

Asaph is using the possessive form to describe **pastures** that are characterized by **violence**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this purpose, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [violent places]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **violence**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [violent deeds]

Here Asaph is speaking of places of oppression and danger as if they were **dark places**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the dangerous places of the land]

Asaph is using this possessive form to mean the places in **the land** that are dark, that is, dangerous. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the dark places that are in the land]

Asaph is using the adjective **weak** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the weak person]

The expression **ashamed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [feeling shame]

Asaph is using the adjectives **poor** and **needy** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [those who are poor and needy]

Here the words **Arise, God** mark a shift to a final urgent appeal for God to act. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [Take action, God]

Here Asaph is speaking of God as if he were a litigant who would **plead** a legal **case** in court. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Contend for yourself]

Asaph is using this possessive form to mean the case that is brought against God, that is, the insults directed at him. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the case against you]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **reproach**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how the fool reproaches you]
Asaph is using this possessive form to mean the reproach that comes from **the fool**. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the way the fool reproaches you]

Here, **the voice of your adversaries** represents what the adversaries are saying. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the words of your adversaries]

Asaph is using this possessive form to mean the voice that comes from **your adversaries**. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [what your adversaries are saying]

Asaph is using this possessive form to mean the uproar that comes from **the ones rising against** God. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the noise that your opponents make]

75.text:
# Psalm 75 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

1. Superscription
2. Community thanksgiving (1)
3. God’s promise of righteous judgment (2–5)
4. Declaration that God alone is judge (6–8)
5. Psalmist’s vow to praise (9)
6. God’s promise to judge (10)

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 75 is a psalm of Asaph that celebrates God as the righteous judge of all the earth.

1. Purpose: to declare that God will judge the earth with equity
2. Content: The psalm moves between different speakers—the community, God himself, and the psalmist—all affirming that God is the judge who humbles the wicked and exalts the righteous.
3. Message: God alone has the authority to judge, and he will do so at the appointed time.

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

1. The psalm contains multiple speakers. Verse 1 is the community speaking. Verses 2–5 (and possibly continuing through verse 8) are God speaking. Verse 9 is the psalmist (Asaph) speaking. Verse 10 contains God’s words in quotation marks.
2. The image of the “horn” appears in verses 4, 5, and 10, representing power, pride, or strength.
3. The image of God’s judgment as a cup of wine appears in verse 8, a common biblical image.

See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/writing-poetry]]

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

The psalmist is repeating the phrase **We give thanks** in order to intensify the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [We thank you so very much]

By **your name is near**, the psalmist means that God is present and accessible to his people. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [you are present with us] or [you are close to us]
The psalmist is using the term **name** to represent God himself and his presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your presence]
The pronoun **they** refers to the people of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state this explicitly. Alternate translation: [we your people recount]

75.quote: כִּ֭י אֶקַּ֣ח מוֹעֵ֑ד אֲ֝נִ֗י מֵישָׁרִ֥ים אֶשְׁפֹּֽט
75.text: This is the beginning of what God said. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of God. Alternate translation: [God said, “When I take the appointed time, I will judge with equity]

God is stating the pronoun **I** twice, even though the verb already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he himself is the one speaking and acting. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the emphasis here. Alternate translation: [I myself will judge]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **equity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what is right] or [uprightly]

The psalmist is speaking of the earth and its inhabitants as if they were **melting**. He means that they are overcome with fear and instability in the presence of God’s judgment. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The earth and all its inhabitants are trembling with fear]

God is stating the pronoun **I** explicitly, even though the verb already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he himself is the one who establishes the earth’s foundations. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the emphasis here. Alternate translation: [I myself established]

The psalmist is speaking of the earth as if it were a building with **pillars** to support it. This image represents the stability that God provides and maintains for the earth. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [made it stable] or [keep it stable]

David is using the adjective **boasters** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [people who boast]

The psalmist is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [wicked people]

The psalmist is speaking of arrogant or defiant people as if they were to physically **lift up a horn** like an animal displaying strength. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [behave arrogantly] or [act defiantly]

The psalmist is speaking of **to the height** as if it were a physical elevation to which one could **lift up** a **horn**. This intensifies the image of arrogance that the horn metaphor conveys. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [act with extreme arrogance]

Here, **neck** represents speaking with an arrogant attitude. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [speak arrogantly]

The psalmist is referring to all directions on earth by naming two (or three) cardinal points, **the east**, **the west**, and **the wilderness** (the south). The word translated **comes lifting up** could possibly mean “mountains” which would refer to the north. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from any direction comes lifting up]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **lifting up**, you could express the same idea with a verb such as “lift” or “exalt.” Alternate translation: [to lift someone up]

The implication is that God brings low the proud and wicked, and lifts up the humble and righteous. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [he humbles this proud person, and he exalts this humble person] or [he brings down the arrogant, and he raises up the lowly]
