The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh’s judgment as if it were **a cup** that Yahweh held **in** his **hand** and forced people to drink. This is a common biblical image. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s judgment is like a cup in his hand]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that **wine** that **foams** and is **a full mixture** refers to wine mixed with spices, making it very strong and intoxicating, representing the full strength of God’s judgment. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the wine foams, full of spices]

The psalmist is speaking of punishment as if it were a cup of wine and God’s enemies **will drain** even **its dregs**, the sediment at the bottom. He means that they will experience God’s judgment completely, even to its most severe and bitter aspects. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they will experience the punishment fully, even its worst parts]
See how you translated the similar expression in [verse 4](../075/004.md).

75.quote: וַ֭⁠אֲנִי אַגִּ֣יד לְ⁠עֹלָ֑ם אֲ֝זַמְּרָ֗ה לֵ⁠אלֹהֵ֥י יַעֲקֹֽב
75.text: This is the beginning of what the psalmist said. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of the psalmist. Alternate translation: [But as for me, I will declare to eternity; I will sing praise to the God of Jacob]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **I** twice for emphasis. He is doing that to emphasize his personal commitment and determination, in contrast to the wicked. If a speaker of your language would repeat a pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that meaning here. Alternate translation: [But as for me, I will declare]

Here, **Jacob** represents the people of Israel, the descendants of Jacob. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to the God of the people of Israel] or [to the God of the Israelites]

75.quote: וְ⁠כָל־קַרְנֵ֣י רְשָׁעִ֣ים אֲגַדֵּ֑עַ תְּ֝רוֹמַ֗מְנָה קַֽרְנ֥וֹת צַדִּֽיק
75.text: This is the beginning of what God said. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of God. Alternate translation: [God says, “And all the horns of the wicked I will cut off; the horns of the righteous will be lifted up.”]

The psalmist is speaking of power and strength as if they were **horns**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the power of the wicked … the power of the righteous]
See how you translated the similar expression in [verse 4](../075/004.md).

The psalmist is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [righteous people]

The expression **will be lifted up** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [I will lift up] or [God will lift up]

76.text:
# Psalm 76 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

1. Superscription
2. God is known in Zion (1–3)
3. God’s judgment destroys the enemies (4–6)
4. God’s judgment causes fear (7–9)
5. Call to worship and vow to God (10–12)

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 76 is a psalm of Asaph that celebrates God’s victory over the enemies of his people and his dwelling in Zion.

1. Purpose: to praise God for his victory and to warn others to fear him
2. Content: The psalm describes God’s power in breaking the weapons of war and striking down the enemies who attacked Jerusalem. It affirms God’s sovereignty over all kings and leaders.
3. Message: God is the supreme judge and warrior who defends his people and dwells among them.

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

### Images of War

The psalm uses several images related to war and judgment, such as “flames of the bow” (arrows), “mountains of prey” (victory), and “gird on wrath” (using wrath as a weapon).

### God’s Names and Titles

The psalm uses “God of Jacob” (v6), “Fear” (or “Awesome One”, v11), and refers to his dwelling in “Salem” and “Zion” (v2).

### Idioms

There are idioms like “stout of heart” (brave) and “found not their hands” (helpless).

See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/writing-poetry]]

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

76.quote: נוֹדָ֣ע בִּֽ⁠יהוּדָ֣ה אֱלֹהִ֑ים בְּ֝⁠יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל גָּד֥וֹל שְׁמֽ⁠וֹ
76.text: These lines mean basically the same thing. Translate according to your team’s decision on parallelism. See the Introduction to Psalms for more information.

The expression **is known** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people know God] or [God has revealed himself]

The psalmist is using the term **name** to represent who God is or to refer to God’s reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his reputation] or [he himself]
These lines mean basically the same thing. Translate according to your team’s decision on parallelism. See the Introduction to Psalms for more information.
The word **Salem** is the name of a city. This is an ancient name for Jerusalem.

The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a person who had an **abode** and a **dwelling place** in Salem and Zion. This represents Yahweh’s special presence among his people in those locations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And his home is in Salem, and where he lives] or [And he is present in Salem, and his presence]
The word **Zion** is the name of a mountain in Jerusalem.

76.quote: שָׁ֭מָּ⁠ה שִׁבַּ֣ר רִשְׁפֵי־קָ֑שֶׁת מָגֵ֬ן וְ⁠חֶ֖רֶב וּ⁠מִלְחָמָ֣ה
76.text: The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh providing peace for his people as if he were physically breaking weapons. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He provides peace by stopping all the enemies’ attacks]

The psalmist is speaking of arrows as if they were **flames of the bow**. This could be because arrows move swiftly like lightning or because they were tipped with fire. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the arrows of the bow]

The psalmist uses some weapons (**the shield and the sword**) to represent all weapons of war and then further uses **the battle** as a summary representing the weapons used in battle. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [shields and swords and all other weapons of war]

The terms **shining** and **majestic** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [are brilliantly glorious] or [are radiant with glory]

The psalmist is speaking of God as if he were **shining** with radiant light. If it would be helpful for your readers, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [are glorious] or [are radiant]

The psalmist is speaking of the mountains as if they were places where God had hunted down his enemies like **prey**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this as a comparison or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the mountains where you defeated your enemies] or [like the mountains of your victory]

The psalmist is using **stout of heart** as a common expression of his culture to mean “brave” or “courageous.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The courageous] or [The brave warriors]

The expression **were plundered** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [lost all their possessions] or [had their possessions taken away]

The psalmist is referring to death in a polite way by using the phrase **slept their sleep**. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [they died] or [they passed away]

The psalmist is using **found not their hands** as a common expression of his culture to mean “were unable to use their strength or weapons.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and … could not lift their hands to fight] or [and … were helpless]

The expression **At your rebuke** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [When you rebuked them]

The psalmist is not using this possessive form **God of Jacob** to indicate that Jacob possessed or controlled God. Rather, the psalmist is using these words to indicate that God is the God whom Jacob worshiped. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [God whom Jacob worshiped]

The psalmist is using **rider and horse** to represent all the military forces of the enemy. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [chariots and horses] or [riders and their horses]

The psalmist is speaking of **fell deeply asleep** as if dying were falling into a deep sleep. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [fell down dead] or [died]

The psalmist is repeating the pronoun **You** in order to intensify the emphasis on God himself. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [You yourself are] or [Truly you are]

The expression **you are to be feared** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [you are fearsome] or [people must fear you]

The psalmist is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [and no one can stand before your face from the time of your nose!] or [and no one is able to stand before your face when your nose begins to burn!]

The psalmist is using **stand before your face** as a common expression of the culture to mean “withstand your judgment” or “endure your presence.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [can survive in your presence] or [can endure your anger]

The psalmist is using the phrase **from the time of your nose** as a common expression of the culture to mean “when you are angry.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when you are angry] or [when your anger flares up]

Here, **heaven** represents the place where God dwells. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [From the sky] or [From your dwelling place]

The expression **caused judgment to be heard** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [you proclaimed judgment] or [you announced your judgment]

Here, **earth** represents the people who live on the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people of the earth were afraid and were quiet] or [everyone on earth feared and were quiet]

The psalmist is using **arose to judgment** as a common expression of his culture to mean “began to judge” or “decided to act in judgment.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when … began to judge] or [when …took action to judge]

The psalmist is speaking of **wrath** as if it were a living thing that could **praise** God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [people’s anger will result in praise to you] or [you will be praised because of how you respond to human anger]

The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he will **gird on** the remainder of wrath like a belt or weapon. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you will wear like a belt] or [you will use like a weapon]

The implication is that the people should fulfill the vows they make to God by doing what they promised. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Make vows to Yahweh your God and fulfill them]

The implication is that **all who are around him** refers to the people of the nations surrounding Israel. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [all the people of the surrounding nations]

Here, **the Fear** represents God, the one who is to be feared. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to the One who is to be feared] or [to the Awesome One]

Here the psalmist is speaking of God as if he were using a tool and **cuts off the spirit of princes**. He means that God humbles or destroys them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He humbles] or [He destroys]

Here, **spirit** represents the courage or pride of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the courage of] or [the pride of]

The expression **is to be feared by the kings of the earth** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the kings of the earth fear him] or [he causes the kings of the earth to fear him]

77.text:
# Psalm 77 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

1. Superscription
2. Lament and sleepless searching (1–6)
3. Questions about God’s favor (7–10)
4. Remembering Yah’s deeds (11–15)
5. God’s power over the waters and leading his people (16–20)

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 77 is a psalm of Asaph in which the psalmist moves from intense distress and questioning to renewed confidence by remembering God’s past saving actions.

1. Purpose: to express a lament and then to renew trust in God by recalling his mighty deeds.
2. Content: The psalm begins with the psalmist crying out in trouble and asking a series of questions about whether God has rejected him. It then turns to remembrance of God’s works and ends with vivid storm-and-sea imagery that recalls God leading his people.
3. Message: When God seems absent, the psalmist responds by remembering who God is and what he has done for his people.

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

1. Rhetorical questions: Verses 7–9 contain a series of questions that function primarily to express grief and uncertainty, not to request information.
2. Figurative language for inner life: The psalm uses terms like “soul,” “heart,” and “spirit” to describe a person’s internal experience.
3. Body-part imagery for God’s power: Expressions like “right hand” and “arm” refer to God’s power and ability to act.
4. Nature imagery: The psalm personifies waters, clouds, skies, and the earth, and uses war/storm imagery such as “arrows” for lightning.
5. Key names and titles: The psalm includes the divine name “Yah,” the title “the Most High,” and references to Jacob, Joseph, Moses, and Aaron.
6. Selah: The term “Selah” appears in verses 3, 9, and 15 as a likely musical direction.

See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/writing-poetry]]

**For the chief musician** is an instruction about who should lead people in singing or playing music with this psalm. This could refer to the person in charge of music for temple worship. If your readers would not be familiar with this role, you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the worship leader]
See how you translated the expression “on Jeduthun” in the superscription to Psalm 39.

Asaph is repeating the expression **my voice is to God** in order to intensify his expression of crying out to God. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [I earnestly cry out to God] or [I cry out with my voice again and again to God]

Here, **My voice** represents Asaph’s act of calling out to God in prayer. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [My prayer]

Asaph is using the term **day** to refer to a specific time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [At the time of my trouble] or [When I was in trouble]

Here, **my hand was stretched out** was a symbolic action by which Asaph showed his persistent prayer and pleading to God. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [I lifted my hands to God in continual prayer]

Asaph is using one part of himself, his **soul**, to represent all of him in his refusal of comfort. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I refused to be comforted]

77.quote: אֶזְכְּרָ֣ה אֱלֹהִ֣ים וְ⁠אֶֽהֱמָיָ֑ה אָשִׂ֓יחָה ׀ וְ⁠תִתְעַטֵּ֖ף רוּחִ֣⁠י
77.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [I remembered God and groaned; yes, my spirit grew faint as I meditated]

Here, **spirit** represents Asaph’s inner strength or vitality. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I felt weak] or [and I became exhausted]

Asaph is speaking of God preventing him from sleeping as if God **held the lids of my eyes** open. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You prevented me from sleeping] or [You kept me awake]

These two phrases **days from antiquity** and **years of long ago** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [times long, long ago]

Here, **days** represents a particular period of time in the past. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the time long ago] or [the era of antiquity]

Asaph is speaking of **my heart** as if it were the place where thinking and reflection occur. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I meditate within myself] or [I reflect deeply]

Asaph is using one part of a person, his **spirit**, to mean all of him in the act of searching for understanding. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I search diligently]

77.quote: הַֽ֭⁠לְ⁠עוֹלָמִים יִזְנַ֥ח ׀ אֲדֹנָ֑⁠י וְ⁠לֹֽא־יֹסִ֖יף לִ⁠רְצ֣וֹת עֽוֹד
77.text: Asaph is using the question form to express his distress and uncertainty. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [The Lord will surely not reject me forever! He will show me favor again!] or [I am afraid that the Lord will reject me forever and will never again show me favor.]

Asaph is using **again add** as a common expression to mean “continue.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And will he not continue to show favor] or [And will he not ever show favor]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **favor**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [will he … treat me favorably] or [will he … be favorable toward me]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [his faithfulness to his covenant] or [his faithful commitment to his covenant]

Asaph is using **for generation and generation** as a common expression of his culture to mean “throughout all generations” or “forever.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [throughout all generations]

77.quote: הֶ⁠אָפֵ֣ס לָ⁠נֶ֣צַח חַסְדּ֑⁠וֹ גָּ֥מַר אֹ֝֗מֶר לְ⁠דֹ֣ר וָ⁠דֹֽר
77.text: Asaph is using the question form to express his deep sorrow and fear that God has abandoned him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [Your covenant faithfulness must be gone forever! Your promise must have failed forever!] or [Surely your covenant faithfulness is gone forever. Surely your promise has failed forever.]

77.quote: הֲ⁠שָׁכַ֣ח חַנּ֣וֹת אֵ֑ל אִם־קָפַ֥ץ בְּ֝⁠אַ֗ף רַחֲמָ֥י⁠ו
77.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Has God forgotten to be gracious and shut up his compassions in his nose]

Asaph speaks of anger as if it were a person shutting a door to keep another person, compassion, from coming out. Alternate translation: [has God stopped showing us compassion because he is angry with us]

77.quote: הֲ⁠שָׁכַ֣ח חַנּ֣וֹת אֵ֑ל אִם־קָפַ֥ץ בְּ֝⁠אַ֗ף רַחֲמָ֥י⁠ו סֶֽלָה
77.text: Asaph is using the question form to express his anguish and doubt, not to seek information. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [God has forgotten to be gracious. He has shut off his compassion in anger.] or [Surely God has not forgotten to be gracious! Surely his anger has not shut off his compassion!]

Asaph is speaking of God’s **compassions** as if they were something physical that his anger could **shut up**, like closing a door or stopping a flow. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [has his anger caused him to withhold his compassion] or [has he withheld his compassion because of his anger]
Here, **nose** represents anger. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in his anger]
This could mean: (1) Asaph was speaking to himself or (2) Asaph was speaking to Yahweh. Alternate translation: [And I said to myself] or [And I said to Yahweh]

Asaph is speaking of his great distress as if it were a physical **wounding**. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [This is my great distress] or [This is what afflicts me]

Here, **the right hand** represents the power of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the power] or [the strength]

Here, **from antiquity** represents the distant past when God did his remarkable deeds. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the wonders you did long ago] or [your wonderful deeds in ancient times]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wonder**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the wonderful things that you did long ago]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [And I will ponder and meditate on all your deeds]

Asaph is speaking of God’s manner of acting as if it were a **way** or path that he travels. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [God, the manner in which you act is holy] or [God, everything you do is holy]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **holiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [is a holy way] or [is a way that is holy]

Asaph is using the question form to emphasize that no god compares to the true God. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [no god is great like God] or [there is no god as great as God!]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how strong you are] or [how powerfully you act]

Here, **arm** represents God’s power and ability to rescue. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [by your power] or [with your mighty strength]

Asaph is speaking of the later Israelites as if they were actually the **sons of Jacob and Joseph**. He means that they are the descendants of these ancestors. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the descendants of Jacob and Joseph] or [the people descended from Jacob and Joseph]

Asaph is repeating the phrase **the waters saw you** in order to intensify his expression of the idea it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [The waters surely saw you, God]

77.quote: רָ֘א֤וּ⁠ךָ מַּ֨יִם ׀ אֱֽלֹהִ֗ים רָא֣וּ⁠ךָ מַּ֣יִם יָחִ֑ילוּ אַ֝֗ף יִרְגְּז֥וּ תְהֹמֽוֹת
77.text: Starting in this verse and extending through verse 19, Asaph is speaking of God’s powerful actions during the exodus as if they were a storm, with **thunder** representing God’s voice, **arrows** and **lightning** representing God’s power striking out, and **the waters** and **the earth** reacting in fear by trembling. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express these images with a comparison or state the meaning plainly.

Asaph is speaking of **the waters** as if they were living things that could see and respond with fear. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [When you, God, came to the waters, they moved back in fear] or [The waters moved away from you, God, as if they saw you]

These two phrases, **they trembled** and **the depths shook**, mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [and they trembled, even the depths shook]

By **gave a sound**, Asaph means that the skies thundered. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the skies thundered]

Asaph is speaking of lightning bolts as if they were **arrows** that God shot. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your lightning bolts also flashed in all directions] or [you also shot lightning across the sky]

Asaph is speaking of the sound of God’s thunder as if it were **in the whirlwind** and as if God’s voice or presence were speaking from within the storm. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Your voice thundered from the whirlwind] or [You spoke with thundering power in the storm]

The terms **trembled** and **shook** mean similar things. Asaph is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [shook violently] or [quaked greatly]

Asaph is speaking of God’s actions and guidance as if they were a **way** and **path** that he traveled. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Your deeds were done in the sea and your works] or [You acted in the sea, and you worked]

These two phrases, **Your way went through the sea** and **your path through many waters**, mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Your way went through the sea, yes, your path went through many waters]

Asaph is speaking of God as if he were a person who could leave **footprints** when walking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but no trace of your presence could be seen] or [but there was no sign of where you had been]

The expression **your footprints were not discerned** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [but no one could discern your footprints] or [but your footprints could not be seen]

The point of this comparison is that just as a shepherd leads and cares for **a flock**, so God led and cared for his people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as a shepherd leads a flock] or [with the care and guidance of a shepherd]

Here, **hand** represents agency and leadership. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [through the leadership of Moses and Aaron] or [by means of Moses and Aaron]

78.text:
# Psalm 78 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 78 is a historical wisdom psalm—a maskil—of Asaph. It recounts Israel’s history from the exodus to the reign of David, teaching each generation to trust God and to not repeat the failures of the past. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/wise]])

1. Call to hear and teach the next generation (1–8)
2. Ephraim’s failure and Israel’s forgetfulness (9–11)
3. God’s wonders in Egypt and the wilderness (12–16)
4. Rebellion in the wilderness and God’s provision (17–31)
5. Continued sin and God’s compassion (32–39)
6. Recounting the plagues and the exodus (40–55)
7. Rebellion in the land and God’s judgment (56–64)
8. God’s renewal: choosing Judah, Zion, and David (65–72)

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a “maskil.” See the discussion of that term in the introduction to Psalms.

## About the Psalm

Psalm 78 is the second longest psalm in the Psalter (after Psalm 119). It belongs to the Asaph collection (Psalms 73–83) and follows a pattern of historical recitation similar to [Psalm 15](../psa/015/001.md), [Psalm 16](../psa/016/001.md), and [Nehemiah 9](../neh/09/01.md). The psalm opens with a didactic framework (verses 1–8) in which Asaph calls his audience to hear a “parable” and “riddles from antiquity.” He establishes the purpose of the recitation: each generation must pass on the knowledge of God’s deeds to the next, so that future generations will trust God and keep his commandments [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/commandments]] rather than repeating the pattern of rebellion.

The historical narrative unfolds in two main cycles. The first cycle (verses 9–39) moves from Ephraim’s failure through the exodus, God’s provision of water, [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/manna]] and quail, the people’s rebellious demands, God’s judgment, and then his compassion. The second cycle (verses 40–64) returns to the plagues in Egypt, recounts the exodus and conquest, and then describes Israel’s idolatry in the land, culminating in God’s abandonment of Shiloh and the capture of the ark. The psalm concludes (verses 65–72) with God choosing Judah, Zion, and David as shepherd-king over his people.

The historical events alluded to include the exodus and sea crossing ([Exodus 14](../exo/14/01.md)), the wilderness provision of water, manna, and quail ([Exodus 16–17](../exo/16/01.md), [Numbers 11](../num/11/01.md)), the plagues of Egypt ([Exodus 7–12](../exo/07/01.md)), the conquest of Canaan ([Joshua 13–21](../jos/13/01.md)), the capture of the ark at Shiloh ([1 Samuel 4](../1sa/04/01.md)), and God’s choice of David ([2 Samuel 5–7](../2sa/05/01.md)).

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

### God’s “nose” as an idiom for anger

The Hebrew word for “nose” is used throughout the psalm to represent God’s anger (verses 21, 31, 38, 49, 50). This is a common Hebrew idiom based on the physical signs of anger (flared nostrils, heavy breathing). Translators should be aware of this recurring pattern and handle it consistently. See the notes on individual verses for guidance.

### Anthropomorphism in verse 65

Verse 65 describes Yahweh awakening “as one sleeping” and “as a mighty man shouting from wine.” This portrays God as having been inactive during the period of judgment, then suddenly rousing himself to action. These comparisons convey sudden, vigorous action after a period of apparent inactivity, not that God was literally asleep or intoxicated.
See how you translated a similar introduction in [Psalms 49:1–4](../049/001.md).

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a **maskil**. Since the meaning of this word is not certain, you may wish to represent it in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language. See the discussion of that term in the Introduction to Psalms.

78.quote: הַאֲזִ֣ינָ⁠ה עַ֭מִּ⁠י תּוֹרָתִ֑⁠י הַטּ֥וּ אָ֝זְנְ⁠כֶ֗ם לְ⁠אִמְרֵי־פִֽ⁠י
78.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine the phrases and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how your team has decided to translate parallel phrases in the Psalms and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Hear my teaching, my people; yes, listen to the words of my mouth]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **teaching**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Listen to what I teach you]

Asaph is using this possessive form **my people** to indicate that he is addressing the Israelites as a leader or teacher among them, not to indicate that they belong to him personally. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [fellow Israelites] or [people of Israel]

Asaph is speaking of paying careful attention to his teaching as if his audience could physically **incline** their **ears** toward him in order to listen better. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [pay close attention] or [listen carefully]

Here, **the words of my mouth** represents what a person says. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to what I say]

78.quote: אֶפְתְּחָ֣ה בְ⁠מָשָׁ֣ל פִּ֑⁠י אַבִּ֥יעָה חִ֝יד֗וֹת מִנִּי־קֶֽדֶם
78.text: See the note on [78:1](../078/001.md) or in the Introduction to the Psalms for more information on translating parallelisms. Alternate translation: [I will open my mouth in parables, yes, I will sing about hidden things from the past]

Asaph is using **I will open my mouth** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I will speak” or “I will begin to teach.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will speak] or [I will begin to teach]

A **parable** is a type of teaching that uses comparisons, stories, or wise sayings to communicate deeper truths. If your readers would not be familiar with this concept, you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [in wise sayings] or [in instructive stories]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **parables** and **riddles**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [my mouth in symbolic sayings; I will pour out what is difficult to understand from antiquity] or [my mouth by speaking metaphorically; I will pour out enigmatic sayings from antiquity]

Asaph is speaking of sharing wisdom as if he were **pouring out riddles** like liquid from a container. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will utter riddles] or [I will proclaim mysteries]

The terms **heard** and **learned** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [These are things that we know well, things]

Asaph is speaking of earlier generations of Israelites as if they were **fathers**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that our forefathers] or [that those who came before us]

Asaph is emphasizing a positive meaning by using a negative word, **not**, together with a mild expression that is the opposite of the intended meaning. If it would be helpful in your language, you could emphasize the positive meaning in a strong way. Alternate translation: [We will certainly tell these things to their descendants]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **praises**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [about the praiseworthy deeds of Yahweh]

The phrase **his strength, and his wonders** expresses a single idea. The word **strength** tells more about **wonders**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [his powerful wonders] or [the mighty miracles]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **testimony** and **law**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [what he decreed and commanded] or [his requirements and commands]

Here, **Jacob** and **Israel** represent all the descendants of the patriarch Jacob, the Israelite nation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [among the people of Jacob and … a law among the people of Israel] or [among the descendants of Jacob and … a law among the descendants of Israel]

**So that** marks the rest of verses 6–8 as the goal or purpose of verse five. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [He commanded this in order that the generation to come]

78.quote: לְמַ֤עַן יֵדְע֨וּ ׀ דּ֣וֹר אַ֭חֲרוֹן בָּנִ֣ים יִוָּלֵ֑דוּ
78.text: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [so that the generation to come might know his decrees, and so that the children not yet born might also know them]

The psalmist is using **rise up** as a common expression of the culture to mean “take action” or “come along.” He does not mean that the children will literally stand up. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they in their turn will tell] or [and they will then tell]

The psalmist is speaking of **confidence** as if it were something that could be physically **placed** in a secure location. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And they would trust in God] or [And they would rely on God]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **confidence**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And they would hope in God] or [And they would confidently trust in God]

The terms **stubborn** and **rebellious** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [a very obstinate generation] or [an extremely defiant generation]

Here, **heart** represents the inner disposition and loyalty of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who were not inwardly loyal] or [whose inner disposition was not right]

Here, **spirit** represents the inner person or will. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they were not committed and faithful to God]

The psalmist is using **turned back on the day of battle** as a common expression of the culture to mean “retreated in battle” or “fled when they should have fought.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [fled when they should have fought] or [retreated instead of fighting]

The psalmist is using the term **day** to refer to a specific time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when it was time to fight] or [at the time of battle]

78.quote: לֹ֣א שָׁ֭מְרוּ בְּרִ֣ית אֱלֹהִ֑ים וּ֝⁠בְ⁠תוֹרָת֗⁠וֹ מֵאֲנ֥וּ לָ⁠לֶֽכֶת
78.text: See the note on [78:1](../078/001.md) or the Introduction to the Psalms for more information on how to translate parallelisms. Alternate translation: [They did not keep the covenant with God; indeed, they refused to obey his law]

The psalmist is using this possessive form, **the covenant of God**, to mean the covenant that God had made with the Israelites. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the covenant that God had made with them] or [God’s covenant]

The psalmist is speaking of obeying God’s law as if it were a path one could **walk** on. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they refused to obey his law]

The psalmist is not distinguishing the **wonders that he had shown them** from other wonderful things that God had not shown them. The psalmist is reminding the people about the character of God’s deeds that they forgot. Be sure that this is clear in your translation. Alternate translation: [which were wonderful things that he had shown them]
The word **Zoan** is the name of a city.

Here, **their fathers** represents their ancestors who were present to see the marvelous things. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when their ancestors were present] or [while their ancestors were watching]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a heap** is a vertical structure, so **the waters** stood upright. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and he made the waters stand upright like a solid wall]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and all the night he led them with the light of fire]

By **the cloud** and **the light of fire**, the psalmist means the pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire that guided Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 13:21–22). You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [with the pillar of cloud … with the pillar of fire]
The pronoun **He** refers to God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [God split open]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the deep** has limitless water, so God provided limitless water for his people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and he gave them water as limitless as the deep]

The psalmist says **and he gave drink abundantly as the deep** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [and he gave them an enormous amount of water to drink]

The point of this comparison is that just as **rivers** are abundant and continuous in their flow, so was the water that God brought from the rock. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [in great abundance] or [in a continuous stream]

The pronoun **they** refers to the Israelites, the ancestors of those whom the psalmist is addressing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the Israelite people added] or [And those ancestors added]

The psalmist uses the word **And** here to indicate a contrast between God’s gracious provision and the people’s sinful response. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [But they added still to sin against him] or [Yet they added still to sin against him]

The psalmist is using the phrase **by asking for food for their appetite** to state the reason for the result that **they tested God in their hearts**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [And they tested God in their hearts when they asked for food for their appetite]

Here, **hearts** represents the inner thoughts and attitudes. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in their minds] or [inwardly]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **appetite**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for what they craved] or [for what they desired to eat]

The Israelites are using the question form to express doubt about God’s ability to provide for them. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [God cannot arrange a table in the wilderness!] or [Surely God is not able to arrange a table in the wilderness!]

The Israelites are speaking of God providing food as if he were **arranging a table** for a meal. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [provide food for us]

78.quote: הֲ⁠גַם־לֶ֭חֶם י֣וּכַל תֵּ֑ת אִם־יָכִ֖ין שְׁאֵ֣ר לְ⁠עַמּֽ⁠וֹ
78.text: The Israelites are using the question form to express their doubt that God can provide different kinds of food. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [But surely he cannot give bread also! Surely he cannot provide meat for his people!] or [But he is not able to give bread also. He cannot provide meat for his people.]

The people are speaking of themselves in the third person as **his people** to acknowledge their relationship with God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [for us, his people]

The expression **a fire was kindled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh kindled a fire against Jacob] or [and Yahweh’s anger burned against Jacob]

The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh’s anger as if it were **a fire** that could be **kindled**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh became furiously angry against Jacob] or [and Yahweh’s anger burned against Jacob]

Here, **nose** represents anger. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and also his anger burned against Israel] or [and also he became angry with Israel]

Here, **Jacob** and **Israel** represent the entire nation descended from this patriarch. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [against the people of Jacob … against the people of Israel] or [against the nation of Israel]

78.quote: כִּ֤י לֹ֣א הֶ֭אֱמִינוּ בֵּ⁠אלֹהִ֑ים וְ⁠לֹ֥א בָ֝טְח֗וּ בִּֽ⁠ישׁוּעָתֽ⁠וֹ
78.text: The word translated as **because** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [since they did not believe in God and did not trust in his salvation]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and that he would save them]

The psalmist uses the word **Yet** here to indicate a contrast between the Israelites’ unbelief and God’s gracious provision. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [But he commanded] or [Even so, he commanded]

78.quote: וַ⁠יְצַ֣ו שְׁחָקִ֣ים מִ⁠מָּ֑עַל וְ⁠דַלְתֵ֖י שָׁמַ֣יִם פָּתָֽח
78.text: The psalmist is speaking of the sky as if it were a building with **doors** that God opened. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yet he gave orders to the sky above and caused the heavens to open]

The psalmist is speaking of **the clouds** as if they were living things that could hear and obey God’s commands. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He controlled the clouds]

The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a weather phenomenon, and **he rained down manna** from the sky. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He caused manna to fall down from the sky]
The phrase **the grain of heaven** could mean: (1) the grain that angels eat or (2) the grain that came from heaven. The next verse supports the first meaning.

The psalmist is using **grain** to represent all of the manna that God provided. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and … the food from heaven] or [and … the provision from heaven]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **Man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [People ate]

The psalmist is using one kind of food, **bread**, to mean food in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the food] or [the grain]
The psalmist assumes that readers will know that **the mighty** refers to angels. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [of angels]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **satisfaction**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [enough food to satisfy them] or [abundant food]

The psalmist is speaking of the meat as if it were rain that God **rained down** on the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent comparison or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He caused meat to fall on them in great abundance] or [He gave them a huge amount of meat]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and he rained down birds of wing as numerous as the sands of the sea]
It might seem that the expression **birds of wing** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [birds]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **birds** that are characterized by having **wings**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [winged birds] or [flying birds]

The psalmist says **like dust** and **as the sands of the sea** as extreme statements for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [in great quantities and … beyond counting]

The pronoun **his** refers to the people of Israel, not to God. The psalmist is describing the birds falling into the Israelites’ camp and near their tents. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [They fell in the middle of the Israelites’ camp, all around the Israelites’ tents]
Here, **his** refers to the Israelites. See the book introduction for more information.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **craving**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [He gave them what they craved]
See how you translated the similar expression in [78:29](../078/029.md).
See how you translated the similar expression in [78:21](../078/021.md).

The psalmist is speaking of the young men dying as if God were physically forcing them to **bow down** to the ground. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he struck down the young men of Israel] or [and he made the young men of Israel fall dead]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wonders**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in the wonderful things he did] or [that he could do wonderful things]

This is poetic language. The psalmist moves from shorter units of time (**days**) to longer units (**years**) to emphasize the completeness of God’s judgment. If your language has a way to indicate poetry, you could use it here. Alternate translation: [So he ended their lives quickly, like a breath, and their years were full of fear]

The psalmist is referring to God ending the lives of the Israelites in a polite way by using the phrase **he consumed their days**. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [So he ended their days] or [So he caused their days to vanish]

The psalmist is speaking of **their days** as if they were something that could be **consumed** (used up) **in a vapor** (as quickly as a puff of breath disappears). If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [So he caused their days to quickly vanish like vapor] or [So he caused their days to pass swiftly like a breath]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and he consumed their years in terror]

Here, **their days** and **their years** represent their lives. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [their lives … and their lives]

The psalmist is describing repeated events, not a single occurrence. The word **When** indicates that this pattern happened multiple times. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a word or phrase that shows this repetition. Alternate translation: [Each time God afflicted them, they would seek him]

78.quote: וַֽ֭⁠יִּזְכְּרוּ כִּֽי־אֱלֹהִ֣ים צוּרָ֑⁠ם וְ⁠אֵ֥ל עֶ֝לְיוֹן גֹּאֲלָֽ⁠ם
78.text: See the note on [78:1](../078/001.md) or the Introduction to the Psalms for more information on how to translate parallelisms. Alternate translation: [They would remember that God Most High was their rock and redeemer]

The psalmist is speaking of God as if he were a **rock** that provided protection and stability. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture, or you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [God was their refuge] or [God was their protector]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and they would remember that God Most High was their rescuer]

Here, **with their mouth** and **with their tongues** represent what the people said by using their mouth and words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [by what they said to him and … in what they told him]

Here, **hearts** represents the people’s inner desires and commitment. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And they were not truly committed to him]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **steadfast**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And they were not loyal to him in their hearts] or [And they did not remain faithful toward him in their hearts]

The psalmist is emphasizing a positive meaning by using a negative word, **not**, together with an expression that is the opposite of the intended meaning. If it would be helpful in your language, you could emphasize the positive meaning in a strong way. Alternate translation: [Many times he chose to be patient with his people]

Here, **nose** represents anger. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he held back his anger] or [he restrained his anger]

The psalmist is speaking of God’s anger as if it were something physical that God **held back** to keep it from going out toward the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he restrained his anger] or [he controlled his anger]

The psalmist is speaking of God’s wrath as if it were something dormant that he could **stir up** or arouse. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and did not cause his full wrath to awaken] or [and did not unleash the full extent of his anger]

Here, **flesh** represents the weakness and frailty of human nature. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they were weak and frail] or [they were mortal]

The psalmist is speaking of human beings as if they were **a wind going and it does not return**. He means that human life is brief and fragile, like a wind that blows by once and then is gone. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [mortal beings whose lives quickly end]

The psalmist is using the expression **they returned and they tested** as a common expression of the culture to mean “they repeatedly tested.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They tested God again and again] or [They continually tested God]

The psalmist is using this possessive form to describe the holy God with whom the Israelites are in a covenant relationship. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and grieved the holy God with whom the Israelites are in a covenant relationship]
The expression **the Holy One of Israel** is a title for God.

Here, **hand** represents the power of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his power] or [his strength]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **day**. He means the time in general when God redeemed the Israelites from Egypt. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the time]

Here, **the adversary** represents Egypt and Pharaoh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [he redeemed them from Egypt] or [he redeemed them from Pharaoh]
See how you translated this in [78:12](../078/012.md). **Zoan** was a city in Egypt.

Here, **the frog** represents frogs in general, not one particular frog. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and the frogs]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and he sent the frog]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **labor**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and what they had labored to produce]

Here, **labor** represents the produce or results of their labor. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and what their labor produced] or [and the fruit of their labor]

The psalmist is speaking of God as if he were a commander who **gave over** the Egyptians’ **cattle to the hail** as if the hail were an enemy army that would attack them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he caused the hail to kill their cattle and gave their livestock] or [And he allowed the hail to strike down their cattle and gave their livestock]

The psalmist is using the phrase **the burning of his nose** as a common expression of the culture to mean that God is angry. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [among them his fierce anger] or [among them his burning anger]

The terms **fury**, **indignation**, and **distress** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the three terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [great wrath]

78.quote: יְשַׁלַּח־בָּ֨⁠ם ׀ חֲר֬וֹן אַפּ֗⁠וֹ עֶבְרָ֣ה וָ⁠זַ֣עַם וְ⁠צָרָ֑ה מִ֝שְׁלַ֗חַת מַלְאֲכֵ֥י רָעִֽים
78.text: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **fury**, **indignation**, **distress**, and **calamity**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [He furiously and indignantly distressed them with disastrous messengers]

78.quote: יְשַׁלַּח־בָּ֨⁠ם ׀ חֲר֬וֹן אַפּ֗⁠וֹ עֶבְרָ֣ה וָ⁠זַ֣עַם וְ⁠צָרָ֑ה מִ֝שְׁלַ֗חַת מַלְאֲכֵ֥י רָעִֽים
78.text: The psalmist is speaking of **fury and indignation and distress** as if they were living things that could be sent as **messengers** to carry out God’s judgment. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He vented on them his great anger and fury, causing them trouble and disaster]

The psalmist is speaking of God’s anger as if it were a weapon or force that **He sent** out to strike the Egyptians. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [His fierce anger struck them with fury and indignation] or [He attacked them with his fierce anger]

The psalmist is speaking of **his anger** as if it were something that could travel along a **path**. He means that God fully released his anger against the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He gave full vent to his anger] or [He released his anger without restraint]

The psalmist is speaking of the lives of the Egyptians as if they were something God could physically give **over to the plague**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but allowed them to die from the plague] or [but caused the plague to kill them]

The psalmist is using **the beginning of strength** as a common expression of the culture to mean the **firstborn** sons. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the firstborn sons] or [the oldest sons]

Here, **tents** represents the families who lived in them, and **Ham** represents the people of Egypt, who were descended from him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the households of Egypt] or [among the people of Egypt]

The point of this comparison is that just as **sheep** need a shepherd to guide and care for them, so did God’s people need God to guide and care for them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [And he made his people journey, guiding and caring for them like a shepherd does for sheep, and he led them, protecting them like a shepherd protects a flock in the wilderness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **security**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [securely] or [safely]
The pronoun **he** refers to God, while the pronoun **them** refers to the Israelites. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And God brought the Israelites]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **the border** that is characterized by **his holiness**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the border of the land he had set apart] or [the border of his holy land]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **holiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [of what is holy to him] or [of what he had set apart]

Here, **his right hand** represents the power of God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that he acquired by his power] or [that his power acquired]

The pronoun **he** refers to God, while the pronoun **them** refers to the Israelites. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [God drove out nations from before the Israelites]

Here the psalmist is speaking of the Canaanites whom God **caused them to fall in a portion of inheritance**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you could use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and caused them to be defeated in each portion that Israel inherited] or [and defeated them in each portion that Israel inherited as they came to it]

The psalmist is using this possessive form to mean a portion for inheriting. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [in each portion inherited by Israel] or [in each portion that Israel inherited]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **inheritance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and gave each tribe a portion to inherit] or [and gave each tribe of Israel a portion as their own]

The psalmist uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between God’s provision and the people’s rebellion. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Despite all this, they tested and rebelled] or [Even so, they tested and rebelled]

The terms **tested** and **rebelled** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [But they continually pushed back] or [But they stubbornly rebelled]

78.quote: וַ⁠יִּסֹּ֣גוּ וַֽ֭⁠יִּבְגְּדוּ כַּ⁠אֲבוֹתָ֑⁠ם נֶ֝הְפְּכ֗וּ כְּ⁠קֶ֣שֶׁת רְמִיָּֽה
78.text: For more information on translating parallelism, see the note at [78:1](../078/001.md). Alternate translation: [They turned back and acted treacherously like their fathers, being as unreliable as a bow of deceit]

The point of this comparison is that just as **their fathers** were unfaithful to God, so were the Israelites. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [in the same unfaithful way as their fathers]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a bow of deceit** is unreliable and does not shoot straight, so were the Israelites unreliable. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as unreliable as a faulty bow]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **a bow** that is characterized by **deceit**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [into a deceitful bow] or [as a faulty bow]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **deceit**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [into a deceitful bow] or [as a faulty bow]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **jealousy**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [they caused him to be jealous]

The term translated as **and** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [God heard, and as a result, he was furious] or [When God heard, he was furious]

The term translated as **And** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [Therefore, he abandoned the dwelling of Shiloh] or [So he abandoned the dwelling of Shiloh]

Here, **his strength** represents the box of the covenant, which showed God’s power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And he allowed the box to be captured] or [And he let the box that showed his power be captured]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what showed he was strong] or [the box that showed his power]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **captivity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to be captured] or [to those who would capture it]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and he gave his splendor]

Here, **his splendor** represents the box of the covenant, and **the hand of the enemy** represents their power or control. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use equivalent expressions or plain language. Alternate translation: [and his glorious box into the power of the enemy] or [and the box that showed his splendor to be controlled by the enemy]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **splendor**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and what was splendid to him] or [and the ark that showed he was glorious]

Here, **the sword** represents warfare or violent death in battle. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he allowed his people to be killed in battle] or [And he delivered his people over to violent death]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **inheritance**, you could express the same idea in another way. See how you translated this in [78:55](../078/055.md). Alternate translation: [and … with the people he had chosen]

The phrases **Fire consumed his young men** and **his virgins were not praised** mean opposite things but work together to show the devastating completeness of the judgment. For emphasis, the psalmist is describing both the death of young men and the corresponding lack of marriage celebrations.
