If a speaker of your language would not use this kind of contrast, in your translation you can convey the emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [Fire consumed his young men so that his virgins had no weddings]

The psalmist speaks of **Fire** as if it were a person that could actively consume people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [His young men died in fires] or [His young men were burned to death]

If your language does not use this passive form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and no one praised his virgins in wedding songs] or [and no one sang wedding songs for his virgins]

Here, **the sword** represents violent death in battle. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [died in battle] or [were killed in war]

The psalmist uses the word **Then** to indicate a contrast between God’s judgment and his intervention. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [But then the Lord awoke] or [After this, the Lord awoke]

The psalmist speaks of **the Lord** as if he were a person who could sleep and wake up. He means that God had seemed inactive during the time of judgment but then became active again to help his people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Then the Lord acted as if he had awakened from sleep] or [Then the Lord began to act again after seeming to be inactive]

The point of this comparison is that just as **one sleeping** must wake up before acting, so the Lord resumed acting after a period of seeming inactivity. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like someone who had been asleep]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a mighty man** who has been drinking wine might shout loudly and powerfully, so the Lord acted with great power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like a powerful warrior shouting with great strength]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **perpetuity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a shame that lasts forever] or [permanent disgrace]

The psalmist uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between rejecting Joseph and Ephraim and choosing Judah. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Instead, he chose the tribe of Judah]

Here, **Mount Zion** represents the tribe of Judah. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Judah’s descendants, who]

78.quote: וַ⁠יִּ֣בֶן כְּמוֹ־רָ֭מִים מִקְדָּשׁ֑⁠וֹ כְּ֝⁠אֶ֗רֶץ יְסָדָ֥⁠הּ לְ⁠עוֹלָֽם
78.text: The phrase **he built his sanctuary like the heights** is parallel to the statement **like the earth he founded it forever** and clarifies the relationship between the sanctuary’s grandeur and its permanence. Alternate translation: [And he built his sanctuary to be as exalted as the heavens and as permanent as the earth]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the heights** are exalted and majestic, so is God’s sanctuary. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as exalted as the heavens]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the earth** is permanent and enduring, so God **founded** his sanctuary to last **forever**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as enduring as the earth, he founded it to last forever]

The term translated as **to** indicates that what follows is a purpose or goal of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [in order to shepherd Jacob his people] or [so that he would shepherd Jacob his people]

The psalmist is speaking of **Jacob his people** as if they were sheep that needed someone **to shepherd** them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to lead and care for Jacob his people] or [to rule over Jacob his people]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **inheritance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the people who belonged to him] or [the people he had chosen as his own]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **integrity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with an honest heart] or [with a pure heart]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **his heart** that is characterized by **integrity**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [according to his honest heart]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **skillfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and with his skillful hands he guided them] or [and he guided them skillfully]

Here, **his hands** represents the actions and capabilities of David. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and with his skill he guided them] or [and he guided them with his abilities]

79.text:
# Psalm 79 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 79 is a psalm of supplication or lament. It includes all the basic elements of that type of psalm except a statement of trust. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Description of troubles (1–4)
2. Cry for help (5–7)
3. Petition: request for forgiveness (8–9)
4. Petition: request for retribution (10–12)
5. Vow of praise (13)

## Translation Issues in this Psalm

### Imperatives

Throughout this psalm, the psalmist is requesting things from Yahweh by using an imperative form which may sound like a command in your language. If this would be impolite in your language, then use a form that would be more appropriate for addressing Yahweh with a request.

### Parallelisms

Parallelisms arise when two phrases occur together which mean the same thing. The second phrase emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea using different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine the phrases and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one and not saying something additional. See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing.

Asaph is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of anguish over the invasion of Israel. If your language has a comparable way to express this feeling, you could use it in your translation. Alternate translation: [O God, nations have invaded your inheritance]

Here Asaph is introducing the **nations** as new participants in the psalm. He does not specify which nations, but refers to foreign peoples in general. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [foreign nations]

Here Asaph is speaking of the land of Israel being different than other parts of the earth by calling it God’s **inheritance**. This means the land that God specially reserved for him and his people. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [into your special possession]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **inheritance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [into what you have inherited]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **holiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [you who are holy]

79.quote: בָּ֤אוּ גוֹיִ֨ם ׀ בְּֽ⁠נַחֲלָתֶ֗⁠ךָ טִ֭מְּאוּ אֶת־הֵיכַ֣ל קָדְשֶׁ֑⁠ךָ שָׂ֖מוּ אֶת־יְרוּשָׁלִַ֣ם לְ⁠עִיִּֽים
79.text: These three phrases all describe the enemy’s attack on what belongs to God. Each phrase intensifies the devastation, moving from invasion to defilement to destruction. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. For more information on how to translate parallel phrases see the Psalm 79 Introduction. Alternate translation: [nations have invaded your land, made your holy temple unclean, and turned Jerusalem into piles of rubble]

Asaph is using the possessive form to describe a **bird** that lives in **the heavens**, that is, the sky. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to the birds that fly in the sky]

Asaph is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and they have given the flesh of your faithful as food to the beast of the earth]

Asaph is using the adjective **faithful** as a noun to mean people who are faithful to God. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [your faithful ones]

Asaph is using the possessive form to describe a **beast** that lives on **the earth**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to the animals that live on the land]

The terms **the bird** and **the beast** are singular collective nouns that refer to all birds and all beasts as a group. If your language does not use singular nouns in that way, you can use plural forms in your translation.

Asaph is referring to all wild creatures by naming two major components, **bird of the heavens** and **beast of the earth**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to every kind of bird … to every kind of wild creature]

Here, **their blood** represents their violent death. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the blood of those they killed]

The point of this comparison is that just as **water** flows freely and abundantly, so the blood of the slain was shed in great quantity. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as freely as water is poured out]
Asaph is providing background information to help readers understand the situation. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

Here Asaph is using the word **We** to introduce the community of Israel as speakers for the first time in the psalm. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [We, your people, have become]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. The poetry of the original language was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [those whom our neighbors insult and mock]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **reproach**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [people whom others reproach]

Asaph is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and we have become scorn and derision to the ones around us]

The terms **scorn** and **derision** mean similar things. Asaph is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [utter mockery]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **scorn** and **derision**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [people whom others scorn and deride]

79.quote: עַד־מָ֣ה יְ֭הוָה תֶּאֱנַ֣ף לָ⁠נֶ֑צַח תִּבְעַ֥ר כְּמוֹ־אֵ֝֗שׁ קִנְאָתֶֽ⁠ךָ
79.text: These two phrases **Will you be angry forever** and **Will your jealousy burn like fire** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. The poetry of the original language was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [How long, Yahweh, will you remain fiercely angry with us]

Asaph is using the question form to express lament and anguish rather than to seek information. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, it has been so long!]

Asaph is using the question form to express anguish at the duration of God’s anger rather than to ask for information. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Please do not stay angry forever!]
Asaph says **forever** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [without end]

Asaph is using the question form to express distress rather than to ask for information. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Do not let your jealousy keep burning like fire!]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **jealousy**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how jealous you are cause us to]

The point of this comparison is that just as **fire** is intense and consuming, so is God’s jealousy. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as intensely as a fire burns]

79.quote: שְׁפֹ֤ךְ חֲמָתְ⁠ךָ֨ אֶֽל־הַ⁠גּוֹיִם֮ אֲשֶׁ֪ר לֹא־יְדָ֫ע֥וּ⁠ךָ וְ⁠עַ֥ל מַמְלָכ֑וֹת אֲשֶׁ֥ר בְּ֝⁠שִׁמְ⁠ךָ֗ לֹ֣א קָרָֽאוּ
79.text: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request to God rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please.” For more information on imperatives, see the Psalm 79 Introduction. See how you as a team have decided to translate imperatives and follow that approach here and throughout this Psalm. Alternate translation: [Please pour out your wrath on the nations that have not known you and on the kingdoms that have not called on your name]

Here Asaph is speaking as if God’s wrath were a liquid that he could **pour out**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Unleash your wrath]

79.quote: שְׁפֹ֤ךְ חֲמָתְ⁠ךָ֨ אֶֽל־הַ⁠גּוֹיִם֮ אֲשֶׁ֪ר לֹא־יְדָ֫ע֥וּ⁠ךָ וְ⁠עַ֥ל מַמְלָכ֑וֹת
79.text: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wrath**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Show the peoples that do not worship you how angry you are and also the kingdoms]

79.quote: וְ⁠עַ֥ל מַמְלָכ֑וֹת אֲשֶׁ֥ר בְּ֝⁠שִׁמְ⁠ךָ֗ לֹ֣א קָרָֽאוּ
79.text: Asaph is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and pour out your wrath on the kingdoms that have not called on your name]
Here, **name** represents who God is. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you]

The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

Here Asaph is speaking as if the enemy were a wild animal that **devoured** its prey. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [one has destroyed the people of Jacob]
The pronoun **one** is indefinite and refers to the enemy nations mentioned in verse 6. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the enemy has devoured]

Asaph is using the name **Jacob** to represent the nation of Israel, which descended from the patriarch Jacob. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Israel]
The pronoun **they** shifts from the singular “one” and refers to the enemy nations. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the nations have desolated]
The pronoun **his** refers to Jacob, that is, the people of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Jacob’s habitation]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquities**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the wicked things we did in the past]

Asaph is speaking of **your compassions** as if they were a living thing that could **meet** the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [show us compassion]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **compassions**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [come to us with your tender care]

Asaph is giving the reason for his urgent request. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this gives the reason for the preceding request. Alternate translation: [because we have become very weak]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [God, the one who saves us]

Here, **on account of the glory of your name** marks the purpose for the preceding request. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [so that your name will be glorified]
Here, **name** represents God’s reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your glorious reputation]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [your glorious name]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **sins**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the wrong things we have done]

Here, **for the sake of your name** marks the purpose for covering over their sins. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [so that people will honor your name]
Here, **name** represents God’s reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [for the sake of your reputation]

Asaph is using the question form to argue that God should act so that the nations will not mock him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Do not let the nations say that their God cannot help them!]

The nations would be using the question form to mock Israel rather than to ask for information. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Their God cannot help them!]
If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this as an indirect quotation. Alternate translation: [Why should the nations ask where their God is]
The pronoun **their** refers to the people of Israel, spoken from the perspective of the nations. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [is the God of Israel]

79.quote: יִוָּדַ֣ע ב⁠גיים לְ⁠עֵינֵ֑י⁠נוּ נִ֝קְמַ֗ת דַּֽם־עֲבָדֶ֥י⁠ךָ הַ⁠שָּׁפֽוּךְ
79.text: The expression **be known among the nations** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Let the nations see you carry out vengeance for killing your servants]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **vengeance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how you avenge]

The psalmist is speaking as if someone had actually **poured out** the **blood** of Yahweh’s **servants** from a vessel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the shedding of the blood of your servants]

Here, **the poured-out blood** represents the violent killing of God’s servants. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the killing of your servants]

The expression **the poured-out blood** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the blood that the nations have shed]
Here, **eyes** represents sight and perception. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [so that we can see it]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **groaning**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how the prisoners groan]
Here, **face** represents God’s presence and attention. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [into your presence]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **greatness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [your great arm]
Here, **arm** represents God’s power and strength. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your power]

Asaph is using **sons of death** as a common expression to mean “those who are destined to die.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those who are condemned to die]
Asaph says **sevenfold** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [many times over]

Asaph is using **into their bosom** as a common expression to mean “directly and personally to them.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [directly upon them]

If it would be more natural in your language, you could put the object **their reproach with which they have reproached you** before the other information in the sentence, so that the reader understands right away what is to be returned. Alternate translation: [And return their reproach with which they have reproached you, Lord, to our neighbors sevenfold, into their bosom]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **reproach**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the insults they have spoken]

Asaph places **And we** at the beginning of this verse to mark a shift from petition to a vow of praise. If it would be more natural in your language, you could indicate this transition in another way. Alternate translation: [Then we]

Here Asaph is speaking of God’s people as if they were a **flock** of sheep that God tends in his **pasture**. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ones you tend and care for]

Asaph is using the possessive form to describe a **flock** that is located in God’s **pasture**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the flock that feeds in your pasture]
This concluding vow of praise signals the end of the psalm. Use the natural form in your language for signaling that a song or poem is ending. Alternate translation: [will always give thanks to you]
Asaph says **forever** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [always]

Asaph says **to generation and generation** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [in every generation that follows]

Asaph is using a poetic device found in the original language by repeating the word **generation** to express the idea of an unending succession. This is poetic language. If your language has a way to indicate this kind of poetic repetition, you could use it here. Alternate translation: [from one generation to the next]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **praise**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how praiseworthy you are]

80.text:
# Psalm 80 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 80 is a psalm of supplication or lament. It includes all the basic elements of that type of psalm except a statement of trust. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the Introduction to the Psalms.

1. Cry for help (1–2)
2. Refrain (3)
3. Description of troubles (4–6)
4. Refrain (7)
5. Description of troubles (8–13)
6. Petition (14–18)
7. Refrain (19)

## Translation Issues in this Psalm

### Imperatives

Throughout this psalm, the psalmist is requesting things from Yahweh by using an imperative form which may sound like a command in your language. If this would be impolite in your language, then use a form that would be more appropriate for addressing Yahweh with a request.

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. See how this is translated in [Psalm 4:1](../004/001.md). Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]
See how you translated the term **testimony** in the superscription to Psalm 8.

Asaph is speaking as if God were a **Shepherd of Israel**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Caretaker of Israel]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. See how you as a team have decided to translate imperatives in the Psalms and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. For more information on how to translate imperatives see the Psalm 80 Introduction. Alternate translation: [please pay attention]
Asaph is using the phrase **give ear** to mean “listen to me.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly as in the UST.

The point of this comparison is that just as a shepherd leads and cares for a flock, so God leads and cares for the descendants of Joseph. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [the one caring for the descendants of Joseph as a shepherd cares for a flock]

Here, **Joseph** represents all the people of Israel, particularly the northern tribes descended from Joseph. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the descendants of Joseph]

Asaph is speaking as if God were one who sits on the cherubim. This refers to God being enthroned above the ark of the covenant. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You who are enthroned above the cherubim]

Here, **To the face of** represents being in front of or in the presence of these tribes. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [In the presence of Ephraim]

Here Asaph is speaking of God displaying his **might** as if it were something that was sleeping and needed to be told to **awaken.** Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [display] or [take action by using]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **might**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and display your power]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to save us]

This phrase indicates that what follows, **let us be saved**, is the purpose or goal of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [and make your face shine so that we will be saved]

Asaph is speaking as if God’s face were a light that could shine. This represents God showing favor and blessing to his people. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and show us your favor]

The expression **let us be saved** is a passive verbal form. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and rescue us]

Here Asaph is using the possessive form **God of armies** to mean “God, the one who commands the armies of heaven.” It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [God who commands armies]

Asaph is using the question form to express strong emotion. If you would not use a rhetorical question for this purpose in your language, you could translate his words as a statement or an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You have smoldered against the prayer of your people for far too long!]

Asaph is speaking as if God’s anger were fire that continues to **smolder**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [will you remain angry at]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **prayer**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when your people pray to you]

80.quote: הֶ֭אֱכַלְתָּ⁠ם לֶ֣חֶם דִּמְעָ֑ה וַ֝⁠תַּשְׁקֵ֗⁠מוֹ בִּ⁠דְמָע֥וֹת שָׁלִֽישׁ
80.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [You have made them eat and drink tears abundantly]
The pronoun **them** refers to the people of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [You have made the people of Israel eat]

Asaph is speaking as if tears were **bread** that people could eat. This means that sorrow has become their constant experience. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [food of sorrow]

Asaph is speaking as if **tears** were a liquid that people could drink in great quantity. This means that God has caused the people to experience overwhelming sorrow. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you have caused them to weep an overwhelming amount]

Asaph uses the phrase **in triple measure** as an exaggeration for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use another way to express this emphasis. Alternate translation: [much more than we deserve]

The first-person pronoun **us** here indicates a shift from the third person **them** in the previous verse. Asaph is now including himself among the suffering people. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use the same person as in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [You have made them strife to their neighbors]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strife**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a cause of quarreling with our neighbors]

Asaph is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and our enemies mock us among themselves]

Here Asaph is using the possessive form **God of armies** to mean “God, the one who commands the armies of heaven.” It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. See how you translated this in [verse 4](../080/004.md). Alternate translation: [God who commands armies]

The word **and** indicates that what follows, **let us be saved**, is the purpose or goal of what came before. See how you translated this in [80:3](../080/003.md). Alternate translation: [and make your face shine so that we will be saved]
Asaph is speaking as if God’s face were a light that could shine. See how you translated this in [80:3](../080/003.md). Alternate translation: [and show us your favor]
If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and rescue us]

80.quote: גֶּ֭פֶן מִ⁠מִּצְרַ֣יִם תַּסִּ֑יעַ תְּגָרֵ֥שׁ גּ֝וֹיִ֗ם וַ⁠תִּטָּעֶֽ⁠הָ
80.text: The structure here indicates events in sequence. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could show this relationship by using a fuller phrase. Alternate translation: [You pulled up a vine from Egypt, and then you drove out nations and planted it]

Asaph is speaking of Israel as if it were a **vine**. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [You pulled up a nation like a vine from Egypt]

The structure here indicates events in sequence. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could show this relationship by using a fuller phrase. Alternate translation: [Then you cleared the ground for it, and it took root and filled the land]
The pronoun **it** refers to the vine (representing Israel). It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [to the face of the vine]

Asaph is speaking of Israel as if it were a vine that became established and spread. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [and the people became established and filled the land]

The phrase **rooted its roots** is an idiom using a verb and noun from the same root. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use an expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and it became deeply rooted]

Asaph is speaking of Israel as if it were a vine whose shadow covered the mountains. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [The people spread even over the mountains]

The expression **were covered** is a passive verbal form. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Its shadow covered the mountains]

Asaph is speaking of Israel as if it were a vine whose branches were like the mighty cedars. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [and the people became as strong as the mighty cedars]

Asaph is using the possessive form to describe the **cedars** as being characterized by extraordinary greatness, as if they belong to God. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [were very great cedars]

Asaph is speaking of Israel as if it were a vine that **sent out its branches**. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this in another way. Alternate translation: [The people extended their territory]

Asaph is referring to the entire promised land by naming its two extreme boundaries, **the sea** (the Mediterranean Sea in the west) and **the River** (the Euphrates River in the east). If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the Mediterranean Sea, and its shoots to the Euphrates River]

Asaph is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from earlier in the sentence if it would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and it sent out its shoots to the River]

80.quote: לָ֭⁠מָּה פָּרַ֣צְתָּ גְדֵרֶ֑י⁠הָ וְ֝⁠אָר֗וּ⁠הָ כָּל־עֹ֥בְרֵי דָֽרֶךְ
80.text: In this context, the second phrase states the result of what the first phrase describes. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [You have broken down its walls with the result that all the ones passing on the way pluck it]

Asaph is using the question form to express strong emotion. If you would not use a rhetorical question for this purpose in your language, you could translate his words as a statement or an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You should not have broken down its walls]

Asaph is speaking as if Israel were a vineyard with **walls** that God has broken down. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [have you removed its protection]
The pronoun **its** refers to the vine (representing Israel). It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the walls of the vine] or [our walls]

The phrase **all the ones passing on the way** is a generalization to emphasize how vulnerable the vine has become. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [so that many people passing by pluck it]

80.quote: יְכַרְסְמֶ֣⁠נָּֽה חֲזִ֣יר מִיָּ֑עַר וְ⁠זִ֖יז שָׂדַ֣י יִרְעֶֽ⁠נָּה
80.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Wild animals from the forest and the field ravage and consume it]

80.quote: יְכַרְסְמֶ֣⁠נָּֽה חֲזִ֣יר מִיָּ֑עַר וְ⁠זִ֖יז שָׂדַ֣י יִרְעֶֽ⁠נָּה
80.text: Asaph continues to draw an extended comparison between the nation of Israel, and a vineyard planted by a gardener. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the comparison. [Their enemies have destroyed your people like wild animals that root and destroy a vineyard]

Here, **God of armies** describes God as the one who commands the armies of heaven. See how you translated this in [80:4](../080/004.md). Alternate translation: [God who commands armies]

Asaph is speaking of Israel as if it were a **vine**. Your language may have a comparable expression you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and care for this people]

Alternate translation: [Enemies have burned it with fire and cut it down]

Here, **your face** represents God’s presence and judgment. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [because you rebuke them]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **rebuke**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because you are angry with them]

Here, **hand** represents power and protection. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Let your protection be on]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [the one whom you have chosen and strengthened]

Here Asaph is using the phrase **son of man** as a common expression of the culture to indicate a person that has the characteristic of being human. 81.text:
# Psalm 81 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 81 begins like a psalm of praise. However, it then presents a direct address from Yahweh. He recalls that he delivered the Israelites from slavery in Egypt, but they nevertheless disobeyed him. He then describes how he would bless the Israelites if they did obey him. Many interpreters believe that this psalm was written for the occasion of one of the annual festivals, when many Israelites would be at the temple in Jerusalem and hear its message of warning and promise. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the Introduction to Psalms.

1. Call to worship (1–3)
2. Reason to worship (4–5)
3. Yahweh testifies against the Israelites (6–12)
4. Yahweh says how he would bless the Israelites (13–16)

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

### Parallelisms

Parallelisms arise when two phrases occur together which mean about the same thing. The second phrase emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea using different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine the phrases and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one and not saying something additional. See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. For more information, see the Introduction to the Psalms.

## Imperatives

The ULT uses the imperative to show that a speaker is expressing a desire that something happen or that someone do something. When Asaph says in verse 1, “Shout joyfully to God”, he means that it is his desire that the people should do this. Translate this form in the most natural way in your language to indicate that the speaker is expressing what he wants someone to do or what he wishes someone would do.

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]
See how you translated the term **Gittith** in the superscription to Psalm 8.

81.quote: הַ֭רְנִינוּ לֵ⁠אלֹהִ֣ים עוּזֵּ֑⁠נוּ הָ֝רִ֗יעוּ לֵ⁠אלֹהֵ֥י יַעֲקֹֽב
81.text: These two phrases **Shout joyfully to God, our strength** and **shout out to the God of Jacob** mean basically the same thing. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. For more information on translating parallel phrases, see the Introduction to this psalm. Alternate translation: [Shout with great joy to God who is the strength of Jacob’s descendants]

Asaph is saying what he wants the people of Israel to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about this form of speech and follow the decision of your team, here and throughout this psalm, of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [I desire that all shout joyfully to God, our strength; you should all shout out]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the one who strengthens us]

Asaph is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [also blow a shofar at the full moon]

The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because it is a statute for Israel]

81.quote: חֹ֣ק לְ⁠יִשְׂרָאֵ֣ל ה֑וּא מִ֝שְׁפָּ֗ט לֵ⁠אלֹהֵ֥י יַעֲקֹֽב
81.text: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the ideas of **statute** and **judgment**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [it is something that God decreed, what the God of Jacob decided]

The pronoun **He** refers to God, and the pronoun **he** in **when he went out** refers to Joseph (representing Israel). It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [God set it as a testimony in Joseph when Israel went out]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **testimony**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [as something to be observed]

The name **Joseph** represents the people of Israel, particularly the tribes descended from Joseph. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [among the people of Israel]
Here, **lip** represents language or speech. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [a tongue]

This is the beginning of what Yahweh said. His speech continues through verse 16. You may wish to mark the words of this speech with a first-level quotation mark at the beginning and end of them or with some other punctuation or convention that your language uses to indicate a first-level quotation.

The phrase **I removed his shoulder from the burden** represents Yahweh completely liberating Israel from slavery in Egypt. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I freed him from his slavery]

The pronouns **his** refer to the people of Israel collectively. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the shoulder of my people from the burden; their palms passed from the basket]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **distress**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [When you were suffering]

Yahweh is speaking as if he were concealed within **the secret place of thunder**. This represents God’s awesome and hidden presence in the storm. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the thunderstorm where I was hidden]

Yahweh is using this possessive form to describe a hidden place that is associated with thunder. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [from the place hidden by thunder]
The word **Meribah** is the name of a desert place.

Here, **if you would listen to me** introduces the first part of a possible condition. Yahweh will only do the things described in verses 13–16 if this condition happens. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen.

Yahweh is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling, a deep longing for Israel to obey. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. If not, you could say what Yahweh was feeling. Alternate translation: [Israel, I so deeply wish you would listen to me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **foreignness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to a foreign god]

Yahweh is speaking as if Israel’s dependence on him were opening a mouth wide to be fed. This represents trusting God to provide abundantly. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Depend on me completely, and I will provide for you abundantly]

The word translated as **Open wide** is an imperative, but it communicates a condition rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a condition for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a condition. Alternate translation: [If you open wide your mouth, then I will fill it]

Yahweh uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between the commands he gave in verses 8–10 and the response of the people. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [However, my people did not listen]

Here, **voice** represents Yahweh’s commands and instructions. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to my commands]
The term translated as **So** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [Therefore I sent them away]

Here, **heart** represents the will and inner attitude of the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the stubbornness of their wills]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **stubbornness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with their stubborn hearts]

Yahweh is speaking of how the people lived as if that were a path that they were walking along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they lived according to their own plans]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **counsels**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the way they themselves chose]

81.quote: ל֗וּ עַ֭מִּ⁠י שֹׁמֵ֣עַֽ לִ֑⁠י יִ֝שְׂרָאֵ֗ל בִּ⁠דְרָכַ֥⁠י יְהַלֵּֽכוּ
81.text: Yahweh is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling, a deep longing for Israel to obey. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. If not, you could say what Yahweh was feeling. Alternate translation: [How I long for my people to listen to me and for Israel to follow my ways]

Yahweh is speaking of how a person lives as if that were a **way** or path that the person was walking along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Israel would live according to my commands]

Here, **hand** represents Yahweh’s power and ability to act. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I would use my power]

The pronoun **him** refers to Yahweh. Even though Yahweh is speaking in the first person, he refers to himself in the third person here. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [would cringe before Yahweh]

Here, **time** represents the duration of their fate or condition. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and their punishment would last forever]

The pronouns **he** and **him** refer to Yahweh and Israel respectively. Even though Yahweh is speaking in the first person, he uses the third person here. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [I would feed Israel]

Here, **fat** represents the best and richest portion of something. Yahweh is speaking as if the finest wheat had a rich fat. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with the finest wheat]
Yahweh is using this possessive form to describe the richest part of the wheat. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the richest part of the wheat]

The pronoun **you** marks an abrupt shift from the third person **him** earlier in the verse to the second person. Both refer to the people of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [I would satisfy them with honey from the rock]

82.text:
# Psalm 82 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 82, like Psalm 81, seems to have been written for the occasion of one of the annual festivals, when many Israelites would have been at the temple in Jerusalem and heard its message of challenge and warning. It depicts God convening an assembly of rulers and passing judgment against them for failing to ensure justice.

1. God takes his place of authority in this assembly (1)
2. God demands that these rulers judge justly (2–4)
3. God passes judgment against these rulers (5–7)
4. The psalmist asks God to judge the earth (8)

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

### Translation of the term “gods”

The psalmist describes these rulers as “gods” in verse 1, and God says to them “You are gods” in verse 6. That has led many interpreters to conclude that this is a depiction of a divine assembly in heaven. However, that same Hebrew term can also mean “judges,” as in Exodus 21:6 and 22:8, so other interpreters understand this as a depiction of God summoning human judges and indicting them for not upholding justice. If possible, translate this psalm in a way that allows for either interpretation. The UST models one way to do that.

### Parallelisms

Parallelisms arise when two clauses occur together which mean the same thing. The second clause emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea using different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine the phrases and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the clauses with a word that shows that the second clause is repeating the first one and not saying something additional. See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of clauses in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing.

The expression **is standing** was a common expression meaning to take one’s position of authority in order to act. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [takes his position of authority]
The term “god,” when applied to a being other than Yahweh, can refer to an idol, but, as here, it can also refer to any lesser spirit being. Alternate translation: [in the midst of the spirit beings]

Asaph is using the question form to rebuke these judges for their corrupt rulings. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for this purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or exclamations. Alternate translation: [You must stop judging with injustice and stop making rulings that favor the wicked!]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **injustice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [unjustly]

The expression **lift up the faces of the wicked** was a common expression meaning “to show partiality or favoritism.” If it would be helpful for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and show partiality to wicked people]

Asaph is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [people who are wicked]

Asaph is using the adjectives **poor**, **orphan**, and **destitute** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [the poor people and the fatherless children; vindicate the poor people and the destitute people]

Asaph is using the adjectives **poor**, **needy**, and **wicked** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [the poor people and the needy people; deliver them from the hand of the wicked people]

Here, **hand** represents the power or control of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the control of the wicked people]

The terms **do not know** and **do not understand** mean similar things. Asaph is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [They are completely ignorant]

Asaph is speaking of these judges as if they were walking around in a dark place. He means that they are morally ignorant and do not act according to what is right. Your language may have a comparable expression that you could use in your translation, or you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they go about in moral ignorance]

Asaph is speaking of the moral and social order of the world as if it had **foundations** like those under a building. He means that because of these unjust judges, the stability of the world is being destroyed. You may have a comparable expression in your language that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [All the stability and order of the world is being undermined]

The phrase **are shaken** is a passive verbal form. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you could state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [shake] or [are trembling]

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. In that case, you could express what God said as an indirect quotation. Alternate translation: [I said that you are gods]

Asaph is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I said** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Yahweh is the one speaking. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [I myself said]
See the discussion of the term “gods” in the introduction to this psalm.

Asaph is speaking of these judges as if they were **sons of the Most High**, that is, as if they belonged to God’s family. He means that God had given them a share in his authority. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and those who share the authority of the Most High]

Asaph uses the word **But** here to introduce a contrast between the divine status declared in the previous verse and the mortality declared here. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [However,]

The point of this comparison is that despite being called gods, these judges will die just as any ordinary human person does. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point clear. Alternate translation: [like any mortal person, you will die]

The point of this comparison is that these judges will lose their position and power just as earthly rulers do when they are defeated. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like any other ruler, you will fall from power]

Asaph is using the imperative forms **Arise** and **judge** to make a request of God. If your language does not use the imperative to make requests, you could express this as a request or wish. Alternate translation: [Please arise, God, and judge the earth]

The word translated as **you** before **you will inherit** represents an independent pronoun used for emphasis in the original language, in addition to the pronoun expressed within the verb. If it would be helpful in your language, you could indicate the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [you yourself will inherit]

Asaph is speaking of God’s sovereign ownership and authority over the nations as if God would **inherit** them as property. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this as a comparison or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you possess authority over all the nations]

Asaph is giving a reason for what he said in the previous phrase. He asked God to judge the earth and he now gives the reason: God possesses authority over all the nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this connection more explicit. Alternate translation: [because you have authority over all the nations]

83.text:
# Psalm 83 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 83 is a psalm of supplication or lament. It is such a desperate, urgent plea for help that it presents only three of the basic elements of that type of psalm. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Cry for help (1)
2. Description of troubles (2–8)
3. Petition (9–18)

Many interpreters believe that this psalm was written during the reign of Jehoshaphat when a large army composed of Moabites, Ammonites, and Meunites, supported by other nations, invaded and attacked Judah, as described in [2 Chronicles 20:1–30](../2ch/20/01.md). Yahweh inspired a Levite from the clan of Asaph to reassure the king and nation that he would defeat these invaders. The outcome was exactly what this psalm envisions and pleads for: “the fear of God was on all the kingdoms of the lands when they heard how Yahweh had fought with the enemies of Israel.” It may be helpful to read this passage before translating this psalm.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **silence**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [may you not be silent]

The expressions **do not be still** and **do not be quiet** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [do not remain inactive]

The psalmist is using the imperative forms **do not be still** and **do not be quiet** to make a request to God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a natural form for making a request. Alternate translation: [please do not be still, and please do not be quiet]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [do not remain silent and inactive]

The psalmist uses **For behold** to introduce the reason for his plea in verse 1. He is saying that God should take action because the enemies are rising up. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make the connection clearer.

The word **behold** is used here to draw attention to what follows. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this with a word or phrase that serves this purpose, or you could leave it untranslated. Alternate translation: [look]

The phrase **the ones hating you** refers to the same people as **your enemies** earlier in the verse. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this explicit. Alternate translation: [those same enemies of yours]
See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [your enemies are boldly rising up against you]

The expression **lift up the head** is an idiom that means to act boldly or defiantly. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [act defiantly]

See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [they are craftily plotting against your cherished people]
The pronoun **They** refers to the enemies mentioned in verse 2. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this explicit. Alternate translation: [Your enemies are cunning]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **counsel**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in counseling together]

The phrase **your treasured ones** refers to the people of Israel, whom God values. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this explicit. Alternate translation: [the Israelites, your treasured people]
The pronoun **They** refers to the enemies mentioned in verses 2–3. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this explicit. Alternate translation: [These enemies have said]

Here, **the name of Israel** represents the nation of Israel itself and its existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the nation of Israel]

If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that no one may remember the name of Israel]

The word **For** introduces the reason why the psalmist said what he said in verses 3–4. The enemies are conspiring because they want to destroy Israel. Use a connector in your language that introduces a reason. Alternate translation: [This is because]
The pronoun **they** refers to the nations listed in verses 6–8. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this explicit. Alternate translation: [these nations have conspired]

Here, **heart** represents the will or intention. The psalmist is saying that these enemies have **conspired** with unified purpose. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with one purpose]

The expression **they have cut a covenant** is an idiom that means they have made a formal agreement or alliance. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they have allied themselves]

The psalmist is leaving out the verb that would be expected in this phrase. The verb can be supplied from the context in verse 5. If it would be helpful in your language, you could supply this verb. Alternate translation: [the tents of Edom and the Ishmaelites have cut a covenant against you]

Here, **the tents of Edom** represents the people of Edom who live in those tents. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people of Edom]

The psalmist is leaving out the verb that would be expected in this phrase. The verb can be supplied from the context in verse 5. If it would be helpful in your language, you could supply this verb. Alternate translation: [Gebal and Ammon and Amalek have cut a covenant against you]
The pronoun **they** refers to Assyria, mentioned earlier in the verse. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this explicit. Alternate translation: [the Assyrians]

# Psalm 84 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

While Psalm 84 is not identified explicitly in its superscription as a “song of ascents” like Psalms 120–134, it nevertheless seems to be that same type of psalm. It encourages and praises going to the temple in Jerusalem. Apparently writing from the perspective of his arrival at the temple, the psalmist describes how he longed to be there and the journey he made to get there. The superscription indicates that a Korahite Levite wrote this psalm, but it was evidently one who lived and worked at some distance from Jerusalem.

1. Celebration of the temple (1–4)
2. The journey to the temple (5–7)
3. Prayer for Yahweh to preserve the king (8–9)
4. Celebration of Yahweh, the God of this temple, for his goodness (10–12)

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]
See how you translated the term **Gittith** in the superscription to Psalm 8.

The psalmist is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of amazement at the beauty of God’s dwelling place. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Your dwellings are so lovely]

The psalmist is using one part of himself, his **soul**, to mean all of himself in the act of longing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I long and even faint]

The terms **longs** and **faints** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [desperately yearns]

The psalmist is speaking of **my heart and my flesh** as if they were living things that could **cry out**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my heart and my flesh groan loudly]

The psalmist is referring to all of himself by naming two major components, **my heart** and **my flesh**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [with my whole being I]

Here, **my heart** represents the psalmist’s desires and feelings. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [my inner self]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and the swallow has found a nest for herself]

The psalmist is using a phrase **The happinesses of** that expresses a strong feeling of joy or blessing. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Oh, how happy are]
The psalmist is speaking of the temple of Yahweh as if it were a **house** in which he lived. Alternate translation: [your temple]
See how you translated the phrase “The happinesses of” in the previous verse.

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the person]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [you make him strong]

The psalmist is speaking of the desire for pilgrimage as if there were **highways** in the hearts of the people. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They desire to make the journey to your temple] or [Pilgrimage journeys are in their thoughts]

The pronoun **their** refers to the kind of person described as **the man** in the first part of the verse. The psalmist shifts from singular to plural because he is speaking of everyone who fits this description. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [are in his heart]

Here, **their heart** represents the desires and intentions of the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [are in their thoughts]

The psalmist is speaking of the pilgrims as if they transformed the Valley of Baca into **a spring** of water. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they find water there] or [they make it a place of refreshment]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **blessings**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with good things from God]
The pronoun **They** refers to the pilgrims described in verses 5 and 6 who are traveling to God’s temple. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The pilgrims go]

The psalmist is using **from strength to strength** as a common expression meaning that the pilgrims grow increasingly strong as they travel. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with ever-increasing strength]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **prayer**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what I pray]

The psalmist is speaking of God as if he were a **shield** that protects in battle. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [our protector] or [the one who shields us]

Here, **the face** represents the person of the anointed king. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your anointed one]

The psalmist is using the adjective **anointed** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [your anointed one]

The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for the request made in verses 8 and 9. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]
