If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wickedness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the tents of wicked people]

Here, **the tents** represents the homes and dwellings of wicked people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the homes of wickedness]

The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a further reason for the psalmist’s desire to be in God’s courts. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh God as if he were **a sun** that gives life and light and **a shield** that protects from harm. If these images communicate well in your language, please use them. If not, you could express them as comparisons. Alternate translation: [the one who gives us life like the sun and protects us like a shield]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **favor** and **glory**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [treats people favorably and honors them]

The psalmist is using the adjective **good** as a noun to mean a certain kind of thing. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [good things]

The psalmist is speaking of how a person lives as if that were a path that the person was **walking** along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ones living in blamelessness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **blamelessness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [blamelessly]

The psalmist is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of joy or blessing. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [oh, how happy is]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the person]

85.text:
# Psalm 85 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 85 is a psalm of supplication or lament. In its core, it presents three of the basic elements of that type of psalm. (See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.) It was most likely written shortly after the first group of Judeans returned from exile in Babylon. Its first part is a recollection of how Yahweh has begun to restore the people, and its concluding part is a vision of how he will do that comprehensively. The supplication in the middle is the psalmist’s plea to him to move the people from their difficult present into their hopeful future in light of what he has already done for them in the past.

1. Recollection of Yahweh’s restoration of the people (1–3)
2. Cry for help (4–7)
3. Petition (7)
4. Statement of trust (8)
5. Prediction of Yahweh’s future mercies (9–13)

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. The psalmist is using the question form to express a plea. If you would not use the question form for this function in your language, you could translate this as a statement or an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Please do not prolong your anger to every generation.]

Up to this point, the psalmist has been speaking on behalf of the community, using **us** and **we**. Now the psalmist shifts to speaking individually, saying **me**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could clarify this. Alternate translation: [Let me, the psalmist, hear]

# Psalm 88 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 88 is a psalm of supplication or lament. Because the psalmist is feeling such despair, he does not make a statement of trust or a vow of praise, and he does not even make a petition. (The psalmist observes instead in verses 10–12 that if Yahweh does not heal him, he will not be able to praise him.) So only two of the basic elements of a psalm of supplication are present. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Cry for help (1–2)
2. Description of troubles (3–8)
3. Cry for help (9–14)
4. Description of troubles (15–18)

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

### Who wrote this psalm?

The superscription to Psalm 88 says that it is both a “psalm of the sons of Korah” and a “maskil of Heman the Ezrahite.” The explanation for this is probably that the first part of the superscription belongs at the end of Psalm 87 (whose superscription attributes it to “the sons of Korah”). See the discussion of this in the introduction to the book of Psalms. As that discussion indicates, there is significant movement among biblical scholars toward seeing the musical instructions at the start of many psalm inscriptions as subscriptions to the previous psalms. However, published versions of the Bible do not yet tend to present them that way. Unless there is a Bible translation in your region that does, we recommend that you follow the current approach and retain both attributions in this superscription. The UST models one way to do that.

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a **maskil**. Since the meaning of this word is not certain, you may wish to represent it in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language. See the discussion of that term in the Introduction to Psalms.

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

The phrase that the ULT translates as **Weakness of Afflicting** could be the name of the tune of this psalm. It might also be a musical instruction See how you translated the term **Weakness** in the superscription to Psalm 53. (The addition of the term **Afflicting** here seems to refer to what the psalmist says in verse 9, “My eye mourns from affliction.”) Alternate translation: [perform this psalm about affliction in a minor key] or [perform this psalm about affliction in a somber tone]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [saving me]

The psalmist is referring to all times by naming two extremes, **day** and **night**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all the time I cry out]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Let my prayer come to your face, indeed, please listen to what I cry out to you]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **prayer**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what I pray]
Here, **to your face** represents being in front of God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [into your presence]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as ‘please’ to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please pay attention to my cry]
The psalmist is using the term **ear** to mean hearing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [listen]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **cry**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to what I cry out]

The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because my soul is full of troubles]

The psalmist is using the term **soul** to mean the entire person from the perspective of his spiritual and emotional existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [my whole being]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **troubles**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [troubling things]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if his life were a journey that had nearly arrived at **Sheol**, which is the name of the realm of the dead. The expression **I am reckoned** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [People reckon me]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if the dead were literally going down into **the pit** which associated with Sheol, the realm of the dead. 89.text:
# Psalm 89 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 89 is a psalm of supplication or lament. It appears to have been written shortly after the destruction of Jerusalem to protest that while Yahweh had promised that David’s descendants would always rule as kings, and Yahweh had the power to make sure that happened, he allowed enemies to destroy Jerusalem and depose the king. The psalmist uses three of the basic elements of a psalm of supplication. (See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.) However, before he does that, the psalmist praises Yahweh for his power, and he cites his covenant with David as grounds for praying for restoration. These two first parts of the psalm correspond roughly to the other two basic elements of a psalm of supplication, a vow of praise and a statement of trust.

1. Praise of Yahweh’s power and greatness (1–18)
2. Yahweh’s covenant with David (19–37)
3. Description of troubles (38–45)
4. Cry for help (46–49)
5. Petition (50–51)

Verse 52 is not part of the original psalm. It is a doxology (an expression of praise to God) that the editors of the book of Psalms added to mark the end of Book Three of the psalms. See how you translated the similar doxologies in [41:13](../041/013.md) and [72:18–20](../072/018.md).

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a **maskil**. Since the meaning of this word is not certain, you may wish to represent it in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language. See the discussion of that term in the Introduction to Psalms.

89.quote: חַֽסְדֵ֣י יְ֭הוָה עוֹלָ֣ם אָשִׁ֑ירָה לְ⁠דֹ֥ר וָ⁠דֹ֓ר ׀ אוֹדִ֖יעַ אֱמוּנָתְ⁠ךָ֣ בְּ⁠פִֽ⁠י

90.text:
# Psalm 90 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 90 is a “wisdom psalm.” It instructs people how to be wise by honoring Yahweh and obeying him. (See the discussion of the types of psalms in the Introduction to Psalms.)

This psalm is a poem, the words to a song, and so the ULT sets its lines farther to the right on the page than ordinary text in order to show that they are poetry.

1. God’s eternity and human mortality (1–6)
2. People perish when God punishes them for sin (7–12)
3. A prayer for God’s mercy and favor (13–17)

The first part of verse 1, “A prayer of Moses, the man of God,” is the superscription to this psalm. Format it in the way that you have decided to format the other superscriptions in the book of Psalms.

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

### Singular “you” and “your”

The pronouns “you” and “your” are singular throughout this psalm because Moses is addressing Yahweh directly. So use the singular forms of those pronouns in your translation if your language marks a distinction between singular and plural “you.”

### Exclusive “we,” “us,” and “our”

The pronouns “we,” “us,” and “our” are exclusive throughout this psalm because Moses is speaking to Yahweh on behalf of the Israelites. So use the exclusive forms of those pronouns in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Here the superscription is providing some background information to remind readers who Moses was. The expression **man of God** is used to indicate that Moses was associated with God in a special way. Alternate translation: [of Moses, who represented God in his covenant with the Israelites]

Moses is speaking as if God were actually a **habitation** or place for the Israelites to live. He means that God has protected the Israelites, just as the walls of a home provide shelter. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you have protected us]

As the introduction to this psalm discusses, the pronoun **you** is singular here and throughout the psalm because Moses is addressing Yahweh directly. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Moses is using **in generation and generation** as a common expression of his culture to mean “in every generation.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in every generation] or [throughout all generations]

90.quote: בְּ⁠טֶ֤רֶם ׀ הָ֘רִ֤ים יֻלָּ֗דוּ וַ⁠תְּח֣וֹלֵֽל אֶ֣רֶץ וְ⁠תֵבֵ֑ל
90.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Consider how you have decided as a translation team to represent Hebrew poetry in your translation, here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Before you created anything at all on the earth]

90.quote: בְּ⁠טֶ֤רֶם ׀ הָ֘רִ֤ים יֻלָּ֗דוּ וַ⁠תְּח֣וֹלֵֽל אֶ֣רֶץ וְ⁠תֵבֵ֑ל
90.text: Moses is speaking as if the **mountains** on earth had actually been **born** and as if God had actually **brought forth**, that is, given birth to, the **earth** and the **world**. He means that God created these things. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Before you created the mountains or formed the earth and the world]

The terms **earth** and **world** mean similar things. Moses is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [the entire earth]

Moses is referring to all of time by naming two extremes, eternity past and eternity future. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [throughout all of time]

As the ULT indicates by using brackets, the verb here is understood, so translators must decide what tense best fits the context. It would be conventional in many languages to use the past tense when describing something that was true a long time ago, so many languages might ordinarily say “you were God.” But Moses means that Yahweh was God long ago, that he is God now, and that he will continue to be God forever into the future. To convey this, the ULT uses the present tense, saying **you are God**. Decide what tense would best convey the meaning in your own language.

90.quote: תָּשֵׁ֣ב אֱ֭נוֹשׁ עַד־דַּכָּ֑א וַ֝⁠תֹּ֗אמֶר שׁ֣וּבוּ בְנֵי־אָדָֽם
90.text: Moses is describing one event, **man** returning to **dust**, before describing another event that preceded it, God telling him to do that. If it would be helpful your language, you may wish to relate these events in the order in which they happened. Alternate translation: [You say, “Return, sons of man,” and you cause man to return to dust]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people]

Moses is using the expression **return to dust** to mean “die.” It is an allusion to the way that God formed the first man from the dust of the ground, as described in [Genesis 2:7](../../gen/02/07.md). This is one of several mild or poetic ways in which Moses refers to death in this psalm. Your language may have a similar expression that you can use here in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [You cause people to pass away… Pass away] or [You cause people to die … It is time for you to die]

The psalmist is using **sons of man** as a common expression of his culture to mean “human beings.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [human beings]
Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an affirmation. Alternate translation: [Indeed]

Moses is using the common expression of his culture **in your eyes** to mean “in your perspective.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in your perspective]

90.quote: כְּ⁠י֣וֹם אֶ֭תְמוֹל כִּ֣י יַעֲבֹ֑ר וְ⁠אַשְׁמוּרָ֥ה בַ⁠לָּֽיְלָה
90.text: The point of these comparisons is that both of the times that Moses mentions seem very short to people: **the day before**, once it is over, and a **watch in the night** that lasts only a few hours. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [seem very short, like yesterday, when it is over, or like a three-hour watch in the night]

The pronoun **them** refers to people, that is, to the “sons of man” whom Moses mentions in verse 3, not to the “thousand years” that he mentions in verse 4. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [You flood people away]

Moses is speaking as if God actually used a **flood** of water to sweep people **away** from the earth. He is using the image to convey the idea that God may cause people to die suddenly, unexpectedly, and with no recourse. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You bring people’s lives to a swift end]

Moses is speaking as if people were actually **sleep**. This could mean: (1) that Moses is using the term **sleep** as a mild way of referring to death. Alternate translation: [then they are dead] or (2) that Moses is illustrating the brevity of human life by comparing it to **sleep** that lasts only a few hours and then is over. Alternate translation: [their lives are short, like a few hours of sleep that soon end]
The pronoun **it** refers to the life of a human being as compared to grass. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [like grass, a person’s life passes along]

The point of this comparison is that just as grass **passes along** through its brief cycle of life, so human life lasts for only a short time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [A person’s life is short, like grass that quickly passes along]

90.quote: בַּ֭⁠בֹּקֶר יָצִ֣יץ וְ⁠חָלָ֑ף לָ֝⁠עֶ֗רֶב יְמוֹלֵ֥ל וְ⁠יָבֵֽשׁ
90.text: Moses says that grass lives for only a single day, lasting only from **morning** to **evening**, as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [Grass blossoms and grows for only a short time; very soon it withers and dries up]

The terms **withers** and **dries up** mean similar things. Moses is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [it dries up completely]

Moses is referring to God’s **nose** as a common expression of his culture to mean God’s anger. Your language and culture may also associate anger with a particular part of the body. If so, in your translation you could use an expression involving that part of the body. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [by your anger we perish, and by your wrath we are terrified]

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to reverse the order of the phrases, since people would first be **terrified** by God’s **wrath** and then they would **perish** when he destroyed them in his anger. Alternate translation: [by your wrath we are terrified, and by your anger we perish]
If your language does not use this passive form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and your wrath terrifies us]

90.quote: שת עֲוֺנֹתֵ֣י⁠נוּ לְ⁠נֶגְדֶּ֑⁠ךָ עֲ֝לֻמֵ֗⁠נוּ לִ⁠מְא֥וֹר פָּנֶֽי⁠ךָ
90.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could connect the phrases with a word to show that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [You have studied our iniquities, yes, you have carefully examined our hidden sin]

Moses is speaking as if God had actually **set** the **iniquities** of the Israelites in front of him where he could see them. The idea is that God is paying attention to the wrong things that the Israelites have done, and God is punishing them for doing those things, as the previous verse indicates. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You examine our iniquities]

Moses is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [yes, you have set our hidden sin in the light of your face]

The term **hidden** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [our sin that we have hidden]

Moses is speaking as if there were actually **light** shining from God’s **face** that allowed him to see clearly what was in front of him. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [where you can clearly see it]

Moses is using **our days turn** as a common expression of his culture to describe **days** turning into nights, that is, to describe the light of day fading as evening approaches. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all of our days fade away] or [all of our days end]

Moses is using the parts of a lifetime, the **days** of which it consists, to mean an entire lifetime. So in this image, he is speaking of a lifetime that consists of many days as if it were a single day. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [our lifetimes fade away] or [our lifetimes end]

In this phrase as well, Moses is using the parts of a lifetime, the **years** of which it consists, to mean an entire lifetime. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [our lives end]

The point of this comparison could be: (1) that just as a **sigh** is a brief utterance, so people come to the **end** of their **years** after only a brief time, Alternate translation: [after only a brief time] or (2) that just as someone might **sigh** when they are sad, so we end our lives in despair. Alternate translation: [in sadness]

Moses is using **The days of our years** as a common expression of his culture to mean “our lifetimes.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [All our born days are 70 years] or [We humans tend to live for 70 years]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [or, if we are strong]
The pronoun **it** refers to the human lifetime. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [our lifetime passes quickly]

Moses is referring to death in a poetic way by using the phrase **fly away**. Depending on what is helpful in your language, you could use a polite or poetic way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [and we depart] or [and then we die]

Moses is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Since Moses says “we” and “us” throughout the rest of the psalm, you could say “we” here in your translation. Alternate translation: [We ought to know the power of your anger, and we ought to know your wrath according to your fear!]
See how you translated the term **nose** in verse 7. Alternate translation: [your anger]

Moses is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [or who knows your wrath according to your fear]

Moses is using the possessive form **your fear** to describe not fear that God has, but fear or reverent respect that people have for God. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [or who fears you in a way that accords with your wrath] or [and we ought to fear you in a way that accords with your wrath against sin]

Moses is speaking as if he actually wanted God to help the Israelites **number** or count how many **days** they would be alive. The implication is that if they did this, they would realize how few days they actually have to live. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [So help us to recognize how short our lives actually are]

Moses may be using the expression **bring in** to speak of the results of learning to number one’s days as if they were actually a harvest of crops that one had cultivated. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that we might acquire a heart of wisdom]
Here the **heart** represents the thoughts. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that we might acquire a mind of wisdom]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wisdom**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [that we might acquire a wise mind] or [that we might understand how to live wisely]

Moses is using an emphatic imperative form here. It may be appropriate in your culture for someone to address God using an emphatic imperative, and your language may have such a form that you can use in your translation. But if people in your culture would not consider it appropriate for someone to address God in this way, you could translate this as a request rather than as a command. Alternate translation: [Please return, Yahweh.]

This could mean: (1) that Moses wants Yahweh to stop being angry and stop punishing the Israelites. He would be speaking as if Yahweh’s anger were literally a place from which he could **Return**. Alternate translation: [Stop being angry, Yahweh!] (2) that Moses wants Yahweh to abide peacefully among his people, protecting them and blessing them. This would be an allusion to the prayer that Moses always prayed in the wilderness when the cloud of Yahweh stopped moving and the Israelites made camp, as recorded in [Numbers 10:36](../../num/10/36.md), “Return, Yahweh, to the multitudes of the thousands of Israel.” Alternate translation: [Dwell peacefully among us, Yahweh.]

Moses is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be helpful in your language. Alternate translation: [Until when will you continue to be angry with us] or [For how long will you continue to be angry with us]

Moses is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I hope that your anger will not last long.]

Moses is speaking of himself and his fellow Israelites in the third person as **your servants** to show humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a humble form in the first person. Alternate translation: [us, your servants]

Moses is speaking as if he actually wanted God to **Satisfy** the Israelites **in the morning**, that is, at the beginning of an actual day. He could mean: (1) that he wants God to be eager to treat the Israelites mercifully. He would be using the expression **in the morning** by allusion to the way that people get up early in the morning to do something they are eager to do. Alternate translation: [eagerly] or [soon]; (2) that he wants God to treat the Israelites mercifully after a time of trouble. He would be speaking of that time of trouble as if it had actually been a night and of the time after it as if it were actually a morning. Alternate translation: [after this time of trouble]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with all the ways you are faithful to your covenant]

The terms **rejoice** and **be glad** mean similar things. Moses is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be helpful for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [and we will rejoice greatly] or [and we will be very glad]

Moses is using the term **days** to refer to a specific time, the human lifetime, since time is made up of days. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for all of the rest of our lives]

Moses is saying that the Israelites will rejoice for **all** of the rest of their lives as a generalization for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [throughout our lives]

Moses is using the terms **days** and **years** to refer to specific times, since time is made up of days and years. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. However, since the Israelites were **afflicted** and did experience **trouble** for a specific number of days and years, you may decide to retain those terms in your translation. Alternate translation: [for the same amount of time that you have afflicted us, yes, for the same amount of time that we have experienced trouble] or [for as many days as you have afflicted us, yes, for as many years as we have experienced trouble]

Moses is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be helpful in your language. Alternate translation: [yes, make us glad for as many years as we have seen trouble]

Moses is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be helpful in your language. Alternate translation: [May your work be seen by your servants, and may your majesty be seen by their sons]

If your language does not use this passive form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [May your servants see your work, and may their sons see your majesty]

Moses is speaking about himself and his fellow Israelites in the third person as **your servants** to show humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a humble form in the first person. Alternate translation: [May your work be seen by us, your servants] or [May we, your servants, see your work]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **majesty**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and may their sons recognize how majestic you are]
Moses is using the term **sons** to mean “descendants.” Alternate translation: [to their descendants]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **favor**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [May the Lord our God favor us]

Here, **hands** represent the capacity to do something. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the work that we do … indeed, the work that we do]

91.text:
# Psalm 91 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 91 is a “psalm of trust.” (See the discussion of the types of psalms in the General Introduction to Psalms.)

This psalm is a poem, the words to a song, and so the ULT sets its lines farther to the right on the page than ordinary text in order to show that they are poetry.

1. The psalmist describes how Yahweh protects those who trust him (1–13)
2. Yahweh describes how he protects those who trust him (14–16)

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

### Singular “you” and “your”

The pronouns “you” and “your” are singular in verses 1–13 because the psalmist is speaking individually to people whom he wants to encourage to trust Yahweh. So use the singular forms of those pronouns in your translation if your language marks a distinction between singular and plural “you.”

The psalmist is speaking as if the **Most High**, that is, God, were actually a **shelter** in which a person could live. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The one who depends on the Most High for protection]

The psalmist is using this expression as a title for God. Your language may have a comparable title that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. If you have already translated Psalm 18, see how you translated this title in [Psalms 18:13](../018/013.md). Alternate translation: [God Most High] or [the Supreme God]

The psalmist is speaking as if God actually had a **shadow**. He is using the image to represent care, the way a shadow provides a cool place to rest in hot climates. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [will continually experience Shaddai’s care]
The word **Shaddai** is a name for God. If you have already translated Psalm 68, see how you translated this name in [Psalms 68:14](../068/014.md). Alternate translation: [the Almighty]

91.quote: אֹמַ֗ר לַֽ֭⁠יהוָה מַחְסִ֣⁠י וּ⁠מְצוּדָתִ֑⁠י אֱ֝לֹהַ֗⁠י אֶבְטַח־בּֽ⁠וֹ
91.text: The word translated **to** could indicate: (1) that the psalmist is saying this to Yahweh. You may wish to use second-person pronouns to indicate this. Alternate translation: [I will say to Yahweh, “You are my refuge and my fortress; you are my God, I trust in you”]; (2) that the psalmist is saying this about Yahweh. You may wish to use third-person pronouns to indicate this. Alternate translation: [I will say regarding Yahweh, “He is my refuge and my fortress; he is my God, I trust in him”]

The psalmist is speaking as if Yahweh were actually a **refuge** and a **fortress**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The source of my safety and my protection]

The terms **refuge** and **fortress** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be helpful for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [The one who keeps me completely safe]

As the Introduction to this psalm discusses, the pronoun **you** is singular here and throughout the psalm because the psalmist is speaking individually to people whom he wants to encourage to trust Yahweh. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **plague**. He means plagues in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [from traps that people set for you and from deadly plagues]

The psalmist is speaking as if the individual whom he is addressing were a bird or small animal that a **trapper** was trying to catch in a **snare**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from anyone who would deceptively try to harm you]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be helpful in your language. Alternate translation: [and he will also rescue you from the plague of calamities]

The psalmist is using this possessive form to describe a **plague** that would cause **calamities**, meaning, specifically, many deaths. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from every deadly plague]

These two phrases mean similar things. Translate them according to the decisions your team has made regarding translating parallelism in Hebrew poetry. Alternate translation: [He will cover you with his feathers, so you will be able to shelter under his wings] or [You will shelter under the cover of his wings]

The psalmist is speaking as if Yahweh were a bird and as if the individual he is addressing were one of its chicks. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He will protect you the way a bird protects its chicks by covering them with its wings]

The psalmist is speaking as if Yahweh’s **faithfulness** were actually a **shield** and **buckler**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [His faithfulness is dependable protection]

The word translated as **rampart** could refer to: (1) a wall around a city that would protect it from enemy attack. In that case, the psalmist would be using a shield that protected an individual soldier and a wall that protected an entire city to mean protection in general. Alternate translation: [His faithfulness is like military protection] or (2) a small shield. In that case, the psalmist would be using a large shield and a small shield together to mean all of the armor that a soldier would wear into battle. Alternate translation: [His faithfulness is like protective armor]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [He will faithfully protect you like a shield and buckler]

The psalmist is using things that might happen at **night** and during the **day** to mean things that might happen at any time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [of any dangers that might harm you at any time]

The psalmist is using this possessive form to describe something that might happen during the **night** that would cause a person to feel **terror**. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [of terrifying things that might happen during the night]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be helpful in your language. Alternate translation: [and you will not be afraid of the arrow that flies by day]

The psalmist is speaking of how an **arrow … flies** without indicating that this is the result of someone shooting it from a bow. This may create the impression that an arrow is a living thing that can fly on its own. If it would be helpful in your language, you could indicate the agent who is responsible for the arrow flying. Alternate translation: [of an arrow that someone might shoot at you]

The psalmist is using one type of weapon, an **arrow**, to mean weapons in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [of any weapon that someone might use to try to harm you]

91.quote: מִ֭⁠דֶּבֶר בָּ⁠אֹ֣פֶל יַהֲלֹ֑ךְ מִ֝⁠קֶּ֗טֶב יָשׁ֥וּד צָהֳרָֽיִם
91.text: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and you will not be afraid of the plague that walks in darkness, and you will not be afraid of the destruction that wastes at midday]

91.quote: מִ֭⁠דֶּבֶר בָּ⁠אֹ֣פֶל יַהֲלֹ֑ךְ מִ֝⁠קֶּ֗טֶב יָשׁ֥וּד צָהֳרָֽיִם
91.text: The psalmist is using things that might happen secretly and things that might happen openly to mean things that might happen in any way. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. It may be helpful to begin a new sentence here. Alternate translation: [You will not have to be concerned about dangers that you cannot see coming or those that you can see coming]

The psalmist is speaking of a **plague** as if it were a living thing that **walks** around. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that spreads]

The psalmist is speaking as if this plague were actually spreading from person to person **in the darkness**, meaning at night. He means that the plague spreads without people realizing it, in the same way that people do not realize what is happening in the darkness of night because they cannot see it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [invisibly]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **destruction**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [of destructive things that cause great damage]

Here, **midday**, the time when the sun is brightest in the sky, represents “openly and obviously.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in broad daylight]

91.quote: יִפֹּ֤ל מִ⁠צִּדְּ⁠ךָ֨ ׀ אֶ֗לֶף וּ⁠רְבָבָ֥ה מִ⁠ימִינֶ֑⁠ךָ אֵ֝לֶ֗י⁠ךָ לֹ֣א יִגָּֽשׁ
91.text: The psalmist is using a hypothetical situation to help his listeners appreciate how confidently they can trust God to protect them. Use the natural form in your language for expressing a hypothetical situation. Alternate translation: [Suppose a thousand fell at your side. Suppose a myriad fell at your right hand. Even then, it would not approach toward you]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [A thousand may fall at your side, and a myriad may fall at your right hand]

The psalmist is using the term **fall** to mean “die,” since people typically fall down when they die. Be sure that it is clear in your translation that he is not referring to people falling down accidentally. Alternate translation: [A thousand may die at your side, and a myriad may die at your right hand]

The pronoun **it** refers to any deadly danger such as the psalmist has described in verses 5 and 6. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [no deadly dangerous thing will approach toward you]

Since the psalmist says that people may die right next to and all around the individual whom he is addressing, he does not mean that danger will actually **not** even **approach** that individual. Rather, he is using this expression as an overstatement to mean that dangerous things will not kill him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [no deadly dangerous thing will kill you]

It might seem that the expression **observe with your eyes** contains extra information that would be unnatural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [observe]

The psalmist is using this possessive form to describe the **wicked** receiving a **recompense**, not the wicked giving a recompense to someone. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and see the wicked receiving their recompense]

The psalmist is speaking as if God were actually repaying the wicked an amount that was due to them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and see God paying the wicked back for what they have done] or [and see God punishing the wicked]

The psalmist is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [wicked people]

91.quote: אַתָּ֣ה יְהוָ֣ה מַחְסִ֑⁠י עֶ֝לְי֗וֹן שַׂ֣מְתָּ מְעוֹנֶֽ⁠ךָ
91.text: The psalmist is speaking as if Yahweh were actually a **refuge** in which a person could take shelter and a **dwelling** in which a person could live. See how you translated the expression “dwelling in the shelter” in [91:1](../091/001.md) and the expression “My refuge” in [91:2](../091/002.md). Alternate translation: [you are depending on Yahweh, the source of my safety, the Most High, for your protection]

91.quote: לֹֽא־תְאֻנֶּ֣ה אֵלֶ֣י⁠ךָ רָעָ֑ה וְ֝⁠נֶ֗גַע לֹא־יִקְרַ֥ב בְּ⁠אָהֳלֶֽ⁠ךָ
91.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The first phrase states the general idea, and then the second phrase gives a specific example. Translate these phrases according to the decisions your team has made regarding translating parallelism in Hebrew poetry. Alternate translation: [evil will not happen to you; no, a plague will not come near to your tent] or [bad things will not happen to you where you live]

91.quote: לֹֽא־תְאֻנֶּ֣ה אֵלֶ֣י⁠ךָ רָעָ֑ה וְ֝⁠נֶ֗גַע לֹא־יִקְרַ֥ב בְּ⁠אָהֳלֶֽ⁠ךָ
91.text: The psalmist is speaking of how **evil will not happen** and **a plague will not come near** without indicating that these are the results of Yahweh’s actions on behalf of those who trust in him. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate Yahweh’s agency explicitly here. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will prevent evil from happening to you; yes, he will keep plagues from coming near to your tent]
The psalmist is using one kind of home, a **tent**, to mean all kinds of homes. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your home]
The pronoun **he** refers to God. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [God will command]

The psalmist is speaking of the activities of the individual he is addressing as if they were **ways** or paths that the individual was walking along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in all of your activities]

The psalmist is using one harmful thing that might happen to a person, hitting his **foot** against a **stone**, to mean every kind of harmful thing that might happen to a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [so that harmful things do not happen to you]

The psalmist is using the word translated as **lest** to introduce an outcome that he does not want to happen. Because of this, he first reassures the person he is addressing that God’s angels will protect him so that this will not happen. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that avoiding this outcome is the purpose of the instruction. Alternate translation: [Otherwise, you might hit your foot against a stone] or [Otherwise, harmful things might happen to you]

91.quote: עַל־שַׁ֣חַל וָ⁠פֶ֣תֶן תִּדְרֹ֑ךְ תִּרְמֹ֖ס כְּפִ֣יר וְ⁠תַנִּֽין
91.text: The psalmist is not referring to a specific **lion**, **adder**, **young lion**, or **serpent**. He means such animals in general. It may be more natural in your language to express this meaning by using plural forms. Alternate translation: [You will tread on lions and adders; you will trample young lions and serpents]

91.quote: עַל־שַׁ֣חַל וָ⁠פֶ֣תֶן תִּדְרֹ֑ךְ תִּרְמֹ֖ס כְּפִ֣יר וְ⁠תַנִּֽין
91.text: The psalmist may be using the terms **tread** and **trample** to mean “defeat.” People in this culture would force defeated enemies to lie down and then place a foot on top of them to show how completely they had defeated them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You will defeat any lion or adder that attacks you; yes, you will defeat any young lion or serpent that attacks you]

91.quote: עַל־שַׁ֣חַל וָ⁠פֶ֣תֶן תִּדְרֹ֑ךְ תִּרְמֹ֖ס כְּפִ֣יר וְ⁠תַנִּֽין
91.text: The psalmist is using a hypothetical situation to help the individual he is addressing appreciate how Yahweh will protect him. Use a natural form in your language for expressing a hypothetical situation. To do that, it may be helpful to combine the two parallel phrases in this verse. Alternate translation: [Suppose a lion or a snake attacks you. Yahweh will enable you to defeat it, and it will not harm you] or [If a lion or a snake attacks you, you will defeat it and it will not harm you]

This is the beginning of a direct quotation from Yahweh. You may wish to indicate that in your translation, using a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says, “Because he clings to me”]

The psalmist assumes that his listeners will know that by **cling**, he means to cling to someone out of love and devotion. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [he is devoted to me]

The word **name** could refer to: (1) Yahweh as a person, since each person has a name. Alternate translation: [he knows me personally]; (2) Yahweh’s reputation, which reflects his character. Alternate translation: [he knows my character and so trusts me]

The psalmist assumes that his listeners will know that by **answer**, he means that Yahweh will help this individual. Yahweh will not simply speak back to the person in response to his **call** for help. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and I will help him]

The psalmist is using the term **days** to refer to a specific time, the human lifetime. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with a long life]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and I will cause him to experience me saving him]

92.text:
# Psalm 92 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 92 is a psalm of praise for God’s kindness and faithfulness. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/faithful]])

1. It is good to praise the Lord (1–4)
2. God’s works are great and his ways are deep (5–9)
3. God strengthens and honors the righteous (10–11)
4. The righteous will flourish (12–15)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Justice

God causes evil people to be destroyed and good people to be happy and useful, even after they grow old. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/justice]]; and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/evil]])
Here **name** represents God himself. If it would be clearer in your language, you could express this explicitly. Alternate translation: [and to sing praises to you]

The abstract noun **covenant faithfulness** refers to God’s faithful love for the people with whom he made a covenant. If your language does not use abstract nouns, you can translate this using another form. Alternate translation: [to proclaim in the morning that you are faithful to your covenant people]

The writer is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and to proclaim your truthfulness every night]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **truthfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and that you are truthful]

A **ten string** is a kind of musical instrument with multiple strings. If your readers would not be familiar with what a ten string is, you could use the name of a similar instrument that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [an instrument with ten strings]

Here, **your hands** represents the capability of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because of the things that you have accomplished]

Here the psalmist is speaking of God’s **thoughts** as if they were a deep pool of water because we cannot see or reach them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. If not, you could state this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [Your thoughts are like a deep pool to us]

The word **thoughts** is an abstract noun that refers to what someone thinks. Some languages may not use abstract nouns. If this is true in your language, you could translate this with a verb, such as “what you think.” Alternate translation: [The things you think] or [Your plans]

92.quote: אִֽישׁ־בַּ֭עַר לֹ֣א יֵדָ֑ע וּ֝⁠כְסִ֗יל לֹא־יָבִ֥ין אֶת־זֹֽאת
92.text: These two phrases **A brutish person does not know** and **a stupid one does not understand this** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [A foolish person neither knows nor understands this] or [The foolish person completely fails to understand this]

The psalmist is using the adjective **stupid** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [any stupid person]
The pronoun **this** refers to what the psalmist goes on to explain in verse 7 about wicked people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the following truth]

This is a simile that speaks of wicked people appearing and growing **like grass**. Grass springs up and spreads quickly but does not last long. This emphasizes that wicked people may seem to prosper for a while, but their success will be brief. Alternate translation: [When the wicked appear quickly and seem to be everywhere as grass does]

The words **they will be destroyed** express in passive form what Yahweh will do to the wicked. If your language does not use passive forms or if the passive form would be confusing here, you can translate this with an active form. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will destroy them completely]
The pronoun **they** refers to the wicked and evildoers. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the wicked and evildoers will be destroyed]

The psalmist is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [wicked people]

The expression **are exalted** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [will live on high]

This text uses the passive verb **will be scattered** without identifying who will do the action. The psalmist of the psalm may have written it this way to focus on what will happen to the evildoers rather than on who will scatter them. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state this in active form with God as the subject, as in the alternate translation. Alternate translation: [you will scatter all those who do evil]

Here, **horn** represents strength or power. The psalmist is describing how God has given him strength like that of a wild ox. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state plainly what the horn represents. Alternate translation: [But you have made me as strong as a wild ox]

Here the psalmist is speaking of himself as if he were an offering that is **saturated with fresh oil**. The abundance of oil represents God’s abundant blessing and the joy that he feels as God has made him able to defeat his enemies. Alternate translation: [you have richly blessed me] or [I am filled with joy]

Here **eye** and **ears** represent the whole person who sees and hears. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have seen my foes … I have heard]

92.quote: וַ⁠תַּבֵּ֥ט עֵינִ֗⁠י בְּ⁠שׁ֫וּרָ֥⁠י בַּ⁠קָּמִ֖ים עָלַ֥⁠י מְרֵעִ֗ים תִּשְׁמַ֥עְנָה אָזְנָֽ⁠י
92.text: Some scholars believe that these phrases imply what it is that the writer saw and heard. You could include this information if a translation of the Bible exists in your region that includes it. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT. Alternate translation: [My eye has looked on my foes, those rising up against me, as you defeat them; those doing evil my ears have heard as you punish them]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the palm tree** is resilient and long-lived, so is **The righteous one**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [The righteous one will be resilient and long-lived like a palm tree]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a cedar** is strong and admired for being tall and stately, so is **The righteous one**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [he will be strong and admired like a cedar tree in Lebanon]

The psalmist is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [Any righteous person] or [All righteous people]
The pronoun **he** refers to any righteous person. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [they will grow]

The psalmist uses the passive verb **are planted** and does not tell who has done the planting. You may need to state clearly who did the planting if your language does not use passive verbs in this way. Alternate translation: [Yahweh has planted them] or [Yahweh takes care of them as if they were trees that he had planted]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if righteous people were actually **planted** trees growing in Yahweh’s house. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. If not, you could state this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [they flourish like trees] or [they live securely]

The pronoun **They** refers to righteous people, who are those who are planted in Yahweh’s house. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Righteous people are planted]

Here the psalmist is speaking of righteous people as if they were plants that **flourish**, which means that they are strong and healthy. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this image differently or state this plainly without the image. Alternate translation: [they grow well] or [they prosper]

The psalmist is speaking of people who are faithful to God as if they were **fruit**-bearing trees. This image emphasizes how they continue to be productive and do good things. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They continue doing good things]
The pronoun **They** continues to refer to righteous people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Righteous people, like trees, bear fruit]

Here the psalmist speaks of **juicy and green** as if the righteous people were plants that are healthy and full of life. This metaphor compares their spiritual and physical well-being to the freshness of a flourishing plant. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state plainly what this means. Alternate translation: [they remain strong and healthy] or [they always do what pleases God]

If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [showing that] or [which shows that]

Here the psalmist speaks of Yahweh as if he were a **rock**, because a large rock can provide protection and safety. You could keep this image in your translation if it is clear, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated this in [Psalm 18:2](../018/002.md). Alternate translation: [the one who protects me]

Here the psalmist is speaking of **unrighteousness** as if it were a substance or object that could be present in or absent from someone. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he is always righteousness]

The phrase **no unrighteousness** uses two negative words to express a positive meaning. The psalmist is saying that God is completely righteous. If your language does not use double negatives, you could express this with a positive statement. Alternate translation: [and he is always righteousness]

93.text:
# Psalm 93 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 93 is a “worship psalm” about the power of Yahweh.

1. Yahweh reigns in glory and strength (1–2)
2. Yahweh is stronger than chaos and opposition (3–4)
3. Yahweh is trustworthy and holy (5)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Yahweh’s power

Yahweh is all powerful; He even controls the ocean.
Verses 1 and 4 of this psalm refer to Yahweh as “he” and verses 2,3, and 5 refer to him as “you.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use “you” throughout the psalm, as in the UST.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **majesty**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [he is majestic]

93.quote: גֵּא֪וּת לָ֫בֵ֥שׁ לָבֵ֣שׁ יְ֭הוָה עֹ֣ז הִתְאַזָּ֑ר
93.text: Here the psalmist is speaking as if **majesty** and **strength** were actually garments that Yahweh **wears**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he displays his majesty; Yahweh’s strength is obvious for all to see]

The terms **wears** and **girds himself with** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Yahweh wraps strength all around himself]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is obviously powerful]

The expression **is firmly established** contains a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [you have firmly established the world]

The expression **be moved** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [no one can ever move it]

The expression **is established** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [You established your throne in ancient times]
Here, **throne** represents royal authority and rule. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Your kingship]

The word translated as **seas** here refers to any kind of moving water; in other contexts it is translated as “rivers” or “floods” (See: “the River” in [Psalms 72:8](../072/008.md)), but “seas” has been chosen here because seas, not rivers, have **pounding waves**.

The psalmist is speaking of **the seas** as if they were living things that could lift their voices. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the seas make a roaring noise]

93.quote: מִ⁠קֹּל֨וֹת ׀ מַ֤יִם רַבִּ֗ים אַדִּירִ֣ים מִשְׁבְּרֵי־יָ֑ם אַדִּ֖יר בַּ⁠מָּר֣וֹם יְהוָֽה
93.text: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **Yahweh on high is mighty** before the comparisons **than the sounds of many waters** and **than the mighty breakers of the sea**. Alternate translation: [Yahweh on high is mightier than the sounds of many waters, than the mighty breakers of the sea]

By **breakers of the sea**, the psalmist means the waves of the sea that crash onto the shore. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [than the mighty waves of the sea crashing on land]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if God were actually in a place **on high**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who is greater than everything else]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if **holiness** were actually a decoration that **adorns** or beautifies the temple. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your house is beautiful because you are holy] or [your holiness is what attracts people to your house]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **holiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [your house is beautiful because you are holy]

The psalmist is using **length of days** as a common expression of his culture to mean “forever.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for always]

94.text:
# Psalm 94 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 94 is a prayer requesting that evil people be punished. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/evil]])

1. A cry for Yahweh’s justice (1–7)
2. Yahweh sees and will judge (8–11)
3. Yahweh disciplines and helps his people (12–15)
4. Yahweh is the refuge of the oppressed (16–23)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Justice

Evil people expect God to ignore their injustices. But God knows what they are doing and will punish them for their evil deeds. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/justice]])

Here, **God of vengeance, Yahweh, God of vengeance** the psalmist is using repetition for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, the God who avenges]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **vengeance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [God who avenges … God who avenges]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if God were actually a light that could **shine forth**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. If not, you could state this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [Reveal yourself] or [Let them see how majestic you are]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if God were actually someone who was sitting or lying down and needed to **rise up**. The psalmist means that God should take action to judge the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Take action] or [Act now]

Here, **the earth** represents all the people who live on the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [of all people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **recompense**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [pay back] or [punish]

The psalmist is using the adjective **proud** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [proud people]

94.quote: עַד־מָתַ֖י רְשָׁעִ֥ים ׀ יְהוָ֑ה עַד־מָ֝תַ֗י רְשָׁעִ֥ים יַעֲלֹֽזוּ
94.text: The psalmist is using the question form **Until when will the wicked, Yahweh, until when will the wicked rejoice** to express his frustration and to make an urgent appeal to God for action. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, the wicked have been rejoicing much too long.]

These two phrases **Until when will the wicked, Yahweh** and **until when will the wicked** are basically the same. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating it again. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. Or if it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, just how long will you allow the wicked to rejoice?]

The psalmist is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [wicked people]

The phrases **pour out** and **speak** express a single idea. The word **pour out** tells more about **speak**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [In large amounts, they speak]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **arrogance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [arrogant words]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **evil**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [evil actions]

The psalmist is speaking as if the wicked people were literally **crushing** God’s people with physical force. He means that they are oppressing them severely. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They oppress]

The psalmist is speaking of God’s people as if they were actually **your inheritance**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your own people]

Here, **the widow and the sojourner** and **the fatherless** represent vulnerable people in general, not specific individuals. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [widows and sojourners & they murder those without fathers]

The terms **kill** and **murder** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [They kill the widow, the sojourner, and the fatherless]
The pronoun **They** refers to the wicked people mentioned in the previous verses. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The wicked people say]

The implication is that the wicked people are thinking these thoughts silently to themselves rather than speaking them aloud to others. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [They say to themselves]

The implication is that God does not see or perceive what the wicked people are doing. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [does not see what we do … does not perceive what we do]

These two phrases **Yah does not see** and **the God of Jacob does not perceive** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Yahweh does not see, no, the God of Jacob does not perceive]

The psalmist is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You fools need to gain insight!]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **insight**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [will you behave insightfully]

94.quote: בִּ֭ינוּ בֹּעֲרִ֣ים בָּ⁠עָ֑ם וּ֝⁠כְסִילִ֗ים מָתַ֥י תַּשְׂכִּֽילוּ
94.text: These two phrases **Understand, stupid ones among the people** and **O fools, when will you have insight** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea in a different form. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Get insight and understanding, you stupid, foolish people!]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if God were actually **planting the ear**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The one creating the ear]

The psalmist is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [he certainly does hear!]

The psalmist is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [he certainly does observe!]

The psalmist is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [he will certainly rebuke you!]

The psalmist is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [The one teaching mankind certainly does not lack knowledge.]

Here, **nations** represents the people of all nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [people of all nations]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **knowledge**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Is there anything that the one teaching mankind does not know]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **thoughts**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the things that people are thinking]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if people’s thoughts were actually **vapor**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. If not, you could state this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [they are unimportant and useless]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **joys**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [How joyful is]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the person]

Here, **to give rest to him** marks this clause as the goal or purpose of God instructing and teaching the blessed person. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [which will allow him to have rest]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **days** that are characterized by **evil**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [during evil days]

The expression **a pit is dug** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language.
