If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [Yahweh digs a pit]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if God’s punishment of the wicked were actually **a pit** being dug. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh punishes the wicked]

94.quote: לֹא־יִטֹּ֣שׁ יְהוָ֣ה עַמּ֑⁠וֹ וְ֝⁠נַחֲלָת֗⁠וֹ לֹ֣א יַעֲזֹֽב
94.text: These two phrases **will not forsake his people** and **he will not abandon his inheritance** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will not forsake his people, no, he will not abandon his inheritance]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if the people of Israel were actually **his inheritance**. He means that they are the people who belong to God in a special way, like a treasured possession that is passed down in a family. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he will not abandon Yahweh’s own people]

The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [It will happen that]

Here, **judgment** represents “judges” or “the judicial system.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [judges will return to making right judgments]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **the right**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [being right]

The implication is that all the upright in heart will support and follow righteous judgment when it is restored. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and all the upright in heart are in favor of that]

The psalmist is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I cannot find anyone who will rise up for me against the evildoers.]

The psalmist is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I cannot find anyone who will stand up for me against the workers of wickedness.]

94.quote: מִֽי־יָק֣וּם לִ֭⁠י עִם־מְרֵעִ֑ים מִֽי־יִתְיַצֵּ֥ב לִ֝⁠י עִם־פֹּ֥עֲלֵי אָֽוֶן
94.text: These two phrases **Who will rise up for me against the evildoers** and **Who will stand up for me against the workers of wickedness** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Who will rise up for me against the evildoers? I say again, who will stand up for me against the workers of wickedness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wickedness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the people doing wicked things]

94.quote: לוּלֵ֣י יְ֭הוָה עֶזְרָ֣תָ⁠ה לִּ֑⁠י כִּ⁠מְעַ֓ט ׀ שָֽׁכְנָ֖ה דוּמָ֣ה נַפְשִֽׁ⁠י
94.text: The psalmist says **Unless Yahweh had been a help to me** to introduce an imaginary situation to help explain what would have happened without God’s help. Use a natural method in your language for introducing an imaginary situation. Alternate translation: [Only because Yahweh was a help to me, my soul did not shortly dwell in silence]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **help**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [had helped me]

The psalmist is using one part of a person, his **soul**, to mean all of him in the act of dying. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I]

The psalmist is referring to death in a polite way by using the phrase **would have dwelt in silence**. Depending on what is helpful in your language, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [would have been killed]

By **When I said**, the psalmist means “When I said to myself” or “When I thought to myself.” You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [When I said to myself]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if his life were actually **a foot that was slipping**. He means that he was in great trouble or danger. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am in big trouble] or [I need help]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Because you are faithful to your covenant, you]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **cares**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [When I am worried about many things]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **consolations**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [your console me, which makes my soul glad]
The psalmist is using **my soul** to represent all of himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [me]

94.quote: הַֽ֭⁠יְחָבְרְ⁠ךָ כִּסֵּ֣א הַוּ֑וֹת יֹצֵ֖ר עָמָ֣ל עֲלֵי־חֹֽק
94.text: The psalmist is using the question form to express that God cannot be allied with corrupt rulers. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You can have nothing to do with a throne of destruction, one who creates injustice by statute.]

Here, **throne** represents a ruler who has authority. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a ruler who destroys people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **destruction**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a throne that destroys]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **injustice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [one who creates unjust statutes]

The pronoun **They** refers to the corrupt rulers from the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Such thrones of destruction conspire together] or [Wicked rulers like that conspire together]

The psalmist is using **against the life of** as a common expression of his culture to mean “to kill” or “to destroy.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to kill the righteous]

The psalmist is using **innocent blood** as a common expression of his culture to mean “innocent people” or “people who do not deserve to die.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they condemn innocent people to death]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **righteous** person. He means righteous people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [all righteous people]

Here the psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were **a high tower** because that is a place of protection. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. If not, you could state this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [my protector]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and my God has been the rock]

The psalmist speaks of having God protect him as if God were a place where the psalmist could go to be safe. See how “rock” and “refuge” are translated in [Psalms 62:7](../062/007.md). Alternate translation: [and my God has kept me safe by his power]
The psalmist is using this possessive form to mean the God whom he worships. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the God whom I worship]

This could mean: (1) that Yahweh will do the same things to them that they did. Alternate translation: [He will do to them the evil things that they have done to others] or (2) that Yahweh will punish them for their evil. Alternate translation: [He will punish them for the evil things that they have done to others]
The pronoun **them** refers to the corrupt rulers mentioned in verses 20–21. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [on those wicked rulers]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the sinful things that they have done]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wickedness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and he will destroy them their wicked activities]

This could mean: (1) that Yahweh will destroy them because of their wickedness. Alternate translation: [because they have done wicked things] or (2) that Yahweh will destroy them while they are doing wicked things. Alternate translation: [while they are doing wicked things]

These two phrases **he will destroy them in their wickedness** and **Yahweh our God will destroy them** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [and he will destroy them in their wickedness. It is Yahweh our God who will destroy them]
The psalmist is using this possessive form to mean the God whom they worship. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the God whom we worship]

95.text:
# Psalm 95 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 95 is the first in a series of six “worship psalms” (Psalms 95–100).

1. Call to worship (1–5)
2. Call to bow in worship (6–7a)
3. Warning to listen and obey (7b–11)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### God’s care

God made everything and takes good care of people. People should not be stubborn, as the Israelites were in the days of Moses. The Israelites with Moses wandered in the desert for 40 years.

Here the writer is speaking as if Yahweh were a **rock**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how “rock” and “of my salvation” are translated in [Psalms 18:46](../018/046.md). Alternate translation: [to our protector and savior]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to our steadfast savior]

Here, **his face** represents being in the presence of God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Let us go into his presence]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **thanksgiving**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [as we thank him]
The term “god,” when applied to a being other than Yahweh, can refer to an idol, but, as here, it can also refer to any lesser spirit being. Alternate translation: [above any other spiritual being]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if Yahweh were actually positioned **above all gods** in a physical sense. He means that Yahweh is superior to all other gods. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who is superior to all other gods]

The psalmist is using **in his hand** as a common expression of his culture to mean “in his control” or “under his authority.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in his control]

The psalmist is referring to all of the earth by naming two extremes, **the depths of the earth** and **the heights of the mountains**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [every part of the earth; they all]

The psalmist is using **are to him** as a common expression of his culture to mean “belong to him” or “are his.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [are his]

The psalmist is using **who to him is** as a common expression of his culture to mean “who owns.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who owns]

The writer is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **he made it** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Yahweh is the one who made the sea. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [and it was he who made it]

Here the word **hands** represents the action of God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he himself formed the dry land]

The phrases **bow down** and **kneel** describe symbolic actions by which people showed submission and reverence to God. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of these actions in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and show that we submit]

Here, **to the face of** represents being in front of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the presence of]
The psalmist is using this possessive form to mean the God whom we worship. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the God whom we worship]

The psalmist is speaking as if the people were like God’s sheep in **his pasture**. He means that the people are like God’s sheep that he provides for. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people who belong to him]

The psalmist is speaking here of God’s people as if they were **the flock of his hand**. This image portrays God as a shepherd who personally cares for and guides his people like sheep. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the group that he directs and guards]

The psalmist says **if only you would listen** to introduce a wish that God’s people would obey him. Use a natural method in your language for introducing a wish. Alternate translation: [I wish you would listen]
Here, **voice** represents what God says. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to what he says]

The psalmist is using **harden your heart** as a common expression of his culture to mean “become stubborn” or “refuse to listen and obey.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Do not be obstinate]
The words **Meribah** and **Massah** are the names of places.

The terms **tested me** and **tried me** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [tested my patience] or [refused to trust me]
Translate this number according to the conventions of your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [For forty years]

God is using **wandering of heart** as a common expression of his culture to mean “tending to stray” or “lacking in commitment.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [blowing hot and cold] or [lacking in commitment]

The pronouns **they, they** refer to the people of Israel whom God is describing. The psalmist is stating the pronoun **they** separately, even though the verb translated as **they have not known** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that these very people failed to know God’s ways. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the emphasis here. Alternate translation: [and those very people have not known]

Here God is speaking of how he wants people to live as if that were **ways** that people could walk along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the way that I teach people to live]

God is using **in my nose** as a common expression of the culture to mean “in my anger.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in my anger]

Following the custom of the culture, God is swearing an oath by stating the first part of a condition (**If they enter into my rest**) but not the second part (“then”). If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explicitly state the second part of this condition. Alternate translation: [If they enter into my rest, then I am not Yahweh]

96.text:
# Psalm 96 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 96 is one of six “worship psalms” (Psalms 95–100).

1. Call to sing and declare Yahweh’s greatness (1–6)
2. Call the nations to worship (7–9)
3. Yahweh’s reign and coming judgment (10–13)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Yahweh, the king

Yahweh is king over all the earth and is worthy of all praise.

Here, **all the earth** represents all the people who live on the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all you people who live on the earth]

Here, **name** represents who Yahweh is. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [bless everything that he is]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [that he is the one who saves]

The psalmist is using **from day to day** as a common expression of his culture to mean “continually” or “regularly.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [every day]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [that he is extremely great]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [recount his marvelous deeds]

The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [Because]

The expression **is to be praised** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and everyone should praise him]

The expression **He is to be feared** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Everyone should fear him]

Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [You see,]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **Splendor** and **majesty**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [His presence is splendid and majestic]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **Strength** and **beauty**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [He is strong and beautiful]
Here, **to his face** represents “in his presence.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [are in his presence]

These two phrases **Ascribe to Yahweh** and **ascribe to Yahweh** repeat the same meaning. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating it again. If it would be helpful to your readers, you say this once and express the emphasis in another way, as in the UST.

The psalmist is using this possessive form to mean clans that belong to various peoples or clans from among the peoples. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [all clans in all peoples]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **glory** and **strength**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [the fact that he is glorious and strong]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Praise Yahweh because he is the glorious one]
Here, **name** represents who God is. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the glory of who he is]

To **Bow down** was a symbolic action by which people showed reverence and submission to Yahweh. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Bow down in worship]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **splendor** and **holiness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [because he is splendid and holy]

To **tremble** was a symbolic action by which people showed reverent fear and awe before God’s holy presence. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [tremble in reverent awe]

The psalmist is using **from his face** as a common expression of the culture to mean “because of” or “on account of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because of him]

Here, **all the earth** represents all the people who live on the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all you people of the earth]

The expression **the world is established** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [he established the world]

The expression **it cannot be shaken** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [nothing can shake it]

This could mean: (1) Yahweh always judges the peoples with evenness, as in the UST, or (2) on the future day of judgment, Yahweh will judge the peoples with evenness. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will judge]

96.quote: יִשְׂמְח֣וּ הַ֭⁠שָּׁמַיִם וְ⁠תָגֵ֣ל הָ⁠אָ֑רֶץ יִֽרְעַ֥ם הַ֝⁠יָּ֗ם
96.text: Here the psalmist is calling on the heavens, earth, and sea to respond with praise to Yahweh. This is the author’s way of expressing that all of creation should respond to Yahweh with joy and praise. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team on how you could express this with statements about what creation should do, as modeled in the UST.

By **its fullness**, the psalmist means all of the creatures that fill the sea. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and all of the creatures that fill it]

This could mean: (1) **the heavens** and **the earth** represent those who dwell in those places. Alternate translation: [Let those who live in the heavens be glad and let those who live on the earth rejoice] or (2) the heavens and the earth are spoken of as if they had emotions like people have. Alternate translation: [The heavens should be glad and the earth should rejoice]

96.quote: יַעֲלֹ֣ז שָׂ֭דַי וְ⁠כָל־אֲשֶׁר־בּ֑⁠וֹ אָ֥ז יְ֝רַנְּנ֗וּ כָּל־עֲצֵי־יָֽעַר
96.text: Here the psalmist is speaking of **fields** and **trees** as if they were living things that could **rejoice** and **shout for joy**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Let it be as though the fields and all that is in them are celebrating. Then let it be as though all the trees in the forest are shouting happily]
Here, **to the face of** represents being in front of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before]

These two phrases **for he is coming** and **for he is coming** are the same. The words are repeated to emphasize their meaning. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [for it is sure that he is coming]

Here, **the earth** represents the people who live on the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people of the earth]

Here, **the world** represents everyone who lives in the world. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [everyone in the world]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [righteously]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [faithfully]

The terms **the earth** and **the world** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [everyone … everyone]

The writer is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and he will judge the peoples with his faithfulness]

97.text:
# Psalm 97 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 97 is one of six “worship psalms” (Psalms 95–100).

1. Yahweh reigns in power and glory (1–6)
2. Idols are exposed as worthless (7–9)
3. The righteous are called to love and rejoice in Yahweh (10–12)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Yahweh’s authority

All people who worship idols are disgraced because Yahweh rules over all the world.

Here, **the earth** represents the people who live on the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [let the people on the earth]

Here, **coastlands** represents the people who live on the coastlands. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [let the people on the many coastlands]

The phrase **Clouds and darkness** expresses a single idea. The word **darkness** tells more about **clouds**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [Dark clouds]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **Righteousness** and **justice**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [Ruling righteously and justly is]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if the way in which Yahweh rules were actually **the foundation of his throne**. The psalmist means that righteousness and justice are the basis on which God rules. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the very basis of his reign]

Here, **throne** represents God’s rule as king. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [of his rule as king]
Here, **to his face** represents being in front of him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before him]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [the earth sees the lightning]

Here, **the earth** represents the people who live on the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people of the earth see and tremble]

The implication is that the earth trembles with fear when it sees God’s lightning. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and trembles with fear]

The point of this comparison is that just as **wax** melts easily when heated, so the **mountains** will easily crumble before Yahweh’s power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [crumble as easily as wax melts]

Here, **from to the face of** represents the mountains reacting to being in the presence of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before the presence of]

These two phrases **from to the face of Yahweh** and **from to the face of the Lord of all the earth** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [from the presence of Yahweh, the Lord of all the earth]

The psalmist is speaking of **the heavens** as if they were a living thing that could **declare** Yahweh’s righteousness. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The heavens display his righteousness so clearly, it is as though they declare it]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [that he is righteous]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [that he is glorious]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [let those boasting in worthless idols feel shame]
The pronoun **him** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [bow down to Yahweh]

To **bow down to him** was a symbolic action by which people showed worship and submission to a deity. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [bow down in worship to him]

The psalmist has been addressing his audience, but now he briefly addresses **all you gods**, even though he knows that these gods cannot hear him. He does this in order to express more powerfully his feelings about Yahweh’s supremacy over all other so-called gods. If it would be helpful in your language, you could introduce this more clearly and put the rest of this address in quote marks. Alternate translation: [I would tell those worthless idols to bow down to him]

Here, **Zion** represents the people who live in Jerusalem. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [The people living in Zion heard and were glad]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Zion heard Yahweh’s judgments]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and was glad to hear them]

The psalmist is speaking as if the towns and cities throughout the territory of Judah were actually **daughters of Judah**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the people in the smaller towns in Judah]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **judgments**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the righteous way that you judge]
**For** introduces not a reason but an explanation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a word or phrase that makes this relationship clearer. Alternate translation: [After all,]

The psalmist is speaking here as if Yahweh were actually **most high above** all the earth in a physical, spatial sense. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [are completely in charge of]

The psalmist is speaking as if Yahweh were actually **exalted** in a physical, spatial sense high above all other things. The psalmist means that Yahweh has supreme authority and power over all creation. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You have much more authority than]
The term “god,” when applied to a being other than Yahweh, can refer to an idol, but, as here, it can also refer to any lesser spirit being. Alternate translation: [every other being]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **evil**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [all that is evil]

The psalmist is using the adjective **faithful** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [of everyone loyal to him]

Here, **hand** represents the power of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the power of]

The psalmist is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [bad people]

The psalmist is speaking here as if Yahweh actually **snatches** his faithful ones from danger. The image is of someone quickly grabbing something to pull it away from harm. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he saves them]

The psalmist is speaking as if **light** were actually seeds that could be sown in the ground. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [He scatters light like seeds]

The psalmist is speaking here of good and beneficial things as if they were **light**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. If not, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He gives good things]

The expression **Light is sown** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh sows light]

The psalmist is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [for those who are righteous]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **gladness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and he makes glad the upright of heart]

The psalmist is using **upright of heart** as a common expression of his culture to mean “sincere in their inner beings” or “honest in their intentions.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and for those who are sincere in their inner beings]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [gladness is sown]

The psalmist is speaking as if being glad were actually something that could happen at a location, **in Yahweh**. He means that the righteous should be glad because of Yahweh or should find their gladness in their relationship with Yahweh. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because of Yahweh]

The psalmist is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [you who are righteous]

The psalmist is using **to the remembrance of his holiness** as a common expression of his culture to mean “to his holy name” or “to him, whose reputation is holiness.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to his holy name] or [to him, whose reputation is holiness]

98.text:
# Psalm 98 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 98 is one of six “worship psalms” (Psalms 95–100).

1. Sing a new song for Yahweh’s saving work (1–3)
2. Shout and rejoice in worship (4–6)
3. All creation celebrates Yahweh’s righteous rule (7–9)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Praise

Everyone and every thing should sing praises to Yahweh because he is worthy of all praise.

Here, **his right hand and the arm of his holiness** represents God’s great power. The psalmist is using body parts to refer to God’s strength and ability to act. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his great and holy power]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **holiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and his holy arm]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Make sure that your translation communicates that Yahweh is the one who saves his people; he is not the one who is saved. Alternate translation: [have saved his people]
The word **Sing**, along with all of the command forms in this psalm, is plural here, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to everyone that he saves people]

Here, **eyes** represents the sight or observation of people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in full view of the nations]

Here, **the nations** represents the people of all the nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people of all the nations]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [that he is righteous]

By **He remembers**, the psalmist does not mean that God could forget something, since God cannot forget anything. He means that God consistently knows and acts according to his covenant loyalty and faithfulness. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [He bears in mind]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **covenant loyalty** and **faithfulness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [that he has committed to love and to be faithful]

Here, **house** means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So **the house of Israel** figuratively means all the people descended from the patriarch Jacob, who was also known as Israel. Alternate translation: [to the people of Israel]

The psalmist is referring to all of the earth by naming the extremes, **the ends of the earth**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [people all over the earth]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Make sure that your translation communicates that Yahweh is the one who saves his people; he is not the one who is saved. Alternate translation: [how our God saves people]
The psalmist is using this possessive form to mean the God whom the people worship. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [from the God whom we worship]

Here, **all the earth** represents all the people who live on the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all people on the earth]

By **burst into song**, the psalmist means that people should suddenly begin singing with great emotion. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. If not, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [express your joy by singing]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **joy**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [sing joyfully]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **harp**. He means harps in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [with harps]

The psalmist repeats the phrase **with the harp** to emphasize its meaning. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [with the harp, yes, with the harp]

The psalmist is using this possessive form to describe singing that is characterized by being vocal rather than instrumental. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and with people singing]

Here, **to the face of** represents being in front of the King, Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before]
Here, **shout** refers to joyfully cheering in front of Yahweh. Be sure that your translation does not communicate that this is angry shouting. Alternate translation: [raise a cheer]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and let its fullness roar]

By **its fullness**, the psalmist means all the creatures that live in the sea. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and everything that fills it]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [let the world and the dwellers in it roar]

Here the psalmist is speaking of **the world** as if it were a living thing that could shout. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [let it be as though the world were shouting]

The psalmist is speaking of **rivers** as if they were living beings that could **clap palm**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Let it be as though the rivers clap palm]

The psalmist is using **clap palm** as a common expression of his culture to mean “clap their hands.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Let the rivers clap their hands]

The psalmist is speaking of **the mountains** as if they were living things that could **rejoice**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [let it be as though the mountains rejoice together]

Here, **to the face of** represents being in front of the King, Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the presence of]

Here, **the earth** represents the people who live on the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people of the earth]

Here, **the world** represents the people who live in the world. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people in the world]

These two phrases **he will judge the world with righteousness** and **the peoples with fairness** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [he will judge the world with righteousness, yes, he will judge the peoples with fairness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [righteously]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **fairness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [equally]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and he will judge the peoples with fairness]

99.text:
# Psalm 99 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 99 is one of six “worship psalms” (Psalms 95–100).

1. Yahweh reigns over all peoples (1–3)
2. Yahweh loves justice and rules rightly (4–5)
3. Yahweh answers his faithful servants (6–9)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Yahweh’s justice

God is just and fair. Moses, Aaron and Samuel each prayed to him and obeyed him, and he answered their prayers. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/justice]])

99.quote: יְהוָ֣ה מָ֭לָךְ יִרְגְּז֣וּ עַמִּ֑ים יֹשֵׁ֥ב כְּ֝רוּבִ֗ים תָּנ֥וּט הָ⁠אָֽרֶץ
99.text: If it would be helpful in your language, you could move the phrase **let the peoples tremble** so that it does not interrupt the larger sentence. Alternate translation: [Yahweh reigns, sitting above the cherubim; let the peoples tremble and let the earth quake]

If it would be helpful, you could explain in the text or a footnote that Yahweh is pictured here as sitting above the cherubim that are on the lid of the ark of the covenant, which is in his temple in Jerusalem. The biblical writers often spoke of the ark of the covenant as if it were Yahweh’s footstool upon which he rested his feet as he sat on his throne in heaven above. Alternate translation: [he sits on his throne above the cherubim on the ark of the covenant]

By **is great**, the psalmist means that Yahweh is powerful and mighty as a ruler. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [is a powerful ruler]

The psalmist is speaking as if Yahweh were actually **high above** all the peoples in a physical sense. He means that Yahweh powerfully rules over all the peoples. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he powerfully rules over]

The psalmist is using the term **name** to represent who Yahweh is or to refer to Yahweh’s reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you, who are great and fearsome]

In this psalm, the psalmist switches between talking about Yahweh in the third person and addressing him in second person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this verse in the third person. Alternate translation: [his great and fearsome name]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And the king is strong]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [he loves doing what is just]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you have established** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Yahweh is the one who has established fairness. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [you are the one who has established fairness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **fairness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [you have given us laws that are fair]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you have done** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Yahweh is the one who has done justice and righteousness. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [you are the one who has done justice and righteousness]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **justice** and **righteousness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [everything that you have done for Jacob is just and right]

By **in Jacob**, the psalmist means in the land of Israel. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in the land of Israel]
The command forms in this verse and verse 9 are plural, so use that form if your language marks that distinction.

If it would be helpful, you could explain in the text or a footnote that the psalmist is continuing to picture Yahweh as sitting above the ark of the covenant, which is in his temple in Jerusalem. Alternate translation: [and worship Yahweh before his throne in the temple]

Here, **calling his name** represents praying to God or calling out to him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [was among those calling out to him]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **answered** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Yahweh himself responded to Moses, Aaron, and Samuel. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [and he himself answered them]

By **he answered them**, the psalmist means that God helped Moses, Aaron, and Samuel when they called out to him for assistance. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [he helped them]

The pronoun **them** refers to Moses and Aaron mentioned in the previous verse, since they were the ones whom Yahweh spoke to out of the cloud. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [he spoke to Moses and Aaron]

The pronoun **They** probably includes Samuel here, along with Moses and Aaron, since Yahweh also spoke directly to him and he obeyed. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Moses, Aaron, and Samuel]
The psalmist is using this possessive form to mean the God whom the people worship. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the God whom we worship]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you answered** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that God himself personally answered them. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [you answered them yourself]
The pronoun **them** refers to Moses, Aaron, and Samuel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [you answered Moses, Aaron, and Samuel]

The implication is that God answered Moses, Aaron, and Samuel by helping them when they called out to him in times of need. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [you helped them]

Here the psalmist assumes that readers will know that **their deeds** refers to sinful or wrongful actions. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [their sinful deeds]
The psalmist is using this possessive form to mean the God whom the people worship. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the God whom we worship]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **the hill** that is characterized by **his holiness**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [at his holy hill]

By **the hill of his holiness**, the psalmist means the hill where God’s holy temple is located. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [at the hill where his holy temple is located]

100.text:
# Psalm 100 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 100 is the last of this group of six “worship psalms” (Psalms 95–100).

1. Call to joyful praise (1–2)
2. Reason for worship: Yahweh is God (3)
3. Enter with thanksgiving and praise (4)
4. Yahweh’s character is the foundation of praise (5)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Yahweh’s care for his creation

God made mankind and takes good care of people.

The command forms such as **shout** are plural in this psalm because the psalmist is calling all people to praise God, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction. See how “shout” is translated in [Psalms 47:1](../047/001.md). Alternate translation: [Raise a shout to Yahweh]

Here, **all the earth** represents all the people who live on the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all people on earth]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **gladness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [gladly]

Here, **to his face** represents being in the presence of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [into his presence]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **rejoicing**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [singing joyful songs]

The word translated as **Know** is a command. If, in your language, someone would not command someone else to know something, then use a form in your language that communicates an exhortation to fully realize something. Alternate translation: [Let us fully realize] or [You must believe that it is true]

The pronouns **Yahweh** and **he** both refer to God. The psalmist is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though it could be omitted, in order to emphasize that it is Yahweh specifically who is God. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the emphasis here. Alternate translation: [it is Yahweh who is God]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **he made us** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Yahweh is the one who made us and no one else. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [he is the one who made us]

Many ancient manuscripts read **and not we**. The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “and we are his.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT. Alternate translation: [and we are his]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and it was not we who made ourselves]

The psalmist is speaking here as if the people were actually **sheep** that belong to God. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he provides for us as though we were sheep in his pasture]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **thanksgiving**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [as you thank him]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **praise**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [as you praise him]
Here, **his name** represents who he is. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [him]

The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [It is right to do this since]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **covenant faithfulness** and **eternity**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [he is eternally faithful to his covenant]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **eternity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [is everlasting]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **truthfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [he is trustworthy] or [he is truthful]

The psalmist is using **generation and generation** as a common expression of his culture to mean “for all time” or “forever.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and his truthfulness endures for all time]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and his truthfulness lasts until generation and generation]

101.text:
# Psalm 101 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 101 is a psalm of David asking God’s help to live as a person should. With God’s help, David pledges to rule uprightly and to get rid of all evildoers.

1. David commits to upright life (1–2)
2. David rejects evil and deceit (3–7)
3. David promises justice and faithfulness (8)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Encouragement

David wanted to encourage all the good people in the land and restrain all the evil people. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/evil]])
See the introduction to Psalms for an explanation of the word **shall**.

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **covenant faithfulness** and **justice**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [about how you are always fair and promised to be faithful to us]

By **the blameless way**, David means the way of living that is morally perfect and without fault. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the blameless way to live]

David is using the question form **When will you come to me** to emphasize the strength of his desire. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I want you to come to me!]

David is speaking of how he will live his life as if it were the way in which he will **walk**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will behave]

The phrase **in the integrity of my heart** was a common expression meaning “with complete honesty” or “with pure motives.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [being honest with everyone] or [with a clear conscience]

David is using **put a worthless thing before my eyes** as a common expression of his culture to mean “consider doing a worthless thing” or “focus my attention on a worthless thing.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will not consider doing a worthless thing]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **transgressions**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [doing sinful things]

David is speaking here as if wrongdoing were actually something physical that could **cling** to a person. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [doing transgressions will not be part of my behavior]

The pronoun **it** refers to the act of doing transgressions, seen in the previous clause. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [doing transgressions will not cling to me]

This could mean: (1) David will not allow himself to have a perverse heart. Alternate translation: [My heart will reject becoming perverse] or (2) David will not tolerate people with perverse hearts. Alternate translation: [People with perverse hearts will be far from me]

Here David is speaking as if a person’s intentions were his **heart**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Desiring to do perverse things]

Here David is speaking as if perverse intentions were actually objects that could physically **turn away** from him. He means that he will not allow himself to be influenced by perverse thoughts or intentions. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will avoid] or [I will not allow myself]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **evil**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [I will not know evil actions]

David is using **I will not know evil** as a common expression of his culture to mean “I will have nothing to do with evil.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will have nothing to do with evil] or [I will reject anything evil]

David is not referring to a specific person **slandering** a specific **neighbor**. He means people who slander neighbors in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Whoever slanders his neighbor]

The terms **lofty of eyes** and **wide of heart** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Any prideful person]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **one lofty of eyes**. He means people with lofty eyes in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Whoever is lofty of eyes]

David is using **lofty of eyes** as a common expression of his culture to mean “haughty” or “arrogant.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Any haughty person]

David is not referring to a specific **one wide of heart**. He means all people with this characteristic. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and whoever is wide of heart]

David is using **wide of heart** as a common expression of his culture to mean “proud” or “arrogant.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and any proud person]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. The full meaning is **him I cannot** tolerate or stand. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [him I cannot stand] or [him I cannot tolerate]

Here, **My eyes are on** represents David’s attention or focus. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am seeking the faithful ones of]

The implication is that these faithful people will **sit with** David as advisors or officials in positions of authority. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [to rule under my authority]

Here David is speaking of living with integrity as if integrity were a path for his **walking**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. If not, you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [The one living with integrity]

David is not referring to a specific **one walking**. He means anyone walking in the way of integrity in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Anyone walking]

101.quote: לֹֽא־יֵשֵׁ֨ב ׀ בְּ⁠קֶ֥רֶב בֵּיתִ⁠י֮ עֹשֵׂ֪ה רְמִ֫יָּ֥ה דֹּבֵ֥ר שְׁקָרִ֑ים לֹֽא־יִ֝כּ֗וֹן לְ⁠נֶ֣גֶד עֵינָֽ⁠י
101.text: These two phrases **A doer of deceit will not remain within my house** and **a speaker of lies will not be established before my eyes** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [A doer of deceit will not remain within my house, no, a speaker of lies will not be established before my eyes]

David is not referring to a specific **doer of deceit**. He means deceitful people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Any doer of deceit]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **speaker of lies**. He means speakers of lies in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [any speaker of lies]

The implication is that David is referring to his royal court or household staff, not just the physical building. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [as a member of my staff]

The expression **will not be established** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I will not tolerate]

Here, **before my eyes** represents “in my presence” or “under my supervision.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in my presence] or [under my supervision]

By **In the mornings**, the psalmist means that he will consistently and regularly destroy the wicked, day after day. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Morning by morning] or [Each morning]

The psalmist is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are wicked of]

The psalmist is using **cut off** as a common expression of the culture to mean “remove.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to remove]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **evil**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [evildoers] or [people who do evil things]

The implication is that this **city** is Jerusalem, where God dwells with his people. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [from this city, which is Yahweh’s city]

102.text:
# Psalm 102 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 102 is a “lament.”

1. Cry of distress and plea for mercy (1–11)
2. Confidence in Yahweh’s eternal purposes and mercy (12–17)
3. Call to record and remember Yahweh’s mercies (18–22)
4. Yahweh sustains and remains unchanging (23–28)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Salvation

The psalmist does not want to die young. He also wants to see Jerusalem saved. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/save]])

102.quote: יְ֭הוָה שִׁמְעָ֣⁠ה תְפִלָּתִ֑⁠י וְ֝⁠שַׁוְעָתִ֗⁠י אֵלֶ֥י⁠ךָ תָבֽוֹא
102.text: These two phrases **Hear my prayer, Yahweh** and **let my cry come unto you** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Hear my prayer, Yahweh, as I cry out to you]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please hear my prayer]

The psalmist is speaking of **my cry** as if it were a living thing that could come to God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [pay attention to what I cry to you]

The psalmist is using **hide your face from me** as a common expression of his culture to mean “ignore me” or “reject me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Do not turn your back on me] or [Do not reject me]

Here the pronoun **it** could refer to: (1) any distressing thing in general. Alternate translation: [when things distress me] or (2) “the day” mentioned just before it. Alternate translation: [that distresses me]

The phrase **on the day** appears twice in this verse with slightly different meanings. The first occurrence refers to any time when distressing things happen, while the second occurrence refers to the specific moment when the psalmist calls out to God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use different expressions to distinguish between these general and specific time references, such as “when” for the first occurrence and “as soon as” or “the moment” for the second. Alternate translation: [when … At the time]
