The psalmist is using **Incline your ear to me** as a common expression of his culture to mean “pay attention to me” or “listen carefully to me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Pay attention to me]

The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [Do this because]
Here, **my days** refers to the author’s life, and the idea of **smoke** is something that quickly disappears. Alternate translation: [my life passes away quickly]

The psalmist is speaking as if his bones were actually **charred like a fireplace**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. If not, you could state this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [and my bones feel like they are charred like a fireplace]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a fireplace** becomes blackened and charred from repeated burning of fires in it, so the psalmist’s **bones** feel burned and damaged from his suffering. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and my bones are charred like a fireplace that has had many fires in it]

The expression **are charred** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and it feels like fire has charred my bones as it chars a fireplace]

The psalmist is using one part of himself, his **heart**, to mean all of himself in the act of withering away. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am struck like grass and withered]

The psalmist is speaking here as if his heart were actually **grass** that has been **struck** and **withered**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. If not, you could state this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [I feel as though my heart has been struck like grass and withered]

Here the psalmist is making a comparison between his heart and grass to show how he feels. The point of this comparison is that just as **grass** becomes **withered** when it is struck down, so the psalmist’s **heart** has become weak and almost lifeless. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [My heart feels as dead as grass that has been struck down and dried out]

The expression **My heart is struck like grass and withered** uses passive verbal forms. If your language would not use those forms, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [My heart feels as dead as grass that the sun has killed and dried]

Here the word **for** introduces not a reason but an explanation. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [indeed,]
The psalmist is using one kind of food, **bread**, to mean food in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a meal]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe a **voice** that is characterized by **groaning**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [From my loud groans]

The psalmist is using the singular **bone** to refer to all of his bones in the act of becoming extremely thin from distress. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my bones cling]

102.quote: דָּ֭מִיתִי לִ⁠קְאַ֣ת מִדְבָּ֑ר הָ֝יִ֗יתִי כְּ⁠כ֣וֹס חֳרָבֽוֹת
102.text: The psalmist is using two comparisons to describe his lonely and desolate condition. The point of those two comparisons is that just as **an owl of the wilderness** and **a screech owl in the ruins** are solitary creatures in desolate places, so is the psalmist in his distress. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [I have become as solitary and lonely as an owl of the wilderness or as a screech owl in the ruins]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **an owl** that is characterized by **the wilderness**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [an owl that lives in the wilderness]

The word translated as “owl” here is obscure. Most scholars believe that the word refers to a type of owl. The ancient Greek translation used the word for “pelican” here, and that was followed by some older versions, although a pelican is a water bird that cannot live in a dry wilderness. If “pelican” is correct, then the psalmist is saying that he feels as though he is living in a place where he cannot survive. If “owl” is correct, then the psalmist is saying that he feels alone and abandoned. You may want to use the word that the major translation in your area uses.

This could mean: (1) The psalmist is awake when he would like to be sleeping. Alternate translation: [I am unable to sleep] or (2) The psalmist is watching for Yahweh to answer him. Alternate translation: [I am watching]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a bird alone** is solitary and isolated, so is the psalmist. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and I have become as solitary as a bird alone]

By **swear by me**, the psalmist means that his enemies use his name as a curse, saying something like “May you become as miserable as he is.” You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [refer to me when they curse people]

The psalmist is speaking as if eating his **bread** were the same as eating **ashes**. He means that his food has no taste or appeal because of his deep sorrow and distress. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Bread and ashes taste the same to me]
The psalmist is using one kind of food, **bread**, to mean food in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [My food is as ashes]
Here, **weeping** represents tears. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [with my tears]

The implication is that the psalmist’s drink is mixed with his tears because he is weeping. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and my drink becomes mixed]

If it is more natural in your language to state the reason before the result, you could do so by moving this sentence to the previous verse. You would then present the combined verses as 102:9–10. Alternate translation: [because of your fury and rage, for you have lifted me up and thrown me, I eat ashes like bread and mix my drink with weeping]

The psalmist is using **from the face of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “because of” or “on account of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because of]

The phrase **fury and rage** expresses a single idea. The word **fury** tells more about the **rage**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [your furious rage]

Here the word **for** introduces not a reason but an explanation. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [you see,]

The psalmist is speaking as if God had literally **lifted** him **up** and **thrown** him away like an object. He means that he feels as though God has rejected and abandoned him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I feel like you have lifted me up and thrown me]

By **My days are** the psalmist means his remaining time to live. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [My remaining life is]

The psalmist is making a comparison. The point of this comparison is that just as **a lengthening shadow** grows longer and fainter as evening approaches, and then it disappears, so **My days** are coming to an end. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [My days are ending like an evening shadow ends the day]

The point of this comparison is that just as **grass** withers and dies, so the psalmist views himself as withering and dying. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and I am dying as grass dies under the hot sun]

By **sit forever** the psalmist means that Yahweh sits on a throne to rule as king forever. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [sit on your throne as king forever]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **remembrance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and you will be well-known]

The psalmist is using **to generation and generation** as a common expression of his culture to mean “throughout all generations” or “forever.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [throughout all generations]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **You** separately, even though the verb translated as **you will arise** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that it is God who will act to show mercy to Zion. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the emphasis here. Alternate translation: [It will be you who will now arise]

The psalmist is using **you will arise** as a common expression of the culture to indicate that God is about to begin taking action to help his people. He does not mean that God is getting out of bed or standing up from a seated position. If this expression does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you will go into action] or [you will do something]
Here, **Zion** represents the people who live there. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people of Zion]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **mercy**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [you will act mercifully toward]

The expression **the appointed time** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [the time that you have appointed]

Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [After all,]

The psalmist says **your servants cherish her stones and favor her dust** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [For your servants absolutely love the city of Jerusalem]

The psalmist is referring to all of Jerusalem by naming two components that are opposite in size, **her stones** and **her dust**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [For your servants love all of the city]

The psalmist is speaking of himself and his people in the third person as **your servants** to show humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a humble form in the first person. Alternate translation: [we, your people,]

Here, **The nations** represents the people of the nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [The people of the nations]
The word translated as **fear** includes the sense of awe and respect. Use a word that includes these ideas, if possible. Alternate translation: [will deeply respect]
Here, **name** represents who Yahweh is. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [who Yahweh is]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and all the kings of the earth will fear your glory]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [you, because you are glorious]

Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [After all,]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [he is glorious as he appears]

These two phrases **He turns to the prayer of the destitute** and **he does not despise their prayer** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [He turns to the prayer of the destitute; certainly, he does not despise their prayer]

The psalmist is speaking as if God were physically **turning** himself toward the prayers of the destitute. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. If not, you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [He pays attention to]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe a **prayer** that is characterized by **the destitute**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the destitute when he prays]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **despise**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [and he accepts their prayer]

The expression **This will be written** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is the psalmist. Alternate translation: [I will write this]

The expression **a people being created** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [and a people whom Yahweh is still creating]
**Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh]

The connecting word **that** introduces the content of the praise mentioned in the previous verse. Use a way that is natural in your language to introduce what the praise is about. Alternate translation: [They will say that]

102.quote: כִּֽי־הִ֭שְׁקִיף מִ⁠מְּר֣וֹם קָדְשׁ֑⁠וֹ יְ֝הוָ֗ה מִ⁠שָּׁמַ֤יִם ׀ אֶל־אֶ֬רֶץ הִבִּֽיט
102.text: These two phrases **that he looked down from the height of his holiness** and **Yahweh from heaven regarded the earth** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [that he looked down from the height of his holiness; yes, Yahweh from heaven regarded the earth,]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe a **height** that is characterized by **holiness**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from his holy high-place]

The phrase **the height of his holiness** refers to heaven, where God dwells. The psalmist assumes that readers will understand that this is describing God’s holy dwelling place above the earth. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [from heaven]

Here, **the earth** represents the people living on earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people living on earth]

Here, **to hear** and **to release** mark these clauses as the goal or purpose of Yahweh looking down from heaven. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [so that he could hear … so that he could release]

By **to hear**, the psalmist means to respond to and help. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [to respond to] or [to relieve]

The psalmist is using **sons of execution** as a common expression of the culture to indicate people who have a certain characteristic. In this case, these people have the characteristic of being condemned to death. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those doomed to die] or [those who would soon be executed]

102.quote: לְ⁠סַפֵּ֣ר בְּ֭⁠צִיּוֹן שֵׁ֣ם יְהוָ֑ה וּ֝⁠תְהִלָּת֗⁠וֹ בִּ⁠ירוּשָׁלִָֽם
102.text: These two phrases **to recount the name of Yahweh in Zion** and **his praise in Jerusalem** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [to extol and praise the name of Yahweh in Zion]

Here, **the name of Yahweh** represents Yahweh’s reputation or who he is. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the great things that Yahweh is known for]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and to recount his praise in Jerusalem]
The psalmist is using this possessive form to mean praise that is given to him. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and to praise him]

The phrase **peoples and kingdoms** expresses a single idea. The word **kingdoms** tells more about **peoples**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [peoples from many kingdoms]

The psalmist is speaking as if his physical vitality were actually an object that God could **break**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He has weakened my body]

The psalmist is speaking of his life as if it were actually **the road** that he was traveling along. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in the middle of my life]
Here, **days** represents the psalmist’s lifetime. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [my lifetime]

The psalmist is speaking as if God would literally **take** him somewhere. He means that God would cause him to die. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [do not end my life]
Here, **days** represents “life.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [my life]

The psalmist is speaking as if God’s eternal existence were actually **years**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your lifespan is]

The psalmist is using **a generation of generations** as a common expression of his culture to mean “forever” or “for all time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [forever] or [unending]

Some translations mark the end of this verse as the place where the direct quotation ends. Other translations consider that the direct quotation continues until the end of the psalm. You may wish to follow what the major translation in your area does.

The psalmist is speaking as if the earth were actually **set** in place like an object that someone positions or establishes. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you made the earth what it is]

Here, **hands** represents the power and creative ability of God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the heavens are your creative work]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **They** separately, even though the verb translated as **they will perish** already contains that meaning. He is doing that for emphasis because he is contrasting the earth and heavens (which will perish) with God (who will remain). If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that meaning here. Alternate translation: [As for them, they will perish]

The pronouns **they** and **them** in this verse refers to the earth and the heavens mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The heavens and the earth will perish]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you will stand** already includes this meaning. He is doing that for emphasis because he is contrasting the permanence of God with the temporary nature of the heavens and the earth. If a speaker of your language would use explicit pronouns for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that meaning here. Alternate translation: [but you, in contrast, will stand]

The psalmist is speaking as if God would physically **stand**. This means that he will continue or endure. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you will continue] or [you will exist always]

The psalmist is repeating forms of the same verb, translated here as **pass**, in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [you will completely remove them, and they will be completely gone]
The pronoun **he** refers to Yahweh, the God who always is. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [But you are the one who is]
Here, **years** represents “existence” or “life.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and your existence]

The implication is that the descendants will be safe and secure under God’s protection. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [will dwell securely]

The psalmist is speaking as if the people who will descend from God’s servants were actually their **seed**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and their descendants] or [and their children]

The expression **their seed will be established** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [and you will establish their seed]
Here, **to your face** represents being in Yahweh’s presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before you]

103.text:
# Psalm 103 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 103 is the first in a series of five “psalm of praise” to God (Psalm 103–107).

1. Call to bless Yahweh with whole being (1–2)
2. Yahweh’s forgiveness, healing, and provision (3–5)
3. Yahweh’s compassionate character (6–14)
4. Yahweh’s covenant faithfulness from everlasting (15–22)
5. Yahweh’s sovereign rule over all (19–22)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Yahweh’s grace

God shows his goodness to us by forgiving our sins and not punishing us as much as we deserve.

103.quote: בָּרֲכִ֣י נַ֭פְשִׁ⁠י אֶת־יְהוָ֑ה וְ⁠כָל־קְ֝רָבַ֗⁠י אֶת־שֵׁ֥ם קָדְשֽׁ⁠וֹ
103.text: The phrases **Bless Yahweh, my soul** and **all of my inward parts, the name of his holiness** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Bless Yahweh, my soul! Yes, all of my inward parts, bless the name of his holiness]

David is using the term **soul** to mean his entire person from the perspective of his spiritual and emotional existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [myself] or [my inner being]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from earlier in the verse if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [bless the name of his holiness]
David is using the term **name** to refer to Yahweh’s holy person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his holy person]

Here, **all of my inward parts** represents David’s entire being from an internal perspective. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and everything that I am]

Here, **my soul** represents David’s entire person from the perspective of his spiritual and emotional existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [myself] or [my inner being]
If it would be clearer in your language, you could avoid using the double negative **do not forget** by expressing the idea in a positive form. Alternate translation: [and remember]

The pronoun **your** in verses 3–5 refers to “my soul” in verse 2. In this way, David is referring to himself. If “your” communicates the meaning well in your language, consider using that. Otherwise, consider using “my” here. Use the same translation decision for these phrases through verse 5. Alternate translation: [My soul, he is the one pardoning all your sins] or [He is the one pardoning all my sins]
Here, **life** represents the entire person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [you]
Here, **the pit** represents death. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from dying]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **covenant faithfulness** and **mercy**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [the one keeping his covenant to love you and be merciful to you]

The psalmist is speaking of God as if he were a king placing a **crown** on the psalmist. He means that God is honoring and blessing him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one blessing you with] or [the one honoring you with]

The phrase **your ornaments** is a translation of the written Hebrew text. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense. It seems that the scribe mistook the word translated as **ornaments** for a similar word that means “existence.” The ancient Greek translation says, “your desires.” You may want to follow one of those readings. Alternate translation: [your existence] or [your desires]

David is using the adjective **good** as a noun to mean good things. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [with good things]

The word **itself** indicates that the object of the verb is the same as the subject of the verb. Use a way that is natural in your language to indicate that the same thing fills two roles in the sentence. Alternate translation: [becomes renewed]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the eagle** is capable and strong, so **your youth** being renewed makes you feel capable and strong. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like an eagle that can go wherever it desires to go]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, he is the one doing righteousness]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **righteousness** and **justice**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [what is right and just]

The expression **those being oppressed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people whom others are oppressing]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [he made known his deeds]

The psalmist is using **long of nostrils** as a common expression of his culture to mean “patient” or “slow to become angry.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [very patient]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and always faithful to his covenant with us]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that **contend** means to contend with us, his people. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [He will not contend with us]

The implication is that God will not **contend** or remain angry for an unlimited length of time, but will eventually cease his anger. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [to the end of time]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and he will not maintain his anger]

103.quote: לֹ֣א כַ֭⁠חֲטָאֵי⁠נוּ עָ֣שָׂה לָ֑⁠נוּ וְ⁠לֹ֥א כַ֝⁠עֲוֺנֹתֵ֗י⁠נוּ גָּמַ֥ל עָלֵֽי⁠נוּ
103.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way, as in the UST. Otherwise, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [He does not deal with us according to our sins; let me say again, he does not treat us according to our iniquities]

103.quote: לֹ֣א כַ֭⁠חֲטָאֵי⁠נוּ עָ֣שָׂה לָ֑⁠נוּ וְ⁠לֹ֥א כַ֝⁠עֲוֺנֹתֵ֗י⁠נוּ גָּמַ֥ל עָלֵֽי⁠נוּ
103.text: The psalmist assumes that readers will know that people’s sins and iniquities deserve punishment from God. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [He does not give punishment to us that is as bad as our sins, and he does not treat us as badly as our iniquities deserve]

Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation of how great Yahweh’s covenant faithfulness is toward those who fear him. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [You see,]

103.quote: כִּ֤י כִ⁠גְבֹ֣הַּ שָׁ֭מַיִם עַל־הָ⁠אָ֑רֶץ גָּבַ֥ר חַ֝סְדּ֗⁠וֹ עַל־יְרֵאָֽי⁠ו
103.text: The point of this comparison is that just as **the heavens** are extremely **high above the earth**, so **his covenant faithfulness** is extremely **strong toward those fearing him**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [For just as it is impossible to measure how high the heavens are above the earth, it is also impossible to measure how strong his covenant faithfulness is toward those fearing him]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [that is how strongly committed he is to being faithful]

103.quote: כִּ⁠רְחֹ֣ק מִ֭זְרָח מִֽ⁠מַּֽעֲרָ֑ב הִֽרְחִ֥יק מִ֝מֶּ֗⁠נּוּ אֶת־פְּשָׁעֵֽי⁠נוּ
103.text: The point of this comparison is that just as **the sunrise** **from the sunset** is an immeasurable distance, so how far **he has removed our transgressions from us** is an immeasurable distance. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Just as it is impossible to measure how far the sunrise is from the sunset, it is also impossible to measure how far he has removed our transgressions from us]

103.quote: כִּ⁠רְחֹ֣ק מִ֭זְרָח מִֽ⁠מַּֽעֲרָ֑ב הִֽרְחִ֥יק מִ֝מֶּ֗⁠נּוּ אֶת־פְּשָׁעֵֽי⁠נוּ
103.text: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from earlier in the sentence if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [As far as the sunrise is from the sunset, that is how far he has removed our transgressions from us]

103.quote: כְּ⁠רַחֵ֣ם אָ֭ב עַל־בָּנִ֑ים רִחַ֥ם יְ֝הוָ֗ה עַל־יְרֵאָֽי⁠ו
103.text: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [As a father has compassion on his children, in the same way, Yahweh has compassion on those fearing him]

103.quote: כְּ⁠רַחֵ֣ם אָ֭ב עַל־בָּנִ֑ים רִחַ֥ם יְ֝הוָ֗ה עַל־יְרֵאָֽי⁠ו
103.text: The point of this comparison is that just as **a father has compassion on his children** very much, so also **Yahweh has compassion on those fearing him** very much. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [As a father has constant and strong compassion on his children, so Yahweh has constant and strong compassion on those fearing him]

103.quote: כְּ⁠רַחֵ֣ם אָ֭ב עַל־בָּנִ֑ים רִחַ֥ם יְ֝הוָ֗ה עַל
103.text: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **compassion**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [As a father loves his children, Yahweh loves]

Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [You see,]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that **form** refers to the physical nature and constitution of human beings. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the weakness of our form] or [what weak stuff we are made of]

The pronoun **he** in the phrase **he, he knows** refers to Yahweh. The repetition of the pronoun emphasizes that Yahweh, more than anyone else, knows the frailty of human beings. If your language has a way to express this emphasis naturally, you may want to use it in your translation. Alternate translation: [he, more than anyone, knows]

David is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Any person]

Here, **days** represents a person’s lifetime. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his lifetime is like the lifetime of grass]

The psalmist is making a comparison to teach that just as **grass** lives for only a short time, so people live for only a short time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [his days are few, like the length of time that grass lives]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a flower of the field** flourishes for only a short time, so does a person’s life last for only a short time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like a flower of the field, the time when he flourishes is short]

Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation of how people are like grass and flowers. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [Indeed,]
The pronoun **it** refers to the flower. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the flower]

The psalmist is speaking of **its place** as if it were a person who could **acknowledge** something. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and there is nothing in its place to indicate that it had been there]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [But Yahweh will be faithful to his covenant from everlasting]

The psalmist is using **from everlasting to everlasting** as a common expression of his culture to mean “eternally” or “forever.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [lasts forever]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and he will be righteous]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that **the children of children** refers to future generations. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [to their descendants]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [to the ones keeping his covenant, that is, to the ones remembering his precepts, to do them]

The pronoun **the ones** refers to people who fear Yahweh, as described in verse 17. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [to those children … and to the children] or [to those descendants … and to the descendants]

The implication is that they are actively keeping God’s precepts in their minds so that they can obey them. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [keeping in mind]

Here, **to do them** marks this clause as the goal or purpose of **remembering his precepts**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [in order to do them]

Here, **throne** represents the authority and power to rule. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [is the supreme ruler]

Here, **kingdom** represents Yahweh ruling as king. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he, as king,]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that **listening to the voice of his word** means obeying what God says. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [obeying]

Here, **the voice of his word** represents what God says. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what he says]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **pleasure**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what pleases him]

The psalmist is speaking to **all his works** that he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about praising Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about all of Yahweh’s works. Alternate translation: [I want all of Yahweh’s works to bless him,]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **his reign**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the places where he reigns]

The psalmist is using the term **soul** to mean his entire person from the perspective of his spiritual and emotional existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [my inner being]

104.text:
# Psalm 104 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 104 is the second in the series of five “psalms of praise” to God (Psalm 103–107).

1. Yahweh’s greatness in creation (1–6)
2. Yahweh’s sustaining care over creation (7–30)
3. Yahweh’s glory declared forever (31–32)
4. Everlasting praise to Yahweh (33–35)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Yahweh’s creation

God has created everything good on earth, in the sky, and in the sea.

The psalmist is using the term **soul** to mean his entire person from the perspective of his spiritual and emotional existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [myself] or [my inner being]

The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were **clothed with splendor and majesty**. He means that Yahweh possesses splendor and majesty just as a king might wear magnificent robes. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture. Alternatively, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you are splendid and majestic]

The terms **splendor** and **majesty** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [extreme magnificence]

The expression **you are clothed with splendor and majesty** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [you are splendid and majestic]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **splendor** and **majesty**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [you are splendid and majestic]

The psalmist is making a comparison to describe how God wears light. The point of this comparison is that just as **a garment** covers and adorns a person, so **light** covers and adorns God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [putting light around you as though it were a garment]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a tent curtain** is stretched out to provide shelter, so the **heavens** are stretched out by God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [spreading out the heavens as a man would spread out a tent curtain]

The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were **setting his upper chambers on the waters**. This image pictures God’s dwelling place as being built above the sky, where the rain clouds are. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [It is as though you have set the upper chambers of your home on the waters in the sky]

The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a king or mighty warrior who rode across the sky with **the clouds** serving as his **chariot**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [It is as though you ride the clouds like chariots]

The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were someone who could **walk on the wings of the wind**. He means that Yahweh moves about freely and swiftly, as if he were riding on the wind itself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you move about freely as though you were flying along with the wind]

104.quote: עֹשֶׂ֣ה מַלְאָכָ֣י⁠ו רוּח֑וֹת מְ֝שָׁרְתָ֗י⁠ו אֵ֣שׁ לֹהֵֽט
104.text: In these clauses, the subjects and objects are not marked, and could fill either role. They could mean: (1) Yahweh makes the winds his messengers and he makes flaming fire his servants, as in the ULT, or (2) Yahweh makes his messengers winds and he makes his servants flaming fire. Alternate translation: [making his messengers winds, and his servants, flaming fire]

The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were **making the winds his messengers**. This image means that Yahweh uses the winds to carry out his purposes, just as a king would send messengers to accomplish his will. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [sending the winds as he would send his messengers]

The psalmist is speaking of **flaming fire** as if it were a person who could serve God. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [controlling flaming fire so that it serves him]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [making flaming fire his servants]

The psalmist is speaking of **the earth** as if Yahweh had placed it **upon** physical **foundations** like a building is constructed on a foundation. The psalmist means that Yahweh created the world to be stable and secure. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He made the earth to be stable]

If your language does not use this passive form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [never can anyone move it]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that **the deep** refers to the waters of the ocean or the primeval waters that once covered the earth. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [with deep water]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a garment** completely covers a person, so **the deep** completely covered the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as completely as if that were its clothing]

The psalmist is speaking of **the waters** as if they were a living thing that could stand in a certain position. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the waters were higher than the mountains]

These two phrases **From your rebuke they fled** and **from your voice of thunder they hurried away** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could combine the phrases. Alternate translation: [From your thunderous rebuke they fled away]

The psalmist is speaking of **the waters** as if they were living things that could **flee** and **hurry away**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they receded … they went away]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe a **voice** that is characterized by **thunder**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [your thunderous voice]

The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh’s **voice** as if it were **thunder** to express how loud it is. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your loud voice]

**They** refers to “the waters” from verse 6. This reflects the idea from Genesis 7:11 that the flood waters came from where they had been stored both above the firmament and underground. Here it is saying that after the flood God returned the waters to those places, so some of it **ascended the mountains** to return to the heavens and some **descended the valleys** to return to their places underground.

Some translations take **the mountains** to be the subject of **ascended** and **the valleys** to be the subject of **descended**. This makes it difficult to translate the following verse however, since verse 9 continues to refer to the waters as “they.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to follow what it does here. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to follow the ULT. Alternate translation: [The mountains rose; the valleys descended]
The pronoun **they** refers to the waters. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the waters]
**The one** in verses 10, 13, and 14 refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, you send]
The pronoun **They** refers to the springs (mentioned in the previous verse). It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The streams of water give drink to]

The psalmist is using **break their thirst** as a common expression to mean “quench their thirst” or “satisfy their thirst by drinking.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [quench their thirst] or [drink and are satisfied]
The pronoun **them** refers to the streams of water mentioned in verse 10. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Alongside the streams of water]

The psalmist is using **they give voice** as a common expression of his culture to mean “they sing” or “they chirp.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they chirp]

The psalmist is using the phrase **The one watering** to refer to God without using a pronoun. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a name or pronoun to clarify the referent. Alternate translation: [Yahweh waters]

The psalmist is speaking of the sky as if it were **upper chambers** in a building from which God sends rain down on the mountains. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from high in the sky]

Here, **fruit** could be both literal and figurative. It could mean either of these things or both: (1) The work of watering the mountains produces literal fruit, which satisfies the creatures on earth. The next two verses list some of that fruit. Alternate translation: [this work of yours produces fruit, which satisfies the earth] or (2) The result of watering the mountains is that the earth is satisfied with the water. Alternate translation: [because you do this, the earth is satisfied]

Here, **the earth** represents the creatures that live on the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the earthly creatures are satisfied]
The phrase **The one** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, who makes grass grow]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from earlier in the verse if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and the one making plants grow]

Here, **to bring forth** marks **bread from the earth** as the goal or purpose of **plants for the work of man**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [in order to produce]

The psalmist is using one kind of food, **bread**, to represent food in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [food]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [And by providing wine]

Here the **heart** represents a person’s inner self, including their emotions and sense of well-being. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all mankind] or [everyone]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **face**. He means faces in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [to make people’s faces shine]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [he gives olives to make the face shine]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and by providing bread]

The psalmist is speaking of **the trees of Yahweh** as if they were living things that could be satisfied. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The trees of Yahweh get plenty of rain]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from earlier in the verse if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [the cedars of Lebanon which he planted are satisfied]

The expression **where birds make their nests there** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in many languages. The word **there** repeats the idea of **where**. If this would be unnatural in your language, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [where birds make their nests]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **stork**. He means storks in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [storks, cypress trees their home]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [the stork makes the cypress tree her home]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [the high mountains are the home for the wild goats]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from earlier in the verse if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [the cliffs are a refuge for the hyraxes]

A **hyrax** is a kind of small, furry animal that lives in rocky areas. If your readers would not be familiar with what a hyrax is, you could use the name of a similar animal that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [for the rock badgers]
The pronoun **He** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh made]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that the **appointed times** are the festivals and religious observances that are determined by the phases of the moon. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [to indicate the times for the special days of each month]

The psalmist is speaking of **the sun** as if it were a living thing that could know when to set. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you made the sun to set at the proper time each night]

The psalmist uses **and** to indicate that **it is night** is the result of God setting **darkness**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [and night happens] or [which creates night]
The pronoun **it** refers to the darkness. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [in the night]

The psalmist is speaking of the young lions as if they were **seeking their food from God**. He means that God provides food for the lions. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as though they are asking God to give them their food]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that he means that the young lions retreat because **the sun rises** and it becomes daytime. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [When the sun rises]

The terms **work** and **labor** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [to all of his work that he does]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **Man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Each person]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wisdom**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [wisely] or [skillfully]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **creation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what you have created]

The terms **great** and **broad of hands** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [enormous in size]

The psalmist is using **broad of hands** as a common expression of his culture to mean that the shores of the sea are far apart. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and with distant shorelines]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that **great** refers to the sea’s vast size or extent. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [large]

The psalmist says **there is no number** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [and there are too many to count]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [the small living things are there with the great living things]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that **great** refers to the large size of some of the sea creatures. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [large]

The psalmist is using the adjectives **small** and **great** as nouns to mean small creatures and large creatures. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you could translate these words with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [small ones with large ones]

The psalmist is referring to all of the living creatures in the sea by naming two extremes, **small** and **great**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [of every size together]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Leviathan travels there]

The pronoun **them** refers to all of the living creatures that the psalmist has been describing, including the sea creatures mentioned in the previous verses. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [All of these living creatures]

The psalmist is speaking of creatures depending on God for their food as if they were physically looking at someone for help. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [need you]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that it is when God provides the food that the creatures gather it. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [When you give to them; then they gather it]

The psalmist is using **you open your hand** as a common expression of his culture to mean “you give generously.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you give generously]

The adjective **good** is functioning as a noun, referring to good things (specifically, good food that God provides). If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this with a noun phrase or indicate what kind of good things are meant. Alternate translation: [they are satisfied with the good food]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that it is when God hides his face from his creatures that they then become terrified. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [When you hide your face; then they are terrified]

The psalmist is using **You hide your face** as a common expression of his culture to mean “You withdraw your care” or “You turn away from them.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [When you ignore them]

The expression **they are terrified** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [that terrifies them]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that it is when God takes the breath away that creatures then expire. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [When you take away their breath; then they expire]

The psalmist is using **return to their dust** as a common expression of his culture to mean “die and decay.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and turn into dirt]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that it is when God sends out his breath that creatures then begin to live. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [When you send out your breath; then they are created]

The same word that is translated as **breath** in this and the previous verse also means “spirit.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to translate as it does. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to translate as the ULT does. Alternate translation: [You send out your Spirit; they are created]

The expression **they are created** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [you create them]

Here, **the face of the land** represents everything living on the surface of the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [everything living on the earth]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [May his creatures honor Yahweh forever]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **creation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in what he has created]
The phrase **the one** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh looks at the earth]

The psalmist uses **and** to indicate that **it shakes** is the result of God **looking at the earth**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [the one looking at the earth, so that it shakes]

The psalmist uses **and** to indicate that **they smoke** is the result of God touching **the mountains**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [he touches the mountains, which causes them to smoke]

The psalmist is using this possessive form to describe his relationship with God. The phrase **my God** indicates the God whom the psalmist worships and serves. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to the God whom I worship]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the idea of **existence**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [while I am alive]

By **my meditation**, the psalmist is probably referring to the things that he has expressed in this psalm. If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **meditation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the things that I have expressed]

The psalmist is speaking of his **meditation** as if it were something that could have a sweet taste. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May my meditation please him]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I will rejoice** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize his personal commitment to rejoice in Yahweh. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [For my part, I will rejoice]

The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a location that the psalmist could be **in**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because of who Yahweh is]

The psalmist is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean wicked people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you could translate this word with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [and wicked people]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from earlier in the verse if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and may the wicked be no more]

The psalmist is using the term **soul** to mean his entire person from the perspective of his spiritual and emotional existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [myself] or [my inner being]

The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Halleluia] or [Praise Yah]
**Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh]

105.text:
# Psalm 105 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 105 is the third in a series of five “psalms of praise” to God (Psalm 103–107). Psalm 105 retells the history of Israel from Yahweh’s covenant with Abraham, to the people’s enslavement in Egypt, to Yahweh’s liberation of the people through the plagues in Egypt, to Yahweh giving them the land of Canaan.

1. Praise Yahweh and seek his works (1–6)
2. Yahweh’s covenant and deeds with the patriarchs (7–15)
3. Yahweh’s guidance over Joseph and Israel in Egypt (16–25)
4. Yahweh’s deliverance and provision in the wilderness (26–45)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Yahweh’s protection

God protected Abraham and Jacob. He worked throughout Israel’s history to bring Israel into the land he had promised them. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/promisedland]])

The psalmist is using the term **name** to refer to Yahweh himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [call on him]

Here, **the name of his holiness** represents Yahweh himself, who is holy. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in Yahweh, who is holy]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe a **name** that is characterized by **holiness**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in his holy name]

Here the **heart** represents where a person’s thoughts, feelings, and desires exist. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [let the people who seek Yahweh rejoice]

The psalmist is speaking of people who desire to know Yahweh as if they were **seekers** of him, or trying to find him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [let the heart of those who desire to know Yahweh rejoice]

The psalmist is speaking of needing to **Seek Yahweh** as if he were a lost object that needed to be sought and found. He means that the people should pray to Yahweh and desire to be in his presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Pray to Yahweh and ask for his strength]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for him to strengthen you]
Here, **his face** represents his presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [seek his presence]

Here, **his mouth** represents Yahweh speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the decrees that he spoke]

106.text:
# Psalm 106 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 106 is the fourth in a series of five “psalms of praise” to God (Psalm 103–107). The book of Psalms is divided into five sections, also called “books,” and Psalm 106 ends book four. Verses 47 and 48 are considered to be a closing petition and praise for book four, rather than belonging specifically to Psalm 106.

1. Praise Yahweh for his goodness and faithfulness (1–3)
2. Plea for pardon and Yahweh’s acceptance (4–6)
3. Recount Israel’s rebellion and Yahweh’s mercy (7–46)
4. Prayer and praise to Yahweh (47–48)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Israel’s sin

Although Israel continually sinned in the desert, God still took them to the Promised Land. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/sin]]; and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/promisedland]])

The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Halleluia] or [Praise Yah]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [give thanks to Yahweh for his covenant faithfulness is to forever]

Alternate translation: [for his covenant faithfulness lasts forever]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the way he is faithful to his covenant]
