By **I shall divide Shechem**, God means that he will divide the land where Shechem is located. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I shall divide the land surrounding Shechem]

By **the Valley of Succoth**, God means the territory or region around the Valley of Succoth. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and measure out the territory of the Valley of Succoth]

By **measure out**, God means “measure out for my people to possess.” You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [for my people make portions of]

108.quote: לִ֤⁠י גִלְעָ֨ד ׀ לִ֤⁠י מְנַשֶּׁ֗ה וְ֭⁠אֶפְרַיִם מָע֣וֹז רֹאשִׁ֑⁠י יְ֝הוּדָ֗ה מְחֹקְקִֽ⁠י
108.text: See how you translated this in [Psalm 60:7](../060/007.md)

God is using **To me is** as a common expression of his culture to mean “belongs to me” or “is mine.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Gilead belongs to me; Manasseh belongs to me]

Here God is speaking of **Ephraim** as if it were **the protection of my head**, meaning a helmet that protects a warrior in battle. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the people of Ephraim are my warriors]

Here God is speaking of **Judah** as if it were a **scepter**. He means that God rules through the kings of the tribe of Judah. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I rule through the kings of the tribe of Judah]

God is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Judah is my scepter]

108.quote: מוֹאָ֤ב ׀ סִ֬יר רַחְצִ֗⁠י עַל־אֱ֭דוֹם אַשְׁלִ֣יךְ נַעֲלִ֑⁠י עֲלֵֽי־פְ֝לֶ֗שֶׁת אֶתְרוֹעָֽע
108.text: See how you translated this in [Psalm 60:8](../060/008.md).

Here God is speaking of **Moab** as if it were **a tub for my washing**. He means that the people of Moab will serve him in a menial way, like servants who bring a basin for washing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The people of Moab are like servants who wash my feet]

Here God is speaking of **Edom** as if it were a servant who removes his sandals. This image shows that Edom will be completely defeated and will serve Israel in the most menial ways. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people of Edom are like servants who remove my sandals]

108.quote: מִ֣י יֹ֭בִלֵ⁠נִי עִ֣יר מִבְצָ֑ר מִ֖י נָחַ֣⁠נִי עַד־אֱדֽוֹם
108.text: See how you translated this in [Psalm 60:9](../060/009.md).

108.quote: מִ֣י יֹ֭בִלֵ⁠נִי עִ֣יר מִבְצָ֑ר מִ֖י נָחַ֣⁠נִי עַד־אֱדֽוֹם
108.text: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **Who will lead me to Edom** before the information about **Who will bring me into the strong city**. Alternate translation: [Who will lead me to Edom? Who will bring me into the strong city?]

David assumes that readers will know that **the strong city** refers to a fortified city in Edom, likely its capital. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Who will bring me into the strong capital city of Edom?]

David is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Only God can bring me into the strong city.]

David is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Only God can lead me to Edom.]
See how you translated this in [Psalm 60:10](../060/010.md).

David is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [God, it seems that you have rejected us!]

108.quote: הָֽבָ⁠ה־לָּ֣⁠נוּ עֶזְרָ֣ת מִ⁠צָּ֑ר וְ֝⁠שָׁ֗וְא תְּשׁוּעַ֥ת אָדָֽם
108.text: See how you translated this in [Psalm 60:11](../060/011.md).

David is not referring to a specific **enemy**. He means enemies in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [against all of our enemies]

Here the word **and** introduces not an additional action but an explanation. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [since futility is the deliverance of man]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **futility**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [since expecting humans to save us is futile]

David is using this possessive form **the deliverance of man** to mean deliverance that comes from human beings. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [any deliverance by human beings]
See how you translated this in [Psalm 60:12](../060/012.md).
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **valor**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [we will succeed valiantly]

David is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **will trample** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that it is God who will defeat the enemies. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [and it is he who will trample our adversaries]

Here David is speaking of God in the third person as **he** even though he has been addressing God directly in the previous verses. This may be to give encouragement to the Israelites who are listening. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the second person to maintain the direct address. Alternate translation: [and you, you will trample our adversaries]

Here David is speaking of God as if he were a warrior who would **trample** the enemies underfoot. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this plainly. Alternate translation: [and he, he will completely defeat our adversaries]

109.text:
# Psalm 109 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 109 is a “psalm of petition,” asking Yahweh to give David relief from his enemies who are falsely accusing him and persecuting him. He also asks Yahweh to curse these people who are enemies of both Yahweh and David.

1. Complaint and accusation (1–5)
2. Curses against enemies (6–20)
3. David’s plea for himself (21–29)
4. Praise and confidence (30–31)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Cursing of Enemies

In this psalm, David takes evil very seriously and calls on Yahweh to punish those who are doing evil to himself and others so that the evil will stop. It is important to note that David does not take vengeance personally, but only calls on Yahweh to combat evil and to perform justice, as Yahweh has promised to do.

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

### Singular and Plural

David refers to his enemies in the singular in verses 6–19 and in the plural in the rest of the psalm. You may want to use the plural throughout the psalm, or you may want to add a footnote at verse 6 that explains that in the section of verses 6–19 David may be speaking of the leader of his enemies or he may be speaking of each one individually.

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

Here David is using the possessive form **God of my praise** to describe God as the one whom he praises. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [God whom I praise]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please do not be silent]

Here, **mouth** represents people who are speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [wicked and deceitful people speak against me]

Here, **tongue** represents the words that people speak. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [they speak untrue things concerning me]

Here, **words of hatred** represents people speaking hateful things. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and people surround me saying hateful things]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **love**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Instead of loving me as I love them]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [they accuse me of doing bad things]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [but I turn to prayer] or [but I continue to pray]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **evil** and **good**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [They do evil things to me although I did good things to them]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **hatred** and **love**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [and they hate me although I was loving to them]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and they put hatred upon me in return for my love]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please appoint a wicked one over him]

Here David is speaking as if God would **appoint** a human judge to preside over his enemy. He means that he wants God to bring judgment upon his enemy. If this image does not communicate well in your language, you could express this as a comparison or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Appoint a wicked one to judge him]

David is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [a wicked man]

By **an accuser**, David means someone who will bring formal charges against his enemy in court. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and may someone accuse him before that wicked judge of doing evil things]

The expression **is judged** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [When the wicked one judges him]

David is using **may he come out guilty** as a common expression of his culture to mean “may the verdict be that he is guilty.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [may the verdict be that he is guilty]

This could mean: (1) The enemy is praying to Yahweh and since his prayer is insincere, Yahweh should count it as sinful. Alternate translation: [and may his prayer be considered as another sin] or (2) The enemy is pleading with the judge, and the judge should count his plea as a further offense. Alternate translation: [and may his plea be considered as an offense]

David is using **May his days be few** as a common expression of his culture to mean “May he die soon” or “May he live only a short time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May he live only a short time]

Here David is speaking of a person’s role or authority as if it were a **position** that someone could physically occupy. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [may another take his authority] or [may another replace him]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and may his wife be a widow]

David is repeating forms of the verb **wander** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [And may his children wander far away]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and beg and seek for food]

By **their desolations**, David means their ruined homes or destroyed dwellings. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [from their destroyed houses]

Here David is speaking as if a creditor were a hunter or trapper who could **snare** the enemy’s possessions. He means that the creditor should seize or take control of everything the enemy owns. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May a creditor take]

David is using **all that is to him** as a common expression of his culture to mean “everything that belongs to him.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [everything that belongs to him]

The implication is that **his work** refers to the things that he worked for or the results of his labor. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the things that he worked for]

David is using **May there not be to him** as a common expression of his culture to mean “May he not have.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May he not have]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [someone who is kindly loyal to him]

The implication is that these would be children who have lost their father due to the curse pronounced against him in the previous verses. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [someone who pities his orphaned children]

David is using **be to cut off** as a common expression of his culture to mean “die” or “be destroyed.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May his posterity be destroyed]

The expression **may their name be blotted out** contains a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [may you blot out their name]

Here David is speaking of making people be forgotten as if their names were written words that could be erased or **blotted out**. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [may there be no one bearing their name] or [may no one remember their name]

The expression **be remembered** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [May Yahweh keep in mind the sin of his fathers] or [May you remember the sin of his fathers]
David is using the term **fathers** to mean “ancestors.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his ancestors]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and may the offense of his mother not be blotted out]

The expression **not be blotted out** contains a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [and do not blot out the offense of his mother]

David is using **not be blotted out** as a common expression of his culture to mean “not be forgiven.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the offense of his mother not be forgiven]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **offense**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the things that his mother did that offended Yahweh not be blotted out]

The pronoun **they** refers to the sins of the enemy’s father and mother mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [May those sins be before Yahweh continually]

Here David is speaking of the sins as if they were objects that could be continually placed **before Yahweh** for him to see. He means he wants Yahweh to notice those sins. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May Yahweh continually consider them]

David is using **cut off their remembrance** as a common expression of his culture to mean “destroy anything that would cause people to remember them.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and may he destroy anything that would cause people to remember them]

The pronoun **he** refers to Yahweh, while the pronoun **their** refers to David’s enemies. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and may he cut off any remembrance of those people]

Here, **the earth** represents any people living on earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from any people living on earth]
The pronoun **he** refers to David’s enemy. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [that man never remembered]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to be kind to others]

Here David is speaking of the man’s treatment of vulnerable people as if he **pursued** them like a hunter chasing prey. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but harassed]

David is not referring to specific **humble** and **needy** and **dejected** people. He means people who were humble and needy and dejected in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people who were humble and needy and dejected in heart]

David is using the adjectives **needy** and **dejected** as nouns to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [and needy people and people dejected in their hearts]

Here David is speaking of people as if their emotions were located in their **heart**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and those who felt very sad]
The implication is that he pursued these people until they died. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [until they died]

Here David is speaking as if cursing were an object that physically **came to** someone. He means that the person experienced the effects or consequences of cursing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and now those curses have fallen on him] or [and now I wish those bad things to happen to him]

David is emphasizing a negative meaning by using a negative word, **not**, together with a mild expression that is the opposite of the intended meaning. If it would be helpful in your language, you could emphasize the negative meaning in a strong way. Alternate translation: [and he hated blessing]

Here David is speaking as if blessing were an object that could be physically **far from** his enemy. He means that his enemy will not receive any blessing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he will not receive any]

Here David is speaking of his enemy as if **cursing** were **his garment** that he put on. He means that cursing other people was habitual for this person, like clothing that someone wears regularly. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he cursed other people continually]

David is making a comparison between **it entered into his inner being like water** and how deeply cursing has become part of his enemy’s character. The point of this comparison is that just as **water** penetrates thoroughly into a person when they drink, so **cursing** has penetrated deeply into this man’s inner being. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and it became a part of him like water does when we drink it]

David is making a comparison between how oil soaks into bones and how cursing has become part of his enemy’s inner being. The point of this comparison is that just as **oil** penetrates deeply and becomes absorbed, so cursing has become deeply absorbed into the enemy’s very nature. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and it became a part of him like oil would after it had entered into his bones]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and it entered into his inner being like oil penetrating his bones]

David is making a comparison between curses and **clothing** that someone wears. The point of this comparison is that just as **clothing** clings closely to a person’s body, so the curses should cling closely to his enemy. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [May it wrap itself tightly to him like the clothing that he wears]

The pronoun **it** refers to the cursing mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [May that cursing be to him like the clothing that he wears]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and may it be for him like the belt]

David is making a comparison. The point of this comparison is that just as **the belt** is something that a person wears constantly, so the curse should cling to his enemy constantly. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and may it always be around him as the belt]

It might seem that the expression **he always girds himself with it** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [he always girds himself with] or [with which he always girds himself]

The pronoun **This** refers to the curse that David has been describing in the previous verses. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [May the effects of this curse be]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [May the effects of this curse be]

Here, **This, the payment** could mean: (1) David is asking Yahweh that this be the payment to his accusers. Alternate translation: [May this be the payment] or (2) David is stating that this is the payment to his accusers. Alternate translation: [This will be the payment]

Here David is speaking of God’s punishment as if it were **payment** that God gives to David’s accusers. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [This, the punishment of my accusers from Yahweh]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and may this be the payment from Yahweh to those speaking evil against my soul]

Here, **soul** represents the entire person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and those speaking evil against me]

By **do with me**, David means “treat me kindly” or “act favorably toward me.” You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [do good to me] or [do what I ask]

Here, **name** represents who God is or God’s reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [on account of your character]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Because you are good and faithful to your covenant]

The terms **poor** and **needy** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [I am very poor]

Here David is speaking of his emotional distress as if his **heart breaks** physically. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am in great despair]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a shadow when it lengthens** quickly disappears, so David’s life is quickly passing away. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Like how quickly a shadow disappears as it lengthens]

The expression **I am made to go** contains a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I will leave]

The expression **I am shaken off** contains a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I will fall off like a locust]

David is making a comparison. The point of this comparison is that just as **a locust** is easily shaken off, so David is easily dismissed or removed from his position. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [I will disappear as quickly as someone shakes off a locust]
Here, **knees** represents the strength of the whole body. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [My body is weak]

The word **from** indicates that **fasting** is the reason for the weakness described in the first part of the verse. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that the fasting is the cause of the weakness. Alternate translation: [because of fasting very much]

By **my flesh is gaunt from fatness**, David means that his flesh is gaunt from the complete absence of fat. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and my flesh is gaunt, very far from being fat]

The pronoun **I** is stated twice here for emphasis. David is emphasizing his own condition or state in contrast to his enemies. If a speaker of your language would use explicit pronouns for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that meaning here. Alternate translation: [As for me, I am]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **disgrace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [I am disgusting to them]

Here the word that is translated **they see me** does not clearly indicate when the action of seeing occurs. It could mean “whenever they see me” or refer to a specific instance. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [whenever they see me]

The expression **shake their head** describes a symbolic action by which people showed contempt or mockery. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [they show that they despise me by shaking their heads]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please help me]

The psalmist is not using the phrase **my God** to mean that he possesses or controls Yahweh, but rather to emphasize that Yahweh is the God he worships as modeled in the UST. See the introduction to Psalms for further discussion.

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [according to your covenant to be faithful]

By **according to your covenant faithfulness**, David means according to God’s promise to be faithful to his people. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [since you have promised to be faithful to me]

Here, **so that** marks **they know that this is your hand; you, Yahweh, you have done it** as the goal or purpose of “Help me, Yahweh my God; save me according to your covenant faithfulness” in the previous verse. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [because I want them to know]
The pronoun **they** refers to David’s accusers. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [so that the people who accuse me know]

Here, **hand** represents the power of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that this is your doing]

David is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you have done it** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Yahweh is the one who has acted. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [it is you, Yahweh, who have done it]

The pronoun **it** refers to Yahweh saving David, as he asked Yahweh to do in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [you, Yahweh, are the one who saved me]
The pronoun **They** refers to David’s accusers. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The people who accuse me, they will curse]

David is stating the pronouns **they** and **you** separately for emphasis, even though the verbs translated as **they will curse** and **you will bless** already include their meanings. He is doing that to create a strong contrast between what his enemies will do (curse) and what God will do (bless). If a speaker of your language would use explicit pronouns for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that meaning here. Alternate translation: [They are the ones who will curse, but you are the one who will bless]

By **they arise**, David means they arise to attack him. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [they arise to attack me]

The psalmist is speaking of himself in the third person as **your servant** to show humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a humble form in the first person. Alternate translation: [and I, your servant]

109.quote: יִלְבְּשׁ֣וּ שׂוֹטְנַ֣⁠י כְּלִמָּ֑ה וְ⁠יַעֲט֖וּ כַ⁠מְעִ֣יל בָּשְׁתָּֽ⁠ם
109.text: These two phrases **May my accusers be clothed with disgrace** and **may they wear their shame like a robe** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [May my accusers be clothed with shameful disgrace as though it were a robe]

Here David is speaking of his accusers as if they were people who could be **clothed with disgrace**. He means that their disgrace should be clearly seen and obvious to everyone. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May it be obvious how disgraceful my accusers are]

David is making a comparison between **their shame** and **a robe**. The point of this comparison is that just as a robe is visible to everyone who sees the person wearing it, so David wants his accusers’ shame to be visible and obvious to everyone. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [may their shame be so obvious to everyone that it is like a robe that they are wearing]

Here, **mouth** represents speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will speak to greatly thank Yahweh]

David is using the adjective **many** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [and in the midst of many people]

Here David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a person who could physically **stand at the right hand of the needy**. The image of standing at someone’s right hand means to be ready to help and defend them. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [he advocates for the needy] or [he helps the needy]

David is using the adjective **needy** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [needy people]

By **the judges of his soul**, David means those who seek to condemn him to death. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [from officials who want to take his life]

110.text:
# Psalm 110 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 110 is a psalm honoring the king as he becomes king and was also recognized as a prophecy about the coming messiah. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/prophet]]; and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/christ]])

1. The divine proclamation (1–2)
2. The people’s response (3)
3. The eternal priesthood (4)
4. The king’s judgment & victory (5–7)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### King

Yahweh will enable the king to conquer his enemies. Christ is seen as both high priest and king. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/highpriest]])

Yahweh is using **Sit at my right hand** as a common expression of the culture to mean “Take the place of highest honor and authority beside me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Sit with me in the honored place]

Here Yahweh is speaking of defeating enemies as if he were making them into **a footstool for your feet**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [until I give you victory over your enemies]

Here, **scepter** represents royal authority and power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will expand the area where you strongly rule]

David is using the possessive form to describe a **scepter** that is characterized by **strength**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [your strong scepter]

The word translated as **rule** is an imperative, but it communicates an invitation to rule rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate an invitation for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates an invitation. Alternate translation: [I want you to rule]

David is speaking of **Your people** as if they were **freewill offerings**. He means that the people will willingly offer themselves to serve the king, just as people willingly bring offerings to God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Your people are like freewill offerings]

David is using this possessive form **the day of your strength** to mean when you show how strong you are. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [when you show how strong you are]

David is using the possessive form to describe a **beauty** that is characterized by **holiness**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in holy beauty]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the ideas of **beauty** and **holiness**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [they will be beautiful and holy] or [because they are holy, they will be beautiful]

Here David is speaking of the king’s youthful vigor as if it were **the dew of your youth** that comes **from the womb of the dawn**. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [you will be as fresh as the dew that comes early every morning]

The pronoun **it** refers to the oath or solemn promise that Yahweh has made and that David is about to repeat. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and will not revoke this oath]

David is using **at your right hand** as a common expression of his culture to mean “near you to help you” or “fighting for you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The Lord is near you to help you]
David assumes that readers will know that **The Lord** refers to Yahweh. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is]

Here David is speaking as if the Lord were a person who physically **crushes kings**. He means that the Lord defeats enemy kings. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He defeats enemy kings]

David is using the phrase **the day of his nose** as a common expression of the culture to mean that the Lord is angry. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [on the day of his anger] or [when he displays his anger]

By **He will judge the nations**, David means that Yahweh will punish the nations for their wickedness. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [He will punish the nations]

Here, **the nations** represents the people who live in the nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people living in many nations]

By **he fills with bodies**, David means he fills the battlefield with dead bodies. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [he fills the battlefield with dead bodies]

David is not referring to a specific **head**. He means the heads of the king’s enemies in general. The word translated as **head** could refer to: (1) the heads of the enemy soldiers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh crushes the heads of the enemy soldiers] or (2) the leaders of the enemy armies. Alternate translation: [Yahweh defeats the leaders of the enemy armies]
The word translated as **land** could refer to: (1) a battlefield. Alternate translation: [on a large battlefield] or (2) the earth. Alternate translation: [over the whole earth]
Here, **He** could refer to: (1) the king. Alternate translation: [The king will drink] or (2) Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will drink]

**Therefore** introduces the result of Yahweh fighting for and strengthening the king, as the previous verses of this psalm describe. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Because Yahweh has fought for him]

David is using **he will lift up the head** as a common expression of his culture to mean “he will triumph over his enemies.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he will triumph over his enemies]

111.text:
# Psalm 111 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 111 is a psalm of praise to God for his miracles and care. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/miracle]])

1. Call to praise (1–2)
2. Yahweh’s majestic works (3–6)
3. Yahweh’s trustworthy and enduring nature (7–9)
4. Wisdom and praise (10)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Yahweh’s character

God is great. He has given his people food, land, and always keeps his promises to his people. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/promise]]; and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/peopleofgod]])

The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Halleluia] or [Praise Yah]
**Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh]

Here the psalmist is speaking of the place where his emotions and will reside as his **heart**. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with my whole heart] or [with all that I am]

The phrase **upright and congregation** expresses a single idea. The word **upright** tells more about **congregation**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [the congregation of upright people]

The psalmist is using the adjective **upright** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the upright people]

The expression **searched by everyone desirous of them** contains a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [everyone desirous of them searches them]

The psalmist is using the adjective **desirous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [searched by everyone who desires them]
The pronoun **them** refers to the works of Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [they are searched by everyone desirous of his works]
This could mean: (1) people examine and study Yahweh’s works. Alternate translation: [studied] or (2) people are looking for Yahweh to do his works. Alternate translation: [eagerly awaited]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **splendor** and **majesty**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [His work is splendid and majestic]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and he is righteous forever]

Here the psalmist is speaking of God’s righteousness as if it were a structure that **stands forever**. He means that God’s righteousness is permanent and will never change or fail. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and his righteousness endures forever]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **remembrance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [He makes sure that people will always remember the wonderful things that he does]

The psalmist is using the adjective **fearing** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [to the people who fear him]
This means that Yahweh will always act according to his covenant. See how you translated this in [Psalm 105:8](../105/008.md). Alternate translation: [He will honor his covenant forever]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **works** that are characterized by **power**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [his powerful works]

The implication is that Yahweh showed his power by means of giving his people the lands that had belonged to other nations as their inheritance. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [by giving to them]

The implication is that this refers to the land that belonged to other nations. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [land that belonged to other nations]

Here the psalmist is speaking of the things that God does as if they were **the works of his hands**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [All the things that he does]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **truth** and **justice**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [are true and just]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that **precepts** refers to God’s commands and instructions. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [We can rely on all of his instructions]

The expression **They are established** contains a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [He established them to last forever]

The terms **forever** and **for eternity** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [for all eternity]

If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. This could mean: (1) Yahweh has given his instructions in a faithful and proper manner. Alternate translation: [made faithfully and uprightly] or (2) his people are to observe Yahweh’s instructions in a faithful and proper manner. Alternate translation: [for his people to observe faithfully and properly]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [done faithfully]

The psalmist is using the adjective **upright** as a noun to mean upright things or upright instructions. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [and they are instructions that are upright]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **redemption**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [He has redeemed his people]

The psalmist is using the term **name** to represent who Yahweh is or to refer to Yahweh’s reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is holy and awesome]

The psalmist is using this possessive form to mean a deep reverence for Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. See how you translated this in [Psalm 19:9](../019/009.md). Alternate translation: [Revering Yahweh]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wisdom**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [is how a person begins to become wise]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [all those doing them will gain a good understanding of how to live well]
The pronoun **them** refers to Yahweh’s precepts, mentioned in verse 7. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [to all those doing his precepts]

Here the psalmist is speaking of **praise** as if it were something that could **stand** in the sense of remaining upright and stable. He means that God will be praised forever. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [His praise endures forever] or [He is to be praised forever]

112.text:
# Psalm 112 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 112 is a “wisdom psalm” teaching the value of a righteous life. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/wise]]; and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/righteous]])

1. The blessings of the Yahweh-fearing (1–3)
2. The character and security of the upright (4–9)
3. The contrast with the wicked (10)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Righteous people

The righteous people will be well-known for their generosity and they will not have to worry about bad news because God is taking care of them.

The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Halleluia] or [Praise Yah]
**Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh]

The psalmist is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of joy or blessing. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Oh, how happy is] or [Truly blessed is]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means any man who fears Yahweh. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [anyone]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [how happy is the one who greatly delights in his commandments]

Here the psalmist is speaking of the man’s children as if they were **seed** that he had planted. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [His offspring]

The expression **will be blessed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will bless a generation of upright ones]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **a generation** that is characterized by being **upright**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [everyone who is upright]

The terms **Wealth** and **riches** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Abundant riches]

The psalmist is using the term **house** to mean an entire household living together. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [belong to his household]
The pronoun **his** refers to the man who fears Yahweh mentioned in verse 1. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [belong to such a person]
The pronoun **his** refers to the man who fears Yahweh from verse 1. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the righteousness of such a person]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and each righteous thing that he does]

This could mean: (1) Yahweh and/or people will always remember the righteous things that such a person does. Alternate translation: [continues to be remembered forever] or (2) Such people never stop doing righteous deeds. Alternate translation: [keeps going continually]

Here, **Light** could be: (1) the subject of the verb **shines** as in the ULT, or (2) the object of the verb **shines**, and then the subject of the verb would be “he,” continuing the subject of the previous verse. Alternate translation: [He shines light in the darkness for the upright]

The psalmist speaks of God blessing the upright person in difficult times as if his blessings were a **light** shining in darkness. Alternate translation: [The blessings that an upright person receives from God are like a light that shines in the darkness]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [such a person is gracious and compassionate and just]

This could mean: (1) it is good to be person who is gracious and lends freely. Alternate translation: [It is good to be a gracious and lending man] or (2) good things will happen to a man who is gracious and lending. Alternate translation: [Life goes well for a gracious and lending man]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [a gracious and lending person]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [he is just in all his dealings]

The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [He does this because he will not be moved for forever]

The expression **he will not be moved** contains a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [For nothing will move him for forever]

Here the psalmist is speaking of the righteous person as if he were an object that could be **moved** from its place. He means that nothing will cause the righteous person to fail or be overcome by difficulties. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [For nothing will ever cause him to fail]

The psalmist is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [righteous people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **remembrance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [will always be remembered]

Here the **heart** represents where a person’s thoughts and motives exist. The psalmist is speaking of a person’s inner confidence as if it were **sure**, meaning firmly established or steadfast. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he is confident]

Here the **heart** represents where a person’s thoughts and motives exist. The psalmist is speaking of the righteous person’s emotional state as if his **heart** were **upheld** or supported, meaning that he is calm. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He is tranquil]

The implication is that the righteous person will remain confident and unafraid while God vindicates him by defeating his enemies. This does not mean that he will begin to fear when he sees his enemies. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [all the way to the time that he looks triumphantly over his adversaries]

The terms **scatters** and **gives** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [He gives generously]

The psalmist is using the adjective **poor** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [to anyone who is poor]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [his righteous works stand forever]

This could mean: (1) Yahweh and/or people will always remember the righteous things that such a person does. Alternate translation: [his righteousness continues to be remembered forever] or (2) Such people never stop doing righteous deeds. Alternate translation: [his righteousness keeps going continually]

The psalmist is using **his horn is high** as a common expression of the culture to mean “he is honored and respected by others.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [people respect and honor him]

The implication is that the wicked will see the prosperity and honor of the righteous person described in the previous verses. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [The wicked will see these things happen]

The psalmist is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [Wicked people will see]
The grinding of teeth is an expression of extreme anger. See how you translated a similar phrase in [Psalms 35:16](../035/016.md). Alternate translation: [he will grind his teeth in rage]

Here the psalmist is speaking of the wicked person as if he were something that could **melt away** like ice or wax. He means that the wicked person will become unimportant and die. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he will become unimportant and die]

Here, **desire** could mean: (1) the emotional desire that wicked people have to do wicked things. Alternate translation: [the things that wicked people want to do will never happen] or (2) it represents the things that wicked people have desired. Alternate translation: [wicked people will lose the things that they desired to have]

113.text:
# Psalm 113 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 113 is a “psalm of praise” to God for his goodness. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/good]])

1. The call to universal and eternal praise (1–3)
2. The greatness of Yahweh’s majesty (4–6)
3. The grace of Yahweh’s compassion (7–9)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Yahweh’s help

God helps the poor and gives children to the wife who cannot conceive children.

The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Halleluia] or [Praise Yah]
**Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh]

Here, **name** represents who Yahweh is or to refer to Yahweh himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [praise everything about Yahweh]

The expression **Blessed be** is a passive verbal form. The psalmist is expressing his desire to praise Yahweh. If it would be unnatural to use that form for this purpose, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [We bless Yahweh] or [Let us all praise Yahweh]

The expression **Blessed be** is a passive verbal form. The psalmist is expressing his desire to praise Yahweh. If it would be unnatural to use that form for this purpose, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Let us bless the name of Yahweh]

The psalmist is using the term **name** to represent who Yahweh is or to refer to Yahweh himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Blessed be Yahweh]

The psalmist is referring to all of time by naming two extremes, **now** and **to forever**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [for all eternity]

The psalmist is referring to all of the earth by naming two extremes, **the rising of the sun** and **its setting**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [All over the earth]

The expression **may the name of Yahweh be praised** contains a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [may people praise the name of Yahweh]

Here, **name** represents who Yahweh is or to refer to Yahweh himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [may Yahweh be praised] or [may everything about Yahweh be praised]

Here the psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were physically **high above** the nations, like someone standing on a mountain looking down. This image emphasizes Yahweh’s supreme authority and power over all earthly kingdoms. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is supreme over all nations]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [his glory is high above the skies]

Here the psalmist is speaking of Yahweh’s **glory** as if it were positioned **above the skies**. The psalmist means that Yahweh’s glory is greater than anything that can be seen in the heavens. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his glory exceeds anything visible from earth]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [he is more glorious than anything visible from earth]

The psalmist is using the question form for emphasis, which begins here and continues through verse 6. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [There is no one like Yahweh our God]

The psalmist is using **the one making high to sit** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the one who sits on high” or “the one who rules in the highest position.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one sitting on high] or [the one who rules in the highest position]

This is the second part of the question form that began in verse 5. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for the purpose of creating emphasis as this does, you could translate these two verses as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [the one making low to look on the sky and on the earth.]

The psalmist is using **the one making low to look** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the one who humbles himself to look” or “the one who condescends to look.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one who lowers himself to look down on the sky and on the earth]

113.quote: מְקִֽימִ֣י מֵ⁠עָפָ֣ר דָּ֑ל מֵֽ֝⁠אַשְׁפֹּ֗ת יָרִ֥ים אֶבְיֽוֹן
113.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [raising up the poor from the dust, yes, he lifts the needy from the garbage]

113.quote: מְקִֽימִ֣י מֵ⁠עָפָ֣ר דָּ֑ל מֵֽ֝⁠אַשְׁפֹּ֗ת יָרִ֥ים אֶבְיֽוֹן
113.text: Here the psalmist is speaking of the extremely poor condition of needy people as if they were sitting in **dust** and **garbage**. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he takes the poor out of their dirty and poor condition]

113.quote: מְקִֽימִ֣י מֵ⁠עָפָ֣ר דָּ֑ל מֵֽ֝⁠אַשְׁפֹּ֗ת יָרִ֥ים אֶבְיֽוֹן
113.text: The psalmist is using the adjectives **poor** and **needy** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [raising up poor people from the dust, he lifts needy people from the garbage]

The psalmist is using **to seat him with princes** as a common expression of the culture to mean “to give him a position of honor and authority.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to cause him to rule with princes]
The pronoun **him** refers to the poor person mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [to seat the poor person with princes]

The phrase **with the princes of his people** clarifies who the princes are from the previous phrase. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [that is, to seat him with the princes of his people]
Here, **his** could refer to: (1) Yahweh. Alternate translation: [with the princes of Yahweh’s people] or (2) the poor person. Alternate translation: [with the princes of the man’s people]

The implication is that God transforms a barren woman into a mother by giving her children. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [He causes a woman who is barren to become the joyful mother of children]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **barren woman**. He means barren women in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [He causes barren women of their houses to dwell]

The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Halleluia] or [Praise Yah]
**Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh]

114.text:
# Psalm 114 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 114 is a “psalm of praise” to God for his miracles in bringing the people of Israel to the promised land. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/miracle]]; and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/promisedland]])

1. God claims his people (1–2)
2. Creation’s astonished response (3–6)
3. Earth’s reverent awe (7–8)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Praise

The psalmist praises God for all the ways he helped his people in the past. This psalm references many miraculous events the Israelites experienced like the parting of the Sea of Reeds (Red Sea), the reversal of the Jordan River, bringing water from a rock, and the awe-inspiring presence of God at Mount Sinai, with creation itself responding, as the earth trembled with, God’s power as he delivered his people from Egypt and led them to the land he had promised them.

114.quote: בְּ⁠צֵ֣את יִ֭שְׂרָאֵל מִ⁠מִּצְרָ֑יִם בֵּ֥ית יַ֝עֲקֹ֗ב מֵ⁠עַ֥ם לֹעֵֽז
114.text: These two phrases **When Israel went out from Egypt** and **the house of Jacob from a people speaking a foreign language** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [When Israel went out from Egypt, that is, the house of Jacob from a people speaking a foreign language]
Here, **Israel** represents the Israelite people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the Israelites]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [when the house of Jacob went out from a people speaking a foreign language]

Here, **the house of Jacob** represents the descendants of Jacob. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Jacob’s descendants]

Here, **Judah** and **Israel** could refer to: (1) the territories of Judah and Israel, since the previous verse talks about leaving the territory of Egypt, as modeled in the UST, or (2) the people of Judah and Israel. Alternate translation: [The people of Judah became those among whom Yahweh lived, the people of Israel became those over whom he ruled]
The pronoun **his** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Judah became Yahweh’s sanctuary, Israel Yahweh’s realm]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and Israel became his realm]

The psalmist is speaking of **the sea** as if it were a living thing that could look and flee. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The sea parted as they approached]

The psalmist is speaking of **the Jordan** as if it were a living thing that could turn around and go in the opposite direction. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the water of the Jordan flowed away]
