The psalmist is speaking of **mountains** and **hills** as if they were living things that could skip and jump. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The mountains seemed to skip like rams, the hills like sons of the flock]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [the hills skipped like sons of the flock]

The psalmist is using **sons of the flock** as a common expression of the culture to mean “lambs.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as if they were lambs]

The psalmist is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [It is amazing that the sea would flee away!]

The psalmist is speaking to the **sea** that he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about God’s mighty power over creation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about the sea. Alternate translation: [What happened to the sea, that it flees]

The psalmist is using **What is to you** as a common expression of the culture to mean “What is the matter with you?” or “What is wrong with you?” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [What is the matter with you] or [What is wrong with you]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [What is to you, Jordan, that you turn backwards]

The psalmist is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [It is amazing that the Jordan would turn backwards!]

The psalmist is speaking to **Jordan** that he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about God’s power over creation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about the Jordan. Alternate translation: [What happened to the Jordan, that it turns backwards]
See how you translated these similar phrases in [verse 4](../114/004.md).

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context of the previous verse if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [What is to you, mountains, that you skip like rams]

The psalmist is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [It is amazing that the mountains would skip like rams!]

The psalmist is speaking of **Mountains** as if they were living things that could **skip**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Why did the mountains seem to skip like rams]

The psalmist is speaking to **Mountains** that he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about God’s power displayed in creation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about the mountains. Alternate translation: [What happened to the mountains, that they skip like rams]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context of the previous verse if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [what is to you, hills, that you skip like sons of the flock]

The psalmist is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [it is amazing that the hills would skip like sons of the flock!]

The psalmist is speaking of **hills** as if they were living things that could skip. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [why did the hills seem to skip like sons of the flock]

The psalmist is speaking to **hills** that he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about God’s power displayed in creation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about the hills. Alternate translation: [what happened to the hills, that they skip like sons of the flock]

The psalmist is using **sons of the flock** as a common expression of the culture to mean “lambs.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as if they were lambs]

114.quote: מִ⁠לִּ⁠פְנֵ֣י אָ֭דוֹן ח֣וּלִי אָ֑רֶץ מִ֝⁠לִּ⁠פְנֵ֗י אֱל֣וֹהַּ יַעֲקֹֽב
114.text: The psalmist has asked in the previous verse why the mountains and hills moved, so this verse provides the answer: it is because of the presence of the Lord. But this verse also is an exhortation to the people who live on the earth to tremble with respect before the powerful God of Jacob. So **earth** here probably refers both to the physical earth and to the people who live on it. You may want to use the parallel structure to bring out both meanings. Alternate translation: [Tremble, earth, from to the face of the Lord, you people of earth, from to the face of the God of Jacob]

114.quote: מִ⁠לִּ⁠פְנֵ֣י אָ֭דוֹן ח֣וּלִי אָ֑רֶץ מִ֝⁠לִּ⁠פְנֵ֗י אֱל֣וֹהַּ יַעֲקֹֽב
114.text: These two phrases **from to the face of the Lord** and **from to the face of the God of Jacob** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation as modeled in the UST. If, however, it would be more clear in your language, you could combine the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Tremble, earth, from to the face of the Lord, the mighty God of Jacob]

The psalmist is speaking to the **earth** that he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about God’s awesome power and presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about the earth. Alternate translation: [The earth must tremble]

The psalmist is using **from to the face of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “because of the presence of” or “on account of the presence of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because of the presence of the Lord] or [on account of the Lord’s presence]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [tremble, earth, from to the face of the God of Jacob]

These two phrases **turning the rock into a pool of water** and **flint into a spring of water** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [the one turning the rock into a pool of water, even flint into a spring of water]

Here the psalmist is speaking as though God turned **rock** into **water**. He means that God miraculously made water come out from solid rock for the Israelites in the wilderness. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one making a pool of water come out of the rock, a spring of water come out of flint]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [the one turning flint into a spring of water]

115.text:
# Psalm 115 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 115 is a “psalm of praise.”

1. Glory belongs to Yahweh alone (1–3)
2. Futility of idols (4–8)
3. Call for God’s people to trust Yahweh (9–11)
4. Yahweh’s Faithfulness and Blessing (12–15)
5. Life, praise, and hope in the living God (16–18)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Yahweh’s power

Yahweh is in heaven and is able to do whatever he wants. Idols can not do anything. Therefore, people and priests should trust Yahweh for their protection.
The psalmist is using the repetition for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Not at all to us, Yahweh]

The phrase **but to your name give honor** is an imperative, but rather than commanding, it is expressing a desire that something happen or that someone do something. If the imperative does not communicate this for your readers, then use a form in your language to indicate the speaker is expressing what he wants someone to do or what he wishes someone would do. Alternate translation: [but people should instead honor your name]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **honor**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [but let people honor your name]

The psalmist is using the term **name** to represent who God is or to refer to God’s reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but let people honor you]

The word translated as **upon** could mean: (1) the psalmist wants Yahweh to be honored for demonstrating his covenant faithfulness and trustworthiness, as in the UST, or (2) Yahweh deserves honor because of his covenant faithfulness and trustworthiness. Alternate translation: [because of your covenant faithfulness and trustworthiness]

If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [by seeing your covenant faithfulness and by seeing your trustworthiness]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **covenant faithfulness** and **trustworthiness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [because they see that you are faithful to your covenant and that you are trustworthy]

The psalmist is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [The nations should not say]

The psalmist is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Their God is doing nothing.]

Here the word **And** is not introducing something additional, but an explanation. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [To that I say, our God is in heaven]
The pronoun **Their** refers to the nations mentioned in verse 2. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The idols of the nations]

Here, **hands of man** represents the craftsmanship and ability of people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the idea with an equivalent expression. Alternate translation: [the work of men] or [made by men]
The pronoun **them** refers to the idols mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [A mouth is to those idols]

The psalmist is using **A mouth is to them** as a common expression of the culture to mean “They have mouths.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They have mouths]

The psalmist is using **eyes are to them** as a common expression of the culture to mean “they have eyes.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those idols have eyes]

The psalmist is using **ears are to them** as a common expression of the culture to mean “they have ears.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those idols have ears]

The psalmist is using **a nose is to them** as a common expression of the culture to mean “they have a nose.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they have a nose]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [The idols have their hands]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [they have their feet]
The pronoun **Their** refers to the idols mentioned in verse 4. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The makers of those idols]

By **are like them**, the psalmist means that the people who make idols become as powerless and lifeless as the idols they create. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [are like them, lacking life and power]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [everyone who trusts in them is like them]
Here, **Israel** represents the Israelite people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Israelite people]

The psalmist switches here from the second person exhortation **trust in Yahweh** to the third person **their help and their shield**. It is probable that when this psalm was sung, a leader would sing the second person exhortation parts and a chorus would sing the third-person parts of verses 9–11. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate the third person parts as second person. Alternate translation: [your help and your shield]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **help**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the one who helps them] or [the one who helps you]

Here the psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a **shield** that protects people in battle. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the one who protects them] or [and the one who protects you]

Here, **House** means all the people descended from a particular person. This image envisions them as if they were one household living together. So **House of Aaron** figuratively means all the people descended from Aaron, the first high priest. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Descendants of Aaron]

The psalmist switches here from the second person exhortation **trust in Yahweh** to the third person **their help and their shield**. It is probable that when this psalm was sung, a leader would sing the second person exhortation parts and a chorus would sing the third-person parts of verses 9–11. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate the third person parts as second person. Alternate translation: [your help and your shield]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **help**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the one who helps them] or [the one who helps you]

Here the psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a **shield** that protects people from attack. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [and the one who protects them] or [and the one who protects you]

The psalmist switches here from the second person exhortation **trust in Yahweh** to the third person **their help and their shield**. It is probable that when this psalm was sung, a leader would sing the second person exhortation parts and a chorus would sing the third-person parts of verses 9–11. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate the third person parts as second person. Alternate translation: [your help and your shield]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **help**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the one who helps them] or [the one who helps you]

Here the psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a **shield** that protects people in battle. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [and the one who protects them] or [and the one who protects you]

The psalmist is using **Yahweh remembers us** as a common expression of the culture to mean “Yahweh thinks about us” or “Yahweh is mindful of us.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh thinks about us]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language as is modeled in the UST.

Here, **house** means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So **the house of Israel** figuratively means all the people descended from the patriarch Jacob, who was also known as Israel. Alternate translation: [the descendants of Israel]

Here, **house** means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So **the house of Aaron** figuratively means all the people descended from Aaron, the first high priest. Alternate translation: [the descendants of Aaron]

The psalmist is using the adjective **fearing** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the people who fear]

The psalmist is using the adjectives **small** and **great** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [the small people as well as with the great people]

The psalmist is speaking of insignificant people and prominent people as if they were physically **small** and **great**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the insignificant people along with the prominent people]

The psalmist is referring to all people by naming two extremes, **the small** and **the great**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from the insignificant ones to the important ones]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know what Yahweh should **add to you**. The context of blessing families suggests that this refers to adding children or descendants. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [May Yahweh add children to your families]

The word **you** is plural here because the psalmist is addressing the Israelites, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction. Alternate translation: [May Yahweh add to all of you]
The psalmist repeats **to you** for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [to you, yes, to you]

The psalmist is speaking as if future generations were actually **sons**. He means descendants in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and to your descendants]

The expression **May you be blessed by Yahweh** contains a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [May Yahweh bless you]

The word **you** is plural here because the psalmist is addressing all the people of Israel, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction. Alternate translation: [May all of you be blessed by Yahweh]

The psalmist is using **The heavens of heavens** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the highest heavens” or “the most exalted heavens.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The most heavenly heavens]

The psalmist is using **are to Yahweh** as a common expression of the culture to mean “belong to Yahweh.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [are Yahweh’s]

The psalmist is using **sons of man** as a common expression of his culture to mean “human beings.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to human beings]

The psalmist is using the adjective **dead** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [Dead people]
The word **Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh” as modeled in the UST.

Here the psalmist is speaking of death as if it were **descending to silence**. This image portrays death as going down to a place where there is no speech or praise. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [going to the grave, where they are silent]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and not any people descending to silence praise Yah]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **we** separately, even though the verb translated as **we will bless** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize the contrast between the living and the dead. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that meaning here. Alternate translation: [But as for us, we will bless]
The word **Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh.” Alternate translation: [we will bless Yahweh]

The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Halleluia] or [Praise Yah]

116.text:
# Psalm 116 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 116 is a “psalm of praise” for saving the psalmist’s life. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/save]])

1. Declaration of love and prayer (1–2)
2. Recounting deliverance and finding rest (3–9)
3. Vows, sacrifice, and public praise (10–19)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Healing

The psalmist was very sick and expected to die but God healed him. So he will pay his vow and sacrifice an offering of thanks. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/promise]])

Here, **my voice** represents the psalmist’s prayers and requests. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh hears me]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [because Yahweh hears my pleas]

The psalmist is using **he extends his ear to me** as a common expression of the culture to mean “he listens to me” or “he pays attention to what I say.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he pays attention to what I say]
The psalmist is using the term **days** to refer to his lifetime. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and throughout my lifetime]

The psalmist assumes that readers will understand that **I will call out** means he will call out to Yahweh. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I will call out to Yahweh]

These two phrases **The cords of death surrounded me** and **the constrictions of Sheol found me** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [The cords of death surrounded me, indeed, the constrictions of Sheol found me]

Here the psalmist is picturing death as if it were **cords** that could wrap around and bind someone. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [It seemed that I would die soon]

Here David is speaking of **the constrictions of Sheol** as if they were ropes or chains that could physically grip and restrain him. He means that he felt as though he was very close to dying. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I felt as though I were dying]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **anguish** and **sorrow**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [I was anguished and sorrowful]

The psalmist is using the term **name** to refer to Yahweh himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Then I called on Yahweh]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. Alternate translation: [I beg you to rescue my life]

Here, **life** represents the person himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [rescue me] or [keep me from dying]

Here **and** introduces not an addition but an explanation. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, our God, is also compassionate]

The psalmist is using the adjective **naive** as a noun to refer to people who are inexperienced or who cannot care for themselves. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who cannot care for themselves]

Here the psalmist is speaking of his difficult circumstances as if he were physically **low**. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I was in a bad way] or [I was in trouble]

116.quote: שׁוּבִ֣י נַ֭פְשִׁ⁠י לִ⁠מְנוּחָ֑יְ⁠כִי כִּֽי־יְ֝הוָ֗ה גָּמַ֥ל עָלָֽיְ⁠כִי
116.text: The psalmist is speaking to himself in the second person as **your** and **you**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in first person as modeled in the UST.

The psalmist is using the term **soul** to mean the entire person from the perspective of his spiritual/emotional existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I must return myself to calmness]
By **rest**, the psalmist means “a state of restfulness.” You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Return to your state of restfulness]

The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh’s good deeds as if they were **repaid** like a debt or wages. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for Yahweh has done good things for you] or [for Yahweh has done good things for me]

Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [After all,]

Here, **my soul** represents the psalmist himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [For you rescued me from death]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **death**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [For you rescued my soul from dying]

The psalmist is using one part of a person, his **eye**, to mean all of him in the act of weeping. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [me from weeping]

The psalmist is using one part of a person, his **foot**, to mean all of him in the act of stumbling or falling. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [me from stumbling]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if he were literally walking **to the face of Yahweh**. He means that he will live in a way that acknowledges Yahweh in all that he does. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will acknowledge Yahweh in all that I do]

The psalmist is using **to the face of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “in the presence of” or “before.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [before Yahweh]

The psalmist is using **in the lands of the living** as a common expression of the culture to mean “as long as I am alive” or “during my lifetime.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as long as I live]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [I trusted Yahweh]

The implication is that the psalmist was speaking to himself or to God about his distress. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [though I said to myself]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **I** twice, even though it is not necessary for understanding. He is doing that to emphasize his personal distress and suffering. If a speaker of your language would use repeated pronouns for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that meaning here. Alternate translation: [woe is me; I am very wretched]

The pronoun **I** is stated twice for emphasis. The psalmist is emphasizing that he himself was the one who made this statement. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the emphasis here. Alternate translation: [As for me, I said]

By **I, I said**, the psalmist means that he said this to himself or thought this to himself. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I, I said to myself]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **panic**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because I was panicking]

The psalmist is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [It is not possible for me to return to Yahweh all of his bestowments to me.]

The implication is that the psalmist cannot fully repay Yahweh for all his goodness. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [How can I pay back to Yahweh]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **bestowments**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [everything that he has done to be kind to me]

This is probably a reference to a drink offering, which was a sacrifice that involved pouring wine on the altar, and which the psalmist will offer as a grateful response to Yahweh for saving him. The full meaning of this statement can be made explicit. Alternate translation: [I will present a drink offering to Yahweh because he saved me]

The psalmist is using the term **name** to refer to Yahweh himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and call on Yahweh]

The implication is that these are people who have gathered to worship Yahweh. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the people who have gathered to worship him]

The word **Precious** here does not imply that Yahweh desires the death of his faithful ones, but that the death of his saints is costly to him and grieves him. See how you translated a similar expression in [Psalm 72:14](../072/014.md). Alternate translation: [Yahweh considers the death of his faithful ones to be a costly thing]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **death**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [When one of his faithful people dies, that grieves Yahweh very much]

The psalmist is using **in the eyes of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “in the judgment of” or “in the opinion of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in Yahweh’s judgment]

The psalmist is using the adjective **faithful** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [is the death of any of his faithful people]

The psalmist here switches to second person by saying **your servant**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could continue using third person as in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [Indeed, for I am Yahweh’s servant; I am his servant, the son of his servant woman; he has undone my bonds]

Here the word **for** introduces not a reason but an explanation. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [definitely I am your servant]

The phrase **the son of your servant woman** adds to the meaning of **I am your servant**. In the culture of the time, the son of a servant woman was a permanent servant, without the right to go free after six years. See [Exodus 21:2–4](../../exo/21/02.md). You could include this information if it would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I am your permanent servant, the son of your servant woman]

Here the psalmist is speaking of his troubles as if they were **bonds** that tied him up and prevented him from moving freely. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [you have freed me from my troubles]

The psalmist is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [I will make a sacrifice to you to thank you]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **thanksgiving**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [I will make a sacrifice to you to thank you]

Here, **name** represents the person of Yahweh himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will call out to Yahweh]
See how you translated this in [verse 14](../116/014.md).

The psalmist says **right in front of all of his people** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [right in front of a gathering of his people]

The psalmist is speaking of the temple of Yahweh as if it were a **house** in which he lived. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the temple of Yahweh]

The psalmist is speaking to **Jerusalem** that he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about his commitment to worship and praise God in the holy city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about Jerusalem. Alternate translation: [in the midst of Jerusalem]

The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Halleluia] or [Praise Yah]
**Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh]

117.text:
# Psalm 117 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 117 is a “psalm of praise.”

1. Call to praise
2. Reasons to praise

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Praise

Everyone should praise God for his love and unending faithfulness. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/love]]; and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/faithful]])

These two phrases **Praise Yahweh, all nations** and **extol him, all peoples** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Praise Yahweh, all nations; yes, extol him, all peoples]

Here, **all nations** represents the people in all nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [you people in all nations]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [For he will never stop being faithful to his covenant to love us]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **trustworthiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh will be trustworthy to do this forever]

The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Halleluia] or [Praise Yah]
**Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh]

118.text:
# Psalm 118 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 118 is a “psalm of thanksgiving” written on the occasion of a military victory. At the same time, it is a messianic psalm that looks forward to the triumph of Jesus Christ. Jesus applied Psalm 118:22 to himself ([Matthew 21:42](../../mat/21/42.md), [Mark 12:10](../../mrk/12/10.md), [Luke 20:17](../../luk/20/17.md)), and the apostle Peter applied it to Jesus both in a speech recorded in Acts ([Acts 4:11](../../act/04/11.md)), and in his first letter ([1 Peter 2:7](../../1pe/02/07.md)). See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Call to Thanksgiving (1–4)
2. Testimony of deliverance (5–18)
3. Messianic celebration (9–29)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Rejected stone

The psalmist praised Yahweh for rescuing him. God enabled him to overpower his enemies. The new Testament, and even Jesus himself, saw the rejected stone as a reference to the Messiah’s rejection by the Jewish leaders. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/christ]])

118.quote: הוֹד֣וּ לַ⁠יהוָ֣ה כִּי־ט֑וֹב כִּ֖י לְ⁠עוֹלָ֣ם חַסְדּֽ⁠וֹ
118.text: See how you translated this in [Psalm 106:1](../106/001.md).

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [thank Yahweh for his covenant faithfulness is to forever]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [he remains faithful to his covenant]

The psalmist is using **to forever** as a common expression of his culture to mean “eternally” or “without end.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [lasts throughout eternity]

Here, **Israel** represents the people of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Let the people of Israel indeed say]

The psalmist is saying what he wants **Israel** to do. See the discussion in the introduction to Psalms about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [May Israel indeed say]
See how you translated this in the previous verse.

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [We praise Yahweh for his covenant faithfulness is to forever]

Here, **house** means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So **the house of Aaron** figuratively means all the people descended from Aaron, who was the first high priest. Alternate translation: [Let the descendants of Aaron indeed say]
See how you translated this in the previous verse.
See how you translated this in the previous verse.

The psalmist is using **From the constriction** as a common expression of the culture to mean “from a distressing situation” or “from a time of trouble.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [From between a rock and a hard place] or [From a distressing situation]
The word **Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh.” Alternate translation: [I called out to Yahweh and he answered me]

The psalmist is using **with wideness** as a common expression of the culture to mean “by setting me free” or “by relieving my distressing situation.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yah set me in a wide place] or [Yah answered me by relieving my distressing situation]

The psalmist is using **Yahweh is for me** as a common expression of the culture to mean “Yahweh supports me” or “Yahweh is on my side.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh wants me to succeed]

The psalmist is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [man do nothing to harm me]

The psalmist is using **Yahweh is for me as my helper** as a common expression of the culture to mean “Yahweh wants me to succeed and so he helps me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh wants me to succeed and so he helps me]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I will gaze** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize his personal commitment to triumph over his enemies. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [and so for my part, I will gaze]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **haters**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [on those who hate me]

Here the psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a **shelter** that people could go into for protection from danger. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to let Yahweh protect us]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [than to trust in people]

The word translated as **I fended them off** could mean: (1) the psalmist’s army pushed back the other armies. The expressions **They surrounded me** and **yes, they surrounded me** mean the same thing. The psalmist is using repetition for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [They had me completely surrounded]
See how you translated this in the previous verse.

The psalmist is making a comparison between his enemies and **bees**. The point of this comparison is that just as **bees** swarm around aggressively when attacking, so his enemies surrounded him aggressively. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [They surrounded me like bees do when they are attacking someone]

The expression **they were extinguished** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they died away quickly like a fire burning thorns]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a fire of thorns** burns out quickly, so the psalmist’s enemies **were extinguished** quickly. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [they were extinguished as quickly as is a fire among thorns]
See how you translated this in verse 10.

The psalmist is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [You pushed me down hard]

Here, **to fall** marks this clause as the goal or purpose of **To push down, you pushed me down**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [so that I would fall]

Here the psalmist is speaking of his enemies’ attack as if the enemies were able to **push** him **down** physically to make him **fall**. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [You attacked me violently in order to defeat me]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and he saves me]

The phrase **a shout and salvation** expresses a single idea. The word **shout** tells more about **salvation**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [The voice of a victorious shout]

The psalmist is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [righteous people]
The psalmist may be quoting a song of victory, starting here and going through verse 16. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark this as the beginning of a song, as in the UST.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **valor**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the right hand of Yahweh does valiant things]

Here, **right hand** represents the power of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the power of Yahweh]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **valor**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [valiant things]

The psalmist is using **The right hand of Yahweh is high** as a common expression of the culture to mean that Yahweh is superior to all others or that Yahweh is victorious. See how you translated this phrase in the previous verse.

119.text:
# Psalm 119 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 119 is a “wisdom psalm” about the law of Yahweh. This psalm is an “acrostic” (see discussion in the Introduction to Psalms), an alphabetic poem with twenty-two groups of eight verses each. Each group begins with a letter of the alphabet in the order of the Hebrew alphabet.

The psalmist uses many different words to refer to Yahweh’s message to us. You could attempt to use a different word for each term (ULT uses words such as “precepts,” “commandments,” and “law”), but most languages will not have that many, so just use the words that your language has.

1. Blessing for those who walk in Yahweh’s law (1–32)
2. Prayer for understanding and guidance from Yahweh’s word (33–72)
3. Comfort and hope in Yahweh’s word during affliction (73–112)
4. Devotion to Yahweh’s law despite opposition (113–144)
5. Cry for deliverance and life through Yahweh’s word (145–176)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### The law

The psalmist loved the law of Yahweh and was blessed by obeying it. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/love]]; and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/bless]])

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

## “your word”

Throughout this psalm, the psalmist uses the phrase “your word” to refer more generally to Yahweh’s commandments, instructions, promises, and messages to us.

## Request form

Throughout this psalm, the psalmist is requesting things from Yahweh by using an imperative which may sound like a command in your language. If this would be impolite in your language, then use a form that would be more appropriate for addressing Yahweh with a request.

The psalmist is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of joy or blessing. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Oh, how happy are] or [How blessed are]

The psalmist is using the adjective **blameless** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [people who are blameless in their conduct]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe a **way** that is characterized by being **blameless**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [people whose way is blameless]

Here the psalmist is speaking of behavior as if it were a **way** that a person walks along. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [conduct]

Here the psalmist is speaking of living according to Yahweh’s instructions as if it were **walking** along a path. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those who live by the teaching of Yahweh]
See how you translated the exclamation starting with “The happinesses of” in the previous verse.
The pronoun **his** refers to Yahweh, mentioned in verse 1. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the testimonies of Yahweh]

The pronoun **They** refers to the keepers of Yahweh’s testimonies, while the pronoun **him** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Those who keep his testimonies seek Yahweh]

Here the psalmist is speaking of wanting to know Yahweh as if people were looking for or seeking him. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They live to know him]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **forgotten** to emphasize that he will carefully remember Yahweh’s commandments. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [I have carefully kept your commandments in my mind]

Psalm 120 is one of the songs of ascents (Psalms 120–134). These are generally understood to be songs that were customarily sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem for one of the three major annual festivals. The term “ascents” is used because going up to the temple in Jerusalem involved a climb up Mount Zion.

1. Plea for deliverance (1–2)
2. Judgment on the deceiver (3–4)
3. Complaint of distant dwelling (5–7)
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **distress**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [while I was suffering]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please deliver my soul]

The psalmist is using **my soul** to represent himself as a whole person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [me]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [from those who speak lies]

The psalmist is using is using parts of a person, **lips** and **tongue** to represent his enemies who are telling lies about him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from people speaking falsehood and deceit about me]

The psalmist is using the question form to warn his enemies of certain punishment from God. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this question as a statement or as exclamation. Alternate translation: [He will give punishment to you, and he will add more to you]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [What severe punishment will he give to you]
The pronoun **he** refers to God. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [will Yahweh give]

As in the previous verse, **tongue of deceit** represents the psalmist’s enemies who are telling lies about him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [O you who speak deceitfully]

120.quote: חִצֵּ֣י גִבּ֣וֹר שְׁנוּנִ֑ים עִ֝֗ם גַּחֲלֵ֥י רְתָמִֽים

Here the psalmist is speaking as if God’s punishment were **coals of broom trees**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [burning destruction]

Alternate translation: [How miserable I am]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. The places named both refer to the people who lived in those places who were considered barbarian or savage. Here, **the tents of Kedar** represents the people who live in those tents. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people of Kedar]

The psalmist is using **My soul** to represent himself as a whole person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have dwelt for a long time]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [but when I speak about peace]

# Psalm 121 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 121 is one of the songs of ascents (Psalms 120–134). These are generally understood to be songs that were customarily sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem for one of the three major annual festivals. The term “ascents” is used because going up to the temple in Jerusalem involved a climb up Mount Zion.

1. Confession of trust (1–2)
2. Assurance of protection (3–6)
3. Promise of preservation (Verses 7–8)

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

### Multiple speakers

This psalm is a dialogue between two individuals as is made clear by the implied information in the UST. Make sure this is clear to your readers.

The psalmist is using **lift up my eyes** as a common expression of the culture to mean “to look up at” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I look up]

The psalmist is using the question form to set up a confident answer that he provides in verse 2. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I know where my help comes from!]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **help**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [someone to help me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **help**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [The one who helps me is Yahweh]

The psalmist is referring to all of creation by naming two extremes, **heaven** and **earth**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all creation]

By using **May**, the psalmist is expressing what he desires or prays will happen. See the discussion in the introduction to Psalms about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [I desire that he will not give your foot to the slipping; that your keeper will not slumber]
The pronoun **he** refers to Yahweh, who was named in verse 2. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers as is modeled in the UST.

The psalmist is speaking of experiencing danger or hardship as if it were a person’s **foot** **slipping** and causing him to fall. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you over to danger]
The psalmist is using this possessive form to mean the one who keeps you safe. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the one who keeps you safe]

The psalmist is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Pay attention]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [he will not slumber, indeed, he will not sleep]
The psalmist is using this possessive form to mean the one who keeps Israel safe. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the one who keeps Israel]

The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were **shade** that protects a person from the heat of the sun. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is your protection]

The psalmist is using **upon your right hand** as a common expression of the culture to mean “at your side” or “close beside you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [at your side]

The psalmist is speaking of **the sun** and **the moon** as if they were living things that could **strike** a person and cause harm. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the heat of the sun will not harm you, and the moon will not harm you by night]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and the moon will not strike you by night]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will protect you from all evil, yes, he will keep your soul]

The psalmist is using the adjective **evil** as a noun to mean evil things in general. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [from all evil things]
The psalmist is using one part of a person, his **soul**, to mean all of him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your very life]

The psalmist is referring to all of a person’s activities by naming two extremes, **your going out** and **your coming in**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [you safe everywhere you go]

The psalmist is referring to all of time by naming two extremes, **now** and **forever**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [for all time]

122.text:
# Psalm 122 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 122 one of the songs of ascents (Psalms 120–134). These are generally understood to be songs that were customarily sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem for one of the three major annual festivals. The term “ascents” is used because going up to the temple in Jerusalem involved a climb up Mount Zion.

1. Joy of arrival and worship (1–2)
2. The commendation of Jerusalem (vv. 3–5)
3. A prayer for peace and prosperity (6–9)

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

### “house of Yahweh”

In this psalm, the phrase “house of Yahweh” is used to talk about the temple. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could state the meaning plainly.

### “Jerusalem”

Many times in this Psalm, the psalmist speaks directly to the city of Jerusalem even though it is not a person and cannot hear. He refers to Jerusalem in both the second and third person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about Jerusalem.

David is speaking of the temple where Yahweh is worshiped as if it were a **house** in which he lived. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the temple of Yahweh]

Here David is using one part of their bodies, their **feet**, to mean all of them in the act of standing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [We are standing]

David is speaking to **Jerusalem**, which is a city that cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him how he feels about Jerusalem. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about Jerusalem. Alternate translation: [within the gates of Jerusalem]

Here the word **gates** refers to the entire city or town. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [within you, the city of]

The point of this comparison is that just as a city whose parts are **joined** together is compact and unified, so is Jerusalem well-constructed and cohesive. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [so that all its parts are compact and unified]

The expression **is joined** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that holds itself together]

David is using this possessive form to mean that the tribes belong to and worship Yahweh because he is their God. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the tribes that worship Yahweh]
The word **Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **testimony**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [as Yahweh instructed the people of Israel to do]

Here, **to** marks **give thanks to the name of Yahweh** as the goal or purpose of the tribes going up. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [so that they can give thanks to the name of Yahweh]

David is using the term **name** to represent who Yahweh is or to refer to Yahweh himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to Yahweh himself]

Here, **For** introduces the reason why the tribes go up to Jerusalem: it is the place where kings will sit on their thrones to render justice. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason. Alternate translation: [Because that is where kings sit on thrones for judgment]

Here, **thrones** represents the kings’ royal authority to rule and judge. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [kings to carry out their judicial authority]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **judgment**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [where kings are judging]

David is leaving out words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [there sit thrones for the house of David]

Here, **house** means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So **the house of David** figuratively means all the people descended from David. Alternate translation: [for the descendants of David]

David is using words with similar sounds for poetic effect. In the original language, the words for **ask**, **peace**, and **prosper** all share sounds similar to the word for **Jerusalem**. David is using this wordplay to connect his prayer for the city with its very name. You may want to reproduce this effect if poetry in your language does this. If not, you could indicate it in a footnote.

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Ask that those in the city of Jerusalem may live peacefully]
Here the name **Jerusalem** represents the people who live in that city. Alternate translation: [those who live in Jerusalem]

In this verse and to the end of the psalm, David is again speaking to Jerusalem, which is a city that cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about the welfare of those who love the city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about Jerusalem. Alternate translation: [may the ones loving Jerusalem prosper]

David is saying what he wants to happen. See the discussion in the introduction to Psalms about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [I pray that the ones loving you will prosper]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the ideas of **peace** and **prosperity**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [May people live peacefully within your rampart, prosperously in your citadels]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. David uses the two phrases together to emphasize his desire for the well-being of Jerusalem. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way, as the UST does. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Let there be peace within your rampart, yes, let there be prosperity in your citadels]

David is asking Yahweh to bless the people of Israel. In your translation, use a form that people would recognize as a blessing in your language. You might express this as a prayer, if that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [May Yahweh bring peace]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [let there be prosperity]

Here, **For** marks **the sake of my brothers and my companions** as the motivation for David speaking peace. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [Because I love my brothers and my companions]

The psalmist is using the term **brothers** to describe people who are descended from the same ancestor or all the Israelites. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my countrymen]

David is using **please, peace in you** as a common expression of his culture used to wish someone well or to pronounce a blessing. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [let me say, “Peace be with you”] or [I pray for peace for you]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [may people live peacefully within you]

Here, **For** marks **the sake of the house of Yahweh our God** as the motivation for David seeking good. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [Because I love the house of Yahweh our God]

David is speaking of the temple where Yahweh is worshiped as if it were a **house** in which he lived. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the temple of Yahweh]
David is using the adjective **good** as a noun to refer to good things. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression. Alternate translation: [what is good]

123.text:
# Psalm 123 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 123 is one of the songs of ascents (Psalms 120–134).
