These are generally understood to be songs that were customarily sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem for one of the three major annual festivals. The term “ascents” is used because going up to the temple in Jerusalem involved a climb up Mount Zion.

1. The servant’s posture: looking to Yahweh (1–2)
2. The servant’s plea: request for mercy (3–4)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Trust

Just as a servant trusts his master to protect him, so the psalmist is trusting God to stop proud people from insulting him. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/trust]])

The psalmist is using **I lift up my eyes** as a common expression of the culture to mean that he looks expectantly toward God for help. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I look expectantly]

Here the pronouns **I** and **my** refers to the psalmist, who speaks as an individual in this verse. However, in verse 2, the psalmist shifts to the plural **our** and **us**, indicating that he is now speaking on behalf of a group. If using the singular form of the pronouns here would not be natural in your language, you could use the plural forms in your translation. Alternate translation: [we lift up our eyes]

The psalmist is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look]

123.quote: כְ⁠עֵינֵ֪י עֲבָדִ֡ים אֶל־יַ֤ד אֲֽדוֹנֵי⁠הֶ֗ם כְּ⁠עֵינֵ֣י שִׁפְחָה֮ אֶל־יַ֪ד גְּבִ֫רְתָּ֥⁠הּ כֵּ֣ן עֵ֭ינֵי⁠נוּ אֶל־יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֵ֑י⁠נוּ
123.text: The point of this comparison is that just as **servants** look to the hand of **their masters** for provision and direction, so the psalmist and his people look to **Yahweh** to provide for them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [just as servants depend on their masters, and just as a maidservant depends on her mistress, so we wait on Yahweh our God]

123.quote: כְ⁠עֵינֵ֪י עֲבָדִ֡ים אֶל־יַ֤ד אֲֽדוֹנֵי⁠הֶ֗ם כְּ⁠עֵינֵ֣י שִׁפְחָה֮ אֶל־יַ֪ד גְּבִ֫רְתָּ֥⁠הּ
123.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. In the first phrase, the psalmist refers to male **servants** and their **masters**, and in the second, to a **maidservant** and her **mistress**. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine the phrases. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [as servants watch the hand of their masters for direction] or [as the eyes of the servants are to the hand of their masters, indeed, as the eyes of a maidservant are to the hand of her mistress]

Here, **hand** represents the provision and direction of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the direction of their masters … the direction of her mistress]

**Be gracious** is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please be gracious to us, Yahweh, be gracious to us]

The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. The psalmist asks Yahweh to be gracious because they have been despised for so long. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [because we are greatly satiated with contempt]

The psalmist is speaking of being treated with **contempt** as if it were food that fills a person. He means that they have experienced so much contempt that they cannot endure any more. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [we have experienced more contempt than we can endure]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **contempt**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with how others despise us]

The psalmist is speaking of being treated with **scorn** as if it were food that fills a person. He means that they have experienced so much scorn that they cannot endure any more. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [we have been treated with too much scorn from]

The psalmist is using one part of a person, their **soul**, to mean all of them in the act of experiencing scorn and contempt. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [we are satiated with]

The pronoun **it** refers to the scorn and contempt that the psalmist specifies later in the verse. The psalmist uses this pronoun before naming what it refers to. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [is satiated with these things]

These two phrases **the scorn of the arrogant** and **the contempt of the proud** mean basically the same thing. See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [the great mockery of arrogant people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **scorn**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [being mocked by]

The psalmist is using the adjective **arrogant** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [arrogant people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **contempt**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [being despised by]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [satiated with the contempt of]

The psalmist is using the adjective **proud** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [proud people]

124.text:
# Psalm 124 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 124 is one of the songs of ascents (Psalms 120–134). These are generally understood to be songs that were customarily sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem for one of the three major annual festivals. The term “ascents” is used because going up to the temple in Jerusalem involved a climb up Mount Zion.

1. Acknowledge Yahweh’s protection from enemies (1–5)
2. Bless Yahweh who did not let us be destroyed (6–7)
3. Confess Yahweh as our help and creator (8)

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

### Various images for enemies

The psalmist depicts enemies through three different images: devouring beasts (verses 3, 6), an overwhelming flood (verses 4–5), and a trapper’s snare (verse 7). Translators should preserve these distinct images.

David is making a conditional statement **If not Yahweh**, that sounds hypothetical, but he knows that the condition is not true. Yahweh was indeed for Israel, and therefore the disastrous results David goes on to describe did not happen. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that the speaker believes is not true. Alternate translation: [If Yahweh had not been on our side]

David is saying what he wants the people of Israel to do and inviting them to join in communal recitation. See the discussion in the introduction to Psalms about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [Israel should indeed say]

Here David is speaking as if the enemies attacking the Israelites actually **rose up** physically above Israel to destroy them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. [when our enemies came to fight against us]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people]

Here and through verse 5, the word **then** introduces what the consequences could have been if the condition proposed in the previous verse (if Yahweh had not been with them when their enemies attacked) had actually happened. Use a natural form in your language for introducing the consequence of this possible condition. Alternate translation: [in that case,]

Here David is speaking as if the enemies who could have killed all the Israelites were wild animals that could have **swallowed** Israel **alive**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [then they would have killed us all]

The pronoun **they** refers to the enemies described as “man” in verse 2. The singular “man” has shifted to a plural pronoun here and following. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [then those enemies]

David is using **nose burned** as a common expression of his culture to mean “to be very angry.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they were fiercely angry with us]

Here David is speaking of the attacks of the enemies as if they were **waters** and a **torrent** that was like a river overflowing its banks or a flood that could overwhelm and drown Israel. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Then the enemies would have overwhelmed us; the attacks would have destroyed us]
Here, **soul** represents the people themselves. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all of us]

This phrase is basically repeating the two phrases from the previous verse; “the waters would have overflowed us” and “the torrent would have passed over our soul,” The second and third phrases emphasize the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could begin this phrase with a connecting word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Then indeed, our enemies would have completely annihilated us]
Here, **soul** represents the people themselves. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all of us]

The expression **Blessed be** is a passive verbal form. The psalmist is expressing his desire to praise Yahweh. If it would be unnatural to use that form for this purpose, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [We bless Yahweh] or [Let us praise Yahweh]

Here David is speaking of the enemies attacking and destroying Israel as if they were predatory animals that could devour Israel as **prey** with **their teeth**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who did not hand us over to be destroyed by our enemies]

The pronoun **their** refers to the enemies described as “man” in verse 2 and “they” in verse 3. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [for the teeth of our enemies]

The point of this comparison is that just as a **bird** that **escaped from the snare of the trappers** flew away to safety, so the people of Israel escaped from the power of their enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [We are like a bird that escaped from the trap of the hunters]

David is using the term **soul** to mean the entire person from the perspective of his spiritual and emotional existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [We are like a bird]

The expression **was broken** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the snare broke]

David is stating the pronoun **we** separately, even though the verb translated as **we escaped** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize the tension of the escape. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing this emphasis. Alternate translation: [and we indeed escaped!]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **help**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [It is Yahweh himself who helps us]

David is using the term **name** to represent who Yahweh is and his authority and power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [is in Yahweh himself]

David is referring to all of creation by naming two extremes, **heaven** and **earth**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [of all things]

125.text:
# Psalm 125 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 125 is one of the songs of ascents (Psalms 120–134). These are generally understood to be songs that were customarily sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem for one of the three major annual festivals. The term “ascents” is used because going up to the temple in Jerusalem involved a climb up Mount Zion. This song is also a “psalm of trust,” expressing communal confidence that Yahweh protects his people as permanently as mountains surround Jerusalem. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Those who trust in Yahweh are secure (1–2)
2. Yahweh preserves the righteous from evil rule (3–5)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Yahweh’s protection as surrounding presence

The psalmist pictures Yahweh’s care as physical encirclement, like the hills around Zion. This spatial metaphor may need adaptation where mountains are unfamiliar.

### The righteous and the wicked

The psalm contrasts the righteous with workers of iniquity, promising that evil rule will not persist over God’s allotted land.

The point of this comparison is that just as **Mount Zion** is immovable and endures permanently, so those **trusting in Yahweh** are secure and will endure permanently. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [are as stable and immovable as Mount Zion]
The pronoun **it** refers to Mount Zion in both instances. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Mount Zion will not be shaken; forever Mount Zion abides]

The expression **be shaken** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [no one can move it] or [nothing can shake it]

125.quote: יְֽרוּשָׁלִַ֗ם הָרִים֮ סָבִ֪יב לָ֥⁠הּ וַ֭⁠יהוָה סָבִ֣יב לְ⁠עַמּ֑⁠וֹ
125.text: David is speaking of Yahweh protecting his people as if he were physically wrapped **around** them like the **mountains** around Jerusalem. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [Yahweh surrounds and protects his people just as mountains surround Jerusalem]

The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh protecting his people as if he were physically **around** his people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh protects his people on every side]

Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation of why those who trust in Yahweh are secure as stated in the previous verse. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [After all,]

Here, **the rod** represents the rule or authority of wicked people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the rule of wicked people]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe a **rod** that is characterized by **wickedness**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the wicked rod] or [the rod of wicked rulers]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wickedness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the wicked] or [those who do wicked things]

Here the psalmist is speaking of the authority the wicked would have over the righteous people as if the ruler’s rod were able to **rest** on them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [will not have authority over the righteous]

Here, **the lot** represents the land that was allotted to the righteous as their inheritance. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the land allotted to the righteous] or [the inheritance of the righteous]

The psalmist is using this possessive form to mean the land that was allotted to the righteous people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the land belonging to the righteous]

The psalmist is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who trust in God]

Here, **so that** marks the clause that follows as the purpose of the rod of wickedness not resting on the lot of the righteous. The goal is that the righteous will not be tempted to do wrong. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [in order that]

Here, **hands** represents actions and participation. The expression **stretch out their hands** means to participate in or engage in something. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [those who trust in God will not participate in unrighteousness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **unrighteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in doing ungodly things]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. The psalmist is praying to Yahweh and asking him to act. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please do good, Yahweh]

These two phrases **to the good** and **to the upright in their hearts** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional, as the UST does. Another approach would be to combine them into a single phrase and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [to those who sincerely try to do good things]

The psalmist is using the adjective **good** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [to good people] or [to those who are good]

The psalmist is using the adjective **upright** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [and to upright people]

The psalmist is speaking of the **hearts** of the upright as if the heart were the location of a person’s true motives and intentions. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in their inner being]

The psalmist is speaking of the behavior of these people as if it were a path that they walk along. He speaks of their disobedience as **twisting their crooked ways**, that is, deviating from the straight path of righteousness. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And those who behave dishonestly]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **workers** who are characterized by **iniquity**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the people who do evil things]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [wicked things]

The psalmist is asking Yahweh to bless the people of Israel. In your translation, use a form that people would recognize as a blessing in your language. You might express this as a prayer, if that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [May Yahweh give peace to Israel]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **Peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Well-being]

126.text:
# Psalm 126 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 126 is one of the songs of ascents (Psalms 120–134). These are generally understood to be songs that were customarily sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem for one of the three major annual festivals. The term “ascents” is used because going up to the temple in Jerusalem involved a climb up Mount Zion. This song is a “psalm of praise” for Yahweh bringing captives home. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Rejoice in Yahweh’s past restoration (1–3)
2. Pray for renewed restoration and blessing (4–6)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Sorrow and joy

People may have sorrow now; but later it will turn into joy. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/joy]])
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **captivity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [those whom our enemies had captured from]

The point of this comparison is that just as people who are **dreaming** have a hard time believing what is happening, so the people of Israel could hardly believe that Yahweh was restoring them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [we could hardly believe it was real]

126.quote: אָ֤ז יִמָּלֵ֪א שְׂח֡וֹק פִּי⁠נוּ֮ וּ⁠לְשׁוֹנֵ֪⁠נוּ רִ֫נָּ֥ה
126.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way, as in the UST. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Then our mouth was filled with laughter, indeed, our tongue with a shout of joy]

The psalmist is using one part of a person, their **mouth**, to mean all of them in the act of laughing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [we were filled with laughter]

The expression **was filled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [overflowed with]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and our tongue was filled with a shout of joy]

The psalmist is using one part of a person, their **tongue**, to mean all of them in the act of shouting. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [we were filled]
If your language does not use abstract noun for the idea of **joy**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with joyful shouting]
The pronoun **they** refers to the people of other nations. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the people of other nations said among themselves]

The words **they said among the nations** introduce a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. Alternate translation: [the people of other nations said]

The psalmist is using **has made great to do** as a common expression of the culture to mean “has done great things.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh has done great things for his people]

The psalmist is using **has made great to do** as a common expression of the culture to mean “has done great things.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh has done wonderful things for us]

The point of this comparison is that just as the dry streambeds in the desert are suddenly restored to flowing **streams** when rain comes, so the psalmist asks Yahweh to suddenly restore the fortunes of his people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Restore those who were taken captive, Yahweh, just as you suddenly restore the dry streams in the Negev with rain]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please return, Yahweh, our captivity]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **captivity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [our people whom our enemies have captured]

Here the psalmist is speaking of people who keep working even while they suffer as if they were farmers **sowing** their seeds even though **in tears**, and of the future joy they will experience as a result as if they would **reap** their harvest with **a shout of joy**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Those who do their work while suffering will celebrate joyfully when they see the results]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **joy**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with a joyful shout]

The psalmist is repeating forms of the verb **go** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [He may indeed go, weeping]

The psalmist is using this possessive form to mean a bag that contains seed. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the bag full of seed]

The psalmist is repeating forms of the verb **come** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [He will certainly come]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **joy**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with a joyful shout]

127.text:
# Psalm 127 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 127 is one of the songs of ascents (Psalms 120–134). These are generally understood to be songs that were customarily sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem for one of the three major annual festivals. The term “ascents” is used because going up to the temple in Jerusalem involved a climb up Mount Zion.

1. Recognize the futility of work without Yahweh (1–2)
2. Receive children as Yahweh’s gift and blessing (3–5)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Blessings

Yahweh wants his people to have rest. It is a blessing to have many children. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/bless]])

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

### “of Solomon”

The superscription of this psalm is “of Solomon.” This may mean that Solomon wrote this psalm. But it may also mean that someone else wrote this psalm in honor of Solomon. We recommend that you translate the superscription in a way that allows for this possibility as well as for the possibility that Solomon was the author.

This phrase introduces the consequence of the condition proposed in the previous phrase. Use a natural form in your language for introducing the consequence of this possible condition. Alternate translation: [then it does not help for its builders to labor on it]

This phrase introduces the consequence of the condition proposed in the previous phrase. Use a natural form in your language for introducing the consequence of this possible condition. Alternate translation: [then it does no good for the watchman to stand guard over it]

Solomon is referring to all of a person’s working time by naming two extremes, **the ones rising early to get up** and **the ones being late to sit down**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the ones working from early morning until late at night]

Solomon is speaking of working hard to raise the food that people eat as if it were **bread of toils**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those toiling to earn your food]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **toils**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [bread gained by toiling]

Solomon is using the possessive form to describe **bread** that is characterized by **toils**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [bread earned through hard work]
The pronoun **he** refers to Yahweh, who is named in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [certainly Yahweh gives to his beloved one sleep]

Solomon is using the word **Behold** to focus the readers’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look]

127.quote: נַחֲלַ֣ת יְהוָ֣ה בָּנִ֑ים שָׂ֝כָ֗ר פְּרִ֣י הַ⁠בָּֽטֶן
127.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [what Yahweh gives as an inheritance is sons, indeed, the fruit of the womb is his reward]
If your language does not use abstract noun for the idea of **inheritance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what Yahweh gives as a gift]
If your language does not use abstract noun for the idea of **reward**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what he gives to reward you]

Solomon is using **fruit of the womb** as a common expression of his culture to mean “children” or “offspring.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [is having children]

The point of this comparison is that just as **arrows** in the hand of a warrior are powerful and useful for defense, so **the sons** a man has in his youth can help defend a man from his enemies when he grows old. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [The sons of a man’s youth are a powerful defense and as useful as arrows in the hand of a warrior]

Solomon is using this possessive form to describe **sons** who were born during a man’s **youth**. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [are sons born during one’s youth]

Solomon is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of joy about the man who has many sons. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [How happy is] or [Truly blessed is]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means any man in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [any man]

Solomon is continuing the arrow imagery from the previous verse, speaking of having many sons as if the father had **filled his quiver** with arrows. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [has been given many children]

A **quiver** is a container that a warrior carries on his back or at his side for holding arrows. If your readers would not be familiar with what a quiver is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [his arrow bag]

The pronoun **They** likely refers to men who have many sons. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The man who have many sons will not have shame when he speaks]

By **have shame**, Solomon means that they will not feel the shame of being defeated by the adversary. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [They will not feel the shame of defeat]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **shame**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [They will not be ashamed by being defeated]

Solomon assumes that his readers will know that **the gate** of a city was where important legal and public matters were discussed and settled. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in the place where public disputes are settled]

128.text:
# Psalm 128 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 128 is one of the songs of ascents (Psalms 120–134). These are generally understood to be songs that were customarily sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem for one of the three major annual festivals. The term “ascents” is used because going up to the temple in Jerusalem involved a climb up Mount Zion.

1. Enjoy the fruit of fearing Yahweh (1–4)
2. Experience peace and prosperity from Yahweh (5–6)

The psalmist is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of joy. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [How happy is everyone fearing Yahweh] or [Truly blessed is everyone who fears Yahweh]

The psalmist is speaking of a person who obeys Yahweh as if that person were **walking** along Yahweh’s **ways**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one living according to his commands]

Here, **labor of your palms** represents the result of the work done with someone’s hands. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [The results of your work]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **happiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [makes you happy]

The point of this comparison is that just as a **fruitful vine** produces much fruit, so the man’s **wife** will have many children. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Your wife will have many children]

The point of this comparison is that just as **shoots of olive trees** are vigorous and healthy, so the man’s **sons** will be strong and thriving. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Your sons will be strong and healthy]

Here the masculine term **sons** has a generic sense that includes both male and female children. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [Your sons and daughters]

The psalmist is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Indeed]

The expression **will be blessed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will bless the man who fears him]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [everyone]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **good**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [that you might see Jerusalem prospering]

Here, **and that** marks **you may see sons to your sons** as a further goal or purpose of Yahweh’s blessing in the previous verse. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [and also so that you may see]

Here the masculine term **sons** has a generic sense that includes both male and female descendants. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [children of your children]

The psalmist is using **sons to your sons** as a common expression of the culture to mean grandchildren. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [many descendants]

The psalmist is asking Yahweh to bless the people of Israel. In your translation, use a form that people would recognize as a blessing in your language. You might express this as a prayer, if that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [May Yahweh give peace to Israel]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **Peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [May well-being come upon]

129.text:
# Psalm 129 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 129 is one of the songs of ascents (Psalms 120–134). These are generally understood to be songs that were customarily sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem for one of the three major annual festivals. The term “ascents” is used because going up to the temple in Jerusalem involved a climb up Mount Zion.

1. Recall Israel’s long affliction (1–4)
2. Trust Yahweh to defeat the enemies of Zion (5–8)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Yahweh saves

Israel’s enemies have always persecuted them but God has saved them from their enemies. He prays that this enemy will be destroyed with no one to wish them well. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/save]])

## Translation Issues in This Psalm

### Israel addressed as a person

The first section of this psalm, verses 1–4, uses first person singular pronouns since the Israelites are asked to speak as a person who is reciting the story of how he has been cruelly treated by his enemies since he was young. This can be seen as the Israelites recitation of Israel’s history as a nation. If it would be more clear in your language you could use plural pronouns in this section.
The word translated as **Abundantly** could refer to: (1) affliction that is frequent. Alternate translation: [Often] or (2) affliction that is severe. Alternate translation: [Severely]

The pronoun **me** here signals that from here through verse 4, people of Israel are speaking together as though they are the nation of Israel. See the discussion in the introduction to this psalm to decide whether your translation will use the plural pronoun forms or keep the singular. Alternate translation: [they have afflicted us from our youth]

The pronoun **they** does not refer to a specific group of people. It refers generally to the enemies of Israel throughout its history. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate that more clearly. Alternate translation: [my enemies have afflicted me]

The psalmist is saying what he wants the people of Israel to say and inviting them to join in communal recitation. See the discussion in the introduction to Psalms about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to say. Alternate translation: [Israel should indeed say]

The psalmist uses the word **however** here to indicate a contrast between the repeated affliction described in the first half of the verse and the failure of the enemies to ultimately prevail. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [in spite of that, they did not prevail against me]

The psalmist is speaking of the enemies’ oppression as if they were farmers plowing furrows on his back. The image of **the plowers plowed** upon his back and **they made long their furrows** represents severe and prolonged suffering. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [They made me suffer, like a farmer plowing a field they made deep wounds in my back]

The psalmist is speaking of the control that wicked people had over Israel as if they were **cords** binding them, and God’s deliverance as if he **cut** those cords. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he has freed me from the control of wicked people]

The psalmist is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to refer to a type of person. If your language does not use adjectives in this way, you could translate this with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who do evil]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **shame**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [May they feel disgraced]

The psalmist is using the name **Zion**, to represent the people who live in Jerusalem and worship God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those who worship God]

The point of this comparison is that just as **grass of the rooftops**, or worthless weeds which grow in a thin layer of soil dry up quickly before anyone can even pull it out, so the psalmist wishes that the lives of his enemies will be insignificant and short-lived. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as insignificant and short-lived as grass on a rooftop which withers before anyone call pull it out]

129.quote: שֶׁ⁠לֹּ֤א מִלֵּ֖א כַפּ֥⁠וֹ קוֹצֵ֗ר וְ⁠חִצְנ֥⁠וֹ מְעַמֵּֽר
129.text: These two phrases are continuing the comparison of the enemies to the grass from the previous verse. Both phrases describe the worthlessness of the grass: **the reaper** cannot gather a handful of it nor can **the one binding sheaves** fill his arms with it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [so insignificant that the reaper cannot harvest it, nor can the one binding sheaves gather an armful to carry]

129.quote: בִּרְכַּֽת־יְהוָ֥ה אֲלֵי⁠כֶ֑ם בֵּרַ֥כְנוּ אֶ֝תְ⁠כֶ֗ם בְּ⁠שֵׁ֣ם יְהוָֽה
129.text: This is a traditional harvest blessing that workers would exchange with those passing by. The psalmist is saying that the enemies of Zion will never receive such a blessing. In your translation, use a form that people would recognize as a blessing in your language. Alternate translation: [May Yahweh make you prosper; may Yahweh bless you]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **blessing**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [The favor of Yahweh]

Here, **the name of Yahweh** represents the person and authority of Yahweh himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [by the authority of Yahweh]

130.text:
# Psalm 130 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 130 is one of the songs of ascents (Psalms 120–134). These are generally understood to be songs that were customarily sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem for one of the three major annual festivals. The term “ascents” is used because going up to the temple in Jerusalem involved a climb up Mount Zion. It is a “psalm of praise” that God forgives sins. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Cry out to Yahweh from the depths (1–4)
2. Wait and hope in Yahweh’s redeeming love (5–8)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Forgive

God forgives sin and helps the sinner. So Israel should trust in God for his forgiveness. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/trust]])

The psalmist is speaking as if being in distress over all his troubles were being in the **depths** or a place of deep water. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Because of my many troubles]

130.quote: שִׁמְעָ֪⁠ה בְ⁠ק֫וֹלִ֥⁠י תִּהְיֶ֣ינָה אָ֭זְנֶי⁠ךָ קַשֻּׁב֑וֹת לְ֝⁠ק֗וֹל תַּחֲנוּנָֽ⁠י
130.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [listen attentively to my pleas for mercy] or [hear my voice, indeed, may your ears be attentive to the voice of my supplications]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **supplications**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to my voice as I plead with you]

Here, **If** introduces a hypothetical condition. The psalmist is saying that this is something that could happen. He is implying that no one could endure God’s judgment if he kept a record of sins. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [Yah, suppose you would mark sins]

The psalmist is using **mark sins** as a common expression of the culture to mean “keep a strict tally of sins.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you, Yah, would keep a count of our sins]
**Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh]

The psalmist is using the question form to emphasize that no one would be able to endure God’s judgment. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [no one could stand!]

The psalmist is speaking about staying alive or surviving attack or punishment as if it were being able to physically **stand**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [could survive] or [could withstand the punishment]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **forgiveness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [you forgive people]

Here, **so that** marks **you may be feared** as the goal or purpose of **there is forgiveness with you**. The psalmist is saying that God forgives so that people will revere him. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [in order that people may fear you]

The expression **you may be feared** contains a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is people. Alternate translation: [people may fear you]

These two phrases **I wait for Yahweh** and **my soul waits** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [I wait eagerly for Yahweh]

The psalmist is using the term **soul** to mean the entire person from the perspective of his spiritual and emotional existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I wait with all my being]

The psalmist is using the term **word** to represent what Yahweh has promised. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and in Yahweh’s promises I hope]

The point of this comparison is that just as **watchmen** stand on guard and eagerly watch **for the morning**, the psalmist eagerly anticipates the Lord’s help. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [I eagerly anticipate the Lord’s help just as eagerly as watchmen wait for the morning]

The psalmist is leaving out one of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the previous verse if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [My soul waits for the Lord]

The psalmist is using the term **soul** to mean the entire person from the perspective of his spiritual and emotional existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I myself wait for the Lord]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the previous verse if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [more than watchmen wait for the morning, watchmen wait for the morning]

The phrase **watchmen for the morning** is repeated as a poetic device for emphasis. If your language has a poetic way to indicate the emotion of this phrase, you could use it here. Alternate translation: [more than watchmen for the morning, even more eagerly than watchmen waiting for the morning]

130.quote: יַחֵ֥ל יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל אֶל־יְה֫וָה כִּֽי־עִם־יְהוָ֥ה הַ⁠חֶ֑סֶד וְ⁠הַרְבֵּ֖ה עִמּ֣⁠וֹ פְדֽוּת
130.text: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second and third phrases give the reasons for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because with Yahweh is covenant faithfulness and with him is abundant redemption, Israel should hope in Yahweh]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **covenant faithfulness** and **redemption**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [Yahweh faithfully keeps his covenant, and he abundantly redeems his people]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **he will redeem** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Yahweh himself will be the one to redeem Israel. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [And it is he himself who will redeem]
The pronoun **his** refers to Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Israel’s sins]

131.text:
# Psalm 131 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 131 is one of the songs of ascents (Psalms 120–134). These are generally understood to be songs that were customarily sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem for one of the three major annual festivals. The term “ascents” is used because going up to the temple in Jerusalem involved a climb up Mount Zion. It is a “psalm of trust.” See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Reject pride and self-exaltation (1)
2. Rest quietly in Yahweh like a weaned child (2)
3. Call Israel to hope in Yahweh (3)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Humility as Contentment

The psalmist expresses humility not as self-deprecation but as willing acceptance of one’s place before God, refusing to pursue matters beyond his scope.

### The Weaned Child

A weaned child resting on its mother is content without demanding anything. This simile pictures a soul at peace with God, no longer driven by unmet desire.

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Both phrases express that David is not proud. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way as in the UST. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [I am not at all proud, nor do I act arrogantly]

Here the **heart** represents a person’s thoughts and attitudes. David is speaking of a proud person’s thoughts as if his heart were physically **high**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my thoughts are not proud]

The expression **are not raised up** contains a passive verbal form. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and my eyes do not look too high]

David is speaking of a proud person’s arrogant attitude as if his **eyes** were physically **raised up**. If your language has a comparable expression, you could use it in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and my attitude is not arrogant]

David is speaking of occupying himself with things as if he were able to **walk** among them. If your language has a comparable expression, you could use it in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I do not occupy myself with great and marvelous things]

David uses the word **Rather** here to indicate a contrast between what he denied about himself in the previous verse and what he now positively affirms about himself. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [On the contrary]

The terms **stilled** and **quieted** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [I have completely calmed]

David is using the term **soul** to mean his entire person from the perspective of his emotional existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [my inner self]

131.quote: כְּ֭⁠גָמֻל עֲלֵ֣י אִמּ֑⁠וֹ כַּ⁠גָּמֻ֖ל עָלַ֣⁠י נַפְשִֽׁ⁠י
131.text: The point of this comparison is that just as **a weaned child** resting **upon his mother** is calm and content, no longer crying for milk, so David’s inner being (**my soul**) is at peace. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [so that I am content and at rest; my inner being is truly at peace]
The pronoun **his** refers to the weaned child in the simile. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [upon the child’s mother]

David is referring to all of time by naming its two extremes, **now** and **forever**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [always]

132.text:
# Psalm 132 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 132 is one of the songs of ascents (Psalms 120–134). These are generally understood to be songs that were customarily sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem for one of the three major annual festivals. The term “ascents” is used because going up to the temple in Jerusalem involved a climb up Mount Zion.

1. Remember David’s devotion to Yahweh (1–9)
2. Affirm Yahweh’s promise to David’s line (10–12)
3. Celebrate Yahweh’s choice of Zion (13–18)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### The Davidic Covenant

Yahweh swore that David’s descendants would reign if they kept his covenant.

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. The psalmist is praying to God. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please remember, Yahweh]
The pronoun **his** refers to David. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [all of David’s afflictions]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **afflictions**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the hardships he endured]

132.quote: אֲשֶׁ֣ר נִ֭שְׁבַּע לַ⁠יהוָ֑ה נָ֝דַ֗ר לַ⁠אֲבִ֥יר יַעֲקֹֽב
132.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way, as the UST does. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [who swore to Yahweh, yes, he vowed to the Mighty One of Jacob]

If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark the end of this verse in a way that shows that the next verse is the beginning of David’s oath. Alternate translation: [vowed to the Mighty One of Jacob, saying,]

132.quote: אִם־אָ֭בֹא בְּ⁠אֹ֣הֶל בֵּיתִ֑⁠י אִם־אֶ֝עֱלֶ֗ה עַל־עֶ֥רֶשׂ יְצוּעָֽ⁠י
132.text: Following the custom of the culture, David is swearing an oath by stating several conditions (“if”) from this verse through verse 5, but not the consequences for not meeting those conditions (“then”). The implied meaning is that something bad will happen to him if he does these things before finding a place for Yahweh.

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [if I give slumber to my eyelids]

132.quote: עַד־אֶמְצָ֣א מָ֭קוֹם לַ⁠יהוָ֑ה מִ֝שְׁכָּנ֗וֹת לַ⁠אֲבִ֥יר יַעֲקֹֽב
132.text: Following the custom of the culture, the psalmist is quoting David as swearing an oath by stating the first part of a condition (“if” clauses in verses 3 and 4) but not the second part (“then”). If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explicitly state the consequence of not meeting this condition. Alternate translation: [until I find a place for Yahweh, dwellings for the Mighty One of Jacob, then may God strike me down]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [until I find dwellings for the Mighty One of Jacob]

The psalmist is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Pay attention]

The pronoun **it** in both clauses refers to the ark of the covenant. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [we heard of the ark of the covenant in Ephrathah; we found the ark in the fields of Jaar]

This is the beginning of what the community of worshipers said. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of the community. Alternate translation: [We said to one another, “Let us go to his dwellings]
The pronoun **his** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s dwellings]

Here, **bow down** is describing a symbolic action by which people showed reverence and submission as an act of worship. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation. Alternate translation: [let us bow down in worship]

Here the psalmist is speaking of the ark of the covenant as if it were **the footstool of his feet**, that is, the place where Yahweh rests his feet as he sits enthroned above the cherubim. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the place where he rests his feet]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. The psalmist is praying to God. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please arise, Yahweh]

The psalmist is using **Arise** as a common expression of the culture to tell Yahweh to take action and come to his resting place. He is not telling Yahweh to stand up from a seated position. If this expression does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly as modeled in the UST.

Here Yahweh is speaking of remaining in one place as if he were **resting** there. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [come where you can remain]

Here, **strength** represents Yahweh’s powerful presence. The box (ark of the covenant) is called the box of Yahweh’s strength because it symbolized his powerful presence among the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and the box where your power resides]

The psalmist is saying what he wants the priests and the faithful ones to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [Your priests should wear righteousness and your faithful ones should shout for joy]

Here the psalmist is speaking of **righteousness** as if it were clothing that the priests could **wear**. He means that the priests should be characterized by righteous behavior. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Let your priests be righteous in all they do]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **righteousness** and **joy**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [righteous acts and let your faithful shout joyfully]

The psalmist is using the adjective **faithful** as a noun to mean people who are faithful to God. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [and your faithful people should shout for joy]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. The psalmist is asking God not to reject the anointed king. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please do not turn back the face of your anointed]

The psalmist is using **turn back the face** as a common expression of his culture to mean “reject.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [reject]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **truth**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [surely]

The pronoun **he** refers to Yahweh, and the pronoun **it** refers to the oath that he swore. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will not turn back from his promise]

Here the psalmist is speaking of Yahweh changing his mind about his promise as if he were going one way and then decided to **turn back from it**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he will not change his mind about it]

After the clause “he will not turn back from it,” Yahweh’s direct speech begins. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh said, “From the fruit of your body]

Here Yahweh is speaking of David’s children as if they were **the fruit** that his body produces. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [From among your offspring]

Here Yahweh is speaking of choosing one of David’s sons to rule his kingdom after him as if he were going to physically **set** him **on the throne**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will cause one of your sons to rule over Israel after you]

Here, **the throne** represents royal authority and the right to rule as king. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [as king over your kingdom]

The terms **covenant** and **testimonies** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [all my commands]

Here, **sit on the throne** represents ruling as king. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [will succeed you as kings]

Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [Certainly,]

This is the beginning of what Yahweh said. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh said, “This is my resting place]

Here Yahweh is speaking of remaining in one place as if he were **resting** there. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [where I will remain]

The word **for** here indicates that what follows is a reason for Yahweh’s decision to dwell in Zion. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [because I have desired it]

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb **bless** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [I will abundantly bless]
Here and through the next verse, the pronoun **her** refers to Zion (see [verse 13](../132/013.md)). It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Zion’s provisions]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [I will bless her needy]

Yahweh is using the adjective **needy** as a noun to mean people who are in need. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [her needy people]
The psalmist is using one kind of food, **bread**, to mean food in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a general expression. Alternate translation: [with enough to eat]

Here Yahweh is speaking the priests being examples of his saving power as if **salvation** were clothing that the priests could wear. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And her priests I will make examples of my saving power]

If your language does not use an abstract nouns for the ideas of **salvation** and **joy**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [with the evidence that I save people, and her faithful people will shout joyfully]

Yahweh is using the adjective **faithful** as a noun to mean people who are faithful to God. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [and her faithful people]

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb **shout** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [they will shout loudly for joy]
The word **There** refers to Zion, which was mentioned in verse 13. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [There in Zion]

Here Yahweh is speaking of son of David’s being born who will be powerful as if he were a **horn** that would **sprout** like a plant growing. A horn represents strength and power, and sprouting represents the arising of something new. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will make a powerful king rise up from David’s line]

Here Yahweh is speaking of the continuing dynasty of the anointed king as if it were **a lamp** that keeps burning. A lamp that stays lit represents the continuation of a family line or kingdom. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a continuing dynasty for my anointed one]

Here Yahweh is speaking of **shame** as if the enemies would wear it like clothing. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [His enemies I will thoroughly put to shame]

Here, **His** and the pronoun **him** later in the verse refer to the anointed one mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The anointed one’s enemies]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **shame**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [I will shame]

Yahweh uses the word **but** here to indicate a contrast between the fate of the anointed one’s enemies and the fate of the anointed one himself. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [however, upon him his crown will flourish]

Here Yahweh is speaking of the anointed one’s crown as if it were a plant that would **flourish** and grow. He means that the anointed one’s reign will prosper and thrive. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his reign will be successful]

133.text:
# Psalm 133 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 133 is one of the songs of ascents (Psalms 120–134). These are generally understood to be songs that were customarily sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem for one of the three major annual festivals. The term “ascents” is used because going up to the temple in Jerusalem involved a climb up Mount Zion.

1. Celebrate the goodness of unity (1–2)
2. Declare Yahweh’s blessing where unity dwells (3)

David is using the word **Behold** to focus the attention of his listeners on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Consider]

The terms **good** and **pleasant** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [truly delightful]

133.quote: כַּ⁠שֶּׁ֤מֶן הַ⁠טּ֨וֹב ׀ עַל־הָ⁠רֹ֗אשׁ יֹרֵ֗ד עַֽל־הַ⁠זָּקָ֥ן זְקַֽן־אַהֲרֹ֑ן
133.text: David assumes that readers will know that the **good oil** being poured on **the head** and **beard** of Aaron refers to Aaron’s anointing as High Priest which was a solemn and joyful occasion. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [It is as good and pleasant as the anointing oil that is pouring down over Aaron’s head and]

Here, **the mouth of his garments** is a common expression that means the opening or neckline of a garment. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the neckline of his garments]

Here the word **there** refers to Zion. David is using this word to refer back to the mountains of Zion that he mentioned previously. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could state that explicitly. Alternate translation: [it was there on Zion that]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the dew of Hermon** is refreshing and life-giving as it falls on the land, so the unity of God’s people is refreshing and brings life. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as the refreshing dew from Hermon falls on the mountains of Zion, so the unity of God’s people refreshes and gives life]
