If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **the blessing**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [that he would bless his people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **life**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [that they would live forever]

134.text:
# Psalm 134 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 134 is one of the songs of ascents (Psalms 120–134). These are generally understood to be songs that were customarily sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem for one of the three major annual festivals. The term “ascents” is used because going up to the temple in Jerusalem involved a climb up Mount Zion.

1. Call Yahweh’s servants to bless him (1–2)
2. Receive blessing from Yahweh the creator (3)

The psalmist is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Pay attention]
The psalmist is speaking of the temple of Yahweh as if it were a **house** in which he lived. Alternate translation: [in the temple of Yahweh]

To **Lift up** the **hands** was a symbolic action by which the Israelites showed their reverence and devotion to Yahweh in prayer. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation. Alternate translation: [Lift up your hands in prayer]

The word translated as **holiness** could refer to: (1) the holy place in the temple. Alternate translation: [to the holy place] or (2) the hands of the worshipers. Alternate translation: [in holiness]

The pronoun **you** here is singular and refers to each individual worshiper among the servants addressed earlier in this psalm. There the psalmist addressed the servants as a group using plural forms, but here the blessing shifts to the singular. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [May Yahweh bless each of you]

Here, **Zion** represents the place where Yahweh dwells among his people. The psalmist is using the name of this location to refer to God’s special presence there. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from his dwelling on Zion]

The psalmist is referring to all of creation by naming two extremes, **heaven** and **earth**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all things]

135.text:
# Psalm 135 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 135 is a “psalm of praise” focusing on worshiping God because his greatness.

1. Call to praise Yahweh (1–4)
2. Yahweh’s power over creation and history (5–14)
3. Idols are worthless but Yahweh is worthy of praise (15–21)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Praise

The people, priests and their helpers should praise God because he is so great. He defeated the Egyptians and led his people to the promise land. Idols have no power.

The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Halleluia] or [Praise Yah]
**Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh]

The psalmist is using the term **name** to represent who Yahweh is or to refer to his reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the idea with an equivalent expression. Alternate translation: [everything about Yahweh]

The psalmist is speaking of the temple where Yahweh is worshiped as if it were a house in which he lived. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in the temple of Yahweh]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [who are standing in the courts of the house of]

By using this possessive form, **our God**, the psalmist is not saying that the Israelites possess or control Yahweh. Rather he is using these words to indicate that Yahweh is the God whom the Israelites worship. See the introduction to Psalms for further discussion. Alternate translation: [the God whom we worship]

The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Halleluia] or [Praise Yah]
**Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh]
Here, **his name** represents who Yahweh is. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the idea with an equivalent expression. Alternate translation: [to Yahweh]
**Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh]

The psalmist is using the name **Jacob** to refer to the people of Israel who were all descendants of the patriarch Jacob, who was also known as Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [he chose Israel for his special possession]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **possession**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [as his own special people]

Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [After all]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I know** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize how confident he is in this knowledge. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [I definitely know]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and our Lord is greater than all gods]
The term “god,” when applied to a being other than Yahweh, can refer to an idol, but, as here, it can also refer to any lesser spirit being. Alternate translation: [than any other spiritual being]

The psalmist is referring to everywhere in all of creation by naming two pairs of extremes, **the heavens** and **the earth**, as well as **the seas** and **all deeps**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [everywhere in all of creation]

Here the word translated **bringing up** does not have an explicit subject. The context of the previous verse makes clear that the subject is Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is bringing up clouds from the end of the earth]

The psalmist is using the phrase **from the end of the earth** as a common expression to mean “from distant places.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from everywhere on earth]

The psalmist is speaking of wind as if it were kept in **storehouses**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from where he has prepared it]
The word **who** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh struck the firstborn of Egypt]
Here, **struck** represents to kill or slaughter. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language as modeled in the UST.

The psalmist is referring to all living beings by naming two extremes, **man** and **beast**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [of every kind of creature of Egypt]

The terms **signs** and **wonders** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [extraordinary demonstrations of his power]

The psalmist is speaking to **Egypt**, which cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about what God did there. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about Egypt. Alternate translation: [right in front of the Egyptians]
The word **who** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh struck many nations]
Here, **struck** represents killing or defeating in battle. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [who conquered]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [He defeated Sihon, king of the Amorite]

The pronoun **he** refers to Yahweh, while the word **their** refers to the defeated kings mentioned in the previous verses. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh gave the land of those kings]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **inheritance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to them as a gift to inherit]

135.quote: יְ֭הוָה שִׁמְ⁠ךָ֣ לְ⁠עוֹלָ֑ם יְ֝הוָ֗ה זִכְרְ⁠ךָ֥ לְ⁠דֹר־וָ⁠דֹֽר
135.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, you will be known and remembered through every generation] or [Yahweh, your name is to forever, indeed, your remembrance is to generation and generation]

Here, **name** represents Yahweh’s reputation and character. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the idea with an equivalent expression. Alternate translation: [your reputation]

The psalmist is using **to forever** as a common expression of his culture to mean “eternally” or “without end.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [lasts throughout eternity]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **remembrance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [people will remember you from generation to generation]

The psalmist is using the phrase **to generation and generation** as a common expression to mean “forever.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [is through all generations] or [is forever]

The word **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

Here, **the hands of man** represents the craftsmanship and ability of people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the idea with an equivalent expression. Alternate translation: [the work of men] or [made by men]

135.quote: פֶּֽה־לָ֭⁠הֶם וְ⁠לֹ֣א יְדַבֵּ֑רוּ עֵינַ֥יִם לָ֝⁠הֶ֗ם וְ⁠לֹ֣א יִרְאֽוּ
135.text: See how you translated the same phrases in [Psalm 115:5](../115/005.md).
See how you translated the similar phrase, “ears are to them, but they do not hear” in [Psalm 115:6](../115/006.md).

135.quote: כְּ֭מוֹ⁠הֶם יִהְי֣וּ עֹשֵׂי⁠הֶ֑ם כֹּ֭ל אֲשֶׁר־בֹּטֵ֣חַ בָּ⁠הֶֽם
135.text: See how you translated the same phrases in [Psalm 115:8](../115/008.md).

Here, **House** means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So **House of Israel** figuratively means all the people descended from the patriarch Jacob, who was also known as Israel. Alternate translation: [People of Israel]
Here the psalmist is using the word **house** to mean all the people descended from Aaron. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly as modeled in the UST.

Here the psalmist is using the word **House** to mean all the people descended from Levi. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [All you Levites]

The expression **Blessed be** is a passive verbal form. The psalmist is expressing his desire to praise Yahweh. If it would be unnatural to use that form for this purpose, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is the worshippers of Yahweh. Alternate translation: [May we bless Yahweh from Zion]
Here, **the one** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [who dwells in Jerusalem]

The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Halleluia] or [Praise Yah]
**Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh]

# Psalm 136 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 136 is a “psalm of thanksgiving.” It is a responsive psalm. One person or group would sing the first part and then the other group would sing the repeated refrain.

1. Give thanks for who Yahweh is (1–3)
2. Give thanks for Yahweh’s works in creation (4–9)
3. Give thanks for Yahweh’s acts of deliverance and care (10–26)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Israel blessed

God has blessed Israel throughout its history and taken care of the needy people. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/bless]])

136.quote: הוֹד֣וּ לַ⁠יהוָ֣ה כִּי־ט֑וֹב כִּ֖י לְ⁠עוֹלָ֣ם חַסְדּֽ⁠וֹ

137.text:
# Psalm 137 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 137 is a “psalm of supplication” or “lament.” See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Grief and remembrance in exile (1–4)
2. Commitment to remember Jerusalem (5–6)
3. Cry for Yahweh’s justice against enemies (7–9)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Songs of Zion

The captives are told to sing songs of Zion there in Babylon but they felt too unhappy to want to sing. The army from Babylon was cruel when it destroyed Jerusalem and the people of Edom encouraged them to destroy Jerusalem. They prayed that God will be cruel to the people of Edom and Babylon.

Here, **Zion** represents the temple and the community of God’s people who worshiped there. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [our homeland]

The psalmist refers to **willows** that are a kind of tree. If your readers would not be familiar with what willows are, you could use the name of another kind of tree that was common in that part of the world that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [On the trees in Babylon]

This is the beginning of what the captors and tormentors said. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote. Alternate translation: [and our tormenters, joy, demanding, “Sing]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and our tormentors requested of us joy]

137.quote: אֵ֗יךְ נָשִׁ֥יר אֶת־שִׁיר־יְהוָ֑ה עַ֝֗ל אַדְמַ֥ת נֵכָֽר
137.text: The psalmist is using the question form to emphasize that the people of Israel were not able to sing the song of Yahweh while in exile. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [We cannot sing the song of Yahweh on the land of foreignness!]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **foreignness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in a land that is not our own]

The psalmist is presenting a possible condition and its consequence. He says that if he forgets Jerusalem, then his right hand should no longer be able to play the harp. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [If I forget you, Jerusalem, then let my right hand forget]
Here the psalmist shifts from speaking about the community as “we” in the previous verses to speaking as an individual using the pronoun **I**. He is making a personal vow.

The psalmist is using **let my right hand forget** as a common expression of the culture to mean that his hand would lose its ability to play a musical instrument. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [let my right hand lose its skill] or [let my right hand wither]

The psalmist is saying what he wants to happen if he breaks his vow. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [I desire that my right hand would forget] or [may my right hand forget]

137.quote: תִּדְבַּ֥ק־לְשׁוֹנִ֨⁠י ׀ לְ⁠חִכִּ⁠י֮ אִם־לֹ֪א אֶ֫זְכְּרֵ֥⁠כִי אִם־לֹ֣א אַ֭עֲלֶה אֶת־יְרוּשָׁלִַ֑ם עַ֝֗ל רֹ֣אשׁ שִׂמְחָתִֽ⁠י
137.text: The psalmist is presenting the consequence first and then the condition. It may be helpful to reorder this sentence so that the conditional statement is first. Alternate translation: [If I fail to remember you, if I do not cause Jerusalem to go up above the head of my joy, then let me tongue cling to my palate]

The psalmist is using **tongue cling to my palate** as a common expression of the culture to mean that he would be unable to speak or sing. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Let me be unable to sing] or [Let my mouth be silenced]

137.quote: אִם־לֹ֣א אַ֭עֲלֶה אֶת־יְרוּשָׁלִַ֑ם עַ֝֗ל רֹ֣אשׁ שִׂמְחָתִֽ⁠י
137.text: The psalmist is using **go up above the head** as a common expression of the culture to mean to the “highest point” or “greatest extent.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [if I do not cause Jerusalem to give me more joy than anything else]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **joy**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what makes me rejoice]
The psalmist is speaking as if the people of the tribe of Esau were actually the **sons** of Edom, another name for Esau. Alternate translation: [the descendants of Esau] or [the people of Edom]

The psalmist is using **the day of Jerusalem** as a common expression of the culture to mean the time when Jerusalem was destroyed. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what happened to Jerusalem] or [the destruction of Jerusalem]

The psalmist is using repetition of the phrase **lay bare** for poetic effect. You may want to reproduce this effect if poetry in your language does this. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Completely demolish]
The pronoun **her** refers to Jerusalem. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [in Jerusalem]

The psalmist is speaking of **Babylon** as if it were a woman by calling it **Daughter**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Babylon] or [The city of Babylon]

The psalmist is speaking to **Babylon** as if the city could hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about the judgment that Babylon deserves. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about Babylon. Alternate translation: [As for Babylon]

The phrase **the devastated one** is a translation of the written Hebrew text. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense. You may want to follow an alternative reading from some ancient Greek and Aramaic translations. The UST follows that reading. Alternate translation: [you destroyer]

The psalmist is using an exclamation to express a strong desire for justice against Babylon. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [how happy is]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **repayment**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in order to repay you for all you did to us]

The psalmist is using an exclamation to express a strong desire for judgment on Babylon. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [How happy will be]

138.text:
# Psalm 138 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm is a psalm of praise.

1. Wholehearted praise (1–3)
2. Global worship (4–6)
3. Confidence in God’s protection (7–8)

Here the **heart** represents the seat of a person’s emotions and will. David is saying that he will thank Yahweh with complete devotion. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with all of my being]

Here, **the gods** could refer to: (1) idols of other nations that the psalmist sees either within Israel or while traveling. Alternate translation: [idols of foreign gods] or (2) God’s heavenly council of angelic beings. Alternate translation: [the heavenly assembly]

David is using the possessive form to describe a **temple** that is characterized by God’s **holiness**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [your holy temple]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **holiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [you, the Holy One] or [all that is holy about you]

David is using the term **name** to represent who Yahweh is and to refer to his reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who you are]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **covenant faithfulness** and **trustworthiness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [the way you are faithful to your covenant and for being trustworthy]

The terms **covenant faithfulness** and **trustworthiness** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [your complete reliability]

The phrase **for you have exalted above all of your name your word** is a translation of the written Hebrew text. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense. Scholars have proposed some alternative readings, and you may want to follow one of those. The UST follows the first alternative. Alternate translation: [for you have exalted above all else your name and your word] or [for you have exalted above all names your word]
David is using the term **word** to represent what Yahweh has spoken. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all that you have spoken]
David is using the word **soul** to refer to his whole self. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **power**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to be mighty]

David is saying **all the kings of the earth** as a generalization for emphasis. If it would be clearer in your language, you could express the emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [kings everywhere]

David is using **the words from your mouth** to represent everything that Yahweh has communicated. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the things you have declared]

David is speaking of what Yahweh does as if those actions were **ways** or paths that he walks along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [of what Yahweh does]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is very glorious]

David uses the word **Though** here to indicate a contrast between Yahweh’s supreme status and his attention to those who are humble. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Even though Yahweh is high, he still sees the lowly]

Here David is speaking of Yahweh’s supreme status as if it were a physical height, saying **Yahweh is high**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is supreme]

David is using the adjective **lowly** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [yet he sees lowly people]

Here David is speaking of Yahweh’s relationship to proud people as if it involved physical distance, saying he **knows** them **from far off**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the proud he keeps at a distance]

David is using the adjective **proud** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [and those who are proud]

David uses the word **Though** here to indicate a contrast between the danger he faces and the protection Yahweh provides. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Despite that I walk in the middle of trouble, you will still keep me alive]

Here David is speaking of experiencing danger as if it were a place through which he walks, saying he will **walk in the middle of trouble**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I experience great trouble]

Here, **hand** represents Yahweh’s power to act. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you will use your power]

Here, **nose** represents the anger of David’s enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the anger of my enemies]

Here, **right hand** represents Yahweh’s power to deliver. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you will powerfully save me]

By **Yahweh will accomplish for my benefit**, the psalmist means that whatever Yahweh does will be to fulfill his purpose for David. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will accomplish his purpose for my benefit]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the way you are faithful to your covenant]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please do not forsake the works of your hands]

Here, **the works of your hands** represents what Yahweh has made and accomplished. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [what you have made]

139.text:
# Psalm 139 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 139 is a psalm of praise.

1. God knows everything about me (1–6)
2. God is everywhere with me (7–12)
3. God formed me wonderfully (8–18)
4. God’s righteous anger guides me (19–22)
5. Inviting God’s search (23–24)

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

Here David is speaking of God examining him thoroughly as if God had **searched** for something. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you have thoroughly examined me]

139.quote: אַתָּ֣ה יָ֭דַעְתָּ שִׁבְתִּ֣⁠י וְ⁠קוּמִ֑⁠י בַּ֥נְתָּה לְ֝⁠רֵעִ֗⁠י מֵ⁠רָחֽוֹק
139.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [You fully know everything I do and think, even from far away] or [You, you know my sitting down and my rising up; indeed, you understand my thought from far away]

David is stating the pronoun **You** separately, even though the verb **know** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that it is Yahweh specifically who knows these things. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, you know]

David is referring to all of his activities by naming two extremes, **my sitting down** and **my rising up**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [everything I do]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **sitting down** and **rising up**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [when I sit down and when I rise up]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **thought**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what I think]

These two phrases **My path and my lying down you have winnowed** and **you are familiar with all of my ways** mean basically the same thing. See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [You have carefully examined everything I do; in fact, you know all of my activities intimately]

Here David is speaking of God examining his life in detail as if God had **winnowed** grain to separate what is valuable from what is not. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [My path and my lying down you have carefully examined]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **path** and **lying down**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [where I go and where I lie down]

David is speaking of how he lives as if that were a **way** or path that he was walking along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you are familiar with all of the things I do]

The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [Certainly,]

Here, **on my tongue** represents what David is about to say. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [that I am about to speak]
The pronoun **it** refers to what David will say. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [all of what I will say]

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about the direction with the information about what God does. Alternate translation: [You have enclosed me behind and before]

Here David is speaking of God protecting and guarding him as if God had physically **enclosed** him on all sides. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Behind and before you have guarded me]

David is referring to every direction by naming two extremes, **Behind** and **before**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [On every side]

Here, **your palm** represents God’s power and protective control. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your protective power]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **knowledge**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [That you know all of this is]

Here David is speaking of God’s knowledge being impossible for him to comprehend as if **it** were physically **high** above him and out of reach. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [it is beyond my understanding]
The pronoun **it** refers to the knowledge David described in the previous phrase. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [this knowledge is high]

139.quote: אָ֭נָ֥ה אֵלֵ֣ךְ מֵ⁠רוּחֶ֑⁠ךָ וְ֝⁠אָ֗נָה מִ⁠פָּנֶ֥י⁠ךָ אֶבְרָֽח
139.text: These two phrases **Where shall I go from your spirit?** and **where shall I flee from your face?** mean basically the same thing. See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [There is truly nowhere I could go to escape your presence!] or [Where shall I go from your spirit? Indeed, where shall I flee from your face?]

David is using the question form to emphasize that there is nowhere he could go to escape from God’s spirit. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I cannot go anywhere to escape from your spirit!]

David is using the question form to emphasize that there is nowhere he could flee to escape from God’s presence. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [There is no place to which I could flee from your presence!]
Here, **your face** represents being in God’s presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from you]

139.quote: אִם־אֶסַּ֣ק שָׁ֭מַיִם שָׁ֣ם אָ֑תָּה וְ⁠אַצִּ֖יעָה שְּׁא֣וֹל הִנֶּֽ⁠ךָּ
139.text: These two phrases **If I ascend to the heavens** and **I spread out in Sheol** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words, using a contrasting image. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [No matter where I go, whether to the highest or lowest place, you are there]

Here, **If I ascend to the heavens** introduces the first part of a possible condition. David is using this hypothetical situation to emphasize that God is present everywhere. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a hypothetical condition. Alternate translation: [Even if I were to go up to the heavens]

David is referring to everywhere in the universe by naming two extremes, **the heavens** and **Sheol**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the highest place and the lowest place]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [behold, you are there]

See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [If I travel to the most distant place in the world]

Here, **If I lift up** introduces the first part of a possible condition that continues from the hypothetical condition David began in verse 8. David is using this hypothetical situation to emphasize that God is present everywhere. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [Even if I lift up]

David is referring to everywhere by naming two extremes, the **wings of the dawn**, representing the east where the sun rises, and the **farthest part of the sea**, representing the distant west. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the farthest eastern horizon and the most remote western shore]

David is speaking of **the dawn** as if it were a bird that had **wings**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the first rays of the morning light]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [if I dwell in the farthest part of the sea]

These two phrases **your hand will lead me** and **your right hand will hold me** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [you yourself will surely guide me and sustain me]

Here, **hand** represents the power and agency of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your strength will lead me]

Here, **right hand** represents the power and strength of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your power will hold me]

If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this as an indirect quotation. Alternate translation: [And I said that surely darkness would crush me and night would be the light around me]

David is speaking of **darkness** as if it were a living thing that could **crush** him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [darkness will completely surround me]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and night will be the light around me]

139.quote: גַּם־חֹשֶׁךְ֮ לֹֽא־יַחְשִׁ֪יךְ מִ֫מֶּ֥⁠ךָ וְ֭⁠לַיְלָה כַּ⁠יּ֣וֹם יָאִ֑יר
139.text: These two phrases **Even darkness does not make it dark to you** and **the night shines like the day** mean basically the same thing. See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [Not even the deepest darkness can hide anything from you, because you see just as clearly at night as during the day]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the day** is fully bright and visible, so **the night** is equally bright and visible to Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [the night is as bright to you as the day]

David is referring to all conditions of visibility by naming two extremes, **darkness** and **light**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [whether it is dark or light, it is the same to you]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [To you, vision in darkness is like vision in light]

The word **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. David is giving the reason why darkness and light are the same to Yahweh: because Yahweh is the all-knowing Creator. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

David is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb **created** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that it was Yahweh himself who created him. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [you yourself created]

Here, **my kidneys** represents David’s deepest inner being, including his emotions and thoughts. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [my innermost being]

Here David is speaking of Yahweh creating him as if Yahweh were a craftsperson **knitting** material together. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you carefully crafted me]

The expression **I am wonderfully made** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [you made me wonderfully]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **works**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the things that you have done]

David is using **my soul** to represent his whole self. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I know it]

The expression **was not hidden** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [No one hid my frame from you]

The expression **when I was made** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [when you made me]

The expression **when I was woven** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [when you wove me]

Here David is speaking of Yahweh creating him as if Yahweh were a craftsperson **weaving** cloth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when you carefully assembled me]

Here David is speaking of his mother’s womb as if it were **the depths of the earth**. He is comparing the hidden, enclosed place where he was formed to the deep interior of the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in the hidden place of my mother’s womb]

Here, **your eyes** represents Yahweh’s perception and awareness. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you perceived] or [you observed]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **unformed substance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [me before my body had taken shape]

Here David is speaking of Yahweh’s plan for his life as if it were a written record **in your book**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And you recorded all of them]

The expression **all of them were written** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [you wrote all of them]
Here, **all of them** could refer to the days of David’s life. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state that explicitly. Alternate translation: [all of my days]

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reorder this clause to clarify its meaning. David is saying that Yahweh recorded his days before any of them actually existed. Alternate translation: [and yet when not one of them had come to be, the days were formed]

The expression **the days were formed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [you formed the days]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **thoughts**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the things that you think]
David is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of amazement at how many things God thinks about. Alternate translation: [You think of so many things]

David is using **their heads** as a common expression of the culture to mean “their total number.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they all] or [they in quantity]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the sand** cannot be counted, so God’s thoughts cannot be counted. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [they are too many to count, like grains of sand]

David says **they are more than the sand** as an extreme statement to emphasize that God’s thoughts are too many to count. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [they are far too many to count]

This is a wish that David is expressing to God rather than a command. If your language has a way of expressing a strong wish, use that form here. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [God, please kill the wicked]

David is using **men of bloodshed** as a common expression of the culture to indicate that a person has a certain characteristic. In this case, these men have the characteristic of being violent. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And violent men] or [And men who love violence]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **bloodshed**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And men who shed blood]
Here, **bloodshed** represents violence and murder. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [violence]

This is a wish that David is expressing rather than a direct command. If the imperative does not communicate a strong wish for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a strong wish. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please depart from me]
The pronoun **who** refers to the men of bloodshed mentioned in the previous verse. The pronoun **you** refers to Yahweh. Alternate translation: [men of bloodshed who speak of you, Yahweh,]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **purpose**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in order to do evil]

David is using **they lift up your name to emptiness** as a common expression of the culture to mean “they misuse your name.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they misuse your reputation] or [they speak your name for worthless purposes]
David is using the term **name** to represent who God is and to refer to God’s reputation. Alternate translation: [they lift up your reputation to emptiness]

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about who these people are before the information about what they do. Alternate translation: [your enemies, they lift up your name to emptiness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **emptiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for what is worthless]

See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, I certainly hate and loathe all those who oppose you!] or [Do I not hate the ones hating you, Yahweh; yes, do I not loathe the ones rising up against you]

David is using the question form to emphasize his loyalty to God. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, I certainly hate the ones hating you!]

David is using the question form to emphasize his loyalty to God. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I certainly loathe the ones rising up against you!]

David is using **the ones rising up against you** as a common expression of the culture to mean ‘those who oppose you.’ If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And do I not loathe those who rebel against you] or [And do I not loathe those who oppose you]

139.quote: תַּכְלִ֣ית שִׂנְאָ֣ה שְׂנֵאתִ֑י⁠ם לְ֝⁠אוֹיְבִ֗ים הָ֣יוּ לִֽ⁠י
139.text: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [I completely hate them, for they are my enemies] or [{With} a completeness of hatred I hate them; indeed, they have become enemies to me]

139.quote: חָקְרֵ֣⁠נִי אֵ֭ל וְ⁠דַ֣ע לְבָבִ֑⁠י בְּ֝חָנֵ֗⁠נִי וְ⁠דַ֣ע שַׂרְעַפָּֽ⁠י
139.text: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [God, please thoroughly examine everything about me]
