Here David is asking God to thoroughly examining his inner being, to **Search** through him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Thoroughly examine me]

Here the **heart** represents where a person’s thoughts and motives exist. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my innermost thoughts]

This is a request that David is making to God rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please examine me and know my cares]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **cares**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the things that concern me]

This is a request that David is making to God rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please see if a way of hurtfulness is in me]

David is speaking of how a person lives as if that were a **way** or path that the person was walking along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [if a harmful way of living]
The word translated as **hurtfulness** could refer to: (1) something that causes harm or pain. Alternate translation: [pain] or (2) an idol. Alternate translation: [idolatry]

This is a request that David is making to God rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [and please lead me in the way of eternity]

David is speaking of how a person lives as if that were a **way** or path along which that the person was walking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in the way of living that lasts forever]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **eternity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the way that lasts forever]

140.text:
# Psalm 140 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 140 is a deliverance psalm. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/deliverer]])

1. Cry to Yahweh for protection from the wicked (1–5)
2. Trust Yahweh as defender and refuge (6–8)
3. Ask Yahweh to judge evil and uphold the righteous (9–13)

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

140.quote: חַלְּצֵ֣⁠נִי יְ֭הוָה מֵ⁠אָדָ֣ם רָ֑ע מֵ⁠אִ֖ישׁ חֲמָסִ֣ים תִּנְצְרֵֽ⁠נִי
140.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, rescue me and preserve me from evil, violent people]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please rescue me]

David is using the possessive form to describe **a man** who is characterized by **violence**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a violent man]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **violence**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from a man who acts violently]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please preserve me]

The word **who** refers to the evil man and the man of violence from the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [these evil people devise evil things]

Here, **heart** represents a person’s thoughts and intentions. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [have devised evil things in their thoughts]

David is saying **all the day** as a generalization for emphasis. If it would be clearer in your language, you could express the emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [constantly] or [all the time]

The phrase **travel around** is a translation of the written Hebrew text. Many translations, however, follow an alternative reading found in one Hebrew manuscript and some ancient translations. The UST follows that reading. Alternate translation: [they stir up battles]

The pronoun **they** refers to the evil man and the man of violence from verse 1. David uses the plural because he has multiple enemies in view. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [these evil people stir up battles]

The point of this comparison is that just as a **serpent** has a dangerous, darting tongue, so the speech of these evil people is harmful. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [They use their words to harm people, as a serpent uses its tongue to strike]
Here, **their tongue** represents their speech. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [their words]

David is speaking of the harmful words of these evil people as if the words were **venom of a viper** under their lips. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the words they speak are deadly and destructive]
Here, **their lips** represents what they say. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in their speech]

140.quote: שָׁמְרֵ֤⁠נִי יְהוָ֨ה ׀ מִ֘⁠ידֵ֤י רָשָׁ֗ע מֵ⁠אִ֣ישׁ חֲמָסִ֣ים תִּנְצְרֵ֑⁠נִי
140.text: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, guard me and preserve me from wicked, violent people]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please guard me]

Here, **the hands** of the wicked represents their power and control. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the control of the wicked]

David is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are wicked]

David is using the possessive form to describe **the man** who is characterized by **violence**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the violent man]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **violence**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from the man who acts violently]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [from anyone of]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please preserve me]

David is speaking of his way of life as if it were a path with **steps** that his enemies could **push down**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who have planned to ruin my life]
The word **who** refers to the wicked and the man of violence. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the wicked people that have planned]

140.quote: טָֽמְנֽוּ־גֵאִ֨ים ׀ פַּ֡ח לִ֗⁠י וַ⁠חֲבָלִ֗ים פָּ֣רְשׂוּ רֶ֭שֶׁת לְ⁠יַד־מַעְגָּ֑ל מֹקְשִׁ֖ים שָֽׁתוּ־לִ֣⁠י
140.text: David is speaking of his enemies as if they were hunters setting **a snare**, **cords**, **a net**, and **traps** to capture him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The proud have made secret plans to ruin me; they have plotted to catch me in their schemes wherever I go]

David is using the adjective **proud** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [Those who are proud] or [Those who act proudly]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please give ear, Yahweh, to the voice of my supplications]
David is using the term **ear** to mean hearing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Listen]

Here, **the voice** represents the words that David speaks. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the words of my supplications]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **supplications**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [my cries for help]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **strength** and **salvation**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [the mighty one who rescues me]

David is speaking of God’s ability to save him as if it were physical **strength**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you who powerfully deliver me]

David is speaking of Yahweh’s protection as if Yahweh had physically **covered** his **head** with armor in battle. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you have protected me when I was in battle]

David is using **in the day of battle** as a common expression to mean “at the time of battle.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when I was in battle] or [at the time of fighting]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please do not grant, Yahweh, the desires of the wicked]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **desires**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what the wicked wish for]

David is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are wicked]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please do not bring forth his plot]

David is using **bring forth** as a common expression of the culture to mean “grant success to.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [grant success to his plot]

The pronoun **his** is singular, even though David used the plural **the wicked** earlier in the verse. This is because he is thinking of the wicked as a group that acts with a single purpose. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [their plot]

It is difficult to know how the word translated as **they rise up** fits with the rest of the verse. The interpretation of the ULT and UST is one way. Some scholars believe that the word belongs with the first line of the next verse in which case it would start a new sentence with something like: “Those who surround me raise their heads.” Here are some other possibilities. Alternate translation: [when they rise up] or [or they will rise up]

David is saying what he wants to happen to his enemies. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants to happen. Alternate translation: [I desire that the mischief of their lips cover them]

David is speaking of the harmful things his enemies have said as if those words could physically **cover them** like a burden. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [let the trouble they have caused by their words overwhelm them]
Here, **their lips** represents what they say. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the mischief of their words]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **mischief**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the troublesome things they have spoken]

David is saying what he wants to happen to his enemies. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants to happen. Alternate translation: [I desire that burning coals fall on them]

David is saying what he wants God to do to his enemies. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants God to do. Alternate translation: [may he cast them into fire]
The pronoun **him** most likely refers to God and **them** refers to David’s enemies. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [let God cast the enemies]

The expression **be established** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [May God not establish a man of tongue in the land]
Here, **tongue** represents slanderous speech. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [slanderous words]

David is using the possessive form to describe **a man** who is characterized by his **tongue**, that is, by his slanderous speech. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a man who speaks slander]

David is using the possessive form to describe **a man** who is characterized by **violence**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a violent man]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **violence**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a man who acts violently]

David speaks of **evil** as if it were a living thing that could **hunt** a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [let him experience one disaster after another]

140.quote: יַעֲשֶׂ֣ה יְ֭הוָה דִּ֣ין עָנִ֑י מִ֝שְׁפַּ֗ט אֶבְיֹנִֽים
140.text: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [will defend poor and needy people and bring them justice]

140.quote: יַעֲשֶׂ֣ה יְ֭הוָה דִּ֣ין עָנִ֑י מִ֝שְׁפַּ֗ט אֶבְיֹנִֽים
140.text: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **cause** and **justice**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will defend the poor and judge fairly for the needy]

David is using the adjective **poor** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. He does the same thing with the word **needy** later in the verse. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [people who are poor]

140.quote: צַ֭דִּיקִים יוֹד֣וּ לִ⁠שְׁמֶ֑⁠ךָ יֵשְׁב֥וּ יְ֝שָׁרִ֗ים אֶת־פָּנֶֽי⁠ךָ
140.text: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [righteous and upright people will give you thanks and live in your presence]

David is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. He does the same thing with the word **upright** later in the verse. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are righteous]
David is using the term **name** to represent who Yahweh is. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [will thank you]

Here, **your face** represents Yahweh’s presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the upright will live before you]

141.text:
# Psalm 141 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 141 is a “lament.”

1. Ask Yahweh to hear and accept the prayer (1–2)
2. Pray for purity in speech and actions (3–5)
3. Trust Yahweh for protection and deliverance (6–10)
This is poetic language. If your language has a way to indicate poetry, you could use it here.

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please hurry to me]

David is using **Give ear to my voice** as a common expression of the culture to mean “listen attentively to what I am saying.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Pay attention to what I say] or [Listen closely to my words]

The expression **May my prayer be established** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [May you establish my prayer]

The point of this comparison is that just as **incense** rises up as a pleasing aroma before God, so David wants his prayer to rise up and be acceptable to God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as a pleasing offering before you]

Here, **to your face** represents “in your presence.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before you] or [in your presence]

141.quote: תִּכּ֤וֹן תְּפִלָּתִ֣⁠י קְטֹ֣רֶת לְ⁠פָנֶ֑י⁠ךָ מַֽשְׂאַ֥ת כַּ֝פַּ֗⁠י מִנְחַת־עָֽרֶב
141.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [May my prayer and my uplifted hands be truly acceptable to you, like a pleasing offering]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the evening sacrifice** is an acceptable offering to God, so David wants his raised hands in prayer to be equally acceptable. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [my lifted hands as an acceptable offering to you]

The **evening sacrifice** is a kind of grain offering that the Israelites presented to God at twilight each day. If your readers would not be familiar with what the evening sacrifice is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [the offering presented at twilight] or [the daily evening offering]

141.quote: שִׁיתָ֣⁠ה יְ֭הוָה שָׁמְרָ֣ה לְ⁠פִ֑⁠י נִ֝צְּרָ֗⁠ה עַל־דַּ֥ל שְׂפָתָֽ⁠י
141.text: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, carefully watch over everything I say]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, please place a guard over my mouth]

Here David is speaking as if his mouth were an opening that needed **a guard** posted over it to control what comes out. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [someone to watch over what I say] or [restraint on my speech]

Here David is speaking as if his lips were **the door** of a building that needed to be guarded. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the opening of my lips] or [what my lips let pass through]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please do not turn my heart toward an evil thing]

Here the **heart** represents where a person’s desires and inclinations exist. David is speaking as if someone could **turn** his heart in a direction toward evil, meaning his desires could be directed toward wrongdoing. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Do not cause me to desire an evil thing] or [Do not direct my desires toward an evil thing]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wickedness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in wicked ways]

Here the masculine term **men** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [with people, doers of evil]

David is using the participial phrase **doers of evil** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [people who do evil things]

David is expressing what he desires for himself. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he desires. Alternate translation: [I desire that I not dine on their delicacies] or [I should not dine on their delicacies]

Here David is speaking as if sharing in the pleasures and rewards of the wicked were dining on **their delicacies**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And may I not partake of their pleasures] or [And may I not share in their rewards]

The pronoun **their** refers to the men, doers of evil, mentioned earlier in the verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [on the delicacies of the doers of evil]

David is saying what he wants the righteous to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [I desire that the righteous hit me] or [The righteous should hit me]

David is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [a righteous person]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because he is being faithfully loyal to me]
The pronoun **he** refers to the righteous person mentioned at the beginning of the verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers.

David assumes that readers will know that anointing someone’s head with oil was a way of honoring or blessing that person. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [May my head not refuse oil for the head, which would be a sign of such honor]

The pronoun **their** refers to the doers of evil mentioned in verse 4. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [For my prayer is continually against the wickedness of the doers of evil]

The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because my prayer is continually against their wickedness]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wickedness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [For my prayer is continually against the wicked things they do]
David is saying **continually** as a generalization for emphasis. If it would be clearer in your language, you could express the emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [again and again]

The expression **Their judges are thrown down** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Someone throws their judges down]
The pronoun **Their** refers to the wicked people described in verse 4. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The judges of the wicked people]

In the phrase **and they hear my words, that they are pleasant**, the first **they** could refer to the wicked people or to their judges, and the second **they** refers to David’s words. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. [and the wicked people hear my words, that my words are pleasant]

The point of this comparison is that just as **splitting and breaking up** the ground scatters clods of earth everywhere, so their bones lie scattered about near death. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Just as clods of earth are scattered when one breaks up the ground]

141.quote: כְּמ֤וֹ פֹלֵ֣חַ וּ⁠בֹקֵ֣עַ בָּ⁠אָ֑רֶץ נִפְזְר֥וּ עֲ֝צָמֵ֗י⁠נוּ לְ⁠פִ֣י שְׁאֽוֹל
141.text: The words of this verse may be (1) the words of the wicked. See the UST for how you could mark this as a direct quote of the wicked. Or this may be (2) the words of the psalmist, describing the danger that he feels from his wicked oppressors. In this case, there would be no quote marks around the verse.

The terms **splitting** and **breaking up** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [breaking apart]

The expression **our bones are scattered** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [death scatters our bones]

The pronoun **our** represents a shift from the singular “I” that David has been using to a plural form. Here David is speaking on behalf of himself and his companions, or he is quoting what the persecuted righteous say together. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers.

David is speaking of **Sheol** as if it were a living creature that could swallow the dead with its **mouth**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the entrance to Sheol] or [the opening of the grave]

David uses the word **Yet** here to indicate a contrast between his desperate situation described in the previous verse and his continued trust in God. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [But despite all of this, my eyes are on you, Yahweh, Lord]

Here, **my eyes are on you** represents “I look to you with trust and dependence.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I put my trust in you] or [I look to you for help]

Here David is speaking as if God were a physical shelter where he could **take refuge** from danger. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in you I find safety] or [you are my protection]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please do not uncover my soul] or [please do not leave my soul unprotected]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please keep me from the hands of the snare they have laid for me]

141.quote: פַ֭ח יָ֣קְשׁוּ לִ֑⁠י וּ֝⁠מֹקְשׁ֗וֹת פֹּ֣עֲלֵי אָֽוֶן
141.text: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [all the traps that evildoers have set to catch me]

Here David is speaking as if the snare had **hands** that could grab and hold him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the grip of the snare] or [the power of the snare]

The pronoun **they** refers to the doers of evil mentioned later in the verse as “the workers of evil.” It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the workers of evil have laid for me]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and keep me from the traps of the workers of evil]

David is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [wicked people]

Here David is speaking as if the punishment that the wicked deserve were nets that they would **fall into**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Let the wicked be caught in their own schemes together] or [Let the wicked be ensnared by their own plans altogether]

The singular pronoun **his** is used to refer collectively to each of the wicked people. David uses a singular form even though he is speaking of the wicked as a group. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [together into the nets of the wicked people]

David is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I will cross over** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he himself will do something different than what the wicked will do. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [while I myself cross over]

142.text:
# Psalm 142 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 142 is a psalm of deliverance from his enemies. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/deliverer]])

1. Pour out complaint and trouble to Yahweh (1–4)
2. Declare Yahweh as refuge and portion (5–7)

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a **maskil**. Since the meaning of this word is not certain, you may wish to represent it in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language. See the discussion of that term in the Introduction to Psalms.

142.quote: ק֭וֹלִ⁠י אֶל־יְהוָ֣ה אֶזְעָ֑ק ק֝וֹלִ֗⁠י אֶל־יְהוָ֥ה אֶתְחַנָּֽן
142.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [I earnestly cry out to Yahweh for favor]
David is using **My voice** to represent his prayer. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [My prayer to Yahweh]

David is speaking of his lament as if it were a liquid that he **pours out** before Yahweh. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I express my lament to his face]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **lament**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what I lament]

Here, **to his face** represents being in the presence of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in his presence]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **distress**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what distresses me]

David is using the word **spirit** to represent his whole self. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [When I grow faint]

The word **you** is repeated for emphasis. David is emphasizing that Yahweh is the one who truly knows his path. If your language does not use repetition for emphasis, you could express this in another way. Alternate translation: [then you alone know]

David is speaking of how he lives and what he does as if that were a **path** that he was walking along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my situation]

David is speaking of his enemies’ schemes as if they were a **trap** that **they** had **hidden** for him to fall into. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they have secretly planned to harm me]

David is using the pronoun **they** in a general sense to refer to his enemies without specifying who they are. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [others have hidden] or [people have hidden]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please look right and see]

Looking to the right was a symbolic action by which a person looked for his defender, since the right side was the position where a protector would stand. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Look for my defender]

David is using the word **soul** to represent his whole self. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [me]

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a **shelter** that could protect him from danger. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my protection]

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a **portion** of inherited land. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all that matters to me]

The expression **the land of the living** was a common expression meaning “among those who are alive on earth.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [during my life on earth]

David is using the adjective **living** as a noun to mean people who are alive. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are alive]

The word **for** indicates that what follows is the reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [because I am very low]

David is speaking of his distress as if he were physically in a **low** position. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am very weak]

The word **for** indicates that what follows is the reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [since they are stronger than I]

David is speaking of his trouble as if it were a **prison** from which he needs to be brought out. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Free me from my troubles]

David is using the word **soul** to represent his whole self. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [me]

Here, **to** marks **praise your name** as the purpose for which David asks Yahweh to bring him out of trouble. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [so that I may praise your name]

David is using the term **name** to represent who Yahweh is and his reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you]

David is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean righteous people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [Righteous people]

The word **because** indicates that what follows is the reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [for you will fulfill for me]

The implication is that Yahweh will fulfill David’s request or his promise. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [you will fulfill your promise to me] or [you will answer my prayer]

143.text:
# Psalm 143 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 143 is a deliverance psalm. The psalmist prays for deliverance from his enemies. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/deliverer]])

1. Plead for Yahweh’s mercy and not judgment (1–2)
2. Describe distress and longing for Yahweh (3–6)
3. Ask Yahweh for guidance, deliverance, and renewal (7–12)

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Hear my prayer, Yahweh; yes, listen to my pleas]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please hear my prayer]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please listen to my supplications]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **faithfulness** and **righteousness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [Because you are faithful, answer me, because you are righteous]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please answer me]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please do not enter into judgment]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **judgment**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And do not judge your servant]

Here, **to your face** represents being in the presence of God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in your presence]

The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

David is saying **everyone living is not righteous** as a generalization for emphasis. If it would be clearer in your language, you could express the emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [no living person is truly righteous]

The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]
Here, **my soul** represents David himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the enemy has pursued me]

Here David is speaking as if his enemy had physically **crushed** his **life to the ground**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he has completely defeated me] or [he has brought me very low]

Here David is speaking as if his suffering were being in **dark places**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in places of despair] or [in places where it is as if I were dead]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the dead of ages** are unable to help themselves, so is David in his suffering. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like people who have been dead for a long time]

David is using the adjective **dead** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [like those who died long ago]

143.quote: וַ⁠תִּתְעַטֵּ֣ף עָלַ֣⁠י רוּחִ֑⁠י בְּ֝⁠תוֹכִ֗⁠י יִשְׁתּוֹמֵ֥ם לִבִּֽ⁠י
143.text: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [So my spirit and my heart lose hope within me]

Here David is speaking as if his **spirit** were a person who could **faint**. He means that he is losing his strength and vitality. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am growing weak inside]

Here the **heart** represents where David’s feelings exist. He is saying that deep inside himself he feels dismay. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I feel hopeless]

See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [In my mind I review all that you have done] or [I meditate on all your works; indeed, I reflect on the works of your hands]

Here, **your hands** represents God’s power and agency. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [on what you have accomplished]

Here David is speaking as if to **spread out** his **hands** were the act of praying itself. He means that he is praying to God. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I lift my hands in prayer to you] or [I pray earnestly to you]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [my soul longs for you as a weary land longs for water]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a weary land** desperately needs water, so David desperately needs God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [I need you the way a weary land needs rain]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please hurry and answer me, Yahweh]

Here David is speaking as if his **spirit** were something that could be **expiring** or used up. He means that he is losing all hope and strength. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am losing all strength] or [I have no more endurance]

Here, **your face** represents God’s attention and favor. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Do not hide your favor from me] or [Do not ignore me]

The word translated as **or** indicates that what follows is a negative consequence that will happen if the previous request is not fulfilled. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [otherwise]

David is referring to death in a polite way by using the phrase **the descenders of the pit**. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [those who descend to their death] or [those who die]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please cause me to hear your covenant faithfulness]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how you are faithful to your covenant]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please make known to me the way that I should walk]

David is speaking of how he should live as if that were a **way** that he was walking along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [how I should live]

David is using **I lift up my soul to** as a common expression of his culture to mean “I completely depend on.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for I completely depend on you]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please rescue me from my enemies]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please teach me to do your will]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **will**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what you want me to do]

David is not using this possessive form **my God** to indicate that he possesses or controls God. Rather David is using these words to indicate that Yahweh is the God whom he worships. Alternate translation: [the God whom I worship]

Here David is speaking as if God’s guidance were leading him on **level land** that is good to walk upon. He means that God gives him a life free from obstacles and difficulties. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [along a safe path] or [help me live in a way that righteous]

The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

Here, **your name** represents God’s reputation and character. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [for the sake of your reputation] or [to bring honor to who you are]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **righteousness** and **distress**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [because you are righteous, please bring me out of my distressing situation]
Here, **my soul** represents David himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [me]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And because you are faithful to your covenant]

The terms **destroy my enemies** and **exterminate all of the adversaries of my soul** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [please completely eliminate all who oppose me]
Here, **my soul** represents David himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [my adversaries]

The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [because]

144.text:
# Psalm 144 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 144 is a specific type of psalm of supplication, a psalm of trust. (See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.) The psalmist does not cry out urgently for help. Instead, he begins by saying how reliable and trustworthy Yahweh is. In the rest of the psalm, the psalmist asks for deliverance from his enemies, but this petition is punctuated by confident expressions of praise for Yahweh as the deliverer.

1. Statement of trust (1–4)
2. Petition (5–8)
3. Expression of praise (9–10)
4. Petition (11–14)
5. Expression of praise (15)

The expression **Blessed be** is a passive verbal form. The psalmist is expressing his desire to praise Yahweh. If it would be unnatural to use that form for this purpose, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I bless Yahweh] or [Let me praise Yahweh]

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a high **rock** that David could climb up to reach safety from danger. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [my protector]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [the one teaching my hands for war, the one training my fingers for battle]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the one who is faithfully committed to me by covenant]

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were **my fortress** and **my stronghold**, strong places where he could go for safety, and as if he were **my shield**, a defensive weapon that protects from attack. If these images communicate well in your language, please use them. If not, you could express them in a different way. Alternate translation: [and my protector, my safe place and the one rescuing me, my defender]

The terms **fortress** and **stronghold** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [my strong fortress]

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a place of **refuge** where he could go to hide from danger. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [and in whom I find safety]

David is not asking for information about **man**. He is using the question form to emphasize how small and insignificant people are compared to God. If you would not use a rhetorical question for this purpose in your language, you could translate his words as a statement or an exclamation and communicate the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [people are so insignificant that you should not pay attention to them, and the son of man is not worth considering.]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [what is man, that you know him; indeed, what is the son of man, that you consider him]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [what is a human being]
Although the term **son of man** is masculine, David is using the phrase in a generic sense that includes both men and women. Alternate translation: [the child of humanity] or [a human being]

David is speaking of **Man** as if he were **vapor**, something that appears briefly and then is gone. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [A person is like a puff of smoke]
Although the term **Man** is masculine, David is using the word in a generic sense that includes both men and women. Alternate translation: [A person]

David uses a comparison to express how quickly a person’s **days** pass. He says they are **like a passing shadow**, something that quickly moves and vanishes. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent comparison or express this meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his days pass quickly]

These are imperatives, but they communicate polite requests rather than commands. Use forms in your language that communicate polite requests. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please bow your heavens and come down]

The phrase **that they may smoke** communicates the purpose for which David asks God to touch the mountains. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that the second phrase describes the purpose for the first phrase. Alternate translation: [touch the mountains so that they smoke]

The psalmist is saying what he wants **Yahweh** to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [please touch the mountains, that they may smoke]

144.quote: בְּר֣וֹק בָּ֭רָק וּ⁠תְפִיצֵ֑⁠ם שְׁלַ֥ח חִ֝צֶּ֗י⁠ךָ וּ⁠תְהֻמֵּֽ⁠ם

However, if it would be unclear in your language, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Light lightning and scatter them; yes, send your arrows and rout them]

David is repeating forms of the word **lighten** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Flash your lightening]
The pronoun **them** refers to David’s enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state this explicitly. Alternate translation: [and scatter my enemies]

David is speaking of lightning bolts as if they were **arrows** that God shoots at his enemies. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [send your lightning bolts]

Here, **hands** represents Yahweh’s power and action. David speaks of God acting on his behalf as if God were reaching out his **hands from above**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Use your power from above]

The phrases **break me free** and **deliver me** mean similar things. David is using the two phrases together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [deliver me to freedom]

David is speaking of his troubles as if they were **many waters** that could overwhelm him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from great troubles]

Here, **the hand** represents the power or control that the foreigners have. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the power of sons of a foreigner]

David is using the possessive form to describe **sons** or people who are characterized by being a **foreigner**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [foreigners]

Here, **their mouth** represents the foreigners themselves speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they speak worthlessness]

144.quote: אֲשֶׁ֣ר פִּ֭י⁠הֶם דִּבֶּר־שָׁ֑וְא וִֽ֝⁠ימִינָ֗⁠ם יְמִ֣ין שָֽׁקֶר
144.text: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **worthlessness** and **falsehood**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [who, their mouth speaks what is worthless, and their right hand is a right hand of what is false]

Here, **their right hand** represents the oath that a person swears by raising the right hand. David says their oath is **a right hand of falsehood**, meaning they swear falsely. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they swear false oaths]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [who provides salvation] or [who grants deliverance]

David is speaking about himself in the third person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [me, David, your servant] or [me, who serves you]

Here, **the evil sword** represents violence and warfare. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from violent warfare]

Here, **the hand** represents the power or control that the foreigners have. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the power of the sons of a foreigner]

Here, **their mouth** represents the foreigners themselves in the act of speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they speak worthlessness]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **worthlessness** and **falsehood**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [what is worthless and they swear to what is false]

Here, **their right hand** represents the oath that a person swears by raising the right hand. David says their oath is **a right hand of falsehood**, meaning they swear falsely. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they swear false oaths]

The word **that** introduces the purpose for which David has been asking God to rescue him and his people. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows describes the purpose for the previous actions. Alternate translation: [so that our sons may be like plants]

Here David compares **sons** to **plants** that are well-established and growing. This means the sons are strong and healthy. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent comparison or express this meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [our sons may be strong and healthy]
If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you could state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that grow large]

Here David compares **daughters** to **corner pillars** that are carved beautifully. This means the daughters are beautiful and strong. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent comparison or express this meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [our daughters may be beautiful and strong]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [that our daughters may be like corner pillars carved in the pattern of a palace]

If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you could state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that someone carved to decorate a palace]

The implication is that the storehouses are full of many different **kind** of food. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could express that explicitly. Alternate translation: [providing many different kinds of food]

In keeping with the conventions of his language, David is using the numbers “thousand” and “myriad” as verbs. He does not mean those exact numbers. He is using them to mean great quantities. Translate these numbers according to the conventions of your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [may our flocks multiply by the thousands and ten thousands in our fields] or [may our flocks multiply in very great numbers in our fields]

If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you could state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [May our oxen carry heavy burdens]

The implication is that there will be **no breach** in the city walls, **no going out** to war, and **no cry** of distress in the streets. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could express that explicitly. Alternate translation: [no enemy breaks through our walls, and no one goes out to war, and no one cries of distress]

David is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of joy or blessing. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Oh, how happy is the people for whom it is thus to it! How happy is]

Here, **it** refers back to **the people**, which is a singular noun which refers to a group. David is saying the people have the blessings he has just described. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make the referent explicit. Alternate translation: [who has all of these blessings]

Here, **its** refers back to **the people**, which is a singular noun which refers to a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make the referent explicit or use a plural pronoun. Alternate translation: [whose God is Yahweh]

# Psalm 145 Introduction

# Psalm 145 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 145 is a psalm of praise. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms. But instead of issuing the usual calls to worship, the psalmist states that he and future generations always will worship Yahweh. He makes this statement repeatedly, interspersing it with reasons to worship.

1. Statement of worship (1–7)
2. Reason to worship: Yahweh is compassionate (8–9)
3. Statement of worship (10–13)
4. Reason to worship; Yahweh provides and help and support (14–20)
5. Statement of worship (21)

145.quote: אֲרוֹמִמְ⁠ךָ֣ אֱלוֹהַ֣⁠י הַ⁠מֶּ֑לֶךְ וַ⁠אֲבָרֲכָ֥ה שִׁ֝מְ⁠ךָ֗ לְ⁠עוֹלָ֥ם וָ⁠עֶֽד

If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [I will exalt you, my God, the King, yes, I will bless your name forever and ever]

David is using the term **name** to represent who God is or to refer to God’s reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [who you are]

The terms **forever** and **ever** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [continually]

David is using the term **name** to represent who God is or to refer to God’s reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [who you are]

The expression **being much praised** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is people. Alternate translation: [people praise him very much]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **greatness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how great he is]

145.quote: דּ֣וֹר לְ֭⁠דוֹר יְשַׁבַּ֣ח מַעֲשֶׂ֑י⁠ךָ וּ⁠גְב֖וּרֹתֶ֣י⁠ךָ יַגִּֽידוּ
145.text: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [Generation to generation will proclaim your works; indeed, they will declare your mighty acts]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **splendor**, **glory**, and **majesty**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [how splendidly glorious and majestic you are]

The pronoun **they** refers to the people and generations mentioned in [145:4](../145/004.md). It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [generations of people will tell]

See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [They will pour forth the remembrance of the abundance of your goodness; indeed, they will sing joyfully about your righteousness]

Here David is speaking as if speech about God’s goodness were a liquid that people **pour forth**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They will eagerly tell their]

David is using **long of nostrils** as a common expression of the culture to mean “slow to become angry.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [slow to anger]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [faithfully keeping his covenant]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **compassions**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [his compassionate acts]

See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [All your works will thank you, Yahweh; indeed, your faithful will bless you]

David is using the adjective **faithful** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [your faithful people]

See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [They will tell the glory of your kingdom; yes, they will speak of your power]

145.quote: לְ⁠הוֹדִ֤יעַ ׀ לִ⁠בְנֵ֣י הָ֭⁠אָדָם גְּבוּרֹתָ֑י⁠ו וּ֝⁠כְב֗וֹד הֲדַ֣ר מַלְכוּתֽ⁠וֹ

Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [so that the sons of man will know his mighty acts and the glory of the splendor of his kingdom]

The psalmist is using **sons of man** as a common expression of his culture to mean “human beings.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to people everywhere]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **glory**, **splendor**, and **kingdom**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [how gloriously and splendidly he rules]

The terms **glory** and **splendor** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [the glorious splendor]

David has been addressing Yahweh directly in the second person, saying **your kingdom** and **your power** in the previous verse, but here he speaks of Yahweh in the third person, saying **his mighty acts** and **his kingdom**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the second person to be consistent. Alternate translation: [your mighty acts and the glory of the splendor of your kingdom]

145.quote: מַֽלְכוּתְ⁠ךָ֗ מַלְכ֥וּת כָּל־עֹֽלָמִ֑ים וּ֝⁠מֶֽמְשֶׁלְתְּ⁠ךָ֗ בְּ⁠כָל־דּ֥וֹר וָ⁠דֽוֹר

If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [succeeding generation]

145.quote: מַֽלְכוּתְ⁠ךָ֗ מַלְכ֥וּת כָּל־עֹֽלָמִ֑ים וּ֝⁠מֶֽמְשֶׁלְתְּ⁠ךָ֗ בְּ⁠כָל־דּ֥וֹר וָ⁠דֽוֹר

Here David is speaking as if those of God’s people who are afflicted were **the ones being bowed down**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ones experiencing hardships]

If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [you yourself are giving]
