Alternate translation: [giving generously]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **desire**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with what they desire]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **truth**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [truthfully]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **desire**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what the ones fearing him desire]

146.text:
# Psalm 146 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 146 is a psalm of praise. The psalmist begins by calling himself to worship Yahweh, and he then gives reasons others to worship him. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Call to worship (1–2)
2. Reason to worship: Yahweh is eternal and powerful (3–6)
3. Reason to worship: Yahweh helps people in need and in trouble (7–9)
4. Reason to worship: Yahweh reigns forever (10)

The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Halleluia] or [Praise Yah]
**Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh]

The psalmist is speaking to his own soul, which cannot hear him. He is doing this to express how strongly he feels about praising Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about himself. Alternate translation: [I will praise Yahweh with all of my being]

The psalmist is using one part of himself, his **soul**, to mean all of himself in the act of praising. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I myself will praise Yahweh]

146.quote: אֲהַלְלָ֣ה יְהוָ֣ה בְּ⁠חַיָּ֑⁠י אֲזַמְּרָ֖ה לֵֽ⁠אלֹהַ֣⁠י בְּ⁠עוֹדִֽ⁠י
146.text: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Let me praise Yahweh my God with music for as long as I live]

The psalmist is using the phrase **the son of man** as a common expression of the culture to mean a human being. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in any human being]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [ability to save]

The pronouns **His** and **he** refer to the mortal person described in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [That person’s breath goes out, that person returns to his ground]

The psalmist is referring to dying in a polite way by using the phrase **His breath goes out**. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [He dies]

The psalmist is referring to the burial of a dead body in a polite way by using the phrase **he returns to his ground**. This alludes to the account in Genesis where God formed man from the ground. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [his body decays and becomes dust again]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **thoughts**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what he was planning comes to nothing]

The psalmist is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of joy. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. If not, you could say what the psalmist was feeling. Alternate translation: [Oh, how happy is]

The psalmist is not using the possessive form **the God of Jacob** to indicate that Jacob possesses or controls God. Rather the psalmist is using these words to indicate that God is the one whom Jacob worshiped. Alternate translation: [the one who has the God whom Jacob worshiped for his help]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **help** and **hope**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [to help him; he confidently waits for Yahweh his God]

The psalmist is referring to all of creation by naming its major components, **the heavens** and **the earth**, and then adding **the sea and all that is in them**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [everything that exists]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [judging fairly]

The psalmist is using the adjective **oppressed** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [for those whom others oppress]
The psalmist is using one kind of food, **bread**, to mean food in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [nourishment]

The psalmist is using the adjective **hungry** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [to hungry people]
Here, **opening** represents giving sight to. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [giving sight to the blind]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is opening the eyes of the blind]

The psalmist is using the adjective **blind** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [blind people]

The psalmist is speaking of those who are discouraged or oppressed as if they were people who were physically **bowed down**. The psalmist is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [righteous people]

Alternate translation: [however, the way of the wicked, he overturns]

147.text:
# Psalm 147 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 147 is a psalm of praise. It presents alternating calls to worship and reasons to worship. These reasons include God’s greatness in creating the world, the way he protects his people and provides for them, and the way he gave his people his laws. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Call to worship Yahweh (1a)
2. Reason to worship Yahweh (1b–6)
3. Call to worship Yahweh (7)
4. Reason to worship Yahweh (8–11)
5. Call to worship Yahweh (12)
6. Reason to worship Yahweh (13–20)

The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Halleluia] or [Praise Yah]
**Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh]

The psalmist uses **For** to introduce the reason for the preceding exhortation. Use a connector that is natural in your language for introducing a reason. Alternate translation: [Because it is good to make music to our God]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **praise**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [praising him]

The terms **pleasant** and **suitable** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [very pleasant]

The expression **the scattered of Israel** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is their enemies. Alternate translation: [the Israelites whom enemies scattered]

The psalmist is speaking of **healing** emotional distress and **binding up their wounds** as if people’s sadness were physical injuries. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [comforting those who are very sad and relieving their pain]

The psalmist is using **the broken of heart** as a common expression of the culture to mean “people who have suffered emotional wounds.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those who are deeply grieving]

The psalmist places the adjective **Great** before the subject for emphasis. If it would be more natural in your language, you could use standard word order. Alternate translation: [Yahweh our Lord is great]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **power**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [abundantly powerful]

The psalmist is using an extreme statement to emphasize how great God’s understanding is. If it would be clearer in your language, you could express the emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [greater than anyone can measure] or [beyond anyone’s ability to assess]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **understanding**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what he understands] or [how much he comprehends]

The psalmist uses the adjective **poor** as a noun to describe a group of people. Your language may use adjectives similarly. If not, you could translate this with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are humble] or [people who are poor]

The psalmist is speaking of God humiliating **the wicked** as if he were physically **bringing** them **down** **to the ground**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [humbling the wicked] or [making the wicked fail]

The psalmist uses the adjective **wicked** as a noun to describe a group of people. Your language may use adjectives similarly. If not, you could translate this with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are wicked] or [people who do wicked things]

147.quote: עֱנ֣וּ לַ⁠יהוָ֣ה בְּ⁠תוֹדָ֑ה זַמְּר֖וּ לֵ⁠אלֹהֵ֣י⁠נוּ בְ⁠כִנּֽוֹר
147.text: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [Make music to Yahweh our God with grateful singing and the harp]

The psalmist uses the imperative form here as an exhortation to worship. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this exhortation in a way that is natural for your language. Alternate translation: [Let us sing to Yahweh and give him thanks]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **thanksgiving**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [giving thanks] or [thankfully]

The expression **the sons of the raven** is an idiom that means young ravens. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use an idiom from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the young ravens]

147.quote: נוֹתֵ֣ן לִ⁠בְהֵמָ֣ה לַחְמָ֑⁠הּ לִ⁠בְנֵ֥י עֹ֝רֵ֗ב אֲשֶׁ֣ר יִקְרָֽאוּ
147.text: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [He gives its food to the beast, and he gives food to the sons of the raven when they call]

147.quote: לֹ֤א בִ⁠גְבוּרַ֣ת הַ⁠סּ֣וּס יֶחְפָּ֑ץ לֹֽא־בְ⁠שׁוֹקֵ֖י הָ⁠אִ֣ישׁ יִרְצֶֽה
147.text: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [He does not value the strength of a horse or the physical ability of a person]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in how strong a horse is]

Although the term **man** is masculine, the psalmist is using it in a generic sense to refer to any person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a phrase that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [the legs of a person]

The psalmist is using one part of the body, **the legs**, to represent physical ability in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a person’s physical ability] or [how fast a person can run]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for him to keep his covenant promises] or [for him to show them kindness because of his covenant]

147.quote: שַׁבְּחִ֣י יְ֭רוּשָׁלִַם אֶת־יְהוָ֑ה הַֽלְלִ֖י אֱלֹהַ֣יִ⁠ךְ צִיּֽוֹן
147.text: The psalmist uses the imperative form here as an exhortation to worship. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this exhortation in a way that is natural for your language. Alternate translation: [You people of Jerusalem should praise Yahweh]

147.quote: שַׁבְּחִ֣י יְ֭רוּשָׁלִַם אֶת־יְהוָ֑ה הַֽלְלִ֖י אֱלֹהַ֣יִ⁠ךְ צִיּֽוֹן
147.text: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [Praise Yahweh, you people of Jerusalem]

The psalmist is speaking to the city of **Jerusalem**, also called **Zion**, as if it could hear, but he is really addressing the people of that city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, people of Jerusalem; praise your God, people of Zion]

The psalmist uses **For** to introduce the reason for the preceding exhortation. Use a connector that is natural in your language for introducing a reason. Alternate translation: [Because he strengthens the bars of your gates]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [The one making your borders safe and secure]

The psalmist is speaking of the best quality of **wheat** as if it were **the fat** part. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with the finest wheat] or [with the best wheat]

The psalmist speaks of God’s **word** as if it were a person who could **run**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his word goes out very quickly] or [what he commands happens immediately]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **swiftness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [goes out very quickly]

The psalmist compares **snow** to **wool** to emphasize how the snow covers the ground in a white, soft layer. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make the point of comparison explicit. Alternate translation: [snow that is white like wool]

The psalmist compares **frost** to **ashes** to emphasize how the frost is spread across the ground lightly and in fine particles. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make the point of comparison explicit. Alternate translation: [frost like gray ashes]

The psalmist compares **hail** to **crumbs** to emphasize that the hailstones are small pieces. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make the point of comparison explicit. Alternate translation: [his hailstones like small crumbs]

The psalmist uses a rhetorical question to emphasize that no one can endure God’s cold. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this question as a statement or an exclamation. Alternate translation: [no one can stand in such cold!] or [no one can endure when he makes it so cold.]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **cold**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in his freezing weather] or [when he makes it freeze]

Here, **the face of** represents the presence or force of something. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when he sends his cold] or [outside in his freezing cold]

The psalmist is speaking of God’s **word** as if it were a messenger that God could **send**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He gives a command, and he makes them melt]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe the **wind** that comes from God. If your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express the idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the wind he sends]

The terms **statutes** and **judgments** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [all his laws]

147.quote: מַגִּ֣יד דבר⁠ו לְ⁠יַעֲקֹ֑ב חֻקָּ֥י⁠ו וּ֝⁠מִשְׁפָּטָ֗י⁠ו לְ⁠יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

Alternate translation: [He declared his word to Jacob; indeed, he declared his statutes and judgments to Israel]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **judgments**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the decisions he has judged]

Here, **Jacob** and **Israel** represent the descendants of Jacob, who was also called Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to Jacob’s descendants] or [to the people of Israel]

The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Halleluia] or [Praise Yah]

148.text:
# Psalm 148 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 148 is a psalm of praise. It presents alternating calls to worship and reasons to worship. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Call to worship Yahweh from the heavens (1–4)
2. Reason to worship Yahweh from the heavens (5–6)
3. Call to worship Yahweh from the earth (7–12)
4. Reason to worship Yahweh from the earth (13–14)

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Praise Yahweh, all of you who are in the heavens above]

The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Halleluia] or [Praise Yah]
**Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh]
See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [Praise him, all of his heavenly beings]

The psalmist is speaking to the **sun and moon** as if they could hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about all of creation praising Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about the sun and moon. Alternate translation: [Let the sun and moon praise him]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **stars** that are characterized by **light**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the glowing stars]

148.quote: הַֽ֭לְלוּ⁠הוּ שֶׁ֣מֶשׁ וְ⁠יָרֵ֑חַ הַ֝לְל֗וּ⁠הוּ כָּל־כּ֥וֹכְבֵי אֽוֹר
148.text: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [Praise him, all you lights in the sky]

The psalmist is speaking to the **heavens** and the **waters** as if they could hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about all of creation praising Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about these things. Alternate translation: [for the highest heavens and the waters above the heavens should praise him]

The psalmist is using **heavens of the heavens** as a common expression in the original language to mean “the highest heavens.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the most exalted heavens]

The psalmist is saying what he wants all the things he has just mentioned to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [They should praise the name of Yahweh]

The psalmist is using the term **name** to represent who Yahweh is, referring to his reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh himself]

The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [because he, he commanded, and they were created]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **commanded** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Yahweh alone is the one who created all things. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [he himself commanded]

The expression **they were created** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [and he caused them to exist]

148.quote: וַ⁠יַּעֲמִידֵ֣⁠ם לָ⁠עַ֣ד לְ⁠עוֹלָ֑ם חָק־נָ֝תַ֗ן וְ⁠לֹ֣א יַעֲבֽוֹר
148.text: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [And he established them permanently by an unchanging decree]

The terms **forever** and **ever** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [to last permanently]

The psalmist is speaking to **sea creatures** and **all depths** as if they could hear him. He is doing this here and in following verses to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about all of creation praising Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about these things. Alternate translation: [creatures of the sea and all that lives below the waters]

The psalmist is speaking of the **wind of tempest** as if it were a living thing that could obey commands. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that goes where he sends it]
The pronoun **his** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [doing Yahweh’s word]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **wind** that is characterized by **tempest** or violence. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [violent wind]

Again, the psalmist is speaking inanimate objects, now to **mountains and all hills, tree of fruit and all cedars**, as if they could hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about all of creation praising Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about them. Alternate translation: [let the mountains and all of the hills, the fruit trees and all the cedars praise Yahweh]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe a **tree** that is characterized by bearing **fruit**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [fruit-bearing trees]

The psalmist is referring to all kinds of small creatures by naming two extremes, **the creeper** on the ground and **bird of wing** in the sky. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [every kind of small creature]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe a **bird** that is characterized by having wings. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the bird with wings]

The psalmist is referring to all of human society by naming two major components, **kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all judges of the earth** who represent both rulers and those who are ruled. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [everyone on earth, both rulers and ordinary people]

The psalmist is referring to all young people by naming two major components, **young men** and **young women**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all the young people]

The psalmist is referring to people of every age by naming two extremes, **old men** and **youths**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [people of every age]

The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [because his name alone is exalted]

The expression **his name alone is exalted** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [his name alone surpasses all others]
If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the abstract noun **splendor** with an adjective. Alternate translation: [he is splendid over the earth and the heavens]

Here the psalmist is using the term **name** twice to represent who Yahweh is and to refer to his reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh himself; for he alone is high above all]

The psalmist is referring to all of creation by naming two major components, **earth** and **heavens**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all of creation]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if Yahweh had given his people a **horn**, which is an animal’s horn that represents strength and power. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [and he has given strength to his people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **praise**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [honoring his faithful people]

# Psalm 150 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

1. Call to worship (1–6)

The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh.
